Your read is almost certainly correct, and here's why it's safe to hold the line without escalating:

The direction of the gap matches the ordering of the definitions, not a product regression.

  v3 = first integration + ≥1 in-product event within 14d
  v2 = first integration + 2 logins within 14d

v3 is strictly a subset of v2. Anyone who logged in twice but never fired an in-product event is counted by v2 and dropped by v3. So v3 rate ≤ v2 rate, always. A materially lower number on v3 is what a tightened def produces — it isn't evidence of a drop. That's the one-paragraph version you can give Owen.

The thing that would make it a real emergency is if v3 itself is moving against its own baseline. So the checklist below is sequenced to prove "definition drift" cheaply before anyone touches labels or forwards May numbers.

Checks to run before any edit or external number:

1. Lock the v3 time series for May vs Mar/Apr on the same def.
   This is the single most important check. v3 has been live since 2023-03-16, and your memory note says the lift has been holding since Mar 7+. Pull May v3 activation on the same 75-200 v2 cohort frame and compare to Mar and Apr v3. If May is in line with the prior two months on v3, you have a clean "definition drift, no product signal" answer. If May is materially below, then it's not just drift and you need a deeper cut before forwarding anything.

2. Compute the gap on the same cohort frame, side by side.
   Re-run v2 activation for May on the exact same cohort (75-200 v2, 14d window, same first-event milestone). The delta between v2 and v3 on the same cohort is the "tightening tax" — the share of May activations who logged in twice but never fired an in-product event. That number is the headline Riley-and-Owen can both defend.

3. Confirm both views use the same "first integration" milestone.

Here is the read.

Why the decision is non-obvious

Billing terms aren't a feature, but they are a self-serve eligibility lever in two distinct ways:

  1. Cash-flow / refund risk. A sub-50 seat on annual commits a non-trivial dollar amount on day one with minimal eval. That's the kind of account that, if it churns in week 2, generates a refund/CS ticket and a Sales Ops cleanup. Month-to-month lowers the activation barrier by removing that sunk-cost dread — but it also lowers the activation barrier in a way that doesn't actually help the cohort you care about (the ones who would have churned anyway now churn faster, noisier signal).

  2. Pricing-page legibility. Whether you offer M/M or annual-only changes what the pricing page has to display, and pricing-page workstream is Marcus's, not yours. Touching billing terms in the sub-50 design is the kind of scope creep that quietly turns into "we should also tweak the pricing page copy" — exactly the lane-bleed you've been disciplined about.

Where billing terms actually belong

The right home is refusal rules / eligibility, not pricing-page constraints. Reason: billing terms don't change *who* can buy the tier, they change *what contract shape* they sign. That's a take-rate / risk-shape decision, not a discovery-legibility decision. Pricing-page constraints are about whether a buyer can self-identify and self-evaluate ("is this for me?"); billing terms are about whether Helio can safely absorb the account if it goes wrong.

Concretely, the four tracks from Tuesday (funnel taxonomy, pricing page, lifecycle, dashboard) cover pricing-page surface and post-purchase motion. None of them is the right home for "what payment cadence do we allow at this tier." That belongs as a fifth track called something like "Eligibility & refusal rules" — or, if you're trying to keep it inside the four, it sits as a hard constraint under funnel taxonomy (because funnel taxonomy is where "who counts as a safe self-serve account" gets defined).

The trap to avoid: putting billing terms inside the pricing-page track because that's where Sales Ops intuitively looks. That makes the pricing-page track own a refusal-boundary decision, which it shouldn't — pricing page owns *display*, not *gate*.

The two scope-guard bullets

Drafted to drop straight into the thread. Plain text, ready to paste:

  - Billing terms (annual vs. month-to-month cadence, refund window, payment method) are a sub-50-seat *eligibility / refusal-rule* decision, not a pricing-page constraint. They govern who can safely self-serve at this tier, not how the tier is displayed. Here's a structure that keeps the two lenses cleanly separated per row. The framing principle (eligibility gates about THEM, product constraints about US) means the refusal language only ever attaches to the eligibility column — that's how it stays "we'd be setting you up to fail" instead of "we don't serve accounts like yours."

HOW TO READ EACH ROW

- Customer state: what we're assessing about the account.
- Eligibility gate (G/Y/R): who we let in. Decision is about THEM.
- Product constraints (G/Y/R per surface): what we can safely support. Decision is about US, across the 5 surfaces Daniela can size — instrumentation, dashboards, permissions, import, migration.
- Refusal language: the customer-facing version of a Red eligibility call. Phrased as protecting them from a setup that would fail, not as a comment on their size.

ROW 1 — First integration
- State: has the account connected ≥1 integration (aligns with activation v3 def: +≥1 in-product event in 14d).
- Eligibility: G = integrated at least once. Y = partial (connected a source, not the core one). R = no integration activity in 14d.
- Product constraints: Instrumentation G. Dashboards G. Permissions G (read-level is enough). Import Y (data shape on import, not on integration). Migration G (greenfield).
- Refusal language (R): "Without a first integration connected, this motion won't close the loop it's designed for. We'd recommend our guided onboarding path first — happy to intro you."

ROW 2 — Admin & permissions complexity
- State: # admin roles, SSO/SCIM need, audit log need, RBAC granularity.
- Eligibility: G = 1–2 admins, no SSO required. Y = multi-role + SSO needed. R = SCIM, granular RBAC, audit logs (ent-procurement-grade).
- Product constraints: Instrumentation G. Dashboards G. Permissions Y at moderate, R at enterprise (Daniela draws the line). Import G. Migration G.
- Refusal language (R): "The permission model this motion assumes doesn't cover SCIM / granular RBAC / audit logs without custom work. We'd be giving you a setup you'd outgrow in 30 days — let's route you to [ent path]."

ROW 3 — Import help
- State: data volume, source system, mapping complexity.
- Eligibility: G = small volume, standard sources, clean schema. Y = medium volume OR non-standard source, mapping help needed. R = bespoke / large / needs dedupe or validation logic.
- Product constraints: Instrumentation G. Dashboards Y (import-validation dashboards may need work). Permissions G. Import Y/R (the constraining surface; R if dedupe needed). Migration Y (overlaps with Row 5).
- Refusal language (Y/R): "Import at this volume / from this source needs hands-on mapping support we can't deliver self-serve. We can either pre-stage with our team or hand you a guided runbook — your call."

ROW 4 — Billing exceptions
- State: contract type, payment terms, multi-entity, procurement involvement.
- Eligibility: G = card on file, standard monthly/annual. Y = PO / net-30 / one-off pricing. R = bespoke MSA, multi-entity, procurement, custom security review.
- Product constraints: Instrumentation G. Dashboards G. Permissions G. Import G. Migration G.
- Note: this row is almost entirely an eligibility gate. Billing sits OUTSIDE Daniela's 5 surfaces — she can't size it, so the constraint column is uniformly G by default. The R/Y/G is really [billing/sales] team's call.
- Refusal language (R): "Custom billing terms need a contract before we can turn this on. Self-serve wouldn't honor net-60 / MSA / multi-entity splits anyway — let's get the contract in place with your AE first."

ROW 5 — Migration support
- State: are they migrating from somewhere, and what kind of source.
- Eligibility: G = greenfield. Y = light (CSV / spreadsheet / single known source). R = heavy (API sync from competitor, dedupe, historical data).
- Product constraints: Instrumentation G. Dashboards Y (pre/post migration parity checks). Permissions G. Import Y (links back to Row 3). Migration Y/R (the constraining surface; R for API-sync / dedupe).
- Refusal language (R): "Migrating from [competitor / historical data] needs a dedicated motion we don't offer self-serve. An API sync without validation + dedupe support would leave you with bad data fast — let's scope a migrations engagement."

ROW 6 — Support handoff risk
- State: in-house technical capacity, self-serve comfort, time-to-value tolerance.
- Eligibility: G = technical buyer with capacity to iterate. Y = needs guidance, can self-serve with docs + chat support. R = needs white-glove, no technical owner on their side.
- Product constraints: Instrumentation G. Dashboards G. Permissions G. Import Y (links to Row 3). Migration Y (links to Row 5).
- Note: this row is also mostly an eligibility gate — product can support, but we can't safely let them in without the right internal capacity. Refusal here is about THEIR org structure, not their account size. Tone matters most on this one.
- Refusal language (R): "This motion assumes a technical owner on your side who can iterate. Without one, the time-to-value math breaks down and you'd end up on a support path we don't have. Let's start you on [lighter-weight / guided] plan instead."

NOTES FOR THE DANIELA CONVERSATION
- The Product Constraint column is what she sizes. Eligibility columns are mine to defend — context, not her scope.
- Where I wrote Y or R, those are the cells she fills in with effort estimates.
- Where the row is uniformly G on constraints (Rows 4 and 6), she's not losing effort there — those are policy gates, not eng work. Flag this explicitly so she doesn't read it as "no work."
- The refusal language column is mine + Ines's tone to set. Daniela doesn't own the customer-facing voice.
- Rows 4 and 6 being mostly eligibility is the structural point worth surfacing — it tells Daniela she can size faster than she might have feared because two rows of the six are not really eng-load.

Here's how I'd frame it, calibrated to Owen's 1-pager cadence (summary first, cuts + raw below) and Priya's gate (no customer-facing claims before eligibility / refusal / instrumentation / lifecycle / support are all ready).

THE FRAME (1-pager top, 4-5 lines)

  Title: "Activation is gated by admin complexity, not seat count."

  Setup line: "Under activation definition v3 (>=1 in-product event in 14d), the under-50 segment is not a single behavioral unit. It splits cleanly by deployment shape. Accounts that can self-onboard hit activation close to the mid-seg+ target band. Accounts that need permissions, import, billing-exception, or migration support lag by more than 15 points. The 50-75 band behaves like starter, consistent with the mid-seg v2 boundary at 75-200."

  Headline (range, not a point):
    Mid-seg+ v2 (75-200):              [Owen's number, target band 60%]
    Under-50, simple deployment shape: [Owen's number]  within or near target band
    Under-50, assisted deployment shape: [Owen's number]  lag of >15 points
    50-75 (starter comparator):        [Owen's number]  closer to starter shape than to mid-seg+ v2

  Mechanism statement: "Eligibility for a self-serve / starter-style tier should be defined by what we can deliver activation-wise, i.e., simple deployment shape, not by seat count alone. Seat count is a correlate, not the cause. An 'under 50' eligibility rule admits the laggard cohort and excludes some simple-deployment accounts above 50. The natural boundary appears to be between 50-75 and 75-200, consistent with mid-seg v2."

WHAT THIS DOES PROVE

  - Under-50 is not a single cohort for tier-eligibility purposes. Admin complexity / deployment shape is the meaningful axis.
  - Simple-deployment under-50 accounts reach activation close to the mid-seg+ target band. They do not need a separate intervention to clear the 60% bar on v3.
  - Under-50 accounts requiring permissions, import, billing-exception, or migration lift lag the target by more than 15 points. The gap is operationally meaningful, not noise.
  - The 50-75 band's behavior is closer to starter than to retained mid-seg, supporting the v2 mid-seg boundary at 75+ rather than at 50.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT PROVE

  - Whether the simple-deployment under-50 group holds activation past the 14-day window. v3 is a 14-day KPI; we have no retention / expansion curves for this subgroup yet.
  - Whether the under-50 laggard cohort can be moved with a specific intervention (import tooling, billing-exception automation, migration support). That's a hypothesis these cuts motivate, not a finding they establish.
  - Whether a Helio Start tier, defined by eligibility built on this signal, would actually retain or expand at acceptable levels. That's a downstream experiment, not a baseline finding.
  - Causal direction. Admin complexity may be the cause of the lag, or a proxy for something else (buyer sophistication, internal champion quality, evaluation rigor). Plausibly both; these cuts don't disentangle.
  - Stability of the under-50 laggard fraction over time, across verticals, or across acquisition channels. These are point-in-time cuts.
  - Whether the "simple deployment shape" signal can be detected reliably enough at signup or week-1 to drive an in-product eligibility decision. That's an instrumentation question, not a measurement one, and Priya's gate won't open until it's answered.

HOW THIS LANDS AS THE MEASUREMENT SPINE FOR THE JUNE READOUT

  - Eligibility is proposed as "deployable without human-assisted onboarding intervention," not "under N seats." Seat count stays as a coarse pre-filter, with admin-complexity flags as the deciding signal.
  - The under-50 headline is reported as a range (simple vs. assisted), with the gap explicit. No reader can summarize it as "under 50 is fine" or "under 50 is bad" without contradicting the cuts in front of them.
  - The 50-75 band sits as the starter comparator, not in mid-seg+. Mid-seg+ comparisons stay at v2 = 75-200.
  - Every claim about Helio Start in the readout is paired with a "what would have to be true" pointer back to the cuts. The cuts don't endorse the tier; they bound what the tier can plausibly promise.

TWO FLAGS BEFORE YOU COMMIT THIS

  1. The "simple deployment shape" wording: do you want a working definition pinned in the readout, or a pointer to a separate doc where Owen defines the buckets? Given Priya's gate, I'd keep the working definition in-line so the readout stands alone.
  2. The refusal-rule framing. The cuts motivate that refusal rules are necessary, but they don't specify them. Worth saying so out loud in the readout so it doesn't read like the cuts imply a specific rule we haven't designed yet.

The depth split is useful but doesn't move the ship/widen decision. The pre-registered decision unit was aggregate, and aggregate is below bar. Anything you read off a subgroup at this stage is hypothesis-generating at best.

WHAT THIS SUPPORTS
- Heterogeneous treatment effects exist — depth is doing real work in how accounts respond to the nudge.
- A pre-registered follow-up test targeting only high-depth accounts, powered for that subgroup. That's the legitimate next step, not a flag change.
- A narrower rollout shape is on the table (high-depth only), as opposed to widening. Smaller blast radius, more aligned to where the signal lives.

WHAT IT DOESN'T SUPPORT
- Shipping or widening the flag. Aggregate is +$6.10 vs the +$8 bar — below bar is no decision change. The standing rule (first sig doesn't ship, wait a stab cohort, p<0.01 second-look) was written for exactly this moment, and we haven't even cleared first-sig on aggregate.
- Reading "high-depth materially ahead" as evidence the treatment works. Three reasons that read is not a decision input:
  - The pre-reg is on aggregate, not depth-conditioned effects. Reading subgroups now is post-hoc.
  - Sample size per slice is roughly halved; CIs widen accordingly. Without p-values on the slice (which Owen didn't surface — ask for them), "materially ahead" is a point estimate with unknown precision.
  - You're picking the winning slice from at least two. That's the garden-of-forking-paths move and it's the class of failure that produced the pricing_page_2023q2_rev rollback.
- Treating a single cohort's slice as a stable estimate of the high-depth effect. Even if it's real, you don't have a stab cohort on it.

THE TRAP MARCUS IS ABOUT TO FALL INTO

Named: subgroup cherry-picking dressed as a widening decision.

The move will sound like: "the high-depth slice clears the bar, so widen the flag and let those accounts convert it." That reframes the question from "does this experiment support shipping?" to "does this experiment contain a slice that looks shippable?" — and the second question is much easier to answer in the affirmative by accident. He'll cite the effect size on the slice, underweight that the aggregate doesn't clear, and want to act before the cohort matures — which is the exact instinct the pre-reg was written to slow down.

If you widen on the slice, one of two things happens: the next cohort regresses to the mean (most likely), or you ship on a result that wasn't pre-registered, which is the same failure mode as the pricing-page rollback.

A quick read first: panting in a cat is not "just spooked." Cats rarely pant, and it tells you he's in a real panic, not mild stress. So treat the next 30 minutes as de-escalation, not waiting-it-out.

On the walk: SKIP IT tonight. Three reasons stacked against you right now:
- Hot pavement. Even at 8:30 PM in early July, sidewalks that got full afternoon sun are often still too hot. Test: press the back of your hand to the pavement for 5 seconds. If you flinch, paws can't go on it.
- Another full adrenaline hit on top of an already-panting cat. He's likely to bolt, freeze, or refuse to move — and then you're chasing a panicked cat in the dark.
- You have a litter box. Use it tonight. If a box isn't set up, a baking dish with a couple inches of soil or even a folded towel in the dry bathtub will do. He may not use it. That's fine.

If he absolutely must go out, the bar is: 10+ continuous minutes of quiet AND the back-of-hand test passes. Don't go before then.

30-MINUTE PLAN (starting ~8:36 PM)

0-5 min — Build a smaller den
- Move the operation from the kitchen table to the most interior room. A bathroom or interior closet (no exterior wall) beats a hallway.
- Set up on the floor: a towel or blanket, ideally something that smells like you (worn t-shirt).
- Keep brown noise on. If you have a second phone or speaker, put it in another room to fill the gaps between booms.

5-15 min — Coax, don't carry
- Don't drag him out from under the table. Lure with a Churu, a treat, or a crinkled toy.
- Once he's moving, walk low and slow toward the new spot. Let him follow.
- Sit on the floor with him. Slow breath. Read aloud quietly, or just be still. Skip the "oh poor baby" voice — fussing can amplify the panic.

15-30 min — Stay put, let him choose contact
- Don't force petting. If he leans in, soft chin or cheek scratches. If he doesn't, just be a calm warm body in the room.
- Pattern to expect: most noise-phobic cats start to settle 20-40 min after the loudest stimulus ends, IF the room is set up right.

Escalation signs (these are "call the emergency vet," not "wait it out"):
- Open-mouth breathing longer than ~5 min after he's in the quiet room
- Drooling, vomiting, or hiding and refusing to come out for hours
- Any wobbling, stumbling, or disorientation

LINE 1 (general: self-serve isn't the right path)

Original: "This workspace isn't a fit for Helio Start self-serve."

LINE 2 (specific cases: sales-assisted)

Evidence-source rule — sub-50-seat tier beta block

Goal: deployment-shape and support-handoff fields can be backfilled, but only with visible evidence, visible staleness, and a status column that keeps unknowns out of beta-ready language.

1) What can be backfilled

Allowed sources (each must be named and dated):
  - AE call note — author + date
  - Onboarding note — author + date
  - Support ticket — ID + date
  - CS owner confirmation — name + date

Disallowed: paraphrased memory, "probably", training-data inference, or values extrapolated from an adjacent field. If we can't point to a named artifact, the cell stays unknown. Backfilled value must be directly stated in the source, not derived.

2) How to label source and staleness

Every cell carries two labels, in the cell itself or in an adjacent column:

  source: <type> | <owner> | <YYYY-MM-DD>
    e.g. source: onboarding note | S. Park | 2023-04-02
    multiple sources: semicolon-separated

  staleness: <fresh | aging | stale>
    fresh:  < 30 days
    aging:  30–90 days
    stale:  > 90 days — must be re-verified before the row can move to beta-ready

Cells with no source are not blank. They carry source: none and value: unknown. Stale cells carry staleness: stale | last-verified <date>.

3) Keeping unknowns out of beta-ready language

Status is its own column, separate from the field value. Three states only:

  unverified — default for any row with at least one source: none on a gating field. Not beta-ready.
  beta-ready — every gating field has a sourced value, no field older than 90 days without re-verification, and a named owner for each backfilled source.
  blocked    — source exists but the value is genuinely unknown or contested; flagged for an owner to resolve.

Rules:
  - A backfilled value alone does not move a row to beta-ready. Staleness and named ownership have to clear too.
  - "Inferred" is never a source label. The cell stays unknown and the row stays unverified.
  - Unknowns roll up. Any row that fails the gate is summarized by its actual status in the 1-pager, not folded into a beta-ready count.
  - Gating fields for this block (per Daniela's 6/26 readout): entitlement state, admin-complexity events, import/migration-help flags, support-handoff taxonomy. All four must clear before a row is beta-ready; support-handoff resolves to unverified until CS confirms the taxonomy rather than eng owning it.

  - A lag is a magic window. If the support handoff event lands at minute 9 the tile still shows null; if it lands at minute 11 it shows real state. The transition is invisible to the viewer and the cutoff is arbitrary in code.
  - A pending label encodes the contract directly: support_state is null until the support handoff event fires. Null = not yet captured, not "no support," not "starter," not inferable to anything.
  - This is the UI mirror of Daniela's 2023-07-19 RED rule on entitlement_state — capture at ws creation, update on support handoff/billing change, no plan_name inference. Between those two events the state is explicitly pending, not inferred.

Six questions, each anchored to a specific failure mode you flagged. One-line probe intent under each so you can listen for the right signal.

1. Cohort hygiene under definitional drift
  "You've got two cohort definitions in flight — v1 uses a 50-200 employee band and v2 uses 75-200. A PM wants a head-to-head retention comparison to decide which to expand. Before you answer, what do you check, and what concerns do you raise?"
  Probes: whether they notice the 50-75 band is silently being dropped in v2 (a "starter" pocket, not the same population), whether they flag that composition changes confound the comparison itself, and whether they ask about field-completeness or definitional drift before running the query. Strong candidates slow down at the question, not the query.

2. Lifecycle email diagnostic instinct (the "don't reach for the send button" test)
  "A nurture sequence sees unsubscribe rate jump 15% week-over-week. Walk me through your first 24 hours — what you look at first, and what you actively do not do."
  Probes: do they reach for a new subject line or a new send, or do they reach for the cohort definition, recent cadence changes, hold-out behavior, and stale-workspace flags first. Listen for whether "send less / send nothing" appears in their instinct before "send differently."

3. Causal claim discipline when a PM is confident
  "PM says: 'the new onboarding email drove the 3% lift in 8-week retention.' Before you agree or push back, what do you need to know?"
  Probes: pre-reg, control definition, what was actually randomized, whether anything else shipped in the same window (product change, pricing-page update, lifecycle cadence tweak), whether the metric was the one pre-committed. Listen for them treating the claim as a hypothesis to falsify, not a fact to confirm.

4. Pre-reg / peeking discipline under shipping pressure
  "An A/B email test has been running 5 days, n=200 per arm, conversion lift 4%, p=0.03. A teammate wants to ship today. What do you do?"
  Probes: do they cave to the clean-looking number, or do they call out peeking + underpowering and propose a continuation rule / hold-out. The specific failure mode is shipping from one lucky peek — strong candidates name it out loud and propose the fix, not just the hesitation.

5. Sequencing and signal hygiene across parallel workstreams
  "We have activation/retention work, a lifecycle email test, and a feature-flag rollout all live at once, all touching the same mid-segment cohort. What concerns you, and what do you propose?"
  Probes: do they see the attribution-collision problem, or do they treat each workstream as independent. Strong candidates will propose pausing or sequencing one out — they're protecting the signal on the others. This is the workstream-sequencing instinct you actually need in the seat.

6. Holding the line on "we don't know yet"
  "A stakeholder asks whether a parked initiative — say, an expansion-assist motion — is worth shipping. You have two weeks of mixed telemetry, no clean controlled test, and a parked status. How do you respond?"
  Probes: honesty under pressure. Do they manufacture a confident read to please the stakeholder, or do they name what would actually resolve it and refuse to ship on vibes. Strong candidates will say "here's the test that would answer this" rather than "here's my best guess."

Two things worth flagging for the loop overall, not as questions:
- The take-home signal you described (cohort instinct OK, causal wobbly) maps directly onto Q3 and Q4 — those are the load-bearing ones. If they nail those, the wobble is teachable; if they don't, the instinct won't save them.
- Q5 is the one that separates "can do growth" from "can do growth at a company our size" — at ~$48M ARR with a Series B clock, parallel-workstream discipline is the actual job.

You already did the two most important things — got the burr out and cleaned the area. Most paw burrs resolve in 24–48 hours with simple monitoring. Here's a calm, structured plan.

TONIGHT

Visual check (one good look, phone flashlight, between every pad and webbed area):
- Any burr fragment still in there
- Active bleeding (small pinpoint OK, steady drip is not)
- Swelling (compare to other front paw — slightly puffier is fine, visibly bigger is not)
- Cut or puncture (a small red dot where the burr sat is normal)
- Discharge (clear = fine; yellow/green/foul = not fine)
- Heat (gently press your inner wrist to the pad — warmer than the other paw is a flag)

Gentle press test (one time):
- Lightly squeeze each toe and the pad. A flinch or pull-away is information — pain on compression suggests something still embedded or a deeper puncture.

If he tolerates it, a quick cool-water or saline rinse (1 tsp salt per cup cooled water) helps. Don't use hydrogen peroxide on a paw — it delays healing.

Discourage the licking, because constant wet maceration is what turns a minor irritation into a vet visit:
- Easy option: a children's sock secured loosely with vet wrap or self-adhering bandage over the paw. Take it off before bed so you can re-check.
- More reliable option: an e-collar (the cone). If you have one, tonight is the night to use it. Licking → swelling → more licking is the loop you want to break.

Then check once more right before you go to sleep. You don't need to set an alarm — if he's resting comfortably, he's fine overnight.

TOMORROW MORNING

First check as soon as he's up and moving:
- Better than last night = great sign, you're done
- Same as last night = continue monitoring through the day, reassess evening
- Worse than last night = see flags below

The trend matters more than any single snapshot.

RED — urgent vet or ER tonight
- Won't bear any weight at all, or worsening limp
- Visible swelling that's clearly increasing
- Pus, foul smell, or colored discharge
- Bleeding that doesn't stop with 5 minutes of gentle direct pressure
- Burr fragment you can see still embedded that you can't easily remove
- Pale gums, panting/shaking at rest, vomiting, or refusal to eat (pain or systemic)

YELLOW — call your regular vet in the morning for advice
- Still licking persistently at the 24-hour mark even if paw looks OK
- Mild limp that hasn't improved by morning
- Slight swelling or redness that hasn't started to resolve
- He's protective of the paw when you touch it

GREEN — keep watching, you're probably fine
- Intermittent licking
- Mild favoring that improves across the evening
- Small red mark where the burr was, no swelling, no discharge
- Eating, drinking, resting normally

One thing to skip: don't apply Neosporin or any OTC ointment unless a vet has seen the paw. Dogs lick it off and some ingredients (especially with pain relievers) cause problems in quantity.

You're not underreacting by waiting this out — you're reacting correctly. The burr is out, the paw is clean, and now you're watching the trend. That's the right call.

Light without definitions is hand-waving.

CONFUSING (in order of risk)
1. "Hypothesis stack" — undefined. Ordered by what? Is the top one pre-registered, or is this just "list of guesses"? The pre-reg rule (lock direction+metric before peek) isn't surfaced. A borrower lists three guesses and calls it a stack.
2. "Effect size, not just direction" — in what unit, against what baseline, with what MDE? Effect size without baseline is unfalsifiable; without CI it's point-estimate theater.
3. "Decision boundary" — three buckets specific to one protocol. A borrower with no stabilization cohort will collapse "first sig" and "observation" together. And "first sig" without the second-look rule (same metric/direction, n≥treatment, p<0.01 before next peek) is exactly the fake-1st-sig failure mode the protocol exists to prevent — the checklist asks for the bucket but doesn't encode the rule that earns the label.
4. (bonus) "Metric, cohort, window" — no operationalization. Is the cohort starter / mid? Is the window event-time, exposure-time, or calendar? Starter vs mid (v2 75-200, v1 50-200) has been the live segmentation choice; the checklist doesn't force the writer to name which one or whether the result transfers.

  - the 10-04 Cust.io fix and 10-05 34-recipient batch were both "controlled-beta move, NOT launch/widening" — the readout needs that axis or it reads a beta move as a launch signal

Here's a v0.2 that keeps both safeguards but speaks to analysts and lifecycle readers instead of looking like a process doc. Two pieces: the revised checklist, then the thank-you note.

INVESTIGATION GUIDANCE — v0.2 (friendly checklist)

Goal: a pre-reg that, six months from now, still tells you what you were trying to learn and what would have made you change your mind.

Four things worth filling in before you ship a test:

1. Problem statement — one line, what we're trying to learn. Not "what are we shipping." If you can't say it in one line, the test is probably trying to answer too much.

2. Hypothesis stack — effect size in two flavors
   Primary + secondary. For each, write both:
     a) Observed lift — what past signal actually showed, if anything. (Write "none yet" if you're flying blind.)
     b) Decision-changing lift — the smallest move on this metric that would make you act.
   The gap between (a) and (b) is where most "uplift" confusion lives. If you only have one number, write (b) — it's the one that drives the call.

3. Metric / cohort / window — spelled out so a future reader sees it the same way you do:
     - Metric: which number, in which direction.
     - Cohort: who's in, who's out.
     - Window: how long you wait before the first peek.

4. Decision boundary — answer this before you run it:
   "What would make me wait instead of ship?"
   First green p-value is not the call. The bar before you act is a second look on a fresh cohort at least as big as the treatment, same metric + direction, p<0.01. If you can't name what would make you wait, you don't have a decision boundary yet — you have a hope.

Two safeguards this checklist exists to protect (don't drop these):
  - Effect size split: observed vs decision-changing. Without this, "uplift" becomes a vibes word.
  - Two-look rule before acting. Without this, first significance = ship, which is how we got burned on the pricing-page rollback.

What this isn't: a sign-off doc, a template anyone needs to approve before you pre-reg, or a checklist of "required fields." Cut anything that doesn't change what you'd do.

Your read hits the four decision points correctly. The metric, the missing holdout, the missing effect definition, and the untailored intervention are the actual holes. A few I'd add or sharpen:

1. The candidate is framing this as a marketing problem. It probably isn't. A day-5 user who hasn't invited teammates AND hasn't connected an integration is more likely blocked by product friction (admin permission, OAuth failure, missing seat, integration not in their stack) than by unawareness. Five more emails won't unstick a permission error. First move should be diagnosis — pull the day-5 cohort, look at where they actually drop in the product. Did they hit an OAuth wall? Bounce on team invite because no eligible teammate? Never reach the integration screen? Each of those wants a different intervention shape, and "email sequence" is the wrong tool for at least two of them.

2. "Segment by job title from the signup form" assumes the form has clean job-title data. It often doesn't — blank, free-text, or stale. Worth flagging because the whole sequencing depends on it. A behavior-based first cut (which setup steps they completed, which admin pages they visited) is usually more reliable than a self-declared attribute from a form field nobody maintains.

3. The candidate proposes email as the sole channel. In-product nudges (banner at the friction point, contextual checklist at admin setup, integration picker at the moment of intent) often outperform lifecycle email for activation work because they reach the user at the point of failure, not on a fixed cadence. Email-only is a defensible choice but it should be made deliberately and acknowledged as such, not defaulted to.

4. "Personalize subject line with company name" is dropped in as an aside. It's actually a second experiment. Conflating two changes in one rollout means you can't attribute effect to either — you won't know whether the sequence worked or the subject line worked. Either test them separately or hold one constant as control.

5. "Open rate above 35%" is also increasingly noisy as a primary signal — Apple Mail Privacy Protection and similar mechanisms inflate open rates unevenly across cohorts. If that's the readout metric, the readout is already suspect before you get to the effect-size question.

What I'd want a stronger answer to look like, in order:

  Diagnose first. What's the actual day-5 failure mode? What does the product data show about where these users stop? Don't propose intervention until you've named the cause.

  Pick one intervention matched to that cause. Email OR in-product, not both at once. If the diagnosis says awareness gap, email. If it says friction-at-step, in-product. State which and why.

  Pre-register everything before shipping: cohort boundary (date range, signup definition, exclusions), holdout (random 10% or whatever fits), primary metric (integration-connected-by-day-10 OR teammate-invited-by-day-7 — whichever the diagnosis pointed at, not opens), guardrails (support ticket volume, day-5→paid conversion in the treatment group, no degradation in any other tier), decision rule with a pre-specified effect size (smallest lift that would change your rollout decision — define it before you look, same lesson as the pricing-page rollback).

  Only then sequence the touches, and keep it short. Three emails is usually enough if the diagnosis was right.

The core pattern your read already names — "jumps to five emails before diagnosing" — is the one that matters most. Everything downstream (metric, holdout, effect size) is downstream of that.

MONDAY COMMUTE PLAN

Two real choices. Pick one, stop second-guessing.

1. Don't ride home Monday (recommended)
   - Transit, rideshare, or a favor from a coworker. Ride or transit in the morning while it's light and dry, get a ride back.
   - One annoying day > one close call in dusk traffic. You already said the no-rear-light ride is a bad idea — trust that read.

2. Ride both ways if you must
   - Leave work well before sunset. Don't gamble on "it's only 20 min."
   - Stay on lit, low-speed neighborhood streets. Skip arterials and highway-frontage roads.
   - Front light + vest help — they do not cover your rear blind spot. That's the actual risk.
   - Skip the ride if rain or fog is in the forecast.

Fastest Monday fix if you skip Option 1 and want to ride:
   - Borrow: Sam, a neighbor, anyone who commutes. A spare rear light is the most-borrowed piece of bike gear on earth.
   - Local bike shop: most are open Sun afternoon or Mon morning. A basic rear light is $15–25, walk-out solution.

REPLACEMENT LIGHT — BUYING CHECKLIST

Filter on these, ignore the rest:

- Brightness: 50+ lumens rear is plenty for city commuting. Day-flash mode matters more than peak lumen number.
- Battery: USB-C rechargeable is the default and what you'll keep charged. AAA-swappable is fine if you'd rather carry spares. Pick the one that matches your actual habit.
- Weather rating: IPX4 minimum. You just learned why.
- Mount: seatpost strap is universal. Confirm it fits your seatpost (most cover 25–35 mm).
- Run time: ≥ 6 hours on the mode you'll actually use, or a flash mode that lasts a round-trip comfortably.
- Side visibility: a small bonus. Pure-rear dots get missed at intersections.

Skip without thinking twice:
- Bluetooth / app / brake-light smart features.
- Anything claiming >300 lumens under $30 (usually lies on the spec).
- Aero / ultralight claims. Irrelevant for commuting.

Local shortcut: any $20–40 light from Cygolite, NiteRider, Lezyne, Planet Bike, or Knog is a safe buy. Online: filter reviews for "runtime" complaints, not just "dim."

Voice-note outline for Marcus — UT Austin supplement

Sunday voice-note fits your usual Sunday-call window with him. Plan for ~2-3 min. Fill in specifics from his actual paragraph as you go; the outline gives you the shape, the warmth, and the two techniques.

  Opener (~15 sec)
  - "Hey. Okay, I read it twice. And before anything else — the version you were panicking about Thursday and this one are not the same essay. This one sounds like you."
  - Name what he actually asked: "You didn't want a line edit — you wanted me to tell you if the idea itself is too bland. So that's what I'm doing."

  What's working (~30-45 sec)
  Pick 2 specific things, not "it's good." The praise has to be specific or it sounds like every admissions-blog pep talk. Patterns to look for in his paragraph:
  - A concrete scene where I can see a place/face/moment vs. an abstract claim
  - A sentence that sounds like something he'd say to me on a call, not something an admissions officer would write
  - An unexpected detail that I genuinely can't imagine anyone else putting in their essay
  Call out the specific moment you're praising by quoting one phrase back to him ("the line about ___" — he'll know exactly what you mean).

  What's still too generic (~30-45 sec)
  This is where you name the bland without rewriting. Two tests to read it against:
  - "Any college could fit" test — if I deleted "UT Austin" and put in [School X], would the paragraph still work? If yes, that's the bland.
  - "Everyone says this" test — anything about wanting to be challenged, finding my people, pursuing passions, contributing to community. If it's in there, it's doing the thing he was worried about.
  Frame it warmly: "this part sounds like the prompt, not like you." Not "this part is weak."

  Two sharpening moves (~60-90 sec — the meat)

  Move 1: One detail only UT Austin has.
  Not "UT's CS department is great" or "Austin is a creative city." The texture move — the smell of a specific hallway, the name of a specific TA, a sentence from a specific paper he read because of a specific professor, the thing the dining hall does on Tuesday. The test: could this detail only be at UT? If yes, it's personal. If it could be at any school with a good program, it's brochure copy.

  Move 2: Show the shift, not just the fit.
  The "why us" essays that actually work don't say "I'm a great fit" — they say "I already started becoming the person I'd be there." A moment in past tense where he ALREADY did the thing — read something because of a UT professor's work, built something because of a detail he picked up at UT, came back from a visit different than when he arrived. Not a future promise. A past-tense shift. Harder to fake, harder to be generic in, and counselors can tell the difference instantly.

  Close (~15 sec)
  - "Don't send it to the counselor yet — try the two moves, then send it back to me. Sunday or whenever, I'm around."
  - One last sister line, not editor line: "And honestly? The fact that you panicked Thursday and then sent something more you on Sunday means you already know how to do this."

One small note for you, not for him: the move-2 framing (past-tense shift, not future promise) is the single highest-leverage thing in here. If he only takes one move, that's the one. Worth saying clearly if the note runs long and you want to cut.

Idea isn't dead. Robotics is fine as the community — what needs work is the angle.

What's flat in the current draft isn't the topic, it's the texture. "Teamwork, leadership, perseverance" is the version of this essay a tired reader has already seen 800 times. "Solve hard problems" / "solve real problems" doesn't tell me anything Marcus-specific. "Build something that works" is the robotics-trope line. Right now I could swap your name for any of a hundred applicants and the paragraph would still work — that's the test it's failing.

What you need is a *moment*. Not "robotics taught me X" — an actual scene where X got earned, or got complicated, or surprised you. A specific failure with a specific lesson. A person on the team who changed how you think. A design call where the right answer wasn't the winning one. The night the robot didn't work and what happened next. The moment the club stopped being a thing you did and became a community you belonged to, or vice versa.

Then the closing line about UT Austin will land differently, because the body will have done real work underneath it.

To find the moment: don't start with "what did I learn." Start with "what do I remember." A scene, a face, a sentence someone said, a week that went sideways. The angle falls out of whatever memory is sharpest — usually the one that still irritates or surprises you.

CLEANING — DON'Ts first

  - Don't soak the pans or the tray. Old binders (casein, honey, early gum arabic) fall apart in standing water; the cracked tray will wick water into the break and swell whatever's underneath.
  - Don't use soap on the pans or tray. Soap strips binders.
  - Don't scrub. No toothbrushes on the pans, no scrub pads, no magic erasers. No abrasives anywhere — especially not on the E.T. on the lid.
  - Don't blow into the pans to clear dust. Breath moisture trapped under a dry surface can grow mildew inside old binders.
  - Don't try to fix the cracked tray. Not your job today.
  - Don't polish the lid. The patina around the E.T. is part of the object.

CLEANING — what to do

  1. Open the tin somewhere dry and room-temp, away from kitchen steam. Photograph the E.T. and the cracked tray first — light from a window if you can. Baseline + sentimental insurance.
  2. Pans: tip the tin over a piece of scrap paper and let loose dust fall out. Then a clean, very soft brush (a clean watercolor mop, a clean makeup brush — anything soft with no splay) to lift the rest. No force.
  3. Rehydrate gently. Lay a damp (not wet) paper towel over the pans for about 5 minutes, lift, then with a clean soft brush and a small drop of clean water, work one pan in slow circles. If it re-wakes, great. If it stays chalky and dry, that pan is probably too brittle to push — leave it.
  4. If a pan releases too much (old honey-bound pans sometimes flood), wick the excess with a clean paper towel. Don't flood and rinse.
  5. Tray: wipe with a barely-damp cloth, dry immediately with a soft dry cloth. Don't run water across the crack.
  6. Lid: soft dry cloth first, then a barely-damp cloth if needed. Stop as soon as it's clean. Let patina stay.

FIRST SWATCH — keep it tiny

  - Use your own paper, not anything that came with the tin. Assume the original paper is brittle and unknown.
  - Pick one friendly pan first — usually an earth tone or yellow ochre. Save the old blues/violets/greens for later; old versions of those are the most likely to be brittle or to misbehave.
  - One pan, one color, a small graded wash on a scrap card. You're testing the tin, not painting.
  - Old pigments sometimes shift as they dry. Wait before judging the color.

OPTIONAL SWATCH-DAY HELPERS (not permanent)

  - A small piece of wax paper or parchment laid over the cracked tray area gives you a smoother mixing surface without touching the crack.
  - A second dry paper towel under the tin while you work catches drips and protects your table.

The toolkit you have is the right one. The trick is sequencing so you set up once and then mostly step out of the loop.

ONE REAL DECISION: WHERE DOES THE BOWL LIVE?

Outside the door (porch, stoop, landing) with the sign taped above it -- "take one please" -- means you don't answer the doorbell at all. Lowest-hover version: Kibo hears fewer rings, you don't move.

Inside with the sign taped to the door means the bell still chimes but you don't answer it. White noise covers the chime.

Outside = fewer rings, one-time setup. Inside = no threshold setup but the bell still fires through the white noise. Either is fine.

BEFORE THE FIRST RING (once, ~30 min before dusk):

  Sign up, bowl placed.
  Water bowl filled, near the under-desk spot.
  Wrap within arm's reach of the spot -- NOT on him yet.
  Get Kibo into the spot while the house is still calm. Preemptive positioning is what reset the post-storm pattern -- same principle tonight.
  White noise on, steady volume (not loud).

DURING THE RUSH:

  Stay in earshot but don't camp by the door or by him. Neutral presence, no soothing voice when the bell rings -- that rule already held after the storm.
  If you read early signs (lip-lick, whale-eye, panting, restlessness), wrap on BEFORE he's fully ramped. Mid-panic is harder to land than preventative.
  If he does ramp: wrap on, move further from the door if a back room works, white noise stays on, you stay quiet and calm. No reassurance talk.

AFTER THE RUSH TAPERS:

  Bowl in if it was outside.
  Don't walk him right away -- let doorbell frequency drop first, then a slow neighborhood loop once it's quiet.
  Water check, wrap off once he's loose and calm.

ESCALATION THRESHOLD: if wrap + distance + white noise isn't landing and he's sustained panting/shaking past the peak window, that's a vet call. Same rule you've been running since the storm.

The whole thing is: one setup pass, then you're a quiet presence in the room while the sign does the front-door work. Sam in service tonight is real coverage, not a failed evening -- you're protecting Kibo's calmer pattern, and preemptive spot + wrap-on-readiness is what already worked Wednesday.

Prompt (give this to the candidate cold, ~10 minutes):

"You're handed a read Monday morning. A teammate ran an A/B test on a new onboarding nudge. Two-week look. Treatment: +4.1% on week-2 retention, p=0.018, n=15,200 control / 15,400 treatment. PM wants to ship Friday. The test was pre-registered for a four-week primary endpoint with one interim peek at two weeks. Walk me through, in order: (1) what you'd verify about the denominator before trusting the read, (2) how you'd think about effect size here, not just significance, (3) what your actual recommendation is and what specific signal would change it. Don't give me the textbook answer — give me what you'd actually do."

Scoring guide for Priya (score each row 0-2, 8 max; 5+ = strong, 3-4 = borderline, ≤2 = no-hire on this dimension):

Denominator first
  2  Names the cohort, asks whether it's pre-registered, checks assignment/contamination BEFORE recommending
  1  Brings up denominator, but only after leaning ship or hold
  0  Trusts the n's as given; never asks

Effect size, not just sig
  2  Translates +4.1% into absolute retained users at current signup volume, weighs against rollout cost, asks if MDE was met
  1  Quotes the lift number; doesn't translate it
  0  Treats the p-value as the decision

Interim peek vs ship decision
  2  Identifies this as the interim look, holds for the 4-week primary, OR names an explicit trigger that would justify shipping now
  1  Knows it's interim but would still ship
  0  p<0.05 = ship

Order and escalation
  2  Checks in order; states a threshold that would flip the call (e.g., "if 4-week confirms direction with p<0.01, ship; if it fades or flips, hold")
  1  Mixes checks and recommendation
  0  Jumps to ship/hold with no structure

Phrases worth hearing out loud: pre-registered cohort, n per arm, absolute lift at current volume, interim peek, primary endpoint, "what would change my call."

Red flags: quotes p without effect size, ships on the interim look, never asks about assignment integrity, gives a generic textbook answer with no concrete decision threshold.

One-line model answer (for calibration, not to share): "I'd hold for the 4-week primary; +4.1% is real direction but it's interim-only and I haven't translated it into absolute retained users at our current signup volume."

Note: the four rows map cleanly onto the 11-14 lane split — denom/effect/order is Owen's lens, the ship/wait/cut/escalate trigger is Riley's lens, and "would I actually recommend this" covers Ines's recommendation-risk check — so Priya can score without re-litigating lanes.

PANEL DRAFT — Onboarding change, p=.04, one week
Lane: Riley (judgment-call escalation). Other panelists can probe other lanes; this draft stays in mine.

THE QUESTION (read verbatim to the candidate):
"An onboarding change has p=.04 after one week. The PM wants to ship it. Would you ship it or not? Explain your decision in five minutes."

WHAT IT SHOULD TEST
Whether the candidate treats p=.04 as a decision input or as a decision. A good answer refuses the yes/no frame until they have:
  - denominator (sample size, segment, pooled vs segmented, was it powered)
  - effect size (absolute lift, practical significance — not just "it's significant")
  - cohort stability (week-1 onboarding cohorts are noisy; do later cohorts agree)
  - support risk (onboarding breakage hits new users; reversibility / rollback)
  - first-sig vs stabilization read (single peek at α=.05 is the classic p-hack;
    pre-reg'd stabilization requires same metric/direction, n≥treatment, and
    a p<.01 second-look BEFORE the next peek)

WHY THE GOTCHA IS RISKY
As written, the prompt rewards a confident yes/no answer with a clean narrative. That is exactly the failure mode we are trying to detect. The signal is in what they ask for FIRST. If they answer ship/not inside 30 seconds without asking for any of the five things above, that is the answer — and it is "no, not from this prompt."

Reframe in your head (do not say this aloud): "Does this person know that p=.04 at one week is the kind of number that ends up in a postmortem six months later?" Listen for the moment they slow down and start requesting inputs.

LISTEN-FORS, BY DIMENSION
Denominator:
  "How many users in treatment? Pooled or per-segment? Powered for the effect we care about, or just for any effect?"
Effect size:
  "What is the absolute lift on activation / retention / the actual metric? Is 0.4pp meaningful at our scale, or noise we would never notice?"
Cohort stability:
  "One cohort or several? Do later cohorts look the same? Week-1 onboarding cohorts churn differently than week-2+."
Support risk:
  "What breaks at 100%? Is this behind a flag? Can we roll back in under a day? Has support seen this change yet?"
First-sig vs stabilization:
  "First peek or Nth peek? Was the metric and direction pre-registered? Did the result hold at p<.01 on a second look, or did we just clear .04 once and stop peeking?"

PROBES (use only if they don't surface these on their own; one per dimension, in order)
1. "Walk me through what you would want to know about the test setup before deciding."
2. "What is the absolute effect, separate from the p-value?"
3. "If we waited another week, what would you expect to see?"
4. "What is the rollback path if support gets hit on day 1?"
5. "How many times has someone peeked at this metric? Is this a stabilization read or a first hit?"

STRONG vs WEAK SIGNALS
Strong:
  - Asks for at least 3 of the 5 dimensions before answering ship/not
  - Distinguishes "ship behind a flag to 10%" from "ship to 100%"
  - Names a concrete rollback / kill criterion
  - Distinguishes first-sig from a stabilization read, and treats them differently
  - Calls out peeking / multiple-testing risk
  - Names a concrete escalation path (wait N days, cut, ship to a segment, escalate for a denom review)

Weak / red:
  - Answers yes or no inside 30 seconds with a clean story
  - Treats p=.04 as a decision
  - Cannot articulate effect size apart from p-value
  - Does not ask about rollback or support
  - Treats "PM wants to ship" as a reason to ship
  - Treats "PM wants to ship" as a reason to refuse (politics-blind is also a fail — they will stall every fight)

CALIBRATION
In five minutes, a strong candidate asks for at least 3 of the 5 dimensions unprompted, gives a conditional answer ("I would ship behind a flag to X%, not 100%, IF Y and Z"), and names one thing that would change their mind. That is a clear hire signal for this lane.

A candidate who answers the yes/no in under a minute with conviction and asks no follow-ups is a clear no-hire. They will be the person shipping pricing-page-style rollbacks in six months.

OPTIONAL REFRAME (only if you want to de-gotcha it before the session)
"Here is an onboarding test result: p=.04 at one week, n=4,000, +0.4pp activation on the new variant. PM wants to ship to 100% Monday. Walk me through your decision."
This forces them to evaluate a concrete number rather than argue with an abstraction, and it surfaces the same five dimensions — but it loses the "do they push back on the yes/no frame" signal, which is itself worth testing. Your call.

Note for the room: stay quiet for the five minutes. The temptation will be to rescue a fumbling candidate with hints. Don't. A candidate who needs the panel to surface the five dimensions is showing you exactly how they will behave when the PM is in the room and the clock is running.

  Candidate prompt — churn cohort investigation (analyst / senior analyst,
  growth-investigations lane)

  Context
    You are joining a growth-investigations team mid-quarter. The team's
    monthly churn metric moved 1.2 percentage points above its trailing
    six-month baseline in October. Whether that movement is decision-
    relevant is part of what the team is investigating. The investigation
    is mid-flight; six lines were opened last week, none are closed, and
    the panel reviewer has already flagged three integrity risks against
    the working frame.

    The team operates under a pre-registration discipline. A line is only
    closed when three conditions hold together: the sample is large
    enough, the test statistic clears a second-look threshold (not a first-
    look one), and the observed effect clears a pre-stated minimum that
    someone has defended in writing. Closing a line does not mean the
    team ships a product change. Shipping is downstream of the panel
    accepting the readout.

  Working state at handoff

    Six investigation lines are open. Each has an owner. No findings are
    attached yet.

      1. New-workspace activation — first-week onboarding events.
      2. Billing-flow error rate — webhook failures on auto-renewals.
      3. Migration-tooling regressions — cohort that used the in-app
         importer.
      4. Lifecycle email deliverability — domain reputation / spam-rate
         shift.
      5. Segment-mix change — fewer mid-segment workspaces than last
         quarter.
      6. Pricing-page experiment residual — the cohort affected by the
         Q2 pricing-page rollback.

    Three risks flagged by the panel reviewer:

      (R1) One line is computing its effect against last quarter's total,
           not last quarter's same-segment baseline.
      (R2) One line's measurement window overlaps with a known non-
           product intervention (a marketing send-out), so any movement
           inside the window is partially confounded.
      (R3) Finance has asked for a forward number. If the team reframes
           the work as "predict Q1 churn," the cohort question collapses
           into a segmentation question with different evidence
           requirements.

  Your task

    A.  Re-frame three of the six lines. For each, write: the hypothesis,
        the metric, the direction you expect, the null, the smallest
        effect you would treat as decision-relevant, and the decision
        rule — the exact condition under which the line ships, holds, or
        is cut. One paragraph per line. Decision rules before outcomes;
        do not look at the data first.

    B.  Diagnose the risks. Which of R1, R2, R3 is most dangerous to the
        investigation's integrity, and what is the cheapest change that
        protects it? Two paragraphs maximum.

    C.  Decision boundaries. Two of the six lines will end the quarter
        closed-but-not-shipped. The team deliberately holds some. Write
        the rules that determine which two, and what the team owes the
        panel before any of them is reopened. One page maximum.

  Submission format
    Markdown, single document. Part A may be a hypothesis table or per-
    line paragraphs — your call. Parts B and C are prose.

    Do not include a final "ship / do not ship" verdict on the churn
    number itself. The team does not ship investigations; it ships
    product changes, and only after the panel accepts the readout.


  Note — what this prompt is evaluating

  This prompt is designed to surface three things, in order: reasoning
  under pre-registration, denominator and effect-size discipline, and
  decision boundaries.

  A candidate who writes a clean "yes, ship it" or "no, hold" verdict
  on the October churn number has misread the role. The whole point of
  the lane is that the ship / no-ship question is downstream of the
  decision rule, and the decision rule has to be defended in writing
  before anyone looks at the data. A prompt that baits a yes/no answer
  rewards the wrong instinct — it selects for confidence, not for the
  discipline the role actually requires.

  The three evaluative dimensions map directly onto the three integrity
  risks in the prompt. (R1) tests whether the candidate catches the
  wrong denominator without being told which line carries it. (R2)
  tests whether the candidate separates product effect from

Short order, do top-to-bottom, stop as soon as one step clears it:

1. Disposal re-check. Run it again with a steady stream of cold water for ~30s. The splash baffle (black rubber flap inside the throat) often catches food even when the disposal sounds fine — peek with a flashlight. Pull visible gunk with tongs or a gloved finger. If you go past the baffle, kill the breaker first; never bare-hand a disposal.

2. Better plunge. Bail the standing water. Stuff a wet rag into the OTHER basin so pressure goes where you want it. Cover the plunger cup with 2–3 inches of water, 8–10 firm strokes. "Helped a little" usually means a bad seal — sealing both basins is what actually moves the clog.

3. P-trap. Bucket underneath, unscrew both slip nuts by hand (channel-lock if corroded). Expect a small flood — keep the bucket low. Clear the trap, then shine a flashlight into the trap arm going into the wall. If you see a soft clog within ~6", pull it with needle-nose pliers.

4. Hand snake (only if trap is clean). 1/4" cable, 6–10 ft is plenty for a kitchen branch. Crank gently, don't force, pull back debris, re-flush with hot water.

5. Reassemble hand-tight + 1/4 turn with channel-locks, run water, check slip joints for drips.

Stop and call maintenance if any of these:

- Snake feeds in 6+ feet with nothing coming back — clog is past your branch.
- Multiple fixtures are slow, or you hear gurgling in the other basin/tub when this one drains — main stack.
- Water backs up into the dishwasher or comes up the other basin.
- You hit a hard object you can't identify.

PATCH THE TUBE.

Reasoning
- Single small pinhole from glass in the tube = textbook patch case.
- Tire casing has no cut, exposed threads, bulge, or bead damage = safe to reuse.
- Saves the spare for a higher-stakes moment (mid-week commute, less time, less daylight).
- Standard caveats that would push you toward the spare: hole within ~1 inch of the valve stem, hole across a tube seam, or a tube with multiple existing patches. None flagged.

PATCH APPLICATION (quick version)
1. Find the hole: inflate the tube and listen for hiss, or dunk a section in water and look for bubbles. Mark it.
2. Rough up the area around the hole with the sandpaper/emery in the kit (patch-sized).
3. Apply a thin layer of vulcanizing cement, wait ~30-60 sec until tacky (not wet/glossy).
4. Peel the patch, press firmly for 1-2 minutes (stand on it against a hard floor, or press with the back of a spoon on a table).
5. Let it set ~5 minutes before reinstallation.

INSPECTION CHECKLIST (before the tube goes back in)
1. Find and remove the debris: run a finger gently along the INSIDE of the tire where the puncture was. A missed shard will re-puncture within minutes. If you can't feel it, angle a bright light inside.
2. Inspect the tire casing from the inside — no cuts, exposed threads, bulges, foreign objects.
3. Rim tape: no tears, no spokes showing through gaps, not shifted into the tire bead channel.
4. Rim well: no sharp edges, burrs, or dents where the tube sits.
5. Mount the tube with a slight pre-inflation so it doesn't pinch. Seat the tire bead evenly on both sides all the way around.
6. Valve stem perpendicular to the rim, not tilted. A tilted valve = improper seating = slow leak.
7. Direction of rotation correct if the tire is marked, and front/rear match if specified.

PRESSURE-TEST CHECKLIST
1. Inflate to the sidewall-rated PSI (road ~80-130, hybrid ~50-70, MTB ~30-50). Do not exceed max.
2. Listen at the patch, valve, and tire/rim interface during inflation — any hiss = stop and recheck.
3. Optional but definitive: spray soapy water on the patch and around the valve. Bubbles = leak.
4. Spin the wheel: tire should look round, no visible wobble or bulge.
5. Squeeze test: firm, not rock-hard but no obvious give.
6. Pressure-hold test: wait 5-10 minutes, or ride a block and recheck. A small drop from cold contraction is normal; anything noticeable = not sealed.
7. Final bead check: both beads seated evenly all the way around, no bulges or "unseated" sections.

If anything in the inspection or pressure test fails, swap in the spare tube. The patched tube can be re-done or kept as a backup once you have time — don't ride on a tire you're not confident in.

Good plan. Two days of sitting is the right re-check window — slow leaks that didn't show on a 3-mile ride will usually show as a measurable pressure drop after 48 hrs of rest. When you do the pre-commute check Tuesday morning:

- Inflate to 62, wait 5 min, re-check. If it holds steady, you're cleared.
- Run a finger around the patch edge — a glue-on patch can lift at the seam if the inside of the casing wasn't fully dry when you applied it.
- If you find any grit or wire that caused the pinhole in the first place and missed it on the hand-check, that's the most common reason a "good" patch fails on day three.

Keeping the spare tube unused is the right call — patch first, swap only if it doesn't hold. 3 miles with no loss is encouraging but not yet proof.

The lifted strip is a fluff of paper fibers that separated from the substrate when the tape pulled. If you lay a wash over it, pigment will pool against the raised fibers and you'll see a dark uneven line that calls more attention to the edge than the fibers themselves do now.

Most conservative: with a small brush, lay a thin line of clean water on just the damaged strip — not the painted wash. Wait 45-60 seconds for the paper to swell and the fibers to relax, then press it flat with a piece of clean blotter or a plain paper towel under light hand pressure (or set a small weight on it) for a few minutes. As it dries the fibers re-bond to the substrate. Mask the painted area with a scrap of paper if the strip sits close to the wash so the water doesn't creep into your color.

If rewetting feels too risky where it sits, the dry-only fallback is to take the back of a clean metal spoon (or a bone folder) and gently burnish along the strip to press the worst of the raised fibers down. It won't fully fix them but it knocks down the catch-points so the wash won't pool as badly.

Last resort if neither of those gives you a clean enough edge: trim 1-2mm off that border with a fresh blade on a cutting mat. Card comes out slightly smaller but you get an undamaged edge, and if it goes in a mat or sits on a backing card the trim disappears.

PRE-REMOVAL

  - Deflate the patched tube fully. 37 psi still holds the bead out and you'll fight the tire on the rim otherwise.
  - Note the tire's orientation on the rim (valve position relative to any tread logo or wear pattern). Less critical for this fix than for diagnosing where on the tread the debris entered, but it costs nothing to mark.

REMOVE THE TIRE

  - Unseat the bead on the side AWAY from the embedded shard first, working the whole circumference, not just near the glass. Concentrating lever force near the shard pushes it deeper.
  - Pull the tube out without levers if you can. Levers only between tire and rim, never against the tube.

PULL THE SHARD + LOOK FOR COMPANIONS

  - Tweezers or needle-nose, not fingers. Hair-thin glass leaves invisible cuts.
  - Strong direct light plus magnification helps. Phone flashlight held close to the inside surface is the minimum.
  - After removal, run a fingertip lightly across the inside of the casing in a 4 to 6 inch radius around the entry point. Hair-thin glass clusters; if one was there, others are likely nearby.
  - Flip the tire and shake it upside down over a clean surface. Small fragments fall out.

CASING INSPECTION (this is your unsafe-to-reuse check)

  Look at the INSIDE of the tire, not the outside. Glass can pass between casing threads without leaving a visible outside cut, so the inside view is the meaningful one.

  - Drag a cotton ball or a wadded paper towel through the inside of the tire all the way around. Snags mean residual debris or fiber damage. A fabric wad pushed through and then shaken out catches things cotton alone misses.
  - Flex the suspect area with both hands, bending the casing back and forth. Grinding, threads shifting, or a bubble forming under flex = internal damage.
  - Inspect the bead all the way around: cuts, fraying, or any kink in the wire/kevlar ring. The bead is what keeps the tire on the rim; a compromised bead is a blowoff waiting to happen.
  - Inspect the sidewalls at the suspect area. Sidewalls flex the most under load, so damage there is the most dangerous.

WHAT MAKES THE TIRE ITSELF UNSAFE TO REUSE

  Replace the tire if any of these are true:

    - Daylight visible through the casing from the inside, even from a pinhole. Will grow under pressure.
    - Exposed casing threads (white nylon or polyester ply showing through the rubber) anywhere, especially inside or at the original glass entry.
    - Any bulge, on sidewall or tread. Internal ply separation.
    - Bead damage: cuts, fraying, kinks.
    - Sidewall cut or scuff that exposes the ply.
    - Inside-surface cuts longer than about 5 mm.
    - A bubble that forms during the flex test.

  If none of those are present, the tire is reusable. Hair-thin glass almost always slips between threads without cutting them, and your "casing still doesn't show a cut, exposed threads, bulge, or bead damage" observation is a genuinely good sign.

RIM AND RIM TAPE INSPECTION

  This is the part that decides whether your spare survives the install.

  - Peel the rim tape back. Replace it (cheap, a couple of dollars) if it's torn, wrinkled, misaligned, or doesn't fully cover the spoke nipple holes. Failed rim tape is the #1 cause of "I changed the tube and punctured it again immediately."
  - Run a fingertip over each spoke nipple inside the rim bed. Any that protrude above the rim tape or have a sharp edge will puncture a tube. File the nipple or shim under the rim tape; replace the nipple if it's badly burred.
  - Inspect the rim well itself: cracks at spoke holes, around the valve hole, or along the seam (on pinned or welded rims). Cracks mean a new rim, not just a new tube.
  - File any burrs at the valve hole or seam.
  - Wipe the rim bed clean with a rag. Worn brake pads shed wire that sits in the rim well and acts like a needle bed.

TUBE AND REINSTALL

  - Don't reuse the patched tube. A patch that loses pressure over a few hours has an unsealed edge. Use the spare as planned.
  - Inflate the spare partway, just enough to give it shape, before installing. This is what prevents pinching between tire and rim.
  - Insert the valve straight, then tuck the tube into the tire all the way around. No twists, no pinches.
  - Mount the bead starting at the valve and work both directions. Thumbs preferred; levers only between tire and rim, never near the tube.
  - Visually inspect the whole circumference: tube must not be pinched between bead and rim.
  - Inflate in stages: about 10 psi first, check seating and that nothing bulges, then up to full. Spin the wheel; any hop means stop and check for a pinched tube.
  - At full pressure, listen for hiss and recheck pressure after 5 minutes. The overnight hold is the real test.

LIKELY REASON THE FIRST PATCH FAILED

  - Most likely the second shard was already inside the tire and re-punctured the patched tube overnight. The 62-to-37 loss rate is consistent with a small, persistent hole, not a catastrophic patch failure.
  - Less likely: the original hole wasn't fully roughed with sandpaper and cleaned with alcohol before patching, so the patch didn't fully bond.
  - Less likely: patch applied without firm pressure across the whole patch area for the full cure time.

If the inside-inspection and rim-tape work both come back clean, the spare should hold. If it doesn't, suspect the rim tape first, the casing second.

What the table is showing mechanically

  An activation rate is computed as:

    activated / cohort

  where the cohort denominator is "everyone who signed up in the window
  being summarized," and the numerator only includes users whose full
  activation window has elapsed AND who hit the activation event. If
  some users in the cohort are still inside their window, they
  contribute to the denominator but cannot contribute to the
  numerator yet. The naive rate is therefore a downward-biased
  estimate of the true eventual rate for that cohort, and the bias
  shrinks as more users age out of their window.

  So "27.8% partial" means: Owen's pulse is computing the rate over a
  cohort that includes some users who haven't had time to activate yet,
  and the rate is being read as if those partial-window users were a
  fair sample of the cohort's eventual behavior. They're not. They're
  a censored sample.

Quick read of what you described — thorn lying *across* the webbing between pads (not into the pad itself), shallow, visible, no bleeding/swelling, Kibo tolerating inspection — that's the most DIY-friendly version of a paw thorn. The sequence below is conservative; bail to the vet list if anything deviates.

Sequence
1. Helper + distraction if possible. Even a lickable treat held at chin-height while you work is enough — you want his head occupied, not a soothing-voice routine (just steady, neutral handling).
2. Flush the area with saline *before* you touch the thorn. A slip is less bad if the skin is already clean.
3. Tweezers as close to the skin as you can get; pull along the same angle the thorn entered, steady — perpendicular yanks snap it.
4. Look at what came out: whole piece, no dark fragment left behind, length matches what you saw going in.
5. Re-flush with saline, pat dry with clean gauze or cloth.
6. Recheck at 10 minutes (bleeding) and again before bed (swelling, heat).

Stop and call the vet instead — tonight (emergency clinic) vs. tomorrow (regular) flagged below
- Thorn broke and any fragment is still in the skin — don't dig for it. → tonight if you can't see/feel it; tomorrow otherwise.
- It turns out to be *in* the pad, not just across the webbing. → tonight.
- Bleeding doesn't stop within ~5 min of gentle pressure. → tonight.
- Paw looks swollen, hot, or red, or favoring gets *worse* (not better) over the next few hours. → tonight if rapid, tomorrow morning if mild.
- He's increasingly painful when you touch anywhere near it. → tonight.
- You can't tell how deep it really is, or you only ever saw one end. → tomorrow for a look.
- Limping or licking persists past tomorrow morning. → tomorrow.

Since it's Saturday evening: if removal goes clean and he's walking normally within an hour, you're fine to monitor at home and only call your regular vet Monday if anything's still off.

Glad it came out clean and he's weight-bearing already — saline + intact extraction is the best-case outcome, and treating resolved as resolved is the right call. The only thing that would change my read is the paw getting *worse* than baseline (new swelling, going off it again, behavior change like hiding or guarding it) rather than just staying the same — in which case it's vet time, not more at-home inspection.
