Lemony cumin chickpeas + kale over rice. One pan, ~20 minutes active, splits cleanly into tonight and a late portion that reheats well.

COOK (one batch, don't split while cooking):
- Warm 2-3 tbsp olive oil in a skillet over medium. Add 2-3 cloves garlic, thinly sliced or smashed. 30 seconds.
- Add 1 can chickpeas, drained, plus a generous pinch of salt, 1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp smoked paprika. Stir and let them warm through, ~3 min. Smash a few with a fork or potato masher so some break down into a light sauce; leave most whole.
- Add 1 big handful of kale, stems removed, leaves torn. Toss until just wilted, ~2-3 min. Pull it while the kale still has some structure — it'll cook more on reheat.
- Squeeze in half the lemon. Kill the heat.

ASSEMBLE:
- Spoon over ~1.5 cups of your cooked rice (warm it separately or pile it on; rice and chickpeas together is fine).
- Plate your portion now: crumble feta on top, a final squeeze of lemon, eat.

PACK SAM'S PORTION (this is the part that matters):
- Put just the rice + chickpea-kale mixture in a container. Refrigerate once cool.
- Do NOT add his feta or his final lemon squeeze yet. Feta gets rubbery and the lemon turns dull after sitting. Both go on after he reheats.

SAM'S REHEAT (he arrives after midnight, keep it dead simple):
- Skillet method (better, ~4 min, worth the small effort): pile his portion into a small nonstick pan with 1 tbsp water. Cover. Low heat. Stir once at the 2-min mark. When hot, kill the heat, crumble feta over the top, squeeze the rest of the lemon over it. Eat.
- Microwave method (fine if he's wiped): bowl, splash of water (1-2 tsp), plate or damp paper towel loosely covering the top (the cover is what saves the rice from going hard and chalky). 70% power for ~2 min, stir, 30-60 sec more. Then feta + lemon on top.

Why it survives the reheat: chickpeas and rice are both forgiving; the smoked paprika and cumin deepen overnight rather than going flat; kale holds up if you underdid it slightly the first time; feta + lemon at the end is what makes a reheated bowl taste like dinner instead of leftovers.

SAME-DAY PLAN

1. Stop running. You already did — don't try to "shake it out" or jog it off.
2. Ice: 15 min on, 45 min off, repeat 3-4x through the afternoon. Thin barrier (sock or towel) between skin and pack.
3. Compression: calf sleeve or a snug tube sock from ankle to just below the knee while you're up and around.
4. Elevate above heart level when sitting — 10-15 min, a few times today.
5. Avoid for the next 48h: heat (no hot bath/sauna), alcohol, deep massage, aggressive stretching of the calf. Easy walking is fine.
6. Hydrate normally. NSAIDs only if you tolerate them — short course, with food, stop if not needed.
7. Pain-free mobility only: ankle circles, light knee bends. If a movement reproduces the soreness, don't push into it.

WHAT WOULD MAKE IT MORE THAN ORDINARY MUSCLE IRRITATION

The picture right now is reassuring (no pop, no sharp pain, no swelling, normal walking). Watch through the next 24-72h and seek same-day care if any of these show up:

- Visible swelling: calf bigger than the other side, or a thumbprint that holds (pitting) when you press.
- Localized warmth or redness over the calf.
- Pain that worsens over 24-48h instead of easing, or pain that's present at rest / when you're not moving.
- Pain reproduced by passive ankle dorsiflexion (someone else pulls your toes up toward your shin).
- DVT risk factors stacked against you: recent >4h flight or car ride, recent illness with bed rest, oral contraceptives or hormone therapy, known clotting tendency, family history of clots, recent surgery, active cancer.
- Compartment syndrome signs: pain out of proportion to what you'd expect, calf feels very tight or full, numbness/tingling in the foot, pain worse with passive stretch.
- A palpable gap in the muscle, sudden bruising, or real weakness on a single-leg calf raise — suggests a tear, not irritation.
- Calf pain plus sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, lightheadedness, or coughing blood — emergency services immediately (pulmonary embolism).

WHEN TO TEST ANOTHER RUN

Not tomorrow. Use a symptom gate — every item needs to be true before you try:

- Pain-free walking, including stairs, for at least 24-48h.
- Single-leg calf raise on the left matches the right, pain-free, 3 x 10.
- Pain-free hopping on the left leg (start single, then a few in a row).
- No calf soreness at rest or on waking.

Once those clear (typically 3-7 days for a low-grade soleus or gastrocnemius strain, sooner if it was just fatigue):

1. Walk 10 min, then jog 1 min / walk 1 min x 5, easy effort, flat ground.
2. If clean the next day: one continuous easy run at about half your usual distance.
3. Build back ~10% per session across the next week.

If tightness returns during or right after the test jog, take another 3-5 days off and retry. If after 10-14 days it's still sore, or if any red flag from the list above appears, get it looked at — a grade I strain that drags on is worth a sports-medicine or PT visit rather than another run-through-the-pain cycle.

Setup-call nudge v1 — one-week operational read

Summary
The nudge shipped clean through call-and-integration: 13/96 booked, 10 calls held, 7 of those 10 accounts connected a first integration within 48 hours, no pressure, suppression, duplicate, or CS-load signals. The booking and call-and-connect mechanics work. The seven connections are a real behavioral correlation. They are not a causal effect, and they should not be used that way.

What this supports
1. Operational quality is intact through a full week and one integration step. No new failure modes appeared past the 24-hour read.
2. The offer + landing + scheduling flow converts on its own terms: 13/96 (~14%) of a hand-reviewed cohort booked without complaints. That is an observation about the treated cohort's behavior, not lift.
3. Among people who actually took the call, the connection rate is encouraging. 7/10 within 48 hours is the right kind of signal from a completed-call readout.
4. Continued absence of harm signals under a slightly longer window — useful for keeping the live cell narrow.

What this does not support
1. Incremental lift. Without a holdout, the seven connections are confounded with self-selection. Admins who book a setup call on a nudge are almost certainly higher-intent than admins who don't. The seven may have integrated on their own timeline regardless of the email.
2. Per-account effect size, ROI math, or anything that needs a counterfactual denominator.
3. Broad scaling. Same rule as the pre-reg rollback: same metric, same direction needs a real comparator before anyone treats the first positive peek as a decision.
4. A claim that "the nudge works." It works mechanically; "useful" is still the deferred question.

Effect, in your terms
Observed: 7 integrations after call, on the booked subset, in a hand-selected 96-account cohort.
Decision-relevant: incremental integration rate vs. doing nothing. Not measured. Not measurable from this read.

Call
Do not let the seven enter any document as lift, ROI, or a scaling case. Two legitimate next moves, pick one:
- Holdout test: same filter, same reviewed cohort, 50/50 split. Same metric (48h post-call-or-equivalent integration), same direction. One pre-registered read, no peeking. The connection comparison then has a real denominator.
- Stay narrow: keep the live cell as-is, continue to treat the read as operational + behavioral among callers, and revisit only when a holdout is feasible. Useful for keeping CS load contained and the offer alive, not for ship decisions.

If someone on the team wants to cite this in a deck, the only framing that survives review is: "the nudge operates cleanly and converts bookings; incremental impact is unmeasured." Anything stronger borrows from the seven and overstates what we know.

CALL: Stay narrow. No lift claim yet. If another batch of reviewed accounts is queued, split it 50/50 for incremental truth; otherwise continue without promoting the result.

OBSERVED (1-wk, n=96):
  96 delivered · 0 dup · 0 leak · 0 complaints · CS load normal
  13/96 booked (13.5%)
  10/13 calls completed
  7/10 connected a first integration within 48h (70%)

WHAT THIS IS: a clean operational readout. Calls convert; the email books calls at 13.5% on a well-targeted cohort.

WHAT THIS IS NOT: incremental lift. No untreated comparison, so 13/96 and 7/10 are observed, not attributable to the nudge. Don't frame as uplift. Don't scale into other segments. Don't promote as a Growth win.

DECISION-RELEVANT SIGNAL: the 7/10 post-call connect rate. Of accounts that took a call, most wired something up in 48h. That's a quality read on the call itself — not on email → call.

USEFULNESS: deferred. 48h integration ≠ retention or expansion. Need 30/60-day read before any retention claim.

  B. Continue to next reviewed-account batch, narrow, no lift claim. Don't scale. Don't promote. Revisit in Q1 once usefulness is read.

Read: classification problem, not behavior. Almost certainly annual-plan handling.

Why not behavior: a behavior explanation would need to account for 7 valid payments not corresponding to 7 paid customers. The behavior candidates — voided, refunded, duplicated, delinquent — you've already ruled out (none apply). What's left is that the dashboard is counting something other than "had a valid first payment."

Most likely cause: the dashboard's "paid workspace" rule filters on monthly-recurring billing — so annual-plan signups get the lump-sum invoice but never trip the "paid" flag. This is common because most SaaS dashboards are built around monthly recurring revenue, and annual plans show up as one big invoice, not a recurring monthly charge. The 7 = the annual-plan subset of the cohort's first payments. That fits the shape exactly.

Minimum verification sequence (3 steps, stop after each if it resolves):

Quick read on the situation: 24°F is way warmer than a working freezer (should be 0°F or below), but it's still well under the 40°F danger zone. 75–90 minutes at that temp is not enough to make any of these items unsafe — quality is the only thing at risk, and even that is mild.

Per-item call (conservative):

  Chicken thighs — KEEP and refreeze. Visible ice crystals = still frozen by the USDA standard. Quality fine. Use within a normal freezer timeline (a few months).

  Frozen vegetables — KEEP and refreeze. "Firm" means they held their frozen structure. Blanched veg that has never fully thawed refreezes with minimal quality loss.

  Bread — KEEP and refreeze (or refrigerate and use within a few days). Bread is low-risk; if it was still cold to the touch when you found it, it stayed under 40°F. Texture will be slightly worse after refreezing, but safety is not in question.

  Ice cream — KEEP and refreeze. Soft edges + frozen center means partial thaw only. Expect an icy, grainier texture after refreezing, but it is safe. If the texture bothers you, eat it this week as a "soft serve" style and don't refreeze.

Nothing in the freezer needs to be discarded based on what's described.

Monitoring the freezer:

  Hour 1 after closing the door: temp should have started falling.
  Hours 2–6: should be visibly trending toward normal (single digits °F).
  Hour 24: should be at or below 0°F.

  Treat it as a problem if:
    - Temp is not clearly dropping within 2 hours of the door being fully closed.
    - It has not returned to 0°F or below within 24 hours. At that point the compressor, thermostat, or refrigerant is suspect and a tech is warranted.
    - You find frost or ice built up along the door gasket, or the door doesn't seat firmly on its own. That means the seal is compromised regardless of how the temperature recovers, and the gasket likely needs cleaning or replacement.

  Also worth a one-time check: a fully loaded freezer holds temp better than a nearly empty one during a door-left-ajar event. If this freezer is usually sparse, consider whether the seal is aging — older gaskets are the most common cause of "door was barely ajar but the temp swung fast" incidents.

One non-food housekeeping note for next time: a simple audible door alarm (or a cheap Wi-Fi temp sensor that pings your phone) catches a 90-minute ajar window down to a few minutes. Cheap insurance for the cost of a freezer of food.

No tools used here — this was a straight food-safety call based on the details you gave. If you want, I can also draft a short note for the household fridge log or a reminder to check the gasket this weekend.

Failure mode has two layers and they're easy to confuse as one.

1. Wrong grain (the 1,642 vs 1,413). The query is fanning out at the join — most likely accounts × admins, or accounts × subscriptions × admins — and never collapsing back to one row per recipient. Admin-checklist emails are sent per admin, so the audience has to be unique admins. 229 rows collapse to 0 once you dedupe at the admin grain; that's noise, not a real audience gap.

2. Suppressions applied late or not at all (the 1,413 vs ~1,325). The ~88 extras are real admins on accounts that should have been filtered: open CS adoption plan = account is being actively worked, support contact in the last 14 days = account is recently served. These need to be hard suppressions for cold admin outreach. Most likely the prompt carried the design intent ("exclude accounts being actively worked") but the query either didn't apply them at all or applied them on the wrong side of a join so they got dropped. This is the same bad-prompt-suppression failure mode as the Expansion Assist case — design input didn't make it into the query.

The 88 delta is what the suppressions should close. The 229 duplicate rows are a separate dedupe problem.

Safer account-level pattern (sketch — adapt to your warehouse):

    WITH base_accounts AS (
      SELECT a.account_id, a.primary_admin_email
      FROM accounts a
      WHERE a.account_status = 'active'
        AND a.primary_admin_email IS NOT NULL
        AND a.year_end_checklist_eligible = TRUE  -- whatever the design input was
    ),
    suppressed_accounts AS (
      SELECT account_id FROM cs_adoption_plans WHERE status = 'open'
      UNION
      SELECT account_id FROM support_contacts WHERE contacted_at >= current_date - 14
      -- add other active suppressions here, in one place
    )
    SELECT ba.primary_admin_email
    FROM base_accounts ba
    WHERE NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM suppressed_accounts sa
      WHERE sa.account_id = ba.account_id
    )
    QUALIFY row_number() OVER (
      PARTITION BY ba.primary_admin_email ORDER BY ba.account_id
    ) = 1;

Three things to keep:
  - Grain is (account_id, primary_admin_email). Suppressions are a separate CTE, joined with NOT EXISTS (or ANTI JOIN) so it's obvious what's filtered and easy to audit before send.
  - Apply suppressions BEFORE you collapse to one row per admin. If you dedupe first, you can lose the suppression signal on the dropped rows.
  - The final QUALIFY is defense in depth — even if upstream dedupe regresses, you can't ship a duplicate.

Pre-send QA checklist:

Counts:
  - Row count == unique recipient count. If rows > unique, the join is fanning out — fix before send, do not just shrug and dedupe post-hoc.
  - Total inside [expected_low, expected_high]. Target ~1,325; flag anything outside ±5%.
  - Suppression delta: count(base) − count(suppressed) ≈ final audience. The 88 from this morning should equal `count(suppressed_accounts)`. If it doesn't, either a suppression is missing or one of the CTEs is over-counting.

Suppression coverage:
  - No accounts with open CS adoption plan (cross-check vs CS team roster).
  - No accounts with a support contact in the past 14 days (cross-check vs support tool).
  - No accounts in any other active suppression list — unsubscribes, role-account blocks, legal-hold.
  - Spot-check 10–20 random recipients: account active, recipient is actually an admin, no recent comms to them.

Sign-off:
  - Ines signs off on the suppression list (her lane — lifecycle rec risk).
  - Suppression CTE contents match what the brief / design doc said.
  - Send log records suppression counts so post-send you can prove what was filtered and to whom.

Ines's stop is the right call. As written, this would have gone to ~88 accounts being actively worked or recently served, and the row count anyone reviewed didn't match the actual recipient count. Fix the query, run the gate above, re-preflight, then ship.

Diagnosis confirmed. This is the OR-across-rows anti-pattern: a LEFT JOIN to a one-to-many table where any single matching row that satisfies the filter lets the parent through. The expired row "wins" the WHERE check even when a sibling active row exists, and the same join fans out 229 duplicate rows.

Impact
  - 1,413 unique admins in output vs ~1,325 expected -> ~88 accounts slipping past active suppressions
  - 229 duplicate rows are the same bug, not a separate one (the LEFT JOIN multiplies parent rows per suppression_history entry)
  - 54 CS adoption plans + 31 recent support contacts live in this pool, so any of those with mixed-history suppressions are also mis-included

Fix -- replace LEFT JOIN + WHERE with NOT EXISTS:

  SELECT ...
  FROM eligible_admin a
  WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM suppression_history s
    WHERE s.account_id = a.account_id
      AND s.expires_at >= CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
  )

Why this is the right shape:
  - EXISTS is true if any row matches; NOT EXISTS is false if any active suppression exists -> bug closed
  - No row fan-out, so the 229 duplicates disappear as a side effect
  - "No suppression row at all" still passes (EXISTS false -> NOT EXISTS true)

Things to also check before re-running
  1. Is "active" really expires_at >= now, or is there a status/flag column? If a status column exists, filter on that, not on time.
  2. Are there legit reasons one admin appears under multiple account_ids (multi-workspace)? If yes, dedupe by admin after suppression is correct; if no, eligible_admin itself has dupes.
  3. Re-run and expect ~1,325 unique rows, no fan-out. If you land at ~1,325 - X where X matches the 88 estimate, the diagnosis was the whole story; if you're off further, the duplicate source is the next thing to look at.

   - Simpson-style inversion: aggregate below bar because the low-depth slice dilutes, while high-depth would have moved even without the prompt.
2. The aggregate missed its bar (+$8 expansion-MRR-per-treated-account). The "materially ahead" language on the high-depth slice is a within-treatment observation Owen layered on after the fact — not a pre-registered sub-arm test. No p-value, no CI inside that slice, no balance check on depth across treatment/control.
3. The 2023-06-22 ruling explicitly closed this door: do NOT widen eligibility from this read; next iteration should use behavior-based eligibility, not blanket day-60. CS adopting "active-admin behavior" as a renewal signal now would invert that ruling and re-create the partial-read → fake-broad-answer failure mode.
4. Intervention imbalance compounds it. Without stratified randomization, even small depth-rate differences across arms would produce the observed within-depth gap because the comparison is happening inside one arm against an implicit baseline. That's a "treat within-arm" footgun.

CALL

MINIMUM STRATIFIED/ADJUSTED RERUN OWEN OWES BEFORE CS ACTS

Pre-register first (cheap, locks the design so it can't be tuned post-hoc):
  - Depth signal: composite (e.g., distinct-admin-event-days last 14d ≥ threshold OR usage-panel session-depth last 14d ≥ threshold). Name the events.

  - Per-stratum primary metric: expansion MRR per treated account, +$8 bar inherited from parent.

2. Stratified rerun (the floor). Per depth stratum:

DRAFT — DATA PROCESSING TERMS (BUSINESS POSITIONS)

Cover: These provisions are drafted to codify the operational positions
on Customer Event Data. "Customer Event Data," "Processor," "Subprocessor,"

1. PRODUCTION DELETION (≤ 30 DAYS POST-TERMINATION)

1.1 Within thirty (30) calendar days after the effective date of
    termination or expiration of the Agreement (the "Deletion Window"),
    Processor shall delete all Customer Event Data from production
    systems, including without limitation production databases,
    primary storage, analytics stores, and any production replica or
    live mirror on which Customer Event Data is actively accessed.

1.2 For the avoidance of doubt, "delete" means removal such that the
    data is no longer accessible in the ordinary course and cannot be
    retrieved, restored, or used by Processor in the operation of the

2. BACKUP RETENTION AND ROLL-OFF (≤ 90 DAYS)

2.1 Customer acknowledges that routine backup media (including

    backup media for no more than ninety (90) calendar days after the
    date of production deletion under Section 1, after which time

    irretrievable on Processor's standard backup lifecycle.

2.2 Processor shall not restore Customer Event Data from backup except
    to recover data lost from production prior to the production
    deletion date, and shall not use retained backup copies to
    continue processing Customer Event Data on an ongoing basis.

    (c) the scheduled backup retention expiry date for any backup

    (d) that no Customer Event Data remains in Processor's active
        control or in any active production system other than as

3.2 Within five (5) business days after the scheduled backup expiry
    date stated in the certification under Section 3.1(c), Processor

----------------------------------------------------------------
4. DEIDENTIFICATION STANDARD

    transformed such that reidentification is not reasonably
    achievable by Processor, any Affiliate, any Subprocessor, or any
    third party:
    (a) workspace identifiers;
    (b) user identifiers;
    (c) message identifiers; and
    (d) event identifiers.

4.2 Aggregations, counts, rollups, model inputs, embeddings, or other

4.3 Processor shall not, and shall not permit any Affiliate,

Quick read on what you're hearing: single chirp about every 45 seconds, steady green power light, no smoke or smell, other units quiet = textbook low-battery chirp. Your detector is still getting AC power; only the backup cell is depleted. You're safe to swap, but you must not leave the unit down or silent overnight.

BEFORE YOU CLIMB
  - Use a proper step stool, not a chair. Have someone spot you if possible.
  - No need to trip the breaker for a battery swap. The interconnect wire means the OTHER detectors stay live, so your home is still protected from a real fire during the few minutes this one is down.
  - Have the fresh battery and a flashlight within reach before you start.

SEQUENCE (don't leave the unit dangling between steps)
  1. Twist the detector counterclockwise off its mounting plate (some models slide straight off — check for arrow indicators). Let it hang by the harness; do NOT yank on the wires.
  2. Squeeze the plastic release tab on the harness connector and pull straight down. The other alarms in the house still detect during this ~2 minute window, so the household is not unprotected.
  3. Slide open the battery drawer (usually back or side). Pull the old cell — likely a 9V, possibly AA or a coin cell — and note the polarity.
  4. Match the EXACT battery type the label specifies. Do NOT substitute rechargeable NiMH (it self-discharges and will trigger false low-battery chirps). Do NOT mix chemistries.
  5. Snap the new battery in, +/− correct, close the drawer.
  6. Reconnect the harness — it only fits one way; should click.
  7. Seat the detector on the plate and twist clockwise to lock. A single brief chirp on power-up is normal.
  8. If it keeps chirping after ~30 seconds, press and hold TEST/HUSH for 15–20 seconds to reset the processor. If still chirping, flip its breaker off for about a minute and back on.

TEST
  - Press and hold TEST. Expect a loud, repeating alarm tone.
  - Verify every interconnected unit sounds, then release. Silence after release = clean reset.
  - Wait 5 minutes in the room. Continued silence = good.
  - Optional but stronger: a quick puff of test aerosol (or a smoldering, then extinguished, cotton string) actually exercises the sensor chamber. The TEST button only checks the sounder and circuit, not the smoke sensor.

A NOTE ON "SILENCING"
  - Some units have a temporary hush that quiets the chirp for ~8 hours. Fine as a stopgap overnight while you source the correct battery, but it is not a fix — the chirp returns and the backup cell is still flat.

STOP AND LEAVE THE HOUSE IF
  - The chirp changes into 3 repeated beeps in a row — that's the fire pattern, not a battery fault. Get out and call 911 from outside.
  - You see smoke, heat discoloration, or smell anything burning.
  - Anyone feels dizzy, nauseous, or headache-y (different chirp cadence — 4 beeps then pause — means CO; evacuate and call 911).

REPLACE THE WHOLE UNIT INSTEAD OF JUST THE BATTERY IF
  - The manufacture date on the back is more than 10 years old. Yours is 2020, so you're well within life.
  - It still chirps after a confirmed fresh correct battery + 20-second reset + breaker cycle.
  - You see yellowing or cracking plastic, corrosion on the battery contacts, or melted/discolored wiring.
  - The chirp pattern is NOT a single chirp ~every 30–60 seconds — e.g., 2 or 3 quick chirps, an unusual cadence, or a "trouble" beep code means sensor fault or end-of-life; replace.
  - You can't confirm the exact battery match.

QUICK UPKEEP WHILE YOU HAVE IT DOWN
  - Gently vacuum the chamber with a soft brush. Dust causes false alarms and sensitivity drift.
  - Replace backup batteries every 6 months (each daylight saving flip is an easy reminder), or switch to a 10-year sealed lithium backup unit.
  - Write today's date on the unit in marker so the 10-year replacement clock is visible.

That's the textbook low-battery chirp recovery — circuit off, fresh battery, hard reset, manufacturer test, steady green. Your read is right.

Small note on confirmation timing: most detectors run a self-check at the top of the next hour or at midnight. If you've got steady green through at least one of those cycles with no chirp, you're genuinely clear. If it chirps again after a self-check, the new battery is marginal or the seating is off — but a clean test pattern + steady green makes that unlikely.

Treating it as resolved is the right call.

Two tablespoons pooled at the front-right corner after a normal cycle, with the machine off, supply/drain dry, no cabinet water, and an apparently intact gasket — that's a plausible signature of the filter hypothesis. The filter assembly sits at the bottom of the tub and on many models IS the sump cover; if it didn't lock, the sump can leak during the spray phases and that water tends to track forward and find the lowest exit at the front-corner of the gasket.

Hold off on running another cycle until step 1 passes. Here's the bounded sequence:

1. FILTER RE-SEAT (highest-probability fix given your read)
   - Open door, pull bottom rack out and set it aside.
   - The filter is a cylindrical coarse filter + flat fine filter in the tub floor, usually near center-front. Twist it out (most are a quarter-turn).
   - Check the sump well (the cavity the filter seats into) for debris — a bone shard, glass, or food lump lodged in the seat is the most common reason a filter won't lock. Remove what you find with your fingers or a soft cloth. Don't use a screwdriver.
   - Reinstall: confirm orientation (arrows usually point to a direction or align with a notch), set it in, and twist until you feel it click.
   - Confirm lock: gently pull straight up. It should not lift out. If it does, debris is still in the seat.
   - Stop and call service if: the filter or its housing is cracked, the sump well has visible damage, or the filter refuses to lock after a careful re-clean.

2. GASKET (focus on the lower corners)
   - With the door open, run a finger along the entire gasket channel, slowly, especially the bottom-left and bottom-right corners where the gasket meets the tub floor. The gasket can pop out of its channel at the corners without showing a tear — it just looks slightly loose.
   - Wipe the gasket with a damp cloth. This removes any food film that could be holding the rubber a millimeter away from the door, and it lets you see the actual surface.
   - Look for: tears, hardening, cracking, flat spots, or any section that doesn't spring back when you press it.
   - Stop and call service if: you find a tear, crack, or visibly deformed section. A gasket replacement is a serviceable part on most models but it's worth a tech confirming the right part number.

3. LOADING
   - Slide the bottom rack in and out without the cycle running. It should roll all the way in without binding.
   - Check nothing tall is leaning against the gasket, the inner door, or the detergent dispenser. A single knife handle or bottle can hold the door a fraction open.
   - Confirm the detergent dispenser is fully clicked shut and the rinse-aid cap is closed.
   - Look at the front lip of the tub (the part the gasket presses against when the door closes). Water tracks along this surface, so any food or mineral buildup here can break the seal at the corners. Wipe it down.
   - Stop and call service if: the rack doesn't seat fully, the dispenser is broken, or you see the tub lip is bent/damaged.

4. DOOR LATCH
   - Close the door and confirm a clean, firm click. The latch should hold the door tight against the gasket with no give when you pull the handle.
   - The strike plate (the small metal hook on the tub frame the latch grabs) can loosen over time. If the door feels "softer" than usual or you can wiggle it when closed, the strike likely needs adjustment — that's a small screwdriver fix on most models, but if the latch itself is worn, it's a service call.
   - Stop and call service if: the latch is visibly damaged, the door springs open under gentle pull, or the strike plate is broken.

5. CONTROLLED TEST CYCLE (only if 1–4 all look fine)
   - Lay a dry towel flat on the floor flush with the front-right corner. Put a second towel at the front-left for comparison.
   - Run the shortest cycle your machine offers — rinse-only if it has one.
   - When the cycle ends, check both towels.
     - Front-right wet only, small amount: leak was door-side, revisit gasket/latch/loading.
     - Both front corners wet or whole-front wet: more than the filter — stop and call service.
     - Both towels dry: the filter reseat did it.
   - Stop and call service if: more than a few tablespoons reappear, water shows up during fill (not drain), water appears under the unit or in the cabinet, or the cycle sounds or behaves abnormally.

OVERALL STOP CONDITIONS — call service regardless of where you are in the sequence:
- Water anywhere other than the floor directly in front of the door.
- Water under the unit, in the cabinet, or back near the supply/drain.
- Filter won't seat, or sump shows damage.
- Any gasket tear, crack, or visibly deformed section.
- Door doesn't latch firmly.
- Leak reappears larger than the original ~2 tablespoons.
- Leak shows up during fill rather than at the end of the cycle.
- Burning smell, unusual noises, or steam where you shouldn't see it.

A couple of things NOT to do, to keep the diagnostic clean:
- Don't run a cycle as a test before step 1. If the filter genuinely isn't locked, a heavy wash phase can leak more substantially than the original 2 tbsp.
- Don't force the filter. Twist-lock assemblies turn by hand; forcing can crack the housing and turn a free fix into a service call.
- Don't ignore a "softer" door close. A latch that isn't fully compressing the gasket will keep producing corner puddles no matter what else you fix.

Most likely outcome, given your read: step 1 resolves it. If not, step 2 is the second-most-common culprit for a corner-specific puddle that size.

Acknowledged — diagnosed, fixed, verified dry through a full cycle with both supply and drain connections staying dry. That's a clean resolution: paper scrap removed, filter quarter-turn locked, cabinet dry. Treating it as resolved.

60% batch (18 cookies):
- Butter: 226 g → 136 g
- Granulated sugar: 100 g → 60 g
- All-purpose flour: 280 g → 168 g
- Egg: 1 large → 30 g of beaten egg (out of ~50 g)
- Orange zest: 2 oranges → 1 whole + part of a 2nd
- Salt: 3 g → 2 g
- Vanilla: 4 g → 2.5 g

Egg — portioning without making the dough wet:

The reason this is fiddly is butter-cookie dough has almost no moisture margin. Treat 30 g as a ceiling, not a target.

Beat one egg lightly in a small bowl (just combine yolk + white — don't whip air in). Weigh it — large eggs run 47-52 g without shell. Pour about 30 g into your mixing bowl and put the leftover ~20 g in a jar in the fridge for tomorrow's scramble.

Then add it in two pours:
- First, about 20 g into the creamed butter and sugar. Mix just until combined.
- Stream in the rest while mixing. Stop the moment the dough clumps when you press a bit between your fingers.
- Stopping at 22 g instead of 30 g is fine — cookies come out a touch more sandy and shortbread-like, which is what orange butter cookies usually are. If the dough still feels tacky at 30 g, dust your hands and the counter with a tablespoon of flour; do not add more egg.

Backup move if you'd rather avoid the partial-egg problem entirely: use just the yolk of one egg (~18 g) plus a teaspoon of cold water. Yolk carries the binding (fat + emulsifiers) with almost none of the water. A lot of old family cookie recipes effectively do this.

Zest — rounding 1.2 oranges:

Zest both whole oranges onto a plate before you juice anything. Don't bother weighing — orange-to-orange variation is huge and grams here are theater.

Practical rounding:
- Use 100% of orange #1's zest.
- Add about two-thirds of orange #2's zest, eyeballed.
- Toss the two together with your fingertips so the oils redistribute.
- Reserve the leftover bit of zest #2 in a small dish — sprinkle on top of the cookies before baking, or save for tomorrow's vinaigrette.

If Mom's card actually gives a gram amount of zest (some do — "15 g zest" is common), just multiply by 0.6 = 9 g. But for "zest of 2 oranges," the eyeball method is what you want. Nobody measures orange zest on a family cookie tray.

Saved a note that the house has 2 ext bibs (one with hose), kitchen + guest bath on ext walls, no sprinklers — for future freeze / plumber calls.

This is a real but moderate event — 6 hours at 27°F in Austin is enough to cause damage in the classic spots, not enough to justify winterizing. Here's the proportionate version.

TONIGHT BEFORE BED (~20–30 min)
  1. Disconnect the garden hose from the bib, drain it, store inside. The hose holding water against the closed valve is the #1 split-pipe source.
  2. Both hose bibs: open the outside valve a quarter turn so the line can drain. If you have inside shutoffs for them (most Austin homes don't), close those. Leave the outside valve dripping onto the ground or into a bucket — even a slow trickle prevents freezing and relieves pressure if ice does form.
  3. Kitchen + guest bath: open the cabinet doors below the sinks (and the guest bath toilet base cabinet if there is one). Goal is warm indoor air reaching the supply lines against the exterior wall.
  4. Drip the kitchen and guest bath faucets. Cold side is enough; both hot+cold if you want extra margin. Pencil-lead stream, not a full flow.
  5. Thermostat: hold steady at the daytime setpoint. Don't drop it to "away" overnight.
  6. Garage door fully closed if any plumbing runs through it.
  7. If the guest bath sits over an unheated space, leave its door open to the heated part of the house overnight.

NOT WORTH IT FOR A SINGLE NIGHT AT 27°F
  - Wrapping pipes / heat tape / foam sleeves
  - Draining the water heater
  - Space heater inside a cabinet (fire risk > benefit at 27°F / 6 hrs)
  - Antifreeze, irrigation shutdown

NEXT MORNING ONCE TEMPS PASS ~40°F
  1. Close the outside hose bibs. Run the kitchen and bath faucets fully open for ~30 sec, then back to normal. Watch the hose-bib walls and under both sinks for 10–15 min — any wet drywall, hissing, or moisture at supply connections is the thing you're looking for.
  2. Flush each toilet once. If one refills slowly or weakly, the supply line somewhere on an exterior wall is partly frozen; usually self-thaws within an hour. Keep that faucet open at a trickle — moving water thaws faster than standing. Don't apply direct heat to a frozen pipe.
  3. Walk the two exterior walls where the bibs sit: look for paint bubbles, bulges, or new water stains.

CALL A PLUMBER IF
  - Active water on a floor or wall that won't stop
  - A faucet that doesn't return to full flow after a few hours
  - Toilet that won't refill at all once the house is fully warm

Worth noting for next time: a quarter-turn frost-free hose bib (~$30 + install) makes bib #2 a non-event, since the actual valve seat sits inside the heated wall. Cheap, durable fix whenever you replace the bib anyway — not urgent for tonight.

Low-risk salvage sequence for a damp, overworked lower third on 140 lb cold-press:

1. Stop and let it dry fully. Bone dry, not "almost dry." Several hours minimum, overnight is safer. Do not use a hair dryer — uneven drying lifts pigment and warps the sheet. Airflow face-up is fine; a low fan helps if the room is humid.

2. Re-read it in raking light once it's dry. Mud often looks worse wet than dry, and some passages settle into something workable once the water leaves. Decide your targets from the dry painting, not the damp one.

3. Mask the figures and red boots before any further wet work. Tape or pin a scrap of paper over them. Anything you put on the grass will creep, and the cleanest part of the painting is the part you cannot afford to lose.

4. Negative shapes first, glazing second. Adding paint is lower-risk than re-wetting mud. Break the lower third into smaller shapes with hard edges — grass blades, weed stems, the edge of a path, a stone, the toe of a boot. Paint the lit planes around them in a cleaner green (sap green, or yellow ochre with a touch of phthalo green) and let the existing mud read as recessed shadow. The eye will take the painted shapes as form.

5. Glaze only where the mud still reads as a flat stain after step 4. Thin mix — pigment plus a lot of water, no thicker than tea. Two hard rules: the paper must be bone dry, and the glaze must not pool. If a bead forms, lift it with the tip of a dry brush before it dries there. A glaze over a damp sheet blooms and makes new mud.

6. Tape or stretch the sheet before step 5 if you can. Rewetting will reintroduce some cockling even on 140 lb, and a buckled sheet holds glaze unevenly.

7. Lift only as a last resort, and lift gently. If a passage is genuinely too dark and not just too gray, a single pass with a damp (not wet) soft natural-hair brush, then let it dry, then re-glaze. A stiff synthetic will scuff the cold-press and that damage cannot be undone. No scrubbing, ever.

8. Stop early. If the lower third reads as "field with form in it" rather than "field," you are done. Over-correcting a salvage is how salvage becomes a second mud.

One thing worth knowing before you commit to step 5: what greens did you use for the original wash? Granulating pigments (earths, viridian, raw umber mixes) take a glaze cleanly and respond well to step 4. Staining pigments (most phthalos, quinacridones) sit on top of the fiber and a glaze will not hide them — you would be relying on negative shapes alone. Knowing which kind of mud you made changes how much of the plan is actually available to you.

The picture you've described — single vomit, mostly grass and foam, soft belly, pink gums, alert, no diarrhea, no known exposure — is consistent with a dog who just ate more grass than his stomach could handle. That's the most likely explanation. Here's a conservative plan:

WATER (start ~1-2 hours after the vomit)
  - Withhold for the first hour or two so the stomach settles.
  - Then offer small amounts often: a few laps at a time, or ice cubes to lick, every 15-20 minutes for the next couple of hours.
  - Aim to gradually rebuild to normal access over 3-4 hours if he's keeping it down.
  - If he vomits the water back up, switch to ice chips only and call your vet if it happens twice.

FOOD (skip the next regular meal, ~6-8 hours)
  - When you reintroduce, go bland: boiled skinless chicken (no skin, no salt/oil) + plain white rice.
  - First portion: about 1/4 of his normal meal size. If that's held down for ~2 hours, offer another small portion.
  - Over 24 hours, build back to his normal portion size. Then mix his regular food back in over 2-3 days (25/50/75/100).
  - Skip treats, fatty food, dairy, and any "people food" today.

ACTIVITY
  - Quiet day. Short leashed potty breaks only. No fetch, no rough play, no off-leash yard time (so you can watch what he tries to chew).

WHAT TO LOG (a few notes on your phone is plenty)
  - Vomit episodes (time + what it looked like)
  - Stool — any diarrhea, blood, or black/tarry stool
  - Water intake and appetite
  - Energy level and gum color

CALL THE EMERGENCY VET (or nearest 24-hour ER) IF ANY OF THESE APPEAR
  - Repeated vomiting or unproductive retching — especially repeated dry-heaving with nothing coming up. In deep-chested dogs this can be the first sign of bloat/GDV and is a true emergency.
  - Vomited material becomes bloody, looks like coffee grounds, or turns bright yellow/green bile and keeps coming.
  - Belly becomes tense, hard, swollen, or he guards it when you touch it. "Prayer position" (front down, rear up, reluctant to move) is also a red flag.
  - Gums turn pale, white, bluish, or feel tacky/dry instead of slick and pink.
  - Energy drops past "a bit quiet" into real lethargy — won't lift his head, won't respond, can't be roused normally.
  - Tremors, wobbliness, seizures, or collapse.
  - Diarrhea with visible blood, or black/tarry stool.
  - He gets into anything suspicious while you're not watching (chocolate, xylitol, grapes/raisins, medications, a wrapper, a sock, etc.).
  - He can't keep even small sips of water down after 3-4 attempts.

CALL YOUR REGULAR VET (non-emergency) IF
  - Vomiting recurs later today or intermittently over the next few days.
  - Appetite hasn't returned to normal within 24-48 hours.
  - He keeps eating grass obsessively and vomiting.

One thing worth saying out loud: you're the best signal here. If his behavior shifts in a way that just feels wrong before any of the red flags above, call. Most clinics have a triage nurse line that can talk you through whether he needs to be seen now or can keep resting — that's a reasonable middle option if you're on the fence.

I'm not a vet and this is general guidance, not a diagnosis. But based on what you described — single grass vomit, normal gums, soft belly, alert, no other symptoms — monitoring at home for the next 6-12 hours is a reasonable call as long as the red flags above don't show up.

The headline sin: the analysis is conditional on a post-randomization event. The right denominator is all 1,920 randomized users, not the 1,105 who reached the eligible state.

If variant B changes who reaches that eligible state — and it plausibly does, otherwise why ship it — then comparing 28% vs 31% only among survivors biases the estimate in whatever direction the survivor mix shifts. With 815 users (42% of those randomized) silently dropped, the +3pp could easily be entirely an artifact.

What makes it worse:

  1. Covariate imbalance is doing you no favors. Secondary admins are 42% of treatment vs 27% of control. That's a 15pp gap on a covariate that almost certainly has a different setup-completion rate than primary admins. The conditional-on-eligible-state subset probably makes this imbalance sharper, not softer. Without stratification or covariate adjustment, the +3pp is confounded by the very mix you're conditioning on. Stratify by admin type, or regress on it, or report the ITT rate per arm.

  2. You are peeking at 8 of 14 planned observation days. Under your own pre-reg stability rule (n ≥ treatment, p < 0.01 on a second look before the next peek), this fails. p = .04 with <60% of planned exposure and no second-look confirmation is exactly the fake-first-sig pattern.

  3. No confidence interval. With this sample and this much covariate imbalance, the CI is wide and may cross zero. A point estimate without a CI is not a readout.

  4. Guardrails are absent. Support contacts and unsubscribe outcomes are not shown. If variant B drove +3pp setup completion at the cost of +20% support tickets or a measurable unsubscribe bump, this is a net-negative ship. Show the full guardrail table or don't ship.

  5. The ship scope overshoots the evidence. "Ship to all trial admins" extrapolates from a conditional subset analysis to the full randomized population, including the 815 users who never reached the eligible state and were never measured. What's the projected effect on them? You don't know, because they aren't in the analysis.

4. Late first integrations, day 8–14
   Of the 1,198 non-activators, count integration_setup_completed events on day 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14. The question: how many would-be day-7 activators just came back from break and finished setup on day 8 or 9? 5. Calendar overlay (the one you're most worried about)

SUMMARY: Kibo is mid-spectrum stressed (still treat-motivated, can briefly settle, no severe signs). Goal tonight is to reduce sound/light/vibration input, keep him oriented to you, and not reward panic. Vet if he crosses any line in the escalation section at the bottom.

INTERIOR SETUP
- Pick one small room, ideally interior (no exterior walls), windowless or with thick curtains. Bathroom, interior bedroom, or large closet work.
- Close all windows and doors. Draw blinds/curtains — flashes are part of the problem, not just the booms.
- Run a fan, white noise, low music, or a calm podcast continuously to mask bangs. Not loud — just constant.
- Lay blankets/towels on hard floors where he'll lie. Better traction, softer settle spot.
- If he uses a crate voluntarily, drape a blanket over three sides and leave the front open so he doesn't feel trapped.
- Keep lights dim. No strobing, no TV flashes.
- Water within reach. Don't worry about food if he skips it.

POTTY TRIPS
- Leash him before any door opens. No off-leash yard time tonight.
- Use a harness if you have one (less neck pressure if he lunges at a bang).
- Short leash, stay out only as long as he needs to pee/poop. No lingering walks, no porch sitting.
- Go during a quiet gap if you can; otherwise just go — don't wait him into a bladder accident.
- Bring high-value treats (kibble, cheese, hot dog). Treat calm behaviors (look at you, sniff, sit). Don't treat the act of pottying — he can't control that.

WHAT NOT TO DO
- Don't coo, soothe, or cuddle him while he's actively panicking — that rewards the panic. Just be near and act normal yourself.

- Don't leave him alone tonight, even if he seems fine right now. Fireworks can run for hours.
- Don't take him outside to "get used to it."
- Don't improvise any sedative — no Benadryl, melatonin, your own anxiety med, untried CBD, or anything from your own cabinet. Wrong dose, wrong drug, or paradoxical excitement is a real risk.
- Don't open windows to "let sound in evenly." That makes it worse.
- Don't change his diet or routine beyond the room swap.

ESCALATION → EMERGENCY VET (call the clinic while you're driving)

- Thick rope drool, can't swallow
- Vomiting or dry-heaving repeatedly, or diarrhea
- Trying to break out — biting at doors, windows, walls, or himself

- Panting so hard he can't settle even briefly, gums pale/gray/tacky
- Growling or snapping when touched, ears pinned, whale eye — even from a normally sweet dog. That's pain-or-panic, not bad behavior.

DIAGNOSE FIRST (do these before deciding):

  1. Plastic anchor that "spins in place" = hole is blown/oversized. Plastic expansion anchors cannot be trusted in a blown hole. Treat the right-bracket location as "no anchor here" going forward.
  2. You said dry, no cracking beyond the anchor hole — drywall is locally sound. (If you find crumbling gypsum, water staining, softness, or a hole > ~1", stop and call a handyman — skip the tree.)
  3. Estimate the load. A loaded linen shelf is roughly 15–30 lb on each bracket. Note this; you'll need it for the load test.
  4. Stud-finder pass along the shelf line. Studs are 16" on center, so there's a real chance one is close to the failed bracket.

DECISION TREE:

  IF a stud is within ~2–3" horizontally of the right bracket:
    → Remount into the stud. Strongest fix, cheapest parts.
       • Wood screw with ≥2" of thread into the stud (#8 or #10 × 2.5" is the usual).
       • Remount the LEFT bracket into the same stud (or its pair) at the same time. Don't leave the left bracket on its old plastic anchor — it's the same age and the same failure waiting to happen. Two-bracket redo on one stud is normal for a closet shelf.
       • The blown hole is cosmetic; spackle it if you care, otherwise ignore.

  ELSE IF drywall is sound but no stud is in reach (or shifting the whole shelf to reach a stud would look wrong):
    → Use a properly rated toggle, not plastic and not a self-drilling threaded anchor.
       • Snap-toggle (Toggler) or a traditional metal toggle.
       • Rated capacity ≥4× the per-bracket load as a working safety factor. For ~15 lb/brkt that's a toggle rated ≥60 lb.
       • Drill the toggle hole at a fresh spot nearby — don't try to reuse the blown hole. Patch the blown hole with spackle if it's visible.
       • Match the drill bit to the toggle's specified diameter (measure the wings, not the bolt).
       • Push the wings through, pull back snug against the back of the drywall, then tighten until firm — don't crush the drywall.

  ELSE (any of these is enough on its own):
    → Stop. Call a handyman.
       • Drywall is crumbling, soft, water-stained, or the hole > ~1".
       • Stud finder flags wiring/plumbing near where you'd drill and you don't know how to relocate.
       • You don't have a stud finder, the right bit, or the toggle.
       • The load is heavy or unknown. Linens are fine; tool storage, electronics, or heavy books on the same bracket are not, without a real anchor.

CONSERVATIVE LOAD TEST (after the repair, BEFORE linens go back):

  1. Empty shelf. Stick a piece of painter's tape on the wall directly under each bracket — any drift, rub, or drywall dust shows up on the tape.
  2. Load the right bracket first. Stack known weight (water jugs, books) to ~1.5× the linen weight you expect — ~25–40 lb hanging on that bracket for a linen shelf.
  3. Hold 10 minutes. Watch for tilt, anchor rotation, drywall dimple. Pull on the bracket with a firm hand tug.
  4. If clean: leave the weight in place for 24 hours. Anything that will fail in service will show creep in that window — a quick pull won't.
  5. After 24 h: recheck. Tape unmarked, bracket hasn't rotated, no drywall bulge or screw backout → good. Any of those → unload, reconsider.
  6. Reload linens in two stages: half the load for a day, then the rest. Don't go straight to a fully packed shelf.

ONE-LINE CALL: stud if one's in reach, properly rated toggle into sound drywall if not, handyman if the wall, the load, or the tools are questionable. 24-hour pull test at ~1.5× expected load before the towels go back, and redo the left bracket at the same time — it's the same anchor and the same age.

Good fix and good discipline — stud-finder + small pilot check before committing to the toggle split is exactly how that should go, and the staged towel load (not just hanging everything on at once) is what gives you actual confidence the brackets aren't creeping. Brackets flush after ~30 min of progressive load means the toggle is properly seated and the stud side is carrying its share.

The "no heavy bottles, period" rule on a closet shelf that size is also the right call regardless of the repair — drywall anchors and chemistry-bottle weight is just a bad match long-term even when everything is sound. If it ever bugs you, a second stud bracket on the right (after a fresh stud find across that span) is the permanent upgrade, but for now this is a clean outcome.

A workflow built around "touch each original once."

STAGE 1 — SETUP (15 min, do once)
- Block one uninterrupted 90-minute session. Pick a moment when the originals can sit out and you're not juggling other things.
- Work at a flat surface next to a window. Indirect daylight beats overhead lights and beats flash — flash causes glare on glossy prints.
- Put a dark cloth or matte board under your working area. It kills reflections and makes photo edges obvious for framing.
- Prop the phone about 12 inches above the surface — small tripod, stack of books, mug-and-shoebox rig, whatever you have. Stability is the goal, not height. Disable flash.
- Have two trays or areas ready: "to scan" and "done". Scanned photos never go back into the to-scan pile.

STAGE 2 — CAPTURE LOOP (~45 min for 36 photos)
For each photo, in this exact order, without setting it down between sides:
  1. Lay it face-up. Snap the front.
  2. Lift, flip once, lay face-down. Snap the back.
  3. Move it to the done pile.

That single-pass rule is what keeps you from rehandling 36 photos four times each. Do not read the backs during capture — just capture. Read later, from the screen.

NAMING (do it on the phone as you go, not after)
Use a numbering pad app or a sticky note so you can rename files immediately:
  2024-01-06_001_f.jpg   (front)
  2024-01-06_001_b.jpg   (back)
  ... through 036

- YYYY-MM-DD = date you scanned. Not the photo's date — you don't know it.
- NNN = sequence number, zero-padded so they sort in any file manager.
- _f / _b is the pairing mechanism. The two files share every character except that suffix, so a plain sort drops them next to each other.

If you want one app recommendation: Google PhotoScan is free, designed for exactly this, and handles glare from glossy prints better than the default camera. It also crops automatically. If you use the default camera instead, leave a little border and crop later in batch.

STAGE 3 — QUICK QC (5 min)
Glance at each pair on the phone:
  - Any handwriting on the back readable? Blurry → reshoot that one only.
  - Whole photo in frame?
  - No glare hiding a face?
Don't chase perfection. These are family copies, not an archive submission.

STAGE 4 — NOTE TRANSCRIPTION (15 min)
About 18 photos have notes. Two options — pick one and stick to it:
  - Leave the back images as-is. Mom can zoom on her screen.
  - Recommended for searchability: make one text file called Notes.txt, one block per photo, formatted like this:

        001_f — Lake Geneva, group of women in garden
        001_b — handwriting: "June 1952, Maman & cousins"
        002_f — ...

This is searchable forever and survives any future format change. Do the transcription from the screen, not by flipping originals again.

STAGE 5 — ONE BACKUP (5 min)
- One copy on your computer — the working folder.
- One copy in cloud auto-sync: Google Photos, iCloud, or Dropbox pointed at that folder. That's your off-site copy.
- Stop. Don't make a third. Two is the right number.

WHAT TO SKIP
- EXIF date editing, color correction, facial tagging. None was asked for; none is worth the time.
- Reading and re-reading backs during capture. Capture is capture; interpretation is later.
- Dragging out a flatbed scanner if it means a setup tax. Phone-on-a-stand is fine at this volume.

DELIVERABLE TO MOM
The folder (fronts, backs, Notes.txt) zipped and emailed, or a shared cloud link. She can keep the originals in the albums; she now has a digital copy that's searchable and survives the shoebox.

Total: ~90 minutes, one session, each original handled exactly once.

No shell/exec tool in this session, so I worked the math by hand (showing the steps so you can verify). Numbers are rounded to the cent — well below noise on a $127 bill.

BILLS
- Prior: 612 kWh, $91.64
- New:   914 kWh, $127.22
- Delta: +302 kWh (+49.4%), +$35.58 (+38.8%)

SHORT ANSWER
The math is clean. If the base charge and per-kWh rate on the bill are unchanged (you said they look unchanged), the two bills are consistent with exactly the same rate structure. All $35.58 of the jump is explained by 302 extra kWh at the same rate. No residual that would require a rate change, billing error, or mystery load.

THE CHECK
If rate = R per kWh and base charge = B (both fixed):
- Bill_old: B + 612·R = 91.64
- Bill_new: B + 914·R = 127.22

Subtract the two equations:
- (914 − 612)·R = 127.22 − 91.64
- 302·R = 35.58
- R ≈ $0.11782/kWh (about 11.78¢/kWh)

Then B from the old bill:
- B = 91.64 − 612·(0.11782) = 91.64 − 72.11 ≈ $19.54

Sanity check against the new bill:
- 914·(0.11782) + 19.54 = 107.69 + 19.54 = $127.23 ✓ (off by a penny from rounding)

So implied rate ≈ 11.78¢/kWh and base charge ≈ $19.54, and both bills fit that exactly.

ONE MORE SIGNAL (free)
The blended $/kWh (dollars ÷ kWh, which includes the base charge spread across usage) actually went DOWN:
- Prior: 91.64 / 612 ≈ $0.1497/kWh
- New:   127.22 / 914 ≈ $0.1392/kWh

If rates had gone up, this number would go up. Going down is exactly what you'd expect from a fixed base charge being diluted by more kWh. Rate-hike hypothesis is basically ruled out on its face.

DOES +302 kWh MAKE SENSE FOR WHAT YOU DESCRIBED?
+302 kWh over a ~30-day cycle = ~10 kWh/day of extra consumption. That's modest given what you said:
- One 1,500W space heater at 6 h/day ≈ 9 kWh/day by itself.
- Two heaters + longer runtime = easily 15–20 kWh/day.
- Electric resistance heat during a cold snap can add another 15–25 kWh/day.
- "Home more over the holidays" (lights, cooking, electronics, extra hot-water reheat) is typically 3–5 kWh/day.

You'd be at the low end of "expected" for that combination. The bill is not suspiciously high — it's actually slightly low for the story.

WHAT WOULD MAKE ME RE-CHECK (none of which apply based on your numbers)
- Per-kWh charge or base charge line item changed vs. last bill → recheck.
- New bill shows a different billing period length or "estimated" flag → recheck.
- $/kWh blended went UP vs. prior → would suggest a rate change.
- Same kWh roughly as last bill but much higher dollars → rate/estimate issue.

None of those flags are present here. You're safe to shrug it off as usage.

ONE SUGGESTION (optional)
If you want a single number to watch going forward, use the implied R ≈ 11.78¢/kWh. Next bill, compute (total − 19.54) / kWh and confirm it's still in the 11.5–12.0¢ range. If it drifts up by more than a cent, that's when to actually call the utility.

Working assumption: single-point rub + lever pulse once per revolution is the textbook signature of a slightly warped rotor — high spot pushing the pad back, pistons push back into the lever, you feel it as a pulse. Often a 5-min trueing at the shop, sometimes nothing. The question is severity. Here's the conservative decision:

RED FLAGS — WALK IT, DON'T RIDE
- Visible crack anywhere in the rotor (look edge-on against a dark background or sky)
- Rotor thickness at or below the stamped minimum — most rotors stamp 1.5 mm; if you don't have calipers, eyeball: a new Shimano rotor is ~1.8 mm, so anything that looks meaningfully thinner than a credit card edge is suspect
- Pad material gone — visible metal backing, or the wear-line/slotted indicator is flush with the pad surface
- Lever bottoms out at the bar or pulls almost to the bar before bite (hydraulic = air or leak; mechanical = stretched housing or cable issue)
- Hot rotor, smoke, acrid smell, shiny blue/brown glazing on the rotor face
- Any wet film around the caliper, hose, or lever (brake fluid, not water)
- Caliper body wiggles when you grab and push it — bolts should be rock solid
- Wheel hop when you spin it (separate from the rub — that's a true issue, also unsafe)
- The pulse is strong enough to startle you at speed or in traffic

YELLOW — RIDE DIRECT TO THE SHOP, AVOID DESCENTS
- Mild pulse you can feel but doesn't yank the bar
- Single-point rub that's been there a while and isn't worsening
- Lever still feels firm and bites high in the stroke
- Pads have plenty of meat, caliper tight, no fluid, no crack, rotor looks straight edge-on

DO THIS RIGHT NOW BEFORE YOU DECIDE
1. Spin the wheel slowly with the brake released. Watch the rotor pass the fixed pad — does it visibly deflect the pad/springs at one point (warp) or rub evenly across the arc (contamination or misaligned caliper)? Single point = your scenario.
2. Squeeze the lever hard. Firm = ok. Spongy or sink-to-bar = walk.
3. Look at the rotor edge-on against the sky. Visible side-to-side wobble = warped; a crack = walk.
4. Eyeball pad material. If you're unsure, measure with a phone photo — any sign of metal or the wear slot gone, walk.
5. Grab the caliper and try to rock it. Movement = walk.
6. Re-bed the brake at walking speed in an empty lot. If it grabs confidently and the pulse stays mild, you're in the yellow category.

PRACTICAL CALL FOR YOUR SCENARIO
Inflated tire, wheel seated, no rim damage, single-point rub, mild pulse, you stopped without incident = almost certainly a slightly warped rotor, not a failure. If your 5-minute parking-lot checks above come up clean, ride it straight to the shop, take the flattest route, skip any long downhills where heat builds, and skip the front brake only test on a hill — that's how people find out the front isn't there. If anything in the red-flag list shows up, walk it or call a pickup.

If you want, take a short phone video of the spinning rotor (side angle, well-lit) — most shops can tell from 10 seconds of video whether it's a quick true or a rotor replacement.

Here's where the data lands under our framework, and where I'd draw the lines.

## Verdict: descriptive association, yes. Bounded experiment proposal, yes. Ship language, no.

**1. The association is real-shaped but not strong.** Two-prop z-test on the 312-account read: z ≈ 1.91, two-sided p ≈ 0.057. That's right on the edge of the conventional sig line and well inside our pre-reg stab rule (n≥treatment + p<0.01 on a 2nd-look before the next peek). So the signal is suggestive, not load-bearing — useful for framing a question, not for declaring an answer.

**2. The risk views support the descriptive read.**
- Support contact: 11.4% (≥2 invites) vs 12.0% (<2 invites) — essentially flat, ~0.6 pp difference.
- Lifecycle unsubscribe: 2.5% vs 3.0% — also essentially flat, ~0.5 pp difference.

So the ≥2-invite cohort isn't behaving like a "happier in every way" cohort — they engage more on invites but they're not markedly less support-burden or less email-fatigued. That actually weakens the "healthier accounts invite more" alternative story a bit: the two risk dimensions you'd expect to differ if it were pure selection (support-touch heavy accounts tend to renew less, fatigue-heavy accounts tend to renew less) aren't moving much. Doesn't *prove* causality, but it keeps the hypothesis space honest rather than collapsing it.

**3. The causality caveat has to stay in the headline, not the footer.** Invite behavior was observed, not randomized. At minimum this could be: (a) invite-driven retention — the causal claim; (b) healthier accounts both invite and renew — selection; (c) an unobserved third thing (team size, admin engagement, growth stage) driving both — confounding. We can't separate these from the observational read.

**4. So what *can* you propose under the framework?** A bounded invite-reminder experiment is exactly the right move and stays clearly descriptive-association-to-design. Specifically:
- One sentence acknowledging the observational association (81.0% vs 70.0%, ~11 pp, p≈0.06, n=312).
- One sentence stating it's descriptive and confounded.
- One sentence proposing a *small, randomized* invite-reminder test as the next step to break the confounding — with explicit bounds (rollout %, duration, success metric, pre-reg stab criteria).
- No claim that invites *cause* renewal. No "ship," "roll out," "we should," or "customers who invite more renew more, so…" framing.

**5. Where I'd draw the line on language.**
- ✓ "The data is consistent with a positive association between ≥2 collaborator invites and renewal, which motivates a bounded randomized test."
- ✓ "Subject to pre-reg criteria (n≥treatment, p<0.01 on 2nd-look before next peek), we propose a randomized invite-reminder."
- ✗ "Customers who invite more teammates renew more, so we should…"
- ✗ "Sending more invites increases retention."
- ✗ Anything with "ship," "roll out to all," or "proven to drive" — those are ship words, and they don't survive the causality caveat.

PRE-START - confirm it's safe to hook up:
  - Jump pack indicator says it's charged
  - Transmission in Park (Neutral if manual), parking brake set
  - Ignition OFF, key out / fob out of range
  - Headlights, climate, radio, USB chargers, dome lights all OFF
  - Battery case not swollen, no wet residue, no rotten-egg smell
  - Skim the owner's manual jump-start section - some cars have a remote positive post under the hood; use it if you can find it

If the case is cracked, swollen, wet, or smells like sulfur, STOP - that battery is being replaced, not jumped.

CONNECTION ORDER (negative-ground, which is almost everything):
  1. RED (+) clamp to the DEAD battery's POSITIVE (+) terminal
  2. BLACK (-) clamp to clean unpainted metal on the engine block or chassis, away from the battery (a bracket, bolt head, or engine lift point). Don't clamp to the negative post - a spark right next to the battery can light any hydrogen gas that's vented.
  3. Power the jump pack on

STOP CONDITIONS - abort if you see or hear any of these, at any point:
  - Hissing, bubbling, or smoke from the battery
  - Rotten-egg smell that wasn't there before
  - Battery case swelling or deforming
  - Cables or clamps getting hot
  - Grinding or whining from the starter
  - Any fuel smell, smoke from the engine bay, or new warning lights
  - Burning smell from anywhere

CRANKING - this is the "don't hammer" rule:
  1. Crank for no more than 5-8 seconds
  2. If it doesn't catch, stop. Wait 2 full minutes before trying again (lets the pack and battery recover, lets any hydrogen dissipate).
  3. Maximum 3 attempts. If it hasn't started by then, continuing just overheats the starter motor and drains the pack. That itself is a result - the battery is too far gone (or something else is wrong), and more cranking won't tell you which.

DISCONNECTION - once the engine is running smoothly:
  1. Leave the jump pack connected ~30 seconds so the alternator starts charging through the cables (avoids a spike at the clamps)
  2. Turn the jump pack OFF
  3. Remove BLACK (-) ground clamp first
  4. Remove RED (+) clamp
  5. Leave the engine running - don't shut it off yet

POST-START - is it an old battery or the charging system?

The smallest test that separates them needs no tools:

Test 1: Drive ~20-30 minutes, then shut the engine off and immediately try to restart.
  - Restarts fine → alternator is putting charge in AND the battery is accepting it. The problem was just the old battery (March 2019 = ~5 years, past typical 3-5 yr life). Replace the battery this week.
  - Won't restart, or cranks weakly → either the alternator isn't charging or the battery can't hold what charge it got. Need Test 2 to tell which.

Test 2 (only if Test 1 is ambiguous): with the engine idling, measure voltage at the battery terminals - multimeter, or the voltmeter mode on many jump packs.
  - 13.8 - 14.7 V → alternator good. Battery won't hold a charge. Replace the battery.
  - Below ~13.5 V → alternator is the real problem (or a loose/corroded big cable from the alternator to the battery - check that first, it's a cheap fix).
  - Above ~14.8 V → regulator overcharging (uncommon, but it will cook a new battery too - replace the alternator).

If you don't own a multimeter, any auto parts store will do both the running-voltage check and a battery load-test free in the parking lot in about 2 minutes. They'll usually tell you straight up which one is bad.

Decision rule, plain language:
  - Jumps, then restarts after a drive → old battery, replace it
  - Jumps, but dies again after a drive, and running voltage is 13.8-14.7 V → battery won't hold a charge, replace it
  - Jumps, but dies again, and running voltage is low → alternator (or its cable), not the battery

Got it — clean resolution. 310 CCA against a 600-amp rating in January is solidly into replace territory (most shops use a ~60% threshold), so roadside's call was right, and the 14.2V charging plus three clean starts confirms the alternator and cabling aren't part of the picture. $198 is in line for a mobile replacement. Closed.

The order I'd use, lowest commitment to highest, with one test per step:

  1. Soften one edge first — the edge of the tree mass closest to the path-bend, on its near side. Damp brush, dry paper, light pass. This costs nothing on the surface (no pigment moves) and creates edge hierarchy: focal point keeps the crispest edges, supporting trees step back. Soften only one tree, then look from arm's length or further.

  Evaluate. Does the eye land on the bend first?

  2. If still flat: lift a bit of value, but only on the tree whose value is *closest* to the focal point's, not all three. Damp brush, soft tissue blot, no scrubbing. Two warnings on this step — lifted watercolor on dry paper tends to leave a slightly chalky, granular patch that's visible at raking light, and you can't put pigment back. So lift less than you think you need.

  Evaluate again. Have you created a hierarchy, or a ghost patch?

  3. If you still need help: add a narrow connecting shadow at the base of the trio, not across their middles. The point of this move is compositional, not value — it lets the three trees read as one supporting mass instead of three competitors. The shadow should be slightly darker than the trees but narrower, and ideally at a different edge quality than the masses themselves, so it doesn't add to the value fight. Only do this if the trees are close enough spatially that a base shadow reads as natural.

  4. If 1–3 didn't get you there, the painting is telling you the cast is wrong. Crop the weakest tree (or two) out. This is the one-way move, so it goes last.

The stop rule, in one line: stop as soon as the path-bend is the first thing your eye lands on from a normal viewing distance. Anything past that point is overwork, and watercolor rewards the version that quits earliest.

Two sub-rules that travel with the stop:
  - Don't stack fixes hoping each adds a little. Two partial fixes usually look like two problems.
  - If a step introduces its own visible issue (a chalky lift, a shadow that looks glued on), skip to the next step rather than correcting it. Corrections accumulate faster than you'd expect.

---

**Call: do not run. Don't even log it as a designed-but-never-started experiment.**

Owen's power math is right. 446/arm (892 total) is the correct figure for 72→80pp, two-sided α=0.05, 80% power. The eligible pool of 112 gives 56/arm, which is **12.6% of the required sample**. That yields ~17% power to detect an 8pp true lift — worse than a coin flip, and it makes the null result non-informative: a flat renewal curve here tells you nothing about whether the treatment works, only that the test can't see it.

MDE at n=56/arm, 80% power = ~22.5pp absolute. So the test as scoped can only "conclude" on a lift almost 3× the design's stated target.

---

**Why an invite-rate secondary won't rescue an underpowered renewal claim**

Three reasons, and they're structural, not rhetorical:

1. **The primary is still null-by-design.** A 17%-powered test gives you a null on renewal either way (effect present or absent). Treating "secondary moved" as a stand-in for "primary works" requires assuming invite-rate is a valid surrogate for 8-week renewal. It probably isn't — invites can move without changing retention, especially at the small effects we're talking about. You're shipping on a proxy while the primary is silent by construction.

2. **Asymmetric cost flips.** When you "rescue" with a faster signal, you're trading Type II error on the slow metric for Type I error on the fast one. Renewal is the outcome that pays the bills; invite-rate is a leading indicator. Letting the cheaper-to-measure signal override the expensive-to-measure one inverts the cost structure without telling you the cheap signal is actually predictive here.

3. **You lose the ability to learn from the test either way.** A powered null is informative (no effect, stop). An underpowered null is just silence. If we ship on the secondary and renewal stays flat in the next 8 weeks, we have no way to distinguish "secondary was a false rescue" from "treatment takes longer than the window." The whole point of the test is to make a decision; an unpowered primary + secondary rescue makes every future decision harder.

---

**Why first significance still needs a stabilization cohort**

This is the rule you've already locked in, and it matters more, not less, when the secondary is moving early:

- **Single-peek p<0.05 has a known false-positive tail under any look schedule.** Once you've peeked and seen green, your next observation is conditionally sampled on "winner-so-far." The second-look bar (n ≥ treatment-arm + p<0.01) is the structural guard against that. Drop it and you ship on noise that the first peek was guaranteed to produce sometimes.
- **"Fake first significance" is the specific failure mode.** A fast proxy will look significant at first peek because early-treatment accounts are the most engaged, the most recently activated, the most observed. That effect decays. The stabilization cohort is the only mechanism that forces you to wait through the decay.
- **Same metric, same direction, second look.** That's the minimum. A secondary metric moving does not satisfy "same metric." If you let secondary sig at first peek satisfy the bar, you've replaced a falsification rule with a vibes rule.

---

**What I'd actually do**

Three options, in order of preference:

1. **Re-scope the cohort.** The exclusions are doing a lot of work — 28 prior-exposed, 15 in active plans/support, 9 window-limited. The prior-exposed carve-out is the obvious lever; if there's a way to include them (different prompt variant, or accept invite-rate dilution and power for it), you roughly double eligible n. Still short of 446/arm, but directionally better than 56.

2. **Change the metric of record** to something the eligible pool can actually power — invite-rate within 4 weeks, if base rates support a detectable effect at n=112. Be explicit that the metric moved, not the renewal claim.

3. **Wait.** If the population ages in fast enough that 8 weeks of waiting gets you to ~446/arm, the design as written becomes runnable. Until then, the draft is parked, not "designed."

The terminal pre-authed $86.42 when the card was run, then settled the final amount when you left. The pending one will most likely drop on its own in 3-7 business days when the merchant doesn't capture it. Threshold — when it becomes a real duplicate:
  - Pending drops within ~7 business days, nothing else posts → not a duplicate, normal auth behavior, do nothing
