Headline: most likely a gritty or stiff chain link failing only where the chainline is worst (small cogs). Cleaning + lube will probably fix it. If it still skips after that, the cassette is likely worn — don't ride to work.

Safe order:

1. Inspect first, before cleaning, so you see wear on a dry surface.
   - Look at the two smallest cogs head-on. Teeth should be symmetric and rectangular. Hooked, asymmetric, or wave-shaped teeth = cassette is worn.
   - Run the chain backward by hand through a rag-wrapped section. Feel for a link that does not flex freely.
   - If you have a chain checker: 0.5% = replace soon; 0.75% = replace now and treat the cassette as suspect.
   - Spin the rear derailleur pulleys. Should turn freely with no crunch.

2. Clean.
   - Wipe the chain with a rag (pedal backward through a folded dry rag first — pulls off loose grit).
   - Degrease the chain and cassette with a brush. Avoid harsh solvents soaking the chain bushings; WD-40 is fine as a cleaner if followed by real lube.
   - Clean the derailleur pulleys.
   - Re-inspect: stiff link visible now? Hooked teeth?

3. Lubricate.
   - Damp commute = wet lube or all-conditions. One drop per roller, pedaling slowly backward. Wipe off all excess. Excess attracts grit, which is what got you here.

4. Low-load test on a quiet flat.
   - Shift into the smallest cog: light pedaling first, then medium, then firm.
   - Repeat on the second-smallest.
   - Ride through the rest of the cassette to confirm shifting is still crisp.
   - If anything skips again, stop.

Do NOT ride to work before a shop checks chain and cassette if any of these is true after the clean-and-lube:

- Skip recurs on either small cog under any load during the low-load test.
- Chain checker reads 0.75% or higher.
- Smallest cog teeth look hooked or wave-shaped on inspection.
- A link stays stiff after cleaning (frozen link — chain must be replaced, and check the cassette too).
- Any chain drop, jam, or new noise during the test.

Why the small-cog caution specifically: the worst-case outcome of a worn chain jumping on a small cog under hard pedaling is the chain wedging between cog and spokes, which locks the rear wheel. That's the failure mode the criteria are guarding against.

If the skip disappears after cleaning + lube, riding to work is fine — but book a chain/cassette check soon. A gritty unlubricated week accelerates wear; the smallest cogs go first because their teeth are thinnest.

Takeaway: clean and lube first; if the small-cog skip survives that, treat it as a worn drivetrain and walk or transit until a shop confirms chain and cassette together.

A loose study fits this palette well — ultramarine, burnt sienna, and quinacridone rose cover the whole porch if you stay disciplined about two-color mixes and let the postcard paper do the work for your brightest accents.

PALETTE (about 6 wells)

  Brick light — burnt sienna, very dilute. Just pigment and water, nothing else.
  Brick shadow — burnt sienna + a small amount of ultramarine. Stop adding blue the moment the warmth goes neutral; one drop too much and it's mud.
  Door green-gray — ultramarine + burnt sienna at roughly 2:1 (more blue than earth). That ratio gives a chromatic gray that leans cool. If it reads purple, add a speck more sienna. If it reads brown, more ultramarine. Muted green-gray does not need a third pigment.
  Door deeper — same mix, less water. No rose here. Rose mixed into an earth-gray goes chalky fast.
  Blue-violet shadow — ultramarine + a small amount of quinacridone rose. The rose shifts the blue toward violet without changing value much. Keep it transparent.
  Terracotta pot — quinacridone rose + burnt sienna. More rose on the lit side, more sienna in the shadow side. This is your cleanest accent; paint it last.

MUD-AVOIDANCE RULES

  Never mix all three pigments at once. Two at a time, always.
  If a puddle on the lid looks like wet cement, rinse it. It is done.
  Change rinse water often. Travel palettes have small wells and cross-contaminate quickly — a trace of ultramarine in your rose will gray the whole pot.
  "Muted" is not a license for mid-value gray everywhere. Let the brick and the door sit at different temperatures.

LAYERING (3 passes on the postcard)

Pass 1 — wet, dilute, shapes only
  Wash the brick wall in one dilute burnt-sienna pass, letting the tone vary slightly across the surface.
  While the brick is still damp, drop the blue-violet shadow mix into the deep shadow shapes only — don't flood the whole wall. Leave crisp paper-white for the brightest brick highlight and the pot highlight. Decide those shapes before the brush touches paper.
  Give the door a dilute cool-gray wash. Don't commit to its final color yet; you're just establishing value.

Pass 2 — dry, deepen only what needs it
  Once Pass 1 is bone dry, work the dappled shadow pattern back into the brick with the brick-shadow mix, in smaller controlled shapes rather than a wash.
  Now commit to the door: edge in with the green-gray mix on a slightly loaded brush. Edges stay crisp here because the paper is dry — that's how the door avoids muddying into the wall.
  Lay the terracotta mix onto the lit side of the pot, leaving a clean white sliver for highlight.

Pass 3 — final accents, dry, small brush
  One loaded stroke of pure burnt sienna on the brightest brick where sun hits. Don't dilute, don't blend.
  A touch of quinacridone rose straight from the well onto the lit edge of the pot if it needs more glow.
  Door hardware, shadow under the pot rim, and the deepest part of the porch shadow: blue-violet mix, undiluted, tiny brush.

KEEPING ACCENTS CLEAN

  The terracotta pot is the focal point. Paint the shadows next to it first, let them dry, then paint the pot — so no cool shadow creeps into the warm accent.
  The brightest brick highlight is paper-white. Never go back over it.
  The blue-violet mix only goes on at full strength in the deepest shadow; everywhere else, dilute it.

WHEN TO QUIT

  Loose study means soft edges are allowed. If a shadow shape softens into the brick, leave it.
  If the door starts looking like wet cement, you're overworking it. Step back. It is done.
  Three passes is the budget. A fourth pass is only for fixing one specific thing, never for general improvement.

Short answer: you can probably ride Monday if you keep it easy and stay out of the two smallest gears, but get it to a shop soon. What you're describing is the textbook signature of chain + cassette wear, not adjustment.

Why this pattern

The two smallest cogs wear fastest on any cassette. The chain crosses them at the steepest angle and articulates the most per pedal revolution, so chain stretch hits them first. As the chain elongates, the rollers ride up the tooth profile; smaller cogs have less tooth depth to absorb that, so skip shows up there first. Crisp shifting is the key clue — it rules out cable tension, B-screw, indexing, hanger alignment, and limit screws, all of which would surface as sloppy shifts before producing load skip.

A stiff chain link can mimic this, but usually shows up across more cogs and has a rhythmic feel (once per crank rev). Worth ruling out, but lower probability given the pattern.

Riding Monday

Skip on the smallest gears isn't catastrophic, but a sudden skip during a hard acceleration or out-of-saddle climb briefly unloads the drivetrain, and in extreme cases a chain can drop off a worn cog. To ride safely:

  - Stay in the middle of the cassette. Avoid the two smallest gears entirely.
  - No sprints, no standing climbs, no hills where you'd naturally reach for the small cogs.
  - If anything changes — skip spreads to other cogs, audible clicking under load, or the chain drops — stop riding.

If you can get to a shop before Monday, do. Chain + cassette replacement is a cheap, fast job.

What to ask the shop

1. Chain wear measurement. Most shops will use a chain checker (Park CC-3.2 or equivalent). Ask for the actual reading: ~0.5% = replace soon, 0.75%+ = replace now.
2. Cassette wear inspection — specifically the two smallest cogs. You're looking for a "shark-tooth" profile: tooth tips hooked or asymmetric instead of symmetric. Side-on view against a light is the quickest check. If those two cogs look like that, the cassette is done.
3. Stiff link check. Have them flex the chain link by link by hand. A non-articulating link can sometimes be freed by flexing it laterally; otherwise the chain needs replacing.
4. Chainring wear check. While the bike's on the stand, ask them to look at the chainring teeth for the same shark-tooth pattern. The big ring wears second-fastest and is often missed.
5. Compatibility confirmation. Chain speed must match cassette speed (10-speed chain on a 10-speed cassette, etc.). A mismatched chain mimics wear symptoms and is an easy thing to rule out.

Likely fix

Replace the chain. If the two smallest cogs show visible wear, replace the cassette at the same time — a new chain on worn cogs will skip, because the new chain's rollers don't seat in the worn tooth profile. Standard practice is to replace both together.

One caveat: if budget pushes you to replace only the chain now, the skipping will probably briefly disappear and then return within a few hundred miles because the new chain accelerates wear on the already-worn cogs. Not a shop mistake — a known compromise.

Compare the two options

  $68 chain-only:
    The mechanic's warning is correct, not a sales tactic. A new chain on worn
    cassette teeth (shark-fin shape from chain stretch) cannot seat properly
    and will skip on those cogs. The skip you feel is at the cassette, not the
    chain. A fresh chain alone will not fix it.

  $214 chain + cassette + adjustment + loaded test:
    This is the actual repair. Both worn parts are replaced together, the
    derailleur is re-tensioned (cable stretch changes with new chain length),
    and the loaded test is what proves the skip is gone under real pedaling
    force. The loaded test is the part that matters most for verification; a
    no-load spin in the stand can look fine and still skip when you stand on
    the pedals.

Is chain-only false economy here?

  Yes. Three reasons:
    1. It does not fix the symptom. You rely on the small cogs during the
       faster part of your commute, which is exactly where the skip lives.
       You'd pay $68 and still have the same problem.
    2. The $68 is not saved, it is spent on top of the eventual repair. The
       chain-only path costs $282 total ($68 now + $214 later) versus $214
       now, and you'd be without a working bike in between.
    3. A new chain on worn cogs can accelerate wear on the remaining (less
       worn) cogs because the chain and cassette want to mesh as a matched
       pair. You'd be trading a small amount of remaining cassette life for
       no functional gain.

  The one narrow case where chain-only is defensible: if you are willing to
  ride only in the middle cogs (easier cadence, no sprints) until the
  cassette is replaced days or a week later. That is a workaround, not a
  fix, and it does not match how you actually use the bike.

    moments of highest torque. That is the unsafe configuration.

    cassette cogs, ease off any acceleration in the small cogs, no

Low-stress plan for future truck mornings

The setup you already used is the right one — closed room, familiar items, white noise. What's worth adding is shifting from in-moment management to prevention, because barking at the front window is partly visual: he sees the truck → barks → truck keeps moving → he "wins" → behavior strengthens. Take the visual and the timing out of the equation.

Three things, in order of leverage:

1. Pre-position him before the truck is audible. Recycling truck arrival at Cherrywood is presumably on a fixed weekday schedule. Beat it by 5–10 minutes: he goes to the workroom with a high-value chew (frozen Kong, lick mat with peanut butter, bully stick — whatever he'll actually work on) before the truck is anywhere near the street. The goal is that he never practices the barking. The workroom becomes the place good things happen, not the place he gets sent when he's already aroused.

2. Close the front blinds the night before, or as part of morning routine. No visual access to the street → no trigger to bark at. Even on non-truck mornings, a partly-draw on street-facing windows during the first month or two of settling in tends to help with this class of reactivity.

3. Keep doing exactly what you did — but not as the first move. If timing's missed and he's already at the window, the calm workroom move with blanket + water + white noise is correct. No verbal correction, no pulling him off the window mid-bark; just walk him out. Note for your own tracking: how long did barking last, and how long until settled. You want the first number to fall week over week.

One thing worth flagging: Cherrywood's only been his home about a week. A single sharp reaction to a loud environmental trigger in a new place, with quick recovery and no post-event symptoms (no panting, shaking, food refusal, destruct), is normal settling-in territory, not a problem to solve yet. Give the pre-positioning routine two to three weeks before judging.

Signs that warrant a vet rather than more settling-in support

Rule out medical first. Pain and sensory issues (ears, teeth, eyes) can present as new reactivity in a new environment:

- Duration gets longer over time despite consistent management, not shorter
- New triggers that aren't environmental — reacting to being touched, to normal household sounds, to you standing up
- Self-injury during or after an episode: chewing paws/flanks raw, scratching hotspots, bumping into things
- Food refusal, weight change, or restlessness at night that wasn't there before
- Panting or drooling when it's not hot and he hasn't exercised
- Any of this showing up on non-truck mornings

Signs that warrant a behaviorist (after vet clears medical)

- Trigger generalizes: he starts reacting to other trucks, cars, joggers, the doorbell — the set of "things he notices" widens
- Settle time stops improving or extends past ~10 minutes
- Anticipation: pacing or whining 15+ minutes before the truck actually arrives
- Any growl, snap, or air-snap during the arousal — toward people, you included
- Recovery behaviors appear after events — even briefly: panting, shaking, hiding, refusing food
- After three or four weeks of consistent pre-positioning + blind management, no improvement at all

Both, urgently

- A bite (toward people or another dog) during an episode
- Self-harm during the episode (broken skin, bleeding)
- Panting or distress that doesn't resolve within an hour of the truck leaving

The headline: what you're describing is a common new-home reactivity pattern with quick recovery and no spillover into the rest of his day. The plan above is the right next move, and the escalation list is for if that plan doesn't bend the curve in a few weeks — not for today.

Lock eligibility at randomization. Keep all randomized accounts in primary analysis as assigned (ITT). Pre-exposure ineligibility is a label, not an exclusion. Run a small separately-randomized reserve (~30% of primary) that replaces only primary slots with a pre-exposure label; the reserve is reported as its own arm and never folded into the primary denominator.

WHY
Replacing within primary after randomization breaks comparability — replacements are non-random conditional on the very outcomes we're measuring. Dropping ineligibles shrinks the exposed cohort unevenly across weeks; ITT stays unbiased but the per-protocol read biases toward healthier accounts. The reserve approach preserves randomization integrity (ITT is clean) AND keeps exposure cadence stable for the secondary per-protocol read.

CUTS / LABELS (snapshot at randomization; updated at each exposure week)
  pre_exposure_churned       subscription cancelled before assigned start week
  pre_exposure_downgrade     ARR or seats dropped below retained-mid before assigned start week
  pre_exposure_sales_led     CSM or AE has a documented expansion conversation in flight before
                             the prompt would have been sent (CS calendar is source of truth)
  pre_exposure_other         primary contact departed, account on hold, etc.

These are reasons exposure didn't happen, not reasons to leave the analysis. Owen (readout shape) sets them from a snapshot at the start of each cohort's exposure week, using the lifecycle surface Ines exposes. Lock the snapshot date in the readout doc.

ANALYSIS
  1. Primary (ITT): assigned-treated vs assigned-control, including assigned-treated that became
     pre-exposure ineligible. Only unbiased comparison; this is the published read.
  2. Secondary (per-protocol / exposed): actually-exposed-treated vs assigned-control. Report with
     explicit caveat — selection bias possible if pre-exposure events correlate with expansion
     propensity.
  3. Reserve arm: separate table, separate narrative. Reserve exposures are not pooled into
     primary. Reserve arm exists so per-protocol cadence stays at ~5/week without breaking
     randomization.
  4. Commercial outcomes: expansion and contraction remain separate per Q1 audit. Do NOT collapse
     to "renewed."

RESERVE ACTIVATION TRIGGERS
  pre_exposure_churned and pre_exposure_downgrade  →  activate reserve (slot is genuinely
                                                       unusable for the prompt).
  pre_exposure_sales_led                            →  activate reserve (prompt would conflict
                                                       with an in-flight sales motion; better
                                                       to give the slot to an account that
                                                       would otherwise wait).
  pre_exposure_other                                →  Owen's call per case (some "other" reasons
                                                       may still allow exposure).

P / PRE-REG
  - Primary metric and direction locked at design. Same metric, same direction across the 6 weekly
    peeks.
  - n ≥ treatment floor before any "first sig" claim. With ITT, this is the assigned-treated count,
    which is robust to pre-exposure loss.
  - p < 0.01 on a 2nd-look before any next-peek action (vs declaring on a fake first-sig).
  - First pre-registered read: the July 8 first-exposure week.
  - Timing: randomize before July 8 (eligibility snapshot taken at randomization); exposures run
    July 8 week onward at 5/week (~6 weeks total).

OPEN QS FOR OWEN (readout shape owner)
  1. MDE for ITT at the planned allocation — does pre-exposure loss threaten per-protocol power
     enough to need a reserve, or does ITT alone carry?
  2. Reserve size — 30% (~10 accounts) vs tighter. CS capacity is 5/week, so reserve can't flow

  3. Where does sales_led_expansion_pre_exposure live — CS calendar export, or a field on the

  4. Is the per-protocol secondary worth the selection caveat on the 1-pager, or is ITT-only

  5. Treatment/control split inside the 30 — is the 5/week cap on treatment only, or on total

TAKEAWAY
Lock eligibility at randomization. Run ITT primary on the full randomized cohort. Label
pre-exposure events as pre_exposure_* flags and never exclude them from primary. Keep the
reserve as a separately-randomized, separately-reported arm. That preserves randomization

Good instinct stopping when something new shows up rather than grinding through. Based on what you described — gradual onset along the lateral ankle, no trauma, full weight-bearing, no swelling or bruising, mild stair pain (~2/10) — the picture is reassuring and consistent with early soft-tissue irritation (peroneal tendon region, lateral ligament/capsule, or sinus tarsi) rather than an acute structural injury. Conservative care is reasonable. Here is how I'd approach it.

Immediate self-care (next 24-72 hours)

- Relative rest from running, jumping, lateral cuts, and uneven terrain. Walking on flat ground is fine if it doesn't reproduce the ache.
- Ice 15-20 minutes, 2-3x/day, especially after any activity that bothers it or at the end of the day. Use a thin barrier between skin and ice pack.
- Compression: a light elastic ankle sleeve or compression sock can help with awareness/swelling prevention, but skip it if it pinches or increases discomfort.
- Elevation when sitting, especially end of day.
- Pain control: acetaminophen is fine as needed. NSAIDs (ibuprofen/naproxen) can help if there's clear soreness/inflammation, but short-course use only and only if you don't have a reason to avoid them (kidney issues, ulcers, bleeding risk, recent GI problems, etc.). If in doubt, default to acetaminophen.
- Avoid heat, deep massage, alcohol, and aggressive stretching in the first 48 hours — these can worsen acute inflammation.

Should you skip your next run

Yes. Treat this as a mandatory rest day at minimum, and plan to skip a second if walking or stairs still reproduce the ache at 48 hours. A common rule: you should be able to walk a mile briskly and descend stairs pain-free (or near it) before you jog again. If the ache has resolved by 48-72 hours, you can start the return progression below. If it has not, hold another few days; if it persists past 7-10 days of relative rest, see a clinician even without other red flags.

Return-to-running progression

Once stairs and brisk walking are pain-free:

1. First session back: walk-run on flat, soft surface (track, grass, treadmill). Example: 5-6 cycles of 2 min jog / 1 min walk, total ~15-20 min. Comfortable shoes you've already broken in.
2. Second session (next day or +1 rest day): 4 cycles of 4 min jog / 1 min walk.
3. Third session: continuous easy run ~20-25 min.
4. Then rebuild weekly mileage by roughly 10%, and avoid adding intensity (speed work, hills) until mileage is back to baseline.
5. Expect some mild awareness — that's OK. Sharp, reproducing, or post-run pain that lingers >24 hours is a signal to back off.

ful additions once pain-free

- Calf and peroneal strengthening: calf raises (straight knee and bent knee), single-leg balance on a folded towel for 30-60 seconds, banded eversion (resisted ankle outward press) — 2-3x/week.
- Footwear check: if your shoes are past ~300-500 miles, or you recently switched models, that's worth noting. Replace or rotate as needed.

Signs that justify prompt medical evaluation

See someone (primary care, sports med, urgent care, or ortho/PT depending on access) if any of the following:

- Inability to bear weight, or a limp that develops/worsens over 24-48 hours.
- Visible swelling, bruising, or deformity around the ankle or foot.
- Feeling of instability, the ankle "giving way," or a sense that something is loose or moving inside the joint.
- Pain at rest or pain that wakes you at night.
- Pain that is worsening rather than improving after 5-7 days of relative rest.
- Pain that recurs at the same point in every run or earlier in the run as you build back (pattern of progressive overload on an irritated structure).
- Numbness, tingling, color change (pale, blue, dusky), or coldness in the foot.
- Calf pain, swelling, warmth, or tenderness — particularly unilateral — given the rare but real risk of DVT after long runs.
- Locking, catching, or inability to fully dorsiflex/evert.
- Any skin break near the area with redness, warmth, or fever.

If none of those show up, the most likely outcome with disciplined early rest and a graded return is full recovery within 1-2 weeks. The biggest avoidable mistake here is running through a low-grade ache that then turns into a peroneal or lateral-ligament issue that takes months to settle.

What you're looking at:

  Provider billed $185 as a separate "post-procedure follow-up facility charge."
  Insurer denied it under N20 — "Service not payable with another service rendered on the same date." That means they treat it as bundled into another service from the same date (most often the procedure itself, or a same-day E/M). N20 is a bundling denial, not a patient-share denial — the insurer is saying the provider shouldn't have billed it as a separate line item.

Do you owe it right now? Not yet. Two questions decide that:

  1. In-network or out-of-network? If in-network, the provider's contract with the insurer almost always bars balance-billing on a service the plan adjudicated as not separately payable. N20 is exactly that kind of denial.
  2. What does the provider's "due May 23" notice actually rest on? Some offices auto-bill the patient whatever the insurer doesn't pay, without checking whether the denial was a true patient-share or a bundling denial.

What I'd do, in order:

  - Don't pay on May 23. Pay only what's undisputed (the $0 the insurer assigned, plus any other adjudicated lines).
  - Call provider billing. The line I want them to answer in writing: "Per your contract and my EOB showing N20, why is this billed to me as patient responsibility?" Specifically ask whether they billed with a -25 / -57 / -59 modifier, or whether they appealed the bundling denial.
  - In parallel, call insurer member services. Ask for written confirmation that this is a bundled service and that patient responsibility is $0. If the provider is in-network, ask them to enforce — they can often force a write-off.
  - If the provider won't budge and it's in-network, escalate to the insurer's formal complaint line and your state insurance commissioner. If it's out-of-network, the exposure is real but the dispute path is the same: get the bundling rationale in writing and challenge it.

Prep-Test Math — Grilled Chicken Plate
======================================

Inputs
- Raw case: 30 lb × $3.10/lb
- Cooked yield: 19.6 lb
- Portion: 7 oz cooked per plate
- Sides + garnish: $3.45 / prepared plate
- Menu price: $19.00

Step 1 — Cooked ounces available
  19.6 lb × 16 oz/lb = 313.6 oz

Step 2 — Complete plates (floor of 313.6 ÷ 7)
  313.6 ÷ 7 = 44.8  →  44 complete plates
  Chicken used: 44 × 7 = 308.0 oz

Step 3 — Leftover cooked ounces
  313.6 − 308.0 = 5.6 oz (not enough for a 45th 7-oz plate)
  In pounds: 5.6 ÷ 16 = 0.35 lb

Step 4 — Case cost (raw)
  30 × $3.10 = $93.00

Step 5 — Chicken cost per complete plate
  Allocate full case cost over the plates you can actually sell:
    $93.00 ÷ 44 = $2.1136 / plate  (≈ $2.11)

Step 6 — Total food cost per prepared plate
  Chicken ($2.1136) + Sides & garnish ($3.45) = $5.5636 / plate  (≈ $5.56)

Step 7 — Food-cost % at the $19 menu price
  $5.5636 ÷ $19.00 = 0.2928  →  29.28%

Step 8 — Gross contribution per plate (after food cost)
  $19.00 − $5.5636 = $13.4364 / plate  (≈ $13.44)

Step 9 — Gross contribution if all 44 complete plates sell
  44 × $13.4364 = $591.20
  Cross-check: 44 × $19.00 = $836.00 revenue
               − $93.00 chicken
               − 44 × $3.45 = $151.80 sides
               = $591.20  ✓

Summary Table
-------------
  Complete plates              44
  Leftover cooked chicken      5.6 oz (0.35 lb)
  Raw case cost                $93.00
  Chicken cost / plate         $2.11
  Sides & garnish / plate      $3.45
  Total food cost / plate      $5.56
  Food-cost % @ $19            29.28%
  Contribution / plate         $13.44
  Contribution, all 44 sold    $591.20

Notes / caveat
- Cooked yield came in at 19.6 / 30 = 65.33% — usable as your yield benchmark going forward.
- The 5.6 oz leftover can't be sold as a plate; it's either eaten by staff, lost, or held for next-day use. If you want to credit that value back, divide $93.00 by 44.8 instead of 44 and chicken drops to $2.0760/plate — but the realistic sellable math is the 44-plate version above.

Q: Who needs to confirm connector access?
A: A qualified admin (or anyone with authority to authenticate the supported connector). The applicant does not need to own the connector. This is separate from Helio admin proof.

Monday morning read

A "no pain / no stiffness / no swelling / no focal tenderness / stairs feel normal" picture, with the minute-16 faint ache absent overnight, is a clean response to Saturday's walk-jog. Overnight resolution without next-day reactivity is the pattern you want before the next step.

Read: green light to keep walking and cycling at comfortable volume this week, and to do one small progression on Saturday rather than a repeat.

This week, Monday through Friday

    Stay in the walk-and-cycle lane. No running, no plyometrics, no cutting or pivoting sports, no new uneven terrain. Walk and ride as normal as long as they stay comfortable; you do not need to push distance.
    
    Layer in the two things that protect you most once running volume starts climbing: calf strength and single-leg balance. Five to ten minutes, most days:
    
        Single-leg stand, eyes open then eyes closed, near a counter
        Double-leg calf raises progressing to single-leg
        Banded eversion with a light band — this is the specific motion that protects a healed lateral ankle
        Ankle alphabets or controlled dorsiflexion for ROM
    
    Keep daily steps normal. Pulling back too much this week actually hurts Saturday more than it helps.
    
    After longer walks or rides, if there is any mild unfamiliar sensation, ice 10 to 15 minutes and elevate. Not because something is wrong, but so any noise does not muddy Saturday's read.

Saturday: small progression, not a repeat

Best progression: keep the same jog interval and walk recovery, add one interval.

    If Saturday was, for example, 5 x (1 min jog / 2 min walk), go to 6 x (1 min jog / 2 min walk). Total session grows by about 3 minutes. That is the right size of step.
    
    Alternative if mid-session you feel unusually good after the warm-up walks: extend only the jog interval to 1:30, keep total intervals the same. Do not combine both progressions in the same session — pick one.

Track where any symptom shows up in time. Last week's "minute 16" marker is useful. The goal this Saturday is either "no symptom at all" or "symptom appears later in the session than last week." Earlier than minute 16, or any new symptom onset, is a yellow flag.

Stop criteria during the session

Stop the session and end the workout if any of these appear:

    Pain that changes how you move, even if the number is low. Limp, hitch, guarding, shorter stride on the jog side — that is the signal, not the pain score.
    
    Sharp or catching pain anywhere in the ankle on push-off or landing.
    
    Feeling of instability, looseness, or "almost gave way," whether or not there is pain.
    
    Pain that does not settle within one to two walk intervals.
    
    Visible swelling during the session, or the shoe feeling tighter on that side than when you started.
    
    Pain that climbs during a jog interval rather than staying stable or fading after warm-up.

You can keep going through:

    Mild diffuse warmth or awareness that does not change mechanics and resolves inside a minute.
    
    A 2/10 or less sensation during the first 30 to 60 seconds of the first jog interval that fades as you settle in — normal warm-up perception, not an injury signal.

Evaluation criteria, before and after

Before the session, the ankle should meet all of these, or you walk only and do not progress:

    No swelling visible compared to the other side.
    
    Full comfortable dorsiflexion equal to the other side, no pinch at the front of the ankle.
    
    Stair descent feels the same on both sides.
    
    No stiffness lasting more than about 5 minutes after you start walking.

After the session, expect all of these to be true by the next morning:

    No pain, stiffness, swelling, or focal tenderness — same list you wrote this morning.
    
    Any in-session sensation resolves within roughly 24 hours.
    
    Stairs and walking feel normal the next day.

If the next-morning picture looks anything like the concerns in your note, you repeat last Saturday's dose next Saturday rather than progressing again. One step forward, two checks back is the right cadence.

When to loop in your PT or clinician

    Any of the stop-criteria triggers actually fire, even if they recover quickly.
    
    Two consecutive sessions show the same symptom at the same time point — a plateau, not noise.
    
    Any instability event, or a sense the ankle "almost went" on uneven ground or stairs.
    
    Swelling that shows up after sessions even when pain does not, or pain that lingers into Tuesday or Wednesday.

Quick summary

    Mon to Fri: walking and cycling as comfortable, add calf strength and single-leg balance, no running.
    
    Saturday: small progression — add one interval at the same jog-to-walk ratio, do not also extend the jog length.
    
    Stop on any pain that changes your gait, any instability, pain that does not resolve in a walk interval, in-session swelling, or a shoe that feels tighter.
    
    Pass to the next session only if next morning matches today's morning: full baseline, no recurrence of the minute-16 type sensation.

Caveat: this is general rehab logic, not a substitute for your PT's or physician's plan. If your clinician gave you a specific walk-jog protocol, follow their numbers and use this as a way to think about progression and stop rules. If anything in your morning picture tomorrow or Wednesday deviates from today's baseline, the conservative move is to hold the line and check in before Saturday.

Safe internal temperature

165°F is the USDA safe minimum for all poultry. For thighs specifically, pulling at 175–185°F is worth considering — dark meat has more connective tissue that softens past 165, so going a bit higher gives noticeably more tender results without compromising safety. Either works; 175+ is just better for thighs.

Thermometer placement

Insert into the thickest part of the thigh. If the thighs are bone-in, push the tip in until it sits in a clear pocket of meat without touching bone. Bone conducts heat faster than meat and will give a falsely high reading, making the chicken look done before it actually is. For boneless thighs, just go into the center of the thickest portion.

Cross-contamination with the marinade

The 2 Tbsp you set aside before the chicken went in is uncontaminated — it's safe to brush on as-is during the last few minutes of cooking.

For everything that touched the raw chicken:
- Use a clean brush or spoon when applying the reserved sauce. Don't use the same utensil that stirred or handled the raw chicken.
- Don't put the cooked thighs back on the plate or tray that held the raw chicken.
- Don't combine the post-thigh marinade with the reserved portion or serve it on the side unless you boil it first — bring it to a full rolling boil for at least 1 minute.
- Wash hands, tongs, and any cutting board or counter that touched the raw chicken or its marinade with hot soapy water before they touch cooked food or anything served raw.

Have a good dinner.

A cautious next-week shape, with the rules you asked for:

NEXT WEEK — three sessions, ~48 h apart (e.g. Mon / Wed / Fri or Tue / Thu / Sat)

Session 1: repeat today's pattern verbatim
  12 min alternating 2 min walk / 1 min easy jog
  12 min alternating 1 min walk / 1 min easy jog
  Total 24 min, ~10 min jogging
  Purpose: confirm the level reproduces on a second day before adding anything.

Session 2: extend duration, hold the ratios
  12 min of 2:1 walk:jog, then 16 min of 1:1 walk:jog
  Total 28 min, ~12 min jogging
  Same route, same shoes, same warm-up.

Session 3: small further extension
  12 min of 2:1 walk:jog, then 18 min of 1:1 walk:jog
  Total 30 min, ~13 min jogging
  Only do this if Sessions 1 and 2 were both fully clean.

REPEAT-A-LEVEL RULE
  Repeat the same session plan before progressing when any of the following is true:
    — any symptoms during the session or in the 24 h after (even mild)
    — effort felt ≥7/10 rather than conversational / easy
    — you missed more than one session in the planned week
    — sleep was poor, fatigue was high, or you felt "off" but not strictly painful
  One repeat is fine. Two repeats in a row means hold that level for the full week, not advance.

STOP RULE (during or after a session)
  End the session and don't finish the planned work when any of these appears:
    — pain that changes your gait, even briefly
    — pain ≥3/10 that doesn't settle within 2 minutes of walking
    — sharp, catching, locking, or "giving way" sensations
    — new swelling, limp, or visible asymmetry developing during the run
    — lightheadedness, chest symptoms, or unusual breathlessness
    — pain that wakes you or persists >24 h after the session
  If you stop, the next session repeats the LAST FULLY CLEAN session, not the one you stopped.

SEEK EVALUATION (don't self-progress through these)
  Contact your clinician or PT within 24–48 h, sooner if escalating:
    — symptoms return at the same or lower load than before (regression)
    — pain is present at rest or with normal daily walking, not just running
    — pain ≥4/10, or any pain that alters your gait
    — new swelling, bruising, clicking, locking, instability, or weakness
    — numbness, tingling, or pain that radiates
    — symptoms that don't fully resolve within 48 h of a session
    — three sessions in a row where you had to stop or repeat the same level

GROUND RULES WHILE YOU BUILD
    — at least 48 h between sessions until you've held a level cleanly for a week
    — easy effort only; you should be able to talk in short sentences
    — same route, surface, and shoes while you're establishing a trend — don't add hills, trail, or new footwear in the same week as a progression
    — 5–10 min walking warm-up and cool-down each session
    — continuous 4-mile running is still several weeks out from this base. A reasonable return path is roughly: weeks 1–2 intervals building to ~30 min, weeks 3–4 extend the jog blocks (e.g. 3:1, then 5:1 walk:jog), weeks 5–6 continuous 15–20 min easy run, then build mileage at no more than ~10% per week

General return-to-load guidance, not a substitute for a treating clinician — if you're under a PT or have a specific diagnosis / post-op protocol, that overrides the defaults above.

SESAME-ALLERGY MEAL — PREP AND SERVICE PLAN

SUMMARY

Leaving off the toasted-sesame garnish does not make this dish safe for the guest. The soy-ginger glaze itself contains sesame oil, and sesame allergy carries real anaphylaxis risk from trace exposure (shared surfaces, shared utensils, airborne particles from toasting, shared fryer oil, hands that have handled sesame that day). The allergy meal needs to be a separately prepped dish on a sesame-free prep track, not a modified version of the standard entrée. The two reconfirmation items that gate everything else are: (1) the guest's severity and comfort level, and (2) the chef-owner's honest read on whether they can deliver a true sesame-free preparation or should swap to a fully different dish.


A. WHAT CANNOT BE GUARANTEED BY JUST LEAVING OFF THE GARNISH

  - Sesame oil is IN the glaze, not only on top. Toasted sesame oil is a concentrated allergen; even refined sesame oil retains protein that triggers reactions.
  - Cross-contact from prep surfaces, even when wiped (sanitize is not the same as wipe).
  - Cross-contact from shared utensils, even after a standard dishwasher cycle.
  - Airborne particles from toasting sesame seeds in the kitchen settling on nearby surfaces and plates.
  - Shared fryer oil if sesame-coated items are fried.
  - Hands that have handled sesame earlier in the service.
  - Shared plating pass.
  Net: the standard entrée is a sesame dish, not a sesame-garnished dish. Removing garnish does not change that.


B. RECONFIRM WITH THE GUEST (before finalizing the menu)

  - Severity: any history of anaphylaxis? Do they carry an EpiPen?
  - Specific triggers: do they react to sesame oil specifically? Any cross-reactive allergies (mustard, peanuts, tree nuts)?
  - What they have safely eaten at restaurants before — establishes a working baseline.
  - Comfort with the kitchen: do they want a clearly separate meal, or are they OK with the chef's modified-dish approach?
  - Will they be carrying emergency medication on the night?
  - Direct contact with chef-owner preferred, or going through Sam?
  - Confirm the guest knows sesame oil is in the standard glaze, so they are not surprised if the modified dish looks or tastes different.


C. RECONFIRM WITH THE CHEF-OWNER (before finalizing the menu)

  - Has the kitchen handled sesame-allergic guests before — what is their standing protocol?
  - Separate prep area, or single line with full sanitize between?
  - Can they produce a TRUE sesame-free version of the entrée (different oil, different aromatics, no sesame used in that dish at all)? Or is the chef-owner's recommendation a fully different dish?
  - What oils are in kitchen rotation — toasted sesame oil used for any other dish same day?
  - Other sesame-containing items being prepped same day (hummus, tahini, Asian sauces, certain breads, certain pastries)?
  - Fryer: shared with anything sesame-coated that day?
  - Plating pass: separate or shared?
  - Chef-owner's own threshold — at what risk level do they say "different dish" instead of "modified same dish"?
  - Serveware: disposable or dedicated for the allergy meal?
  Default rule: if the chef-owner has any doubt, default to a fully different dish, not a modified one.


D. PREP SEQUENCE (conservative)

  1. Allergy meal prepped FIRST in the service window, or in a fully separated prep window when no sesame is in the kitchen.
  2. Dedicated cutting board, knife, pan, tongs, spoons — never previously touched sesame. New or fully sanitized.
  3. Work area cleaned AND sanitized (true sanitize step, not just wipe-down).
  4. Disposable aluminum or deli containers for the allergy meal, or thoroughly washed dedicated containers.
  5. Clear label on the container AND on the finished plate: "ALLERGY: SESAME — DO NOT CROSS-CONTACT."
  6. Chef-owner personally inspects the finished plate before it leaves the kitchen.
  7. Garnish for that plate is sesame-free (scallion, herbs, lime zest, microgreens) — not just "no sesame seeds."


E. SERVICE SEQUENCE

  1. Allergy plate covered or plated last, on a separate pass if possible.
  2. Server briefed on the allergy, the dish contents, and the rule: no sesame-containing sauces or sides on or near the plate.
  3. Server confirms with the guest visually when serving (label check, plate contents check).
  4. Chef-owner personally delivers OR personally signs off on delivery before it leaves the pass.
  5. Seat the guest near an exit, not near the kitchen pass, in case of reaction.
  6. Sam and chef-owner both should know where the EpiPen is and who is calling 911 if needed.


F. ITEMS WORTH PUTTING IN WRITING BEFORE JUNE 1

  - The exact modified or alternative dish the chef-owner will produce for the allergy guest (ingredients, prep, garnish).
  - The chef-owner's sign-off that the dish is safe per their professional judgment.
  - The guest's acknowledgment of the plan.
  - Sam's standing rule: if the chef-owner has any doubt at any point on the day, the allergy meal becomes a fully different dish, not a modified one.


Two practical asks of Sam right now: (1) loop the guest in early so severity and comfort drive the dish choice, not the dish choice driving them, and (2) ask the chef-owner directly whether they want to modify the standard entrée or swap to a different dish — that answer sets the rest of the plan.

RULE 1 — SAME-DAY FULL REFUND  (HS-011, HS-019, HS-027, HS-046)

  Rule. Drop any invoice.paid where cash_collected > 0 AND a full_refund fires with refund_amount == cash_collected AND (refund_timestamp - paid_timestamp) < 24h.

  Why. Same-day full refund = no durable cash-in. The likely paths are accidental card re-run, dispute auto-resolved as friendly fraud, or chargeback-then-return. In every path the customer never actually retained the payment, so labeling them "first-paid" is false.

RULE 2 — ZERO-CASH / CREDIT-APPLIED  (HS-031, HS-044)

  Rule. Drop any invoice.paid where amount_due == 0 AND cash_collected == 0 AND credit_applied > 0.

  Why. amount_due = 0 means there is no new revenue event. credit_applied is a draw on existing liability (refund credit, promo credit, account credit) — balance-sheet activity, not new acquisition. Counting these as first-paid conflates the two.

  Effect. -2 from customer-level numerator. The $1,100 of credit-applied ($500+$600) is not first-paid revenue.

DIAGNOSIS

The mock buckets each row by raw status string, treating the event log as a flat status table. But this is a state machine: provisional_* transitions to final_*. Each entity should sit in exactly one current bucket at any moment — the bucket corresponding to its MOST RECENT event, not to every event it has ever emitted.

That is why the two flagged rows are wrong:

  A-117: 08:03 provisional_pending → 08:22 final_assisted.
    Latest = final_assisted. The 08:03 row is stale and should not place A-117 in "pending."

  A-219: 10:01 provisional_admitted → 10:19 final_ineligible.
    Latest = final_ineligible. Two compounding errors:
      (a) the 10:01 row leaks A-219 into "admitted" when its current state is ineligible;
      (b) the provisional_admitted → final_ineligible transition is a PROVISIONAL-TO-FINAL REVERSAL, which the side-by-side display silently flattens into two unrelated facts instead of flagging.

A-204 (single final_admitted row) is correctly bucketed — the bug only surfaces for entities with ≥1 provisional AND ≥1 final row, where naive aggregation double-counts.

A second hidden issue: this view has no place for entities still stuck in provisional. Per Ines's 24h abandoned-intake definition (latest row is provisional_*, no final row, age > 24h), those need an explicit bucket or they vanish entirely once you suppress stale provisional rows.


CORRECTED LOGIC (raw event table untouched; rebuild the read path)

(1) Current-state view — one row per entity, bucketed by latest event only.

  Rule: an entity's current bucket = status on the row where (entity_id, timestamp) = MAX(timestamp) for that entity.

  Applied to the mock:
    A-117 → final_assisted
    A-204 → final_admitted
    A-219 → final_ineligible

  Buckets in this view: ONLY final_* values (final_admitted, final_assisted, final_ineligible). provisional_* disappears from the current-state axis — correct, because once a final row exists the provisional state is no longer current.

  Sketch:
    SELECT entity_id,
           (SELECT status FROM events e2
            WHERE e2.entity_id = e1.entity_id
            ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 1) AS current_status
    FROM events e1
    GROUP BY entity_id;

  Caveat to document for Owen: this is "as of latest event," not "as of clock now." If clock-now semantics matter, left-join entity_id to a now() anchor and flag entities whose latest event is >N hours old separately.

(2) Exception view — additive, never mixed into the current-state axis.

  Three exception types, each its own row in its own view. Do not collapse them into a status column; the value is in the contradiction.

  (a) Provisional-to-final reversal. Entity has at least one provisional_* row AND a later final_* row whose route ≠ the provisional route.
        A-219 matches: provisional_admitted → final_ineligible.
        Materialize as: (entity_id, provisional_status, provisional_ts, final_status, final_ts).
        This is the reversal Owen's current mock hides. Surface it; it's the highest-signal exception in his dataset.

  (b) Abandoned provisional (Ines cohort). Entity's latest row is provisional_* AND no final_* row exists for that entity AND (clock_now - latest_ts) > 24h.
        Sketch:
          SELECT entity_id, MAX(timestamp) AS stuck_since, status
          FROM events
          GROUP BY entity_id
          HAVING status LIKE 'provisional_%'
             AND MAX(timestamp) < clock_now - INTERVAL '24 hours';
        In the May 29 mock, none of A-117 / A-204 / A-219 qualifies (all resolved same-day) — but this is the bucket that will populate once the dashboard extends past day-0.

  (c) Provisional-then-final-of-same-route-but-with-gap. Entity has a final_* row whose route MATCHES its last provisional_* route but with a long gap (>X minutes, configurable). Suggests delayed routing rather than reversal; usually a workflow latency signal, not a routing error. Optional but worth defining now so it doesn't get conflated with (a).

  Crucially: do NOT fold exception (a) into the current-state view. A-219 belongs in "final_ineligible" on the current-state axis AND in the reversal-exception view simultaneously — that's the correct representation, not a contradiction.


WHAT TO TELL OWEN

The bug is bucketing by raw status instead of by latest-status-per-entity. Fix the read path, not the source: keep all five rows in events, derive current_status via MAX(timestamp) per entity_id, and add a second derived view for reversal/abandoned exceptions. A-117 and A-219 stop double-bucketing, and the provisional_admitted → final_ineligible flip becomes visible as a named exception instead of two silent rows.

Recommendation: repeat the same dose for one more session before progressing, then advance cautiously if it stays clean.

Reasoning tied to your specific findings:

The faint delayed outer-ankle ache, 1/10, on stairs only, resolving within an hour, with no swelling, limp, instability, bruising, or focal tenderness, reads as a mild tissue-load signal rather than a structural warning. The session itself was pain-free, and going from 24 to 30 minutes with the same 4:2 walk-jog ratio is roughly a 25% volume jump in a single step, which sits on the aggressive end of a return-to-run progression. That is why the right move is to hold and confirm tolerance at this dose, rather than stack another increment on top or step all the way back to the 24-minute session (which was itself clean and would discard useful information).

Concrete plan:
- Next session, 48 to 72 hours later: repeat the exact 30-minute dose on flat ground in the same shoes — 6 minutes walking, 3 rounds of 4 minutes easy jogging and 2 minutes walking, 6 minutes walking to cool down.
- If that session is pain-free during it and for the following 24 hours, the next session after that can take a small step up — for example one extra jogging minute per interval, or about 5 more total minutes, not both at once.
- If it reproduces the same delayed outer-ankle ache, step back to the prior 24-minute walk-jog dose for one or two sessions, add peroneal and hip-stability work, then re-attempt the 30-minute dose.
- If any of the thresholds below trips, pause and arrange an evaluation before the next progression.

Thresholds that should prompt evaluation (any one is enough):
- Pain during the session itself, not only after.
- Pain still present at the 24-hour mark, or recurring unprompted the next day.
- Pain that worsens or recurs on a repeat of the same dose.
- Any swelling, bruising, warmth, or visible change around the ankle.
- Mechanical signs — catching, locking, clicking with giving-way, or a sense of instability.
- A limp or any subtle gait change, even if you can "walk it off."
- Pain at 3/10 or above, or any pain that changes how you walk.
- Focal bony or tendon-insertion tenderness you can point to with one finger.
- Pain at rest, or pain that wakes you from sleep.
- Numbness, tingling, or color change in the foot.
- Two failed attempts to repeat the same dose without the delayed ache returning.

This is reasoning from the pattern you described, not a substitute for an in-person exam — but for the specific picture you've reported, repeat-and-confirm is the load-appropriate next step, and the list above is the line at which that calculus flips.

For the corner that intrudes 1/8 inch:

The least-invasive option is to widen the mat opening on that corner by about 1/4 inch (the damage plus a small buffer). It is a frame-only fix that leaves the painting completely untouched and the disturbed fibers sit behind the mat. Under mat and glass, the texture irregularity will be near-invisible anyway, and the wash itself is intact, so the image is not compromised.

If you want to do something on the paper itself:

  If fibers are standing up: lay a sheet of glassine or clean tracing paper over the area and gently press the lifted fibers back down with a bone folder or the back of a spoon. Light pressure, no rubbing.

  If there is any sticky residue (sometimes shows as a faint sheen on cold-press): lightly dab with a kneaded eraser, kneaded until soft, rolling it across the residue rather than rubbing. Test on the margin first.

  Do not rewet the area. Water risks pulling more pigment from the edge of the wash and swelling the lifted fibers so they cockle.

Avoid localized touch-up paint. A 1/8-inch re-painted edge will almost always read as a repair, and on a wash it is very hard to blend.

For future sheets, in rough order of impact:

  1.  Pull tape while the paper is still slightly damp, right after the last wash has dried to the touch but the sheet still feels cool. Fully dry cold-press is when the adhesive locks into the paper's tooth. This single change prevents most of the lifting you just saw.

  2.  Pull at a low angle, back along the line of contact (close to 180 degrees), slowly and steadily. Pulling straight up at 90 degrees is what tears fibers.

  3.  If you do need to pull from dry paper, switch to a tape with a less aggressive adhesive: drafting tape such as 3M 2090 Long-Mask, or 3M / ScotchBlue "Delicate Surface" painter's tape. Even lower-tack options exist in the form of gum-based yellow masking tapes (Japanese washi "hoshi" tape, or the traditional Kleen-Wrap), which are designed for water media and release cleanly from cold-press.

  4.  Pre-test any new tape on a scrap of the same paper before committing a sheet.

  5.  If tape has been sitting on fully dry paper and you suspect it will grab, warm it briefly with a hair dryer on low, just enough to soften the adhesive, then pull low and slow.

  6.  For straight borders, many watercolorists skip tape entirely. Painting to a T-square edge, or freehand with a rigger brush, or using liquid masking fluid only where shapes demand it, avoids the failure mode altogether. Tape on cold-press is one of the more common ways to lose a sheet.

I'm not a vet, so treat this as practical triage, not a diagnosis. A small piece of fatty skin in a dog who otherwise seems comfortable is usually a watch-and-wait situation, with the main concern being pancreatitis (delayed onset, sometimes 12–48 hours later). Here's how I'd handle tonight:

TONIGHT
- Keep Kibo in a quiet, low-stress area where you can watch him. Dim lights, no rowdy visitors.
- Note the time of the single vomit (about 8:50 pm if your message was 8:30) so you can talk concretely with a vet if anything changes.
- Skip dinner tonight. A short fast (about 8–12 hours, then reintroduce bland food) is gentler on his gut after a fatty insult. If he seems hungry and agitated, a few bites of plain boiled skinless chicken are fine — don't force a full meal.
- Take a quick "baseline check" so you know what's normal for him tonight and can spot change: gum color (should be pink and slick, not pale/tacky), breathing rate at rest (under ~30/min is typical for a mid-size dog), and his behavior (alert, following you, etc.).

WATER
- Don't let him gulp a full bowl right now. Offer small amounts frequently — a few laps every 15–30 minutes.
- If he keeps water down for an hour, you can leave a small bowl out; if he vomits water, pull it for 30–60 minutes and offer ice chips instead, then retry small sips.
- Watch for repeated trips to the bowl and gulping — that's a nausea sign.

FOOD (STARTING TOMORROW)
- Bland diet for 2–3 days: boiled skinless chicken breast (no salt, no skin, no fat) + plain white rice, roughly 1 part chicken to 2–3 parts rice.
- Small frequent meals: about 1/4 of his normal portion, 3–4 times a day, then taper back to his regular diet.
- Avoid anything fatty, rich, or new for the next several days — no treats, no table scraps, no fatty add-ons.

URGENT VET — GO TONIGHT (ER, not waiting for morning) IF ANY OF THESE
- Repeated vomiting (more than 2–3 times in a few hours, or vomiting that resumes after seeming to stop).
- Repeated retching/dry heaving without producing anything — that's a bloat red flag, especially in deeper-chested dogs, and time-sensitive.
- Abdomen becomes firm, swollen, or painful to touch. The classic pain posture is "praying position" — front down, rear up, reluctant to settle.
- Restlessness — pacing, can't get comfortable, keeps getting up and switching spots.
- Lethargy that's worse than just being tired: not responding to you, won't get up, glassy or unfocused.
- Gums go pale, white, gray, yellow, or tacky/sticky instead of pink and wet.
- Refuses water for several hours, or signs of dehydration (pinch a bit of shoulder skin — it should snap back in under a second; if it tents, that's dehydration).
- Any diarrhea that's watery, frequent, or has blood/mucus.
- Panting, drooling, or shaking that's out of character for him — these read as nausea/pain, not just stress.
- Difficulty breathing, collapse, weakness in the legs, or stumbling.

CALL A VET (your regular clinic's after-hours line, or ASPCA Animal Poison Control 888-426-4435 — fee may apply) — even if not ER-level urgent — if
- He seems "off" in a way you can't quite pin down but you're worried.
- Vomiting returns even once after the bland-diet start.
- He refuses food for more than 24 hours.
- You're not sure whether a symptom is concerning (the after-hours line exists for exactly this).

WHY THIS MATTERS
The reassuring signs right now are: one vomit only, alert, normal breathing, soft abdomen, not retching, still drinking. The risk isn't usually the chicken skin itself — it's that a fatty meal can trigger pancreatitis 12–48 hours later in a susceptible dog, so the next 24 hours of monitoring are the real watch window. If he stays well tonight and into tomorrow, the odds are very much in his favor.

Short answer: No. One test gives Sam a working hypothesis, not a validated process. Require a repeatability test before proposing a sale run.

What's been demonstrated (n=1):
- Labor: 58 min, under the 60-min ceiling
- Yield: 19.1 cooked lb = 43 complete 7-oz portions + 4.6 oz leftover
- Process change works end-to-end (pre-staged marinade, new tray sequence)

What hasn't:
- That 58 min is the typical figure, not Sam-on-a-good-day
- That 43 portions is the new steady-state yield and not measurement noise
- Anything about customer reception, sell-through, or margin

Why the one-portion loss doesn't settle the yield question:
44 → 43 is 2.3%. That's inside normal kitchen variance — raw-case water content, thermometer calibration, rest time, even which cook trims. You can't separate signal from noise on one observation. Labor has the same problem: a multi-hour prep by one person on one day can swing 10-15% on pace, interruptions, and how complete the staging actually was that morning.

Evidence Sam needs before proposing a sale run:

1. Labor repeatability. Minimum 3 runs of the new method. Ideally one of those with a different operator, to confirm 58 min isn't person-specific. Pre-register the bar (e.g., "labor ≤65 min on 3/3 runs").

2. Yield repeatability. Same 3 runs. Pre-register: "≥42 complete portions AND QC acceptable" — and write down what QC means before the run (no raw spots, no overcooked batches, rest loss within an expected band). If a measurement rule isn't fixed before the test, Sam will redefine "good" after he sees the number.

3. Sell-through design. Kitchen yield isn't the commercial question. Even at 43 portions, what matters is price × units sold vs. cost. Sam needs a sale-run plan that sets a price, a sell-through target, and a stop rule (e.g., "if <X portions sold by hour Y, revert to the old plan"). Without this, the sale run is just another untested kitchen day with customers attached.

4. Honest baseline check. Was the old 3-hour / 44-portion figure also one run, or averaged? If both sides are n=1, the comparison is anecdotal on both ends and a single paired repeatability run (old method vs. new method, same day, same case) is the minimum honest test.

What would change my call:
- If the old labor figure is well-characterized across many runs and the only new variable is the tray sequence, one new timing run is closer to sufficient — but yield still needs repetition because raw cases vary.
- If Sam frames the next step as a soft sale (limited quantity, easy revert, pre-registered stop rules), that can substitute for a formal repeatability study — but only if it's framed that way going in, not sold as a launch.

Framing for Sam: this isn't "wait for perfection." A repeatability test is small — 3 runs, same week, same supplier, same operator if possible — and gets him to a defensible sale-run proposal by midweek. One positive kitchen result doesn't earn a commercial step when the commercial variables (price, demand, margin) haven't been touched at all. Conditional plan stays conditional until the data's there.

Scam indicators — this message has essentially every flag a refund-claim phishing text has:

  1. Unsolicited. Mom didn't initiate contact; legitimate refunds are processed to bank details already on file and don't require inbound confirmation.
  2. Phantom refund. The statement shows zero due and she never paid the removed balance. Real refunds correspond to real payments — this one is invented.
  3. URL shortener (bit.ly). Hides the destination. Legitimate providers link to their own domain. Shorteners are a near-universal phishing tell.
  4. "Confirm your bank details." Real providers don't ask you to confirm bank info via a text link — they credit the account they already have. This phrasing is the bait.
  5. Urgency — "today." Pressure to act before Mom thinks it through.
  6. STOP-to-opt-out framing. Mimics TCPA compliance language to look legit; replying also confirms her number is live and gets it sold/used more.
  7. Plain SMS for money movement. Banks, insurers, and most providers use signed portal mail or account notifications, not inbound text links, for refunds.

What NOT to do (worth stating because it matters most):
  - Don't tap the bit.ly link — even on Wi-Fi with the phone in a sandbox. The landing page can fingerprint the device, harvest any entered data, and phish more credibly next time.
  - Don't reply STOP. That confirms the number is active and active numbers get reused/resold.
  - Don't call any number or use any URL that came in the text.

Safe verification sequence — using only the provider's known portal or the statement phone number:

  Step 1. Pull the actual paper/email statement. Confirm the provider's real customer-service number and the official portal URL printed on it. (If she doesn't have a statement handy, search the web for "[provider name] official site" and confirm the domain matches what's on a past bill or correspondence — never trust a URL forwarded by the text.)
  Step 2. From a desktop browser, navigate to that portal directly (typed or via her own bookmark, not via the text). Sign in with her normal credentials. Look for: any pending refund, any account note about a balance adjustment, any message in the provider's message center.
  Step 3. Independently, call the phone number from the statement. Ask the rep to confirm in the system whether a $185 refund is actually outstanding, and whether the provider sends refund-confirmation texts via shortened links. (They won't. If they do text at all, it will reference the provider's own domain.)
  Step 4. If portal + call both confirm no such refund exists, treat it as confirmed phishing. If, against expectation, a real refund does exist, it will be visible in the portal without her doing anything, and the provider will never need her to "confirm bank details" via an inbound text.

Reporting sequence — once she's confirmed it as phishing:

  1. Forward the text to 7726 (SPAM). This is the carrier-side reporting short code used by AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile, etc. After forwarding, follow any prompts the carrier sends back. This routes the message into carrier spam/abuse tracking.
  2. Report to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov. Select "Text message scam" and paste the message verbatim, including the sender number. The FTC uses these for cross-carrier pattern detection.
  3. Report to the FCC at consumercomplaints.fcc.gov under "Unwanted calls/messages." SMS phishing falls under this and feeds into the FCC's Robocall Response Team data.
  4. Notify the provider. Use the same portal/call path from Step 2 — "report a phishing attempt impersonating us." Most providers have a fraud/abuse mailbox (often abuse@ or security@ their domain) and they actively warn other customers when these campaigns hit.
  5. Block the sender number on Mom's phone. iOS: Messages → tap the number/profile → block. Android: long-press the conversation → block.
  6. Delete the message after the above are done — keep screenshots for the reports, then remove it so a follow-up tap can't happen later.

One forward-looking note: because she received this, her number is now on a list that will be reused. Worth checking haveibeenpwned.com for the number/email, and turning on carrier-level spam filtering (most carriers offer a free "call/text filtering" toggle, and iOS/Android both have "Filter Unknown Senders" settings that route these to a separate inbox so they can't be tapped accidentally). If she's ever tempted by a future text in this pattern, the rule of thumb is the same one that worked here: real refunds don't need inbound confirmation; verify only through a channel she already trusts.

Quick recap in plain form: do not engage with the text in any way; verify through the statement's phone number and the portal she logs into on her own; once confirmed fake, report to 7726 + FTC + FCC + the provider, then block and delete. No action she can take in the next hour is more important than not clicking.

The "cleanliness" of the photograph isn't a neutral aesthetic; it's the product of a frame, and every frame excludes. The mosquitoes, the sour bank, and especially the brother's shout are the irreducible mess of the lived event — sensory, embodied, ungovernable. What matters is that the brother isn't passively cropped: he is a SHOUTING presence, actively trying to be part of the scene, which makes his absence from the frame feel like silencing rather than accident. The prose then quietly counters the photograph it describes: it puts the brother back inside what the image cropped out, suggesting writing can recover what images leave behind precisely because writing doesn't share the photograph's commitment to cleanness. The real tension, then, isn't memory versus image — it's that the image was always an edited version, and what we end up "remembering" is simply what survives that edit.

The "pasted on" effect is almost always two things together: an even, continuous rim line, and full-strength pigment meeting the cool shadow at a hard boundary. With ultramarine under burnt sienna, that boundary wants to neutralize to gray the moment the two overlap wet — that's the mud you saw on scrap.

Three-part sequence to keep the cool luminous and the rim glowing:

1. SOFTEN THE SHADOW EDGE FIRST
   Take a clean damp (not wet) brush and gently pull along the dry blue-gray edge where the rim will land. You want a 1–2mm feather of paler gray, not a re-wet of the shadow body. This gives you a transition zone that's still cool but receptive.

2. FIRST RIM GLAZE — THIN, SOFT, OFFSET
   Mix quinacridone rose + a touch of burnt sienna, watered to weak-tea consistency. More rose than sienna — the rose is the halo underlayer. Apply with a damp brush starting just inside where the bright rim will live, then immediately use a clean damp brush to feather the outer edge OUTWARD into the dampened shadow band. Stop short of the dry shadow body. Never let the orange glaze sit on top of the cool shadow — only kiss its softened edge.

   The mud-avoidance rule: keep them physically separated. The only place orange and blue-gray meet is the transition band, where both are at their most transparent. Any gray that forms there reads as atmosphere, not mud.

   Let this dry completely.

3. SECOND PASS — THE CORE GLOW, DISCRETE
   Now a slightly more concentrated burnt sienna (rose still present, but sienna leaning up), applied as separate touches only in the brightest hit zones — not as a continuous outline. Think 3–5 short dabs along the curve of Kibo's back, ear, and cheekbone where the light catches. Leave gaps. Let the rim die into the shadow in 2–3 places — real backlit fur isn't a uniform stripe.

   Optional final: a hair-thin pass of nearly-pure quinacridone rose on the brightest speck or two. That's the luminous hit.

WHY IT HOLDS TOGETHER
- The first thin rose-sienna glaze does the optical heavy lifting; it stays transparent so the cool shadow keeps its luminosity.
- Softening the shadow edge (rather than re-wetting it) feathers the transition without lifting the wash or causing blooms.
- The bright core is built in layers, not one stroke — layered transparencies glow; single thick strokes sit.
- Varying rim width and saturation is what kills the cutout feeling.

TWO THINGS TO AVOID ON THE NEXT SCRAP TEST
- Don't pre-mix the rim to one even value. Paint it in stages.
- Don't re-wet the shadow to blend the rim into it. If the transition still reads hard, fix it by feathering the rim outward with a damp brush on the rim side, not the shadow side.

One small thing on the scrap test itself: the orange looked pasted on partly because you tested it as a single stroke. Try the same mix in the actual sequence — feathered first pass, dry, then discrete bright dabs — on a scrap with a dried blue-gray stripe under it. The behavior changes a lot.

Bottom line: Option B is the only one plausibly meeting 90 minutes with margin. Option A is short even on its best day.

Load assumption (modem + wired AP):
- Cable modem: ~10-15 W (DOCSIS 3.1 typical)
- Wired AP: ~8-12 W
- Real load: ~18-25 W, comfortably under the 30 W reference both datasheets use

Option A (425 VA / 225 W, 50 min @ 30 W, sealed battery):
- At your real load (~20 W) you'd expect roughly 65-80 min on a new battery, before aging/derating
- After 2-3 yr sealed lead-acid aging in a typical indoor location: ~50-60 min
- Cannot plausibly cover a 90 min outage even under favorable assumptions
- Sealed battery also means end-of-life = replace the whole UPS

Option B (850 VA / 450 W, 100 min @ 30 W, user-replaceable battery):
- At ~20 W load: roughly 130-160 min on a new battery
- After 3-4 yr aging: still ~100-120 min
- Comfortable margin over 90 min target even at end of useful battery life
- Swappable battery extends useful UPS life to ~8-10 yr total
- Extra VA headroom also handles brief inrush if the modem/AP stack ever spikes

Recommendation: Option B. Option A fails the requirement on paper; Option B clears it with margin and stays serviceable.

Confidence in published runtime:
Treat published numbers as best-case upper bounds, not field expectations. Discount for:

1. Battery aging (sealed lead-acid, the common UPS chemistry):
   - Year 1: ~90-95% of rated capacity
   - Year 2-3: ~75-85%
   - Year 4-5: ~60-70%
   - Hot locations (closet, attic, near heat-producing gear) add ~10-20% derating

2. Conversion / overhead loss:
   - Line-interactive UPS: ~90-95% efficient
   - Online/double-conversion: ~85-90%
   - The UPS itself draws 3-10 W just to run, which is included in the published load figure but worth knowing
   - Net effect on runtime: roughly 5-15% shorter than the battery-only number would suggest

3. Test conditions vs reality:
   - Published at 25 deg C, new battery, full charge, resistive load reference
   - Real loads are SMPS (modem/AP) with modest power-factor quirks; minor effect at these wattages
   - Battery not always at 100% if recent outage or poor storage

Realistic expectation for Option B:
- New: ~85-95 min (close to published 100, with ~10% efficiency/aging haircut)
- Mid-life (2-3 yr): ~70-85 min
- Late-life (4 yr, before swap): ~60-70 min

So Option B clears 90 min for roughly its first 1-2 years, and clears it comfortably if you replace the battery at the 3-year mark (which you can, because it's user-replaceable — the main reason it beats Option A structurally, not just on the spec sheet).

Practical add-ons worth doing either way:
- Plug the UPS into a surge-protected outlet (most are, but check)
- Don't daisy-chain surge strips
- Note the replacement battery model now while the UPS is fresh, so it's on hand when needed
- A $10 plug-in wattmeter (Kill-A-Watt style) lets you measure actual draw and refine runtime estimates per your specific gear

WHY CURRENT STATE MUST BE REEVALUATED NEAR EXPOSURE
Between flagging and exposure, accounts churn, downgrade, enter a CS hold, get acquired, or otherwise become ineligible. Re-checking at exposure is what makes the cohort a cohort rather than a snapshot. Substituting the historical 37 now would make staleness the cohort's defining feature.

STATUS OF THE LOCKED PRIMARY COHORT (30)
Randomized and locked. Two of the 30 were lost to pre-exposure eligibility and remain labeled as such — not silently folded into a different list, not "replaced" by the 37, not re-randomized. The remaining 28 proceed unless exposure-time checks surface new issues, which would be labeled the same way the original two are.

STATUS OF THE RESERVE ORDER
Randomized separately and independently of the primary. It is not a re-cut of the primary, and it is not a re-expression of the 37. It exists to backfill exposure-time losses without re-opening the primary's randomization. It gets used in order, only if and as needed, and only via the reserve order — never by quietly swapping in a different list.

WHAT HAPPENS AT EXPOSURE
Re-verify eligibility on the locked primary cohort (28 currently live) and on the reserve order, against the same criteria used originally. Any new losses get labeled exposure-time losses, same convention as the existing two. If, after exposure-time checks, the team wants a structurally different cohort drawn from the underlying universe, that is a new decision the review can make — not a substitution into the existing one.

ONE-LINE ANSWERS IF OWEN PUSHES BACK
"Why doesn't 37 just replace 30?"  Because 37 is historical; eligibility is current, and only the locked cohort has had eligibility checked.
"Why are the two pre-exposure losses still labeled?"  Because the label is the audit trail. Renaming or absorbing them would erase the loss and break the read at d30/d90.
"Why can't we just top up from the reserve?"  We can, in reserve order, if exposure-time losses exceed what the reserve was sized for. We cannot top up by swapping in the 37 — that is a different list with a different provenance.
