The least-damaging path is to lift it from a fully dry state before re-wetting anything, and to stop at the first step that does enough work. Here's the sequence in escalating order, with the constraint that the roof edge stays intact.

1. Dry lift with a barely-moist brush. Take a clean synthetic brush (a small dagger or soft mop, not a stiff scrubber), dampen it, then press it out on a paper towel so it's nearly dry — just enough moisture to pick up pigment, not enough to flow. Pounce, don't scrub, on the bloom. Blot with a tissue between passes. This is the gentlest option because it doesn't reactivate the surrounding sky wash and won't disturb the roof line a half inch away.

2. Local rewet and blot, tightly bounded. If the dry pass only lightens it, switch to a slightly wetter brush and work only inside the bloom's footprint, not out to its edges. Wait five or ten seconds, then press a folded tissue firmly onto the spot and lift straight up. Working inside the mark keeps the hard edge from softening into a new halo. Expect quinacridone rose to leave some stain — that's normal and not a failure.

3. Stop and assess. If the bloom is now reading as a soft cool patch instead of a hard dot, leave it and let the paper dry completely before deciding on integration. Going further usually costs more than it returns.

If after step 2 it's still a defined dark mark, don't chase it. Restraint matters more than removal here. Two clean ways to integrate without overworking the sky:

  - Glaze the whole upper sky once bone dry. Mix a very dilute wash of the same ultramarine and rose and lay a single even pass over the bloom and the sky around it. The bloom becomes one darker passage inside an overall slightly varied sky, and the hard edge dissolves because the values next to it are no longer pure paper-white. One pass, not two — a second glaze will start to look worked.

  - Read it as atmospheric variation. A pale ultramarine sky in real life isn't uniformly light; a soft darker passage a half inch above a roof reads plausibly as distant haze or a thin cloud shadow. If that interpretation fits the study, leave it and let the eye take it as part of the sky's range. The mark stops being a mistake and becomes a feature only if you don't touch it again.

Things to avoid: scrubbing the paper surface, rewetting a wide area around the bloom (this lifts the original sky wash and invites a new backrun), and trying to paint the mark out with white or opaque paint — that muddies watercolor and is the fastest path to an overworked sky.

One practical note for next time: a bead that collects near the lower edge of a wash is usually the sky drying faster at the top while gravity pulls pigment down. Tilting the board a few degrees more during the wash, or pulling the wash with a slightly damper mix so it levels before setting, usually prevents the bead from forming in the first place.

$720.00 ÷ 7 = $102.857142857… per share

Rounded to the nearest cent, the standard share is $102.86 (since the third decimal is 7, it rounds up from .85 to .86). Holding Sam at exactly twice that rounded standard share gives $205.72.

Rounded-share totals
- Sam (lead, 2 shares):  2 × $102.86 = $205.72
- Each of 5 staff (1 share): $102.86
- Subtotal at full rounded shares: 7 × $102.86 = $720.02

That is $0.02 over the $720.00 pool. Because the constraint locks Sam at twice the rounded standard share, the $0.02 overage must come out of the 5 equal-share allocations.

Cent-difference allocation (transparent options)

The 5 staff must together receive $720.00 − $205.72 = $514.28, while the unadjusted total would be 5 × $102.86 = $514.30. The unavoidable $0.02 difference has to be trimmed from that group. Two clean ways to distribute it:

Option A — single-person trim (most concentrated, easy to audit):
  4 staff × $102.86 = $411.44
  1 staff  × $102.84 = $102.84
  Staff subtotal       = $514.28

Option B — two-person trim (more evenly spread):
  3 staff × $102.86 = $308.58
  2 staff × $102.85 = $205.70
  Staff subtotal       = $514.28

Either option totals exactly $720.00 with Sam at $205.72 (2 × $102.86 standard share). Pick by whatever convention Sam already uses for rounding residuals on his closeouts — by role, by tenure, alphabetically, or split evenly. The rule of thumb to record alongside the policy: round each share to the nearest cent first, hold the lead at twice the rounded standard share, and let any residual penny land on the equal-share group rather than on the lead.

Quick sanity check
- Ideal Sam share = 2 × ($720/7) = $205.7143
- Sam at $205.72 is $0.0057 above ideal — closer than the alternative $205.70 ($0.0143 below), so $102.86 is the right standard share to anchor on.
- 0.0057 = less than half a cent, so the nearest-cent rounding on the standard share is the tightest the policy allows.

Assumption: 900 VA / 540 W SOHO UPS with a sealed lead-acid battery (CyberPower, APC Back-Ups, Tripp-Lite, Eaton, etc.). Generic procedure — cross-check the manual that came in the box for model-specific charge time, alarm pattern, and button layout.

1. BEFORE YOU TOUCH CABLES

Goal: exactly two loads on the UPS — modem and wired AP. Nothing else.

  - Trace every cord near the UPS spot. Most SOHO units split the outlets into "Battery + Surge" and "Surge Only." Modem and AP go on Battery + Surge. Laptop, monitor, phone charger, anything else, go on Surge Only or straight to the wall.
  - Label the two UPS-side plugs with a small piece of tape: "MODEM" and "AP." This matters during a real brownout when you'll be grabbing fast.
  - Confirm whether your unit shows load (watts or %). If yes, you have a clean way to catch laptop contamination during the test. If no, you'll catch it by process-of-elimination instead.

2. INITIAL CHARGE

  - Plug the UPS into a known-good wall outlet. No loads connected.
  - Charge time: 8 to 12 hours minimum. Some manuals say 24 — use the longer number if you don't have the manual. SLA batteries ship partially discharged for transit safety; running a test on an undercharged battery gives you a falsely short runtime reading and you don't get a second chance at a clean number until you replace the battery.
  - Keep it upright, ventilated (don't shove it in a closed cabinet), room temperature. Heat shortens battery life and skews capacity.
  - Done when: solid charge LED, "100%" on the display, or fan stops cycling. A short beep on first plug-in is normal (the unit detects a low battery) and should silence within a few minutes.

3. LOG SETUP — WRITE THESE BEFORE THE TEST

One line per timestamp, plain notes are fine:

  - Time charge completed and the unit's stated level.
  - Input voltage if displayed.
  - Load in watts with the modem and AP connected and idle (no traffic spike). This is your actual load — modem plus wired AP is usually 10 to 25 W, not the chart's 30 W. Note it.
  - Ambient temp near the UPS.
  - UPS model and serial — for the replacement battery in 3 to 5 years.

4. RUNTIME TEST — STEP BY STEP

Schedule it for a window with no work calls, no meetings, and no one else likely to need the internet. If a call might still happen anyway, hotspot the laptop as backup so an unexpected UPS failure doesn't drop you mid-call.

  a. With the UPS charged and both loads connected, re-read load wattage to confirm steady state. Log it.
  b. Pull the UPS plug from the wall. Do not press any button on the UPS — let it transfer to battery on its own. Start a stopwatch.
  c. Every 10 to 15 minutes, log: time, estimated battery %, any beep pattern, load wattage, AP LED state, modem LED state. If a wired device is handy, ping the modem and log the result.
  d. Stop at the 60-minute mark OR when the low-battery alarm first sounds — whichever comes first.
  e. Plug the UPS back into the wall. Confirm it returns to charging (LED behaviour, fan).

5. STOP CONDITIONS — DO NOT RUN TO FORCED SHUTDOWN

Stop the test at any of these, immediately:

  - Low-battery alarm first sounds. SOHO UPS units typically chirp every 1 to 2 seconds at roughly 20 to 25% capacity remaining. Runtime-to-first-alarm is your real outage budget — that's the number to plan around, not a wall-clock runtime that includes a dying battery.
  - Load wattage starts climbing (UPS is sagging and compensating; voltage drop imminent).
  - Modem or AP LEDs dim or flicker (internal brown-out; reboots likely).
  - Casing is hot to touch, smells sharp or sulphurous, or the battery looks swollen. Ventilate, contact the manufacturer.
  - Loud relay clicking, repeated restarts, or fan pinned at max for more than a couple of minutes.

Reason not to exhaust the battery: deep discharge is hard on SLA cells, shortens service life, and gives you a worse data point — the bottom 10 to 20% of the discharge curve is noisy and not usable for planning.

6. AFTER THE TEST

  - Recharge back to 100% — typically 4 to 8 hours from ~50%, longer from deeper discharge.
  - Optional: repeat the test a week later. Capacity rises over the first 3 to 5 cycles as the battery formats. The second runtime is usually a few minutes longer, then plateaus. Two readings beat one.

7. WHAT YOU GET OUT OF IT

  - Actual load wattage (replaces the chart's 30 W assumption).
  - Runtime to low-battery alarm — your conservative outage budget.
  - A second-reading trend if you repeat.
  - Implicit confirmation the laptop is not on the UPS: if the load readout shows only the modem+AP figure (~10 to 25 W) during the wall-pull, and your laptop on wall power behaves normally, the laptop was never on the UPS. If the load shows 50+ W, you've accidentally included the laptop — replug it to wall before you trust this for an actual outage.

One practical note for the test window: pick a time that isn't one of your protected blocks. You don't want a half-discharged UPS when Sam's on a late shift and the truck wakes Kibo, or when you need the connection for a real call.

SCHEMA REDESIGN — replaces the one-funnel mock

SUMMARY
Drop the funnel. Keep five independent measurements. Make non-exposure a visible cohort with reasons. Let the account row carry timestamps without forcing a single order. Add expansion_source so post-CS and organic expansion are not summed.

WHY THE FUNNEL FAILS (the cuts)
1. Eligible-but-not-exposed vanishes — they fall out of the denominator with no label.
2. Prompt exposure and CS handoff are different surfaces. Product vs human. A handoff source is usually a help request, not the prompt.
3. Linear funnel implies eligible → prompted → handoff → expanded is the only path. Expansion can be organic, post-handoff, or self-serve.
4. A single conversion_rate column credits the prompt for outcomes the prompt did not cause.

REPORT-LEVEL COLUMNS (each a count, not a stage)
- eligible_accounts
- exposed_accounts (prompt actually delivered within the planned window)
- non_exposed_eligible (see breakout below)
- help_request_accounts
- cs_handoff_accounts
- expanded_accounts

LOCAL RATES (each its own row, not a single conversion_rate)
- exposure_rate = exposed / eligible
- help_rate_per_exposed
- handoff_rate_per_help_request
- expansion_rate_post_handoff
- expansion_rate_organic

NON-EXPOSURE BREAKOUT (so the missing cohort has a reason, not silence)
- suppressed
- held_out (control bucket)
- failed (delivery / technical)
- outside_window (timing miss vs planned exposure window)

ACCOUNT-LEVEL ROW FIELDS
- account_id
- eligible_at
- exposure_status (enum: prompted | suppressed | held_out | failed | outside_window)
- prompt_sent_at (nullable)
- first_help_request_at (nullable)
- handoff_at (nullable)
- expanded_at (nullable)
- expansion_source (enum: post_handoff | organic | self_serve | unknown)

EFFECT ON THE READS
- Sequence still inspectable per account — timestamps present, nullable, no forced ordering. You can still pull "eligible then never exposed then expanded organically" as a path.
- Non-exposure cohort is visible with a reason rather than silently dropped.
- No causal claim implied between prompt and handoff or between prompt and expansion.
- Help request is its own event, not a funnel stage.
- Post-CS and organic expansion are reported separately, so the prompt is not credited for organic.

CALL
Send back to Owen with the four cuts above and the schema. Ask him which non-exposure reason categories he wants — minimum above is what we need; he may want finer (suppression reason) or coarser (suppression + held_out combined).

For today, a tiny superficial scrape with no active bleeding, swelling, puncture, embedded material, torn nail, and a dog who bears weight and lets you handle the paw is something you can manage at home. Pad wounds heal slowly because the pad takes weight constantly, so the goal today is gentle cleaning, brief protection outside, and a close eye on it.

Clean and protect

1. Rinse with lukewarm water or a simple saline rinse (1 tsp plain salt per cup of water, or store-bought saline). Gentle stream from a cup or low-pressure sprayer for 30–60 seconds is enough.
2. Pat dry with a clean cloth. Don't rub.
3. If you want an antiseptic, use dilute chlorhexidine (2% solution diluted to the color of weak tea) or dilute betadine (povidone-iodine) to the same weak-tea color. Apply with a gauze pad, not by pouring.
4. Skip hydrogen peroxide and alcohol — both damage healing tissue. Skip Neosporin unless your vet has previously okayed it for him; some dogs react to it and ingestion during licking is a concern.
5. Cover with a non-stick gauze pad loosely held by self-adhering vet wrap (not human bandaids — too tight, trap moisture, dogs shake them off). A breathable dog bootie is fine. Keep it on outside; take it off indoors so the wound airs out.
6. Discourage licking. If he won't leave it alone, an e-collar for a day or two is reasonable.

Check it again tonight and once tomorrow morning. A little pinkness and mild tenderness on first touch is normal.

Walks

Shorten and soften them for the next 2–3 days, then return to normal once the scrape is closed and he's moving evenly:

- 10–20 minutes on flat, clean surfaces (sidewalk, clean pavement, chemical-free grass).
- Avoid hot pavement (back of your hand to the ground — if you can't hold it 5 seconds, too hot; heat dries and burns the wound).
- Avoid sand, gravel, muddy trails, and chemical-treated lawns until closed.
- No fetch, no off-leash running, no stairs or jumping for a couple of days.
- Leash walks only so you control pace and footing.

The right-front favor for two minutes this morning fits a small pad scrape — most dogs take a few ginger steps, realize it stings less than expected, and move on. The pattern to watch is whether the favor returns later today or on later walks.

Vet call warranted the same day for any of these:

- Active bleeding that doesn't stop with gentle, steady pressure within 10 minutes, or bleeding that soaks through gauze.
- New or worsening swelling, heat, or clear pain on handling — pulling away, growling, or snapping when he normally tolerates paw handling.
- Limping that returns, worsens, or shows up at rest.
- Discharge — pus, cloudy fluid, foul smell.
- A pad flap, deep cut, or anything that gapes open. Pad injuries can hide a deeper wound; if you can't see the wound bed clearly, that's a vet visit.
- Anything still embedded or debris you can't rinse out.
- Redness that spreads, red streaks, or skin around the scrape getting darker/tender.
- Loss of appetite, lethargy, or behavior change that lasts more than a few hours.
- No improvement or no healing by 48–72 hours.

If it's still a clean, dry, non-bleeding scrape tomorrow and he's walking evenly, keep managing at home until it closes over, usually 7–10 days for a pad.

I'm not a vet — these are standard first-aid steps for a minor pad scrape. If anything looks off before the above triggers, your own vet's judgment on the phone is the right call.

Bottom line: the tech has identified two specific, cheap, symptom-matching failures (weak capacitor + pitted contactor) and found no leak and normal compressor amperage. The $468 repair addresses the diagnosed fault directly; the $9,240 replacement is throwing away a compressor and sealed refrigerant system that show no problem. Default lean: do the repair. But Mom should still ask the questions below before signing anything.

Comparison of the two choices

  $468 repair (capacitor + contactor)
  - Targets the actual fault. Capacitor weakness is the textbook cause of intermittent afternoon shutdowns (compressor can't get enough starting torque under high load, thermal protector trips, unit restarts when it cools). Pitted contactor causes voltage drop and arcing, same symptom pattern. Both findings explain what she's experiencing.
  - Leaves the compressor, coils, refrigerant charge, and blower motors untouched. Those are the expensive components. None of them showed a problem today.
  - Does not stop the next failure from happening eventually. An 11-year unit has wear elsewhere the tech didn't measure.
  - Low risk: if the diagnosis is wrong and the symptom returns, Mom is out $468 plus another diagnostic fee, but she hasn't replaced anything that was still working.

  $9,240 replacement
  - Replaces a unit whose compressor amperage is normal and refrigerant system is sealed. That's roughly 20x the cost for a fix that targets two $30-80 parts.
  - Mid-life discard. Typical AC life is 15-20 years; she's at 11. Replacement now throws away 4-9 years of remaining useful life on the major components.
  - Gets a new manufacturer warranty (typically 10 years parts) and a more efficient unit (depends on SEER rating chosen — confirm below).
  - Justified only if the tech found, and is hiding, a second problem. There is no evidence of that in what you've reported.

  The asymmetric risk that matters: if the $468 repair fails for a different reason later (say, evaporator coil leak next summer), Mom still has the option to replace then on her own schedule. If she replaces now and the install is sloppy, she's locked into a $9K outcome she didn't need.

Questions to resolve before Mom commits

Warranty (ask in writing)

  Repair:
  1. How long is the workmanship warranty on the labor — 30 days, 90 days, 1 year?
  2. Are the capacitor and contactor themselves warrantied separately by the manufacturer? For how long?
  3. If the same intermittent-shutdown symptom returns within the warranty window, is the follow-up diagnostic free?
  4. If the unit fails for an unrelated reason during the warranty window (compressor, fan motor), is that covered?

  Replacement:
  5. Manufacturer parts warranty — how many years, and is it parts-only or parts + labor? Labor coverage after year 1 is the usual surprise.
  6. Installer labor warranty — separate from manufacturer, how long?
  7. Is registration required within a deadline to keep the warranty in force?
  8. What is explicitly excluded? (Common exclusions: refrigerant, diagnostic fees, labor after year 1, damage from power surges.)
  9. Is the warranty transferable if Mom sells the house? (Matters for resale.)

Failure-risk

  10. Did the tech inspect the evaporator coil? An 11-year-old evaporator coil is a known leak point and a $1,500-2,500 repair on its own. If they didn't look, ask them to.
  11. Did they inspect the condenser coil and the outdoor fan motor? Any noises, hot air discharging weakly, or visible oil staining at the refrigerant line connections?
  12. Did they check static pressure / airflow across the indoor coil? A clogged filter or weak blower can overheat a perfectly good compressor; the capacitor symptom can be downstream of an airflow problem.
  13. After the repair, what's the realistic next failure and when? Compressor (amperage normal now, low near-term risk), refrigerant leak (none now, rubber seals age), blower motor, control board. Get the tech's written opinion on remaining useful life of the major components.
  14. If the repair doesn't fix it, what's the diagnostic path? Will the same company credit the $468 toward a replacement if they misdiagnosed?
  15. Is Mom comfortable that, if a major failure happens later (coil leak, compressor), she'll have time to get 2-3 replacement quotes rather than being forced into an emergency swap mid-summer heatwave? If not, replacement now becomes more defensible.

Replacement-scope (only if she goes that direction — and only after getting a second quote)

  16. Second quote. Get one. From a different company. Same equipment class. $9,240 is a price where 2-3 quotes is standard practice.
  17. What's in the $9,240, line by line: outdoor unit, indoor coil/air handler (or keeping existing — see next), line set (refrigerant lines), thermostat, electrical disconnect/wiring, concrete pad, condensate drain, permits, haul-away, startup/commissioning.
  18. If keeping the existing indoor coil/air handler, is it being flushed and is it rated compatible with the new outdoor unit? Mismatched indoor/outdoor pairs can void the manufacturer warranty.
  19. What brand, model, SEER, and tonnage? SEER 14-16 is mid-range; anything quoted as standard should be in that band unless the quote specifies higher. Tonnage should match the home's Manual J load calculation, not "what was there."
  20. Permits: who pulls, who schedules inspection, and is the inspection included in the price?
  21. Rebates and credits: utility company rebate, federal energy credit (25C, if applicable this year), manufacturer promotion, state/local. Apply before signing.
  22. Surge protection: is a surge protector on the outdoor unit included or recommended? Compressor and control board damage from power surges is the single most common preventable AC failure.

Recommended next step for Mom: ask the tech questions 1, 3, 10, 12, 13 in writing, then get one more company to do an independent diagnostic and a replacement quote in parallel. If the second tech confirms only the capacitor and contactor, do the repair.

The 73-minute result is signal, not just first-cycle noise.

What 73 vs 100 actually means:
- 73% of rated capacity on cycle 1 is a wider gap than the usual first-cycle dip. A fresh lead-acid UPS typically delivers ~85-95% of rated on cycle 1, climbing toward 95-100% over the next 2-3 cycles as the plates condition. A 27% shortfall points to real shelf age — the battery sat in a warehouse or shipping container long enough that some active material has degraded. Conditioning recovers some of that, but it does not reverse calendar aging. You are unlikely to claw back the full 27-point gap.

What one more cycle is likely to give you:
- Most likely (~55-65%): ~78-85 min. A real improvement, but still short of your 90-min target and well below the published 100-min claim. You'd be keeping a unit that doesn't do what you bought it for.
- Optimistic (~15-20%): jumps to 90+ min on cycle 2. Possible but unlikely given how far off you started.
- Pessimistic (~20-25%): stays in the 73-78 range. The battery is what it is.

The deadline math:
- One conditioning cycle = ~75 min discharge + 8-12 hr recharge = roughly 14 hr
- Starting now (Sat ~9 AM): cycle finishes ~11 PM Sat, retest Sun late morning
- If the retest disappoints, you're scrambling for a same-day return or swap with no margin. Stressful gamble.
- If you return today, you keep full optionality. A replacement may well come from fresher inventory, and you can run 2-3 conditioning cycles on it on your own clock before trusting it for a real outage.

What I'd do: return it today, and if the replacement is the same model, run 2-3 full cycles on it before you treat any single runtime number as the real one. Only count runtime from cycle 3 onward.

Three things worth checking on the way out the door, just so you know what you're dealing with:
- Was the unit stored anywhere below ~50°F before you got it? Cold batteries read artificially low and recover at room temp, but that doesn't usually explain a 27-point gap.
- If the UPS has a battery-age or "replace by" indicator in its menu/log, note what it says. It'll tell you how the manufacturer dates the cell.
- Confirm you're using the supplied charger at its native current, not a third-party or under-amped supply.

None of those are likely to flip my recommendation — the gap is too wide for a simple environmental explanation — but they will tell you whether to be more or less suspicious of the replacement when it arrives.

- Work outdoors on a clean dry surface, or indoors with a window fan pulling air OUT of the room (pointed away from your face, never across the photos toward you).
- PPE: an N95 respirator (not a surgical or cloth mask — those don't filter mold spores), nitrile gloves, long sleeves. The fuzzy spots are biological growth and you don't want to aerosolize them.
- Have ready: clean cotton swabs, plain white paper, wax paper or unbuffered archival tissue, clean cardboard for temporary supports, a soft pencil (never pen on a photo back).

STEP 2 — ISOLATE THE TWO PROBLEM GROUPS FIRST

For the 6 stuck prints (Group B):
- Do not pull, flex, slide, or peel. Glossy prints (typically resin-coated / RC paper) can fuse emulsion-to-emulsion when wet, and forced separation almost always destroys both images.
- Slip a sheet of wax paper or clean plain paper around the stuck stack so nothing rubs against it.
- Lay the stack flat on a piece of stiff cardboard.
- Keep at normal room conditions, dry, until you can deliver to a conservator. They are stable in this state — the rule is "don't handle," not "rush."

For the 2 prints with fuzzy edge spots (Group C):
- Treat as mold-contaminated. Don't brush, blow on, or wipe them. Don't use a household vacuum — it exhausts spores back through the filter.
- Slide each print onto its own sheet of clean paper using the gloves; don't touch the fuzzy areas directly.
- A conservator will likely handle these with HEPA vacuum at very low suction, single-pass swabs in one direction, and sometimes localized humidity or freeze-thaw cycles.
- Until then, store them in a paper folder or on cardboard in a breathable container — NOT sealed in a plastic bag. Sealed plastic traps moisture and lets mold keep growing. Keep them physically separate from Group A.

STEP 3 — HANDLE THE ~32 DRY PRINTS ONLY AFTER B AND C ARE OUT
- Rehouse each print in its own archival polyester sleeve (Mylar / Melinex), or interleave with acid-free tissue in an acid-free archival box. Acceptable materials: polyester sleeves, acid-free tissue, acid-free boxes. Avoid: regular printer paper, self-adhesive envelopes, "magnetic" photo albums, PVC sleeves, lamination.
- Don't write on the backs with ballpoint or marker — those inks can bleed through or emboss into the emulsion. Soft pencil only, lightly, along the edge, away from the image.
- Store flat (not leaning on edge), in the dark, at stable household humidity. Target roughly 30–50% RH; a closet away from bathrooms, kitchens, and exterior walls is usually best. Avoid basements, attics, and garages — humidity swings are what caused the original damage.

DECISION: WHO NEEDS A CONSERVATOR
Send Groups B and C to a photographic conservator. Home treatment is not appropriate because:
- The stuck six will be destroyed by any separation attempt. A conservator has controlled-humidity chambers and the training to attempt separation without tearing the emulsion.
- The fuzzy spots are biological growth on a gelatin emulsion. Surface cleaning is possible in principle, but home attempts either scar the image or spread spores through the rest of the box.

For the ~32 dry prints, you do not need a conservator. Standard archival rehousing is enough.

FINDING A CONSERVATOR
- American Institute for Conservation (AIC) "Find a Conservator" directory at culturalheritage.org — filter by specialty = photographs.
- Expect an initial consultation fee; ask whether they offer a triage visit. Many will look at the whole box, separate the must-handle-by-them items from the home-rehouseable items, and bill accordingly, which often saves money.
- Lower-cost alternatives: regional museum conservation labs, state historical societies, and university conservation programs sometimes take outside work at reduced rates.

THINGS NOT TO DO
- Don't try to peel the stuck prints apart — biggest single risk in this whole situation.
- Don't brush, wipe, or blow on the fuzzy spots.
- Don't put any of these photos in sealed plastic bags.
- Don't laminate, tape, or apply any "preservation" spray or adhesive from a craft or office-supply store.
- Don't store the whole batch in a basement, attic, garage, or anywhere with humidity swings.
- Don't use a household vacuum on any of the prints.

ONE FOLLOW-UP QUESTION THAT WOULD CHANGE THE PLAN
If you can tell me roughly when the photos were made (1950s? 1970s? 1990s?) and whether the affected ones look black-and-white or color, I can sharpen the conservator-handoff note — early color prints (especially Kodachrome home prints and 1960s–70s dye-based color) are more vulnerable than black-and-white silver gelatin, and that affects how urgent the conservator visit is.

The diagnosis is concrete, the system is currently running healthy on all measured parameters, the price asymmetry is ~20x, and the 30-day same-fault credit effectively converts the repair into a one-month diagnostic trial rather than a sunk cost. Main residual risk: intermittent shutdowns have several possible causes and this repair only addresses two visible suspects (capacitor + contactor); if the symptom returns after the repair, it points at something else and the replacement decision becomes clearer on its own.

WHY THE REPAIR IS SUPPORTED

1. The diagnosis points at two specific, plausible causes of intermittent shutdown. Capacitors degrade and cause hard starts / protective trips; pitted contactors cause intermittent power interruption to the compressor and condenser fan. Both are routine wear parts. The fault isn't speculative.

2. Current readings say the rest of the system is healthy. An 18-degree supply-to-return split is a normal-looking delta-T (roughly 14-22 is typical depending on humidity and indoor conditions). Compressor amperage is in spec. No refrigerant leak detected. The system is running normally aside from the intermittent fault.

3. Price asymmetry is large. $468 vs $9,240 is a roughly 20x ratio. Worst case where the repair fails and she proceeds to replacement shortly after, the added cost is a second diagnosis visit or a second opinion — cheap relative to a premature full replacement.

4. The 30-day credit is a real option, not a gimmick. If the intermittent shutdown recurs within 30 days and she buys THIS contractor's quoted replacement, the $468 is credited. That makes the repair a 30-day diagnostic trial with a known worst-case downside.

5. Both repairs are routine field work. Capacitor and contactor swaps don't require system commissioning, don't touch refrigerant, and don't carry meaningful collateral risk of breaking something else.

MATERIAL RISK THAT REMAINS

1. Component-level diagnosis doesn't rule out other causes. Intermittent shutdowns can also come from failing compressor windings (sometimes not visible on a single amp reading), thermostat or low-voltage control faults, control board issues, high-pressure switch trips from a slowly-fouled coil, low charge from a slow leak not detectable on the day of testing, or condensate/drain safeties. The repair fixes two suspects; it doesn't prove they're the only suspects. If the shutdown returns after the repair, that's information — and the credit does not apply because it wouldn't be the "same" fault.

2. The 30-day credit is tied to this contractor. If replacement becomes the path, going with a different contractor forfeits the $468. That's soft pressure to stay with the original quote even if a competitor undercuts it. Worth knowing before anything is signed.

3. Labor warranty is only 90 days. If a related electrical issue surfaces at day 100, parts may be covered but labor is not. Limited comfort on a contactor/capacitor repair.

4. The warranty disparity itself is signal. 1yr/90day on repair vs 10yr/2yr on replacement tells you the contractor is less confident in the repair's durability than in a new system's. Not a reason to skip the repair — a reason to keep the option open.

5. System age and refrigerant type aren't in what you sent. On a 5-10 year-old R-410A system, repair is obviously right. On a 20+ year-old R-22 system approaching the refrigerant phase-out, the calculus tilts toward replacement even when a repair "works," because future coil or compressor failures get more likely and R-22 service more expensive.

WHAT I'D DO BEFORE APPROVING

- Ask the contractor for three things on the visit: equipment age, refrigerant type (R-22 vs R-410A), and what else was inspected beyond the capacitor and contactor (coil condition, control board, thermostat, drain). These don't change the repair decision; they change how aggressively to plan a replacement budget.
- Approve the repair. Schedule it; it's cheap, specific, and reversible via the credit.
- Monitor for the intermittent shutdown for the full 30 days after the repair. If it recurs, get a second opinion before agreeing to replacement — but use the credit window if the second opinion confirms the same recommendation.
- If the repair holds past 30 days, the question becomes system age and refrigerant. On modern R-410A equipment, the repair essentially resets the clock on the two most common wear parts. On aging R-22, plan a replacement budget within 1-2 years regardless of how the repair performs.

  - "Reliable 90 min" implies headroom. A unit that lands at 73 under your measured 31 W load will land lower under degraded batteries, higher ambient temperature, or after a year of use. If 90 is your floor, you actually want a unit that comfortably exceeds it on day one. The refund lets you buy that (different model, higher VA rating, or a unit with published runtime well above 90 min at your load).

  - A refund also restores your optionality. You can rebuy the same model if you decide the price/feature tradeoff is still right, after independent confirmation that 90 min is actually achievable. Right now you have evidence it isn't, on this unit.

  - One thing the exchange does give you, for free: a data point. If you do take the exchange and test the new unit under the same 31 W load, you'll know whether 73 was a lemon or systemic. That information has some value — but it's not what you asked the retailer to solve, and it doesn't get you to 90 min any faster than a refund-and-repurchase does.

Practical recommendation: take the refund. If you have an immediate coverage gap, the cheapest interim fix is a cheap二手 UPS or a small online UPS sized to carry the load for 20–30 minutes while you wait for the right replacement — that buys you time without committing to a unit whose spec you now have reason to distrust.

No shell tool available in this session. The math is simple enough to verify by hand: 25 + 5 + 3 + 1 = 34. If the disputed workspace moves from "paid and active" (uncorrected truth) into "canceled" because of current status, the table becomes 25 + 6 + 3 + 1 = 35 — which contradicts Owen's stated 34-window count. So the current-status label is double-counting one workspace.

Here's the classification and the fix.

══════════════════════════════════════════════
Day-90 classification
══════════════════════════════════════════════

The disputed workspace belongs in "paid and active."

At the day-90 timestamp (July 1, 12:00am Central), it had paid active entitlement through July 2 at 11:59pm Central. Its cancellation did not become effective until July 3 at 12:00am Central — which is day 92, two full days after the snapshot. A day-90 snapshot is defined by status at the snapshot instant, not by what happens afterward. At the snapshot instant, this workspace was:

  - Entitled: yes (paid through day 91)
  - Past due: no
  - On billing hold: no
  - Effective cancel date: not yet

So its day-90 bucket is paid and active. The current-status "canceled" label is a current-state field, not a snapshot field, and applying it here is what put the table at odds with itself.

The math exposes the error. Owen's 34-window count has to reconcile against the four buckets:

  Current uncorrected: 25 paid & active + 5 canceled + 3 past due + 1 on billing hold = 34. Mathematically that already sums to 34, but with the disputed workspace sitting in "canceled," that bucket is really 6 canceled and paid & active is really 24 — a phantom fifth canceled that does not match any day-90 cancel effective date.

The clean reconciliation is 26 paid & active + 5 canceled + 3 past due + 1 on billing hold = 34, where the 5 canceled are the workspaces whose cancellation was effective on or before the day-90 timestamp, and the disputed workspace stays in paid & active with a separate note for what happens on day 92.

══════════════════════════════════════════════
How Owen should preserve the later cancellation without rewriting the snapshot
══════════════════════════════════════════════

Two things have to be kept distinct: the state of the workspace at the snapshot instant, and the state of the workspace between the snapshot and now. Right now Owen is collapsing both into a single "current status" field, which is what's causing the mis-bucketing. The fix is to keep them as separate fields in the report.

1. Snapshot bucket = the workspace's day-90 state.

The rules for placing a workspace into a bucket should be read at the day-90 timestamp, not today. Concretely:

  - paid and active: paid entitlement extends past the snapshot timestamp, no past-due flag, no billing hold, no effective cancel on or before the snapshot timestamp.
  - canceled (effective on or before day 90): effective cancel timestamp is on or before the snapshot timestamp. This is the only way a workspace earns "canceled" in the day-90 table.
  - past due: past-due flag is set at the snapshot timestamp.
  - on billing hold: billing-hold flag is set at the snapshot timestamp.

Under those rules the disputed workspace is paid and active. Its effective cancel is day 92, two days after the snapshot, so it has no path into the canceled bucket at day 90.

2. Post-snapshot events = a separate column, not a bucket change.

The fact that this workspace canceled on day 92 is real and worth keeping in the report — d90 retention is a downstream metric and Owen will want to know which of the 26 paid & active workspaces churned before day 92, 93, 95, etc. But it should live in a separate column or a separate downstream table, with its own effective date. A standard shape:

  workspace_id | day90_bucket | cancel_effective_date | days_to_cancel_post_snapshot

For the disputed workspace: paid and active | 2024-07-03 | +2.

Workspaces that canceled on or before day 90 stay in the canceled bucket and get a cancel_effective_date on or before 2024-07-01. Workspaces that cancel after day 90 stay in paid and active at day 90 and only appear as churn in the d90-plus or d120 retention reads.

3. The principle, stated once so Owen can reuse it.

Snapshot buckets are a function of state at the snapshot timestamp. Current status is a function of state today. The report can carry both, but the day-90 column is governed by the snapshot timestamp and the d90-plus churn column is governed by the effective cancel date. Never let a current-status field overwrite a snapshot bucket, and never let a future-effective cancel pull a workspace backward into an earlier bucket.

If Owen wants a single line of defense in the pipeline: gate the bucket assignment on the relationship between the cancel effective date and the snapshot timestamp — "canceled" requires effective_date <= snapshot_timestamp, full stop — and route any workspace whose cancel effective date is after the snapshot to a post-snapshot churn register rather than to the day-90 canceled bucket. That's the rule that prevents the same mistake on the next report.

Recommendation for this week: controlled indoor ride, not the commute.

The three reasons, in order of weight:

1. Untested stacking. The new loading exercises and cycling have not been combined on the same day. Even if each is tolerable alone, the combined load is unknown, and you can't separate the effects after the fact. The indoor ride lets you hold one variable (dose/duration/resistance) constant while you find out how the loading exercises land overnight. The commute cannot offer that.

2. "Easy cycling" is most defensibly read as controlled easy riding, not a commute. Two short rises, gradient variability, wind, and time pressure all push intensity above what you'd dial in indoors. You have less ability to back off in the moment on a commute than on the indoor bike, which is the relevant comparison the therapist was likely approving.

3. Your downside is asymmetric, and you already named it. The cost of one indoor ride instead of commuting is small. The cost of overloading on day one of stacking and losing pain-free cycling for weeks is large. Given that asymmetry and an unknown combination, the conservative choice is the right one this week. You're trying to preserve cycling as a sustainable option, not prove you can complete a specific ride.

How to apply the during-session and next-day symptom rule:

During the session:
  - Mild awareness that does not change your form, breathing, cadence, or effort is acceptable. Note it and move on.
  - Any symptom that makes you change form, reduce effort, slow down, or want to stop means the session was too much. End it there. Do not push to complete the planned dose.
  - "I can finish this" is not the test. "Nothing is asking me to adjust" is the test.

Next day (this is the real gate):
  - Symptoms should return to near baseline by the next morning. "Baseline" means how you felt yesterday before the session, not zero.
  - If you wake up more symptomatic than the day before, the previous day's combined load was too much. Do not repeat that dose. Hold or reduce next time, do not push through.
  - A symptom that shows up new the next morning and wasn't present during the ride still counts. Overnight reactions are information.
  - Two consecutive next-day flares on the same dose is a clear signal to step back further before progressing.

A practical sequence, so Friday has a clear answer and next week is set up:

  - This week: indoor ride only, on a day you are also doing the new loading exercises. Pick a short, easy dose you can repeat identically.
  - End-of-week check: did next morning return to baseline both times you stacked loading exercises + indoor ride? If yes, you have a known-good baseline.
  - Next week, if baseline held: first commute can be a test, with permission to walk the two rises if anything asks you to adjust. The rule still applies — during and next day — you're just running the same gate on the commute.
  - If next morning did not return to baseline: stay on indoor rides, reduce one variable (duration or loading exercise volume), and retest. Don't escalate to the commute until a clean next morning.

One thing worth saying out loud: skipping the commute this week is not falling behind. It's the move that lets you keep cycling at all. If you treat the commute as the thing you must complete, you've already converted it from rehab into a running substitute — exactly the framing you said you wanted to avoid.

Immediate plan — Kibo, July 4th evening

NOW (next 60–90 min)

1. Stay with him. His pacing between you and the hallway is seeking behavior — your presence is the main anxiolytic. Don't leave the room.
2. You already closed the blinds. If light is still strobing through, pin a blanket over the rod as a second layer.
3. White noise louder than usual — fan + a podcast/playlist at moderate volume to mask booms. Keep it consistent; don't change tracks mid-burst.
4. Bring his water bowl to him. Panting dehydrates and he may not leave the spot to find it.
5. Skip the evening walk. Do not force it. Leash + door = highest-trigger zone tonight.

BATHROOM BREAKS

- Wait for a real lull (10–15 min of quiet) before opening any exterior door.
- Leash on BEFORE the door opens. Short leash, not retractable.
- Walk the closest, most sheltered spot — the driveway apron or just outside the front door. No around-the-block, no off-leash, no yard time alone.
- If bangs restart mid-walk, turn around immediately.
- If he refuses to step outside, that's fine — use a potty pad or a piece of grass-turf just inside the door. One missed evening is not a medical issue.

WHAT HELPS IN THE ROOM

- Long-lasting chew: frozen stuffed Kong, lick mat with peanut butter, bully stick. Licking/chewing lowers heart rate. Only offer if he'll take it.
- Snug wrap / Thundershirt if you have one — many dogs settle within 10–15 min.
- Bed against an interior wall, not near a window. Your worn t-shirt draped over the bed helps.
- Calm energy. Avoid repeated soothing phrases ("it's okay, buddy") — that can reinforce the alarm. Quiet presence + slow breathing is enough.

MEDS — DO NOT IMPROVISE

- No Benadryl, melatonin, Trazodone, or anything OTC without his vet's dose for his weight. Some sedatives + noise phobia = paradoxical agitation.
- If you want pharmaceutical support tonight: call his regular vet's after-hours line now and ask for a one-dose acepromazine or trazodone script. Many clinics phone-in for known patients on July 4th specifically.
- For future July 4th / NYE: book a pre-season vet consult 2–4 weeks ahead so meds are on hand rather than scrambling tonight.

GO TO THE ER IMMEDIATELY IF YOU SEE

- Panting that does NOT slow between bursts, or open-mouth breathing at rest with ribs heaving.
- Gums pale, grey, blue, or tacky. Lift his lip now so you have a baseline color to compare against.
- Collapse, staggering, or unable to stand.
- Repeated vomiting or unproductive retching (bloat signal — separate from anxiety).
- Seizure, or sudden rigid posture with glazed eyes.
- Attempts to bite when handled — either pain or panic past the point he can override; both warrant evaluation.
- Any injury from pushing through a door, window, or crate.
- Rectal temp above 104°F (heatstroke from sustained panting).
- Hiding that becomes non-responsive — not just tucked away, but won't look at you or respond to his name.

WHAT IS NOT AN ER SIGN — monitor, don't panic

Pacing, panting, whining, trembling, clinginess, refusing food/treats, hiding behind furniture, drooling, dilated pupils. Distress, uncomfortable, not dangerous. The plan above addresses them.

REST OF THE EVENING

- 6:00–9:00 PM: heaviest window. Stay in the room, white noise + chews, water nearby.
- 9:00–10:30 PM: usually tapers. Try a brief leashed, sheltered potty break during a lull.
- After 10:30 PM: if he's settled and sleeping, dim the white noise gradually. Don't move him to his normal sleep spot yet — keep the setup stable until morning.
- Tomorrow morning (7/5): expect a "hangover" — lethargy, clinginess, reduced appetite for 12–24 hours. Normal. Resume routine; he doesn't need a special day-after.

SAFETY CHECKS

- Front, back, and any low windows latched. Panic-pushing dogs go through screens and cracked windows fast.
- Crate only if he already loves it. Don't introduce the crate tonight — a panicked dog in a closed crate can break teeth or nails.
- Yard is off-limits tonight. Even a fenced yard becomes a flight risk when fireworks are popping.

YOU

It's a long night. Set up water + phone charger + a snack in the room with you. The single biggest variable is your calm presence — you've already done the right things (blinds closed, moved rooms, kept him responsive).

The pattern you're describing (2/10 in the final set, settled within an hour; 1/10 only on the very first loaded descent next morning; pain-free walking; no swelling, bruising, limp, instability, or rest pain) is a mild, acceptable, *reactive* response. It's not a red flag, but it is a yellow light: the tissue tolerated the volume but is signaling it's right at its current reactive ceiling. The right move is to repeat the same load next session, confirm the response is reproducible (not trending up), and only then add a small variable. Pushing on a 2/10 in the final set is how you turn a tolerable session into a setback.

Next loading session (resisted eversion plus the rest of the block):

  - Same exercise, same load and variables as last session. Do not add a set, rep, band, or range today.
  - Sub-session rule: if you reach ≥2/10 during any working set, stop that set. Don't push through to "finish."
  - Tempo and technique unchanged. Avoid compensations (e.g., hip abduction to get through a fatigued set).
  - Keep the rest of the session as planned — symptoms at this level are a reason to hold, not to swap in a different exercise today.
  - Finish with an easy 5–10 min cool-down (walk or easy spin), partly because a clean next-morning reassessment is easier when the acute session load is over.

Cycling (resume as a symptom probe, not a training stimulus today):

  - Low-to-moderate, steady, lower-cadence effort in a pain-free range. No surges, no hill repeats, no out-of-saddle climbing.
  - Stop any interval that produces ankle symptoms ≥2/10. End the ride at or below the duration/intensity that reproduced no symptoms.
  - Position: avoid deep dorsiflexion — drop the heel slightly if cleats allow, or run the saddle a few mm higher for this ride. Deep dorsiflexion under load is the position that loads the lateral structures.
  - If the ride is fully 0/10 and next morning is clean, normal riding is fine from the next session on.

Next-morning reassessment (same checks you just did):

  - First loaded movement (first stair descent): target 0/10, acceptable ≤1/10 and gone within a few steps.
  - Walk, sit-to-stand, single-leg calf raise: target 0/10.
  - No swelling, no stiffness that lingers past ~10 min, no after-activity flare.

Progression rule — only when two consecutive sessions are clean both in-session and next-morning:

  - Add ONE small variable at a time, in this order: reps → sets → band/load → range → speed of eccentrics.
  - A small variable is ~10–20% volume, not a step change.

Regression / stop rule — if next-morning symptoms are equal or worse, in-session pain reaches 3/10, or any new clinical sign appears (swelling, catch, giving way, rest pain, sharp localized pain):

  - Drop volume ~20–30% or substitute isometrics or shorter-range eversion for the dynamic resisted work for 1–2 sessions, then re-test.
  - If a true red flag appears (giving way, sharp localized pain, swelling, rest pain, or pain that escalates session-to-session), stop self-managing and get assessed in person rather than continuing to titrate yourself.

Running and hopping:

  - Running stays paused, as you decided.
  - Hop testing stays supervised (clinician or qualified coach), as you decided — an unsupervised failed hop is exactly how a manageable reactive episode becomes a real lateral sprain. Bring it back in only when the current load has been asymptomatic for 2+ sessions and a supervised hop test is clean.

Bottom line: repeat the same dose, don't add anything, ride easy as a probe, and progress only after two consecutive clean sessions. Your response warrants caution, not alarm — but it does warrant holding the line for one more session before moving forward.

Short answer: keep the full sheet. Option 1. The 1/8" overlap is tight-but-adequate for a flat study, and $46 is not worth lopping off content you composed deliberately.

Mat overlap (1/8" per edge)

  Sheet 9 x 12, opening 8.75 x 11.75 -> exactly 0.25" total bite, 0.125" per edge on all four sides. Correct.

  Conservation-grade framing (PPFA / museum guidance) treats roughly 1/8" to 1/4" as the working range for flat works on paper. 1/8" sits at the floor. It's fine if:

    - the sheet is dry and lies flat under the backing (archival backing is specified, so it is)
    - the paper hasn't cockled from the wash (porch studies in cold-press often relax flat once dry under weight - if this one is still wavy, press it first or ask the framer to open the window to ~8.5 x 11.5, which gives ~1/4" overlap and is safer)
    - the mat board is rag, not wood-pulp (saying "archival mat" should cover this; confirm)

  One side note on the visible mat border: frame 12 x 16 with a 9 x 12 sheet gives a 1.5" border on the short sides and 2" on the long sides. That's slightly narrow on the short side for a study but normal; not a reason to switch options.

Why not Option 2

  Cutting the sheet to 8 x 10 is irreversible. It specifically removes the pale right-side wash you wrote the composition around. Three things stacked against it:

    1. It destroys original material to save $46.
    2. It trades your compositional intent (the wash as negative space / balance / atmosphere) for a cheaper frame.
    3. A stock 8 x 10 frame is not archival mat and backing - it's the format, not the material. You may end up paying for archival materials separately anyway if the piece matters to you.

  If budget is the real pressure point, the honest move is to ask the framer for an archival 8 x 10 mat+backing build around a stock-looking frame, and keep the full 9 x 12 sheet. Don't cut the paper.

Recommendation

  Take Option 1. Two small asks to put in writing when you drop it off:

    - confirm mat board is 100% rag (not "acid-free" lignin-loaded wood-pulp)
    - confirm the sheet will be hinged at the top edge with archival tape, not dry-mounted or corner-taped (dry-mounting a watercolor on paper is a no)

  If the sheet is wavy when you bring it in, mention it so they open the mat window a touch and give you ~1/4" overlap instead of 1/8".

Short answer: yes, a 20-minute easy indoor ride is a reasonable next step under a pain-free rule, given that walking, stairs, and a reduced resisted-eversion session have all been pain-free during, after, and the next morning. Cycling is closed-chain, non-impact, and lets you control ROM and load — it's a sensible intermediate step before you reintroduce running or hopping.

Before you start, set the bike up so it isn't doing extra work for you: seat height with a slight knee bend at the bottom of the stroke, flat pedal (no cleats/clip-in forcing a fixed ankle angle), low resistance, easy cadence (roughly normal talking-pace effort). If anything feels off in the first few minutes, stop — you don't need to "push through" a 20-minute test.

Stop or defer cycling if you see any of the following:

During the ride
- Any pain at all — sharp, pinching, catching, or a dull ache that builds
- Loss of smooth pedal stroke (guarding, hitching, favoring one side)
- Heel lift or forefoot gripping that you didn't have walking

Within the first few hours after
- New or increased resting pain compared to the last 48 hours
- New swelling, warmth, or visible change in the joint
- Stiffness or soreness that doesn't settle back to your recent baseline by that evening

The next morning (this is the real gate under a pain-free rule)
- First-step stiffness or pain out of bed that wasn't there the previous mornings
- Pain during ordinary walking or stairs that had been absent for 48+ hours
- Tenderness on palpation returning around the lateral malleolus, peroneals, sinus tarsi, or anterior joint line
- Reactive soreness in the calf, peroneals, or tib anterior that reads as overload rather than just "I used the leg"
- Any sense that you're compensating or guarding without realizing it

If any of those show up, treat the ride as having failed the rule: back off to where you were (walking + the reduced eversion dose), give it another 48 hours of pain-free baseline, and then retry. If it's cleanly pain-free during, after, and the next morning, cycling is in the clear and the next decision is whether to reintroduce the full resisted-eversion dose before moving toward walk-run or hopping.

Sounds like a routine exertional/humidity-driven panting episode, not heat stroke — Kibo settled within the normal 5–15 min cooling window, perfusion looks good (pink, moist gums), gait and mentation normal, no GI or airway signs. The 8 min recovery is reassuring.

Rest of this evening
  Keep him in the AC, water available but don't force a big drink.
  Skip any second walk or play. Quiet evening is fine.
  Recheck gums and resting respiratory rate a couple of times over the next few hours — should be down to ~15–30 breaths/min at rest and gums staying pink/moist.
  Normal dinner is fine if he wants it; don't push food if he's not interested.

Outdoor breaks while it's hot/humid
  Dusk is usually still heat-loaded and humid — humidity specifically blunts panting's evaporative cooling, so don't assume "dusk = safe."
  Cut to bathroom-only trips; no walks, no sniff strolls.
  Pre-cool the house (AC down before you head out) so the cool environment is waiting.
  Bring water; offer a few laps on return.
  Test pavement with the back of your hand for 5 sec — if you can't hold it, he shouldn't walk on it.
  If a heat-index day is bad enough, a temporary indoor pee-pad setup is a reasonable swap, not a regression.
  Aim for first real walk for the day being early morning (before the sidewalk warms), not the evening one.

Urgent vet signs (any one of these, and now — not "watch and wait")
  Gum color change: bright red/brick, purple, blue, gray, or pale/white.
  Gums going from moist to dry/tacky/sticky (dehydration taking hold).
  Thick ropey drool or sudden heavy salivation.
  Vomiting, retching, or any diarrhea — especially if bloody or repeated.
  Stumbling, weakness, head tilt, blank/staring expression, disorientation.
  Collapse or inability to stand.
  Seizure, or any sudden behavior change that doesn't resolve in a minute or two.
  Noisy breathing — stridor, gagging, raspy inspiratory noise (laryngeal edema can escalate fast).
  Resting respiratory rate that stays elevated and is not trending down with rest/AC, or effort that looks heavy rather than just fast.
  Restlessness/agitation that won't break — inability to settle despite a cool house and water.
  Glassy eyes, unresponsiveness when you call his name.

Mechanism worth keeping in mind: heat injury in dogs can look deceptively OK and then decompensate over the next 1–6 hours as core temp effects on gut, kidneys, and clotting show up. So "fine at 9 pm" doesn't fully clear "fine at 2 am" — tonight I'd keep him in sight, not behind a closed door, until morning.

If he repeats this pattern (longer to settle, gets worse next time, or any of the signs above start), it's a vet call, not another wait-it-out.

Call: hold the reduced dose through the next 1-2 sessions, then step to 3x10. Do not couple the eversion dose to run-readiness.

Why now (one paragraph)
- Two consecutive pain-free exposures (ride + 2x8) is not yet a stable baseline. Restoring the printed dose is a load jump, not a return to baseline. The cost of holding one or two more sessions is essentially zero; the cost of stepping up and getting even a mild flare is that you lose the clean signal you've built.
- Pain-free walking and stairs are ADL-level. Resisted eversion at 2x8 is strength-level. Hopping is plyometric — a bigger jump than either, and a more relevant gate for run than eversion dose is.

Cuts
- "Ride was fine" is not load clearance. Ride is steady-state cardio at sub-bodyweight load.
- "Symptoms are gone" ≠ "tissue is loaded enough to take more." Pain is a lagging, coarse signal; absence of pain after one session is necessary but not sufficient to add load.
- Run-readiness is a separate decision and should not be unlocked by an eversion-dose increase. The relevant gates, in order: pain-free hopping → short walk/run intervals → continuous easy run. Eversion dose is rehab adherence, not run clearance.

Plan
- Hold 2x8 resisted eversion for 1-2 more sessions (so 3-4 total consecutive pain-free at the current dose), then step to 3x10 at the next session if everything stays symptom-free.
- Keep ride at current easy dose; no change there.
- Run remains on hold. The next live test in that lane is a single set of hops, separately and only when you decide it's time — not as a response to the eversion dose going back up.

Effect of the call
- Conservative, but the conservative choice here is cheap and protects the signal. Holding costs you a couple of sessions at a sub-target dose; stepping up prematurely risks losing the streak you've built.
- The "improvement is not clearance to run" line is preserved by design — the run lane has its own gate (hopping) that is independent of the eversion dose.

Plain version: stay at 2x8 for a couple more sessions, then go to 3x10. Hopping and running are a separate track and don't get unlocked by either number.

OVERNIGHT PRECAUTIONS

The leak stopped when you closed the dishwasher's local shutoff — that is your main control right now and the strongest clue. Keep it closed.

Tonight, in order:
1. Leave the local shutoff closed. Do not open it for any reason overnight.
2. Close the under-sink hot-water valve that feeds that shutoff. Most are quarter-turn. This is belt-and-suspenders: even a slow drip past the local valve will stop. Reopen it only when you run the diagnostic in the morning.
3. Leave the sink cabinet doors open all night. Airflow dries residual moisture, and you can hear or see anything new without pulling anything out.
4. Lay one dry paper towel flat on the cabinet floor directly under the supply connection. In the morning, dry = no overnight leak. This is your overnight tell.
5. Slide a shallow tray, cookie sheet, or a folded thick towel under the connection as a catch in case anything weeps past the valves.
6. Make sure the dishwasher cannot run on its own: cancel any delay-start, and if your model latches electrically, leave the door cracked. Unplugging is optional — the supply is already isolated — but a fine extra step if it helps you sleep.
7. Confirm the cabinet floor and the area under the dishwasher are dry to the touch before bed. No water near an outlet was already verified — keep it that way; don't shift anything wet toward outlets overnight.
8. Normal sink use in the kitchen is fine. Only the dishwasher branch is isolated.

DIAGNOSING SUPPLY FITTING vs DRAIN LEAK, NO DISASSEMBLY

Your facts already lean strongly toward supply: clean water, under the supply connection, and the leak stops when the supply shutoff is closed. A drain-side leak would not be affected by that valve. Still, a cheap confirmation in the morning:

Phase test (most decisive, one cycle):
- Dry the cabinet floor with a towel.
- Lay two fresh dry paper towels: one flat under the supply hose and valve connection, one under wherever the dishwasher drain hose enters the cabinet (usually a knockout or rubber boot at the back wall or side, dropping to the disposal or sink tailpiece).
- Open the local shutoff just enough to fill. Start a short cycle and watch.
- The supply side pressurizes during FILL — the first 2 to 5 minutes of the cycle. The drain side flows only during DRAIN, the last few minutes. Whichever towel darkens first identifies the source.
- If your model has a drain-only or cancel-drain function, run that first. A leak during drain-only with the supply closed proves drain side and lets you skip the fill phase.

Touch and listen test (faster, less certain):
- With the supply open and the dishwasher idle, put your hand on the supply hose and fitting. Dry = not leaking there right now. Start a fill and feel again — wet or a cold spot during fill = supply.
- A supply-side leak often hisses or ticks audibly when the valve is open and the dishwasher is idle, because of static pressure on the inlet. Drain-side leaks are silent until the pump runs.

Visual confirmation:
- Supply-side water is clean and cold or hot only. Drain-side water is often faintly gray and may carry food debris or soap foam. Clean water under the supply connection, with valve-stopped behavior, is almost certainly the supply fitting or hose.

Most likely culprits given what you saw, in order:
- Supply hose nut at the shutoff valve (worn gasket, slipped thread, or loose packing)
- Supply hose itself (small split, usually near the crimp)
- 90-degree elbow at the dishwasher inlet
- Valve packing nut
- Dishwasher internal inlet/fill solenoid (less likely — those usually drip whenever the supply is open, not only during cycles, so your valve-stopped symptom fits upstream of the unit better)

URGENT CALL vs WAIT

Call an emergency plumber tonight or first thing tomorrow — do not wait for a routine appointment — if any of these is true:
- The local shutoff will not close fully, or it spins freely without stopping flow. You cannot isolate.
- Water drips or runs despite both valves being closed.
- Water has reached or is approaching an electrical outlet, GFCI, junction box, the dishwasher's own electrical hookup, or any appliance cord.
- Water is spreading onto the kitchen floor beyond the cabinet base.
- Cabinet floor is swelling, bubbling, peeling, or soft to the touch — moisture intrusion is active.
- The supply line or shutoff valve looks bulged, cracked, corroded (green or white crust), or visibly deformed — burst risk.
- You smell sewage, rotten eggs, or gas. Different system, but flag it.
- The leak recurs and is clearly larger than two tablespoons when you run the diagnostic cycle.

Wait for a normal-schedule plumber (same-day or next-day) if:
- The cabinet stays dry overnight with the supply closed.
- No water near electrical.
- No structural swelling.
- The diagnostic confirms a small supply-side leak at a fitting — that is a 30 to 60 minute repair (new gasket, new hose, or new angle-stop) and is not urgent once isolated.

You can likely DIY-repair without a plumber at all if the diagnostic points to:
- The supply hose nut at the valve: close the local valve, unscrew the nut, replace the gasket/rubber washer, retighten. Use two wrenches — one on the valve body to hold it still, one on the nut — so you do not torque the valve and crack a solder joint behind it.
- The hose itself: replace it. A stainless-braided supply hose is about 15 to 25 dollars at any hardware store and takes 15 minutes with the same two-wrench technique. This is the most common fix for exactly the symptom you described.

If the leak turns out to be from the dishwasher's internal inlet valve, that is an appliance repair, not plumbing — a different tech, and not urgent while the supply is closed.

One last thing: do not run a diagnostic cycle tonight. The phase test wants you watching it, and any water you cannot immediately see is water you cannot immediately stop. Morning, cabinet doors open, towels in place, flashlight ready, is the right time.

Verdict: repeat the original intervals one more time (1-min jog / 2-min walk, 8 rounds). Do not step up to 90-second jogs on Sunday.

The plan's gate is technically met by your own report — both earlier sessions symptom-free, Friday through Saturday morning symptom-free, stair descent included. So you are not blocked. But "permitted" and "conservative" are different questions, and you asked for the conservative read. Here is why one more hold is the safer call:

1. The next step changes a parameter, not just volume.
   Going from 1-min to 90-sec jog bouts introduces a new variable — longer continuous stress per interval on the same tissue. Adding rounds is a volume change; lengthening the interval is a load-pattern change. Conservative progression usually wants more than one clean cycle at the current load before altering interval duration. You have one fully-reported cycle (Friday) plus the following-day observations. That is enough to keep going at 1-min, not quite enough to add a new parameter.

2. Stair descent is reassuring but is not a direct test of the next step.
   Stair descent is eccentric and largely single-leg. A 90-second continuous jog bout is repeated concentric loading at a sustained intensity. It corroborates recovery, but it does not replicate the specific demand you'd be adding. Don't count it as evidence for the 90s interval specifically.

3. Asymmetric downside.
   If you step up Sunday and get even a minor symptom during or after the session, the realistic next move is back to 1-min × 8, which costs you at least one full session and resets confidence. If you repeat 1-min × 8 and it passes clean, you go into the next progression decision with two consecutive clean sessions at the current load — strictly better evidence for stepping up to 90s after that. Cost of one more hold is small; cost of one premature step is larger.

4. "Permits" is not "requires."
   The plan gives you the choice. The conservative reading of a permitted step is to take it once the prior load has been clearly tolerated across more than one cycle, especially when the next step changes interval duration rather than round count.

Short version: gate is open, but the conservative move is one more clean 1-min × 8 session. Use the 90s × 7 step the session after that if this one passes clean.

Caveat: this is judgment based only on what you've reported here. If your therapist's written plan specifies a tighter or looser criterion than I'm reading into "both earlier sessions and following days pass," follow the plan over this read. But on the information you've given, repeat once more.

Sequence, in order from least to most risky — stop at the first step that gets you the soft edge you're after:

  1. Dry pass with a clean damp brush (not wet, just barely
     loaded). Drag it once along the bloom's hard edge, away
     from the eye and nose. This alone often breaks the
     cauliflower contour because bloom pigment sits loose on
     the surface. If the edge softens here, stop — you're done.

  2. If the dry pass isn't enough, lay clean water on the
     bloom zone only — a small pointed brush, no flood.
     Wait 10–20 seconds for the dry pigment to soften, then
     lift with a clean damp brush or a tissue blot. Keep the
     water envelope strictly on the cheek-to-muzzle transition;
     don't let it touch the eye or nose shapes.

  3. One pass. Then stop, regardless of outcome. Each repeat
     lifts a little eye/nose pigment along with bloom pigment,
     and you cannot selectively release one without the other —
     that's what produces mud.

Stopping point — name it before you start: stop when the
cauliflower edge has lost its hard contour and reads as a soft
tonal transition into the muzzle. Residual bloom texture is
the correct outcome. A perfectly clean edge is not the goal
and is not safely reachable without sacrificing the features.

If after one pass it's still too dark and you're tempted to go
again, switch tactics instead of re-lifting: glaze a thin
transparent wash of the muzzle value back over the bloom to
harmonize it. Additive glazing is safer than a second
subtractive pass because it won't disturb the eye and nose.

One environment note for future backlit Kibo studies: the
cauliflower bloom is a sign the cheek-to-muzzle edge went
in while the neighboring wash was still wet enough to push
pigment. On the next one, let the muzzle pale dry to a true
matte before laying the shadowed cheek into it — that kills
the bloom at the source rather than in correction.

Net change vs. June 28: same 30 lb case, same tested pre-staging sequence, same 60-min ceiling, same 44-portion floor. One person sequential becomes two people in parallel. The ceiling stays meaningful only if it's enforced on wall-clock (start-to-finish span), not on summed person-minutes — because summed minutes inflate the moment you split work between two people, and that inflation isn't labor you can recover.

**Task sequence (Friday)**

1. T-15 → T-10  Line cook pre-stages sheet pans, racks, hotel pans, probes, timer. Slot into existing prep window; log only marginal minutes.
2. T-10 → T-0  Sam confirms seasoning mix, sets oven temp/rack plan, lays probe.
3. T-0 (clock-stamp trial start)  Sam breaks down case, portions, seasons. Continuous run.
4. Concurrent with Sam's seasoning → load  Line cook moves finished pans from prep surface to oven-load position as each rack fills.
5. Sam stages oven (position racks, set timers, hand off probe target to probe-log).
6. Cook to target internal temp. Log only active checks; oven idle time is not labor.
7. Sam pulls, rests, portions to yield count.
8. Line cook clears empty pans and breaks down. Slot into a lull; log marginal minutes only.
9. T-end (clock-stamp trial close). Log final yield.

**Labor-logging method (marginal-minute stopwatch, per person)**

A. One card per person — Sam, line cook. Columns: Task | Start | End | Marginal min | Notes. Pre-print the trial task list so non-trial tasks don't get logged by mistake.

B. Counts (incremental only):
  - Sam: seasoning, oven staging, temp checks, pull/portion — only the slice beyond his normal closing shift. If Sam seasons chickens on a normal Friday close, those minutes don't count.
  - Line cook: pan pre-stage, pan clear, breakdown — only the slice between existing duties. If the line cook is already passing the dish pit, marginal cost is near zero; if it's a special trip, log the full round-trip.

C. Does NOT count:
  - Full scheduled shift hours.
  - Passive oven time (bird is cooking; nobody is laboring).
  - Anything the person would have done that night anyway, even if it falls inside the trial window.
  - Line cook's normal side work, even if it falls inside the trial window.

D. No-double-count rule — ceiling enforced on wall-clock, not summed minutes:
  - Trial start = first person begins a trial task. Trial end = last person finishes a trial task.
  - Wall-clock span (end − start) ≤ 60 min. This is the ceiling. Directly comparable to June 28, which was one person sequential — wall-clock equaled that person's minutes.
  - Person-minute sum (Sam marginal + line cook marginal) is logged separately for analysis. It will exceed 60 min and that's fine; it does not bust the ceiling.

E. June 28 comparability:
  - Primary comparison: wall-clock span. Apples to apples.
  - Secondary comparison: per-task minutes by task name (e.g., "seasoning 30 lb case — June 28 X min, Friday Y min"). Lets you see whether Sam is faster/slower at seasoning than the prep cook was.
  - Both numbers go on the card. Don't roll them into one figure.

F. Yield floor: 44 portions, counted at portioning, not raw case weight. Count goes on the same card.

G. Guardrail: if wall-clock span is past 55 min by the portioning step, stop the trial, count what was portioned, log it, and call it. Don't push past 60 to chase the yield floor — ceiling and floor are independent; missing one is a data point, not a failure.

Net result: a Friday number directly comparable to June 28, Sam's contribution separated from the line cook's, no inflation when the two overlap, and neither person's normal shift billed to the trial.
