REMOVAL (do this first)

1. Have someone steady Kibo's head — behind-the-ear is a sensitive spot and he'll likely flinch when you pull.
2. Part the fur so you can see the tick's mouthparts meeting the skin. With your fine-tipped tweezers, grasp the tick as close to the skin as possible — pinch the head/mouthparts, not the body. Pinching the body can squeeze more pathogen-laden saliva into the bite.
3. Pull straight up with steady, even pressure. No twisting, no jerking, no rocking. Slow and constant is the goal; it usually takes 3–5 seconds.
4. If the mouthparts break off and stay embedded: don't dig. Clean the area and let it work out on its own over a few days. Mention it to the vet at the next visit, but it's not an emergency on its own.
5. Do a quick once-over of the rest of his coat while you're hands-on. In Austin we mostly deal with Lone Star ticks and their nymphs are poppy-seed sized and easy to miss, especially in ear folds, under the collar, armpits, groin, and between toes.

AFTERCARE

1. Drop the live tick into a small sealed bag or jar with a slightly damp paper towel or a cotton ball with a few drops of rubbing alcohol. Label it with the date and "Kibo, behind left ear." This keeps it intact for ID if symptoms show up later — don't crush it between your fingers.
2. Clean the bite site on Kibo with mild antiseptic (chlorhexidine or diluted betadine). Don't use harsh alcohol or hydrogen peroxide on broken skin.
3. Watch the site daily for 2–4 weeks. A small pink bump that flattens in a few days is normal. A red ring that expands (especially a bull's-eye pattern) is not.

WHAT TO DO WITH THE TICK

- Keep it in the sealed container at room temperature or in the fridge for ~4 weeks, in case your vet wants to send it for species testing later.
- Don't flush a live one or burn it — flushing doesn't always kill them and burning risks releasing aerosolized pathogens.
- If you want to dispose of it sooner, submerge in rubbing alcohol for several days, then toss.

LOCAL SIGNS — call the vet (not urgent, but book soon)

- Red ring expanding outward from the bite, especially with a clearing center (bull's-eye / erythema migrans). This can appear anywhere from 3 to 30 days post-bite.
- Redness, swelling, warmth, or discharge at the site that worsens past day 2–3 instead of improving.
- A small hard nodule that persists more than a couple of weeks.

WHOLE-BODY SIGNS — urgent vet / urgent care

Any of these within 2–4 weeks of the bite (some diseases have longer incubation):

- Lethargy, reluctance to move, or sudden lameness / stiff gait that shifts legs.
- Fever (warm ears, panting at rest, shivering).
- Loss of appetite or refusing food for more than a meal.
- Vomiting or diarrhea.
- Pale or tacky gums.
- Wobbliness, weakness in the back legs, or change in bark/voice (think tick paralysis, which can progress fast).
- Facial swelling, hives, or sudden itch all over (allergic reaction).
- Difficulty breathing.

CALL THE VET ABOUT THE TICK ITSELF IF

- You think it was attached more than ~24 hours (longer attachment = higher pathogen transmission risk; worth a phone consult even with no symptoms).
- It is engorged when you find it (already fed).
- You can't get it out cleanly.
- Kibo isn't current on tick-borne disease prevention (we can talk about year-round preventatives for Central Texas — it's tick season essentially year-round here).

ONE AUSTIN-SPECIFIC NOTE

Lone Star tick bites (very common in Travis County) have been linked to alpha-gal syndrome — a delayed allergic reaction to red meat and sometimes dairy that can develop weeks to months after a single bite. Worth knowing as a longer-term possibility, but not something to act on now. If Kibo ever develops hives, vomiting, or restlessness 2–6 hours after eating beef, pork, lamb, or dairy down the road, mention the tick history to the vet.

He's acting normally, you have the right tool, and you avoided the old bad advice (oil/heat/alcohol) — you're already on the right track.

Lifting step (dry paper, single transparent glaze — pigment is bound but still liftable):

1. Pre-dampen a soft mop (sable or synthetic equivalent) with clean water, then blot it so it's damp, not wet. Touch, don't flood.
2. Lay the damp mop on a small zone of the warm bank for ~10–15 seconds — just long enough to swell the binder, not long enough for water to migrate toward the horizon opening.
3. Press a clean dry blotter/paper towel onto the swollen zone and lift straight up. Don't rub — rubbing drives pigment into the tooth and kills the granulation you're trying to keep.
4. Repeat in adjacent zones, working top-down toward the bank base. Stop while the area still reads slightly warm rather than pushing it to chalky white — chalky is unrecoverable without re-glazing over it.

Edge control near the pale opening: approach from inside the bank, never cross the edge. If you need a barrier, hold a small piece of torn paper towel as a mask along the horizon line while you lift the zone closest to it.

Let it bone-dry before the next pass.

Cooler glaze (after the lift is dry):

- Mix a thin wash of Payne's grey with a touch of dioxazine purple — Payne's granulates, the purple knocks the warmth toward storm-violet without going chalky. Dilute until it reads as a tea-stained tint on a test strip.
- Optional: a half-drop of burnt sienna if you want the lower bank to still register as warm-ish storm light rather than going pure slate.
- Lay it with the same soft mop in one even pass over the bank, leaving the horizon opening untouched. Thin enough that the existing granulation still reads through.
- While the glaze is still damp, drop a slightly stronger Payne's grey or a touch of burnt umber into the very base of the bank and let it settle — that gives you a darker anchored bottom without restating the whole shape.

Dry flat. Don't go back in.

The whole sequence is lift → dry → cool glaze → dry. No scrubbing, no wet-on-wet against the reserved opening.

Summary: both problems are capture-side, not condition-side, so the fix is a targeted reshoot of only those two sides under adjusted lighting, with the original files kept for audit. No print is touched, IDs stay on the prints, the treated cohort is never re-staged.

Procedure

1. Scope lock (before anyone handles a print)
   - Work only with P007 and P014. Confirm the eight treated photographs remain in their separate housing and are not on the staging surface at any point.
   - Read the temporary IDs aloud and match them to the prints before the reshoot and again after; do not reissue or relabel.
   - Use a clean, dust-controlled staging area; clean hands or clean cotton gloves; no pens, no solvents, no labels anywhere near the prints.

2. P007 front (glare)
   - Cause is specular reflection from the capture lighting, not a print defect. Fix at the copy stand, not on the print.
   - Reposition: two diffused lights at roughly 45 degrees each side, equidistant, at a lower angle than the first pass; or a single raking light from the side opposite the obscured region.
   - Add a polarizing filter on the lens crossed with polarizers on both lights to kill surface reflection if the diffused setup still glares.
   - Bracket three exposures around the original setting so the obscured area is recoverable in at least one frame.
   - Keep the camera square to the print; do not tilt to dodge glare, since tilt distorts geometry.

This pattern — small (≈4 mm), pink, mildly raised, with a dry center, no warmth, no drainage, no marked tenderness, and a normally behaving dog five days after tick removal — fits a common minor local reaction to tick saliva and the small mechanical injury from the bite/removal. Local immune response to tick antigens often produces a papule that lingers for days to a couple of weeks. The absence of systemic signs (normal eating, gait, breathing, no feverish behavior, no facial swelling) is reassuring at this point.

That said: a tick bite is also a potential pathogen-exposure event, so the answer isn't really "yes, ignore it" — it's "yes, it fits a minor local reaction, and here is how to keep watching it without making it worse." I'm a personal assistant, not a veterinarian, so treat this as general care guidance, not a diagnosis.

Caring for the site without irritating it

  - Don't squeeze, lance, scratch, or pick at the bump. Don't pull off the dry crust if it isn't ready to come off.
  - Don't apply over-the-counter antibiotic ointments, hydrocortisone, essential oils, alcohol, hydrogen peroxide, or anything not specifically approved by your vet — dogs lick, and several of those are problematic if ingested.
  - If you want to clean it, plain lukewarm water on a soft cloth or a dilute chlorhexidine solution your vet approves is fine. Pat dry, don't rub.
  - Keep Kibo from scratching or rubbing the spot. If she's bothering it, a soft e-collar, a snug t-shirt, or a snood behind the ears tends to work better than bandaging (bandages slip behind the ear and often irritate the area more).
  - Photograph it once a day next to a ruler or coin for scale. That gives your vet a clean size/color record if anything changes.
  - No need to restrict normal activity; normal walking and playing won't worsen a local reaction.

Routine veterinary call (next-day or scheduled appointment, not an emergency)

  - Bump grows past roughly 7–10 mm, becomes more raised or firm, or develops a ring/donut shape around the original center
  - Mild itch develops or the crust repeatedly falls off and reforms
  - It looks unchanged at the 2–3 week mark rather than fading
  - You find additional ticks on Kibo, or weren't sure the head/mouthparts all came out and the spot stays firm
  - Any low-grade behavior change that lasts more than 24 hours — slightly off food, slightly quieter than usual, mild stiffness — even without dramatic symptoms

Urgent or same-day vet visit (or ER if after hours)

  - Rapid enlargement, spreading redness (especially a "bull's-eye" with central clearing), or new redness tracking away from the site
  - Significant swelling, heat, obvious pain, or any pus/drainage
  - Lethargy, weakness, reluctance to move, or sudden lameness / joint swelling
  - Feverish behavior — panting at rest in a cool room, warm ears/footpads, shivering
  - Vomiting or diarrhea lasting more than ~12–24 hours, or a noticeable drop in appetite lasting more than a day
  - Facial swelling, hives, sudden intense itching, or any breathing changes — these are allergic-reaction red flags
  - Pale gums or yellowing of the whites of the eyes or gums

A useful frame on timing: tick-borne illness incubation windows don't line up neatly with the bite date. Anaplasma and Ehrlichia tend to surface in roughly 1–3 weeks; RMSF in 2–14 days; Lyme arthritis often shows up 2–5 months later. So "she looked fine at week one" doesn't close the book — the watchfulness for low-grade changes is the more useful long-tail habit than the first-week spot check. If you want to flag the exposure to your vet now (just by phone or message) so it's on Kibo's record, that's reasonable and doesn't require a visit.

SHORT ANSWER
The hallway wall is the safest of the three for the watercolor.

WHY THE LIVING ROOM IS NOT SAFE
- West-facing direct sun from roughly 3 to 5 pm is the harshest light exposure a typical home wall gets. Even with UV-filtering acrylic, that is still two hours of unfiltered visible light and heat on the glazing.
- UV-filtering acrylic typically blocks about 97 to 99 percent of UV radiation. It does not block visible light, and visible light alone fades many watercolor pigments over time. Some pigments used in watercolor are fugitive (notoriously light-sensitive) and will shift noticeably at lower light levels than people expect.
- Direct sun also heats the acrylic. Heat accelerates every form of degradation on paper and on the acrylic itself, and heat buildup behind glazing is a real risk on a west wall.

WHY THE KITCHEN IS NOT SAFE
- No direct sun is good for the light side of the ledger, but the humidity problem is real. Watercolor paper is hygroscopic; it absorbs and releases moisture, and repeated cycling is what does the damage (not a single humid day).
- Beyond humidity, kitchens put grease aerosols,油烟, and acidic vapors (citrus, vinegar, wine reduction) into the air. Those deposit on the frame and can work past the glazing seal onto the paper.
- A tightly sealed frame can trap that moisture against the paper. If you cannot see condensation, that is good. If you ever do, the backing has failed.

WHY THE HALLWAY WINS
- Indirect light means low UV and low overall visible-light exposure. Cumulative fading is what destroys watercolors, so low light is the single biggest lever.
- Steady humidity means the paper does not cycle, which removes the cockling/mold/false-mount risk.
- The farther viewing distance is purely an aesthetic trade-off, not a preservation one. If the piece matters, viewers will cross the room.

PRACTICAL PLACEMENT PRECAUTIONS FOR THE HALLWAY

1. Verify "indirect" really is indirect, all year.
   Direct sun shifts seasonally. Check the wall at the summer solstice when the sun is highest; a window across the hall can cast a beam onto a wall that is safe in winter.

2. Prefer an interior wall over an exterior wall.
   Exterior walls swing more in temperature and relative humidity. Interior walls track room conditions, which you can actually control.

3. Stay clear of HVAC supply and return vents, and any radiator.
   Forced air dries and re-humidifies paper faster than the room does. A return vent directly behind the piece is a hidden culprit.

4. Hold indoor relative humidity around 40 to 50 percent.
   Use a small hygrometer near the piece. Below about 35 percent the paper gets brittle; above about 55 percent mold risk climbs. A dehumidifier in humid months is a cheap insurance policy.

5. Make sure the frame is built right (or have it reframed if any of this is missing).
   - UV-filtering glazing (you already have this).
   - Acid-free, lignin-free mounting board and backing.
   - A spacer or window mat so the artwork never touches the acrylic. If condensation ever forms inside the frame, that gap is what saves the paper.
   - Backing paper or foil tape sealing the rear against dust and minor moisture migration.
   - The frame should NOT be airtight. It needs to breathe so humidity inside equilibrates with the room instead of building up.

6. Light levels on the wall, not just at the window.
   Aim for under about 150 lux on the surface for fugitive watercolor pigments (museum guidance for highly light-sensitive works on paper). If you add a picture light, use LED, never incandescent or halogen. LEDs emit very little UV and almost no heat on the surface.

7. Use proper hanging hardware.
   D-rings and braided wire rated for the framed weight. A single sawtooth on a heavy frame is a future floor incident. In a hallway, also think about traffic: a frame at shoulder height in a narrow corridor is a bump risk.

8. Inspect quarterly.
   Look for foxing (small reddish-brown spots), any visible cockling through the glazing, frame-seal gaps, and dust inside the glazing. If moisture ever appears between the acrylic and the paper, the seal/backing has failed and the piece needs a reframer.

9. Plan for rotation if you want it to last decades.
   Cumulative fading is irreversible. Limiting total hours of exposure is the only real lever. Rotating the piece off display for a few months every couple of years (or having a second piece to swap in) is the simplest long-term plan.

10. Never relocate it to the kitchen or a bathroom "temporarily."
    That is the single most common way a piece like this gets quietly damaged. If you ever move homes or rearrange, the hallway-grade spot is the one to preserve.

ONE NOTE ON YOUR UV-FILTERING ACRYLIC
It is doing real work, but treat it as one layer of a system, not a shield. It buys you time against UV specifically; it does not protect against visible-light fading, heat, humidity cycling, or pollutants. The other layers are the wall choice, the wall conditions, the frame build, and light level on the surface. Those four are what actually decide how the piece looks in 10 and 30 years.

TRADE-OFF

Same coverage both ways ($40k property / $300k liability). The only things changing are the annual premium and the deductible:

  $1,000 deductible  -> $312/year
  $2,500 deductible  -> $276/year  ($36/yr savings)

The $36 is what you gain. The $1,500 is what you give up per claim. Those are not comparable units:

  - Premium: certain, paid every year, small.
  - Deductible exposure: contingent, paid only when you file a claim, large.

For the higher deductible to be the rational pick, you'd need the $1,500 extra out-of-pocket per claim to be outweighed by $36/year in premium savings. Break-even probability is roughly 2.4% per year (36 / 1,500) -- and that's the bare breakeven; it doesn't price in the fact that real claims are lumpy and indivisible. You don't get to claim $750 of deductible; you pay all $2,500 or $0.

The framing trap: "lower premium" sounds like a discount, but it's really the insurer paying you $36/year to absorb $1,500 of risk. That is a bad price for risk transfer.

WHY THE $1,000 DEDUCTIBLE IS THE SENSIBLE CHOICE

1. Renters claims are moderate-loss, not catastrophic. Typical events (theft, small fire, upstairs-neighbor water damage) often run $2k-$10k in personal property loss. On those, the deductible is the dominant out-of-pocket piece -- the $1,500 bump shrinks the band where insurance actually helps. At $1,000 deductible, insurance meaningfully engages at ~$1k+ losses. At $2,500, you're effectively self-insuring up to $2,500, which is the same risk profile as having meaningfully less coverage.

2. The savings don't compound meaningfully against the exposure. $36/year over a 5-year policy span is $180 saved against a $1,500 contingent hit. A single claim in that window reverses the "savings" by 8x or more.

3. $36/year is not a real budget lever. It's $3/month. Optimizing $36 of certain spend against $1,500 of contingent risk is the wrong direction to spend decision-making energy.

4. No information in the conversation suggests claim frequency is unusually low (high-rise fire risk, prior claims history, very low-value contents, etc.). In the absence of a reason to think claims are rare, default to keeping the deductible low.

RECOMMENDATION

Keep the $1,000 deductible at $312/year. Renew at the original terms.

The insurer structured the offer so the lower premium *looks* like the better deal on the surface -- that is the point of the framing. The actual economics ($36 certain vs. $1,500 contingent, break-even ~2.4% claim probability, no offsetting benefit to you) favor the lower deductible unambiguously. File the renewal at $312 before Friday.

The overall picture you describe — flattening, fading pink color, no heat, drainage, swelling, tenderness, or enlargement, and a dog acting normally two weeks out — is a reassuring normal-healing trajectory. A small dry scab at this stage is expected.

1. Should you leave the dry scab alone?
Yes. Don't pick, pull, soak, or scrub it. The intact dry scab is the body's own dressing; it will shed on its own over the next days to a couple of weeks. The only mechanical risk here is that the spot is behind the ear, where Kibo can reach it with a hind paw and can also rub it on furniture or carpet — so the main job is to make sure he leaves it alone.

2. Is any cleaning still useful?
Minimal to none. With no inflammation or exudate, antiseptic scrubs are counterproductive. If the area gets visibly soiled after a walk, a damp cloth with plain water (or very dilute chlorhexidine) can wipe AROUND the scab gently, then pat dry. Skip alcohol, hydrogen peroxide, and topical antibiotic ointments — dogs lick them off and they slow epithelialization. No need to bathe the spot or apply anything to the scab itself.

3. Changes that would justify a routine (non-emergency) vet call despite the improvement:
- The scab or the bump under it enlarges, or a new firm lump appears at the site (a persistent "tick-bite granuloma" can form; usually benign but worth a look if it doesn't resolve by 4–6 weeks).
- Pinkness, heat, or tenderness returns after having faded.
- Any new discharge — pus, blood, or persistent clear fluid.
- Kibo starts scratching the area, rubbing it on furniture, or shaking/flapping the ear more than usual — self-trauma behind the ear is the most common reason a healing tick site goes sideways.
- The scab is still firmly adherent past 4–6 weeks with no progress.
- Any systemic sign over the next 4–8 weeks: lethargy, appetite drop, fever, unexplained lameness or joint stiffness, or swollen lymph nodes. Tick-borne pathogens (Lyme, ehrlichia, anaplasma, RMSF) typically incubate 2–4 weeks, so a routine call — not an emergency — is appropriate if any of those show up, even if the bite site itself still looks fine.

If none of those appear and the scab lifts on its own in the next week or two, no call is needed.

The "pasted" read comes from a shadow that's chromatically unrelated to the lit fur. Neutral grays sit on top of the figure instead of reading as absence of light. Cool shadows share pigment DNA with the warm object: ultramarine mixed with a small amount of burnt sienna produces a slate that cools without looking "added."

Mix to make before touching paper:
  - Ultramarine blue + burnt sienna, stirred on the palette until you reach a soft blue-slate with a whisper of warmth. The burnt sienna is the cohesion move — without it the shadow reads as a separate thing laid beside the fur.
  - Optional depth: a touch of cobalt for a softer cast, or a hint of dioxazine violet for atmospheric cool. Not required.
  - Avoid: ivory black, lamp black, paynes gray straight (too dead); phthalo blue (stains and goes chalky when dry).

Dilution:
  - Tea-strength for every pass. A wash that looks almost too pale wet is the right amount dry. Pigment darkens as it dries — go pale.

Sequence (each layer dry before the next):

  1. Contact shadow first. The single anchor — the small, darkest band where the body meets the floor. Same mix, not diluted further. Small pointed round, loaded but not wet. Keep it tight; it shouldn't extend more than a body's thickness from the underside. This is the move that makes Kibo sit on the floor instead of float on it.

  2. Cast shadow, far half. Same mix, slightly cooler (more ultramarine, less burnt sienna), equally dilute. Lay it on the bare paper trailing away from the contact zone as a single confident stroke. Stop short of the rim-light zone with a clean edge there; soften the far/dissipating edge with a barely-damp brush tip while still wet.

  3. Cast shadow, near half — between the contact zone and the figure edge, on bare paper. Slightly warmer (more burnt sienna) to harmonize with the fur above. Same dilution. This is what tells the eye the figure is one object, not a sticker.

  4. Optional: ambient occlusion accents — under the chin, inside leg creases, where the belly meets the floor. Almost dry-brush, very dilute, almost no pigment transfer. A whisper.

What protects the preserved rim light:
  - Brush only as wet as you need. A loaded round will bleed across dry paper within a millimeter of contact.
  - Work with strokes moving TOWARD Kibo, not away. Pulling a stroke away from the figure into the shadow leaves a clean edge on the body side; pushing outward toward the figure risks creeping into the rim.
  - Never rewet the rim-light zone. If a stroke ends too close, soften with a barely-damp brush and patience, not a loaded one.
  - The glaze lives on bare paper in the cast-shadow zone. It does not go over the rust fur — that path is what contaminates the warm reading.

Order with what's still pending:
  - Do this glaze before facial details. Both dark eye/nose work and the cast-shadow glaze want a dry figure and a clean dry rim. Anchoring the floor plane first means facial features get placed against a properly seated figure rather than guessed.

Here is a conservative temporary plan for the 40 stabilized photographs (32 dry + 8 retouched in sleeves/boxes) until the A/C is restored.

1) Decision on whether to move them at all
- 67% RH for ~6 hours is a real excursion from the 30–50% target, but for a single overnight event with dry, non-condensing boxes and sleeves, it is below the threshold where mold growth, dye bleed, or gelatin softening actually starts to occur. Six hours at 67% does not, by itself, require a relocation scramble.
- Verdict: do NOT move the boxes as a reflex. Movement introduces handling, jostling, and the real risk of a fast RH/temperature swing if boxes are opened into dry air. The first move is to stabilize conditions in place.

2) Where to relocate IF conditions worsen or boxes must be moved
- Best room in the house: the interior room most distant from the failed A/C closet, on an interior wall, off the floor (on a bed or chair seat), away from any window, kitchen, bathroom, or exterior door. Climate-controlled interior closet with a working door is ideal.
- Acceptable substitute: the coolest interior closet that is NOT the failed one. Keep the closet door closed.
- Avoid: garage, attic, basement, car trunk, bathroom, laundry room, kitchen, or any room with a humidifier, dehumidifier cycling on/off, or active airflow.
- Transport rule: carry boxes flat, do not tilt, keep lids seated (do not latch/unlatch), no stacking changes. Use a clean sheet or pillowcase as a sling if you need to cover a box in transit. Do not open sleeves to "check on" photos en route.

3) How to monitor WITHOUT opening boxes or causing a swing
- Place a small hygrometer/thermometer on the OUTSIDE of the closet — on the door exterior at mid-height, not inside. Read it without opening the door. Note time and reading each check.
- Second, even cheaper monitor: a strip of plain white paper towel taped to the exterior of the closet door. If humidity is bleeding through, the paper will feel cool/damp to a fingertip without opening anything. Touch only briefly; do not move the strip.
- If you want an in-closet reading without opening repeatedly, slide a small Bluetooth hygrometer (e.g., Govee/HygroSet) inside on the shelf next to the boxes ONCE, leave the door closed, and read the phone app remotely. If you don't have one already, don't go buy one and crack the door repeatedly — skip.
- Check cadence: every 60–90 minutes while awake. Never more often than every 30 minutes. Do not open the closet door just to "look."
- Do NOT run a household dehumidifier pointed at the closet door — the on/off cycling creates larger swings than the steady elevated RH.
- Do NOT run a fan or open windows for "cross ventilation" — that exchanges humid outdoor air for indoor air and can make things worse.

4) What signs would warrant conservator advice (call before opening anything)
- Any visible condensation on box lids, sleeves, or the closet walls.
- Any new odor when the door is opened briefly — musty, sweet, or chemical.
- Any tackiness or curl on a sleeve surface (only check by opening ONE box briefly if a smell is detected; otherwise don't).
- RH staying above 60% for more than 24 cumulative hours, OR rising above 70% at any single reading.
- Room temperature rising above ~80°F (26.7°C) — heat + humidity together is the damage multiplier.
- Any sign of water intrusion from an unrelated source (roof leak, plumbing, spill near closet).

5) When the A/C is restored
- Do NOT bring the closet back to 50% RH instantly. Let it drift down over 12–24 hours with the door closed. A fast drop from 67% to 40% in minutes can cause emulsion cracking and sleeve curl on gelatin prints — the swing is more dangerous than the excursion itself.

Short answer: a boot is a get-home measure, not for ordinary riding, and yes — visible casing on a sidewall cut means replace before your next loaded commute.

Why a boot isn't enough here:

A boot's job is to keep air in long enough to ride to a place where you can fix the problem properly. It's an emergency patch, not ongoing repair. Sidewalls flex under load every rotation, and a boot doesn't restore structural strength — it just covers the hole. Under your weight, road vibration, and heat buildup, sidewall cuts tend to grow, and a booted cut still lets debris and water work into the casing plies. If the boot fails mid-commute, you're looking at a sudden flat at speed.

Why visible casing tips it to replacement:

The casing is the tire's structural layer. Once it's exposed on a sidewall, the tire's integrity is compromised at that point and the damage will propagate under normal flexing. Patches and boots don't restore casing strength — that's why manufacturers treat exposed casing on a sidewall as a retire-the-tire condition, regardless of whether it currently holds air.

What "holds pressure, no bulge" actually tells you:

Good news: the casing isn't actively separating yet and you don't have an immediate blowout. But that's "not failing yet," not a safety clearance — those conditions can change quickly once the tire is loaded and hot on a real ride. The absence of bulge is not the absence of risk.

Practical recommendation:

If you need to ride today, boot it just to get home or to a shop, and carry a spare tube. Replace before your next loaded commute. A commuter tire in the $25-50 range is cheap insurance compared to a crash or a roadside repair in traffic — and given that you bike in three days a week, the tire sees real load regularly, so don't push this one to its limit.

If you want to keep the tire around, it's fine as a shop spare for non-loaded errands, but I'd retire it from road duty on the commuter.

Here is the distinction, framed for Marcus (and for the record on the proposal):

SUMMARY
The $364.62 is the average refund-adjusted cash per admitted workspace in a matched mature Helio Start cohort. It is not a paid CAC, and treating it as an allowable ceiling for a paid-acquisition test would be a relabel, not a measurement.

WHAT THE $364.62 ACTUALLY IS
$18,960 in refund-adjusted cash, collected from 52 workspaces in this cohort, divided by those 52 workspaces. That is the average cash a workspace paid once it was already in, observed under whatever acquisition mix produced the cohort in the first place. It describes earnings from an already-admitted group, not the cost of getting the next workspace in.

WHAT MAKES A PAID CAC, AND WHY THIS NUMBER IS NOT ONE
A paid CAC needs four things, and none of them are in this calculation:

  1. A paid-media spend line that the conversions are credited against.
  2. An acquisition mix — paid vs organic vs referral vs other — so you can isolate the paid slice.
  3. A paid-channel response comparison — what changes in conversion when paid spend is on vs off.
  4. An incrementality read — how many of the conversions would not have happened without the paid spend.

The $18,960 / 52 figure has zero spend, zero mix, zero channel comparison, and zero incrementality. The cohort came in through whatever channels produced it; the cash reflects that mix, not a paid cost.

WHY THIS MATTERS FOR A PAID TEST

Two framings, one arc. Opening surfaces the divergence; follow-up makes the costs visible from both sides.

Opening: "Reader A sees the narrator as competent; Reader B doesn't. Whose reading is closer to what the narrator themselves believes — and what do we miss if we're wrong?"

Follow-up: "If the narrator stopped performing competence the way Reader A admires, who actually loses more — the narrator, or the people who'd been getting to lean on the role?"

What each is doing, plain: the opening forces readers to choose between rewarding the role and reading the person, and to notice whose self-conception they've been tracking. The follow-up makes the costs land on different parties — and once the costs split that way, personal responsibility stops being a single question (was the narrator competent?) and becomes two (whose need was the role actually serving, and what does the narrator owe themselves vs. the people the role has been feeding). Distinct from needed-vs-known: that one was about being valued for use vs. for selfhood; this one is about whether the competence on display was ever owned or only ever rented out.

A paid-acquisition model built today would need fabricated CAC, channel mix, and conversion assumptions — and a fabricated-inputs model that *looks* rigorous is more dangerous than gut feel, because it produces false confidence in a number that will drive real spend.

- **Bad-decision risk.** A premature model could justify a premature spend commitment before retention unit economics are validated. That's a one-way door we don't need to walk through 2.5 weeks early.

PHASE 0 — Pre-flight (do this BEFORE touching the next photo)

  0.1  Switch the scanner to TIFF / RAW mode. Turn OFF every "auto" setting:
       auto-exposure, auto-color, auto-contrast, sharpening, descreening,
       dust removal, fade correction, backlight correction. None of these.

  0.3  Include a color target AND a grayscale step wedge in the first capture

  0.4  Decide and write down the ID scheme now, before handling anything:
       - Continue from P024 onward. P023 and P028 are already taken.

  0.5  Open the log. One row per photo, columns:
       temp_id | front_master_path | back_master_path | access_copy_path
       | sha256_master | condition_notes | inscriptions
       | attribution_status | pairing_verified
       The log row is the source of truth — not the sleeve, not the filename.


PHASE 1 — Per-photo loop (repeat 8x, in this exact order)

  Step 1.  Assign next temp ID. Write it in the log FIRST, before scanning.

  Step 2.  Conservator condition note. With the photo on a clean surface
           under raked light, BEFORE any capture, record:
           - corners, edges, surface (emulsion vs. paper)
           - tears, creases, foxing, tape residue, water damage
           - visible inscriptions on BOTH sides at handling time
             (do not rely on the scan to find them)
           - anything that must NOT be cleaned off
           If a family memory conflicts with what's physically on the photo,
           mark "superseded family attribution" — record both, do not erase.

  Step 3.  Capture FRONT.
           - Photo face-up, color target in frame.
           - TIFF, no auto-correction, full optical resolution.
           - File: PNNN_front_master.tif
           - Spot-check on screen: open it, confirm it matches the print.
             If it doesn't, re-capture now before moving on.

  Step 4.  Capture BACK. Every back, every time — even blank ones.
           This is what makes front-to-back pairing unambiguous.

           - Back with faint pencil: confirm legibility in capture under
             raked light. Do NOT rely on software to surface it.
           - File: PNNN_back_master.tif
           - Spot-check on screen before moving on.

           - The log row is the join. temp_id is the only thing tying
             front_master and back_master together.
           - Filenames contain ONLY the temp ID. No "Austin", no "Uncle Bob",
             no speculative names anywhere on disk.

  Step 6.  Checksum.
           - SHA-256 of each master TIFF, recorded in the log.

           - File: PNNN_front_access.jpg / PNNN_back_access.jpg

  Step 9.  Re-sleeve.

  Step 10. Attribution status.

Where you are now: 2 copies (laptop + external drive), 2 media types (SSD + HDD), and 1 offsite once the drive is at Mom's house. That is close to the 3-2-1 rule but missing the third copy. The gap to close before the drive goes is adding that third copy and proving every copy matches. Practical sequence, in order:

1. Verify on the laptop first, before anything moves
   - Confirm the eight P033-P040 filenames are exactly what the session verified (case, extension, no truncation by the filesystem)
   - Generate SHA-256 hashes of all eight TIFF masters into a manifest file (for example, sha256_P033-P040_2024-08-29.txt). Do the same for the access copies in a separate manifest. These files travel with every backup copy
   - A manifest is what lets you prove "this is the verified state" later. Filenames alone don't catch silent corruption; hashes do

2. Build the external drive layout before copying
   - Top-level folders that separate masters from access copies by intent, not just by file type:
       tiff_masters/        (unaltered, archival)
       access_copies/       (altered, working/reference)
       manifests/           (the hash files from step 1)
   - Filenames stay P033.tif through P040.tif inside tiff_masters/ and the matching access-copy names inside access_copies/. Do not mix them in one folder, and do not give access copies the .tif extension just because the basename matches. Different folder plus different extension is belt-and-suspenders, and either one alone has failure modes
   - Reason: future-you or Mom opening the drive six months from now must not be able to grab an access copy by accident and treat it as the archival master

3. Copy with verification, not just copy
   - Copy the TIFF masters first using a tool that verifies on write (rsync -c, teracopy, or similar), so hashes are checked at copy time rather than at a separate pass
   - Re-run the hash manifest against what's now on the drive and confirm every line matches
   - Then copy the access copies and their manifest the same way
   - Catches a bad sector on the destination drive before the laptop is your only remaining copy

4. Close the 3-2-1 gap with a third copy
   - The two you have cover local and offsite but only two copies total. Add a third. In rough order of preference:
     a) Cloud archival (Backblaze B2 at roughly $0.005/GB/mo is the typical pick; 8 TIFFs is a rounding-error cost). Offsite, automatic, survives drive failure at either physical location
     b) Second external drive at a third physical location (office, bank safe deposit box, a sibling's house). Cheap upfront, but you own the rotation and refresh cycle
     c) A NAS at home with redundancy is third-place here because it shares the laptop's risk envelope for fire, flood, and theft
   - Whichever you pick, replicate the same tiff_masters/ + access_copies/ + manifests/ layout and verify hashes on receipt

5. Hand the drive to Mom with a small README
   - One page (or a sticky note on the drive) that says: what is on the drive, where the canonical master folder is, that access copies are NOT masters, when it was last verified, and where the third copy lives
   - Mom does not need to run anything; she needs to know not to "tidy up" the folders, not to plug the drive into a Mac and let Photos import it, and not to reformat it if her computer asks

6. After-care cadence
   - Once a year (and before any media migration), re-run the hash manifest against every copy. Bit rot is rare on healthy drives but it is the failure mode you cannot see
   - Treat the external drive as a 3-5 year item, not permanent. When Mom's drive nears that age, migrate to a fresh drive, regenerate the manifest, and replace. Cloud handles this automatically; physical drives do not

On the "physical originals are not the only fallback" point: this is the right call. Treating archival storage as the only safety net means a single handling event at the storage facility can take the only true master. The arrangement above gives you three independent digital copies, each verifiable, with the physical collection as a fourth independent source rather than the load-bearing one.

Two small flags worth raising before you start:

  - If any access copy was saved with the same basename as the TIFF and only a different extension, double-check that the destination filesystem does not hide one of them. Some tools and OSes will show only one when extensions are mismatched. Separate folders solve this; it is just worth eyeballing once
  
  - If the external drive is the same one that held an earlier batch (P001-P032 or similar), confirm it has been reformatted, or at minimum that the older batch sits in a clearly separated folder. Mixed generations on one drive are how filenames drift across batches

"Rhythmic, only under load, fine on the stand" almost always means something that changes geometry when you put weight on the bike, not a rotational defect you can see unweighted. For a freshly-installed 700x32 with a puncture belt, the most likely culprits in rough order of probability:

1. QR / thru-axle not fully tensioned. The wheel can shift laterally in the dropouts the moment you load the bike. Standing over the bike, close the QR lever with full palm pressure; for a thru-axle, torque to spec. Then bounce-test.

2. Tire bead not fully seated all the way around. A puncture belt makes the casing stiffer and harder to seat evenly. Look at the bead line — the narrow ridge running circumferentially just inside the tread. It should sit the same distance from the rim edge the full 360°. Any high spot means the bead hasn't snapped into the rim hook there; under load that section grows and the tire tracks off-center. Inflate to sidewall max, deflate to operating pressure, and recheck — the bead often seats on the second cycle.

3. Brake caliper not centered. The single most common cause of post-service rub.
   - Rim brake: spin the wheel and watch the gap between rim and each pad. Recenter via the caliper's centering screw, or loosen the mounting nut, pull the caliper body by hand until pad gaps are equal, retighten.
   - Disc brake: loosen the two caliper bolts a half-turn, squeeze and hold the brake lever (this self-centers the caliper on the rotor), retighten the bolts while still holding the lever.

4. Wheel true. Spin the unloaded wheel and watch the rim-to-pad gap (or the rotor-to-pad gap through the caliper window). It looks fine unweighted because the rim runs in a wider arc than the pad clearance. Under load the rim deflects inward at the bottom and that section sweeps the pad. A fresh install can shift spoke tension enough to introduce this. The shop should true before you accept.

5. Tire pressure. A low-pressure squirm under load feels rhythmic because the carcass deforms once per rotation. Bring pressure into the middle of the sidewall-printed range, not the max.

6. Frame clearance. A 700x32 is meaningfully larger than a 28 or 30. With your weight on the bike, eyeball the gap between the new tire and the seat-tube bridge and chainstays. If it's under 3–4 mm, the tire is contacting the frame under load, not the brake — different problem, the shop needs to know it's a fitment issue.

Recommendation: don't ride it home. A pre-acceptance test catching this is exactly the right time to push back. The first three fixes above are 5-minute bench jobs; if it needs a true or a re-dish, that's the shop's problem to solve before pickup, not yours to absorb. Given that you weight predictable commute over rotational performance, a load-dependent rub is the kind of small issue that becomes a not-small one on wet pavement or with a loaded bag — pushing back now is the cheap version of the conversation.

Good news on the presentation: oozing stopped with pressure, no flap, no gape on flexion, weight-bearing normally, no debris visible — that's a textbook "superficial abrasion," which is home-manageable as long as the escalation thresholds below stay quiet.

CLEANING (once, then daily at bandage change):
- Lukewarm water rinse first to remove any grit. A dilute chlorhexidine solution (0.05%, the light blue or colorless kind sold for dogs) on a gauze pad is ideal. Plain mild soap is fine if that's what you have.
- Do NOT use hydrogen peroxide — it damages the new granulation tissue and slows healing. No alcohol, no essential oils, no Neosporin unless you know Kibo tolerates it (some dogs react to the neomycin).
- Pat dry; don't rub. Inspect under good light for any remaining grit or a seed awn tucked at the edge.

SHORT-TERM PROTECTION (7-10 days minimum):
- Non-adherent pad (Telfa) over the wound, then a thin layer of plain petroleum jelly to keep the pad from sticking and to keep the surface slightly moist.
- Wrap with conforming gauze (1-2 layers, snug but not tight — you should be able to slide a fingertip under the wrap at the top).
- Outer layer: cohesive bandage (Vetrap) — stretch it just enough to hold; over-tightening at the top of the paw cuts off venous return and the toes swell. Check the toes 10 minutes after wrapping: if they're puffy, cool, or discolored, re-wrap looser.
- Cover for outdoor walks with a dog bootie, or a child-sized sock taped at the carpus. Avoid plastic bag-only coverage for more than a few minutes — it traps moisture and macerates the wound.
- Change the bandage every 24 hours, or sooner if it gets wet or dirty. A wet bandage is worse than no bandage.

ACTIVITY:
- Leash-only, short walks for the first week. No off-leash, no running, no jumping. Pads flex with every step and re-tear easily.
- Avoid hot pavement, sand, and chemically treated grass. Early-morning and late-evening walks only while healing.
- Lick prevention matters more than it looks: a single focused lick session can reopen a pad wound in seconds because the tongue acts like sandpaper on moist tissue. Use an e-collar (the rigid plastic kind — Kibo will hate it for ~20 minutes then accept it) or a secured sock cover when you can't watch.

VET ESCALATION:

Same-day vet call (not ER, but don't wait for a regular appointment):
- Oozing or bleeding restarts after you controlled it.
- Spreading redness, swelling, or warmth up the paw or into the toes — that's cellulitis starting.
- Discharge turns yellow, green, creamy, or develops any odor.
- Kibo starts limping or refuses to bear weight (he's loading it now — a change is the signal).
- Persistent licking despite the e-collar/sock.
- The wound looks the same or worse at the 48-hour mark instead of cleaner and smaller.
- Any behavior change — inappetence, lethargy, panting at rest.

Urgent care / ER now:
- Bleeding you can't stop with 10-15 minutes of firm direct pressure.
- You find or suspect glass, a thorn, or a metal fragment embedded — don't pull it; it may be sealing a deeper tract.
- A deep puncture rather than a scrape (pads seal over punctures fast and abscess below).
- The wound gapes, or a flap develops, or a chunk of pad is missing.
- Any sign of systemic illness — vomiting, pale gums, collapse.
- Kibo steps through antifreeze, paint, lawn chemicals, or any unknown irritant — rinse the paw and go in immediately.

Two things worth knowing for the recovery window: paw pads heal slowly even when superficial — full epithelialization typically takes 3-4 weeks — and watch for "proud flesh," a firm red bumpy bulge that grows proud of the pad surface. It looks like the wound is healing aggressively but it actually blocks the skin from closing over it, and a vet needs to trim it back.

Quick frame before the steps: I am not a vet, and a wound Kibo re-opened by licking is no longer a clean superficial scrape even if the visible picture is still reassuring. The good news from your own check is real — weight-bearing fine, no gape, no heat/swelling/discharge, bleeding stopped with a minute of pressure — but oral bacteria are now in the wound, so the next 24–48 hours are the window where infection would show up. Treat what follows as triage + dressing, then watch the thresholds at the bottom.

Immediate cleaning (one pass, then re-bandage):
  - Rinse with lukewarm saline or plain lukewarm water. If you have dilute chlorhexidine 0.05% (the blue "scrub" diluted to weak-tea color, or the pre-diluted 0.05% spray), use that — it's safe for paws and the standard first choice.
  - Do NOT use hydrogen peroxide (damages granulation tissue and slows healing), rubbing alcohol (stings and damages tissue), or essential-oil sprays. Avoid any "-caine" or "-caine PLUS" pain-relief creams (lidocaine, pramoxine) — toxic if licked even in small amounts.
  - Gently flush for ~30–60 seconds to lift any saliva and debris. Pat dry with clean gauze — don't wipe.
  - Inspect again after drying. If you now see a flap, deeper tissue, or anything you couldn't see before, that moves you toward same-day vet (see below).

Re-covering (and fixing the sock-slip failure):
  - Thin layer of a dog-safe ointment — plain triple antibiotic (bacitracin/polymyxin/neomycin WITHOUT pain reliever), or Vetericyn, or a vet-supplied paw balm. Nothing ending in "-caine."
  - Non-adherent pad (Telfa) cut to cover the scrape with a few mm of margin, plastic/shiny side up so it doesn't stick to the clot.
  - Rolled gauze or a piece of clean soft cloth as a comfort layer over the Telfa.
  - Self-adhering wrap (Vetrap/Coflex) — loose. The two-finger rule: you should be able to slide two fingers under the wrap at the top, and the toes should not swell, cool, or change color. Too tight on a paw cuts off venous return fast and is a real risk.
  - Top layer: a clean cotton sock. The reason yesterday's sock came off is almost always that it wasn't anchored above the carpus (the "wrist") or wasn't taped to the fur/leg. Anchor it this time:
    - Pull the sock well up the leg, above the carpus joint.
    - Tape the top of the sock to itself with a couple of wraps of medical tape, or use a strip of self-adhering wrap around the top of the sock (not the leg, the sock), so the sock can't slide down and pool at the paw.
    - Alternative: a baby Onesie-style sock or a dedicated dog paw boot (e.g., a soft rubber-soled bootie) is more secure than a loose human sock.
  - Change the dressing once daily, or sooner if it gets wet or soiled.

Cone question — yes, use one now, because this is the second failure mode:
  - The pinpoint bleed you saw came from friction-licking on an exposed edge. That's exactly when an e-collar earns its keep: even short licking disrupts clotting and seeds bacteria.
  - Standard hard plastic "lamp shade" cones are the most reliable. Inflatable/comfy cones work for some dogs but many can still reach a front paw with them — Kibo reaching a back or front paw, you'll know which one fits his reach.
  - Memory note that Kibo is reactive in some contexts — if a hard cone stresses him badly, a soft/comfy cone plus constant supervision (he stays in your sight line, you redirect on the first head-down toward the paw) is a reasonable compromise for the first 24 hours while the surface re-seals.
  - If you have a basket muzzle and he's muzzle-trained, that's an alternative during supervised indoor time and lets him eat/drink normally.
  - Practical tip: feed and water dishes need to be raised or use a wide shallow bowl while the cone is on — dogs bonk the dishes constantly otherwise and stop eating.

Same-day vet / urgent-care thresholds now that the surface is disturbed:
  - Go in today (or call your vet's triage line right now) if any of these appear:
    - Bleeding recurs, or doesn't stop within 5–10 minutes of firm direct pressure.
    - Redness or swelling spreads beyond the immediate wound edge (cellulitis — a halo of pink/red expanding outward over hours).
    - Any heat, discharge (cloudy, yellow, or green = pus), or foul odor.
    - Lameness worsens, dog stops bearing weight, or starts guarding the leg when standing.
    - Wound gapes, you see a flap, deeper tissue, or you can no longer see the bottom of the scrape.
    - Anything embedded you couldn't flush out — gravel, a thorn, a hair tuft driven in.
    - Kibo seems painful beyond mild (whimpering, panting at rest, won't settle, won't eat), or runs a temp (dog normal is ~101–102.5°F; over 103 is a fever).
  - Specifically urgent (ER, not waiting for your regular vet) if:
    - Bleeding is pulsing or soaking through gauze repeatedly (could be a digital artery nick — pad arteries run through there).
    - Paw is rapidly swelling or feels boggy.
    - The dog is in obvious distress, or has a known condition that compromises healing (diabetes, immune disease, on steroids).
  - If none of those fire and the dressing stays clean and dry through tonight: a regular vet visit within 24–48 hours is still reasonable for a re-check, but it's not a same-day emergency.

One thing worth flagging just because it changes the calculus: if Kibo keeps getting the sock off, the dressing protocol isn't going to save you, and you may want your vet to apply a proper paw bandage and possibly prescribe a short course of a topical antibiotic and/or a course of an e-collar at the right length for his neck. That's a same-day-call question rather than same-day-visit — your vet's front desk can usually answer it in two minutes and save you a trip.

PRE-FLIGHT — WHY TIMESTAMP AND SIZE ARE NOT AUTHORITY

- File size is not a content fingerprint for TIFF. Two files with identical pixel data can differ by tens of KB if they carry different tag sets (ICC profile, XMP/IPTC, embedded preview, strip vs tile layout) or different compression. A 12 KB delta in a TIFF is almost always metadata or organization, not pixel data — but that is a hypothesis to test, not a fact to act on.
- mtime is not provenance. The newer timestamp can be set by any copy/backup/indexing/sync operation that touches atime or mtime without changing content; conversely, a verbatim byte-copy can preserve the older mtime. The scanning-session log is a stronger witness than any filesystem timestamp.

All steps below are read-only against the two originals until Stage 4. Nothing in Stages 0–3 mutates the bytes, names, or locations of either file.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
STAGE 0 — FREEZE STATE AND CAPTURE WITNESS METADATA
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Goal: make accidental writes impossible, and record the on-disk state of both files before any further inspection.

0.1  If either volume is mounted read-write and you have the option, remount read-only for the comparison (e.g., `mount -o remount,ro /mnt/external`). Skip if impractical.

0.2  Capture witness metadata for both files in a side log you keep outside both volumes:

      stat /path/to/laptop/P037_back.tif
      stat /path/to/external/P037_back.tif

  Record: size, mtime, atime, ctime, inode, device, blocks. The fact that size differs by 12 KB is itself a witness — confirm it here before going further.

0.3  If the laptop or external supports a hardware write-protect switch (SD adapter, some external enclosures), engage it now on the one that holds the file you most suspect of being the master. This is advisory only — do not skip Stage 0.1 if you cannot.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
STAGE 1 — NON-DESTRUCTIVE FORENSIC COMPARISON
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

All operations here read the files. On Linux, reading typically updates atime; if your workflow treats atime as evidentiary, run the comparisons with the filesystems mounted `noatime`/`relatime`, or use `chattr +A` to suppress atime updates before reading. `chattr +A` is reversible and does not touch content.

1.1  Cryptographic hash (byte-identity test). If hashes match, the size report is wrong and the files are identical — re-check size with `stat` from both locations and stop here. If hashes differ (expected), the 12 KB is real and you are looking at two genuinely different byte streams:

      sha256sum /path/to/laptop/P037_back.tif \
                /path/to/external/P037_back.tif

  Save both hashes into the side log. These are your content fingerprints regardless of what mtime says.

1.2  TIFF structural comparison. Read tag layout, compression, photometric interpretation, strip/tile layout, bits-per-sample, embedded profiles. Any of the following tools works; pick whichever is installed:

      exiftool -G -s -a -ee /path/to/laptop/P037_back.tif
      exiftool -G -s -a -ee /path/to/external/P037_back.tif

  Or, with libtiff:

      tiffinfo -D /path/to/laptop/P037_back.tif | tee laptop.info
      tiffinfo -D /path/to/external/P037_back.tif | tee external.info

  Diff them:

      diff -u laptop.info external.info

  Common benign explanations for a ~12 KB delta that you may see here:
    - Embedded JPEG/XMP preview thumbnail in one, absent in the other.
    - ICC color profile in one, sRGB tag only in the other.
    - IPTC/XMP block added by post-processing software (Lightroom, Photoshop, Bridge, darktable).
    - Strip layout vs tile layout with the same compression.
    - LZW vs Deflate vs no compression — usually a larger delta than 12 KB, but worth checking `Compression` tag.

1.3  Pixel-level comparison. This is the decisive test for "did the picture itself change." Render both to a lossless intermediate using a tool that does not re-encode, then diff the renders. Do not save the renders on either source volume.

      mkdir -p /tmp/P037_quarantine_compare
      cd    /tmp/P037_quarantine_compare

      # Lossless render (PIL/Pillow reads and re-writes pixel-identical PNG
      # when the source is uncompressed or LZW; for safety, render to PNG).
      python3 - <<'PY'
      from PIL import Image
      for label, p in [("laptop",   "/path/to/laptop/P037_back.tif"),
                       ("external", "/path/to/external/P037_back.tif")]:
          im = Image.open(p)
          im.save(f"/tmp/P037_quarantine_compare/{label}.png")
      PY

      # Pixel diff. AE = number of differing pixels; if AE=0 and
      # RMSE=0, the picture is identical and the 12 KB is purely
      # metadata/organization.
      compare -metric AE  -fuzz 0% \
              /tmp/P037_quarantine_compare/laptop.png \
              /tmp/P037_quarantine_compare/external.png \
              /tmp/P037_quarantine_compare/diff.png
      compare -metric RMSE -fuzz 0% \
              /tmp/P037_quarantine_compare/laptop.png \
              /tmp/P037_quarantine_compare/external.png \
              null:

  Also produce a perceptual diff using a tool that ignores sub-pixel resampling artifacts (e.g., `compare -metric PAE` or `image-compare` in Python with a tolerance) — but the strict AE=0 / RMSE=0 result is what tells you the pixel content matches.

1.4  Cross-reference the scanning-session log. Look for: nominal file size at capture time (many capture logs record it), capture software and version, whether post-processing was logged, target compression, target profile, and operator notes. The log is your strongest external witness; the hash is your strongest internal witness; pixel equality is your strongest content witness.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
STAGE 2 — DECISION CRITERIA (NO WRITES YET)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Walk this list in order. The first criterion that produces a clear verdict wins; stop at that criterion and record it in the side log.

  C1. Scanning-session log explicitly records file size for this capture.
        → Whichever file matches the recorded size is the master, unless
          the log also records a post-processing step that would change
          size without changing pixel content (then read C2 first).

  C2. Pixel diff (1.3) shows AE > 0 or RMSE > 0.
        → The files are not pixel-identical. Whichever matches the
          physical photograph (you have the original in its sleeve) is
          the master. Do a side-by-side visual compare against the
          physical print/slide/negative — viewing both PNGs from 1.3 on a
          calibrated display, not the TIFFs in a viewer that may apply
          its own transforms.

  C3. Pixel diff (1.3) shows AE = 0 and RMSE = 0, but hashes differ (1.1)
      and tag diff (1.2) shows a real tag-set difference.
        → Pixel content matches; metadata diverges. The master is the
          file whose tag set matches what the capture workflow was
          configured to write. Tie-breakers, in order:
            (a) Scanning-session log specifies expected profile/tags —
                match against that.
            (b) The other ten treated-photo TIFFs in the verified set
                share a tag fingerprint with one of the two candidates.
                Whichever candidate matches the cohort's tag
                fingerprint is the master.
            (c) If (a) and (b) both fail, defer to institutional
                policy: for most archives, the capture-time, untagged-
                since-capture version is master and the
                downstream-tagged version is a derivative.

  C4. Pixel diff shows AE = 0 and RMSE = 0, and tag diff (1.2) shows
      only compression or strip/tile layout differences (no extra tags).
        → Both files represent the same image. Master is whichever
          matches the cohort convention from C3(b), or — if the cohort
          is split — the file with the compression/layout that the
          capture software was configured to produce.

Do not let "newer mtime" override C1–C4 under any circumstance.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
STAGE 3 — PREPARE THE QUARANTINE HOLDING AREA
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

The quarantine is a separate directory tree, not a rename in place. Keep it on a third volume if possible, so it cannot accidentally be mistaken for the working archive.

3.1  Create the quarantine area outside both source volumes:

      mkdir -p /path/to/quarantine/P037_investigation/$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)
      cd       /path/to/quarantine/P037_investigation/<timestamp>

3.2  Record the decision from Stage 2 in a `DECISION.md` (or `.txt`) in this directory: which file was judged master and why, with the hash values from 1.1 and the diff outputs from 1.2/1.3 referenced.

3.3  Copy — do not move — the file judged to be the non-master into the quarantine directory, with a name that cannot collide with the working archive:

      # Adjust source based on your Stage 2 verdict.
      cp -p /path/to/<non-master-location>/P037_back.tif \
            /path/to/quarantine/P037_investigation/<timestamp>/P037_back.NON_MASTER.tif

  `cp -p` preserves mode, mtime, atime. After the copy, re-hash the copy and confirm it matches the original hash from 1.1:

      sha256sum /path/to/quarantine/.../P037_back.NON_MASTER.tif

  If the copy hash does not match the recorded original hash, do not proceed — the copy itself is suspect. Re-run from 1.1.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
STAGE 4 — ISOLATE THE NON-MASTER IN PLACE (NON-DESTRUCTIVE)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

This is the only stage that touches the originals' locations, and it does so by renaming, not by deleting or overwriting. Renaming on the same filesystem is content-preserving and reversible.

4.1  Rename the non-master on its original volume so it cannot be picked up by the working archive's discovery/import step, while leaving the master untouched:

      # Replace <non-master-location> with whichever path holds the
      # file judged non-master in Stage 2.
      mv /path/to/<non-master-location>/P037_back.tif \
         /path/to/<non-master-location>/P037_back.QUARANTINED_NON_MASTER.tif

  After the rename, re-hash:

      sha256sum /path/to/<non-master-location>/P037_back.QUARANTINED_NON_MASTER.tif

  Confirm the hash matches what you recorded in 1.1 for the non-master. If not, the rename path has a problem — investigate before going further.

4.2  Confirm the master is untouched: hash, size, and mtime on the master should match what you recorded in Stage 0/1.1. Any drift here means something else touched the file between Stages 0 and 4 — that itself is a finding.

4.3  Confirm the rest of the archive set still resolves: re-run whatever verification step you used for the other ten captures and confirm they still pass with the renamed non-master excluded from the comparison.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
STAGE 5 — ROLLBACK / RECOVERY NOTES
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Reversibility of the sequence:

  Stages 0–3: fully reversible, no writes against the originals.
  Stage 4.1:  reversible by `mv` back to the original name. The bytes
              are unchanged. The only evidence of the quarantine is the
              filename suffix and the `DECISION.md` in the holding
              area.
  Stage 4.2 onward: still reversible as long as the holding-area copy
              and `DECISION.md` exist.

Things that would make this sequence non-reversible, which you should guard against:

  - Running a tool that "fixes" the file in place (Photoshop "save", `jpegtran -copy all`, any TIFF re-writer that touches pixel data).
  - Letting a sync/backup/indexing daemon touch the volume between Stage 0 and Stage 4.
  - Deleting the quarantine holding-area copy or `DECISION.md` before you've confirmed the working archive is stable with the new name.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ONE-LINE SUMMARY OF THE PRINCIPLE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Hashes identify content, the scanning log identifies intent, and the physical photograph identifies truth. mtime and size identify neither. The sequence above uses those three witnesses — in that order — to name the master, then isolates the loser by rename so the working archive can no longer confuse the two.

Ruling — Expansion Assist CS request classification when source event crosses a calendar-date boundary in UTC vs. local time.

RULE (for Owen's QA record and Ines's lifecycle-audit review):

1. Window anchor = exposure timestamp, canonicalized to UTC.
   The 45-day Expansion Assist window begins at the exposure timestamp expressed in UTC. UTC is the canonical form for window arithmetic. Local time-of-day is not the window anchor under any condition.

2. Eligibility test = continuous elapsed time, not calendar days.
   A CS request is in-window for exposure E iff:
       (CS_request_UTC − E_UTC) ≤ 45 × 24 hours  (i.e., ≤ 1,080 hours)
   measured as a single continuous duration. Calendar-date boundaries in either UTC or any local timezone are not consulted. A request originating at 23:58 Pacific on day N is treated identically, for window-membership purposes, to one originating at 09:00 Pacific on day N.

3. Both representations retained side-by-side; neither overwrites the other.
   The exposure / raw channel event record keeps:
       - original local timestamp (e.g., 2024-09-03 23:58 America/Los_Angeles)
       - UTC equivalent        (e.g., 2024-09-04 06:58 UTC)
       - original IANA tz + offset (e.g., America/Los_Angeles, −07:00 PDT)
       - source channel, raw event ID, session correlation IDs
   Local is retained for channel/forensic fidelity. UTC is retained for canonical window math. Neither is "corrected" into the other.

4. No calendar-date correction on accepted exposure records.
   The exposure row is not edited to shift its warehouse calendar date so the local and UTC dates agree. Per the standing exception-review ruling, accepted point-in-time tables stay fixed; this is a separate forward classification event, not a revision to the historical snapshot.

5. Dashboard calendar cells are display-only.
   Whatever calendar date a dashboard surfaces (UTC view vs. local view) is presentation. It does not change eligibility. If a dashboard and the elapsed-time test disagree, the elapsed-time test governs, and the discrepancy is logged with the request record.

6. Unit-of-count discipline still holds.
   Per the 2024-08-28 measurement-grain ruling, the unit of count remains the account-level CS request. The local and UTC timestamps are evidence on that one request, not separate counts. Cross-boundary timing does not create a second request and does not change the channel-event-vs-CS-request distinction.

7. Per-request annotation (mandatory).
   The request record / brief carries one explicit line:
       "Window computed from exposure timestamp [UTC] using continuous elapsed time
        (≤ 1,080h); local timestamp [America/Los_Angeles, PDT] retained for
        forensic reference only."
   This makes the rule visible on Owen's shape+ex pass and Ines's lifecycle-aud-risk pass without requiring a reader to re-derive the convention.

8. Scope note.
   This ruling addresses window classification only. No complete outcome count, conversion count, or pipeline figure is being requested, reported, or implied by applying this rule to Owen's flagged record.

Unit math first, because it's the obvious comparison:

- Single sheet: $8 / 4 quarters = $2.00 per quarter
- Five-sheet pack: $32 / 20 quarters = $1.60 per quarter (20% cheaper per quarter)

So on paper the pack wins. But the conditions you flagged flip it:

Storage. You have room for one flat full sheet. Four extra full sheets stored somewhere else is where paper goes wrong — curling, damp pickup, dog-nose dents, dust. A quarter sheet that's been stored loose in a closet for months doesn't behave like a fresh one.

No planned use. "Bulk is cheaper" only matters if you actually use the bulk. Four sheets with no current purpose is $24 of inventory sitting in conditions that may degrade it. If you later need quarters, you'll likely want fresh stock anyway.

Recommendation: buy the single sheet ($8). It covers the opening exercise with three spare quarters in case the clinic has additional exercises, fits your storage, and doesn't strand $24 in paper you can't keep properly. The 20% per-quarter saving is real arithmetic but not realized here.

Bulk would be the right call only if (a) you have a second flat storage spot, and (b) you'd realistically use the other four sheets within a few months. Neither condition holds, so don't pay for inventory you can't house.

One thing to confirm before buying: the instructor named the opening exercise as one quarter sheet — if the full clinic run uses more than four quarters total, the math tips back toward the pack. Worth asking how many exercises are planned before you commit to the single.

Pattern looks more like tissue-load irritation than an acute structural event: delayed onset around minute 28 of an easy effort, 2/10 lateral ache that faded to near zero over ~30 min after you stopped, no swelling/tenderness/limp/instability/sharp pain immediately afterward, and a longer fade than the brief Aug 28 stiffness. That's a "capacity was just under the load" signal rather than a sprain/fracture pattern. It deserves a structured Mon-AM read, not panic. Below is the monitor, the run-decision rule under your +dur OR +freq/wk constraint, and the clinical-escalation list.

PART 1 — MONITOR THROUGH MONDAY MORNING

Five checkpoints. Any one of them breaking pattern changes Part 2.

(a) Sunday afternoon (~2–4 hr post-run)
  - Re-inspect: any new swelling, bruising, warmth, or point tenderness over the lateral malleolus (outer ankle bone) or just below/anterior to it.
  - Stair test: walk a flight both directions. Note any catch, hesitation, or sharp pain on push-off (plantarflexion + inversion).
  - Single-leg balance, affected side, eyes open, 30 sec — compare to the other side. Wobble or guarding = signal.

(b) Sunday evening
  - Pain at rest: still 0/10, or drifting back to 1–2/10?
  - Repeat the stair test.
  - Side-lying on the affected side: any ache that surfaces with pressure?

(c) Overnight / Monday wake
  - First steps out of bed: any stiffness, ache, or guarded feeling in the lateral ankle?
  - Walk to kitchen/bathroom: any limp at all, even subtle.

(d) Monday AM, after ~10 min of normal movement
  - Stairs again.
  - Single-leg balance, both sides, 30 sec eyes open.
  - Single-leg calf raises: 10 slow reps on the affected side (up on 2, down on 3), wall-touch for balance only. Note lateral pain during the raise, or a clear rep-count or quality drop vs the other side.

(e) Monday AM, light load test
  - 10 min brisk walk on flat ground. Note any return of the ache during the walk, and again 10 min after stopping.

PART 2 — DECISION RULE FOR YOUR NEXT RUN

Your rule is +dur OR +freq/wk, not both, and your hold template is "prescribed run min + 8-min walk/transition buffer, no pace target, no extension." So the only available knobs are hold-at-34, shorten, or skip. No extension is on the table regardless of how Monday reads.

Gate the decision on checkpoints (d) + (e).

HOLD at 34 min (your normal slot, + 8-min walk buffer) IF ALL are true:
  - Monday first-step stiffness is 0/10, or a brief <2-min mild stiffness that clears completely.
  - No limp at any point Monday morning.
  - Brisk 10-min walk reproduces nothing, and nothing in the 10 min after.
  - Stairs, single-leg balance, and single-leg calf raises all feel symmetric with no lateral pain.
  - No new swelling, bruising, or point tenderness since Sunday afternoon.
  - Sunday evening and overnight were pain-free at rest.

SHORTEN (e.g., 20–22 min easy + 8-min walk/transition buffer) IF:
  - First-step stiffness is mild but clears within ~5 min.
  - No limp, no swelling.
  - Brisk walk reproduces a faint ache (≤1/10) that fades within minutes of stopping.
  - Stairs, balance, and calf raises are clean.
  - In that case run shortened easy (no pace target, no extension) plus the 8-min buffer. If the in-run ache does not return, hold at the shortened duration for two runs before stepping back to 34 — do not jump back up after one clean shortened run.

SKIP IF ANY of these are true:
  - Monday first-step ache >0/10 and still present past 5 min.
  - Any limp Monday morning.
  - Brisk walk reproduces ache ≥2/10, or ache that lingers more than ~30 min after.
  - New swelling, bruising, warmth, or point tenderness over the lateral malleolus or sinus tarsi.
  - Single-leg calf raise on the affected side reproduces the in-run ache or shows clear asymmetry.
  - Stair push-off reproduces a sharp or catching sensation.
  - Single-leg balance is meaningfully worse than the other side.
  - Sunday-evening or Monday-morning pain at rest is not back to 0/10.

If you skip, do not try to add the missed minutes onto another day. Your load rule does not trade a symptom-driven skip for a +dur token elsewhere — and bike days (Tue/Thu/Fri as usual) stay as planned unless a Part 3 flag appears.

PART 3 — CLINICAL FOLLOW-UP CRITERIA

Contact your PT or a sports-med clinician this week (do not wait it out) if any of the following shows up:

  - Swelling, bruising, or visible change in ankle contour.
  - Point tenderness over the lateral malleolus, the ATFL (just below and anterior to the malleolus tip), or the sinus tarsi.
  - Any sense of instability — "giving way" on the affected side, or a single-leg balance that is clearly worse and does not normalize after a day or two.
  - Pain persisting at rest into Monday (you are aware of it without loading).
  - Ache that returns with every walk, not just with running-equivalent load.
  - Pain that trends worse over the next 48 hr instead of toward zero.
  - Any sharp, catching, or locking sensation in the ankle.
  - Numbness, tingling, or color change in the foot.

Also worth a call (not urgent) if, after you return, the same delayed-onset pattern repeats at the same time-into-run with the same ~30-min fade. Repeating-load reproduction at the same minute is a load-tolerance finding your PT will want to see — that's exactly the kind of thing PT follow-up is for, and it's also a useful data point for any future +dur decision.

If Part 1 trends clean and Part 2 lets you hold or shorten without any in-run return of symptoms, no clinical visit is needed — this is normal capacity-adjustment territory, which is what the load rule is built to handle.

- **Account-level support effort: not addressed.** No tickets/account, no CSM-hours/account, no handle-time assumption, no support-cost line.

So the package provides *inputs to one side of the acquisition economics* — the gross cost side — and provides nothing for the other three pieces the gate requires.

**Verdict: the package does not satisfy the gate.** It is a necessary-but-far-from-sufficient input. The unit-cost mechanics it enables ($26,400 outlay, $150 media-only, $165 fully-loaded per signup start) are calculable, but the three gate-relevant quantities — mature retention, refund-adjusted cash, support effort per account — remain unaddressed. Calling the gate "met" on the basis of this package would conflate *having gross-cost inputs* with *having the evidence the gate actually requires*.

## What to ask Finance for next (so the gate can be evaluated)

To move from "gross cost mechanics calculable" to "gate evaluable," Finance would need to supply, in the same package:
1. An expected paid-activation count or activation rate, so cost-per-activated-account is derivable.
2. A refund-rate assumption and a stated treatment (cash-back vs. recognized-revenue reversal), so net cash per signup is derivable.
3. A support-load assumption at the account level (tickets/account or hours/account), so support cost per acquired account is derivable.
4. A statement of the maturity status of the paid-acquisition cohorts being costed — specifically, whether retained cohorts from this channel have reached the maturity threshold (e.g., D90/D180) and what the observed retention looks like at that age.

Items 1–3 are forward assumptions Finance can reasonably supply alongside the test inputs. Item 4 is the empirical piece that has to come from the retention/cohort data, not from Finance's assumptions — so it's the part where the gate genuinely depends on evidence the package doesn't carry.
