Design — Two-Wash Sky Study, Angle as Sole Variable

Format
  Four cells on a single sheet, laid out as a horizontal strip (one row,
  four panels). Each panel is a self-contained sky study with the same
  horizon line and same paper orientation. The only thing that changes
  between panels is the board tilt during both washes.

Held constant across all four panels
  - Paper, brush, pigment, and pigment load (same mix for wash 1 across
    panels; same deeper mix for wash 2 across panels).
  - Pre-wet timing of the sky area (same dwell, same water amount).
  - Wash 1 application: same edge, same stroke order, same pigment
    volume per stroke.
  - Edge touch: 20 seconds, one touch per edge, brush not returned.
  - Blotting: exactly one firm blot, at the same location within the
    panel, performed at the same point in the sequence.
  - Inter-wash wait: sheen allowed to dull before wash 2 begins
    (no bloom trigger — mirroring what worked in the exercise).
  - Wash 2 application: same edge, same stroke order, same volume.
  - Edge touch and blot rules repeated identically for wash 2.

Variable — board tilt
  Tilt direction is the same in every panel: the TOP edge of the sky
  area is the LOW point, so pigment pools toward the zenith. Only the
  magnitude changes.

  Panel A  —  0°  (flat). Control. No directional pooling; gradient is
              driven purely by wash application and the edge-touch hold.
  Panel B  —  ~10°. Gentle directional pull. Slight deepening at the
              top edge.
  Panel C  —  ~20°. Clear gradient. Pigment collects at the zenith line;
              edge-touch hold has to work against a moving bead.
  Panel D  —  ~30°. Aggressive pooling. Tests whether the one-firm-blot
              and the no-return rule still contain the seam risk.

Procedure per panel (run identically in A → D)
  1.  Pre-wet the sky area with clean water; let the sheen dull to the
      same point each time.
  2.  Wash 1 — light mix. Lay it in from the horizon edge upward.
  3.  At the meeting edge between wet wash and dry paper, touch the
      brush once and hold 20 seconds. Move to the next edge: one touch,
      20-second hold. No return passes.
  4.  One firm blot at the designated spot. Stop.
  5.  Wait for the sheen to fully dull (your "no bloom because I did not
      return" condition).
  6.  Wash 2 — deeper mix. Repeat steps 2–4 against the now-damp
      surface.

What the panels will surface
  - Whether a 20-second edge hold can still control a bead that is
    migrating under gravity, and at what angle it stops controlling.
  - Where the one firm blot starts to over-correct (Panel D is the
    likely failure point — pooling fights the blot).
  - Whether the "no return after sheen dulls" rule interacts with tilt:
    a tilted, damp surface dries unevenly, so the dull-sheen cue may
    arrive earlier at the low (top) edge than at the high (horizon)
    edge. Worth noting in a margin note beside each panel.

One operational note
  Because tilt changes drying rate across the panel, set a single
  external cue (e.g. the horizon-edge sheen) as your "start wash 2"
  trigger rather than a clock — otherwise angle will smuggle itself
  into the wait time and you will no longer be isolating it.

Suggested record per panel: angle, sheen-dull time observed at the
horizon edge, whether the 20-second hold visibly fed pigment into the
dry edge or just held it back, and whether the single blot left a
seam.

WHAT THE NOTICE CONFIRMS
- She is enrolled in a Part D plan that will continue into 2025 (auto-enrolled unless she acts during Open Enrollment, Oct 15 – Dec 7, 2024, for a Jan 1, 2025 effective date).

WHAT IT DOES NOT ESTABLISH (the actual cost drivers)
- Her out-of-pocket cost for her specific drug list. Deductible + premium is only ~$345 of the headline math; tier copays/coinsurance are the real swing factor.
- Whether her current drugs are still on the 2025 formulary, at what tier, or with prior authorization, step therapy, or quantity limits.
- Whether her current pharmacy will be preferred, standard, or out-of-network next year. Network changes can quietly move a pharmacy from preferred ($5 copay) to standard ($15) and double her costs without any premium change.
- 2025 catastrophic coverage position. Note: the IRA eliminated the coverage gap for 2025 and capped Part D out-of-pocket at $2,000/year — a structural benefit the notice does not quantify.
- Whether her Extra Help (Low-Income Subsidy) status or IRMAA (income-related adjustment, billed separately by SSA) still applies. The plan premium is a different number from what she actually pays.
- Whether a different plan in her county would be cheaper for her actual drug regimen. Premium is a weak proxy for total annual cost.

CHECKLIST BEFORE SHE COMPARES OR SELECTS

Documents to pull (get the 2025 versions of each — last year's are misleading):
  1. Full 2025 ANOC from her current plan (the multi-page version, not just this summary page).
  2. 2025 Summary of Benefits (SB) — shows copay/coinsurance per tier.
  3. 2025 Formulary (drug list) with tier assignments for every drug she takes.
  4. 2025 Pharmacy Directory — preferred vs. standard network, filtered to her ZIP.

  - Copay/coinsurance at preferred vs. standard pharmacy for each tier she uses.
  - Which nearby pharmacies will be preferred in 2025, and is her current one on that list.
  - Does the plan offer the Medicare Prescription Payment Plan (the new monthly-smoothing option under the IRA $2,000 cap)? Useful if her costs front-load in January.
  - Are any of her drugs being removed from formulary or shifted to a higher tier for 2025?

Comparison questions to run, not just reason about:
  - On medicare.gov/plan-compare, enter her exact drug list, dosages, and pharmacy, and pull the personalized total annual cost estimate for: (a) her current 2025 plan, (b) the 2-3 lowest-cost alternatives in her county.

INDOOR TEST (~6 min) -- usable fit vs. return-before-outdoor

  - Y-junction centered on breastbone, no rotation around chest axis
  - Belly strap sits 1 finger-width behind BOTH front legs
  - Two fingers under neck strap and chest strap

  Clip a leash, apply steady moderate forward pull (walking tension, not a lunge). Hold 60 sec, walk 30, hold 30, side-step 30. Re-measure clearance at both front legs.

    Fail: clearance drops to <1 finger-width at either leg OR harness rotates around chest

Step 2 -- Range-of-motion (2 min):
  Sit -> down -> stand -> back up 3 steps -> sit. Repeat 3x. Re-measure.
    Pass: clearance unchanged within +/- 0.5 finger-widths through transitions
    Fail: any forward migration, especially during the back-up (that's the migration vector)

    Pass: belly strap does NOT slide forward into the armpit; neck opening does not visibly enlarge

WATERCOLOR STUDY — 35° TILT, LOWER-BEAD WICKING FREQUENCY

Instructor diagnosis recap: at 35°, the lower bead gets too heavy and feeds back into the drying wash, so the wash dries twice and gives you two cauliflower edges. The fix is wick more often — NOT more brush moisture.

QUESTION
How does wick interval affect cauliflower edges at 35°, holding brush moisture, 20-second contact, and the one-touch rule constant?

HELD CONSTANT (every wash)
- One firm blot after loading (brush moisture = fixed)
- 20-second touch window after the wash is laid
- One-touch rule — single pass, no re-entry
- Tilt 35° (prop the board, verify the angle)
- Same paper batch; 12 pre-cut strips, equal size
- Same pigment, dilution, brush, load amount
- Same lighting and phone position for photos

VARIABLE: wick interval
  Level   Interval   Wicks in 20s window
  A       40 s       0   (validation: should reproduce two cauliflower edges)
  B       20 s       1   (current practice)
  C       10 s       2
  D        5 s       3

REPS & ORDER
- 3 reps per level = 12 washes, one session (~25–35 min)
- Randomize the order of all 12 before you start
- Label each strip with its condition code (A1..D3) before painting, so scoring stays blind to where you are in the sequence

PER-WASH PROCEDURE
1. Load brush, one firm blot — done.
2. One-touch lay the wash on the strip.
3. Tilt board to 35°, start timer.
4. At the prescribed wick interval, touch tissue to the lower bead ~1 s. (Level A: do NOT wick during the window — that is the failure case.)
5. At t = 20 s, lower the board, photograph the strip under fixed lighting.
6. Score on the rubric.

SCORING (per strip)
- Cauliflower edges: count (0 / 1 / 2+)
- Lower bead weight at t=20s: none / light / medium / heavy
- Feed-back into drying wash: yes / no
- Edge evenness: 1–5 (1 = broken/cauliflowered, 5 = clean)
- One-line note

READING THE RESULTS
- Level A should reproduce two cauliflower edges. If it does not, wick interval alone is not the driver.
- Expect edge count and evenness to improve as interval shortens.
- Diminishing returns: if 10 s and 5 s look the same, your working interval is ≤10 s — pick the longer of the two that still looks clean.
- If even 5 s still cauliflowers, the next variable to isolate is brush moisture (load amount or blot count) at the best wick interval found here.

NEXT STUDY (IF NEEDED)
Isolate brush moisture at the winning wick interval.

SUMMARY
Need: 27 GB free for OS update, 19 GB available. Reclaimable you've already identified: 19 GB across Desktop (9), call-cache (6), Downloads (4). Sequence: verify + refresh backup, then clear call cache, triage Downloads, archive non-active Desktop exports (active Helio untouched or compressed in place), system-cache sweep, confirm, update. Typical net: 35-45 GB free. Only non-negotiable order: backup verification before any destructive step. Steps 2+3 alone close the 8 GB gap, so the Desktop bucket is buffer, not load-bearing.

WHY THIS ORDER
Call cache is fully regenerable and zero-boundary-risk, so it goes first, instant 6 GB back. Downloads triaged next, case-by-case. Desktop is the only bucket with a real constraint, but "active Helio analyses" is a subset, not the whole 9 GB. Most of that bucket is finished CSV/image exports that can be compressed in place (zip, verify, delete originals) or moved to work OneDrive/SharePoint — still inside company boundaries. System sweep runs last because size is unpredictable; usually the biggest single win.

SEQUENCE

1. BACKUP — VERIFY, THEN REFRESH
   Confirm the Oct 19 backup actually exists and is restorable, not just flagged "successful." Open the backup client, check size/date, browse a sample file. Then run an incremental backup now to capture Oct 20-26, before you free space. If the backup target is external or company-managed cloud, this doesn't fight you for local disk.

2. CLEAR 6 GB CALL CACHE — SAFE
   Quit Zoom, Teams, Meet, etc. Clear their cache folders (Zoom: ~/Library/Application Support/zoom.us/data or %AppData%\Zoom\data; Teams cache under %AppData%\Microsoft\Teams). These rebuild on next call.

3. TRIAGE 4 GB DOWNLOADS — REVIEW FIRST
   Oldest first. Delete installers (.dmg/.exe/.pkg/.msi), old archives, one-off PDFs older than 30 days. Keep anything you can't replace. If you want to keep but not locally, move to work OneDrive/SharePoint, not a personal account.

4. ADDRESS 9 GB DESKTOP — KEEP HELIO, ARCHIVE THE REST
   Identify active Helio analyses (open in Helio, modified in the last few days). Do not delete or move these.
   For non-active Desktop items:
       Compress in place — zip the folder, verify the zip opens, then delete originals. Same machine, same account, no boundary issue.
       OR move to work OneDrive/SharePoint/Google Drive workspace. Verify the sync completes before deleting local copies.
   Active Helio files: leave in place, or compress-in-place if you want them smaller.

5. SYSTEM SWEEP — UNPREDICTABLE BUT LARGE
   Empty Trash. Clear browser caches. Mail attachment cache if local. Old iOS/iPadOS backups (MobileSync/Backup). Local Time Machine snapshots (sudo tmutil deletelocalsnapshots on macOS), ONLY after step 1 is verified, because deleting snapshots removes those restore points. Slack, Docker, IDE caches typically 1-5 GB each.

6. CONFIRM >=27 GB FREE
   Re-check storage view. If still short, the usual remaining suspects are Mail, Photos library, or VM disk files, each needs its own decision, don't auto-delete.

7. RUN THE OS UPDATE
   The installer package is removed after install, so the 27 GB requirement is temporary.

EFFECT
19 GB + 6 GB cache + ~4 GB Downloads + ~6 GB Desktop archive + ~8 GB system sweep ~= 43 GB free, with active Helio files intact and all data inside company-managed storage.

CALL
Steps 1-3 take ~15 min and are risk-free once backup verifies. Step 4 needs ~10 min per folder to decide what's active vs. finished. Step 5 is weekend work. Don't start any destructive step until step 1's verification is done — that's the only order that actually matters.

This is the most important framing: the $48 net gap shrinks or reverses depending on whether she realistically switches to mail order. If she does switch to mail order, the $48 figure stands.

Both pages left these unstated. None of them are dealbreakers on their own, but each can swing the decision:

Study design — single-variable test:
whether the 20-second bead-wicking interval stays consistent across a longer passage.

The variable (only thing being tested)
  - Consistency of the 20s wicking interval across a continuous, longer wash:
    timing of each tick, bead character at each tick, lower-edge behavior, front shape.

Fixed (held constant from the prior study)
  - Paper: same sheet, same batch, same orientation.
  - Mix: same water-to-pigment ratio, same load volume.
  - Brush: same brush, same load.
  - Angle: same steep angle — log it with a protractor/angle-finder at start and end.
  - Pre-wash blot: one firm blot, same pressure and dwell.
  - Edge touch: one 20-second touch at the same starting point.
  - Boundary rule: one-touch — do not revisit any spot.

The longer passage
  - One continuous wash — no breaks, no re-wetting, no second edge touch.
  - Length: longer than the prior strips by a meaningful margin. Target a passage
    that spans 6–10 wicking intervals at 20s each — enough data points to call
    consistency without dragging past the point where paper hydration starts to
    itself become a variable.

How "consistent" is measured at each 20s mark
  1. Timing — stopwatch running; log actual elapsed at each expected tick.
     Drift > ~2s from the 20s cadence = flag.
  2. Bead character — photo at each tick (same camera, same light, same framing).
     Compare to the prior 20s reference: same density, no pale skips, no
     over-wicking halos.
  3. Lower edge — confirm the edge stays clean through every interval; any
     re-bloom at the lower edge = flag (the failure mode from the no-wick strip).
  4. Front shape — straight line through the full passage, or starts to scallop/lag.

Replication
  - N = 3 longer strips on the same sheet, same session. Controls for
    session-to-session variance.
  - If any of the three shows drift, run a second session of N = 3 before
    drawing conclusions.

Pass / fail call
  - Holds: timing drift ≤ ~2s at every tick, bead matches the reference at every
    tick, lower edge stays clean for the full passage, front stays straight.
  - Does not hold on any signal across all three strips: fall back to a shorter
    wash OR revisit blot/angle before changing the interval. Do not change the
    interval on this evidence alone.

Per-strip log
  - Header: start time, angle reading, mix ratio, brush load.
  - Per tick: tick #, actual elapsed, bead note, edge note, photo file name.
  - Footer: end time, post-wash scan note, one-line call — consistent / drift / fail.

The single read-out that decides the next move
  - Did the 20s interval hold across all six-to-ten ticks on all three strips?
    If yes, the interval is stable at this passage length and you can extend.
    If no, the failure pattern (timing drift vs. bead fade vs. edge bloom vs.
    front scallop) tells you which control to revisit before touching the
    interval itself.

Two questions, both answered in the conservative direction you asked for.

WHICH FOOD CAN RETURN

Anything held continuously at or below 40°F goes back in:

  - Food in the ice-filled cooler at or below 38°F returns to the refrigerator.
  - Food in the freezer at 1°F returns or stays.
  - Perishable food with an unknown temperature history during the outage is discarded, not returned.

The cooler's verified 38°F holding is what protects most of the load. The 2°F margin is real, and you documented it.

CHICKEN AND RICE: DISCARD

Throw out the container. Three reasons stack, and none of them is rebutted by smell or appearance.

1. The 2-hour rule is breached by an unknown margin.

   The first confirmed reading, 46°F, is itself inside the USDA danger zone (40-140°F). The 2-hour cumulative limit applies. You have no way to confirm the dish spent less than 2 hours total above 40°F in the failing refrigerator. Given the unknown duration of the fan failure, the conservative assumption is that the 2-hour mark was crossed. Perishable food past that mark is discarded.

2. Cooked rice carries a specific, separate hazard.

   Bacillus cereus spores survive cooking and can produce cereulide toxin when cooked rice is held at temperatures that allow germination, including temperatures in the upper part of the refrigerator-danger zone. Cereulide is heat-stable. Thorough reheating will not make unsafe rice safe. There is no "reheat it well and it is fine" option for the rice portion.

3. Cooked chicken adds the usual Salmonella and Campylobacter risk.

   These are killed by thorough reheating to 165°F, but combined with the rice problem above, the conservative call is to discard the dish as a whole, not to separate and judge the components.

WHY SMELL AND APPEARANCE DO NOT COUNT

Cereulide is odorless and invisible. Pathogens on chicken can reach harmful levels with no off-odor or visible change, especially in the first 24 to 48 hours. "It looks and smells fine" is exactly the failure mode the conservative path is designed to avoid. Discard the dish regardless of how it appears.

WHAT TO DO

  - Bag and discard the chicken and rice now, so it cannot be retrieved and reheated later.
  - Wipe down the refrigerator interior before restocking.
  - Return the cooler food and freezer food to the refrigerator and freezer.
  - One hour after restocking, with the door closed, recheck the refrigerator thermometer to confirm 37°F holds under normal loading.

The rest of the load is fine. The chicken and rice is the only item that fails the conservative test.

Bottom line: copy Desktop → Managed (Desktop as source of truth for that file),
never Managed → Desktop. Pause the sync client before touching anything. Hash-
verify the copy. Only then delete the Desktop originals. Only then run the OS
update.

Why this shape: the client's "all synced" is a per-volume report from a snapshot
captured before your last save. Its next reconcile would treat the older
Managed copy as authoritative and could overwrite your newer Desktop edits.
Pausing removes that race; explicit copy + hash puts you in control of direction
and content.


Phase 0 — Stop the race
  - Quit or pause the corporate sync client (the one managing "Helio Secure
    Analysis"). Don't just close the window — pause syncing or quit the process.
    If there's no explicit pause, sign out / disable network for that client.
  - Close the CSV in the spreadsheet app. A still-open file can flush another
    save at the worst moment.


Phase 1 — Audit, don't trust the one observation
You noticed one CSV. The "saved while sync was finishing" window can have
touched others. The audit is the truth, not the one observation.

Replace the two path variables with your real ones (no trailing slash on
DESKTOP). The `stat` flag differs by OS — pick the right one.

  AUDIT=/tmp/audit_q4
  mkdir -p "$AUDIT"
  DESKTOP='/path/to/Desktop/Q4 exports'
  MANAGED='/path/to/Helio Secure Analysis/Riley/Q4 exports'

  # macOS:  stat -f %m   |   Linux:  stat -c %Y
  MTIME='stat -f %m'

  : > "$AUDIT/mismatches.log"

  find "$DESKTOP" -type f -print0 | while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do
      rel="${f#"$DESKTOP"/}"
      m="$MANAGED/$rel"
      if [ ! -f "$m" ]; then
          echo "ONLY_ON_DESKTOP  $rel" >> "$AUDIT/mismatches.log"
      else
          d=$($MTIME "$f"); mg=$($MTIME "$m")
          if [ "$d" -gt "$mg" ]; then
              echo "DESKTOP_NEWER  $rel  d=$d mg=$mg" >> "$AUDIT/mismatches.log"
          elif [ "$mg" -gt "$d" ]; then
              echo "MANAGED_NEWER  $rel  d=$d mg=$mg" >> "$AUDIT/mismatches.log"
          else
              echo "MTIME_EQUAL    $rel" >> "$AUDIT/mismatches.log"
          fi
      fi
  done

  cat "$AUDIT/mismatches.log"

The cases you care about are DESKTOP_NEWER and ONLY_ON_DESKTOP. Note any
MANAGED_NEWER rows too — those are files where the client has something you
don't, and you don't want to clobber them in Phase 2.


Phase 2 — Resolve each mismatch in the safe direction
For every DESKTOP_NEWER and ONLY_ON_DESKTOP file: Desktop → Managed. Use `cp -p`
or `rsync -a --update`. `-p` / `--update` matter: plain `cp` resets mtime, which
confuses the sync client into thinking nothing changed.

  cp -p "$DESKTOP/$rel" "$MANAGED/$rel"
  # or, equivalent and resumable for many files:
  rsync -a --update "$DESKTOP/$rel" "$MANAGED/$rel"

`--update` is the safety net: it refuses to overwrite a Managed file that is
newer, so a stray MANAGED_NEWER row in the audit log can't be silently
clobbered by the copy step.


Phase 3 — Verify, byte-for-byte
Hashes must match. Sizes must match. If they don't, stop and re-copy. Do not
proceed to deletion on a mismatch.

  shasum -a 256 "$DESKTOP/$rel" "$MANAGED/$rel" | tee -a "$AUDIT/post_copy_hashes.log"
  # Linux: sha256sum ...

  ls -l "$DESKTOP/$rel" "$MANAGED/$rel"   # sizes must match

Both SHA-256 lines for a given file should be identical. Anything else means
the copy didn't take or the wrong file was sourced; investigate before
deleting anything.


Phase 4 — Confirm the sync client agrees
Resume / re-enable the sync client. Trigger a manual sync if it has one.
Confirm in the client UI:

  - No "conflict" prompts for the file(s) you reconciled.
  - No pending uploads for the Desktop originals.
  - The managed folder's reported size still equals 6.8 GB. A smaller number
    means a file was lost somewhere; a larger one means something
    duplicated.

If the client offers "resolve conflict → keep newer," reject it. You've
already done the resolution manually; letting the client redo it re-introduces
the race.


Phase 5 — Delete the Desktop originals
Only after Phase 4 is clean. The client will see Desktop deletions as delete
events and propagate them. Managed is now your source of truth.

  rm -v "$DESKTOP/$rel"

Bulk-delete only after you've spot-checked a few `rm -v` lines and confirmed
only the files you intended are being removed.


Phase 6 — OS update
Only after Phase 5. Re-open the CSV from the Managed folder before launching
the update to confirm the recent edits are present. Then run the update.


Pitfalls to avoid
  - Do not let the sync client auto-resolve. Many clients pick the older mtime
    as winner when they think they "finished."
  - Do not copy Managed → Desktop. That direction overwrites your newer work.
  - Do not run the OS update first. An interrupted update can lock you out of
    reconciling cleanly.
  - Do not trust the "all synced" status as per-file currency. It's per-volume
    at best; per-file verification is on you.
  - Do not skip the audit assuming only one file was affected. The save-
    during-sync window is the risk window and can cover more than one file.

If at any point a hash check fails after a copy, stop. Re-source the file
from whichever side has the right content and re-run the copy. Don't proceed
to deletion on a mismatch.

No relevant prior context on this specific wash — proceeding with a focused technical answer.

WHAT WENT WRONG

Paper lifting with tape is usually bond failure at the surface, not a deep problem. The tape adhesive pulled harder than the paper's surface bond to the sizing layer. Even on a fully dry sheet, water just under the surface film + tight contact = the weakest layer tears off with the adhesive.

Two changes reliably fix this: lower the tape's adhesion demand at the moment of removal, and peel in a direction that splits the load rather than raking it across the sheet.

— -

PRACTICAL SALVAGE FOR THE LIFTED STRIP

Do not press it back down and hope it re-bonds. You will trap a weak, raised edge that takes pigment unevenly on the next wash and lifts again on the next tape pull.

Use this instead, in order:

1.  Trim any fibers standing proud of the line. A fresh razor blade, held flat, drawn once along the edge. Do not dig. Goal is a clean line, not a smooth surface.

2.  Re-wet only the damaged strip with a damp brush (clean water, not the wash solution). Just damp, not soaked. Let it sit 30 seconds. This swells the loose fiber back up and relaxes any crease.

3.  Press it flat under a clean blotter with light, even weight. A heavy book on a blotter is enough. 10–15 minutes. Do not rush this with heat.

4.  Check the edge. If it lies flush and the line reads as a hairline rather than a ridge, the sheet is back in shape. If it still reads as a ridge, the fibers are torn below the surface layer and no amount of pressing will hide it — accept the line, do not sand or fill. Wet-on-wet pigment flows into a torn fiber zone and re-bonds it on its own.

5.  If you re-coat, apply paint right up to and over the repaired edge on the next pass. Let the wash bridge the repair, do not fight it.

— -

TAPE-REMOVAL TEST (ONE VARIABLE CHANGED)

Keep everything from today's successful run identical: the steep-angle wash, the 20-second bead-wicking interval, the single firm brush blot, the one-touch edge boundary.

Change only how the tape comes off.

Pull direction: pull back along the tape's own length, not straight up. Angle the tape low, close to the paper, so the adhesive releases in a rolling line rather than across the whole strip at once. The leading edge of the release runs ahead of the trailing edge instead of the whole strip fighting the paper at once.

Pull speed: slow, steady, continuous. No pauses, no re-grabs mid-pull.

Pull hand: hold the tape with the flats of your fingers, not pinched. A pinch concentrates load at one point and rakes. Flat fingers spread the load across the full width.

Timing: remove the tape while the sheet is still slightly damp from the last blot, not bone-dry. The next-to-last blot — lift tape immediately after the blot, before the surface goes matte. Adhesive releases more cleanly from a surface with a touch of moisture in it. If your current run fully dries before tape removal, this is your single biggest variable to test.

Test sequence for one sheet:

-   Run the full wash with today's controls.
-   At the post-blot moment (sheet still evenly damp, not shiny wet), pull the bottom-edge tape first using the low-angle, flat-finger, slow-continuous method.
-   Pull the side tapes second the same way.
-   Inspect all four edges under raking light.

Pass criterion: no lifted fiber on any edge. If you see lift on one edge but not another, the failure is technique on that specific pull, not the method — re-pull the lifted edge the same way and check whether the lift is recoverable.

If you still see lift with damp removal, the next test is switching to a low-tack tape (standard washi or painter's tape rated "14-day clean removal"). Keep the damp-pull method. That isolates tape adhesion as the remaining variable.

Run the test on a throwaway sheet first if you have one. Same paper, same wash, same controls. You want to confirm the method before trusting it on a sheet that matters.

— -

Save the November 9 wash result, the lift event, and this test plan so the next session can pick up where you left off?

LOWEST-RISK OPTION, IN ORDER

1. Buy a small bag of the exact same formula locally
   - Same brand, same product line, same protein first on the ingredient panel. Most major brands (Royal Canin, Hill's, Purina Pro Plan, Orijen, etc.) are stocked at PetSmart, Petco, or independent pet stores; some are at grocery.
   - Check the ingredient panel — same ingredients in the same order means same formula. Regional variants exist for some brands under the same name.
   - A 4–6 lb bag covers ~3–4 days for a typical adult dog. Roughly $15–30.
   - This is the genuinely zero-disruption option. Same kibble, same gut response.

2. Bland bridge if you cannot find the same formula
   - Plain skinless chicken breast (boiled, no salt/oil/seasoning) + plain long-grain white rice (cooked soft, no butter/salt).
   - Ratio ~1 part chicken to 2 parts rice by volume. Shred the chicken finely.
   - No skin, no dark meat, no bones, no broth with onion/garlic.
   - Feed smaller, more frequent meals (3 small portions vs 1–2 large) — gentler on the gut.
   - Rough total for ~30 hours: ~1 lb chicken + ~1.5 cups dry rice.

3. Hybrid (most robust)
   - Buy whatever local bag is closest in formula for primary meals; keep bland ingredients on standby in case the new kibble causes a soft stool.

WHAT TO AVOID ON A BRIDGE
- Rich or fatty foods (table scraps, bacon, hamburger, dairy — many dogs are lactose intolerant).
- New proteins Kibo hasn't had before (turkey, fish, lamb) — adds a second variable on top of the swap.
- Switching multiple meals in a row to the same unfamiliar food — creates a sustained gut challenge rather than a brief bridge.
- Letting him skip water access. Rice-heavy meals are drying; make sure water is freely available.

CALL THE VET IF YOU SEE
- Vomiting — especially repeated, or any vomit with blood or coffee-ground appearance.
- Diarrhea that is watery, bloody, black/tarry, OR persists beyond 12–24 hours. One soft stool in 24 h is normal adjustment, not vet-worthy by itself.
- Refusing both food and water for more than ~12 hours.
- Lethargy beyond "a little quiet" — not getting up, not responding normally, hiding.
- Signs of abdominal pain: praying posture (front down, rear up), reluctance to be touched near the belly, tense or visibly distended abdomen. (Distention + restlessness in a deep-chested dog is an emergency — go now.)
- Dehydration signs: dry/tacky gums, skin that doesn't snap back when lifted at the scruff, sunken eyes.
- Any neurological change (disorientation, tremors, wobbliness) — low likelihood, but worth flagging.

CONTEXT I AM ASSUMING
- Kibo is a generally healthy adult dog with no known kidney disease, pancreatitis, food allergies, diabetes, or recent GI episodes. Your description ("eating and acting normally") supports that baseline.
- The gap is ~30 hours, covering Mon lunch, Mon dinner, Tue breakfast, and possibly Tue lunch — about 3 meals.
- I don't have his breed, age, or weight on file. If any of those change the math (very small dog with low caloric reserve, deep-chested breed where bloat is a worry, senior with kidney issues, etc.), tell me and I'll revise.

Plain gut check: a healthy adult dog handles 30 hours of bland or near-identical food without incident. The reason to call is rapid deterioration or any of the red flags above, not the bridge itself.

POST-VALVE-WORK FLUSHING SEQUENCE

The fine bubbles you're still seeing are almost certainly trapped air in the lines (a normal consequence of valve work), not contamination. Air in pipes causes sputtering and a milky/white look that clears from the BOTTOM up when you fill a glass and let it sit. If it clears that way, it's air. If it stays uniformly cloudy or anything settles, that's sediment and needs more attention.

Keep the stored water for you, Sam, and Kibo until cold lines are fully clear everywhere.

STEP 0 - BEFORE YOU FLUSH
  - Confirm no boil-water / do-not-use notice (you have).
  - Have towels and a bucket ready.
  - Remove aerators from kitchen and bathroom faucets. Sediment collects in
    aerator screens and will keep the stream cloudy even when the lines are
    flushing clean. Put the screens in a cup so you don't lose the gaskets.

STEP 1 - FLUSH COLD LINES, ENTRY -> FARTHEST
  Run COLD only at full flow. The goal is to push air and any dislodged
  sediment OUT of the system, not back through it. Order:
    1. Fixture nearest where water enters the unit (often kitchen cold).
    2. Bathroom sinks, in order of proximity to the entry.
    3. Shower(s) and tub(s) - use the shower, not just the spout, so the
       showerhead line gets flushed. Take the showerhead off if you can.
    4. Toilet tanks - flush several times and let them refill.
    5. Outdoor hose bib / laundry cold tap - briefly.
  Run each for 5-10 minutes, or until the stream is glass-clear with no
  bubbles and no particles. The kitchen cold may be the last to clear since
  it's often the longest horizontal run from the riser.

STEP 2 - THEN FLUSH HOT
  Only after ALL cold is clear:
    - Run hot at each fixture for several minutes.
    - This pulls any sediment through the water heater and out, rather than
      letting it settle in the tank.

STEP 3 - APPLIANCES (COLD FIRST, THEN HOT)
    - Washing machine: run an empty rinse/spin cycle on cold, then hot.
    - Dishwasher: run an empty rinse cycle.
    - Ice maker: empty the bin, discard the first 2-3 batches of ice
      (or stop the ice maker and let it cycle a few times before using).
    - Coffee maker / kettle / filter pitcher: run 2-3 full cycles of cold
      water through and discard.
    - Humidifier, pet water fountain (relevant for Kibo): empty, refill,
      run a cycle, discard.

STEP 4 - REASSEMBLE
  - Clean and reinstall aerators. If a screen is clogged with grit, soak it
    in white vinegar for 10 minutes, scrub with an old toothbrush, rinse.

DO NOT USE YET (until cold is clear throughout and aerators are clean)
  - Tap water for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, washing produce.
  - Ice from the ice maker.
  - Dishwasher or washing machine for actual dishes/laundry.
  - Hot water for anything that goes in a mouth or on skin (shaving,
    face-washing) until hot has been flushed too.
  - Refilling Kibo's bowl from the tap - use stored water.

CALL MAINTENANCE OR STOP USING THE WATER IF YOU SEE
  - Cloudiness that does NOT clear from the bottom up in a glass, or
    cloudiness that persists at a fixture after 15-20 minutes of flushing.
  - Brown, yellow, orange, red, or rust-colored water at any point - or
    water that clears and then turns discolored again after several
    minutes (intermittent sediment means the lines are still shedding).
  - Visible particles, grit, or flakes in the stream or settled in a glass.
  - Any odor beyond a mild chlorine/chloramine smell. Specifically: rotten
    egg / sulfur, sewage, fuel, oily, or sweet/chemical smells are stop-use
    signals even without a formal notice.
  - Pressure changes: a sudden drop, no flow at one or more fixtures while
    others are fine, or banging / "water hammer" in the lines.
  - Any visible leak - under sinks, around toilets, at the water heater,
    or wet spots on walls/ceilings. Air in lines can dislodge fitting
    seals that were already marginal.
  - The property manager issues a boil-water, do-not-drink, or do-not-use
    notice at any point during or after your flushing.

For Kibo specifically: the stored water covers drinking; the only change
is that bath-time / paw-rinse water can come from the tap only once cold
runs clear and you're confident no sediment is flushing through.

Practical stop-point: if the cold kitchen stream is glass-clear, bubble-
free, odor-free, and stable for 5+ minutes, and the same is true at the
farthest fixture, you're done and you can resume normal use in the order
above (cold first, then hot, then appliances).

ASSESSMENT

Don't ride it. Your own rule applies: sidewall cut with casing visible → shop, not ride. The tube holding pressure is temporary — under your weight on the rear wheel plus road flex, the cut will widen and a sudden blowout under load is a real loss-of-control risk. Most shops won't patch a sidewall with casing exposed; they'll recommend replacement. Plan to walk, take transit, or rideshare home and bring the bike with you.

SEQUENCE: PHOTOS FIRST, THEN DEFLATE, THEN TRANSPORT

1. Photos before deflating. The cut's behavior under pressure is what the shop actually wants to see. Take them now.
2. Move the bike to a flat, stable spot — wall, rack, or kickstand. Keep it upright so the rear wheel isn't loaded.
3. Cover the cut with a piece of tape (electrical or even masking). Stops debris from getting into the casing during handling and transport.
4. Remove the valve cap. Identify the valve type:
   - Schrader (car-style, threaded): press the core in with a small Allen key, coin edge, or a dedicated valve core tool.
   - Presta (skinny, locknut on top): unscrew the small knurled nut at the tip, then press the stem down to release air.
   Press and hold until the hiss stops and the tire is fully slack.
5. Decide transport mode — this changes what else you do:
   - Bus with front-mounted bike rack: leave the wheel on, just roll it on. The rack holds the frame, tire pressure is irrelevant. Confirm the rack fits your wheel size and that a slack tire is OK on that agency's rack (most are fine; a few want a firm tire).
   - Light rail / subway: roll it on, no disassembly needed.
   - Rideshare (Uber XL / Lyft XL): deflate as above, then drop the front wheel off for a flat load in the trunk or back seat. Loosening the rear is optional and only needed if you're fitting the bike somewhere tight; otherwise leave it on.
6. If you remove the front wheel, protect the rotor or the exposed fork ends — a piece of cardboard or a rag prevents damage and complaints from the driver.

  - Close-up of the cut with a coin or ruler next to it for scale. Make sure the casing ply is visible in the frame.
  - Slightly wider shot of the same area showing how the cut opens when you squeeze the tire.
  - Whole-tire profile shot showing the cut's position relative to the tread centerline and the rim.
  - Tire sidewall — manufacturer logo, model name, and the size stamp (e.g., 700x32c, 650bx47). This is what they need to order a replacement.
  - If you can pop the tire off the rim at any point, an inside-view photo of the cut is gold.

Given what you described — shallow scrape at the pad edge, gravel already rinsed free, bleeding stopped, full weight-bearing, no swelling or embedded material — this is a reasonable at-home situation. Here's a conservative plan.

CLEANING (once or twice daily for 3-5 days)

  1. Rinse the paw with lukewarm water or sterile saline. A gentle stream from a cup or low-pressure faucet is fine.
  2. If you see caked dirt, soak the paw in a shallow bowl of lukewarm water for 2-3 minutes, then pat dry.
  3. Clean the scrape itself with dilute chlorhexidine (0.05%) or povidone-iodine (Betadine) diluted to a weak-tea color. Apply with gauze or cotton, wipe gently, rinse lightly.
  4. Pat dry. Optional: a thin smear of plain triple-antibiotic ointment — use the plain version, not the "pain relief" / lidocaine one.
  5. Skip hydrogen peroxide and rubbing alcohol — both damage healing tissue.
  6. If he'll tolerate it, cover with a non-adherent pad and a light wrap or a breathable dog bootie for walks; remove indoors so the paw can air out.

ACTIVITY AND ENVIRONMENT

  - Short leash-only potty breaks for the next 24-48 hours. No park, no running, no rough pavement, no muddy trails.
  - Keep the paw clean and dry between outings — wipe with a damp cloth after each walk, dry the pad and between the toes.
  - Discourage licking. A few licks right after the scrape is normal; persistent licking delays healing and drags in bacteria. If he won't leave it alone, use an e-collar or a snug sock he can't shake off.
  - Watch his gait on the next outing. Full weight-bearing is reassuring, but don't push distance yet — let the pad rest a couple of days.

CALL THE VET IF YOU SEE

  - Bleeding restarts or won't stop with gentle, direct pressure after 5-10 minutes.
  - Increasing swelling, warmth, or obvious tenderness when you touch near the scrape.
  - Spreading redness or red streaks tracking up the leg.
  - Pus, cloudy or colored discharge, or a foul smell from the wound.
  - Limping that worsens, or refusal to bear weight, persisting beyond about 24 hours.
  - The wound gapes, deepens, or shows no visible improvement in 48 hours.
  - Anything still embedded that you can't rinse free, or a deeper puncture you didn't initially see.
  - Systemic signs: appetite drop, lethargy, panting at rest, or fever-ish behavior.

For tonight specifically: since bleeding has stopped, he's bearing weight, and the gravel is out, a single gentle rinse and a few minutes of close observation are enough. The bigger overnight risk is him licking the pad raw — if he keeps circling back to it, get a sock or e-collar on before bed, since you won't catch every quiet licking session once you're asleep.

Organic: 78/120 = 0.65 = 65.0%

Interpretation — descriptive only, on Owen's cut:

What this shows. Partner leads on the observed activation rate, Organic sits in the middle, and Paid social trails by a wide margin. Read as three point estimates of activation within each channel's eligible population in Q3, that's the picture.

What this does not show. The rates are not channel-quality effects. We don't have a causal comparison here, so none of these gaps should be read as "Partner is a better channel than Paid social" or as a basis for reallocating spend. A few reasons it can't carry that weight:

- Unequal denominators. The eligible populations differ in size (120 vs 45 vs 90), so each rate is estimated with different precision. Partner's 73.3% is built on 45 eligible users — small enough that a handful of activations moves the rate materially. Organic's 65.0% on 120 is the most precisely pinned of the three; Paid social's 46.7% on 90 is in between. The rank-order is real-looking, but the *magnitude* of the gaps, especially anything hinging on Partner, isn't.
- Selection into channel. The eligible set in each channel is who we managed to reach / who showed up, not a random assignment. The people Partner delivers are a different population than the people Paid social delivers, and activation propensity is plausibly correlated with whatever drives that selection. A 27-point Partner-vs-Paid-social gap is at least as likely to reflect who's in each channel as what's true about each channel.
- No controls, no experiment. We haven't adjusted for segment, intent, tenure, creative, or time-of-Q3 mix. We also haven't randomized traffic across channels. So the cut is a description of three non-comparable cohorts, not an effect estimate.

What it's good for. As a descriptive cut this is a reasonable starting signal — it tells us Paid social is the one worth looking at first, and that Partner's lead is small-sample enough that we shouldn't act on it yet. The next step, if we want anything causal, is either a holdout/readout-style cut that holds the audience definition constant across channels, or an actual randomized allocation test, before any reallocation or forecast credit.

Bottom line: three channel-level activation rates with very different sample sizes and self-selected denominators. Observed gap ≠ channel-quality gap. Descriptive only — no lift, no rollout, no reallocation call from this.

Five signup-survey comments split into five distinct themes. Three are guidance-shaped (next step, closure, correctness), one is an authority blocker outside Helio's setup flow, one is a product-state signal mismatch. None of these redefine activation v3, and n=5 is not prevalence — these are themes present in this set, not claims about the cohort.

THEME CODES

[1] Guidance — next-step ambiguity. User has completed a step (Google Ads connected) and lacks a clear "what comes next" cue from the product.

[2] Guidance — closure ambiguity. User isn't sure whether the action they took (contact import) constitutes completion of setup. Asking for a definition, not a fix.

[3] Product-state — signal mismatch. User believes they completed the step (invited team) but the checklist still says incomplete. Either the action didn't update state, the checklist checks a different condition than the user thinks, or there is a sync delay. Can't tell which from the comment alone.

[4] Authority — external dependency. User is blocked by an authority outside their control (security team's Salesforce access review). They cannot progress regardless of in-product guidance.

[5] Guidance — post-completion correctness doubt. User has technically completed setup (first sync worked) but is unsure the configuration is right (lifecycle stage mapping). Distinct from [2]: [2] is "did I finish?"; [5] is "is what I finished right?"

CAUTIOUS SYNTHESIS

Authority:
  One blocker pattern in the set: external approval gates (security review). Not addressable inside Helio's setup flow directly. Flag for Ines's lifecycle-audit-risk view; don't propose activation changes from a single comment.

Guidance:
  The dominant theme is guidance, not state. Three of five comments are users asking what to do, what counts as done, or whether their setup is correct. This is a guidance-surface signal, not a flow-shape signal. Note: it overlaps with activation v3 only if v3 specifies a completion signal the guidance isn't surfacing — and we are not changing v3 to address guidance gaps.

Product-state:
  One signal: checklist says "incomplete" after a step the user believes they completed. Could be a real product-state bug, a definition mismatch (checklist checks X, user did Y), or a latency issue. Without instrumentation, can't tell which. If it recurs, that's Owen's shape+ex lane, not a definition change.

CAVEATS

  - n=5 signup-survey comments is anecdotal. Themes here, not prevalence claims.
  - Activation definition v3 is unchanged. None of these comments argue for redefining it.
  - Sampling/response conditions for the survey aren't visible from the comments.

Reading the instructor's note through your reframe: the technique being introduced is the clean 45° tape pull on a fully dry passage, and tape-removal direction is the only thing to vary in this study. Everything else stays locked. Design follows.

WATERCOLOR STUDY — ISOLATED VARIABLE: TAPE-REMOVAL DIRECTION

Locked across every cell:
  - Paper (single sheet, same block)
  - Tape type, width, application pressure
  - Wash recipe: pigment, water ratio, brush, load
  - Wash technique: longer stroke, steep angle
  - One firm blot at the lower edge (same blotter, same dwell)
  - 20-second bead-wicking interval
  - One-touch edge control
  - Drying: ambient only — no heat
  - Pull angle: ~45°
  - Pull speed: slow and steady

Variable (the single thing that changes):
  - Direction of tape pull relative to the masked edge.

Test grid — one sheet, five cells:

  A. Pull AWAY from the wash at 45° — baseline best practice
  B. Pull TOWARD the wash at 45° — drags back over the painted edge
  C. Pull PARALLEL to the edge at 45° — lateral slide along the boundary
  D. Pull PERPENDICULAR straight back at 45°
  E. Lift straight up at 90° — no horizontal component; control for angle itself

Per-cell procedure (identical except step 7):

  1. Apply tape — same pressure, same smoothing pass.
  2. Lay the wash — longer stroke, steep angle, same load.
  3. One firm blot at the lower bead.
  4. Wait 20 seconds.
  5. One-touch edge control — single clean brush touch.
  6. Wait until the passage is FULLY DRY — touch-test before pulling; any cool damp spot will lift.
  7. Pull tape in the assigned direction — slow, no jerk.
  8. Inspect and log.

Log per cell:
  - Edge crispness: sharp / faint feather / bleed-under
  - Any pigment lift along the edge
  - Dry-down: even or uneven
  - Bead behavior at the edge

Decide:
  Which direction produces the cleanest edge with no lift. That direction becomes the locked parameter in the NEXT study, where heat is introduced as the new variable.

Session rules:
  - Same water pot, same brush (rinse between cells)
  - One session — drying conditions stay comparable across cells
  - Redos go adjacent to the original cell, not on a fresh sheet
  - No heat at any point — the next study, not this one

Pre-pull checklist (run before each cell's step 7):
  - Passage fully dry to the touch
  - Tape line visible and clean along the wash boundary
  - Brush, blotter, and towel unchanged since the prior cell

The echo is doing real work in the ending, and I don't want to dismiss it. When Mara teaches the narrator where to put the key, she frames that location as a shared address: "where anyone who knew me would look." The stone isn't really a hiding place — it's a convention between people who know each other. So when the narrator ends the book by sending the key back to the same spot, the location carries everything Mara put into it. It reads as continuity. It reads as: the arrangement that connected us is still in force. Whoever knows, still knows. That's the member's reading, and the text supports it.

But I keep stalling on the sentence before it. "I locked the gate." That isn't inherited from Mara. Mara taught a hiding place; she didn't teach a locking. The narrator is doing something new, and doing it deliberately — first person, simple past, the kind of grammar the book reserves for actions the narrator owns. The lock adds a threshold that wasn't in the original arrangement. Under Mara's instruction, the key was simply where a friend could find it. Under the narrator's own practice, the gate is closed, and then the key is placed.

So the ending holds two acts at once. The location is the same, and sameness is the invitation reading. The lock is the new act, and the lock is what makes the location function differently now — because a key under a stone, with the gate open, is just a key in a yard; a key under a stone, with the gate locked, is something a visitor has to know to look for, and to reach. The narrator has built a small obstacle and then, separately, ensured it can be undone by the right person.

What I can't resolve, and what I don't think the book resolves, is whether the narrator believes anyone still knows. Mara knew. The arrangement was built for a relationship. The ending shows the narrator performing both halves of the practice alone — locking and replacing — without telling us whether anyone is expected. That silence is what lets the ending be both things at once. The boundary and the invitation don't have to be reconciled, because the narrator hasn't told us who, if anyone, the locked gate is for.

Kibo is very likely fine. Let me give you the assessment, the math behind it, and the watch-window.

BOTTOM LINE
  No emergency call needed. A sub-teaspoon of gravy where onion and
  garlic are flavoring components (not the bulk ingredient) is well
  below the toxic dose for a 42-lb dog. Kibo's current behavior is
  consistent with no immediate problem. Monitor, don't panic.

WHY (dose math, roughly)
  Kibo ~ 19 kg. Allium toxicity thresholds (cooked or raw, cooking
  does not destroy the toxic organosulfur compounds):
    - Onion: ~ 5 g/kg → ~ 95 g for Kibo
    - Garlic: ~ 5 g/kg, more potent → ~ 95 g for Kibo
  Your teaspoon of gravy ~ 5 mL, and gravy is mostly fat / stock /
  thickener. Real allium content in that teaspoon is on the order of
  fractions of a gram. Even being generous and assuming the entire
  teaspoon were onion, that's ~ 5 g — about 1/20th of the toxic dose.
  Margin is wide.

WHAT YOU ARE WATCHING (and when)
  Allium toxicity is a delayed oxidative hemolytic anemia. The
  timeline matters:
    12-24 h   GI phase: vomiting, diarrhea, drooling, appetite loss,
              abdominal discomfort. Most common early sign.
    24-48 h   Urine color: red, brown, or "coffee"-colored urine
              (hemoglobinuria from RBC breakdown). Easy to miss in a
              dog that goes outside — actively check.
    2-5 days  Hematologic phase: pale or jaundiced (yellow) gums,
              lethargy, weakness, rapid breathing, tachycardia. This
              is the dangerous window. Heinz bodies can show on blood
              smear by 24 h; frank anemia lags a couple of days.
    Up to 7 d  Late phase: collapse in severe untreated cases.

  Kibo has no current symptoms and the dose is sub-toxic. The realistic
  odds of any of these developing from this exposure are very low. But
  the watch window extends to ~ 5-7 days because of the delayed
  hematologic phase.

WHEN TO ESCALATE (any of these, any time in the next week)
    - Repeated vomiting or refusal of more than one meal
    - Red / brown / dark urine (lift a tail or check the yard)
    - Pale, white, or yellow-tinged gums (normal = bubblegum pink)
    - New lethargy, weakness, or exercise intolerance
    - Fast or labored breathing at rest
  If any of those show up, call your regular vet the same day and
  mention the allium exposure — they may want a CBC to check for
  Heinz bodies / hemolysis. Kibo eating a teaspoon of gravy at
  sub-toxic dose does not warrant an ER visit on its own.

PEACE-OF-MIND OPTIONS (your call, not required)
    - ASPCA Animal Poison Control: 888-426-4435 (consult fee applies)
    - Pet Poison Helpline: 855-764-7661 (consult fee applies)
    - Your regular vet's office line — many will answer a "is this
      dose concerning?" question from an established client for free.
  These exist for the cases where the dose math is unclear or
  symptoms are developing. Yours is neither, which is why I'd skip
  the call unless you want the confirmation for your own nerves.

Given the constraints — fully cooked now, about a 3 hour gap, the countertop oven tied up with the mac and stuffing, and the roaster's minimum being 200°F — the move that is both safe and protects quality is to cool the turkey now and reheat at mealtime. Holding it at 200°F in the roaster for three hours is safe temperature-wise (it's above the 140°F hot-holding floor) but it is still oven heat on white meat for three hours, so the breast will overcook and dry out. The 200°F floor is the reason the "just leave it in the roaster" answer is a quality trap.

The cool-and-reheat method:

1. Right now (~11:10am): Carve the turkey. Pull the breast off in whole pieces or thick slices and separate the thighs and drumsticks. Smaller, thinner pieces cool faster and reheat more evenly than a whole bird.

2. Cool it down fast. Lay the pieces in a shallow metal pan (not plastic, not glass from a hot oven). Set that pan inside a larger pan or your sink filled with ice water, and stir or turn the meat every few minutes. You are trying to hit two USDA targets: get from ~170°F down past 70°F within about 30–45 minutes, then from 70°F down past 40°F within the next few hours. The ice bath is what makes this workable at home — without it, a whole turkey cools too slowly and you spend too much cumulative time in the 40–140°F danger zone, past the 2-hour rule.

3. Cover and refrigerate once it is below 40°F (around 11:55–12:15pm). A light film of broth or melted butter over the top before covering helps with fridge surface drying.

4. About 1:15–1:30pm: Pull the turkey out. While the mac, stuffing, and rolls finish in the countertop oven, put the turkey on a sheet pan with a splash of broth or a couple pats of butter, cover tightly with foil, and slide into the countertop oven at 325°F. It should hit 165°F internally in about 20–30 minutes depending on thickness. If timing with the other dishes is tight, do the reheat in the roaster instead — 200°F with broth and foil for 30–40 minutes works fine for already-carved meat, because a short moist reheat is a very different problem than a 3-hour dry hold.

5. Rest 5 minutes, then serve.

If carving that early feels like too much, a workable middle path: leave the turkey whole, set it on a rack over a bed of ice in a cooler or on a sheet pan in the fridge, and put it into the countertop oven at 1:00–1:15pm at 325°F covered with foil and a splash of broth until it reads 165°F in the thickest part. Whole-bird reheat from fridge temp runs 45–75 minutes, so start earlier; the carved version is just faster and more even.

One thing not to do: tent the turkey in foil on the counter for three hours. Even fully cooked, that puts you well past the 2-hour cumulative danger-zone window by 2:00pm.

Scale factor: 14/8 = 7/4 = 1.75

Scaled quantities (each base x 1.75):
- Cornmeal: 1.5 × 1.75 = 2.625 = 2 5/8 cups
- Flour: 0.5 × 1.75 = 0.875 = 7/8 cup
- Sugar: 2 × 1.75 = 3.5 = 3 1/2 tbsp
- Baking powder: 2 × 1.75 = 3.5 = 3 1/2 tsp
- Salt: 0.75 × 1.75 = 1.3125 = 1 5/16 tsp
- Buttermilk: 1.25 × 1.75 = 2.1875 = 2 3/16 cups
- Eggs: 2 × 1.75 = 3.5 eggs (the awkward one)
- Butter, melted: 4 × 1.75 = 7 tbsp

Recipe scaled from 8 to 14 servings (1.75x)
============================================

Cornmeal            1 1/2 cups  ->  2 5/8 cups
All-purpose flour   1/2 cup     ->  7/8 cup
Sugar               2 tbsp      ->  3 1/2 tbsp
Baking powder       2 tsp       ->  3 1/2 tsp
Salt                3/4 tsp     ->  1 5/16 tsp
Buttermilk          1 1/4 cups  ->  2 3/16 cups
Large eggs          2           ->  3 1/2  <-- awkward
Melted butter       4 tbsp      ->  7 tbsp

Bake at 400°F for 22-25 minutes (check earlier rather than later; see below).

Awkward consequences, named instead of hidden
---------------------------------------------

Eggs. 1.75 x 2 lands on exactly 3.5, not a whole number. Rounding either way changes the batter: 3 eggs makes it slightly dry/crumbly; 4 eggs shifts the fat-and-protein balance and tightens the crumb toward a cakey texture. Neither is what the original 8-serving recipe gives you.

Pan size. 1.75x the volume does not fit a single 8-inch square pan. The original batter fills that pan at roughly the right depth; multiplying by 1.75 would overflow or rise into a dense, underdone brick. A 9x13 is the standard step up from an 8x8, but it only holds about 1.5x by area, so a single 9x13 is too small for 1.75x. A single 10-inch round or 11x7 would be a closer fit, but they change shape and edge-browning.

Bake time. A larger volume in a proportionally larger pan sets up almost identically for heat penetration, so 400°F for 22-25 minutes is still a defensible starting window - but it is a starting window, not a guarantee. Doneness cues beat the timer.

Recommended treatment
---------------------

Eggs. Beat one egg in a small bowl, then measure 1 1/2 tablespoons (about 1.75 oz / 49 g) into the batter. Discard the remainder or save for another use. This keeps the original recipe's egg contribution exact, rather than rounding the recipe itself.

Pan. Use a 9x13-inch pan. It will be slightly shallow for 1.75x the batter - expect a thinner, more crust-edged cornbread rather than the taller, plush square of the original. That is the honest trade for keeping one pan. If you want the original's depth and browning pattern, bake in two 8-inch square pans side by side; divide the batter roughly 60/40 (the deeper pan gets more) and start checking the shallower pan first at about 18 minutes.

Bake-time check. Start checking at the low end of the window (about 22 minutes) regardless of which pan you use. The recipe's doneness cues already work: a wooden pick should come out with a few moist crumbs but no wet batter, and the top should spring back lightly when pressed. If the 9x13 is browning fast on the edges before the center is set, tent loosely with foil for the last few minutes. Pull it when the pick is clean rather than cooking to the timer's max.

INTERPRETATION

The two methods aren't really "different angles" — they're different kinematic regimes. A 45° peel back over itself runs along the paint film and spreads stress across more of the tape/paint interface; a 90° straight pull concentrates stress at the leading edge. The mechanism matches what you observed: lower peak stress per unit width at 45°, higher at 90°. So the result is consistent with a real method effect, not just noise.

The "two places" detail matters too. Localized fiber lift at two points reads more like local adhesion variation (a fingerprint, dust, a thicker paint bead, two thin-paper spots) than a wholesale edge problem. That nudges the interpretation toward "angle is doing it," but it doesn't rule out edge.

WHAT YOUR DESIGN CONTROLS
- Same painting, so paper, paint film, and dry state match
- Same tape, same dwell time, no warming on either side
- The two edges are spatially close

WHAT IT DOESN'T CONTROL
- Which edge got which treatment (no randomization)
- Anything edge-specific you might not have noticed: paint thickness gradient, paper variation, how that edge was handled or whether tape was repositioned there

RECOMMENDATION

Run one minimal confirmation before changing your default. The cost is tiny and the confound you flagged is exactly the sort of thing that produces false positives in a single-edge comparison.

Minimal design, on the same painting:

1. Lay two short tape strips in an interior area away from the edges you already tested — top center or bottom center, where paint and paper state should be most uniform.
2. Randomize which strip gets which method (coin flip).
3. Remove one at 45° back-over-itself, one at 90° straight pull, same dwell as before, no warming.

How to read it:
- 45° clean, 90° lifts → angle is the dominant factor. Adopt 45° back-over-itself as default.
- Both clean → your original right-edge lift was edge-specific; don't generalize yet. The n=1 was driven by an unnoticed edge difference.
- Both lift → something else is wrong (tape batch, paint film, paper). Investigate before committing to any change.

If you don't have spare painting area for two strips, lay one interior strip and remove it at 90° straight pull. Clean → edge-specific. Lifts → angle is the cause. Either outcome resolves the confound for less work than another full painting.

Net: don't adopt 45° yet on this evidence. The result points the right way, but one confirmation in an interior position separates removal direction from edge position cheaply, and your wash study was clearly built to that standard.

CONSERVATIVE CALL

Run: STOP. No test jog, no slow shakeout, no "see how it feels." Your PT clearance rule fires here — recurrent focal pain means renewed clinical follow-up, not self-clearance by another run.

Cycling: HOLD too, pending therapist input. It is low-impact but it still loads the medial ankle / tib post. Don't use it as a back-door test.

Walking: keep ordinary daily walking at your normal level. No extension, no added hills, no uneven-terrain "let's check." Kibo walks: same routine, easy pace. If a walk makes it worse, shorten it — don't push through.

Other: no hop test, no calf raise probe, no stretch-into-it, no massage gun on the spot. Treat it like something you're protecting, not something you're diagnosing.

WHAT TO SEND YOUR THERAPIST

Paste-ready, short and factual:

"Onset Sat 11/30 at the end of an easy 22-min continuous run. Focal ache, inside (medial) right ankle. Worst ~2/10; still locally tender to palpation Sun evening. Did not settle with ordinary walking — different from the recent bilateral calf stiffness, which did. No swelling, bruising, gait change, numbness, or pain at rest. I've stopped running and cycling pending your input. Walking only, at normal daily level. Is in-clinic follow-up indicated, and is there anything I should add or avoid in the meantime?"

URGENT-EVAL TRIGGERS — same-day contact if any of these show up

  - swelling, bruising, or warmth at the site
  - can't bear weight, or a new limp you didn't have yesterday
  - numbness, tingling, or color / temperature change in the foot
  - pain at rest, or pain that wakes you from sleep
  - calf pain or calf swelling (flag separately — different concern)
  - a snap or pop, locking / catching, or a sense of giving way
  - rapid pain escalation, fever, or any skin change over the area

If it stays a focal 2/10 tenderness with none of the above through Monday, the right move is the therapist message above — not another run to settle the question.

The point isn't to find it — it's to rule out the obvious so the utility/maintenance call is productive.

BOTTOM LINE

  Do not use that hair dryer at that outlet until the cause is
  identified. The GFCI tripped twice on dryer use, which means the
  dryer is leaking current to ground at or above the ~5 mA trip
  threshold - that is the same magnitude that can injure or kill a
  person, which is exactly what the GFCI exists to prevent. The lamp
  working after reset only tells you the outlet itself is not dead;
  it tells you nothing about the dryer or the wiring.

  Treat this as BOTH until evidence separates them:
    - Report the outlet/circuit to your landlord/management today
      in writing (it is their wiring, not a tenant repair).
    - Stop using the dryer at any outlet until you can isolate it
      or replace it.


WHY THE EVIDENCE IS AMBIGUOUS, NOT REASSURING

  A GFCI trips when hot and neutral currents differ by ~5 mA. Two
  trips on the same appliance, same outlet, with no other warning
  signs is consistent with three causes, and you cannot distinguish
  them from this side of the outlet face:

    1. The dryer itself is leaking (most likely if it is old, has
       been dropped, has a marginal cord, or has any moisture
       history).
    2. The outlet or wiring is leaking (nicked insulation, moisture
       in the box, a GFCI aging past ~10 years).
    3. Both at once.

  The lamp working rules out "the circuit is dead" - that is all it
  rules out. A 12-15 A hair dryer will expose leakage that a 0.1 A
  lamp cannot.


SAFE ISOLATION SEQUENCE

  Do these, and do NOT do more.

  1. Dryer: parked, unplugged, not used at any outlet until sorted.
  2. Outlet: still fine for a low-draw lamp or phone charger after
     a successful reset. Do not use a heater, curling iron, straightener,
     or other high-draw device there.
  3. GFCI self-test, once: press TEST - it should trip and cut power.
     Press RESET - power should return. If TEST does not trip the
     GFCI, the GFCI itself has failed protection. That IS urgent -
     go straight to the urgent-signs path below.
  4. Map downstream: if any other bathroom or nearby outlets went
     dead when this GFCI tripped, they are on its LOAD side. Note them;
     they belong in the same report.
  5. Visual check (eyes only, do not touch): outlet face, screw-on
     plate, wall around it. Stop and escalate urgently if you see
     anything in the urgent-signs list below.


REPORTING SEQUENCE

  Open the maintenance ticket or email to your property manager
  today, in writing. The two trips, the dryer, and the post-reset
  lamp behavior is the whole story they need - keep it factual.

  Include:

    - Date and time of each trip (Dec 5, ~9 pm local, both events).
    - Appliance in use each time (hair dryer; model/age if known).
    - That a low-draw lamp worked normally after each reset.
    - That there is no heat, smell, discoloration, buzzing, or
      moisture observed.
    - That you have stopped using the dryer at that outlet.
    - That you request a licensed electrician to evaluate the
      circuit and the GFCI before the outlet is returned to
      normal use.

  After-hours note: many landlords have a 24-hour emergency line
  for electrical even when general maintenance is next-day. If yours
  does, this qualifies - "GFCI tripped twice, occupant has stopped
  using the appliance, no active hazard signs." If no after-hours
  line, opening the ticket tonight still creates the paper trail
  and puts you on Friday's first dispatch.

  Keep the dryer available to show the electrician. Do not run it
  for them "to see if it trips again" - the two trips are already
  the demonstration.


HOW TO LATER DISTINGUISH DRYER vs. OUTLET

  Only a licensed electrician with a megger or leakage tester can
  do this safely. Do not try to DIY it.

  If you want a low-risk hint before the visit, with the dryer
  unplugged and your hands dry:

    - Plug the dryer into a GFCI-protected outlet in a DIFFERENT
      room (a kitchen-counter GFCI, for example). Use it briefly.
    - If it trips there too, the dryer is the source. Replace it;
      do not bother with a repair shop.
    - If it behaves normally there, the original outlet/circuit
      is the suspect, and the electrician visit is what confirms.

  This is a hint, not a verdict. Still file the report either way.


LIKELY OUTCOME

    - Dryer is the source (common for older units or any with cord
      damage): retire it. Hair dryers are not cost-effective to
      repair, and any "fix" cannot give back the ground-fault
      margin the unit used to have.
    - Wiring or GFCI is the source: electrician replaces the GFCI,
      inspects the box for moisture or damaged insulation, may pull
      a new circuit if the cable run is compromised.
    - Both: dryer goes, electrician handles the rest.


URGENT SIGNS - escalate immediately, do not reset

  Any one of these turns this from "report today" into "report now
  and do not use the outlet at all":

    - Burning smell, even faint, from the outlet, wall, or dryer.
    - Discoloration, scorch marks, or melted plastic on the outlet
      face or wall plate.
    - Buzzing, crackling, sizzling, or popping from the outlet.
    - Outlet, plate, or surrounding wall warm or hot to touch.
    - Trip of the BREAKER (not just the GFCI reset button) - that
      is a different, more serious fault.
    - Shock, tingle, or "pins-and-needles" sensation when touching
      the dryer, the outlet, faucets, or any metal in the bathroom.
    - Visible moisture, water staining, or rust in or around the
      outlet box.
    - Trip happens the instant the dryer is PLUGGED IN, before the
      switch is moved - indicates a hard ground fault, not a
      load-dependent leak.
    - Any other outlet, light, or appliance on what seems to be the
      same circuit misbehaving (flickering, dimming, buzzing).
    - The GFCI TEST button does not trip the device when pressed
      (protection is silently failed).

  For any of the above: treat the outlet as live-but-unsafe. If you
  can confidently identify the breaker for that bathroom, switch it
  off. Call your landlord or an emergency electrician immediately.
  If you smell burning or see scorch and cannot reach anyone quickly,
  treat it as a fire risk and call your local emergency number.


WHAT NOT TO DO

    - Do not keep resetting and trying the dryer "to see if it
      happens again." It will, and each trip is one where the
      protection worked - the next event is the one you cannot
      rely on the protection still working.
    - Do not move the dryer to a non-GFCI outlet via extension cord
      or adapter. Removing the protection is the worse direction.
    - Do not assume "it's fine because the lamp works." That is a
      category error - the lamp cannot expose what the dryer
      exposed.

Opening observation

The two passages do something subtle together, and the scene's whole weight lives in the way they pull against each other. The first stages a future the narrator has made inescapable for herself: by sliding the letter beneath the tax papers, she has guaranteed her own annual rediscovery of it. The line is not decorative — "where every April her hands would have to find it again" is a small mechanical prophecy. She has chosen a hiding place that does not hide; it reschedules. The second passage stages a present that is, by contrast, fully closed. "Not tonight," the key turned, the hour refused. So the scene is built on two different temporal logics running at once — one that loops back to her, one that locks shut in front of her. The question for the room is not which one wins, but what kind of act it is to choose the lock when you have also chosen the loop. That is the door both readings are standing at, and I want us to keep it open.

Three questions

1. What does the choice of hiding place actually do? Tax papers are not a neutral drawer — they have a season, a deadline, a forced handling, an obligation attached to fingers and a calendar. Did the narrator put the letter there because the place guarantees eventual confrontation, or because it guarantees a ritualized deferral that looks like confrontation? Is the April rediscovery an appointment she has made with herself, or a recurring postponement she has quietly dressed up as one?

2. How should we read "Not tonight"? The phrase is small and ordinary — the kind of thing said to an invitation, a drink, a child's request — and it is paired not with another sentence but with a physical act, a key turned in a lock. Is she naming a real boundary ("there is a right time, and this is not it"), or is she performing one in language so she does not have to examine whether she means it? And if she means it tonight, what would actually have to be different on another night for the letter to be opened — and is that condition ever something she controls?

3. The letter is unopened in both readings. In one, that is a temporary state on its way to being changed. In the other, it is the permanent condition the scene is really about, and everything else — the tax papers, the locked night, the eventual April — is costume and cover. What in the text, and what in our own experience of letters we know we should open, lets us tell the difference? Or does the scene quietly suggest that, sometimes, the difference is not tellable from inside the person's life, only from the outside, and only after a long time?

Image 8.5" x 11.25" on 9" x 12" paper, assumed centered on the paper (standard watercolor practice, and consistent with the framer's numbers):
  Paper border around image: 0.25" on sides, 0.375" top/bottom

Signature (relative to image, origin top-left):
  Right edge at x = 8.5 - 0.2 = 8.3"
  Bottom edge at y = 11.25 - 0.2 = 11.05"

For the signature to be fully visible, the mat opening must crop at least 0.2" from the right and bottom painted edges. Both options crop less than that, so the signature is visible in both — the question is by how much.

OPTION 1 — 8.15" x 10.9" opening ($68), centered on the image

  Image crop per edge:
    Horizontal: (8.5 - 8.15) / 2 = 0.175"
    Vertical:   (11.25 - 10.9) / 2 = 0.175"

  Paper overlap (under mat border):
    Sides:      0.25 + 0.175 = 0.425"
    Top/bottom: 0.375 + 0.175 = 0.55"

  Signature clearance (right and bottom): 0.2 - 0.175 = 0.025"

  -> Crop is 0.175", below the 0.2" threshold, so the signature IS visible — but only by 1/40". Your "almost no signature clearance" reading is correct.

OPTION 2 — 8.25" x 11" opening ($76), centered on the image (also centered on the paper)

  Image crop per edge:
    Horizontal: (8.5 - 8.25) / 2 = 0.125"
    Vertical:   (11.25 - 11) / 2 = 0.125"

  Paper overlap:
    Sides:      0.25 + 0.125 = 0.375"
    Top/bottom: 0.375 + 0.125 = 0.5"

  Signature clearance (right and bottom): 0.2 - 0.125 = 0.075"

COMPARISON

                              Option 1            Option 2
  Cost                        $68                 $76
  Paper overlap (sides)       0.425"              0.375"
  Paper overlap (top/bottom)  0.55"               0.5"
  Image crop per edge         0.175"              0.125"
  Signature clearance         0.025"              0.075"

RECOMMENDATION

Use Option 2 (8.25" x 11") for the placement proof.

The signature is the irreversible element. Option 1's 0.025" clearance is below the practical ~1/32" tolerance for mat cutting and centering — a small miss clips the signature. Option 2's 0.075" (3/32") margin is still tight but gives you a real buffer against mat-cutting variation and any minor image-or-signature placement error.

Both openings are secure on paper overlap. Option 1's 0.425"/0.55" is generous; Option 2's 0.375"/0.5" is still well above the ~0.25" minimum usually cited for a 9x12 piece. So this isn't really a "secure overlap vs. signature" trade — it's "tighter image vs. signature margin," and the margin wins. The $8 premium buys real insurance against a permanent mistake on the signature, which is exactly the risk a placement proof is meant to flush out.

  Redness that is RAPIDLY INCREASING — markedly worse hour to hour or morning to evening, or new redness spreading

  THICK discharge — yellow or green, sticky, crusting, or any "pus-like" appearance

  PERSISTENT nausea or vomiting — not just one queasy moment, but ongoing or repeated, or anything keeping her from keeping meds or fluids down

  Anything else that just feels wrong to either of you and isn't on this list — the handout isn't exhaustive; instinct is a signal


Practical Saturday notes

  Most eye clinics don't have a Saturday phone line. Find the after-hours or emergency number on the discharge paperwork NOW, before you need it, and save it in your phone. It's usually the surgeon's exchange or a partner on call.

  If something crosses into the "call now" category today and you can't reach the clinic, the reasonable next step is the ER or an urgent ophthalmology visit — call before driving in so they can prep.

  If it's borderline (say pain goes to 3/10 but everything else is stable), you don't have to panic-call at 9:30 PM Sunday — but DO call the clinic first thing Monday morning rather than waiting for Wednesday.


What "stable enough to wait for Wednesday" looks like

  Pain stays at or below 2/10 and trends DOWN over the days, not up
  Vision stays at or near discharge baseline
  Redness, if any, stays mild and doesn't expand
  No thick discharge, no persistent nausea or vomiting
  She's tolerating her drops and meds and sleeping okay

If that holds, Wednesday is the right venue. If anything blurs the line, the plan above covers it.
