   This is the single most informative field. A working sensor should reduce aux minutes on days where the actual temp doesn't warrant them.

4. Setpoint changes
   Default = none. Record any manual override with time, new setpoint, and whether it was restored.
   Treat setpoint changes as their own column. Folding them into kWh comparisons will invalidate the boundary below.

5. Daily kWh (where available)
   Source: utility interval data or smart-meter daily read. If only a monthly bill is available, leave the field blank and note "monthly resolution" once at the top of the log. Monthly resolution cannot support the kind of attribution the question is asking about.

WHAT "SUCCESS" LOOKS LIKE OVER THE 7 DAYS
  - Field 2 deltas stay ≤ 2°F.
  - Field 3 aux minutes drop on days with ambient low above ~30°F (where aux previously ran heavily under a sensor that read 18–32°F low).
  - Field 4 stays empty or near-empty.
  - Field 5 trends with HDD, not with calendar day.

EVIDENCE-SAFE COMPARISON BOUNDARY

What the 7-day log supports:
  - The new sensor is operating in tolerance.
  - A new operating baseline under accurate outdoor readings.
  - A qualitative direction ("aux heat usage is lower on mild days than it would have been under the old sensor").

What the 7-day log does NOT support, by itself:
  - "X% of November's electricity increase was the faulty sensor."
  - A retrofit savings estimate computed as (November kWh − this-week kWh).
  - Any quantitative causal share attributed to the sensor from this short window.

Why a simple before/after fails as attribution:
  - Heating load is nonlinear in outdoor temp; HDD differs across the two windows.
  - Occupancy, schedule, and setpoint behavior differ between November and this week.
  - The pre-window is itself contaminated by the faulty sensor, so it cannot serve as a clean counterfactual.
  - n = 7 is too small to separate a sensor effect from weather noise even with a perfect match.
  - There is no control group (no parallel home with a working sensor in the same weather).

If a number is ever needed downstream, the defensible method is:
  - Compute kWh per HDD for the post-replacement week.
  - Compare that ratio to a pre-failure reference period with an accurate sensor and similar occupancy — early October, or the same calendar week a prior year.
  - Report the result as "consistent with the sensor being a major driver" or "inconsistent with the sensor being a major driver." Never as "the sensor caused X%."

ONE-LINE FOR ANY DOWNSTREAM NOTE OR CLAIM
  "Outdoor sensor replaced 12/19. Seven-day post-replacement monitoring through 12/25 establishes a baseline under accurate outdoor readings. The November electricity increase is not attributed to the sensor on the basis of this short before/after window; any quantitative share requires HDD-normalized comparison to a like-condition reference period."

This is textbook smishing. The good news is you already did the right thing by telling her not to open the link.

Safe verification (use only the airline app and the number printed on her ticket/boarding pass - never anything in the text):

  1. Open the airline app from the home screen icon, not from the text. Go to the trip / baggage section and confirm there is no hold, no fee, and no bag matching her name or bag tag.

Find the airline's customer service number on the printed boarding pass, the e-ticket email she received at booking, or by typing the airline's URL directly into the browser (e.g. aa.com -> Contact Us). Ask the agent to confirm whether any bag is on file for her reservation and whether any fee is owed.
  3. While she has the agent on the line, ask whether the airline ever sends bag-hold SMS from a plain 10-digit number or asks for payment via a link. The answer will be no - they bill the card on file.

Reporting (independent channels, not anything in the text):

  1. Forward the text to 7726 (SPAM). This is the GSMA short code used by AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile and most US carriers; forwarding is free and feeds carrier anti-spam filters.
  2. Report to the airline's fraud/abuse team via the contact page on their official site (typed URL, not the link). Many carriers have a "report phishing" form; include the screenshots.

12:52pm — CHICKEN OUT
  Verify 165°F in the thickest part of the thigh. Tent loosely with foil on a cutting board or rack — NOT sealed tight, or the skin goes soft. Leave on counter. Rest until 1:30pm = 38 min.

  Oven action: leave door cracked 2-3 min to shed the 375°F residual, then set to 350°F. It should be ready by 1:00pm.

11:22am — CHICKEN IN
  Oven at 375°F, middle/lower rack. 90 min → out at 12:52pm.
  Tip: chicken on a rack inside the sheet pan = better air = crispy skin. Start at room temp (pull from fridge by ~10:30am, salt early).

11:12pm — ROLLS OUT, OVEN BUMPED TO 375°F
  Pull rolls, tent with foil on the counter — they'll hold fine for 80 min.
  Set oven to 375°F; it'll be ready in ~10 min.

11:00am — ROLLS IN
  Oven at 325°F. 12 min → out at 11:12am.
  (Doing rolls FIRST is the trick — the oven's already at 325, then climbs to 375 for the chicken, then drops to 350 for the mac. No awkward last-second temp swings.)

WHY THIS ORDER
  Rolls (325, 12 min) → Chicken (375, 90 min + rest) → Mac (350, 30 min).
  Each step moves the oven's set temp in the direction it's already going, so recovery is fast. Chicken gets a real rest. Mac finishes exactly at service. Rolls hold comfortably because bread is forgiving.

MARCUS (arrives 12:45pm)
  He's there for the final stretch — good time to set the table, toss the salad, and help carve/portion at 1:30pm. The cooking is done before he walks in.

Revised plan below. The key insight: separate the chicken from oven heat entirely so it stops cooking, and run the sides in the oven after the chicken rests.

CHICKEN — hold in the cooler (starting 12:35pm)

  1. Rest uncovered on the counter for 5 minutes. Carryover heat is still pushing the internal temp up 5–10°F right now; an open rest lets the surface shed heat so it plateaus instead of climbing toward 175°F (which is where breast meat turns dry).
  
  2. Optional but worth it: spoon or brush 2–3 Tbsp of warm chicken broth (or melted butter) over the pieces. This creates steam inside the foil and keeps the surface moist.
  
  3. Wrap tightly in heavy-duty foil — two layers, pressed to the surface, seams folded sealed. No tenting; you want a tight seal.
  
  4. Wrap the foil package in a clean kitchen towel (two if you have them).
  
  5. Place in the insulated cooler. Pack extra towels around the package on all sides. Close the lid.
  
  6. Do NOT open the cooler until service. Every open drops the temp 5–10°F.

Expected temp at 1:30pm: roughly 150–160°F. Well above the USDA 140°F hot-holding floor, well below the overcooked zone.

OVEN — sides only

  12:45pm  Drop oven to 350°F. Macaroni in. (If the oven was at roasting temp 375–400°F, give it ~5 min to settle at 350 before loading.)
  
  1:15pm   Macaroni out. Bump oven to 325°F.
  
  1:18pm   Rolls in. (3 min for the oven to come down to 325°F.)
  
  1:30pm   Rolls out. Plate immediately.

Total cook time for the sides: 42 minutes, finishing exactly at 1:30pm.

WHY THIS WORKS

  - The cooler-with-foil-and-towels is a recognized catering hot-hold method. It removes the chicken from oven heat entirely, so no further cooking — that addresses your dry-out concern directly.
  - Running the sides after the chicken rest means the chicken is never sitting in residual oven heat.
  - The tight foil + broth inside traps moisture against the surface, so the chicken steams gently in its own juices rather than drying.
  - The 5-min uncovered rest before wrapping is the move most people skip; it’s what keeps breast meat from drifting past 170°F.

QUICK SAFETY CHECK AT SERVICE

  If you have an instant-read thermometer, probe the thickest piece at 1:25pm before plating. Anything 140°F or above is safe to serve. A properly packed cooler will land 150–160°F, which is the sweet spot — safe and juicy.

A slow drain in BOTH basins with the disposal still working usually means a soft blockage (grease, starch, soap film) in the shared drain line just past the disposal, or in the P-trap. Holiday cooking is the classic trigger — fats and starches coat pipe walls and then set as they cool.

Below is a sequence that escalates gently. You can stop at any step and call maintenance; nothing here is mandatory.

STEP 1 — HOT WATER + DISH SOAP FLUSH (zero hazard)
  Squirt a generous amount of liquid dish soap down both drains.
  Boil a full kettle.
  Slowly pour the near-boiling water down both basins, alternating.
  Wait 5 minutes, then run the hot tap for a minute.
  Repeat once if improved but not fully cleared.
  Why it helps: dish soap is a degreaser; hot water softens solidified fats from gravy, butter, bacon, etc.

STEP 2 — CHECK THE DISPOSAL BAFFLE
  Turn off the disposal at the wall switch.
  Shine a flashlight into the disposal opening. There's a black rubber splash baffle at the top.
  Sometimes a film of food/grease sits on the baffle and chokes flow from that basin.
  If you see debris on top, lift it out with wooden spoon handles or tongs. NEVER fingers.
  If the baffle looks clean, skip ahead.

STEP 3 — BAKING SODA + VINEGAR (mild, safe for pipes and disposal)
  1/2 cup baking soda into each drain.
  1 cup white vinegar into each drain. It will fizz — that's normal.
  Let sit 20–30 minutes. Do not run water during.
  Flush with hot tap water for a minute.
  Note: this is gentle foaming action, NOT a chemical drain cleaner. No fumes, no pipe damage, no disposal harm. It won't dissolve a tough clog, but it loosens soft buildup.

STEP 4 — PLUNGE, CAREFULLY
  The disposal makes plunging trickier. The rule is: seal the disposal side first.
  Stuff a wet rag firmly into the disposal-side drain, or use a sink stopper.
  If your dishwasher drain hose ties in under the sink and you can see the connection, clamp it or have someone hold a tight rag around it. (If you can't find it, don't worry — water may spit up through the dishwasher air gap, which is harmless and self-draining.)
  Fill the other basin with 2–3 inches of water.
  Use a cup-style sink plunger (not a toilet plunger). Get a solid seal.
  Pump gently 10–15 times — steady, not violent.
  Pull the stopper, run hot water into both basins.
  Repeat up to 2–3 times. If no change, stop.

STEP 5 — CLEAN THE P-TRAP (only if comfortable)
  This is the natural point to call maintenance if you'd rather not.
  Bucket under the U-shaped pipe.
  Unscrew both slip nuts by hand, or gently with channel-lock pliers.
  Water and gunk will spill out — expected.
  Clean the trap, peek into the horizontal arm going into the wall.
  Reassemble hand-tight, then run water and check for leaks before moving the bucket.

STOP AND CALL MAINTENANCE IF ANY OF THESE HAPPEN:
  - Water backs up into the dishwasher or its air gap (the small round hole near the faucet).
  - Another fixture in the house drains slowly or gurgles when the kitchen sink runs (tub, bathroom sink, toilet).
  - The sink stops draining entirely, or water rises when you run it.
  - Any water appears under the cabinet — even a small drip.
  - Foul or sewage smell from the drains.
  - The disposal hums when switched on but does not spin (it's jammed — needs a specific unjamming procedure; do NOT use water or your hands).
  - The drain clears but slows again within a day or two (suggests a main-line issue, not a local clog).
  - You are uncomfortable at any step. There is no prize for fixing it yourself.

THINGS TO AVOID ENTIRELY:
  - Chemical drain cleaners (Drano, Liquid-Plumr, lye-based products). They can splash into eyes, generate heat that cracks porcelain or softens PVC joints, damage disposal seals, and create a hazard for whoever works on it next. You already avoided this — keep doing so.
  - Reaching into the disposal with hands or any tool while it's wired up.
  - Running the disposal without water flowing.
  - Using a drain snake/auger unless you know your plumbing layout — you can puncture a pipe or wreck the disposal.

REALISTIC EXPECTATION: a post-holiday slow drain in both basins usually resolves at step 1 or step 3 within a few hours. If steps 1–4 don't move it, the blockage is likely past the trap or is a grease plug that needs mechanical clearing — that's a maintenance call, not a homeowner failure.

Want me to also draft the one-line summary that should sit above it (the "summary first" convention in your rulings), or leave that to you?

OPENING OBSERVATION

Two early readers came to opposite framings of the house, and I want to start there. One reads the house as the only thing that survives every loss — every new pair of residents quietly changing what it means. The other pushes back: the house may not be unifying the lives so much as holding the frame still enough for the breaks between them to show. We don't have to pick between those tonight. Some of us finished every section, some didn't, and the book gives each of us a different cut of it depending on where we stopped — so let's meet in the rooms we each have.

THREE QUESTIONS

1. Whatever sections you got through: is there a detail — a room, the apple tree, a piece of light, a sound — that felt like it actually carried from one stretch of the book into the next? Or did the specifics change so completely that the only thing left was the address?

2. The book keeps changing shape — letters, naturalist lists, a case file, a deposition, plain narrative. Did those shifts feel like the same book wearing different clothes, or like different books that happen to share a building? And does your answer change if you think about the house instead of the form?

3. Each stretch seems to leave something behind for whoever comes next — an object, a name, a stain on the floor, a story someone tells slightly wrong. Which inheritance stuck with you — the one the book described, or the one you carried into the next section in your own reading? And did any of those inheritances actually reach the next residents, or did they die in the room where they were left?

A note on order: Q1 has the lowest barrier — anyone can answer from any section, and it lets the note-1 / note-2 tension surface without anyone having to name it. Q2 builds on that by pushing the same question onto form rather than content. Q3 is the most synthetic — better once people have already talked, since it asks readers to compare across stretches.

LEAD SUMMARY
------------
Capture Mom's knowledge in a fast triage pass BEFORE any scanning, then have Marcus scan in parallel while Riley keeps the index. Use a single ID scheme on every photo (no writing on the photo itself), and let uncertainty be explicit — flagged in the filename and the index, never hidden, never resolved by guessing. Anything we cannot get to today stays in clearly labeled "hold" trays; nothing gets discarded, including uncertain duplicates.

ROLES (stay rigid for the whole 2 hours)
----------------------------------------
Mom   — narrator only. Stays at the triage table. Talks, points, holds photos briefly, never touches the scanner or types. Her job is to say ONE line per photo: who, when, what. If she goes long on a story, Riley writes the one-line caption and tucks the rest into the Notes column.

Riley — intake/indexer. Writes one row per photo (paper card or laptop), assigns the ID, applies the post-it, manages the trays, runs the timer, and keeps the queue feeding Marcus. Sole owner of the index file — no one else edits it.

Marcus — scanner. Owns the scanner, runs a fixed loop, follows the file-naming scheme verbatim. Does not edit metadata, does not relabel photos, does not make duplicate calls. If something is weird, he sets it aside and keeps moving.

PRE-SETUP (do these before the 2-hour clock starts, ~10 min)
------------------------------------------------------------
  -  Scanner warmed up, default = 300 dpi, JPEG, color. Test scan a throwaway.
  -  Four trays on a clean surface, labeled: TRIAGE / QUEUE / HOLD / DUP-CHECK.
  -  Index ready (printed paper cards OR a single shared laptop spreadsheet). Columns:
       ID | Box# | Era | People | Event | Flags | Notes | Scan_filename
  -  Post-its + Sharpie. Phone nearby for snap-of-the-back (some prints have pencil dates on the reverse).
  -  Cheat sheet for the naming scheme printed and taped next to the scanner (see end).
  -  Coffee + water for Mom. Two-hour clocks start NOW.

STAGE 1 — TRIAGE WITH MOM  (target 25–30 min, hard stop)
--------------------------------------------------------
Goal: every photo in the three boxes is touched, ID'd, and slotted. Zero scanning this stage.

Loop, in order, one photo at a time, Riley pulling from the unsorted pile:

  1.  Riley picks up a photo. Reads any writing on the back aloud to Mom ("says 'July 1968, Jo's porch'") — that often unlocks the identification.
  2.  Mom says one line: era/decade, who's in it, what it is. Riley does NOT prompt for more than one line. If Mom launches a story, Riley writes the story into the Notes column and gently moves on.
  3.  Riley assigns the next ID (see scheme below) and writes it on a post-it stuck to the bottom edge of the photo. NEVER on the face, NEVER on the back.
  4.  Riley places the photo in QUEUE. If it's a probable duplicate of something already triaged, place in DUP-CHECK with a post-it "see ID XXXX". If it has zero info from Mom and no writing on the back, place in HOLD with the post-it and a single "?" on it.
  5.  Snap a phone pic of the BACK of any photo that had writing or pencil marks — these often vanish in scanning.
  6.  Repeat. Do not stop to scan. Do not debate duplicates in real time.

End-of-stage check: every photo is in QUEUE, HOLD, or DUP-CHECK, and has a post-it ID. The three boxes are empty.

STAGE 2 — SCAN + INDEX  (target 80–90 min)
------------------------------------------
Marcus works QUEUE in order. Riley's job during this stage is to keep Marcus fed and to update the Scan_filename column as Marcus finishes each item. Mom is now DONE and can rest, or can be moved to a quiet task like sorting the HOLD tray by what she thinks the era might be — but no further additions to the index from her.

Marcus's loop per photo:
  -  Pull from QUEUE.
  -  Scan at 300 dpi JPEG. If the print is fragile or curled, scan twice and flag in the index; do not try to flatten it.
  -  Save the file using the naming scheme below, exactly. No spaces, all lowercase, ASCII only.
  -  Say the filename out loud; Riley confirms it against the post-it ID and writes it into the Scan_filename column.
  -  Photo goes back into the original pile (clean side up) with post-it still attached.
  -  If anything is ambiguous (e.g., the post-it ID is unclear), Marcus does NOT guess — he sets the photo in HOLD with a sticky "verify ID" and Riley resolves at the wrap.

End-of-stage check: as many QUEUE photos scanned as time allows. Unscanned QUEUE photos stay where they are with their post-its; that becomes next session's starting point.

STAGE 3 — WRAP  (last 10 min)
-----------------------------
  -  Save the index (paper cards stacked in order; laptop file named with today's date).
  -  HOLD tray: take 60 seconds with Mom to re-skim the "?" pile and see if anything she missed on the first pass now sparks a memory. Capture anything new as a row. Anything still unknown stays as-is — do not force a date.
  -  DUP-CHECK tray: do NOT resolve today. Tape the tray shut, label it "verify next session," and put it next to the unscanned QUEUE pile.
  -  Unscanned QUEUE: pile them face-up with post-its intact. This is next session's queue.
  -  Back-of-photo phone snaps: rename the phone album to today's date and back it up before anyone leaves the room.

FILE-NAMING + UNCERTAINTY SCHEME
--------------------------------
The ID is the only thing written on the photo. Everything else lives in the filename and the index row.

ID format (on the post-it):
  B{box}-{seq}     e.g.,  B02-037
  Box number is 01, 02, or 03 (the three mixed boxes as they sit today). Seq is zero-padded, assigned in the order Riley triages. Globally unique.

Filename pattern (Marcus types exactly this):
  {ID}_{date-or-era}_{people-or-event}.jpg

Date slot, in this priority order:
  -  Exact:           1968            Mom said July 1968, or back says it
  -  Decade-precise:  1960s           Mom knows the decade
  -  Circa:           c1968           Mom says "around 1968" or "maybe 1968"
  -  Unknown:         uncdt           No date from Mom and nothing on the back

People/event slot:
  -  Use short, lowercase, hyphenated tokens. Names first if known.
       mom-and-aunt-jo
       marcus-as-baby
       porch-group
  -  If people are uncertain, keep the token but add the flag (below).

Uncertainty flags (appended after the slot, before .jpg, comma-separated):
  _uncdt    already covered by date slot; do not duplicate
  _uncid    people in the photo are uncertain
  _dup-NNN  appears to be a duplicate of ID NNN (do not delete the original; the dup just lives in DUP-CHECK)
  _frag     print is fragile / scan is best-effort, may need rescanning
  _rev      Mom revised this identification later; original caption kept in Notes

Examples:
  B02-037_1968_mom-and-aunt-jo.jpg
  B02-038_c1960s_uncle-ed_uncid.jpg
  B02-039_uncdt_porch-group.jpg
  B02-040_c1968_marcus-as-baby_dup-B02-031.jpg

Index columns (paper card or spreadsheet — same shape):
  ID | Box# | Era | People | Event | Flags | Notes | Scan_filename
  Flags cell can hold multiple values comma-separated: "uncid, frag"

DUPLICATE + UNCERTAINT HANDLING (today's rules)
-----------------------------------------------
  -  DUP-CHECK tray is NEVER discarded today. Even if two prints look identical, there may be a different crop, a different print generation, or a penciled note on one back that the other doesn't have.
  -  Each suspected dup gets a post-it "see ID NNN" and a row in the index with flag "dup-NNN". Resolution is a separate future session with the original prints side-by-side.

Practical freeze-prep for tonight, in order:

Before the temp drops (do this Sunday afternoon/evening)

1. Disconnect anything attached to the two exterior hose bibs. If there's an indoor shutoff for each bib (often in a nearby utility room, basement, or crawlspace), close it and open the outside bib to drain the line, then leave the outside bib slightly open. Confirm with property management whether the bibs are frost-free before you skip this step — frost-free bibs still want covers, but don't need an indoor drain-down.
2. Put the insulated faucet covers on both exterior hose bibs. Make sure they seat fully and cover the valve, not just the spout.
3. Open the cabinet doors under the kitchen sink and the guest bath sink. Both are on exterior walls and that wall cavity is the most likely freeze point for interior plumbing.
4. Set the thermostat to a steady 65°F overnight. Do not use "auto" setbacks to lower it overnight — let it hold. Auxiliary/emergency heat running for hours at 27°F is expected and not a fault signal (separate from your HVAC diagnostic rule, which is for mild-weather aux-heat runtime).
5. Leave interior doors open so heat circulates past the exterior-wall sinks and any closed rooms.
6. Locate the main water shutoff and make sure it's accessible. If a pipe does burst at 2am, you want to know where it is before you need it.
7. Note the after-hours emergency number for property management now, not after something breaks.

Overnight (once outdoor temp is at or below ~28°F, Mon→Tue)

8. Drip the kitchen cold and the guest bath cold — those are the runs on exterior walls. A pencil-thin stream is enough; the goal is moving water, not volume. If you can only drip one, drip the one farthest from the main shutoff.
9. Open both corresponding cabinet doors (already done in step 3, just confirm).
10. Don't crank the thermostat above ~68°F — oversized t-Δ won't help interior wall cavities warm meaningfully and just runs the strip heat longer.
11. Keep a working flashlight near the bed and listen for any sudden loss of furnace airflow (frozen condensate line on a high-efficiency unit is a real failure mode at these temps; if airflow stops, the furnace shutoff is usually the right move, and that's a property-management call).

Tuesday morning, once temp is back above ~35°F

12. Turn off the drips, close the cabinet doors.
13. Run each exterior-wall faucet and look under the sink and around the hose bib for any new drip or wet spot. Frozen pipes often leak at a joint once thawed, not at the burst point.
14. If anything is wet, shut the main and call property management. Don't wait — Texas-style homes with uninsulated exterior-wall plumbing can crack a pipe that was fine all winter.

What to confirm with property management before you drip or change any equipment setting:

a. Lease-required minimum thermostat setting (commonly 55–65°F). They need to tell you what number to hold, and what's a violation if you go below it.
b. Whether tenants are expected, required, or prohibited from dripping faucets during a freeze. Some leases require it and hold tenants responsible for burst pipes if they didn't drip; others treat dripping as wasted water. Get this in writing or at least in a text/email reply.
c. Whether the exterior hose bibs are frost-free and whether they want tenants to use an indoor shutoff to drain them. Don't close an indoor valve you're not sure is the hose-bib shutoff — closing a domestic cold branch by mistake is how you flood a ceiling later.
d. Whether there's any submetering or water-cost concern with running a faucet overnight. Usually trivial, but worth knowing if bills are allocation-based.
e. After-hours emergency contact and the procedure if a pipe bursts (do they want you to shut the main and call, or attempt something else first).
f. Whether the furnace has a high-efficiency condensing unit and where the condensate drain exits — at 27°F the condensate line can freeze and trip the furnace off. Ask them in advance what they want you to do if that happens overnight, so you're not guessing at 3am.

If property management doesn't respond in time tonight, the safe default for a 27°F / 6-hour event is: bibs covered and drained if possible, cabinet doors open, thermostat held at 65°F, both exterior-wall cold lines dripping, and the main-shutoff location confirmed. None of those steps modify equipment in a way the lease would object to, and they cover the failure modes that actually matter in this forecast.

Every scan traces back to its physical source (box + handwritten sequence), uncertain dates are visible at a glance in the filename, and any two prints that may depict the same image stay as separate, linkable objects.

  B{box}              Box identifier, zero-padded. Match the box label Marcus uses.
  S{seq}              Handwritten sequence number within that box, zero-padded to 3 digits so listing sorts correctly.
  -D{seq2}            Optional. Only used if the same handwritten number is reused inside ONE box (rare, but covers it).
  __                  Separator between provenance and content fields. Double underscore marks a new group.
  date                See DATE CONVENTIONS below.
  _print-{a|b|1|2}    Optional. Only when two physical prints may depict the same image.
  __slug              Short kebab-case description (people + scene). Omit if unknown — leave the trailing underscores.
  .ext                .jpg / .tif / .png — match the master format you keep.

Examples:
  B03-S007__1958__jane-and-tom-at-creek.jpg
  B03-S007__ca1958__jane-and-tom-at-creek.jpg          (year tentative)
  B05-S007__1962__family-at-farm.jpg                   (same handwritten "7" as B03-S007 — box disambiguates)
  B03-S012__ca1960_print-A__dad-with-prize-cattle.jpg
  B03-S012__ca1960_print-B__dad-with-prize-cattle.jpg  (possible duplicate print of the one above)

Slug rules: lowercase, hyphens only, 1–5 words, no people initials (write full names).

DATE CONVENTIONS — four visually distinct states
  1958          Year confirmed (by mom, caption, or context).
  ca1958        Year tentative — mom thinks it's right but isn't sure. The lowercase "ca" (circa) is the flag.
  ca1955-1960   Range tentative — mom can narrow to a window but not a year.
  undated       No usable year at all. Don't guess.

What you're seeing is almost certainly an authorization hold plus the real charge, not a duplicate. Here's how to handle it.

Why it looks like a duplicate
Restaurants routinely place a pre-authorization on the card for the estimated bill (sometimes including a tip cushion) before the final tip is added and the payment is settled. Both transactions flow through your statement: one as pending (just a hold on available funds, no money has actually moved) and one as posted (the real charge). Same dollar amount usually means the tip was either zero, or the pre-auth already included it. The pending line is not a second charge.

What to do right now
Do nothing to either entry. Specifically:
  Do not dispute the posted charge. It matches your receipt and is valid; a dispute on it can create more problems than it solves, including the merchant pushing back with the signed receipt.
  Do not call the merchant or issuer yet. There is nothing for either to "fix" until/unless the pending line converts into a second posted charge or fails to drop off.

Evidence to preserve (do this once, now)
  - Photograph or screenshot your full card statement page showing both entries, with timestamps and the pending/posted status. Capture the merchant descriptor exactly as printed.
  - Photograph or scan the signed receipt showing the $86.40 total.
  - Note the date and approximate time of the visit, and the date you first saw the pending entry.
  - If you have any email/SMS confirmation from the restaurant (OpenTable confirm, loyalty receipt, etc.), save it.
  - Keep these until the pending entry has been gone for at least one full billing cycle.

Whether to wait for the pending to fall away
Yes. That's the normal outcome. Most pending authorizations release automatically within 2 to 7 business days; card networks allow merchants up to about 30 days in edge cases, but for an in-person restaurant charge a week is typical. Once it drops, your available balance rebills and there is nothing further to do.

What change would justify contacting the merchant or issuer
Contact only if one of these actually happens:
  - The pending entry converts into a second posted $86.40 (true duplicate posted). In that case, contact the merchant first for a refund; only escalate to the issuer's dispute process if the merchant is unresponsive within a couple of weeks.
  - The pending entry sits for more than 7 to 10 business days without dropping or posting. A quick call to the card issuer can ask them to release the hold on your available balance without disputing the posted charge.
  - The amount on the pending line changes. That would be unusual and worth flagging.

Bottom line: keep the receipt and a statement screenshot, leave both lines alone, and expect the pending $86.40 to vanish on its own within a week.

The address printed on a 1099-R is simply what the plan administrator had on file when they issued the form. For federal filing, the address that matters is the one on Form 1040 — the IRS matches the 1099-R to the return by SSN, not by address.

How to handle it:

1. VERIFY before requesting anything
   - SSN on the 1099-R matches Mom's SSN exactly. This is the only field the IRS uses to match the form to her return.
   - Legal name matches (watch maiden vs. married, hyphenation, middle initial).
   - "Corrected" box is unchecked — if blank, this is the original; a later reissue would be marked Corrected.
   - Box 1 (gross distribution), Box 2a (taxable amount), Box 4 (federal withholding), and Box 7 (distribution code) all match what Mom actually received. Code 7 = normal, 4 = death, G = direct rollover, etc.
   - Payer/plan info in Boxes 11–15 is correct.

2. FILE THE RETURN using Mom's current address on Form 1040. A 1099-R printed with the old address does not require a corrected form and does not block e-filing. If using a paper return, attach the 1099-R as usual.

3. WHAT TO REQUEST FROM THE ADMINISTRATOR
   - Do NOT ask for a corrected 1099-R solely to fix an address. The IRS will not accept a corrected form that only changes the address.
   - Do ask for an address update on their records so future year-end forms (1099-R, 1099-DIV if applicable, RMD notices) go to the right place. Most administrators accept either:
       - a signed W-9P with the new address, or
       - a short letter: full legal name, SSN (last 4 only is fine), old address, new address, signature, date.
   - If the original 1099-R was mailed to the old address and never forwarded, request that they resend a duplicate to the new address.
   - Only request a corrected 1099-R (1099-Rc) if there is a real error in SSN, name, gross/taxable amount, withholding, or distribution code. If a corrected form is issued, file with the corrected version and keep the original in the tax file.

4. KEEP BOTH COPIES if a corrected form is ever issued. The IRS already received the original; the corrected copy supersedes it, but having both avoids questions later.

5. STATE RETURN — if Mom files a state return, check whether the state uses its own 1099-R variant. Same logic: match by SSN, file with current address.

Quick summary: address mismatch on a 1099-R is informational, not a filing problem. File the federal return with Mom's current address, do not request a corrected 1099-R just to fix the address, send the administrator a W-9P or signed letter to update their records, and only request a corrected 1099-R if there is an actual error in SSN, name, amount, withholding, or distribution code.

3. Pause any cloud sync (iCloud Drive / OneDrive / Dropbox / Google Drive desktop) before the move, or move the file into the sync client's "ignore" folder, then pause. Any copy that already synced is now a separate item — track it, don't lose it.

   sha256sum ~/secure-incident/<customer.csv>
   stat    ~/secure-incident/<customer.csv>     # size, mtime, owner
   wc -l   ~/secure-incident/<customer.csv>     # row count
   file    ~/secure-incident/<customer.csv>     # confirms it's CSV, not a renamed xlsx
6. Schema only, no rows.
   head -1 ~/secure-incident/<customer.csv>                       # column header line
   csvkit: csvstat --names ~/secure-incident/<customer.csv>       # names + inferred types
   Do not pipe rows into `less`, `cat`, or screenshot them.
7. PII classification based on the header: direct identifiers (name, email, phone, postal address, SSN/tax ID, DOB, account number, payment data) vs quasi-identifiers (postal code, IP, device ID, timestamps). This drives the report severity.

SUMMARY
The readout invites a "risk reduced" read (escalation rate 6/10 → 5/12) that the readout itself admits it cannot support. The numbers, even taken at face value and assuming definitional parity is real, do not establish process effectiveness — they are a single-period shift on a self-selected, small, structurally incomparable sample. The parallel-period layout is doing the work of a comparison that isn't there. This isn't a ruling that the process is broken; it's a ruling that this readout cannot carry the conclusion it is set up to deliver.

WHAT THE READOUT ACTUALLY SHOWS
- Current: 5 of 12 reviewed accounts escalated (~42%)
- Prior: 6 of 10 reviewed accounts escalated (60%)
- Movement: -1 escalation on +2 reviewed; rate shift ~18 points across ~11 accounts

WHAT THE READOUT DOES NOT SHOW
- No comparison group. No counterfactual (what would have escalated without the process), no control cohort. The "rate" is not a treatment effect; it is a ratio inside one team's workflow.
- No defined "risk reduced" outcome. Even if fewer accounts escalated, the readout has not named what the process is meant to move. "Reduced" has no referent.
- "Reviewed" denominator is not stabilized. Going from 10 to 12 reviewed accounts means the sample composition could have shifted along with the size. Rate changes on a changing denominator are not clean comparisons even within one team.
- Definitional parity is asserted, not evidenced. "Escalated uses the same definition in both periods" is a verbal claim. The audit-relevant pieces — same trigger criteria, same threshold, same reviewer pool, same case-mix — are not shown.
- Sample size forecloses inference. A swing of one escalation across ~11 reviewed accounts is noise. There is no signal here at any reasonable bar.

WHAT THE READOUT INVITES (AND SHOULDN'T)
The side-by-side period structure pushes the reader toward "we're improving." With this data, that read is unsupported. The honest summary is descriptive: counts moved, rate moved, neither is a result. The CS team's own disclaimer ("No comparison group or defined `risk reduced` outcome is supplied") is doing real work — it makes the gap explicit rather than hiding it — but a disclaimer does not cure the gap. The implicit comparison is still being invited by the layout.

Without those controls, the supported rows inherit the held exceptions by default — that is the failure mode this ruling is built to prevent.

WHY

Standing principle: exception review does not rewrite. Accepted point-in-time tables stay fixed, and later state = separate forward events, not revisions to the historical snapshot. So the question is not whether the 53 can ship without the 5 — they can — it is whether the release mechanism is structured so the 5 do not ride along through a shared key, a sum-from-base read, or a downstream join.

THREE INHERITANCE VECTORS (each must be broken before approval)

1. Shared parent key. If any of the 5 held exceptions shares a parent/group ID with a supported row in the 53, a parent-level re-statement drags the exception back in. Mitigation: split the write by row, not by parent. The supported row writes its accepted state; the exception sits as a forward event under the same parent but in a different manifest reference.

2. Sum-from-base aggregation. If downstream totals are computed from a base table containing both A (supported) and B (held) rows, releasing A without B does not actually release A — the read path still pulls B in. Mitigation: pair the manifest release with a snapshot-as-of timestamp that excludes B, OR scope aggregation to read from A directly (manifest-scoped read, not base-table read).

3. Downstream join-by-key. Any consumer joining A on a shared key (customer ID, subscription ID, account ID, etc.) must have the join scoped to manifest=A, otherwise the exception rides along via the join. Mitigation: explicit join-scope declaration in the consumer contract, OR row-level filter on manifest reference.

Safe call: bus home with the bike. Sunset in ~10 minutes + 4 miles of road + a backup that only lights the patch under your wheel is not a combination worth negotiating. Even if the main light comes back, you won't know it holds until you're already in the dark, and a flicker that survives a battery reseat is exactly the failure mode that comes back mid-route.

Use the remaining daylight for a short isolation test. Swap one known-good component at a time and see which substitution brings the main light back.

1. Battery first (most common cause of flicker-then-shutoff):
   - Inspect the battery and contacts. Look for green/white crust, swelling, leaks, or a torn wrapper.
   - Clean contacts with a pencil eraser; follow with an alcohol wipe if you have one.
   - Try the suspect battery in the backup clip light. If backup lights up, the battery is fine and the main light is suspect.
   - Try a known-good battery (fresh spare or one pulled from another device) in the main light. If it lights, the battery was the problem.

2. Light body next, only if the battery checks out:
   - Check the charge port and any rubber cover. Water in the housing is the classic flicker-then-die pattern, especially after a wet ride.
   - Cycle the power button several times; grit or a sticky switch can mimic a dead unit.
   - If it's rechargeable, confirm it actually took a charge by plugging it in and watching the indicator.

3. Mount and cable last:
   - Reseat the light fully. Many mounts need a firm click or a twist-lock to seat the contacts.
   - If there's an external cable, wiggle it while the light is on to expose an intermittent.

Read the result:
- Known-good battery fixes it -> battery (replace or recharge).
- Known-good battery doesn't fix it, but suspect battery works in backup -> main light is bad (repair or replace).
- Neither works -> mount, switch, or internal wiring; bench diagnosis, not a ride-home fix.

If the light holds steady for a few minutes under power before sunset, you can ride. If anything still flickers, bus it.

Verdict: the opening is the best part of this. The conclusion walks it back into generic. A protocol for this, in three phases. Treat as: stabilize first, assess after drying, decide last.

PHASE 1 - STABILIZE (no adhesive yet)

The fiber is still attached to the sheet, just raised. That is the best possible starting state - your goal is to coax it back into plane with moisture and pressure, not glue.

Work surface: clean glass or plexiglass, not wood. Wood can transfer grit under the lift.

Clear debris from under the lift. Use a soft hake or wide mop brush, working from the center of the lift outward toward the loose edge. Then a bulb syringe (or breath through a piece of screen) to blow out anything trapped beneath the lifted strip. Tweezers and probes tend to make this worse - do not poke under the fiber.

Humidify the lift, from above. Cut a piece of clean blotter slightly larger than the lift. Dampen it with distilled water (wring until moist, not dripping) and lay it OVER the lifted strip. Tape the blotter in place with low-tack tape at its corners only - not on the sheet itself. Wait 3-5 minutes. The moisture relaxes the paper fibers so they want to lie flat again. Check by touch through the blotter: cool and damp, not wet.

Coax the fibers down. Remove the blotter. With a soft brush, work from the middle of the lift outward in short strokes, pressing the fiber gently back into plane. For stubborn spots, press through a slip sheet (silicone release paper, Mylar, or a scrap of the offcut) using a bone folder or your fingertip. Never press directly on the dampened paper - it will bruise.

Weight-dry. Sandwich:
  sheet, paint side up, on glass
  blotter covering the affected area
  smooth rigid sheet (glass or plexi)
  light, evenly distributed weight (a few pounds; a flat board with a few books works)

Leave 24-48 hours in stable humidity. Away from a heating vent, direct sun, or a drafty window. Slow, even drying is what sets the fibers into their new (old) plane.

PHASE 2 - ASSESS (only after it's dry)

Snag test: brush lightly across the area with a soft brush in multiple directions. Any catch means the fiber is still proud of the surface.

Raking light: hold the sheet at an angle under a single light source. Any ridge, shadow, or sheen difference means the lift is visible.

Visual vs. tactile: a fiber can lie flat and still show a slight tonal shift if the surface texture was disturbed. Look AND feel.

Then ask:
  Will the lift fall inside the mat window? Standard 4-ply or 8-ply mats cover roughly 1/4" or more of paper edge. If your planned window sits inside the lift, the mat hides it.
  Is the mat going to be a floating mat (paper fully visible at edges)? If yes, the lift will show even if planed down.

If invisible AND inside the mat window: stop. No repair. Mat it. That is the most conservative outcome.

PHASE 3 - REPAIR (only if Phase 2 says you must)

Use the wheat-starch paste only if the fiber refuses to settle, or if a visible ridge remains that the mat won't cover. Paste is a commitment; the protocol above leaves it as the last option.

When you do:
  Thin the paste well - thinner than you think. A 1:4 or 1:5 paste-to-water mix is typical; follow your recipe but err toward the thin side.
  Lift the edge of the fiber only as far as you need to slip a thin brush or microspatula underneath. Do not peel it back further.
  Apply paste to the underside of the lift or the sheet below it - never to the top surface.
  Press the fiber back into place immediately. Blot excess paste with a damp (not wet) blotter, working from center outward.
  Re-weight using the same sandwich. Full cure is 48-72 hours; do not handle before then.

The offcut is your donor material only if a later repair needs a fiber-fill (i.e., actual loss). For a lift that re-settles, the offcut is not needed.

NOTES ON WHAT TO AVOID

  No household adhesives, no glue stick, no tape applied to the sheet.
  No iron or hair dryer - heat sets cockling unevenly and can scorch watercolor.
  No full-sheet immersion. Localized humidity only.
  Do not frame or mat before the weight-dry is complete. Moisture trapped under a mat will cause new problems (tideline, mildew, cockling).

If at any point in Phase 1 the lift begins to detach further or pigment at the edge of the painted area looks compromised, stop and bring it to a paper conservator rather than continuing - AAD guidelines and AIC referral directory are the standard starting points if you need one. But for a 1.5-inch fiber lift outside the image, the moisture-and-weight settle almost always works.

Framing: this is a price-vs-judgment question, not a complexity question. Both options can technically handle her documents. The $236 difference buys (or doesn't buy) a credentialed human reviewing the return and owning the result.

WHAT EACH OPTION ACTUALLY BUYS

Guided software ($89)
- She reads each form, types numbers into the right boxes, answers yes/no prompts, reviews the output, e-files.
- No human reviews for accuracy. No one flags anything she missed. No audit representation. Support is generic chat/help articles.
- Best when: forms are unambiguous and she's comfortable answering the prompts herself.

Enrolled agent ($325)
- A licensed federal tax practitioner (enrolled agents are IRS-credentialed, not generic "preparers") interviews her, prepares the return, signs as preparer, and can represent her if IRS has questions later.
- She provides documents, answers interview questions, reviews the draft, signs.
- Best when: forms have edge cases, she has judgment questions, or she wants a credentialed human to own the result.

WHAT ACTUALLY DRIVES THE CHOICE

The dollar gap matters less than these variables:
1. Filing status (single vs. spouse) — changes standard deduction and Social Security taxation thresholds.
2. Age 65+ — extra standard deduction amount, plus credit eligibility.
3. 1099-R character — pension, traditional IRA, inherited IRA, or Roth conversion. Each has different rules. Whether the "Taxable amount" box is blank, zero, or filled is meaningful.
4. Federal income tax withheld on any form — changes refund-vs-owed math.
5. State — same state as last year? (You said no interstate move, but residency and domicile aren't identical.)
6. Last year's return — how it was filed, any IRS notice.
7. Health-insurance records — context matters: Marketplace with advance premium tax credit, retiree coverage, COBRA, Medicare, or other. "Ordinary health-insurance records" is ambiguous on purpose.
8. Anything else in 2024 not yet mentioned — large charitable gifts worth itemizing anyway, estimated payments, HSA, sale of a personal asset, etc.
9. Her own tolerance for being the one who decides each prompt.

QUESTIONS MOM SHOULD ANSWER BEFORE CHOOSING

 1. Filing single, or is there a spouse with income to combine?
 2. Was she 65 or older at the end of 2024?
 3. For the 1099-R: what kind of account is it, and is the "Taxable amount" box filled in?
 4. Did any of the forms show federal income tax withheld?
 5. Same state of residence as last year?
 6. How did she file last year, and was anything unusual about that return?
 7. What kind of health insurance is it — Marketplace (with or without premium credit), retiree plan, Medicare, COBRA, or other?
 8. Anything else in 2024 that might show up on a return, even small things, that hasn't been mentioned yet?
 9. If a human reviews and signs, what's her annual ceiling for that?
10. Does she want a credentialed preparer to own the result, or is she fine being her own reviewer?

ONE-LINE RULE OF THUMB

If she can read the 1099-R and tell you what each box means without help, the software is fine. If she'd rather ask a human than guess on any box, the EA is worth the $236.

The "three counts" problem is exactly the trap you'd hit if a report rolled them up as a single "total exceptions" line. Here are corrected labels and the why-not-sum explanation.

================================================================
PROPOSAL — three-lane exception reporting, unit-correct
================================================================

1. CORRECTED LABELS (use these in any report)

Lane A — Ines (lifecycle-aud-risk):
  Label: "Lifecycle risk findings raised"
  Unit: findings / reporting period (each finding = one reclassification,
        one preflight artifact, or one stale-state fail-closed event
        surfaced by Ines). Reported with risk class (routine / higher /
        stale-fail-closed) as a sub-attribute, not as a separate count.

Lane B — Owen (shape + exception review):
  Label: "Exception reviews opened"
  Unit: opened cases / reporting period (each case = one shape review or
        one post-release exception review flagged on Riley's request).
  Note: "Opened" ≠ "resolved" and ≠ "rewrite." Resolved and rewritten
        belong to a separate forward-events view, not this count.

Lane C — Riley (judgment-escalation):
  Label: "Higher-risk decisions called"
  Unit: decisions / reporting period (each = one release/hold/escalate
        call on a higher-risk send, an exception-review stop, or a
        cross-surface judgment). Each decision maps to one Ines
        preflight artifact as a prerequisite; the count is not
        derivable from Lane A.

  Sidebar — standing-lane cap (NOT a fourth count; a per-week ceiling
  that applies across all three lanes):
  Label: "Standing-lane neutral exposures (week)"
  Unit: neutral-equivalent exposures / week, max ≤ 3 (cap, not target).
  This is a rate, not a count of exceptions, and it caps the *sum of
  neutral touches* across lanes, not the Lane A/B/C counts themselves.

2. WHY NOT SUM (concise explanation)

The three counts cannot be summed because they are unlike units:

  - Lane A counts *findings raised* (auditor work product).
  - Lane B counts *reviews opened* (reviewer cases).
  - Lane C counts *decisions called* (judgment calls).

A finding can become a review and a review can produce a decision, but
they are not three measurements of the same thing. Summing them would
be like reporting "5 doctors + 3 teachers + 2 lawyers = 10
professionals" and presenting the 10 as a single metric — the total
is well-defined arithmetically but carries no operational meaning,
because the three numbers answer different questions:

  - Lane A: "How much aud-risk surface did Ines surface this period?"
  - Lane B: "How many shape/ex cases did Owen open this period?"
  - Lane C: "How many higher-risk judgment calls did Riley own?"

A reader of a summed total cannot answer any of those three questions
from the sum, and cannot tell whether a change in the sum came from
more risk, more review, or more decisions. The cap (Lane D, standing
neutral-exposure / week) is the only one of the four numbers where a
"do not exceed" framing is correct, because the cap is genuinely a
ceiling on a single kind of event (neutral-equivalent exposures) over
a single window (week).

3. REPORTING PATTERN (recommended)

Display the three counts as a 3-row table, one row per lane, with the
unit named in the column header:

  Lane                    | Count | Unit              | Period
  ------------------------+-------+-------------------+--------
  Lifecycle risk findings |  n    | findings          | wk/fort
  Exception reviews opened|  n    | cases             | wk/fort
  Higher-risk decisions   |  n    | decisions         | wk/fort

Show the standing-lane neutral-exposure / week figure separately,
labeled as a cap check, not as part of the table total. Never display
a "total exceptions" line. If a downstream reader asks for one,
respond with: "the three lanes measure unlike units and do not sum;
the standing-lane neutral-exposure / week figure is the only cap."

4. ONE-LINE EXPLANATION (for Ines / Owen / Priya if asked)

"The three lanes are unlike units — findings, reviews, and decisions —
so a total would be arithmetically valid and operationally meaningless.
Report them as three separate counts with units named; report the
standing-lane neutral-exposure / week as a cap check, not as part of
the total."

Diagnosis: this pattern is a textbook internal open circuit — almost certainly a broken solder joint, fractured wire strand, or failing internal connector inside the housing. Nothing you've tested externally explains it.

Reasoning, in order of elimination:
  - Vibration / tap reproduces the cutout → connection is mechanically intermittent
  - Mount is tight → ruled out at the mount interface
  - Known-good battery + clean external contacts → ruled out the external contact side
  - Remaining suspects: LED board solder joints, wire-to-board joints, internal wire break at a flex point, or the switch

Next steps:

If you want to attempt repair (only if the housing opens cleanly):
  - Inspect the solder joints where wires meet the LED board first — vibration cracks these most often
  - Then wires at flex points (where they bend when the housing is tapped) — broken strands inside the insulation
  - Then the switch
  - Reflow suspect joints or replace the wire
  - If the housing is ultrasonically welded or glued shut, don't force it — not worth the damage risk

If sealed or under warranty:
  - Contact the manufacturer. Vibration-induced cutouts are a known defect class and most major bike-light brands (Light & Motion, Cygolite, Garmin, Lezyne) replace under warranty for exactly this symptom. Even out of warranty, this is usually a $20–40 repair at a bike shop if the model is worth keeping.

For tomorrow's dark commute:
  - Do NOT rely on the clip backup alone for the 4-mile route after dark — you already identified it's visibility-only, not route-lighting, and that's the right call.
  - Viable interim options, in order:
    - Borrow a real front light (shop, friend, or buy a basic commuter light locally tonight)
    - Take transit / drive / shift the ride to daytime until a replacement arrives
    - Order a replacement today so it ships immediately
  - The backup clip light is fine as a supplement to a real headlight on streetlit segments; never sole-source on unlit road.

One quick distinguishing check before you crack anything open: does the light cut out cleanly (full off → on) or flicker / strobe? Clean cutout points more to a broken wire or joint; flicker points more to the switch or a loose connector. Useful for warranty claim language either way.

If you tell me the make/model I can look up whether it's a known issue and whether the housing is user-serviceable.

ASSESSMENT: Retire it from primary-commute duty.

An intermittent front light is not a "mostly working" light — it's an unreliable one. These failures typically worsen (loose connections loosen further, dying cells die faster, switch contacts pit more) and tend to drop out at the worst moments: cold start, end of battery cycle, vibration from rough pavement. Given your stated priority (predictable commute > rotational weight), reliability is the metric that matters, and this light no longer clears it.

  1.  What Mom can prepare before retrieving the prior-year AGI

The retrieval has two realistic paths, and each has different prep:

  IRS Online Account (irs.gov/profile or via login.gov / ID.me)
    - Pulls the AGI immediately once she's in.
    - Have ready: SSN, date of birth, filing status from 2023, current mailing address (must match what IRS has on file — a move in 2024 is the most common reason this fails), and a phone or camera for identity verification through ID.me.
    - If she's been on this account before and lost the login, "forgot password" is fine; if she's never created one, the ID.me selfie step can take a day and occasionally gets flagged for manual review.
    - Pre-flight: a phone or laptop with a working camera, a clean photo of her driver's license or passport, and a second device or email for one-time codes.

  Get Transcript by mail (online request at irs.gov/individuals/get-transcript, or Form 4506-T)
    - Useful as a fallback if the online account path stalls. Arrives in ~5–10 business days.
    - Online request needs the same identity info; Form 4506-T can be mailed in but takes longer.
    - Pre-flight: confirm the address the IRS has — a forwarded transcript is the second-most-common failure mode.

  Before she starts either path, the cheapest prep is just this: locate a copy of her 2023 return (paper, PDF, or last year's e-file acknowledgment). The AGI is on line 8a of the 2023 Form 1040. If she has that, she may not need the IRS at all.

  2.  The 1095-A question, given her Medicare coverage

1095-A is issued only by the Health Insurance Marketplace (ACA plans). Medicare beneficiaries do not receive 1095-A — they receive 1095-B (from Medicare / Social Security, for Parts B and D) or 1095-C (from a former employer, if she had employer coverage that counted as creditable).

Practical consequences for the software / EA interview:

  - If Mom has been on Medicare (Parts A and/or B) the whole year, she should not have a 1095-A, and the software should be told she's covered by Medicare — she leaves the 1095-A section blank and nothing is reconciled against Form 8962.
  - If she has a 1095-A in hand and has been on Medicare, that's a real problem to surface, not a routine input. It means a Marketplace plan was active for at least one month, which usually means either (a) she kept an ACA plan she shouldn't have after Medicare started — and she'd owe back any premium tax credits, or (b) the form is wrong / sent in error. Either way, this is the one case where the $325 enrolled agent earns its fee, because the reconciliation involves Form 8962 with figures that have to match the 1095-A exactly.
  - If she had Marketplace coverage for part of the year and switched to Medicare mid-2024, she does have a legitimate 1095-A, and the software can handle it — but the answer depends on the exact months, and the agent would be more reliable if her return has anything else going on.

So the screening question to ask Mom before she sits down to file: "Did you get a 1095-A in the mail?" If yes, that's the case where filing-method choice matters the most.

This is the one I can't lock in without a couple of facts you have and I don't:

  a) Why does she need the prior-year AGI specifically? The IRS no longer requires the prior-year AGI as the e-file signature PIN (that requirement was relaxed after 2022). The remaining reasons are: creating an IRS online account, retrieving an Identity Protection PIN, or verifying identity after a lockout. Each has a different workaround — paper file, request IP PIN by mail (Form 15227), wait. If the gap is a few days, it likely doesn't change the cost-benefit; if the gap is weeks and there's no workaround, it could.

If you tell me her income mix I can give a sharper call.

  c) What is the AGI gap actually? Lost 2023 return (then software probably can't finish without reconstructing it, and the agent earns their fee) versus just can't log in to IRS online (then software is fine, she waits or uses Get Transcript).

Default answer if nothing else is true: the temporary AGI gap, by itself, doesn't tip the decision. The diagnostic in your first sentence is the answer.

"Lies flat without spreading" after a week under blotter is the key signal. It means the lift has relaxed, the fibers are still hinged (not severed), and nothing is actively deteriorating. Combined with intact pigment and no through-tear, you have a stable, surface-only defect.

Recommendation: do not paste. Mat it and leave the wheat-starch on the shelf.

Why hold off:

1. Minimal intervention. WSP introduces moisture and pressure into an area that is currently stable. Moisture near a watercolor edge is exactly how you introduce tidelines or cockling. WSP is reversible, but unnecessary treatment is still treatment.

2. The mat does the protective work for you. A 1/4" overlap means the window mat will hold the area flat against the backing board. That is mechanical consolidation without adhesive.

3. If it stayed put under blotter for a week, it will stay put under a mat.

When paste would be the right call (not here):
  - the fiber is still mobile or catches under a finger
  - blotter didn't hold it
  - pigment is lifting or flaking nearby
  - mat overlap is too narrow to cover the damage

Middle-ground option if you want it: a tiny WSP application only under the loose edge (not on the face), dried under blotter with light weight. For a 1.5" lift that has relaxed cleanly and will be matted over, this is usually overkill.

One caveat: if the piece is high-value and you want certainty, a paper conservator's hands-on look is cheap relative to the work. What I can offer is the principle, not the inspection.

Short answer: usually fine to leave alone if it's truly stable — but a lifted tuft under a mat is a slow-failure mode, not a static condition. The default is "monitor, don't repair"; the trigger to escalate is any sign the defect is propagating.

WHEN IT'S OK TO LEAVE IT
- The lifted area is a single tuft or small loop, not a seam or backing tear
- The mat fully covers it and lays flat with no edge pressure on the raised fiber
- No other fibers in the surrounding 6-12 inches are pulling or loosening
- No visible discoloration, odor, or moisture under the mat
- Foot traffic across that spot is light (under a stationary mat, not a doorway or walk path)

SIGNS THAT JUSTIFY PROFESSIONAL REPAIR (not DIY patching)
- Growth: more tufts lifting, or the affected area has expanded since you first noticed it
- Unraveling: a run is forming along a row — once a carpet row starts, it accelerates
- Backing visible: the primary or secondary backing is torn, not just face fiber
- Buckling or wrinkling radiating outward from the spot
- Mat no longer lays flat because the raised fiber is pushing it up (creates a low-grade trip lip and accelerates wear on the mat)
- Any dampness, staining, or odor under the mat — suggests moisture wicking into the backing, which can delaminate the carpet
- Located at a threshold, transition strip, or high-traffic pivot point even if currently small

LEASE NOTE WORTH FLAGGING
If this is in a common area you'd want on record anyway (entry, hallway), take one dated photo now and re-shoot in 30 days. Not because it's damage you caused — wear is normal — but because a dated baseline is the difference between "pre-existing condition" and "move-out charge" if it later looks worse than it is. That said: don't repair proactively just to protect the deposit; a small stable lift under a covered mat is well within normal wear.

THE PRACTICAL RULE
Stable + covered + localized + not propagating → leave it, check monthly.
Any single one of: growth, run, backing exposure, buckling, moisture → call a carpet pro for a re-tuft or patch before it becomes a re-stretch.

SUMMARY
Daniela's 2h warning / 4h critical shape is directionally right for an hourly-refreshing export, but on its own it is a labeling exercise, not an operational alarm. To be useful, the acceptance criteria need to commit to (a) where the warning actually surfaces and what action it triggers, (b) a real page path at 4h, (c) forward-only resolution that does not reopen eligibility closed during the stale window, and (d) no per-incident override. Two additions: missing/null timestamp is critical immediately, and the criteria describe the alarm mechanism only — not field-level freshness semantics for downstream consumers.

ASSESSMENT OF THE TWO THRESHOLDS
- 2h warning = one missed refresh + buffer. Reasonable as a "look now" trigger for an hourly producer, but only operationally useful if it lands somewhere a named owner reads within the next 2h.
- 4h critical = three missed cycles. Reasonable as a page-level trigger, but only if a named on-call rotation actually pages out. A dashboard tile going from yellow to red is not operational.
- Both thresholds assume the producer's actual cadence is hourly with high reliability. If the producer routinely runs 80–100 min cycles, the 2h warning will fire often enough to lose signal. The producer's observed cadence over the last 30 days should be checked before these numbers are locked.

RECOMMENDED ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
1. Deterministic, time-bounded transitions. Warning fires at consumer_timestamp_age ≥ 2h ± 5 min; critical at ≥ 4h ± 5 min. Clock-skew tolerance is explicit and small; it is not a delay mechanism.
2. Auditable transitions. Every clear → warn → critical → clear transition is logged with timestamp, the consumer_timestamp value at the transition, and any actor for forced transitions. Retention follows the standing audit policy, not just the UI.
3. Warning routes to a watched surface. 2h warning creates a ticket or surfaces in a queue a named owner reads during business hours. If no such surface exists, the warning state has no operational value and should be dropped from the criteria.
4. Critical pages a named rotation. 4h critical fires a page (not a dashboard color change) to a defined on-call. Acceptance includes a test that demonstrates the page path works end-to-end.
5. Resolution is forward-only. When a fresh consumer_timestamp arrives after a stale period, the alarm clears and downstream re-checks current state. Eligibility or decisions closed during the stale window are NOT reopened — consistent with the standing lag-recovery rule. A delayed refresh resolves forward; it does not restore pre-lag eligibility.
6. No per-incident override. No role can silence, lower, or extend the threshold for a specific occurrence. Class-level suppression is allowed only for a planned upstream maintenance window, with explicit time bounds and a named owner, and is itself logged.
7. Missing/null timestamp is critical immediately. A missing consumer_timestamp is treated as ≥ 4h stale on detection, not after the 4h wait. Missing is a stronger signal than stale.
8. Mechanism, not semantics. The criteria describe the alarm's behavior on the consumer_timestamp field. They do not encode what "fresh" means for any specific downstream consumer or field — that remains a separate, unsettled workstream and this document does not pre-empt it.

QUESTIONS
- For Daniela: does a watched surface for the 2h warning already exist, or does that need to be stood up before these criteria can be signed off?
- For Daniela: what is the producer's observed cadence over the last 30 days? If 80–100 min is normal, 2h warning will be noisy and the threshold should be revisited.
- For Ines (lifecycle-aud-risk): the fail-closed policy for downstream consumers during a critical alarm is her lane. The alarm criteria should reference that policy but not define it — does she want a separate document?
- For Owen (shape + measurement/definitions): the choice of consumer_timestamp as the watched field, and any clock-skew tolerance, may belong in his measurement definitions. Are these criteria the right home, or should they defer?
- For Priya: once live, this counts as a standing lane — confirm it fits inside the ≤3 neutral/wk ceiling.

SUMMARY: Answer "pension or annuity" — not IRA.

Why:
- Code 7 by itself just means "normal" distribution (vs. early, disability, death, etc.). The IRA/SEP/SIMPLE checkbox is what distinguishes an IRA from an employer plan.
- Box is blank → this is from an employer pension/annuity/profit-sharing/ESOP, NOT an IRA.
- Gross = taxable is about taxability (e.g., all contributions were pre-tax, so 100% is taxable as ordinary income). It says nothing about the source type and doesn't change the answer.

Quick sanity check on the form itself: confirm the IRA/SEP/SIMPLE box on the 1099-R is actually unchecked. If it is, the software answer is "pension or annuity" and you can move on.

One related thing worth knowing: Code 7 means the payer already classified it as a normal (not early) distribution, so the 10% early-withdrawal penalty shouldn't apply — assuming Mom is 59½ or older, which is the most common reason a payer codes it 7. If she's under 59½ and this wasn't a qualifying exception, double-check that the payer used the right code (sometimes code 7 is used when the payer can't verify age).

[Note: this is interpretation of the 1099-R instructions, not a CPA ruling — but the code-7 + blank-IRA-box combination is unambiguous.]

This is purely a knowledge question, so no tools are needed. The answer below is a plain-text walkthrough for Mom (or whoever is helping her at the keyboard).

    QUICK FRAMING

The IRA-versus-pension prompt in tax software is asking a specific legal question: which IRC framework governs this distribution — the IRA rules (Subchapter D, Sec. 408) or the qualified-plan / annuity rules (Sec. 401(a), 403(b), 457, 72, etc.). The visible 1099-R fields are clues, not proof. The software pre-fills an answer based on those clues, but the answer can be wrong if a single clue is misread or if a past rollover changed the character of the account.

    WHAT THE VISIBLE FIELDS ACTUALLY SAY

Box 7 (Distribution code). This is the single most informative field. Codes carry different implications depending on what they are paired with:
  - Code G = direct rollover TO an IRA — implies origin was a qualified plan or 403(b)/457, not an IRA
  - Code H = direct rollover TO a qualified plan — implies origin was an IRA
  - Code P = in-plan Roth rollover — implies a qualified plan
  - Code Q or T = Roth IRA distribution — implies an IRA
  - Code 1, 2, 7, M (early, exception, normal, RMD) — universal, not type-specific

Payer name and account labeling. Look at the literal legal name on the form, not just what the software infers:
  - "Vanguard ... FBO Jane Doe IRA" or "Schwab Traditional IRA" → IRA
  - "Acme Corp Pension Plan" or "ABC 401(k) Plan" → qualified employer plan
  - "MetLife" / "Prudential" / "Jackson National" with no IRA language → non-qualified annuity (different from both IRA and pension)

Box 10 (Amount allocable to IRR). If this box has a number, the payer is reporting an insurance company annuity under Sec. 72(e). This is NOT an IRA, and the prompt should not be answered as if it were.

Box 11 (First year of designated Roth). Indicates Roth treatment, but Roth exists inside both IRAs and qualified plans — confirms Roth but not the broader type.

Box 2a (Taxable amount). If blank, marked "not determined," or flagged with a 2b value of "1," the payer has punted the basis work to the taxpayer. This matters because basis recovery rules differ between IRAs and pensions.

Boxes 1, 4, 12-16. Amount, withholding, state info — they don't help distinguish IRA from pension, but they're worth scanning for consistency.

    HOW THESE FIELDS FEED THE SOFTWARE PROMPT

The software uses the field pattern to:
  1. Pre-select "IRA" or "Pension" (often based on payer name keywords and Box 7)
  2. Route the entry to Form 1040 Line 4a/4b (IRA) vs Line 5a/5b (pension/annuity)
  3. Pick the early-withdrawal exception list (Sec. 72(t) exceptions differ between the two)
  4. Apply the correct basis recovery order (after-tax IRA contributions come out tax-free first; in pensions, basis was already recovered at start of payments, so distributions are usually fully taxable)
  5. Apply the correct RMD method (separate tracking per IRA; aggregated for 403(b) accounts)

A wrong answer at the prompt cascades through all five of these.

    FACTS MOM MUST VERIFY BEFORE CLICKING AN ANSWER

1. The actual account type from the most recent plan statement or trust agreement, not from the 1099-R alone.
2. Whether the account is a SIMPLE IRA — SIMPLE distributions within the first two years of participation are subject to a 25% early-withdrawal penalty, not 10%. The 1099-R does not always flag this clearly.
3. Whether any prior rollover or conversion occurred. A 401(k) rolled into an IRA becomes an IRA going forward; a SEP-IRA that received employer contributions is still an IRA. Character follows the receiving account, not the original source.
4. Whether the account is an inherited IRA / inherited Roth IRA. Death distributions follow their own rules (10-year rule for deaths after 2019; the software's prompt logic may misclassify these).
5. Box 7 reading — confirm the code matches Mom's age and the actual event (e.g., Code 7 = age 59½ or older, normal; Code 1 = under 59½, no known exception).
6. Box 2a status — if "not determined," she has basis-tracking work to do before answering the prompt accurately.
7. Whether multiple 1099-Rs from the same payer represent different accounts (e.g., a 401(k) and a pension from the same employer) — each gets answered separately.
8. The payer's actual legal name. "Charles Schwab & Co. Inc." can be a brokerage for either an IRA or a 401(k) rollover IRA; the form alone may not make the original source clear.

    WHEN TO STOP AND CALL THE PLAN ADMINISTRATOR (THE PAYER ON THE FORM)

  - The payer name is ambiguous (could be brokerage, could be plan administrator)
  - Box 7 code is unfamiliar or appears inconsistent with what Mom believes happened
  - Box 2a is blank and she cannot reconstruct basis from her own records
  - The 1099-R is for a death distribution and she is the beneficiary — confirm whether it should be reported as inherited IRA or as an estate distribution
  - There are two or more 1099-Rs from the same payer and she is unsure which account each one represents
  - The form lists a default code she doesn't recognize (e.g., K, L, N, S, W) and she wants to confirm before answering

    WHEN TO STOP AND CALL A TAX PROFESSIONAL

  - Any rollover or conversion occurred within the past five years — recharacterization and 60-day rollover rules interact with the prompt's classification
  - A backdoor Roth or mega backdoor Roth contribution is in the picture
  - A SIMPLE IRA 2-year window applies
  - An inherited IRA is involved and the original account holder died after 2019 (10-year rule)
  - Box 2a is blank ("not determined") and the basis story is non-trivial — Pub. 590-B or the IRA trustee may need to be consulted
  - The distribution was made to satisfy an RMD and there is any question about whether it was timely
  - A 1099-R correction (corrected form received after the original) was issued and the original return was already filed
  - State return treatment of the same distribution differs from federal (some states exempt pension income but tax IRA income, or vice versa)
  - A non-qualified annuity (Box 10 populated, or insurance company payer) is involved — the 10% additional tax rules and basis recovery are substantially different
  - A Qualified Plan Loan Offset (QPLO) flag appears
  - The total distribution includes employer securities with net unrealized appreciation (Box 6) — this is not IRA territory

    THE UNDERLYING RULE

If the IRA-versus-pension answer is not clearly supported by the 1099-R AND confirmed by the plan document, do not guess. The cost of one short call to the plan administrator is the cost of getting this right; the cost of a wrong answer is a return that has to be amended, an early-withdrawal penalty assessed in the wrong direction, or an IRS notice about an incorrect 1040 line. Filing season is a poor time to find out a single prompt answer was the wrong one.
