Most likely cause: typo, or the AGI on the copy she's reading from isn't what IRS actually has. Re-type from line 11 of the as-filed 2023 Form 1040 and retransmit — that fixes it more than half the time. If it rejects again, walk this tree:

1. Was her 2023 return ever amended (1040-X)? If yes, IRS holds the amended AGI, not the original. Her paper copy may show the pre-amendment number. This is the most common silent cause of IND-031-04.

2. Did her filing status or primary SSN change between 2023 and 2024 (marriage, divorce, name change)? If she's now primary on a different SSN than last year, IRS is matching against the wrong account. The AGI she needs is the one tied to whatever SSN is primary on the 2024 return.

3. Is she confusing prior-year AGI with the Identity Protection PIN (IP PIN)? Different thing, different reject — but worth ruling out. The IP PIN is a 6-digit annual code mailed/issued by IRS; she wouldn't have one unless IRS assigned it.

4. If she doesn't have her 2023 return at all: IRS "Get Transcript" online → Tax Return Transcript shows the AGI line exactly as IRS holds it. Or call IRS and request one by mail (5-10 days).

Resubmit path: most guided software will let her re-enter AGI and retransmit without starting over. Alternative — she can self-select any 5-digit prior-year PIN instead of AGI (IRS just verifies the PIN against her records; the digits don't have to mean anything).

Timing: not urgent. April 15 deadline, the e-file is just dead in the water until corrected.

Plain Q: Did she ever file a 1040-X for 2023, or was the 2023 return filed as-is?

IND-031-04 means the prior-year AGI entered on the return doesn't match what the IRS has on file. Don't retry the e-file until you know which situation you're in — work through these in order.

STEP 1 — Confirm last year's return was actually processed
Before assuming a typo, verify the IRS has the prior-year return on file. If it was filed late (after Oct 15 extension), was an amended return, or just finished processing, the e-file database may not yet reflect it.
  - IRS online account (irs.gov/payments/view-tax-account) — shows processed returns and the AGI on file.
  - "Where's My Refund?" / "Where's My Amended Return?" for status.
  - Phone (long waits; the online account is faster).

If the prior-year return is not yet processed, the cleanest fix is usually to wait — or, if eligible, use the $0 prior-year-AGI option (see Step 3).

STEP 2 — Pull a transcript to read what the IRS actually has
If last year's return was processed, request an IRS Tax Return Transcript (free, online via the IRS account, or by mail with Form 4506-T). The transcript shows the AGI the IRS recorded. Compare line-by-line to what was entered:
  - Filing-status change between years (MFJ → Single is the single most common cause of IND-031-04).
  - Spouse SSN/Name Control mismatch if MFJ.
  - An amended return that changed the AGI (IRS may still be using the original figure).
  - Simple data-entry typo (extra digit, decimal in wrong place).

This step turns the problem from "guess and retry" into "match what's actually on file."

STEP 3 — Use $0 only if the conditions are met
The IRS allows entering $0 as the prior-year AGI only when the taxpayer (a) didn't file a prior-year return and wasn't required to, or (b) is filing for the first time. Two constraints:
  - This is a one-time-use per taxpayer.
  - It's not a fallback for "I can't find the AGI" — using it when you filed last year and it was processed will trigger a different reject or delay.

If your mom filed last year and it was processed, $0 is the wrong answer — go back to Step 2 and get the transcript.

STEP 4 — If the AGI matches but it still rejects
Rare, but possible if there's an identity-theft marker or a CPF freeze. At that point:
  - File Form 14039 (Identity Theft Affidavit) if theft is suspected.
  - File a paper return with Form 8948 (the IRS's "e-file reject — paper alternative"). This is the other filing method provided for unresolvable rejects — print, sign, and mail the return with a short explanation.
  - If an IP PIN was issued, it must be entered; you can also request one proactively if there's been a data breach.

STEP 5 — Don't keep re-transmitting
Each reject/fix cycle leaves a footprint, and repeated mismatches can flag the account. Resolve the AGI question fully (usually via transcript) before re-filing.

Plain-language order of operations:
  1. Was last year's return processed? No → wait, or $0 if eligible. Yes → continue.
  2. Get the transcript, read the IRS's AGI, match it.
  3. Retry e-file with the correct AGI.
  4. Still rejects → Form 8948 paper file.

SHADOW-REPLAY ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
Post-9-fixture gate, pre-production-release decision
For: qualifying-human-admin status transformation (Helio Start reporting, Expansion Assist selection, lifecycle-preflight)

────────────────────────────────────────
WHY
────────────────────────────────────────
The corrected nine-record fixture proves the transformation no longer silently inherits prior true values when current governed value is missing, and that three consumers converge on those nine hand-picked cases. That is necessary but not sufficient for release:

  - Fixture cases are small-volume and likely over-fit to the prior-mismatch pattern Owen was chasing.
  - They exercise one snapshot in time, not lag conditions, stale windows, or the full state distribution (admitted / assisted / ineligible / final-reconciliation / pending).
  - They do not validate that the hold-on-missing behavior fires consistently when a record enters a lag, not just when the field is genuinely empty at rest.
  - Cross-consumer agreement on nine records cannot speak to agreement on the broader surfaced-state subset where the three consumers are intentionally non-overlapping.

Shadow replay runs the corrected transformation against production-bound data pipelines with production writes held back; it exists to falsify the fixture result before any release consideration. These criteria are the bar the shadow run must clear.

────────────────────────────────────────
CUTS (six gates, each independently pass/fail)
────────────────────────────────────────

GATE 1 — VOLUME & SAMPLING (not the same nine)
  - Replay covers the full qualifying-human-admin population over a defined window (suggest ≥30 days rolling, or full available window if shorter), not the original nine fixtures.
  - Sample must be stratified to include all five Helio Start states (admitted / assisted / ineligible / final-reconciliation / pending) at their natural distribution, not oversampled on previously-mismatched states.
  - Include at minimum:
      * N ≥ 200 records with current governed value present (truth-available cohort)
      * N ≥ 50 records with current governed value missing at snapshot (hold-cohort)
      * N ≥ 50 records that transitioned during the window (transition-cohort)
  - The original nine fixtures must be retained as a regression baseline inside the shadow run, not as the gate's primary evidence.

GATE 2 — CROSS-CONSUMER AGREEMENT (bounded, not blanket)
  Pass criterion: 100% agreement on the surfaced-state subset where the three consumers are scoped to overlap.
  "Agreement" is defined as: identical current governed value, or identical hold-flag, where the consumer is in scope for that record's state — not byte-equality of underlying payloads.
  
  Required carve-outs (must be enumerated, not implicit):
    - `pending` is pre-admission and not in Helio Start rate/activation denom. EA and lifecycle-preflight may legitimately diverge from Helio Start on pending records; divergence here is not a failure.
    - `final-reconciliation` is in lifecycle-preflight scope and out of Helio Start rate denom. Surfaced divergence on final-reconciliation is not a cross-consumer failure if each consumer is reading its own scope correctly.
    - Expansion Assist remains descriptive / non-forecast; it must not surface governed values that Helio Start has already closed. Divergence on forecast-shaped fields is not in scope of this gate.
  Any divergence outside the documented carve-outs is a gate failure, regardless of count.

GATE 3 — FAIL-CLOSED ON MISSING CURRENT VALUE
  For the hold-cohort specifically:
    - 100% of records with current governed value missing must surface as HOLD on all three consumers.
    - Zero records may surface as inherited-true on any of the three consumers.
    - Zero records may surface as inherited-false on any of the three consumers (silent-false is as bad as silent-true for selection logic).
  This is the exact regression the nine-fixture test proved; the shadow run must prove it holds at population scale and across the lag boundary, not just at rest.

GATE 4 — STALE & LAG BEHAVIOR (forward-only)
  Inject or observe records where the upstream export is delayed beyond the staleness threshold:
    - On staleness: all three consumers must hold, not proceed on cached/inherited prior value.
    - On lag recovery: forward-only. Pre-lag eligibility is NOT restored. The post-recovery governed value is whatever the current export now says, applied forward, not retroactively rewriting the lag window.
    - No consumer may "re-fill" prior-true values into the lag window after recovery.
  This gate is the operational reality check that the nine-fixture test cannot provide.

GATE 5 — EXPLICIT-BOUNDARY INVENTORY
  Before the shadow run completes, the team must publish a written inventory of every known intentional boundary where the three consumers are expected to differ (pending / final-reconciliation / preflight-only states / etc.). For each boundary: name it, name which consumer(s) it applies to, name what the expected surfaced value is.
  The shadow run is then evaluated against this inventory. Any divergence not on the inventory is an undocumented boundary — which is itself a gate failure requiring either documentation or a fix before re-run.

GATE 6 — NO SILENT INHERITANCE, PERIOD
  Aggregate check across the full replay window:
    - Count of records where any consumer output a governed value that was not present in the current input AND was not explicitly held = must be 0.
    - Count of records where any consumer's output can be traced back, by lineage, to a prior-period true value not present in the current period's input = must be 0.
  This is the unified "the inheritance path is dead" gate, irrespective of which consumer or which state.

────────────────────────────────────────
PASS / EFFECT
────────────────────────────────────────
Shadow replay PASSES when Gates 1–6 all pass on the same replay window. On pass:

  - The transformation is approved to advance to production-validation (a separate, distinct phase — shadow pass is not production pass).
  - The boundary inventory from Gate 5 becomes the standing reference document for ongoing cross-surface reconciliation.
  - The lag-recovery forward-only behavior is confirmed operationally, not just from the transformation's static logic.

Shadow replay FAILS on any of:
  - Any silent-inheritance event (Gate 6) — automatic fail, no override.
  - Any undocumented cross-consumer divergence (Gate 5) — automatic fail.
  - Hold-cohort showing non-hold on any consumer (Gate 3) — automatic fail.
  - Stale data proceeding on any consumer instead of holding (Gate 4) — automatic fail.
  - Stratified sampling missing required state cohorts (Gate 1) — replay is incomplete, not failed; must be re-run, not waived.

────────────────────────────────────────
CALL
────────────────────────────────────────
Recommended sequencing after this 1-pager:

  1. Daniela + Owen publish the boundary inventory (Gate 5) first — it sets the evaluation frame for everything else.
  2. Owen runs the shadow replay against the defined window and sampling (Gates 1, 2, 3, 4, 6).
  3. Ines reviews lifecycle-aud-risk surface from the shadow output before any production-validation conversation.
  4. Shadow pass → escalate to Riley for judgment-esc on whether production-validation is warranted. Shadow pass alone is not a release decision.
  5. Production-validation is its own gated phase with its own criteria; it does not inherit approval from shadow.

This sequence keeps the fixture result as evidence, the shadow as falsification, and production as a separate decision — matching the existing audit-role split (Ines on lifecycle risk, Owen on shape + measurement, Riley on judgment escalation and cross-surface cuts) without collapsing any of those boundaries.

Staging Freshness Alarm — Acceptance Criteria
=============================================

Scope: staging ingestion lag alarm. Repaired lag must not keep firing; held rows must stay held by the alert; fail-closed posture preserved on ambiguous signal.

1. Automatic-clear criteria (lag is no longer treated as active)
---------------------------------------------------------------
A lag event clears from "active" state only when ALL of the following are observed in the same evaluation window:

- Freshness watermark advances to within the freshness SLO (current lag <= SLO threshold), AND
- That recovery watermark is sustained for a configurable dwell time (default: 2 consecutive evaluation cycles, >= the alarm's normal polling cadence — not a single lucky read), AND
- The watermark reflects a genuine forward export, not a roll-back or replay from an earlier point (monotonic, non-decreasing relative to the pre-lag watermark).

Any of the following keeps the event ACTIVE regardless of watermark movement:

- Freshness still > SLO at evaluation time.
- Watermark recovered but the dwell window has not elapsed.
- Recovery signal derived from a backfill, replay, or clock skew correction rather than a normal forward export.
- Suppression flag set by the on-call (manual hold) — alert stays quiet, event stays active.

2. Audit-history criteria (what the trail must show)
----------------------------------------------------
Every state transition for a lag event is recorded in the audit log with:

- Event id (stable across the lifecycle).
- From-state and to-state (e.g., active -> clear-suppressed; active -> clear-recovered; suppressed -> active on re-lag).
- Timestamp (UTC) and evaluation cycle id that drove the transition.
- Watermark value and lag-seconds at transition.
- Dwell completion evidence (cycle count, not just one sample).
- For clears: the rule path that triggered it ("recovered+dwell-satisfied" vs. "manual-suppress").
- For re-activations within 24h of a clear: an explicit "reopened" flag, not a fresh event id, so reviewers can see the flap as one incident.

Audit history is append-only; transitions are not rewritten retroactively. A lag that was active at 14:00 is recorded as active at 14:00 even if the underlying row is later reclassified or backfilled — later state is forward-only (consistent with the standing exception-review rule).

3. Held-row guardrail (alert must NOT release held rows)
--------------------------------------------------------
The alarm is a signal surface, not a release authority. Concretely:

- The alarm has no write path to held rows. Clearing a lag event changes alarm state only.
- Held rows remain held until an explicit, out-of-band release action by an authorized role (the same release path that would be used without the alarm — the alarm does not bypass it).
- A clear during a held window does NOT auto-release. The held flag is independent state; the alarm can be green while rows are still held.
- Conversely, a held row does not silence the alarm. The alarm can still fire and stay active on a separate held-row's own lag.
- On reactivation within 24h of a clear, the prior release path (if any) is not re-invoked — held rows stay held unless explicitly re-released by the same authorized role.

4. Fail-closed handling (ambiguous signal stays latched)
--------------------------------------------------------
When the recovery signal is ambiguous, the event fails closed — i.e., stays ACTIVE — until disambiguated:

- Watermark present but source can't be confirmed as a forward export (e.g., exporter restarted, replay tool used, clock jumped): treat as not-recovered.
- Dwell satisfied on only one evaluator when a second evaluator disagrees: treat as not-recovered.
- Suppression window open with no manual decision recorded: stay ACTIVE; do not auto-clear.
- Post-clear, if any subsequent evaluation within the flap window (24h) re-detects lag above SLO: transition back to ACTIVE with the same event id and "reopened" flag; do not open a new event.

Net effect: a repaired lag clears only on sustained, forward-exported recovery, the trail records why and when, the alarm never touches held rows, and any ambiguity keeps the page open until a human resolves it.

Bottom line: Don't drive it as-is, but a short, low-speed trip to a nearby shop after reinflating to 35 psi is reasonable. Do not pull the screw. Do not highway-drive it underinflated.

Why 27 psi matters
- You're running ~23% below spec. The sidewall is flexing more than designed, generating heat. At 27 psi, city-surface driving for a few miles is survivable; sustained highway speed (heat + load) is where a slow leak turns into a blowout.
- Other three tires at 34-36 are fine and consistent with cold readings — they're not the story.
- Overnight 35 → 27 with a visible screw is a slow leak pattern, not a catastrophic failure.

The screw: leave it in place
- The screw is currently partially plugging the hole. Pulling it converts a slow leak into a fast one and makes the shop's job harder (they lose the visible leak marker and have to submerge the tire to find it).
- Center-tread punctures are the repairable zone. Shoulder/sidewall punctures generally are not — yours being center tread is the best-case location for a plug/patch repair.

Adding air solely for a short trip — reasonable only if all of these hold:
- Distance: a few miles, not across town on the highway.
- Speed: stay under ~50 mph. No freeway on-ramps at full throttle.
- Pressure: inflate cold to the full 35 psi spec, not partial. Cold = driven less than a mile in the last 3 hours, or add 3-4 psi if the tire is warm to compensate.
- Route: surface streets, gentle inputs, no hard cornering.
- Direct: drive straight to the shop. No side errands, no "I'll just swing by…"
- Recheck pressure before you leave — if it won't hold 35 for even a couple of minutes in the driveway, the leak is faster than slow and you should not drive.

Stop-driving / abort immediately if any of these appear:
- Pressure drops more than ~3 psi between driveway and shop.
- Any vibration, thumping, or pull to one side.
- New hissing sound, visible sidewall bulge, or cracking.
- TPMS warning light (if equipped — at 27 it's probably already near threshold on many cars).

If the nearest tire shop is far, highway-only, or you're on an AWD vehicle with strict tire-matching requirements in the manual: call a mobile tire service or flatbed. Don't "just drive and see."

- If your car is AWD, check the owner's manual — some require all four tires within ~2-3 psi of each other, which the current setup already violates. Same caution applies post-inflate until repaired.
- The 27 reading is likely a "drive-now-fix-soon" situation, not a "stop in the road" situation — but the margin is thin and the answer changes fast if conditions change.

================================================================
SUMMARY
================================================================
Owen's v1 collapses five exception classes (entitlement, authority, qualifying-human-admin, suppression, cosmetic reporting) into a single priority pool with two terms that misread every class differently. Time-open is the wrong axis for entitlement (deadline-driven) and authority (approver-blocked); surface-count is the wrong axis for suppression (by definition invisible). The fix is class-bucketed triage with field_criticality as the inner sort key — age never crosses class boundaries, so field severity is preserved. The score is labeled operational priority, never customer impact.

================================================================
CRITIQUE — WHERE V1 BREAKS, BY CLASS
================================================================
Entitlement (billing/refund/chargeback). Time-open understates tail risk — a wrongly-billed user accruing interest isn't less urgent at hour 6 than hour 5, and a refund-window or chargeback deadline is event-driven, not linear. Surface count understates per-surface financial exposure. The formula can rank a 5-hour cosmetic typo on 3 dashboards (score 35) above a 5-hour entitlement breach on 1 surface (score 15) — wrong routing.

Qualifying-human-admin. By-design slow — the queue is doing its job by waiting for the right human. The 1pt/hr term penalizes the queue, not the exception. These belong in a separate lane ordered by routing-unblock, not by age.

Authority. Blocked on a named approver. "Open N hours" measures org latency, not severity — Owen's formula will pull authority items into the high-priority queue when they're really waiting on a person, not on a fix. Needs a decision-ready substate (ready-for-approver vs. waiting-on-approver), not a flat age term.

Suppression. By definition near-zero consumer-visible surfaces. Surface-count auto-deprioritizes suppression issues even when the suppression rule itself is wrong — e.g., wrong segment suppressed, or a rule swallowing a high-severity class. Shape inverts intent: the more invisible the failure, the lower it scores.

Cosmetic reporting. A label typo on a dashboard is not 10pt/surface equivalent to a wrong refund amount on the same dashboard. Without a class term, formula can't distinguish presentation bug from data bug.

================================================================
PROPOSED TRIAGE RULE
================================================================
Inputs per exception row:
  - class ∈ {entitlement, authority, qualifying-human-admin, suppression, cosmetic}
  - field_criticality ∈ {high, medium, low} — assigned at intake by lane owner
  - active_holds ∈ ℕ — surfaces currently in held/blocked state BECAUSE of this exception
  - affected_surfaces ∈ ℕ — total surfaces the exception touches (open or held)
  - age_hours ∈ ℝ

Step 1 — Bucket by class. Lane order (this is the outer key — age cannot cross lanes):
  1. Entitlement
  2. Authority (substate: decision-ready first, then waiting-on-approver)
  3. Qualifying-human-admin
  4. Suppression
  5. Cosmetic reporting

Step 2 — Within a bucket, sort by composite key (descending on each):
  (field_criticality → active_holds → affected_surfaces → age_hours)

Step 3 — Class-specific age handling (age never accelerates cosmetic or authority-wait):
  - Entitlement: effective_age = age_hours × 2.0  (age = deadline proximity, not decay)
  - Suppression: effective_age = age_hours × 1.5   (silent exceptions accumulate operational debt)
  - Authority / qualifying-human-admin / cosmetic: × 1.0 (age is not a severity signal here)

================================================================
WHY ACTIVE_HOLDS IS SEPARATE FROM AFFECTED_SURFACES
================================================================
Affected_surfaces = total blast radius. Active_holds = blast radius that is currently STALLED because of this exception. A 5-surface exception where 1 surface is on hold outranks a 10-surface exception where 0 are on hold, because the operational consequence is immediate. Conflating them loses the "this is actively blocking another surface right now" signal.

================================================================
WHY THIS IS NOT A CUSTOMER-IMPACT METRIC
================================================================
The score is operational priority — it drives queue position and unblock order, not customer comms or reporting claims. Affected_surfaces and active_holds capture operational scope (other surfaces blocked on this fix), not customer reach. A consumer-facing claim like "this affects N customers" is a separate derivation and is NOT what this score says. Label it that way in any doc, dashboard tile, or Slack relay — otherwise ops reads will get re-cast as impact reads downstream.

================================================================
WORKED EXAMPLE — BACKLOG OF 4
================================================================
  A. 5hr cosmetic label typo, 3 dashboards.          Owen v1: 35
  B. 5hr entitlement breach, 1 surface.              Owen v1: 15
  C. 12hr suppression rule, 0 active holds, 4 surf.  Owen v1: 52
  D. 8hr authority-blocked, decision-ready.          Owen v1: 28

  Owen v1 order:  C (52) → A (35) → D (28) → B (15)
  — cosmetic suppression beats the entitlement breach. Wrong.

  Proposed order: B → D → C → A
  — B (entitlement, age-accelerated to effective 10) leads
  — D (authority, decision-ready substate) next
  — C (suppression, 0 active holds) below authority
  — A (cosmetic) last, age does not accelerate it
  Field severity preserved: A cannot leapfrog B under any age.

================================================================
CUTS FROM V1
================================================================
  - Drop "1pt/hr" as a universal term. Replace with class-specific effective_age.
  - Drop "10pt/surface" as a flat additive. Replace with (active_holds × w_h) + (affected_surfaces × w_s), w_h > w_s.
  - Add field_criticality as the inner sort key (assigned at intake by lane owner).
  - Add class as the outer bucket — this is what stops age from erasing field severity.

================================================================
EFFECT ON CURRENT BACKLOG
================================================================
  - Entitlement items move to the head of the queue regardless of age.
  - Authority items stop floating up on age alone — they queue behind entitlement and behind decision-ready ordering.
  - Suppression issues with zero active holds drop below authority/qualifying-human-admin even when old — which is correct, because the failure is silent.
  - Cosmetic reporting stays at the bottom; age never accelerates it.

================================================================
CALL
================================================================
  - Adopt the class-bucketed sort. Keep Owen's surface term shape, but split it into active_holds + affected_surfaces and weight active_holds higher.
  - Age is a within-bucket tiebreaker plus a class-specific accelerator — never a class-crosser.
  - Label the score "operational priority" everywhere it appears. Do not let it be re-cast as customer impact.
  - field_criticality is assigned at intake by the lane owner (Ines for lifecycle, Owen for shape, Riley for judgment escalations) — not derived from the score.

Here's the plan. Plain text because the CLI doesn't render markdown.

================================================================
8-HOUR NO-USE METER TEST — RILEY'S APARTMENT
================================================================

Important precondition (check first):
  If your building has one shared meter for all units (common in
  apartment complexes), this test catches ALL tenants' water use,
  not just yours. You cannot isolate a unit-side leak that way.
  Confirm with your landlord/utility before running it. If it is
  a shared meter, the equivalent test is a shut-the-unit-main test:
  close your unit's shutoff valve, watch the meter for 8 hours. If
  the meter still moves, the leak is between the meter and your
  shutoff (building's responsibility). If it stops, the leak is in
  your distribution.

Best daytime window:
  9:00am–5:00pm on a workday. Avoids the typical 2am water-softener
  regen cycle and the 4–6am irrigation cycle. Mid-day building use
  is also lower than morning/evening peaks. Tuesdays, Thursdays,
  Fridays you bike-commute, so pick a day you'll be home (e.g., Mon,
  Wed, weekend) and start the test after the morning rush is done.

================================================================
PREPARATION (the day before or earlier in the test day)
================================================================

1. Confirm the meter's units
   - US residential meters are usually cubic feet (CF) on the
     odometer, with a separate leak indicator (small triangle, gear,
     or disc that spins with any flow).
   - 1 cubic foot = 7.48 gallons. Write down which units yours uses.

2. Find and read your shutoff valve
   - Locate the apartment main shutoff (under sinks, near water
     heater, or where the line enters the unit). You don't have to
     use it for the test, but know where it is in case you find a
     leak mid-test.

3. Walk every fixture and appliance; tape a "DO NOT USE" note on each
   - Bathrooms: toilets, sinks, shower/tub
   - Kitchen: sink, sprayer, instant-hot dispenser, filtered water tap
   - Laundry: washing machine (door ajar, latch undone is a good
     visual lockout)
   - Refrigerator: ice maker + water dispenser (turn ice maker OFF
     via the switch if you can reach it; empty the tray and prop the
     ice bin lid up so it's obviously not in service)
   - Dishwasher (door ajar, latch undone)
   - Humidifier (whole-house or room units — OFF and unplug if
     portable)
   - Hot water heater (typically passive; just know it)
   - Evaporative cooler, if present
   - Outdoor spigot / hose
   - Irrigation controller: verify schedule is OFF for the test day
   - Water softener: skip regen cycle — most are timer-set; if you
     can force regen NOW before the test, fine; otherwise avoid a
     regen during the window
   - Pool/hot tub autofill — N/A in your unit but check the building
   - Steam oven, coffee maker plumbed-in line
   - Plant watering cans — empty or fill from a pre-collected source
   - Reverse-osmosis / under-sink filter with auto-flush valve

4. Pre-water everything that needs water
   - Plants: water them now
   - Pets: this is Kibo's section, see below
   - Yourself: fill a kettle, water bottles, anything you might want
     during the 8 hours — all BEFORE the start reading

5. Charge your phone / clear storage
   - You'll want timestamps on photos. Make sure the camera app is
     set to embed date+time+GPS in EXIF, or at minimum visible on
     the screen.

6. Notify household
   - Even if it's just you at home, text Sam / roommate / anyone who
     might drop by: "No water use in unit from 9am to 5pm today —
     literally no flushing, no faucet, nothing. If you need water,
     go downstairs to the lobby restroom."

================================================================
KIBO'S WATER (the daytime-friendly piece)
================================================================

Goal: zero meter-side draw for Kibo during the 8-hour window.

Method — pre-fill, dispense from container:

  Before the start reading, fill a measured container from the tap
  (this draw IS captured by the meter before your start reading,
  so it doesn't count against the test). Suggested amounts for an
  adult dog over 8 hours in mild indoor weather:
    - 2–3 quarts in his regular bowl
    - 1–2 quarts reserve in a sealed jug in the fridge (cold water
      is more appealing and he'll drink more of it)
  Total ~1 gallon of pre-fill.

  During the 8 hours:
    - Kibo drinks from the bowl.
    - If the bowl needs a top-up, pour from the reserve jug.
    - NEVER refill from the tap. NEVER run the tap to rinse the bowl
      or to add ice from the fridge dispenser.
    - If he somehow runs the bowl dry and the reserve is gone, the
      test is invalidated. Note the time, restart with a fresh
      reading after a stabilization wait.

  Optional belt-and-suspenders: add a few ice cubes (made the day
  before, pre-test) to the bowl at the start so the water stays
  cool and he drinks less.

Note: if the day is hot, or Kibo is more active than usual, or he
has any condition that increases thirst, scale the pre-fill up.
Healthy adult dogs on a normal day do fine with ~1 gallon over 8
hours. If in doubt, lean toward more pre-fill rather than refilling
mid-test.

================================================================
START-OF-TEST PROCEDURE (T = 0)
================================================================

1. T-15min: do one last full walk-through. Open every toilet lid
   so they're visibly inert. Run nothing.

2. T-5min: lay out the recording sheet (see "RECORD" section
   below). Phone camera ready.

3. T-0: walk to the meter with the phone.

================================================================
BEFORE PHOTO (at T = 0)
================================================================

Capture four photos, in this order, with timestamp visible in frame:

  Photo A — meter face, straight-on, flashlight if needed
    - Entire dial face fills the frame
    - All digits on the odometer legible (typically 6–8 digits)
    - Serial number visible
    - Leak indicator (small triangle / disc / gear) clearly visible
    - Sub-register if present (the small dial showing fractions of
      a cubic foot, or a gallon sweep hand)
    - EXIF timestamp and date embedded
    - Optional: a piece of paper next to the meter with start time
      written ("START 9:00 AM 2025-02-19") so it's unambiguous

  Photo B — wide shot of meter + surrounding context
    - Shows the meter box, lid, and the wall/floor around it
    - Useful to prove nothing was altered (no kinked hose, no
      shutoff valve turned)

  Photo C — Kibo's bowl at T-0
    - Pre-filled, sitting on the counter or floor
    - Reserve jug next to it
    - Visible "DO NOT REFILL FROM TAP" sign
    - Date and time on a sticky note in frame

  Photo D — kitchen overview
    - Faucet with "DO NOT USE" note
    - Dishwasher door ajar
    - Refrigerator with ice maker indicator off

Optional but ideal: one photo of every "DO NOT USE" tagged fixture
so you can later show you had them all under control.

================================================================
DURING THE 8 HOURS
================================================================

  - Do not run any water. Period.
  - Check the meter visually at the 2-hour, 4-hour, and 6-hour
    marks. Each check: glance at the leak indicator. If it's
    spinning at any point, the test is already detecting flow —
    note the time and let the test finish (don't stop early; you
    still want the before/after numbers). Quick phone photo of the
    meter at each check is good evidence.
  - Stay home. Leaving the unit doesn't help if a fixture cycles
    on while you're gone (ice maker, water softener, irrigation).
  - Use the bathroom before T-0. Plan meals that don't need
    cooking-water access (sandwiches, takeout eaten cold, etc.).
  - Do not flush, do not wash hands in the unit, do not rinse a
    dish, do not run the shower for "just a sec."
  - Kibo water protocol as above.

================================================================
END-OF-TEST PROCEDURE (T = 8 hours)
================================================================

  1. T+7h55m: get the phone, flashlight, recording sheet.
  2. T+8h00m on the dot (or as close as you can get):
     - Take Photo E (identical framing to Photo A) — meter face,
       straight-on, all digits + serial + leak indicator.
     - Take Photo F (identical framing to Photo B) — wide context.
     - Take Photo G — Kibo's bowl at T+8h (level noticeably lower
       if he drank normally).
  3. Walk through the unit and resume normal use only after
     photos are taken and saved.

================================================================
STOP / INVALIDATE CONDITIONS
================================================================

Stop the test (note the time, what happened, restart fresh):

  - Any household member or guest uses ANY water in the unit
  - Kibo somehow gets tap water (e.g., jug knocked over and you
    refill from the tap)
  - Building water shutoff event you didn't initiate (utility
    work, fire system test) — wait 24 hours after restoration,
    then restart
  - Water softener regen cycle fires mid-window (if you can hear
    or see the regen start, restart)
  - Irrigation runs mid-window
  - You accidentally use a fixture (e.g., reflex flush) — note it
    honestly, restart; do not "compensate" by extending the test

Let the test finish and report the leak (do NOT stop):

  - You hear dripping or running water
  - You see a wet spot, ceiling stain, or pooling
  - The leak indicator spins at any intermediate check
  - The end reading differs from the start reading

  These are exactly what you're trying to find. Record them and
  let the test complete so you have the documented leak rate.

Conditions that make the test inconclusive (consider rescheduling):

  - Refrigerator ice maker cycles on during the test. You cannot
    isolate how much of any change came from the ice maker vs a
    leak. If you can verify the ice maker is OFF and the bin is
    empty, this is moot. If not, reschedule or plan around the
    known cycle (the test still works if you read the meter RIGHT
    BEFORE an ice-maker fill and RIGHT AFTER it stops — but that
    requires careful timing and is harder to defend in a dispute).
  - Water softener regen scheduled during the window
  - Irrigation scheduled during the window
  - Anyone else has legitimate access to the unit (cleaner,
    maintenance, roommate) during the window
  - Building shutoff / pressure event within 24h of the test
  - Heavy rain or freeze event that could cause transient
    distribution-side movement unrelated to your unit

================================================================
INTERPRETATION (after you have end numbers)
================================================================

  - End odometer == Start odometer, AND leak indicator did not spin:
    no leak detectable in your service line during the window.
    Document and keep.
  - End odometer > Start odometer:
    Compute delta:
      cubic feet change x 7.48 = gallons used in 8 hours
      gallons x 3 = gallons per day (linear extrapolation, rough)
      gallons x 365 = gallons per year (same caveat)
    A toilet flapper can leak 1–3 gal/day silently. A pinhole in
    a pressurized line can leak 10–100+ gal/day. Document and
    report to landlord.
  - Leak indicator spun but odometer barely moved:
    very slow leak below meter resolution. Still actionable — it
    means water is moving somewhere. Investigate toilets (food
    coloring in the tank, see if it reaches the bowl without
    flushing) and visible piping.

================================================================
RECORD — write this all down, then photograph the page
================================================================

Total elapsed (hours): ______  Ambient indoor temp: ______
Outdoor temp / weather: ______

  Serial number: __________

Fixtures confirmed OFF / locked out (initial each):
  _ Toilet 1     _ Toilet 2 (if applicable)
  _ Kitchen sink _ Bathroom sink _ Shower/tub

  _ Humidifier   _ Evaporative cooler
  _ Outdoor spigot / hose
  _ Irrigation controller (schedule off for the day)

Kibo water:
  Pre-fill volume (gallons): ______
  Pre-fill tap draw recorded before T-0: yes/no

Anomalies during test (with time):

Witness (optional but useful for landlord disputes):

================================================================
QUICK-REFERENCE TIMELINE (T = 0 at start reading)
================================================================

  Day before:
    Walk the unit, identify fixtures, pre-water plants,
    pre-make ice for Kibo's bowl, plan no-cook meals.

  Test day, T-15min:
    Final walk-through. Kibo's bowl filled from tap. Reserve
    jug filled from tap. Recording sheet ready.

  T-0:      Photo A, B, C, D. Note start time and odometer.
  T+2h:     Check meter. Quick photo.

  T+6h:     Check meter. Quick photo.
  T+8h:     Photo E, F, G. Note end time and odometer. Resume
            normal use only after end reading is locked.

================================================================
WHAT TO DO WITH THE RESULTS
================================================================

  - No change: file with your records. If you were running the test
    because of a high water bill, the leak is likely on a fixture
    inside the unit (running toilet, dripping faucet) — those won't
    always show on a static 8h test if they're intermittent. Test
    individual fixtures next: a few drops of food coloring in each
    toilet tank, wait 10 min without flushing, see if color reaches

  - Change detected: notify landlord in writing (email, with the

Daniela's right that the gap is real. Three independent restore paths (reporting deploy, monthly-selection job, Customer.io config) means the rollback has a structural coordination window where one consumer is on the new feed while another is still on its old selector. That's not a hypothetical.

But I'd push back on the assertion goal as she's framed it. "All consumers return to the same authority at the same time" is the same shape as "eliminating mismatches" — it overreaches on shared-state claims. In a system with intentional authority boundaries across surfaces, you can't assert atomic convergence. The right assertion is bounded reconciliation on the surfaced-state subset, with named intentional boundaries where divergence is expected.

What the assertion should actually check:

  1. Reconciliation window — concrete and bounded. All surfaced-state paths reconcile within [X] minutes on the [subset of state that drives downstream customer-visible decisions]. X tied to the longest of the three restore channels, validated against your clean nonproduction replay. The subset is the activation-driving and send-gating slice, not the entire state surface.

  2. Named intentional boundaries — where divergence during the window is a feature, not a bug:
     - Helio Start `pending` (pre-admission) is intentionally outside rate/activation denom. A consumer reading `pending` during rollback is reading a real state, not a mismatch.
     - Expansion Assist selection is descriptive, nonforecast. Its restore timing doesn't gate activation or downstream sends, so it's not in the surfaced-state subset that needs bounded reconciliation — it's a read-only surface for this purpose.
     - Lifecycle preflight on `routine education` is a lifecycle-aud-risk lane (Ines's), not a Helio Start one. Its restore timing is governed by the lifecycle runbook; the Helio rollback assertion shouldn't own it.

  3. What's left after those carve-outs is the subset that actually drives a customer-visible decision inside the rollback window. That's what the assertion covers. Everything else gets documented as intentional.

One other thing: Daniela's draft focuses on the rollback direction (kill switch → restore prior). The same coordination gap exists going the other way — first rollout of the new feed has three independent activation paths in the same shape. If the nonproduction replay only tested one direction, the assertion needs to cover both, or you're testing half the picture.

Want me to draft the assertion language for the runbook itself, or a Slack note back to Daniela with this framing?

SUMMARY
The non-atomic rollback is NOT itself a release blocker. Three independent restore paths are a feature of intentional surface boundaries, not a defect. The blocker is shipping without rehearsal-proven bounded reconciliation on the surfaced-state subset, named authority, and operator visibility during the window — same package that gates any release, applied specifically to the rollback direction. Same coordination gap exists in forward rollout (new-feed activation). Rehearsal must prove both directions, not one.

WHY
- Atomic rollback across the three channels isn't architecturally available without collapsing intentional surface boundaries (Helio Start reporting vs Expansion Assist selection vs lifecycle preflight are independent for good reason — different owners, different cadences, different blast radius).
- "All consumers return to the same authority at the same time" overreaches on shared-state claims (per cross-surface exec-lang memory). The right assertion is bounded reconciliation on the surfaced-state subset, with named intentional boundaries where divergence is correct.
- The gap is symmetric: rollback has it (kill switch → three independent restores), forward rollout has it (new feed → three independent activations). Rehearsing only one direction tests half the picture.

CUTS — surfaced-state subset for bounded reconciliation
IN (must reconcile within the bounded window):
  - Helio Start reporting on admitted / assisted / ineligible / final-reconciliation states (activation-driving slice)
  - Lifecycle preflight on non-`routine education` lanes (send-gating slice)

OUT (intentional divergence — documented, not reconciled):
  - Helio Start `pending` (pre-admission) — intentionally outside rate/activation denom; reading it during rollback is correct state, not a mismatch
  - Expansion Assist selection — descriptive, nonforecast; restore timing doesn't gate activation or downstream sends in this window
  - Lifecycle preflight on `routine education` — Ines's lifecycle-aud-risk lane; rollback timing governed by the lifecycle runbook, not the Helio rollback assertion

EFFECT — coordinated rollback behavior the next rehearsal must prove
1. Bounded reconciliation window on the IN subset, measured in minutes tied to the longest restore channel for that subset. X bound to observed restore latency from the rehearsal, not assumed.
2. Kill-switch order: stop new shared-state transport first, then trigger the three restores in parallel with per-channel timestamps captured. Sequencing the restores just widens the window for no benefit.
3. Within the bounded window: surfaced-state paths reconcile on the IN subset. Any divergence is a real mismatch, classified and remediated before the window closes.
4. Outside the window OR on the OUT subset: divergence is correct behavior, not a rollback trigger.
5. Symmetric: same coordinated behavior proven for forward rollout (new-feed activation across the same three paths).
6. Per-channel completion criteria, not vibes:
   - Reporting deploy: selector restored, no records showing new-feed values
   - Monthly-selection job: selection restored (EA excluded from bounded reconciliation; restore observed for record)
   - Customer.io config: preflight restored on non-routine-education lanes
7. Stale-fail-closed throughout: no record inherits prior eligibility post-rollback, even mid-window.

CALL — rehearsal evidence the next rehearsal must produce
Artifact, not verbal:

A. Per-channel rollback replay snapshot
  - Each of the three restore channels: trigger time, completion time, observed selector / selection / preflight state
  - Max divergence window observed on the IN subset (start, end, duration)
  - Per-record data: which consumer read what during the window, classified matched / divergent / OUT-subset-intentional

B. Pre-fix vs post-rollback diff on a fresh dataset
  - At least one example per consumer of mismatch the rollback resolved
  - At least one example per OUT lane where divergence is correct post-rollback (pending reads correctly; EA selection doesn't drive activation; routine education held in its own restore timing)

C. Stale-fail-closed proof
  - Hold list: every record that intentionally remained held, with reason
  - Confirmation: no record inherited prior eligibility post-rollback, even mid-window

D. Forward-direction proof (symmetric)
  - Same artifact shape for new-feed rollout: three activation paths, per-channel timestamps, IN-subset reconciliation, OUT-subset intentional divergence
  - If rehearsal only covers rollback direction, it's testing half the picture

E. Per-consumer sign-off
  - Three consumer owners (Helio Start reporting, Expansion Assist, lifecycle preflight) confirm consumed values from the rehearsal artifact, not just the operator's run summary

F. Rollback authority + triggers + revert SLA
  - Named authority: Riley or named delegate, per audit-role boundary (cross-surface + lifecycle + judgment-esc lands here)
  - Triggers: any IN-subset divergence past the bounded window; any record displaying Central date earlier than its UTC source timestamp (the Feb 18 timestamp-display failure mode); any record inheriting prior eligibility; freshness outcome flipping held → released without an intake event
  - Revert path: revert the transformation, not the data, with SLA in minutes
  - Last-known-good replay snapshot retained and re-runnable on the same dataset version

G. Operator visibility proof
  - Divergence alert fires correctly on a planted IN-subset divergence during rehearsal (not just a daily report)
  - Per-run held vs released counts available, with alert on drift
  - On-call aware of the change before it ships, not after the first page

WHAT THIS IS NOT
  - Not a release. No production change ships on the back of a clean rehearsal alone.
  - Not "atomic rollback." That goal overreaches; the assertion is bounded reconciliation on the IN subset.
  - Not Daniela's draft as written. "All at the same time" framing has to be replaced with bounded reconciliation + named boundaries.
  - Not a one-directional proof. Forward rollout has the same coordination gap.

THREE PLAIN QUESTIONS
1. Daniela — bounded reconciliation on the IN subset with named boundaries (recommended), or stay with "all at the same time" and accept the overreach?
2. Owen — what's the bounded window X observed in the clean nonproduction replay? The next rehearsal needs to reproduce it on a fresh dataset, not just confirm it once.
3. Ines — confirm the routine education lane carve-out: her rollback timing for `routine education` is governed by the lifecycle runbook, not asserted by the Helio rollback. If that's wrong, the IN subset shifts.

Next step on my end, if you want it: draft the runbook assertion language itself (replacing Daniela's "all at the same time" with the bounded-reconciliation framing + IN/OUT cuts), or send a Slack note to Daniela with this spec for her to redraft against. Your call.

Short answer: everything in there is safe to keep and refreeze. The thermometer reading is what matters here, and 24°F (-4°C) is well below the 40°F safety line.

Per-item
- Sealed chicken portions with ice crystals — safe to refreeze. Quality may drop slightly (some texture change once thawed), but safety is fine.
- Frozen vegetables (sealed) — safe to refreeze. Veggies handle this well.
- Bread — safe, no real change.
- Ice cream soft at the edges — expected; texture loss only, not a safety issue. Rehardening won't fully restore the original texture.
- No leaking package, no cross-contact — that rules out the one thing that would have made this a real problem (raw juices on ready-to-eat food).

What to do now
1. Make sure the door is fully shut and latched this time. A slightly-ajar door for 3 hours usually means a gasket issue, a recent bump, or something on a shelf leaning against it.
2. Give it a few hours, then recheck the thermometer. It should drop back to 0°F or below. If it stalls above 10°F, the door isn't sealing or the freezer is struggling — worth investigating before you load it back up with $100 of groceries.
3. Once the freezer is back down to temp, refreeze the items. Use the chicken first once it's thawed later.

One small note for next time: a 3-hour door-ajar event at 24°F is a normal household incident, not a recall. The reason food is still safe is the freezer was doing its job the whole time. The 40°F / ice-crystal rule is the real test, and you cleared it.

Situation as of 2025-02-22 17:30 CST: freezer door was ajar for ~3 hours and is now closed. Treat this as a likely partial-thaw event. Below is a conservative framework (no smell/taste required), a category-by-category call, and the restore/monitor plan.

================================================================
1. THE DECISION RULE (objective, no senses needed)
================================================================

The only thing that matters is whether any given item crossed 40°F (4°C) for more than 2 cumulative hours. You don't actually know that for sure because you almost certainly didn't have a probe in the freezer during the event. So the conservative move is:

  - If you CAN verify it stayed at/below 40°F → refreeze.
  - If you CAN'T verify it → assume it crossed, and use the table below.

The 3-hour open-door event is meaningfully worse than a 3-hour power outage with the door shut, because warm room air was actively washing the interior the whole time. The door gasket and ice mass buy you some buffer, but not much once the door is cracked.

What you have to work with (objective signals, no smell/taste):

  - Instant-read thermometer probe (the single most useful tool).
  - Visual ice crystals inside the package.
  - Firmness of the item — still rock hard = still frozen; pliable but cold = thawed-but-cold; soft and warm = fully thawed and warmed.
  - Freezer interior: is there still visible frost on walls/coils? (Some frost left = interior stayed near or below freezing longer.)
  - Package condition — swollen/bloated bags or rigid vacuum-packs = gas from bacterial growth = discard regardless.
  - Discoloration, separation of liquids from solids that shouldn't separate, purge liquid that looks milky or stringy.

================================================================
2. FOOD-BY-FOOD CALL (conservative)
================================================================

KEEP AND REFREEZE (only if ice crystals still visible OR probe reads ≤40°F):

  - Raw beef, pork, lamb — steaks, roasts, chops, ground. Thawed-but-cold is fine to cook; refreezing ground beef is acceptable but quality loss is real.
  - Raw poultry — whole or parts. Same rule.
  - Raw fish/shellfish — IF still icy/cold. If fully thawed and warmed, cook immediately, don't refreeze (quality tanks, and shellfish is the most temperature-sensitive thing in the freezer).
  - Hard vegetables — corn, peas, beans, broccoli, spinach (blanched). Refreeze with quality loss.
  - Fruits — berries, chopped fruit, juice concentrates. Refreeze; texture suffers but safe.
  - Bread, rolls, baked goods, tortillas.
  - Butter, hard cheese (block parmesan, cheddar — not fresh cheeses).

COOK NOW, DO NOT REFREEZE (still safe to eat, just don't refreeze raw):

  - Any raw meat/poultry/fish that is fully thawed but still cold to touch. Cook to safe internal temp, then refrigerate and eat within 3-4 days, OR refreeze the cooked dish.
  - Thawed vegetables intended for a specific dish — cook into something.

DISCARD (conservative — don't try to rescue):

  - Ice cream, frozen yogurt, sorbet, gelato — dairy + sugar + often eggs; melts into a perfect bacterial medium; texture is unrecoverable anyway. If it's fully soft/liquid, it's gone. Even partial melt + refreeze produces an icy grainy mess that masks any safety question.
  - Frozen prepared meals with dairy, cream, cheese, custard, or egg sauces (lasagna with béchamel, mac-and-cheese, pot pies with cream fillings, frozen quiche, cheesecake). These are the highest-risk items in any freezer.
  - Frozen prepared seafood — crab cakes, shrimp dishes, fish in sauce. Seafood + dairy/egg binder + pre-cooked = highest discard priority.
  - Fresh/soft cheeses — ricotta, cream cheese, mascarpone, brie, burrata (if you had any frozen, which is unusual but possible).
  - Anything with visible ice crystals thawed AND a bloated/swollen package or off-color purge.
  - Anything you're not sure about. The cost of replacing is lower than the cost of a foodborne illness.

EDGE CASES:

  - Ice cubes / trays: dump and refreeze. If the tray water sat warm for hours, just dump it.
  - Gel packs: fine to refreeze.
  - Vacuum-sealed items still rigid and cold: refreeze.

================================================================
3. IMMEDIATE RESTORE STEPS
================================================================

  1. Take inventory FIRST, before you open and close the freezer repeatedly. One pass: pull everything out onto towels or into coolers, sort into Keep / Cook-now / Discard piles. Decide before putting anything back.
  2. Throw out the Discard pile. Don't ask the freezer to recover around spoiling food — it slows recovery and contaminates the chamber.
  3. Wipe down interior walls and shelves with hot water + a small amount of baking soda or diluted bleach (1 tbsp per gallon). Dry.
  4. If anything leaked (especially meat juices or dairy), clean that shelf/area thoroughly before restocking.
  5. Restock the freezer. Don't overpack — air needs to circulate to recover fast.
  6. Close the door. Leave it shut. Do not open for at least 4-6 hours while it recovers.

================================================================
4. MONITORING (no smell/taste needed)
================================================================

GET THESE NOW if you don't have them:

  - An appliance thermometer — small, cheap, sits in the freezer permanently. Place it where you can see it when you open the door. Target reading: 0°F (-18°C) or below.
  - OR a wireless/remote thermometer probe (Bluetooth or WiFi) that alerts your phone. Worth it if this kind of event is even slightly likely to repeat.

TIMELINE:

  - 1 hour after closing: freezer will likely still read above 0°F. That's expected.
  - 4-6 hours: should be approaching 0°F if the door has stayed shut and the unit is healthy.
  - 24 hours: should be solidly at 0°F or below. If not, the unit has a problem (compressor, refrigerant, door seal) — call service.
  - 48 hours: steady-state. Probe individual suspect items that you kept — anything still showing internal temp >0°F after 48 hours is a sign it never fully refroze; cook it soon.

GOING-FORWARD CHECKS:

  - Glance at the appliance thermometer every time you open the freezer. Takes one second.
  - Once a month: pull the thermometer, verify it against an ice-water bath (should read 32°F in a slurry of ice + water). Cheap thermometers drift.

5. WHY DID THIS HAPPEN (worth one minute)

A door ajar for 3 hours is not a normal event. Likely causes:

  - Gasket failure — do the dollar-bill test: close the door on a bill, try to pull it out. Should resist. If it slides freely, the seal has failed in that spot. Inspect gasket for cracks, debris, or warping.
  - Door not latching — the strike/latch may be misaligned. A quarter-inch misalignment can hold the door a crack open. Close slowly and watch whether the latch fully seats.
  - Recently added or shifted contents pushing the door open — common after grocery runs.
  - Something wedged against the door (kid, pet, bag).

Pick whichever fits and fix it before restocking, or this happens again.

TL;DR
================================================================

Assume interior went above 40°F during the 3-hour interval. Refreeze only what still has visible ice crystals or what an instant-read probe confirms is ≤40°F. Discard ice cream, dairy/egg-based prepared foods, prepared seafood, and soft cheeses outright. Sort into Keep / Cook-now / Discard piles in one pass, clean the interior, restock loosely, leave the door shut 4-6 hours, and verify 0°F within 24 hours using a permanent appliance thermometer. SUMMARY

Do not ship as written. The proposed headline and body together re-open the pricing page as a self-serve Start entry point and erase the assisted-routing explanation that the bounded launch was built on. The draft is closer to the 2024-03-05 overclaim than the 2024-03-07 fix. Replace with copy that keeps the access-review requirement visible, names a real eligibility shape (not a blanket sub-50), keeps the assisted paths for migration / import / permissions / SSO, and keeps the non-self-serve CTA. I have a replacement below. Pricing-page exposure of Helio Start is still gated — that gate is unchanged by this draft and is not in scope to relax here.

WHY THIS DRAFT IS WRONG

  1. "Start Helio instantly — no review required" is a launch announcement, not pricing copy. The current gate is first-paid + day-90, with `pending` (pre-admission, not in the rate/activation denom) and `assisted` as real states in the state model. "No review required" contradicts both. The headline alone is enough to scrap the draft.

  2. "Every team under 50 seats can create a workspace and connect data in minutes" is the same overclaim the 2024-03-05 draft made and that we cut. Blanket sub-50 invites the path we don't support unattended and reads to out-of-segment prospects as in-scope. The bounded launch uses a real eligibility shape (e.g., "5 to 50 people running one sales motion") plus admin access, supported billing, and a first integration that can be connected in week one — not seat count alone.

  3. "If you can sign in, you're ready" removes the assisted-routing block. This is the second thing the 2024-03-05 draft got wrong. Migration, import, SSO/permissions, and multi-pipeline setups are staff-led, not self-serve. The pricing page has to keep telling those teams to come in via the assisted path, not sell them the self-serve one.

  4. Removing the assisted-review explanation makes the page worse for the customers it actually serves. The whole point of the 2024-03-07 fix was that help reads as a feature, not a workaround. Erasing it pushes the team that needs help into the wrong surface and creates the "product defect" read we explicitly wrote against.

Walk the bike the six blocks to the parallel neighborhood street.

WHY (briefly)

The only thing that changes between now and the evening ride home is whether the trench is still open. Three quick checks, in order of effort:

1. On your way in, walk past the barricade and look for a project / permit notice. Active utility trenches almost always post a permit number, contractor name, and an "anticipated reopen" date or ETA. Photograph it — that one image answers the question for the rest of the week.
2. If the sign is missing or vague, pull up your city's active road-closures or active-construction map on your phone (most have a 311-equivalent page or app). Search the street name; status updates usually lag the sign by a day at most.

RULING: HOLD — do not send as-is.

Why (top issues):
1. Subject "Your connection failed" misframes pending as a terminal failure. Helio Start pending is forward-only pre-admission, not "failed." Also charged language runs against the standing-lane neutral-tone cap (≤3 neutral/wk).
2. CTA is generic ("Reconnect it now"). Body never names the specific artifact or step that's pending. A pending-state nudge should point to the missing step, not gesture at a vague "connection."
3. "We couldn't verify your integration" — "verify" and "integration" are ambiguous to the user. A pending user likely doesn't know what's being verified, which raises support load.
4. Payoff line "your workspace will be ready" is OK as forward-state language, but only earns its keep if the body establishes which step unlocks it. Right now the body doesn't.

Cuts I'd ask for:
- Subject → forward-pointing, not failure-framed. Candidates:
    - "One step left to start Helio"
    - "Finish setting up Helio Start"
    - "Your Helio setup is almost ready"
- "We couldn't verify your integration" → name the actual pending artifact (whatever step is unresolved — need Ines to specify)
- "Reconnect it now to continue setup" → replace with the specific action verb + step. Generic "reconnect" reads like a placeholder.
- Tie payoff line to that step: "Once [step] is complete, your workspace will be ready."

Two open questions before a clean redraft:
- What is the pending user actually being asked to do? (the email needs to name it)
- Does pending resolve only by user action, or can it also resolve forward to ineligible on its own (per stale-fails-closed)? If the latter, the copy should not imply the user can self-resolve at any pace.

p/effect:
- Send as-is → confused/alarmed users, possible support spike, risk of users re-running something they shouldn't (if pending isn't strictly user-resolvable).
- Revised → neutral standing-lane nudge, names the missing step, forward-only framing intact.

Call: hold release. Ask Ines to (a) replace subject, (b) name the pending step in body, (c) tie CTA + payoff to that step. Once the pending step is named, the copy can be specific. Right now it reads like a template dressed as final.

    Album index: "Marcus and Keiko, Barton Springs, summer 1962"
        Grandma's handwriting, creation date unknown.
    Back of photo: "Barton — 61?"
        Faint pencil, explicit question mark.

How I'd read each:

    The pencil note reads as a working/tentative mark. The "?" is doing work —
    whoever wrote it was guessing the year, not stating it. "Barton" without
    "Springs" reads as shorthand from someone who already knew the location,
    which points to Grandma (or another family member sorting later) rather than
    Marcus or Keiko themselves.

    The album index entry reads as a finalized record: people + place + season
    + year, all four slots filled cleanly with no hedging. That structure
    suggests it was written with more context than the back-of-photo note —
    likely after the dating question had been resolved (one way or the other)
    to 1962.

Plausible reconciliation (most likely):

    Grandma wrote "61?" on the back as a first pass, then later confirmed the
    year against other photos or family context and committed to "1962" in
    the index. The index supersedes.

Plausible alternative (cannot rule out):

    Both notes are Grandma's, both are uncertain, and the index is off by a
    year because she never resolved the ambiguity. The "?" was honest.

What would actually settle it:

    - Other photos from the same trip/summer. A sequence is the strongest
      date evidence and usually settles "61 vs 62" cleanly.
    - Drugstore/Kodak date stamps on the print edge. Common on 1960s
      drugstore prints, faint but usually legible against a backlight.
    - Keiko's or Marcus's letters/diaries from that period.
    - The pencil note's handwriting vs Grandma's later writing — if it's
      not Grandma's, that changes who we trust.

My current read: album index is probably authoritative over the back-of-photo
note, but I would not assert "1962" without flagging the "61?" tension in the
record. Silently picking one over the other is a small but real integrity loss
on a primary-source document.

  - If Mom also files a state return that hasn't been filed yet, use $12.01 (the bank-issued 1099 is the authoritative figure, not the dashboard total). The dashboard figure is preliminary and the bank 1099 trumps it.

Here's how to think about a $12.01 Form 1099-INT and what reconciliation actually requires. A 17-cent difference does not automatically mean a refile or amendment — the right answer depends on a few factual checks first.

RETAIN
- Keep the 1099-INT itself (paper or PDF) with Mom's 2024 tax records.
- Keep the supporting statements that explain it: December and early-January bank or brokerage statements, any year-end tax-form summary, and any earlier version of the 1099-INT from the same payer (in case the $12.01 is a corrected form).
- Standard retention is at least 3 years from the later of the filing date or the due date. Conservatively, 7 years covers almost every individual scenario.
- If the "CORRECTED" box is checked, that form supersedes any earlier one. Keep both — the corrected form is the controlling figure going forward.

RECONCILE
The 1099-INT is the payer's statement of what they reported to the IRS. Mom's return should match it unless she has a documented reason it shouldn't. Reconciliation is just the comparison:
- Payer-reported Box 1 vs. Mom's own year-end records.
- Payer-reported amount vs. any prior version of the form from the same payer.
- The other boxes vs. what she expects — Box 3 (U.S. Savings Bond interest), Box 4 (federal income tax withheld), Box 8 (tax-exempt interest), Box 13 (bond premium).

VERIFY BEFORE ANY FILING DECISION
1. Is it the original or a corrected form? "CORRECTED" checked = the new number controls; the original is dead.
2. Which box is the $12.01 in? Box 1 (ordinary interest) is the most common and simplest. A 17-cent discrepancy in Box 3, Box 8, or any other box has different reporting implications even when the dollar amount is tiny.
3. What do Mom's own records show? Interest frequently accrues through Dec 31 but posts in early January — the year-end statement may not capture that.
4. Is Box 4 (federal income tax withheld) populated? If yes, she claims that as a payment credit on Form 1040 regardless of the gross interest amount. The 17-cent gross-interest difference is irrelevant to the credit.
5. Whose name/SSN is on the form? Joint accounts, trust accounts, UTMA, inherited IRAs — these affect who actually reports the income.
6. Has she already filed? If she filed using $12.01 and the 1099 also says $12.01, there is no issue.

SHOULD SHE AMEND
- Ordinary Box 1 interest, 17-cent delta: do not amend. The IRS does not assess tax on differences this small, and the cost of amending outweighs any benefit. This is the specific trap the question is pointing at.
- If she has not yet filed, file using the 1099-INT amount. Matching the payer is what avoids a CP2000 notice.
- If she filed using her own record ($11.84) and the 1099 says $12.01, the IRS may or may not match. Even if a CP2000 arrives, respond with the 1099 attached and the notice will close at zero additional tax — the IRS tolerance absorbs sub-dollar discrepancies.
- The one scenario where amendment actually matters: the form is a CORRECTED 1099-INT and she already filed using the original (different) number. Amend so her return matches the corrected figure, even at 17 cents — the alignment, not the refund, is the point.

WHEN TO INVOLVE A PROFESSIONAL
- The form is corrected and Mom disagrees with the corrected number.
- It's a Box 3 Savings Bond with a discount or complex acquisition history.
- There is an estate, trust, or inherited-account wrinkle behind the form.
- Box 4 withholding is non-zero and she wants to confirm the credit is claimed correctly.

BOTTOM LINE
Retain the form and supporting statements per the standard 3–7 year window. Reconcile by comparing the 1099-INT to Mom's own records, confirming it is not a corrected form, and checking the relevant boxes. For a $12.01 / 17-cent gap on ordinary interest, the right move is almost always: file using the 1099-INT amount, do not amend a previously filed return, and respond to any IRS notice with the 1099 attached. Don't reflexively amend for small dollar items.

There's no DMV/vin/plate record in this environment, so I can't pull your specific jurisdiction's accepted-docs list — but the safest-ordering question is answerable from general procedural logic. Here it is, with the variables you need to apply locally.

Safest order: address correction FIRST, then renewal.

Why this order:
- The renewal triggers a mailing (new card, sticker, or both) to the address of record. If the old address is still on file when the renewal posts, the new credential is mailed to the wrong place and you have a real recovery problem on top of the original error.
- An address change, by contrast, is usually an in-file update with its own confirmation receipt — no outbound mail you have to chase. Doing it first means the renewal that follows lands at the correct address.

Which proof to use:
Pick the single strongest document you have that shows (a) your full name and (b) the new address, dated within whatever window your DMV accepts (commonly 30 or 60 days). In rough order of acceptance strength:
1. A recent utility bill (gas, electric, water) in your name at the new service address — usually the cleanest single doc because it ties name + address + recent date.
2. A bank or credit-card statement showing the new address — widely accepted as a fallback when the utility isn't in your name (e.g., landlord's account).
3. An insurance declaration page (homeowners or renters) showing the property address.
4. Lease or mortgage statement.

If your jurisdiction requires two proofs, pair the utility bill with a bank statement — that's the most universally accepted combo. Avoid using the registration card itself as proof (it's the document being updated) and avoid any document that only shows a PO box.

What confirmation to retain:
- Address change: the transaction/confirmation number, the date, and a screenshot or PDF of the confirmation screen. If done in person, the clerk-stamped receipt. This is the artifact that proves the address was correct on file BEFORE the renewal was triggered — important if the renewal card ever gets lost in the mail.
- Renewal: the renewal receipt or confirmation page with its own confirmation number, the date processed, and the new card/sticker once received. Keep the mailing tracking number if one is issued.
- Keep the OLD registration card (and the old address-change receipt) until the new card physically arrives and you've verified the address printed on it. Only retire the old card once the new one is in hand.

Two flags worth checking against your actual paperwork before you act:
- Some jurisdictions won't process an address change and a renewal in the same transaction even if you go in person — in that case the order above is also the only available order, so you're covered.
- If the renewal deadline is imminent and the address change involves a mailed credential you might not get back in time, check whether your jurisdiction lets you do the renewal online or at a kiosk with the new address already on file from the same-day update — that avoids a mail round-trip.

  Session structure
    Warm-up walk ~5 min
    Cycle 1: 4:00 easy run  →  2:00 walk
    Cycle 2: 4:00 easy run  →  2:00 walk
    Cycle 3: 4:00 easy run  →  2:00 walk
    Walk cool-down ~5–10 min to fill the 40-min slot
    Pace stays conversational. No strides, no hills.

  Work-period math
    3 cycles × (4:00 + 2:00) = 18 min active work period
      12 min running  +  6 min walking breaks
    Prior pattern at 4 cycles × (3:00 + 2:00) = 20 min active
      12 min running  +  8 min walking breaks

  Why this fits the progression

    1. Single-variable advance. Only the run bout lengthens
       (3:00 → 4:00). Walk break stays at 2:00. Cycle count drops
       (4 → 3) to compensate so total running time stays flat at
       ~12 min. This is the cleanest possible test of whether a
       LONGER bout is tolerated, without adding total load.

    2. Matches "+dur OR +freq, not both" in spirit. You are
       reshaping how the running is distributed, not adding volume.
       Frequency stays 2/wk, total running minutes flat at ~12,
       no new surface, no third session.

    3. Continuous running remains deferred. Walk breaks still
       appear every 4 min. Linking two run bouts (4:00 → 4:30 →
       5:00...) or shortening the walk break is the NEXT gate —
       not this step. Don't conflate "longer bout" with
       "continuous running"; they're different.

    4. Active work period stays in the prior range. 18 min is
       close to the prior 20 min and well within the 20–25 min
       band from the earlier template. Not a step backward in
       conditioning, just a redistribution.

    5. Ankle-and-calf strengthening continues unchanged on
       non-run-walk days — it has to keep pace with the
       lengthened bouts, but you are not adding new exercises.

    6. The step is earned. Four prior sessions and four following
       days all symptom-free is a stable base for a small change.

    Escalate earlier (call PT) if: pain at rest, walking →

5. Do not pay. Wait for explicit acceptance of the proof of residency — usually a status change on the renewal page or a portal/email message. If there is no clear acceptance signal, treat the proof as not yet accepted. Fulfillment is not verification.
6. After acceptance, re-screenshot the renewal detail page. Read the address field. If the portal accepted the utility statement but did not update the displayed address to the corrected one, stop. Escalate before paying — the system read the document but not the address on it.

- Portal accepted the statement but the displayed address did not update to the corrected one.
- Cherrywood address-correction WO is not on track to close before 2025-03-31.

Field-by-field, between:

  (a) The corrected 1099-INT just received (labeled CORRECTED)
  (b) The original 1099-INT she saw on March 1 — if she has no paper copy, pull it from the bank's online document center or request a duplicate from the bank
  (c) The bank's year-end interest statement for the tax year — this is usually the source document for the 1099 and should reconcile to Box 1
  (d) The monthly or quarterly statements for the underlying deposit (savings, CD, money market) — confirms interest actually accrued
  (e) Her accepted Form 1040 — specifically Line 2b (taxable interest) and Schedule B if filed
  (f) Her IRS Wage & Income Transcript for the tax year (pull via her IRS online account or Form 4506-T) — shows what the IRS has on file from this payer right now
  (g) The guided-filing provider's intake record / payment summary explaining why the 1099 was omitted in the first place
  (h) The envelope or email showing the date she received the corrected form — proof of receipt date matters for any reasonable-cause argument
  (i) The bank's written explanation of what was actually corrected — when Box 1 is unchanged, the correction is almost always a non-amount field (TIN, address, payer EIN, account number, or a re-file after an IRS rejection)

Compare on every field, not just Box 1: payer EIN, payer address, recipient TIN (Mom's SSN), recipient address, account number(s), tax year, Box 1, Box 2 (early withdrawal penalty), Box 3 (US savings bond interest), and any state or backup-withholding boxes.

Keep all nine items in one folder. The corrected form, the original, the bank statements, and the IRS transcript are the four that matter most if she ever has to substantiate the position to the IRS.

WHY THIS COMPARISON ACTUALLY MATTERS

The CORRECTED label is a filing instruction to the IRS, not a description of what changed. Banks reissue corrected 1099s even when Box 1 is identical to the original, because something other than the dollar amount had to be corrected, or because the IRS rejected the original filing and required a re-file. The IRS treats the corrected form as authoritative either way. Because Mom's return reported $0 from this payer and the IRS now has $12.01 on file under her SSN, there is a reporting mismatch that the Automated Underreporter (CP2000) process is built to detect. The fact that the number "matches what she saw on March 1" does not, by itself, resolve the mismatch — it just means the dollar effect of resolving it is small.

Verbatim, before deciding on Form 1040-X:

"Based on the corrected Form 1099-INT I just received showing $12.01 in Box 1 — which matches the $12.01 I would have reported had the form been available when I filed — please tell me, in dollars: (1) the exact change to my federal taxable interest, (2) the exact change to my AGI, (3) the exact change to my federal income tax, (4) any underpayment interest that would accrue, and (5) any failure-to-pay or accuracy-related penalty that would apply if I file Form 1040-X to add this 1099-INT; and (6) confirm whether your platform will prepare that amendment if I elect to file it."
