A cautious sequence for sealed wood, escalating only as needed. The "shadow" suggests most pigment already lifted; further effort risks the finish more than the stain.

BEFORE ANYTHING
  Find an inconspicuous spot (under a furniture leg, back edge) and test each
  agent there first. Different sealants (polyurethane, lacquer, shellac,
  conversion varnish) react differently to water, alcohol, and abrasives.
  Give the test spot 2-3 minutes to show any softening, dulling, or whitening
  before proceeding on the visible stain.

STEP 1 — Re-blot with clean water + soft microfiber
  Damp (not dripping) cloth, gentle pressure, dry immediately with a second
  cloth. Many "remaining shadows" are loose pigment that wasn't fully lifted
  the first time. This is the safest possible step.

STEP 2 — Mild dish soap
  One drop clear dish soap in a small bowl of water. Soft microfiber, gentle
  circular motion, immediate dry. Most pigment residue that survived plain
  water comes up here.

STEP 3 — Isopropyl alcohol (70%) on a cotton swab
  Only if 1 and 2 did nothing. Alcohol dissolves some pigment binders and
  can lift stain particles without attacking cured polyurethane or lacquer.
  Dab, do not rub. Brief contact — 5-10 seconds. Dry immediately.
  Skip this step if your test spot showed any dulling or softening.

STEP 4 — Melamine sponge (Magic Eraser), very lightly
  Last resort before calling a refinisher. It IS a micro-abrasive and will
  almost certainly leave a faint dull spot even on cured poly. Use the
  lightest possible pressure, damp (not wet), and stop at the first sign of
  sheen change.

DO NOT USE
  Acetone or nail polish remover (attacks most film finishes).
  Bleach, vinegar in concentration, or any unknown "all purpose cleaner."
  Abrasive powders, Scotch-Brite, steel wool, or scrubbing pads.
  Prolonged soaking of any agent — brief contact, immediate dry.

WHEN TO STOP
  Any color lifting onto your cloth or swab means you're either moving
  pigment into the wood or removing finish. Stop and reassess.
  Any visible change in sheen at the test spot or the stain site — dulling,
  hazing, whitening, or tackiness — means the finish is being affected.
  Stop that agent immediately.
  After 2-3 attempts at a given step with no visible progress, the pigment
  has likely penetrated below the surface. Further effort trades finish
  integrity for marginal cosmetic gain. Stop.
  If the remaining shadow is only visible at certain angles/light, it may
  be permanent and acceptable — true staining pigments (phthalo, ultramarine,
  indigo) are designed to lodge in surfaces and may not fully release without
  refinishing.

If the spot is in a prominent location and the shadow bothers you after
gentle cleaning has done what it can, a furniture refinisher can sometimes
feather the area or spot-restore the sheen without redoing the whole piece.
That's a better next step than escalating to harsher solvents.

PROCEDURE — Sidecar reconstruction & audit log
(for working docs / handoff / preflight)

Principle (1 line)
  Reconstruct = derive from captured evidence. Missing is a valid state.
  Fulfillment != verification: building the sidecar is not validating it.
  No field is backfilled from plausibility, neighbor rows, prior state,
  dashboards, or operator memory.

1. Sidecar file convention
   - One sidecar per source artifact (event, snapshot, row, file).
   - Naming: <source-id>__<source-ts-utc>__<reason>.<ext>
     e.g. evt_8814__2025-03-22T15-03-11Z__recon.json
   - Layout — three required sections:
       a) header    : sidecar_id, source_id, source_ts, operator,
                      tool+version, build_ts
       b) evidence  : list of {field, source, locator, retrieved_at, value,
                                note?}
                      one row per field actually captured
       c) derived   : the assembled record, fields in declared order,
                      value OR MISSING[<reason-code>]
   - Source artifact is read-only. Never overwrite or "fix in place."

2. MISSING reason codes (closed set)
   NOT_PRESENT       field absent in source
   REDACTED          removed by source/system
   OBFUSCATED        present but encoded, key not held
   TRUNCATED         cut off at boundary
   UNREADABLE        binary parse failed
   OFFLINE           source unreachable at retrieval
   AUTH_DENIED       credential not authorized for this scope
   LAG               export delayed; refresh forward-only, do not impute
   DROPPED           consumer-side loss (pipeline dropped the row)
   CONFLICT          sources disagree; both recorded, none picked
   NEIGHBOR_INFERENCE_REJECTED   cardinal sin — recorded for traceability
                                  so reviewers see the temptation was noted

3. Field-level provenance rules
   - A value is admissible iff it appears in evidence[] OR is a deterministic
     derivation from admissible fields. Formula + every input cited.
   - Type coercions are derived. Mark "derived: cast int->str" in evidence.
   - Timestamps carry source-tz AND utc. If only one survives, MISSING the
     other with reason LOST_IN_TRANSIT (or similar specific).
   - Identifiers copied verbatim. No case-fold, trim, or unicode-normalize.
     If a join key demands normalization, store both raw and normalized,
     label clearly.

4. Audit log
   - Append-only ledger. Entry:
        {ts, actor, action, target, sidecar_id?, evidence_hash, notes}
   - action vocabulary (closed set):
        OPEN, READ_SOURCE, READ_FAIL, RECONSTRUCT, DERIVE,
        MARK_MISSING, VERIFY, VERIFY_FAIL, CLOSE, REOPEN,
        ESCALATE, AMEND
   - AMEND is the only mutating verb; it cites a prior entry id + reason.
     Amendments supersede; they do not erase history.
   - Hash chain: hash(entry) = sha256(prev_hash || entry_payload).
     Walk on read; any link break fails loudly.
   - No silent entries. Writes blocked if evidence_hash is absent.

5. Reconstruction workflow
   1 OPEN          skeleton + first audit entry
   2 EVIDENCE      read source, populate evidence[]; failures -> READ_FAIL
   3 DERIVATION    for computed fields -> DERIVE entries (formula+inputs)
   4 MISSING       every non-evidenced, non-derivable field -> MARK_MISSING
   5 ASSEMBLE      derived view; each cell is (a) evidence pointer,
                                                (b) DERIVE result, or
                                                (c) MISSING[<code>]
   6 VERIFY        independent replay of evidence+DERIVE -> diff vs assembled;
                   discrepancies -> VERIFY_FAIL -> REOPEN, never silent AMEND
   7 CLOSE         only after VERIFY passes; closed sidecars are read-only

6. Temptations to refuse (worked examples)
   - "Looks like a typo"           -> keep ORIGINAL_TEXT; add DERIVE proposing
                                       a cleaned form alongside. Do not replace.
   - "Probably 10:15:03"           -> MISSING NO_SOURCE_TS. DERIVE only if a
                                       deterministic rule (bucket boundary)
                                       is cited and label DERIVED_NOT_OBSERVED.
   - "Other rows had X"            -> MISSING NEIGHBOR_INFERENCE_REJECTED.
   - "Dashboard shows it"          -> out of scope; dashboards are not sources.
   - "We had it last week"         -> LAG / forward-only recovery, do not restore
                                       pre-lag values (see lag ruling).

7. Conflicts and lag
   - Two sources disagree: record both, mark CONFLICT, escalate. Resolution
     requires AMEND with named rule + actor.
   - Delayed/incomplete export: MISSING LAG. Re-VERIFY on refresh; do not
     re-eliminate pre-lag refusals.

8. Edge cases worth pre-deciding
   - Screenshot/PDF: OCR text is DERIVED; store artifact pointer + confidence.
   - Human-spoken: transcript is source of record; audio is a pointer.
   - Batched with overlap: identical field+value -> one row;
                           identical field, different value -> CONFLICT.

9. Release checklist (a sidecar is releasable iff all true)
   [ ] Every populated cell traces to evidence[] or a DERIVE entry.
   [ ] No MISSING cell has an unstated reason.
   [ ] Audit log hash-valid end-to-end.
   [ ] VERIFY replay produced a matching derived view.
   [ ] No source artifact modified.
   [ ] No "fix later" cells left UNRESOLVED.
   [ ] All CONFLICTs have an AMEND trail (or are still open with ESCALATE).

Summary: One meal, currently asymptomatic, no need to panic — but you're right that "wait and see" is the wrong frame. The plan below is built around pulling two specifics from the recall notice (contaminant + any ingestion guidance) because they drive the monitoring window. Everything else is general scaffolding that holds up across most recalls.

EXPOSURE (log now, while it's fresh)
  Date/time Kibo ate from the recalled bag: March 22 (done — single meal)
  Amount eaten: estimate in cups or grams if you can; "one meal" is fine if not
  Lot/best-by you switched to: lot number, brand, package size
  Kibo's weight today (kg or lb) — load-bearing for any dose-based risk call the vet does later
  Photo/scan of the recall notice (lot + brand + reason for recall) — saves you digging if you need the vet on day 4
  Other pets or food bowls in the house that could have cross-contacted (probably none, but note it)

MONITORING — this is where the recall notice matters
The contaminant sets the clock. From your notice, identify which class:
  Bacterial (Salmonella, Listeria, E. coli): GI signs — vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy, inappetence. Onset typically 6 hr to 7 days. Watch for blood in stool, dehydration, fever.
  Mycotoxin / aflatoxin: liver. Subtle early signs in 24–72 hr (inappetence, quiet) → jaundice (whites of eyes, gums, inner ears yellowing) can appear out to 1–2 weeks. Aflatoxin is the one where "looks fine on day 3" doesn't mean done.
  Vitamin D toxicity: vomiting, lethargy, increased thirst/urination. Onset hours to ~5 days. Polyuria is the diagnostic tell.
  Pentobarbital / sedative contamination: sedation, ataxia, hypersalivation. Fast onset — usually within hours, often the same meal.
  Foreign object / metal: depends on object. Look for oral injury or GI distress on the next meal.

Do the timeline math: if you're past the typical onset window for the named contaminant with no signs, acute risk drops meaningfully — but not to zero for the slower-onset classes (aflatoxin in particular).

CLEANUP — you're mostly there, three more steps
  Discard the recalled bag in a sealed bag inside a sealed trash bag. Don't compost, don't leave accessible to any other animal.
  Wipe down the storage surface (bin, shelf, pantry floor) where the bag sat. Bacterial recalls in particular contaminate the surface.
  Bowl + scoop + any measuring cup that touched the food: hot soapy wash, then dishwasher sanitize cycle OR dilute bleach (~1 tbsp per gallon, 5 min contact) then rinse well.
  Wash your hands after handling the bag and bowl. Recall bacteria don't care whose hands they're on.

VETERINARY ESCALATION — concrete triggers, not "if concerned"
Call your regular vet (not emergency) within 24 hours if any of:
  Vomiting (especially >2x or any with blood), diarrhea (especially bloody or black/tarry), inappetence past 24 hr, marked lethargy, any visible jaundice
  Persistent increase in thirst or urination beyond normal post-meal noise

Go directly to emergency if:
  Repeated vomiting that won't stop (>3–4x in a few hours, or anything keeping water down)
  Collapse, pale gums, severe weakness
  Any neurological signs: ataxia, tremors, seizures, deep sedation
  Aflatoxin specifically: ANY yellowing, ANY unexplained bruising/bleeding — liver damage moves fast once clinical signs show

When you call, have ready: weight, "one meal from recalled lot L25-0317A on March 22," the contaminant from the notice, current symptoms (none), and the new lot number you're feeding.

CALLS (short list, in order)
  1. Pull contaminant class + ingestion guidance from the recall notice — sets the monitoring window
  2. Weigh Kibo today; record the new lot number
  3. Call your vet now even though Kibo is fine — most clinics will chart it and tell you exactly what they want flagged for that specific recall. Cheap, converts "should I call?" into "they told me what to watch for"
  4. Bag disposal + storage wipe-down today
  5. Keep the recall notice photo in a folder you can find from your phone

Steps to take now:

1. STOP feeding the recalled bag. Pull it out of rotation. Put the rest of the bag (with the lot label L25-0317A and best-by 2026-02-01 visible) into a sealed bag so you have it if a vet asks for the lot info — and so no one (human or animal) accidentally opens it again.

2. Switch to a different food for Kibo going forward. If you don't have an unopened alternate bag, a plain bland option for tonight/next meal is fine: boiled chicken (no skin/bones/seasoning) + plain white rice, ~1:2 ratio, small portions.

3. Salmonella incubation in dogs is typically 6–72 hours, often 12–36 hours. Kibo is at ~8.5 hours post-meal with no symptoms — that's reassuring, NOT a clean bill. Symptoms can still appear through tomorrow (Sun). Keep him where you can watch stool and behavior.

4. Call your vet Monday morning regardless, even if he stays asymptomatic. Mention the lot number and approximate amount eaten. Many clinics will just note it in the chart and tell you to monitor. If Kibo shows any of the listed signs — vomiting, diarrhea (especially bloody/mucousy), fever (warm ears, panting at rest, warm nose is NOT reliable on its own), lethargy, or refusing food — call sooner. With bloody diarrhea, persistent vomiting, or any sign of dehydration (gums tacky, skin tenting), it's ER, not wait-until-Monday.

5. Wash anything that touched the food: the bowl (hot soapy water or dishwasher), the scoop, the counter, your hands. Salmonella is zoonotic — humans handling the recalled food can get sick too. Kids / immunocompromised household members should not handle it.

6. Save the recall notice itself (screenshot or print). If Kibo does get sick, the lot/best-by/upc are what the vet and any reporting pathway need.

- Cohort-edge slips introduced between approval and release — feed-current at approval is not feed-current at release.

KIBO — HOME MONITORING PLAN
Single loose stool, one week post Salmonella-class recall exposure (asymptomatic until now)
As of 2025-03-29

QUICK READ
The baseline you describe is reassuring. Grass chewing commonly causes a single loose stool in dogs, and a one-off episode with full appetite, normal drinking, and normal energy is most often self-limiting. The reason to run a conservative plan is the recall context: Salmonella incubation is typically 6–72 hours (occasionally longer), the organism is zoonotic, and Kibo is kitchen-employed indoors — which makes hygiene the highest-yield piece of this plan.

1. HYDRATION

Keep free access to fresh water; refresh the bowl twice daily. If he drains the bowl fast, offer small amounts every 15–30 minutes rather than a full refill at once, since large boluses can trigger another loose stool. Unflavored Pedialyte is fine as an occasional offering if you suspect mild depletion; if you're planning to use it as the primary fluid, call your regular vet first.

Dehydration checks, twice daily:
- Skin tent: lift scruff between shoulder blades, release. Should snap flat in under 2 seconds. Over 3 seconds is concerning.
- Gums: should be pink and slick. Dry, sticky, tacky, or pale = concerning.
- Capillary refill: press a gum until it whitens, release. Color should return in under 2 seconds.

2. FEEDING (next 24–48 hours)

Continue feeding — he's alert and interested, so fasting isn't indicated for a single loose stool in a well dog.

Bland diet:
- Boiled skinless chicken breast. No bone, no skin, no fat, no salt, no oil, no seasoning.
- Plain white rice (not brown — easier to digest).
- Ratio roughly 1 part chicken to 2–3 parts rice.
- Small frequent meals: 3–4 per day, starting at about 1/4 of his normal portion and ramping up if tolerated.

Avoid for now: treats, table scraps, dairy, fatty foods, bones, new foods, the recalled product line (already disposed, per you), anything that could itself be contaminated.

Return to normal food over 2–3 days once stool is consistently formed:
- Day 1: 75% bland + 25% regular
- Day 2: 50/50
- Day 3: 25% bland + 75% regular
- Day 4: full normal ration

3. HYGIENE (highest priority given Salmonella + kitchen-employed)

Hand hygiene:
- Wash with soap and warm water for at least 20 seconds after touching Kibo's feces, food/water bowls, bedding, muzzle, or anything that contacted the recalled food.
- Wash before preparing human food, before eating, and after using the bathroom.
- Hand sanitizer is acceptable between contacts but not a substitute after feces or food handling.

Feces handling:
- Pick up yard stool promptly; bag and tie, sealed trash. Do not compost.
- Gloves if convenient, but wash hands regardless of glove use.
- Remove stool from the yard daily for at least the next 4–6 weeks even after he's back to normal — Salmonella shedding can persist that long in dogs who clear the clinical signs.

Bowls:
- Wash food and water bowls daily in hot soapy water; rinse well. Dishwasher on a hot cycle is fine if the bowls tolerate it.

Bedding:
- Wash soiled blankets/towels in hot water, regular detergent, high-heat dry. Swap to clean bedding daily while symptoms are present.

Yard and surfaces:
- Disinfect any floor or crate surface Kibo contacts with dilute bleach (about 1 tablespoon per gallon of water) or an accelerated hydrogen peroxide cleaner; rinse and dry.
- Clean any storage container, scoop, lid, or counter that touched the recalled food in the same way.

Recall-related housekeeping:
- Confirm the recalled food is gone from pantry, counters, trash Kibo could reach, vehicle, and any treat-dispensing toys.
- Discard anything that may have been cross-contaminated and that Kibo can access.

Household members:
- Children, elderly, pregnant, or immunocompromised people should minimize direct contact with feces and bedding until Kibo is back to normal and ideally until a vet clears him.
- If any household member develops diarrhea, fever, or stomach cramps in the next 1–2 weeks, they should see a physician and mention a dog with Salmonella-class exposure.

4. MONITORING (log twice daily for 7–14 days)

Per check, capture:
- Stool: number of bowel movements, consistency (formed / soft / loose / watery), color, any mucus or blood (specks vs. streaked vs. mixed).
- Appetite: full / partial / skipped.
- Water intake: normal / increased / decreased.
- Vomiting: none / single / multiple, and what it looked like.
- Energy: normal / mildly quiet / lethargic.
- Gums: pink and moist, or pale / tacky / yellow.
- Abdomen: soft, or tight / distended / painful.
- Temperature if you have a rectal thermometer: normal 101–102.5°F. Lubricate with petroleum jelly, insert about 1 inch, don't force. Skip if he's uncomfortable.
- Any new exposures: grass, plants, trash, other dogs, new treats.

5. THRESHOLDS — CALL YOUR REGULAR VET (within 24 hours, sooner if you're worried)

- More than 2–3 loose or watery stools in 24 hours.
- Loose stool persisting beyond 48 hours on the bland diet.
- Any visible blood in stool (fresh red streaks, drops, or dark/black/tarry).
- Mucus recurring in stool, or a marked color change to black, yellow, green, or grey/pale.
- Decreased appetite for more than 24 hours.
- Mild lethargy or quietness that doesn't resolve within a few hours, or a clear drop from his baseline.
- Any abdominal tenderness, repeated "praying" posture (front down, rear up), or reluctance to be handled around the belly.
- Recurrent vomiting (a single isolated spit-up of grass is not the same).
- Drop in water intake.
- You want a stool sample submitted (Salmonella culture, fecal float, parvovirus test depending on age/vaccines).
- Anything new that you can't explain.

6. THRESHOLDS — URGENT OR EMERGENCY CARE (go now, or call the nearest ER en route)

- Repeated vomiting (3+ times in 24 hours, any vomit with blood, or any vomit that looks like coffee grounds).
- Profuse watery diarrhea or many episodes in a short window.
- Large-volume fresh blood in stool, or melena (black, tarry, foul-smelling).
- Severe dehydration: skin tent stays up over 3 seconds, dry/tacky gums, sunken eyes, weakness, collapse.
- Gums that are pale, white, blue, grey, or yellow (jaundice).
- Temperature over 103.5°F or under 99°F.
- Abdominal distension, guarding, or obvious pain — especially if restless and unable to settle in a deep-chested dog (bloat/GDV risk).
- Collapse, severe weakness, sudden ataxia, tremors, or seizures.
- Refusal to drink for more than 12–24 hours in a dog that was drinking normally.
- Any suspicion of a new toxin, foreign body, or ingestion of another recalled product.
- Any rapid deterioration from his current baseline.

7. RECALL-SPECIFIC NOTE

A single loose stool is more likely to be grass-irritation than Salmonella, given the timing and the absence of other signs. But because the recall organism was on the list and Kibo is kitchen-employed, the heightened hygiene plan above is the part that earns its keep regardless of cause. A negative fecal culture is the only way to confirm he isn't shedding; your regular vet can tell you whether and when that's worth doing.

8. WHAT TO HAVE READY IF YOU CALL

- Timeline: recall date, last exposure date, disposal date, today (3/29/2025), and timing of the loose stool.
- Stool description: color, consistency, mucus, blood, approximate volume.
- Last normal stool: when, what it looked like.
- Appetite and water intake today.
- Energy and behavior today.
- Recent exposures: grass, new treats, new food, other animals, yard items.
- Current medications, supplements, preventives (heartworm, flea/tick, joint, etc.).
- Vaccination status, especially parvovirus.
- His weight, if you have a recent number.

A small disclaimer is fair: this is a structured home-monitoring plan, not a diagnosis. If anything in sections 5 or 6 triggers, the plan is to call or go — don't wait to see if it passes.

One practical thing given today's date: if he has another loose stool in the next 12–24 hours, or any of the regular-vet thresholds trips, having a fresh sample (within 1–2 hours, refrigerated, in a clean bag) ready to drop off can save a trip later.

VALUE-SEP STUDY — design

Hypothesis: the drying-time convergence you saw between the cool window wash and the warmer counter edge is driven by relative pigment value at laydown, not by hue or by timing. Find the value offset that survives drying and the problem is localized.

What you hold constant
  - Paper: one sheet, 140 lb cold press, single orientation, no pre-stretch variance
  - Brush: same round, same size, rinsed and blotted the same way between every pass
  - Pigment load: pre-mix one cool pigment and one warm pigment, each in two measured dilutions (e.g., 1:8 and 1:4 paint:water by volume). Same cup, same dilution, used across every cell
  - Water: same source, same temperature
  - Wash timing: pre-wet each cell with a fixed water volume, tip off; lay cool wash at t=0; lay warm wash at t=15s into the damp side
  - Drying conditions: same room, same air, evaluate at a fixed drying point (~30 min)

What you vary
  - Cool pigment value: light dilution vs dark dilution
  - Warm pigment value: light dilution vs dark dilution
  Two axes, four cells. Nothing else moves.

Layout (quarter sheet, four equal cells; soft pencil midline in each):

  Cell A: cool light  + warm light
  Cell B: cool light  + warm dark
  Cell C: cool dark   + warm light
  Cell D: cool dark   + warm dark

In each cell: pre-wet, tip, lay cool wash on the left half, wait 15s, lay warm wash on the right half with a 2–3 mm overlap into the damp cool side so the edge behaves like a real counter-meeting-window junction.

Run the grid twice in mirrored orientation (or rotate which combo sits in which cell on a second pass) to rule out position-on-paper effects. Cheap insurance.

How to read it
  Score each cell at three points — wet, damp (~5 min), dry (~30 min):
    1. Value separation at the edge  (5 = strong contrast, 1 = flat)
    2. Hue separation at the edge    (cool stays cool, warm stays warm)
    3. Edge softness                 (no hard line, no muddy bloom)
  Plot the wet-vs-dry delta for each cell. If B and C hold and A and D collapse, the lever is relative starting value — not pigment identity, not timing, not paper.

What this isolates
  - The single variable behind the wet/dry flatten: the value offset you laid down. Two dilutions, four pairings, one answer.

What it does not isolate
  - Pigment choice. You tested one cool and one warm. To compare pigments (e.g., Phthalo vs Cerulean, Raw Sienna vs Yellow Ochre), swap and rerun the same grid on a second sheet.
  - Edge technique. Wet-into-damp is held constant. Wet-into-wet vs wet-on-dry is a separate study.
  - Scene geometry. Flat plane, not a real window-meeting-counter angle. The actual light falloff is still missing.

Optional anchor strip
  Reserve a narrow strip along the bottom of the same sheet for one cell using your actual scene pigments at their actual values, painted at the same timing. It ties the grid results back to the original Sunday study so the conclusion transfers, not just lands in the abstract.

Plain question before you start: do you want one cool and one warm pigment throughout (cleaner read, fewer variables), or do you want to compare pigments in the same sheet (more information, more noise)? The design above assumes the first.

Good finding — and a clean comparison given the constants you held. Value separation is structural: the warm edge has a darker neighbor to stop against, so the wash can do its natural work without flattening the read. Added orange is optical, fighting the wash's own tendency to cool on drying — which is why the convergence case went flat. The structural approach works with the medium; the saturation approach tries to override it.

The reason both readings stay live is that "calling it resilience" is the speech act you'd see in either case. The planner's vocabulary doesn't disambiguate because both positions can co-opt the same word. So the disambiguation has to come from somewhere else in the text — and the question is whether you want it to.

A few axes that often do the work:

Who does the labor, and who gets named for the outcome. This is probably the strongest pressure you have. In the adaptation reading, the residents' rerouting *is* the resilience — distributed, embodied, theirs — and the planner is recognizing what's already there. In the avoidance reading, the residents absorb the inconvenience and the planner absorbs the credit; the discourse does the institutional work of not-building while making not-building sound like a feature. Your three scenes are consistent with either reading because they don't yet show what happens when a real alternative is on the table.

Temporality and verb tense. Genuine interim adaptation usually carries "until" language — scoped, bridged, conditional on a real timeline. Settled avoidance drops the conditional: this is how the system now operates. Tracking whether the planner's "resilience" speech has a horizon, or has gone equilibrium, is telling.

What the planner does when a fix is proposed. The diagnostic scene, if you want one. If a real alternative appears and the planner engages with it — even to argue against on cost or feasibility — that's adaptation territory. If a fix arrives and gets recast as unnecessary because the workaround already exists, that's the avoidance tell, and it's usually sharp enough to break the ambiguity for the reader.

If you don't want a diagnostic scene — if the ambiguity is meant to hold all the way through — that's defensible, and arguably the more politically serious move. It puts the reader in the same position as the residents: the planner's discourse has been built to resist resolution, and reproducing that in form is part of the argument. The risk is that readers experience irresolution as authorial indecision rather than as a feature of the discourse being depicted. The way to keep the second reading alive is to make sure the three scenes aren't merely repeating the same setup — each one should put slightly different pressure on the framing, so the reader accumulates evidence rather than just accumulating scenes.

The question I'd actually sit with: do you have a scene where the planner is alone with the choice — no audience, no minutes, no one to perform for — and what they do or don't do there? That's usually where the discourse drops, because there's no one to perform it for.

THE FOUR GAPS, NAMED

   Risk: owner can sit on the number indefinitely; Sam has no signal of when (or whether) he'll see it. Ask for: "Calculation delivered to Employee within [20/30] days after quarter-end." Stronger version: tied to completion of quarterly close or reviewed financials.

2. Reserves are not disclosed

4. No error-correction / dispute process
   Risk: even an honest math error is unrecoverable; Sam has no standing. Ask for:

   - Owner must respond in writing within a defined time

Yes — this fits trapped air (microbubbles). The diagnostic pattern matches: planned common-line work lets air into the lines, and microbubbles scatter light, giving a milky/cloudy appearance. They rise and dissipate, so a glass clears from the bottom upward over ~30 seconds. No sediment, color, odor, or leak in the unit all point the same direction. The Kibo pre-fill is also the right play during a planned shutoff.

Conservative cold-water flushing sequence:

1. Skip the hot tap for now. The air is in the cold lines; running hot can also stir sediment in the water heater.
2. Remove the aerator from the kitchen cold faucet. It can trap stray particles and slows flow.
3. Open the cold tap fully — not a trickle. Velocity pushes air pockets out.
4. Run 2–3 minutes, then refill a clear glass and recheck. If still milky, run another 2–3 minutes.
5. Once the kitchen clears, run each other cold tap in the unit for ~10–15 seconds (bathrooms, laundry, tub). Air pockets in branch lines are common after a main shutoff.
6. Washing machine: run a quick rinse/spin on cold, or just let it fill once and drain.
7. Ice maker: discard the first batch of ice (it's mostly trapped air and any loosened sediment).
8. Reattach the aerator once water is fully clear.

Stop flushing and contact management if you see any of these instead of assuming it's air:

- Discoloration — yellow, brown, reddish, or black water. Points to rust, disturbed sediment, or a main issue, not air.
- Persistent particles — anything that doesn't clear after extended flushing. Could be sediment or a failing fixture.
- Odor — rotten egg (often bacterial, frequently in the water heater), heavy chlorine (possible backflow/contamination), or any fuel/chemical smell (stop running water immediately and call).
- Pressure loss — a sudden drop can mean a closed valve, a leak in the building system, or a main issue.
- Visible leakage anywhere in the unit — under sinks, around toilets, the water heater, walls, or ceilings. Don't keep running water into a suspected leak.

If only the milky clears-from-bottom behavior shows up and none of the above appear, it's almost certainly air and the sequence above resolves it within a few minutes per fixture.

CONSERVATIVE STATIONARY INSPECTION

The goal is to gather information without loading the bike. Don't pedal hard on a stand or hop on to "reproduce" the skip — that's exactly what we're avoiding. Walk it, look at it, measure it.

1. Visual chain check (no tools): With the bike on the ground or in a stand, lift the chain at the front derailleur and slowly walk it forward link by link. Every link should flex freely through its pivot. A frozen/stiff link stays rigid as the chain moves around it. That's a one-per-revolution problem that can feel like a skip and is a cheap fix.

2. Chain wear (if you have a chain checker): Drop it on the chain. If it's at or past 0.5% stretch, the chain is at end-of-life and is the single most likely cause of skip-under-load. (0.75% is the worn-cassette risk threshold.) If you don't have a checker, skip this — a rough eyeball is not useful here.

3. Cassette tooth profile: Look at the smallest 3-4 cogs (the climbing gears) from behind the bike with a flashlight, peering through the spokes with the wheel in. Healthy cogs have symmetric trapezoidal teeth. Worn cogs develop a hooked, asymmetric, "shark fin" shape. That's the visual fingerprint of cog wear and the second most likely cause.

4. Chainring teeth (visual only): Look down at the front chainring(s). Same check — symmetric vs. hooked/sloped teeth. Front rings last much longer than cassettes, so this is "rule in if obvious, ignore if not obvious."

5. Rear derailleur hanger: Look at the hanger from directly behind the bike. It should be vertical and parallel to the frame's seat tube / dropouts. If the bike has been recently hit (curb, pothole, transport), a bent hanger can cause skip and ghost shifting. No recent impact → unlikely.

6. Rear wheel security: Confirm the rear axle is fully engaged (thru-axle lever fully closed, QR fully clamped). Skip can present as the wheel shifting in the dropouts under load if the axle is loose. Look and feel — don't load it.

7. No-load shifting pass: With the bike stationary, run through every gear once in each direction. Listen and feel for hesitation, slow shifts, chain not settling on a cog, or unusual noise. This is not a load test — it's just confirming indexing is clean. No hard pedaling.

8. Cleat / pedal interface: If you're on clipless, unclip and reclip a few times. If the cleat moves on the shoe or engagement feels mushy, "skip" can actually be the cleat releasing under load. Quick check, no tools.

9. Sidewall and tire: You said normal, but a 10-second pass for cuts exposing casing, embedded debris, or bulges. Treat sidewall cuts with casing visible as shop-today, per your standing rule.

If you find a stiff link, that's a low-cost DIY fix (flex the link back and forth until it frees, lube, then a low-traffic flat-only verification ride — not a climb). If you see visible cog wear or the chain checker reads stretched, the bike is going to a shop regardless.


KEEP OUT OF COMMUTE USE

Yes — until the cause is identified and corrected.

Two skips under climbing torque on a normally-riding bike is the drivetrain telling you it has lost the margin to handle normal use. The next skip could be a chain throw into the spokes, a hard lurch on a climb, or a pedal-stroke dropout in traffic. None of those are acceptable outcomes on a commute. The whole point of a commuter is that it works predictably; this one just demonstrated it doesn't.

Walking the remaining half mile was the correct call. Don't do a "confirmation ride" — that's loading an unverified safety-critical system on public roads.

Minimum bar before returning the bike to commute use:
  - Shop has either (a) replaced the chain and confirmed the cassette is within spec, or (b) identified a specific cause (stiff link, loose axle, bent hanger) and corrected it.
  - You've done a low-traffic, flat-only test ride in the climbing gears with zero skips.
  - Then it goes back on the commute.

Flat, easy-cadence, no-torque recreational riding is a different question — that can be acceptable while you wait for the shop appointment, but the commute stays parked.


SYMPTOMS TO REPORT TO THE SHOP

The shop can do most of the diagnosis from your description. Be ready with:

1. Frequency: Twice in one ride. Both occurrences. No prior warnings in the recent past that you recall.

2. Trigger: Both skips happened under firm pedal pressure while climbing — high torque, not high cadence. Note whether you were seated or standing; the shop cares.

3. Gear state at the time: Which chainring (front) and approximately which rear cog. Climbing gears are small cogs in back + big ring in front. Skip in those gears under load is a classic wear signature; skip in any gear under load is still concerning.

4. Pedal-stroke angle: Roughly where in the rotation did the skip happen — downstroke at peak pressure, top, bottom, random? Same angle both times, or different?

5. Sound and feel: Describe it — hard snap/klunk, momentary hesitation, lurch forward, click? Both skips sounded and felt the same?

6. Other behavior: Brakes, tires, and steering felt normal. You did not crash. Nothing else in the bike's behavior changed that day.

7. What you did: Stopped riding. Walked the bike the remaining half mile. Did not attempt to ride further.

8. Conditions that day: Wet, dry, dusty? Recently washed or lubed the chain? Recently replaced any drivetrain part?

9. Recent impacts: Any curb hit, pothole, dropped bike, or transport damage in the last few weeks? Tells the shop whether to suspect hanger misalignment.

10. Service history: Approximate miles on the current chain, when the chain was last replaced, when the cassette was last replaced, when cables were last serviced.

11. Shifting behavior: Normal before and after the incident? Any ghost shifting, slow shifts, hesitation, chain not settling, or chain falling off?

12. Chain maintenance: When was the chain last cleaned and lubed, and with what?

13. Cleat state: Clipless? Do cleats feel secure on the shoes? Any recent cleat replacement?

Hand the shop the list. Their stationary inspection will most likely cover items 1-3 and 8-12 from the inspection sequence above, and they'll want to put the bike in a stand and check hanger alignment and shifting indexing under no load — that's appropriate and won't replicate the skip.

Conservative phone cleanup, two weeks before Portland. Three phases — reversible first, verification gate, then targeted removals.

PHASE 1 — REVERSIBLE, NO DATA LOSS

Start here. Each step below restores fully by reinstalling the app or re-fetching from the cloud.

1. Offload unused apps. On iOS: Settings → General → iPhone Storage → enable Offload Unused Apps. The binary is removed but documents and data stay; reinstalling from the App Store restores everything. (On Android, the equivalent is "clear cache" + reinstall where needed, but uninstalling is non-reversible for app data, so prefer cache-clearing.)

2. Clear browser caches. Safari: Settings → Safari → Clear History and Website Data (keeps passwords/bookmarks). Chrome: Settings → Privacy → Clear Browsing Data → Cached Images and Files only.

3. Clear streaming app caches — Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube, Netflix. These remove cached streams (re-buffered on demand), not your downloaded playlists or offline content.

4. Reboot and idle overnight, plugged in. Both iOS and Android recalculate system/Other storage and clear some purgeable cache on their own after a quiet cycle.

PHASE 2 — VERIFICATION GATE (run before Phase 3)

Do not delete a single downloaded episode, offline map, or app's local data until you have confirmed three things for each item:

  a) Cloud source still exists. Open the source app, find the album / playlist / show / region, and confirm it is still in your library and downloadable. If it shows "no longer available," do NOT delete the local copy.

  b) Subscription / license is active. A lapsed Spotify, Netflix, or Prime sub can make "downloaded" items un-redownloadable later.

  c) You can re-authenticate. For any app whose data you're clearing, confirm you have a working 2FA method that does not depend on that app. (You said auth apps are protected, so leave Authy / Google Authenticator / 1Password / Bitwarden alone entirely — but for any *other* app that uses TOTP, double-check you can still get in.)

Concrete pre-flight, run through once:

  - Spotify: Settings → Storage — list every downloaded playlist; tap each in Your Library to confirm it still resolves.
  - Apple Music / Apple Podcasts / Pocket Casts: confirm each show is still in your Library, not removed by the publisher.
  - Google Maps / Apple Maps: confirm Portland and any transit corridors you'll use are still downloadable as offline regions.
  - Netflix / Prime Video / YouTube Premium: confirm titles still appear under My Downloads eligibility (licensing rotates).
  - Kindle / Audible / Libby: confirm books are in your cloud library, not device-only.
  - Photos: if iCloud Photos / Google Photos backup isn't visibly on and syncing, fix that before you touch any local media.

PHASE 3 — TARGETED REMOVALS (only after Phase 2 passes)

5. Downloaded podcasts and music you won't need on the trip. Keep one travel-day playlist and one long-form listen; delete the rest.

6. Old offline map regions for cities you aren't visiting.

7. Watched downloaded videos in Netflix / Prime / YouTube Premium.

8. The Files app "On My iPhone/iPad" (Android: Files by Google → Downloads). Safari downloads, PDFs, voice memos, screen recordings, ZIPs from old emails. Often the single largest non-photo space hog.

9. Messages → Large Attachments (Settings → General → iPhone Storage → Messages → Review Large Attachments). If iCloud Photos / Google Photos backup is on, these are usually synced; if not, save keepers first.

LEAVE ALONE

  - Photos / Camera Roll — family photos are protected.
  - Authenticator and password-manager apps — clearing app data here can lock you out.
  - Travel confirmations — Wallet passes, airline apps, hotel and confirmation emails.
  - Full message history — Settings → Messages → Message History → Keep Messages → Forever if it isn't already set.

AFTER CLEANUP

Recheck at Settings → General → iPhone Storage. Aim for meaningful headroom before you fly — boarding-pass updates, offline maps, photos, and video from the trip all consume space, and a trip-day "Storage Almost Full" alert is the worst time to deal with it.

ASSESSMENT

Ordinary kraft or corrugated cardboard is the issue here, not the painting itself. Cardboard is made from unpurified wood pulp that contains lignin and acidic residues; over time it off-gases acids that yellow and embrittle adjacent paper ("acid burn"), and it absorbs and releases moisture, which can encourage mold and cockling. The good news from what you've described — no staining, no buckling, no odor, no transfer — is that the piece appears stable so far. You can address this carefully and at your own pace; nothing here is an emergency.

CONSERVATIVE OPTIONS (least intervention first)

1. Insert an isolation sheet between the painting and the cardboard.

   This is the lowest-risk move. You don't touch the artwork's surface or alter its mounting — you only add an inert barrier between the painting and the acidic board.

   Acceptable materials, in rough order of common preference:
     - Mylar (polyester film), 4- or 7-mil. Dimensionally stable, chemically inert, doesn't off-gas. The transparency lets you see the painting. Mild static is a concern for very friable media (pastel, charcoal); for watercolor it's generally fine.
     - Acid-free buffered tissue, 100% alpha cellulose with a calcium carbonate reserve. Soft, breathable, archival. Buffered tissue is appropriate for watercolor since the binder (gum arabic) is not protein-based and won't be harmed by mild alkalinity.
     - 100% cotton rag interleaving tissue, unbuffered. Equally safe; the choice between buffered and unbuffered matters more for photographs or protein media than for watercolor.

   Materials to avoid as the isolation layer:
     - Glassine. Acid-free and smooth, but can stick to soft media over time and is not preferred for long-term contact.
     - Regular tissue paper, copy paper, plastic wrap, wax paper, kitchen parchment — all carry acids, plasticizers, or surface treatments.

   Procedure: lay the clean isolation sheet on the cardboard, then place the painting face-up on it. Keep the painting in its current orientation; don't flip, fold, or slide it against the cardboard fibers.

2. Replace the cardboard backing with an archival board.

   Lift the painting straight off the cardboard without flexing or dragging it (this avoids abrading the surface on cardboard fibers). Set it face-up on a clean sheet of glassine or tissue as a temporary rest.

   Cut a new backing from one of:
     - 100% cotton rag matboard (Crescent Ragmat, Bainbridge Alpharag, or equivalent with alkaline reserve, pH ~8.5–9.0).
     - Acid-free buffered corrugated board (the blue/grey archival version from Talas, Gaylord, University Products, or Archival Methods). The most economical choice for a non-display backing.
     - Archival foam board specifically labeled acid-free. Standard black foam core is NOT acceptable — its inner polystyrene off-gases.

   The new backing should sit behind the painting with no overhang pressing on the artwork; if the frame has a rebate, the backing can fill it flush.

   If you don't already have a window mat in front of the painting (a mat with a cut opening that suspends the artwork away from the glazing), that's the larger upgrade to consider. Direct contact with glass risks sticking and condensation; a window mat keeps a breathing gap.

3. Mount the painting properly when re-backing (only if you want it secured).

   Use Japanese tissue hinges (kozo fiber, e.g., from Hiromi Paper or Talas) attached with wheat starch paste or methylcellulose. T-hinges at the top edge, or corner hinges at the top corners, allow the painting to be lifted out later for inspection. Never use dry-mount tissue, white glue, rubber cement, spray adhesive, or pressure-sensitive tape — including "archival" tape, which conservators generally avoid for original art.

HANDLING PRECAUTIONS

  - Clean, dry hands. If you prefer gloves, unbleached cotton is best for paper (good fingertip feel). Nitrile reduces tactile sensitivity and tempts you to grip harder.
  - Always lift by the edges; never touch the image surface.
  - Work on a clean, dry, flat surface, away from food and drink, with room to maneuver.
  - Keep the painting face-up when possible. If you must flip it, lay a sheet of glassine on the surface first.
  - Don't stack other work on top, and don't press down on the painting while working around it.
  - Keep the room at stable humidity (~45–55% RH). Avoid storing or displaying on exterior walls, in bathrooms, kitchens, attics, or basements.

SIGNS THAT JUSTIFY A PROFESSIONAL

A trained archival picture framer can do everything in Options 1 and 2 — replacing backings and installing a proper window mat is well within their scope. Bring the piece in person so they can see the current state.

A conservator (American Institute for Conservation — culturalheritage.org, "Find a Conservator") is the right call if you see any of the following, and you should not attempt home treatment for any of them:

  - Foxing: small reddish-brown spots, often mold-related. Don't apply bleach, peroxide, or sunlight.
  - Tide lines, water stains, or any visible staining.
  - Tears, creases, losses (missing paper), or cockling (buckling) that doesn't relax in normal humidity.
  - Powdery, flaking, or lifting media — a sign the binder is failing.
  - Adhesive residue, prior tape, or any sign of earlier improper mounting.
  - Yellowed or brittle edges that crack on flex — advanced acid degradation.
  - Musty odor, visible mold, or persistent fogging inside the glazing (frame seal failure and a moisture history).
  - Mat burn: a rectangular ghost of the previous mat opening, meaning the painting has already had prolonged acid contact.
  - Pastel, charcoal, silverpoint, or other friable/sensitive media on the sheet — these need different handling from watercolor.

If the piece has sentimental or insurance value, or you don't know its history, a conservator consultation before any work is a reasonable hedge.

FRAMER VS CONSERVATOR, IN SHORT

  - Archival framer: re-backing, re-matting, glazing upgrades, proper hinging. Faster and less expensive.
  - Conservator: any surface cleaning, stain reduction, washing, de-acidification, tear repair, media consolidation, flattening. Slower and more expensive; needed only if the signs above appear.

PRACTICAL NOTES

  - Replacement materials are inexpensive. A single sheet of rag matboard runs roughly $5–10; Japanese tissue or Mylar is similar. For a one-piece job, asking an archival framer to handle it is often cheaper than buying tools and supplies.
  - Reliable US suppliers for archival materials: Talas (talasonline.com), Gaylord, University Products, Archival Methods, Hollinger Metal Edge. Big-box and general craft stores usually don't carry truly archival stock; Blick carries some, but read the specifications.
  - Keep the cardboard you remove. If the piece ever shows unexpected degradation, knowing the exact backing it was in contact with helps a conservator diagnose the cause.

  - "Authority verified = Helio allowed to contact the admin" — Authority verified is connector readiness (external system is permitted to push/pull), not contact permission. Conflating the two means a clean connector can be read as admin-contact approval, which it is not.

SUMMARY
No. The CS auto-nudge closing is not blanket authorization for a new consumer on the same shared feed. Shared state being MANDATORY for Growth+CS lifecycle does not make it SAFE for any consumer. Before the renewal-risk notif can subscribe, four preconditions must clear, in this order: (1) per-field semantic map signed by the source owner, (2) freshness limits per field, (3) operator view that explains Hold / Suppressed by field, (4) rollback rehearsal end-to-end. Without these, consumer five couples renewal outreach to CS-purpose semantics we have not pinned down — exactly the failure mode the disputed-semantics pattern was written against on 2025-05-13.

WHY
The CS auto-nudge feed publishes four states: Proceed / Suppressed / Hold / Authority verified. Those definitions are purpose-fit to the CS nudge, not generic:

  Proceed ≠ "fresh enough to act on" for renewal purposes. CS Proceed means "no CS-specific suppression." Renewal outreach needs recency against contract end, not against CS adoption state.

  Hold = a specific field is stale, unresolved, or conflicting — NOT "bad data." A renewal-risk consumer reading Hold would suppress outreach even when the renewal clock is live and the unresolved field is unrelated (e.g., a billing-connector freshness gap with no bearing on contract end).

  Suppressed is multi-causal. CS adoption / renewal work is one cause, not the definition. A renewal-risk consumer cannot read Suppressed as "do not outreach for renewal reasons."

  Authority verified = connector readiness (external). It does not confer contact permission for renewal messaging.

Same field names, different meaning by consumer. "The states sound similar" is the disputed-semantics hazard in textbook form.

CUTS (what approving as-scoped would cut)
  Semantic ownership: only the CS nudge has been mapped. A second consumer without a map means the renewal team is inferring from CS-purpose semantics.

  Freshness: the CS auto-nudge freshness contract matches the CS cadence. Renewal-risk cadence is tied to contract end, not engagement. Different cadence → different freshness floor.

  Operator view: there is no shared reader today that answers "why is this account Hold?" for a non-CS team. The renewal team will escalate; we will have no shared answer.

  Rollback: pausing the CS surface reverts consumer one. There is no analogous revert path for the renewal-risk surface. A bad shared-state event fanning out to two surfaces doubles the blast radius.

P (preconditions, in order)
  1. Semantic map. Owen (Lifecycle Systems semantics owner) drafts the per-field map: what each of the four states MEANS for the renewal-risk consumer, with explicit "differs from CS nudge" rows where meaning diverges. Ines (lifecycle-aud-risk) signs the consumer-side definition. I redline disputed terms before sign-off.
  2. Freshness. Per-field max-staleness values, signed off against renewal-risk cadence (contract-end window, not engagement). Stale fails closed per field, not per account — same rule as the CS nudge, applied correctly.
  3. Operator view. A reader that shows, for any account, which fields are stale / unresolved / conflicting and WHY, so the renewal team can interpret Hold / Suppressed without guessing. Not the CS nudge's internal reader — a shared one.
  4. Rollback rehearsal. End-to-end test of pulling the renewal-risk consumer off the feed and reverting to the legacy renewal-risk source under a forced-stale condition. Timing and blast radius documented. Pass/fail written.

EFFECT
Preserves the disputed-semantics pattern established 2025-05-13. Keeps renewal-risk out of shared-state fan-out until the mapping is real. Avoids the "first consumer succeeded, so all consumers are safe" inference — which is precisely what the pattern was written against.
Costs one sprint of delay on pointing renewal-risk at the shared feed. Legacy renewal-risk source keeps running. That is the right cost.

CALL (plain questions for the growth team)
  Can you name the four states as they apply to renewal-risk, in writing, with per-field definitions? If yes, send to me and Owen — that IS the semantic map, and we can size the rest against it.

  Who on the renewal-risk side owns the operator-side interpretation of Hold / Suppressed today? If the answer is "we'd figure it out from the feed," that is the gap.

  Is there a rollback path off the shared feed to the legacy renewal-risk source? If no, that is precondition four and we are not skipping it.

  Is Owen aware this proposal is being scoped? Source-owner review is precondition one, not a courtesy.

If any of those four answers is "no" or "we haven't done that yet," the answer to "point renewal-risk at the same feed next sprint as consumer five" is: not without the preconditions, not as-scoped.

Lightning is the dominant risk here, and the 4-mile exposed stretch is exactly the wrong place to be during a storm producing frequent lightning — a metal-framed bike on an open path, often the tallest object around, with lightning documented to strike 10+ miles from the parent cell. Hail is secondary but adds real head/eye injury risk if it materializes while you're moving and can't take cover.

Ranking the three options with lightning + hail as the deciding risks:

  1. Wait out the warning, then bike home after ~6:30pm. Safest overall. You're indoors during the active lightning/hail window, you keep the bike, no separate retrieval trip, no rideshare cost. Trade-off: ~2 hours at the office. If you can work late, grab dinner, or just be patient, this is the move.

  2. Rideshare now, collect bike tomorrow. Second safest. You get off-site immediately, zero exposure to lightning or hail. Bike stays in secured storage. Costs a rideshare fare and a short retrieval trip in the morning. Right call if you have a hard reason to leave now (kid pickup, dinner, partner waiting) and can't wait 2 hours.

  3. Bike home now. Don't. Even at 4:18pm, "frequent lightning" means the cell is already active. The 30/30 rule says if you can't count 30 seconds between flash and thunder, shelter in place — and on a 4-mile open stretch you can't shelter. Hail can injure without you being able to stop and cover up. This is genuinely unsafe, not just inconvenient.

If you leave the bike in secured storage overnight (either of the top two paths):

Securing:
  - Lock to an immovable object inside the storage (rack bolted to floor/wall) with a U-lock or sturdy chain — not just to itself or to a freestanding rack.
  - Remove everything detachable: front and rear lights, computer/GPS, bags/panniers, water bottle, helmet if clip-mounted. Anything small and valuable goes home with you or into your desk.
  - If storage is genuinely secured (badge access, locked room), a lighter lock is fine; if it's just a shared bike room, lock aggressively.
  - Note your lock combo/key location so tomorrow-you isn't searching.

Retrieval:
  - Quick walk-around before riding: tires firm (no slow leak from debris blown in), chain not crunchy, brakes responsive, lights charged, frame intact.
  - Lights matter even more if you end up biking home after 6:30pm in the dark.

Bottom line: wait out the warning in the office until ~6:30pm, then bike home. If you can't wait, rideshare now and grab the bike tomorrow morning. Don't ride the 4 miles in this storm.

Recommendation first: pick Option A.

Why A wins on variable isolation

    Drop.       A keeps 8 mm identical to what you've already adapted to.
                B adds 2 mm. Drop is the highest-leverage geometry variable
                for Achilles/calf loading; preserving it eliminates the
                single largest biomechanical change you could introduce.
    Firmness.   "Slightly firmer" sits closer to how a 480-mile shoe
                actually behaves underfoot than a softer platform does.
                A broken-in shoe has lost midsole rebound; a soft new
                shoe changes proprioception even when walk-tested and
                easy-jogged briefly.
    Weight.     A is 1.2 oz lighter. Less mass = less cumulative load
                across 30 min, less fatigue on a return-to-run.

Why B is the riskier pick despite the comfort

    The 2 mm drop increase is a real change in calf/Achilles stretch
    demand across a full 30 min, even if 5 min on a treadmill felt fine.
    Softer cushioning also tends to mask small form drift (heel-strike,
    cadence) that firmer foam surfaces sooner. Heavier mass adds work
    per step on top of both.

Transition protocol — single variable only

    1.  First new-shoe run replaces one of the two weekly 30-min runs.
        Same route, same effort feel, same 30 min. No third run.
    2.  Do not stack any duration or frequency change with the shoe
        switch. The shoe is the variable under test; nothing else moves.
    3.  Symptom during the run -> stop, end session, revert to old shoes
        for the next scheduled run.
    4.  Symptom the day after -> hold dose. Repeat the same 30 min in
        the new shoes on the next scheduled run; do not progress.
    5.  Six clean sessions (no symptoms during AND no symptoms the
        following day) before any reassessment.
    6.  Keep the ankle/calf strength routine unchanged. It is the
        safety net, not a variable to drop while the shoe changes.

One small pre-flight before run #1

    Wear the new pair on a non-running day for roughly an hour of
    walking first. Your treadmill test was brief; an hour surfaces any
    hot-spot or upper fit issue before you're committed to 30 min.

Bottom line: Option A matches the largest biomechanical input (drop),
is closer in feel to a worn shoe, and is lighter. Under the standing
"isolate the only variable, 6-session obs before reassess" rule, that
is the conservative transition.

Short version for Marcus:

Different thing. "Failed to deliver" and "refused to deliver" are not the same event.

A delivery failure is operational — the system tried to send and something broke in transit. You retry, fix the transport, page someone.

A hold is governance — the shared-state path (the single contract path) saw that a governed field wasn't in a state that authorized a send, so it deliberately refused. The hold comes with a contract rule attached: stale qualifying-human-admin past freshness, unresolved external-system authority, or active CS adoption/renewal work in flight. The path being healthy is exactly what makes that refusal legible. It's the contract working as designed, not the path malfunctioning.

If you reclassify holds as failures, three things break at once:

  1. The held-queue and the "no silent releases" rule stop being separate categories. The monthly Q2 reliability evidence (the (a)–(e) list, especially held-row count and held-queue disposition) stops lining up because you'd be counting failures and refusals in the same bucket.
  2. Suppression-as-yield inverts meaning. Suppression isn't "the path broke" — it's the contract deliberately stepping aside for in-flight CS work. Calling that a delivery failure says the contract did something wrong when it did the right thing.
  3. The forward-only rollback obligation stops making sense. Held rows survive rollback by contract — they don't rewind. Failures retry. Those are different behaviors and different evidence trails. If a "held" record could have been a "failed" record instead, the audit trail no longer tells you which one it actually was.

Healthy single path = holds produced on purpose, with a rule attached, audited separately. That's the signal, not the noise. The whole point of the shared-state contract is that refusal-with-a-reason is more reliable than send-and-hope.

If Marcus wants the receipts, the cleanest one is the production-shadow close from May 2: 204 live decisions, 191 agreed with legacy, 13 contract-blocked (9 field-specific holds + 4 suppressions). Every one of those 13 had a contract rule attached. None of them were transport failures.

Subject: Hold vs. fail-closed check vs. delivery — drawing the lines

Two distinctions that tend to collapse in reports, so flagging them up front:

1. Each customer gets ONE evaluated decision — the lifecycle call that lands in shared state. That is the row we ship.

2. Intermediate fail-closed checks happen earlier in the pipeline. They are guardrails: if required state is stale, unresolved, or internally conflicting, the audit pauses and the row is held. The check is the mechanism; the hold is its output — not the decision itself.

What a hold is NOT:

  - Not a final outcome. We haven't called the lifecycle state. It is a deliberate non-decision, pending state resolution. Forward-only: when the state arrives, we re-evaluate against current conditions, not pre-lag eligibility.

  - Not a delivery failure. No customer-facing send is attempted on a held row. Holds live entirely in the audit / state layer — they do not appear in message-state or contact logs.

Why the distinction matters:

  - Holds are not harmless noise to be averaged into denominators. They are signal that something upstream needs resolution (stale export, conflicting signals, missing ingestion). Smoothing them out silently masks the very state issues that produced them.

  - Treating holds as customer sends breaks CS suppression logic and inflates activation / support-load numbers against the wrong denominator.

If a row is held, the next step is state resolution (re-pull, refresh, or escalation to the right owner). Not a retry, not a send.

MATERIALS (small, easy to source before August)
  - Glassine envelopes or acid-free interleaving tissue (7+ sheets)
  - One acid-free folder, archival envelope, or clean manila envelope
  - Two pieces of clean cardstock or chipboard, each ~1/2 inch larger than
    the largest photo on every side
  - A soft pencil (HB / No. 2 only — never pen, marker, or pen on photos)
  - Small clean paper slips for order markers
  - A rigid small box, small archival clamshell, or a hardcover book with
    a flat cavity; clean cotton T-shirt or acid-free tissue for padding
  - Optional: clean cotton gloves (clean dry hands are usually fine for
    modern prints)

BEFORE PACKING — ORDER ONLY, NO IDENTIFICATION
  - Have mom remove the six photos one at a time, in the exact stacking
    order she finds them in the stored box.
  - Mark each slip with a single digit 1–6, one slip per photo.
  - Slip placement: BACK side of each photo, never touching the image
    surface and never against the handwritten back.
  - Do not write names, dates, places, or guesses. Only the sequential
    number.

PER-PHOTO WRAPPING
  1. Before flipping anything, set aside the photo whose back carries
     handwriting. Keep it face-up; do not turn it over until step 3.
  2. For every photo: lower a glassine sheet flat onto the image side
     (no sliding, no rubbing). Lift; do not wipe.
  3. For the handwriting photo: gently flip it face-down onto a clean
     surface; lower a glassine sheet flat over the writing side. Lift it
     back face-up by the edges only.
  4. Each photo becomes a sandwich:
        glassine (image side)
        photo
        glassine (back side)
     with the order slip sitting on the BACK of that rear glassine,
     never against photo paper or ink.
  5. Sleeve each sandwich into its own glassine envelope if available,
     fold flap closed, do not tape the envelope.

STACKING + BUNDLING
  - Stack the six envelopes in numerical order (pick a direction — 1 on

  - Align all long edges. Do not rotate any photo.
  - Do not use rubber bands, paper clips, staples, tape, or Post-its on

The calorie shift is 380 to 365 per cup, about a 4% drop. That's small. For a stable-weight dog with no symptoms, the calorie number by itself isn't a concern.

What actually matters is whether "updated recipe" is a minor reformulation or a meaningful one. Two things to check on the new bag:

1. Does it explicitly say "transition recommended" or "no transition needed"? Minor calorie tweaks usually don't, but real reformulations (different protein source, new fiber, etc.) typically do.
2. The ingredient panel. If proteins, fats, and fiber sources look largely the same, it's a tweak. If there's a new primary protein or a substantial shift, treat it as a new food.

What to do, depending on how you handle the remaining old bag:

If you finish the old bag first
  No action now. When you crack the new bag, follow the revised feeding table for portions and watch stool and appetite for the first week.

Standard 7–10 day blend — only because the label changed, not as a treatment protocol. Treat each stage as 2 days minimum unless a symptom forces a hold.

  - Refusing the new mix entirely for more than 24h (one skipped meal is not a signal)
  - New itching, hives, ear scratching, paw licking, or skin redness
  - Clear behavior shift you can't explain — lethargy, restlessness, hiding

BOTTOM LINE
44°F in the fridge after a 4-hour closed-door outage is above the 40°F safety line. Most perishable items that spent time in the 40–140°F danger zone for more than 2 hours should be discarded, regardless of odor. The freezer looks intact — items still solid with ice crystals means it held.

TRIAGE SEQUENCE (now, in order)
1. Confirm the freezer held. Items still hard and icy = SAFE. Refreeze OR cook today — your call. Anything thawed and soft = treat as perishable (step 3).
2. Reset the fridge. Leave the door closed 30–60 min with power back; wait for the thermometer to drop to ≤40°F before reloading anything you save.
3. Inventory by category. Do NOT sniff-test perishable proteins or dairy to "save" them — dangerous bacteria often produce no odor or off-flavor.
4. Sort into three bins: DISCARD, COOK NOW (to 165°F internal), KEEP.
5. Wash hands, surfaces, and any container that held discarded food before reuse.

DISCARD (perishable proteins, dairy, and cooked items — heat-stable toxins from Staph and spores from Clostridium cannot be rescued by re-cooking)
- Raw or cooked meat, poultry, fish, seafood
- Soft cheeses: cottage, ricotta, cream cheese, queso fresco, brie, feta, fresh mozzarella
- Milk, yogurt, sour cream, half-and-half
- Cut fruit, cut vegetables, prepared salads, coleslaw, fresh salsa
- Cooked leftovers, soups, stews, casseroles
- Deli meats, hot dogs, sausages, pâté
- Prepared egg dishes: scrambled, quiche, custard, hollandaise
- Gravy, cream-based or butter-based sauces
- Opened creamy dressings and opened mayo
- Opened fresh-squeezed or cut-juice products

COOK NOW (165°F internal throughout, then either eat immediately or cool rapidly to ≤40°F within 2 hrs in shallow containers)
- Fresh raw meat/poultry/fish that is still cold to the touch (≤40°F)
- Freezer items that just started to thaw but still have visible ice crystals
- Any safe protein you'd rather save than discard

KEEP
- Whole uncut fruits and whole uncut vegetables
- Hard cheeses (parmesan, aged cheddar, swiss, romano) — trim ~1" around any mold
- Butter, margarine
- Opened high-acid or high-sugar condiments: ketchup, mustard, soy sauce, vinegar-based dressings, hot sauce, jam, jelly, peanut butter
- Unopened shelf-stable items (canned goods, jars, sealed drinks)
- Bread, rolls, bagels, crackers, chips, dry pasta, rice, flour
- Whole spices, vinegar, oils
- Unopened shelf-stable juice boxes, UHT milk

CAUTIOUS CASES (treat conservatively)
- Shell eggs in the carton: borderline at 44°F. Generally safe if uncracked and the carton was not above 45°F for long; discard if cracked, washed, or if you want strict caution.
- Items from the top shelf and door bins (warmest spots) — lean toward discard even if the category above says "keep."
- Hard cheese with a large exposed cut face — trim generously.
- Anything with mixed temp history (pulled out and put back during the outage?).
- Anything where you're tempted to "sniff test" — that's not a valid safety check at this temp.
- 44°F reading 15 min after power return is NOT the peak — the fridge may have risen higher mid-outage and is now falling. If you can't rule out >2 hrs above 40°F, default to discard for perishable proteins and dairy.

SANITY CHECK
When in doubt, throw it out. The cost of replacing a few items is far lower than a foodborne illness. Source: USDA/FDA food-safety guidance (the 2-hour rule above 40°F for perishable foods).

CALL: keep scheduled-decision IDs in the source ledger. In the deck, use narrative anchors only ("carried forward from [cycle]; reevaluated [date]") for identity continuity. Do not put IDs in the deck body, footnotes, or appendix.

WHY
- Identity-linkage is a ledger function, not a deck function. "Held decision + fresh reevaluation = one decision" is true iff the ledger says so. The ledger enforces one ID per decision with reevaluation events attached — that's the authoritative answer to "is this still one decision?" and the deck doesn't need to re-prove it.
- Deck audiences verify by reading the rationale, not by ID lookup. Putting IDs in the deck invites three failure modes: (1) readers treat them as rank/sort keys or significance markers, (2) the deck picks up schema noise every time the ledger changes, (3) reviewers spend cognitive budget on tokens instead of the call.
- Audit pattern is consistent with the rest of the org (Helio Start, lifecycle shared-state). Owen already owns ledger semantics — extending that surface is the right boundary; extending the deck surface is the wrong one.

CUTS
- IDs in deck body: out.
- IDs in deck footnotes / appendix: out (same noise, less visible — worst of both).
- A "ledger: [link]" line at the bottom of the deck channel post: in (cheap, opt-in lookup for anyone who actually wants to verify).

P / EFFECT
- P(this convention is right): ~0.9. Matches the audit pattern, matches Owen's lane, and the failure mode if wrong is mild.
- Effect if wrong: a reviewer can't independently verify identity from the deck alone and has to ping the team. Mitigation is a one-line ledger link in the deck-channel post — cost is low.

OPEN Qs
- Is the ledger actually readable to deck reviewers today? If not, that's the real fix — make it readable, don't drag IDs into the deck.
- Is there a real case where two decisions look like one (same topic, different cycles) but aren't? If yes, the ledger is where that's adjudicated; the deck can flag it narratively ("supersedes prior held decision") without exposing IDs.

STRUCTURE RECOMMENDATION

Three layers, strict separation. Each layer ties out to the next via documented references; nothing in the main deck asks the reader to take a number on faith.

  1. MAIN DECK — broad audience. Aggregates only. No record keys, no customer names, no account IDs. Every number carries a small footer citing the appendix table and ledger range it ties to.
  2. RESTRICTED APPENDIX — Owen + Riley + reviewers who need to verify. Definitions, reconciliation logic, and aggregate movement tables. Still no record-level identifiers.
  3. SOURCE LEDGER — Owen + audit. Raw export from the shared state, hashed internal IDs only. The mapping from hash to customer sits outside this artifact entirely.

Owen's denominator lives in the main deck as a single, attributed line — label, value, owner, definition pointer, source pointer. Every downstream rate or percentage that uses it explicitly references this line, not its own count. That keeps the denominator as the single source of truth and makes Owen's ownership visible at a glance.

MAIN DECK (~6-8 slides + a 1-pager exec summary up front, per the ruling format)

  - Slide 0 — 1-pager: why / cuts / proposal / effect / call
  - Slide 1 — Denominator. Definition, current value, "Owner: Owen (Lifecycle Systems)", App. A ref, Ledger ref
  - Slide 2 — State distribution. Counts by state (admitted / assisted / ineligible / pending / final-reconciliation), with an explicit "snapshot, mutually exclusive, no double-count" caption
  - Slide 3 — Movement reconciliation. Waterfall: opening → admits → reevaluations → holds opened/closed → exits → closing. Tie-out check that opening + net movement = closing
  - Slide 4 — Hold overlay. Count of records currently on hold, broken down by underlying state. Shown as a sub-flag, NOT a separate state bucket
  - Slide 5 — Reevaluation pathway. Count of records that returned from ineligible/closed. Shown as a flow metric over the period, NOT a current-state bucket; reconciled separately against the closing-vs-opening delta
  - Slide 6 — Notable patterns (the 22 stale fail-closed, etc.) — aggregate only
  - Slide 7 — Decisions / asks for leadership

RESTRICTED APPENDIX

  - App. A — Definitions. Each lifecycle state, hold rule, reevaluation trigger. Owned-by attribution per definition (most by Owen). Version + last-updated date.
  - App. B — Reconciliation. Aggregate movement table (week or month granularity). Tie-out cells matching each main-deck number. The no-double-count proof: show that every record in the snapshot sits in exactly one state bucket; holds are a sub-flag, not a bucket; reevaluations are transitions, not states.
  - App. C — Exception log (aggregate only). e.g., the 22 stale fail-closed: how identified, what state they ended up in, what action was taken. Category descriptions, no record keys.

SOURCE LEDGER

  - Tab 1 — Raw export from shared state. Columns: record_hash, current_state, hold_flag, last_reevaluation_date, state_entered_at. No PII.
  - Tab 2 — State transitions (event log). Columns: record_hash, from_state, to_state, transition_date, reason_code. This is what proves no double-count.
  - Tab 3 — Tie-out manifest. For each aggregate in the main deck → specific filter/range in this ledger, with the row count that should match.

HOLDS AND REEVALUATIONS — THE DOUBLE-COUNT RISK AND HOW IT'S NEUTRALIZED

The risk is that a record on hold gets counted in both its underlying state and a "hold" bucket, and that a reevaluated record gets counted in both admits and reevaluations. The structure handles both as overlays, not buckets:

  - Holds are a sub-flag of the underlying state. A record on hold still belongs to exactly one state bucket. Slide 4 reports hold counts broken down by underlying state; the sum across states equals the total hold count, and that sum is the only number carried into leadership.
  - Reevaluations are transitions, not states. Slide 5 reports them as a flow count over the period, NOT added to the admit count. The reconciliation in Slide 3 explicitly verifies: opening + admits − exits + reevaluations − non-recovery closures = closing, tied out to Tab 2's transition rows.
  - Forward-only lag handling (per the standing rule): records resolved from lag are NOT counted as reevaluations; they sit in their current state and are surfaced as a separate "lag-resolution" line in the movement reconciliation so reviewers can see the adjustment without conflating it with genuine reevaluations.

IDENTIFIERS — WHAT LIVES WHERE

  - Main deck: none. Aggregates and percentages only. Cohort labels (e.g., "mid-segment cohort") are fine; record keys are not.
  - Restricted appendix: aggregate only — counts by category. Exception log uses category descriptions.
  - Source ledger: hashed internal IDs only. The hash-to-customer mapping is held outside this artifact (presumably Owen's side or a secured system) and is not part of the deck package.

REVIEWER VERIFICATION PATH

A reviewer can walk the numbers three ways:
  1. Read the main deck, follow the tie-out footer to the appendix table.
  2. Open the appendix, see the same number in the reconciliation table, confirm the no-double-count logic.
  3. Open the source ledger, apply the documented filter from the tie-out manifest, confirm the row count matches.

A spot-check (pick 5 records, walk their transitions in Tab 2 against their current state in Tab 1) closes the loop on any specific concern. Any break between layers is detectable and attributable.

  - Denominator definition: do we use a point-in-time snapshot at a specific date, or a period-average? Owen's call; needs to be locked before the deck is built so the appendix can document it precisely.

  - Distribution: who gets the restricted appendix vs. the main deck only? Affects the cover-page handling.

The flatting you're seeing is value collapse, not hue collapse — the warm and the two neutrals are all heading for the same middle-value band as pigment consolidates on drying. You don't need more orange; you need to widen the value gap and pick one edge to hold.

Recommended single controlled pass:

  1. Timing — wait for leather-damp. Surface matte, slightly cool to the back of a knuckle, no standing water, no shine. Not wet, not bone-dry. This is the only stage where you can both lift and glaze without either bleeding or beading.

  2. Value, direction A (deepen the warm) — mix the same orange/brown at roughly 1.3–1.5× the pigment load of your first pass. Same hue, less water. Lay it only inside the interior zone, stopping a few mm short of the existing soft edge so you don't flood the boundary. This drops value without raising chroma, which is the lever you asked for.

  3. Value, direction B (lift the neutrals, if you prefer not to add pigment) — at the same leather-damp stage, take a clean damp brush and gently draw out one or two small lifts in the doorway or street wash where it sits closest to the warm in value. Push them lighter, leave the pigment on the paper. Separation widens the other direction, zero added chroma, zero commitment.

  4. Edge — pick one short segment, not the whole boundary. The deepest-shadow corner or the side facing the light source. With a damp (not loaded) brush, draw a clean crisp line where the new glaze meets the cooler zone. One edge, held for 2–3 cm, is enough to re-read the form. Don't try to define the full interior perimeter — that turns it into a finish move.

  5. Hands off — let it dry fully without rewetting or reworking. Evaluate at bone-dry, since wet reads darker than the final value.

Decision shortcut:
  - If the warm is already reading as the darkest zone → use direction A (glaze).
  - If the surrounding neutrals crept up and now sit on top of the warm → use direction B (lift).
  - If you're unsure, lift first — it's reversible, a glaze isn't.

This stays a study because it's one intervention, one localized edge, and chroma is held constant. You can abandon, overpaint, or re-wet the whole sheet later without it costing anything structural.
