If you want a provisional sketch pending your call, here's the shape I'd default to — a single quarter-sheet, three reads stacked, every other variable locked:

PROVISIONAL DESIGN — three reads, one sheet

Held constant across the whole sheet: 140 lb cold press, one round brush, two pre-mixed dilutions per pigment (1:8 light, 1:4 dark), same water source/temperature, same room, same drying window (~30 min). No pre-stretch variance. All wet-into-damp edges use the same 15 s offset unless a read specifically isolates timing.

**Read 1 — Value separation** (top strip, 4 cells, 2×2 grid)
Re-run the March 30 design, but as a *confirmation*, not a discovery. Score wet / 5 min / 30 min on value-sep, hue-sep, edge softness. If B and C hold and A and D collapse, the hypothesis lands; if any cell surprises you, that surprise is the input to the dark-mix read.

**Read 2 — Edge timing** (middle strip, 3 cells)
Same pigments, same dilutions, one cool + one warm at the values Read-1 tells you survive drying. Vary only the offset between cool wash and warm wash: 5 s / 30 s / 60 s into the damp side. Score edge softness and value-sep at the same three timepoints. This isolates whether timing is a separate lever or just a proxy for dampness.

**Read 3 — Separate dark-mix test** (bottom strip, 3 cells)
Hold everything from Read 1's surviving cell. Vary only the *dark* dilution: 1:4 / 1:3 / 1:2 paint:water. If value-sep survives drying across all three, your dark mix isn't the bottleneck; if the 1:2 collapses, you've found where the dark end of the scale stops being controllable on this paper.

Why stack them: each read's output is the next read's input. Read 1 sets the value offset that survives drying; Read 2 uses that offset and only varies timing; Read 3 holds that offset and that timing and only varies the dark mix. One sheet, three isolated levers, one Sunday block.

What this isolates vs. doesn't:
- Isolates: the relative contribution of value offset, timing offset, and dark-mix density to wet/dry convergence.
- Does *not* isolate: pigment identity (one cool + one warm only), edge technique beyond wet-into-damp, or scene geometry. Those stay separate studies.

SUMMARY

The 8/5 CS support-load cut on the mature day-90 cohort (52 ws, Owen closed 7/30) shows a concentrated, low-burden touch pattern: ~60% zero-touch, ~29% light (16m median), ~12% heavier (41m median), 0 manual billing/import-migration.

That is a real operational read. It is an EFFORT read, not a cash or acquisition read. Until refund-adjusted cash lands, do not let this favorable shape drift into any LTV, CAC payback, or "raise acquisition spend" claim.

WHY THIS CUT, WHY THIS COHORT

Mature = day-90 closed by Owen on 7/30. The 8/5 cut is a one-shot, point-in-time audit of CS touch-type and time across the 52 active weekly subs. It is NOT a longitudinal trend and NOT a comparison against earlier cohorts.

CUTS — WHAT THE DISTRIBUTION SAYS

  31 no-contact                       59.6%
  15 light touch (16m median)         28.8%
   6 heavier touch (41m median)       11.5%
   0 manual billing/import-migration  0%

Operational read:
  - Effort is concentrated in ~40% of the cohort; the majority are zero-touch.
  - Conditional on touch, median burden is modest and splits cleanly by severity (16m vs 41m).
  - The "heavier" tail exists but is small (n=6) and is NOT the catastrophic billing/import-migration class.
  - No cohort member required the most expensive known intervention.

LIMITATIONS OF THE OPERATIONAL SIGNAL

  - n=52 is small. The 11.5% heavier share has a wide confidence interval; one or two cases move the bucket.
  - Taxonomy is coarse. Light vs heavier is bucketed, not a continuous time histogram — skew, max, p90/p95 are invisible.
  - We do not see WHY each tier was touched: proactive vs reactive, success vs failed fix, expansion-related vs retention-saving.
  - No control cohort. "Concentrated" is asserted, not benchmarked against a day-30, day-60, or earlier mature cohort.
  - "No-contact" is silent — could be healthy self-serve OR disengaged. Effort-zero does not equal revenue-positive.
  - One snapshot from 8/5. No trend line into the next month.
  - CS time is not loaded cost — no fully-loaded hourly, no overhead/tooling allocation.

WHAT IS NOT DEMONSTRATED — PAID-ACQUISITION AND UNIT-ECONOMICS

Nothing in this cut speaks to:

  - LTV, CAC payback, channel ROI, or acquisition-spend appetite.
  - Gross margin per customer after CS load.
  - Cohort-level net revenue retention.
  - Whether touched customers retain BETTER or WORSE than no-touch (selection on need is not selection on churn risk).
  - Expansion or contraction behavior by tier.

WHAT WE STILL CANNOT CONCLUDE WITHOUT REFUND-ADJUSTED CASH

  1. Whether the 6 heavier-touch cases are retention RISKS or retention SAVES — refund/credit patterns tied to touch would tell us.
  2. Whether the 31 no-contact are net-positive cash contributors or net-zero after dormant credits.
  3. True cohort NRR. Gross MRR is visible; net-of-refunds is not.
  4. Whether the CS time spent on the 6 heavier cases is dollar-justified — saved churn ≥ cost.
  5. Any acquisition-spend recommendation. Payback math requires net revenue, not effort shape.
  6. Whether the favorable 0% billing-import-migration rate reflects product stability OR just cohort composition — these customers may never have had legacy data to migrate, which would make the 0% uninformative rather than reassuring.

CALL

Treat this cut as an EFFORT SIGNAL ONLY: concentrated burden, no catastrophic tail, modest medians, small n. Do not promote it to a unit-economics or paid-acquisition claim.

At ~3 min the surface still carried free water, so re-entry displaced pigment and pulled the cool into the warm by capillary action — that's the bleed across the doorway. So 5 min isn't "the right timing." It's the first timing past 3 where the wash is stable enough to accept the interruption without breaking. The bloom is residual — the surface is still damp enough that the dark mark feathers into the wash instead of sitting on it. You can work in that window, but you're trading off, not winning.

One next study — change only the interruption timing, hold everything else:

Run at 7 minutes. Same paper, same blue-plus-brown mix, same brush load, same large cool wash, same warm doorway setup, same dark interruption mark. Move only the interruption from 5 to 7 minutes.

Why 7, not 6 or 8:
- 6 is too close to 5 — likely just gives you a slightly smaller bloom and tells you little new.
- 8 is a bigger leap and risks trading the bloom problem for a crisp warm edge (the surface may have crossed into matte by then, which would break the second goal).
- 7 is the step with a reasonable chance of suppressing the bloom without overshooting into edge crispness. It's the informative midpoint.

Track all three outcomes, not just the bloom. A single-variable study only pays off if you read the trade across measures. If 7 kills the bloom but hardens the warm edge, you've located the threshold and the next move is back toward 5–6 with a smaller step, not further toward 8. If 7 suppresses the bloom and the edge still reads soft, you've found the upper bound of the working window.

One methodological note: define "bloom present" vs "no bloom" before the run so the result is unambiguous. "Small bloom" is doing too much work in your current notes — it'll read differently next Sunday than it did this morning.

Yes — ride in this morning, lock the bike at Helio, do not ride home during the 3:00–7:00pm 108°F window. Pre-decide your return method NOW — rideshare, transit, or pickup — so you're not improvising at 3pm in 108°F heat. The conservative move is a paid ride home, not a heroic bike ride.

MORNING RIDE IN
- Leave early, ride at conversational pace — no intervals, no PR attempts today
- Pre-hydrate: 16–20 oz water + electrolytes 60–90 min before departure
- Carry two bottles minimum (one plain water, one electrolyte mix); refill at Helio
- Sun: SPF 30+ applied before kit goes on, reapply on neck/ears at Helio, sunglasses, light long-sleeve or arm sleeves if you have them
- Kit: light-colored moisture-wicking jersey, well-ventilated helmet, gloves optional but helpful for grip if palms get slick
- If anything feels off mid-ride (dizziness, nausea, cramping, sudden fatigue) — stop in shade, fluids, don't push through

AT HELIO (BIKE STORAGE)
- Park indoors or in shade if at all possible — full-sun rack for 8+ hours cooks tires, brake fluid, and any exposed electronics; if outdoor rack is the only option, at least note position and double-check the lock
- Bring inside: bike computer, lights, phone mount if removable, anything heat-sensitive
- Don't leave a water bottle mounted on the frame — bake-out

RETURN TRIP — PICK ONE NOW, BEFORE THE WINDOW OPENS
1. Rideshare home (preferred) — predictable, A/C, zero exertion. Pre-book if you have a preferred app and surge worries.
2. Transit — covered platforms + A/C usually; check the schedule now so you're not standing on a hot platform waiting.
3. Wait past 7:00pm and rideshare, OR ride home if temp has dropped below ~95°F and you feel good and have rehydrated all afternoon. Only this one involves the bike.

Avoid during the window: walking more than a couple of blocks in direct sun; any bike portion; "I'll just tough it out." Those are the failure modes.

HYDRATION + CLOTHING THROUGH THE DAY
- Sip steadily at the office — aim ~8 oz every 30–60 min, plus one electrolyte drink per hour through the window even if not thirsty
- Wear loose, light, breathable office layers; keep a cold water bottle at your desk
- Eat normally — skipping lunch to "save time" before a rideshare is unnecessary but don't load up on heavy/hot food either

ESCALATE IF
Dizziness, headache that doesn't resolve with water and shade, confusion, stops sweating in heat, rapid pulse, or any chest discomfort = stop activity, cool location, fluids, call someone. 108°F heat index is CDC "danger" territory for sustained exertion — heat illness is easier to prevent than reverse.

WHY THIS CALL
A 108°F heat index on a bike at 3–7pm is not a "be smart and you'll be fine" situation — it's a real heat-illness risk for a 20–40 minute hard exertion, easy to avoid, hard to undo. CONSERVATIVE ONE-SHOT 35-MIN EASY TEST — LAKE TRAIL, NEW SHOES

Why this is the right next step, briefly
- 6-session obs in the new pair is symptom-rule-clean (no focal ankle pain, no gait change, no following-day symptom across multiple weeks of 2x30).
- A single, isolated +5 min duration bump is a minimal-variable probe — only duration moves; route, effort, terrain, and shoes are held constant. Frequency stays at 2/week. That's the smallest legible signal you can get.
- Calf and ankle strengthening continues throughout. No new exercise or load change is layered onto the test week.

Spacing
- Test session on whichever of your two nonconsecutive run days falls earlier in the week (e.g., Tuesday if that's a normal run day), so the test gets a full rest day before and a full rest day after within the standard Tue/Thu/Fri pattern, and the following-day symptom window covers a real off-day, not a race against the next session.
- Unchanged second run stays on its normal nonconsecutive day later that week (e.g., Thursday or Friday), still 30 min, still easy, same lake-trail route.
- No third run. No "bonus" walk-run. The week is two sessions; one of them is just longer.

Effort
- Genuinely easy. Conversational pace, nasal-breathing-capable, RPE roughly 3-4 / 10. Same perceived effort as your recent 30-min runs, not faster.
- First 25 min identical to a normal easy 30. Last 10 min stay at the same effort — the extra 5 min is a duration probe, not an intensity probe. If you're tempted to "get something out of it," that's the wrong move.
- Same warm-up pattern you've been using (walking to the trailhead and the first few minutes easy), no strides, no hill surges.

What to do with the unchanged second run
- Keep it exactly as it has been: 30 min, same route, same effort, same shoes, on the usual nonconsecutive day.
- Do not "make up" the test by shortening the second run or skipping it. Skipping = lost signal. Shortening = confounds the comparison with the prior weeks.
- Treat the second run as a second data point: a clean 30-min session ~48-72 h after the test, at the same easy effort, gives the symptom-rule a fair second look.

Stop or rollback conditions (session-plus-following-day symptom rule)
The rule still applies to both sessions that week. Any one of these triggers rollback to the prior 2x30 baseline and the test is shelved until cleared again:

In-session / end-of-session
- Focal ankle pain at any point — even mild, even only in the last 5 min. Roll back. "Awareness" is not a pass.
- New gait change (visible or self-noticed compensation) during the run. Roll back.
- Effort drift past easy — if RPE climbs to 5+ or you can't hold nasal breathing because of the duration, that's the test failing on its own terms. Roll back to 30.

Following day (both the day after the 35 and the day after the unchanged 30)
- Focal ankle pain, new or worse than baseline. Roll back.
- Following-day symptom (stiffness, ache, swelling, sleep disturbance tied to the run) that wasn't there during the 2x30 baseline weeks. Roll back.
- Any gait change noticed the next day (limping on stairs, unloading the ankle on the walk to Kibo's morning loop, etc.). Roll back.

Rollback protocol
- Drop back to 2x30 easy, same route, same effort, same shoes, for at least 2 full weeks symptom-rule-clean before re-attempting.
- Do not bump duration again until those 2 weeks pass. If a second test fails on the same trigger, treat it as a shoe-or-load mismatch signal, not a test-design problem — pause duration changes and reassess.

Pass criteria for the test
- Session felt easy throughout, no focal pain, no gait change.
- Following day symptom-rule clean.
- The unchanged second 30 later that week also symptom-rule clean.
- All three boxes → you've earned a one-shot 35-min slot in the rotation, still capped at 2/week, still easy. The next move (a second 35, or a first 32-33, or holding 35 for another week) is a separate decision; don't pre-commit.

What to track the week of the test
Just enough to make the signal legible:
- Date and minute of the test session.

Read: you're bracketing a wetness window, and the timing lever is real. The wash passes through three states between laydown and sealed — wet (pigment flows), damp (pigment integrates without flowing), dry (pigment sits on the surface and keeps its edge). Your two results place the interruption at opposite ends of that spectrum: at five minutes the wash was still wet enough to bloom the mark outward; at six it had sealed enough to reject the mark and hold a crisp edge. The pair tells you a working point exists somewhere in the last third of that minute. It doesn't tell you where inside it, or how wide the working zone is.

On 5:30 as the next test — yes, it is the most useful single next step, for three reasons:

1. It keeps timing as the only variable. If you changed pigment load or brush wetness at either bound, you'd be testing a different lever and would lose the bracket you've already built.
2. A midpoint is exactly what a smooth wetness curve predicts. A clean integrated mark confirms timing is the lever and gives you the target. A slight bloom points you toward 5:40–5:50; a slightly crisp edge points you toward 5:10–5:25.
3. It costs one study and produces a third anchor so you can interpolate cleanly rather than guess between two endpoints.

What it won't tell you:

- Whether the working zone is wide (say, 5:20–5:50 all integrate cleanly) or narrow (only one timing works). That requires a tighter pair afterward.
- Whether other levers (concentration of the rain pigment, brush dampness) could rescue the 5- or 6-minute timing if you ever needed to shift the schedule. Worth pursuing later only if timing becomes unreliable in practice.

Run the 5:30 study with the same paper, mix, brush load, wash, and warm-edge goal. Hold everything else. If it lands clean, you've identified both the lever and the target in three studies. If it's still ambiguous, the next move is two more studies bracketing inside the result (e.g., 5:15 and 5:45), not changing variables.

OPERATING INTERPRETATION — ELIGIBILITY vs EXPOSURE
Riley, 2025-09-03
================================================================

SUMMARY (read first)
  ELIGIBILITY is not EXPOSURE.
    Eligible (E)  = account meets gating criteria. Set membership.
    Exposed  (X)  = account actually encountered the treatment /
                    surface / event in-window and was measurable.
                    X is a subset of E.
    Treated  (T)  = subset of exposed that completed the measured
                    action or held the measured state long enough
                    to count as a conversion / retention / expansion.
                    T is a subset of X.
  Eligible accounts are NOT pipeline, NOT causal evidence, NOT
  forecast credit. They are addressable universe — nothing more.
  Any readout, brief, forecast, or exec line that cites a population
  must state E, X, and T separately. The three are nested; do not
  collapse.

WHY
  Eligibility is a precondition, not an outcome. Counting it as one
  inflates impact, contaminates experiment readouts, and biases ARR
  bridges — the classic "ghost lift" pattern: credit claimed for
  accounts that never touched the treatment surface.
  Q3 work touched all three pools (state-guide, mature Day-90 cohort,
  Expansion Assist). Without a shared definition the team reads each
  readout through different lenses.

DEFINITIONS (precise)
  E — property of the account at time t. Computed from filter
      (state, segment, signal, tier, permission).
  X — property of the system AND the account. Requires actual
      receipt of treatment / message / surface / state change AND
      measurability (state allows measurement, identity resolvable,
      no blocker).
  T — property of the readout. Requires X plus completion / dwell
      per the readout's definition.

SCOPE
  Applies to:   lifecycle, expansion, retention, experiment, exec
                readouts; pipeline views; causal claims; ARR-bridge
                and forecast entries; Slack / doc headlines.
  Does NOT apply to: targeting inputs (eligibility IS the targeting
                     filter — correct there); reach / saturation
                     estimates (eligible universe IS the correct
                     denominator for "how big is the pool to reach").

OPERATIONAL RULES
  1. Pipeline lists = exposed-and-pending-decision OR
                      treated-and-in-cohort.
                      NEVER eligible-only. Eligible accounts have
                      not entered the funnel.
  2. Causal evidence = (T_treatment − T_control), measured on X,
                        not on E. Eligibility is not in the
                        estimand. Including eligible-but-not-exposed
                        accounts in either arm dilutes or
                        double-counts.
  3. Forecast credit = (eligible × measured E→X rate × measured
                        X→T rate) at most. NEVER eligible × assumed
                        conversion. Do not book ARR / retention /
                        expansion from E alone.
  4. If only E is available, label exactly:
        "addressable universe — not exposed; not causal; not booked."
  5. Retro-check prior readouts (Q3 cohort cut, Expansion Assist
     descriptive, any expansion-stage pipeline view) that may have
     collapsed the three. Restate with corrected cuts before they
     ship, get cited, or roll into a forecast.

CALL
  Lock as the team standard (Owen / Ines / Priya / Riley) for Q4
  readouts. Surface in the next cohort cut with Owen and in any
  expansion / lifecycle brief that crosses Q3 → Q4. Add a one-line
  E / X / T population cut to the standing readout template so the
  discipline is structural, not heroic.

Dish: chicken fried rice with corn, spinach, and lime.

PORTION FIRST
Plate half for you now, transfer half to a shallow container for Sam. Loosely cover (paper towel under a loose lid) so steam escapes — sealed hot rice goes gummy in the fridge.

TIMED SEQUENCE (25 min)

 0:00  12" skillet on medium-high to preheat. While it heats: shred/dice the chicken, thinly slice the scallions keeping whites and greens in two piles, halve the lime.
 0:05  Oil the pan. Chicken in flat — warm through and pick up a little color, ~3 min.
 0:08  Push chicken to one side. Crack both eggs into the empty side, scramble in the pan, then toss together. The eggs are the moisture insurance so the rice doesn't dry out.
 0:12  Add the rice, breaking up clumps. Add the corn. Toss 2–3 min until the rice is hot and just starting to toast at the edges. (Cold day-old rice actually works better here — clumps break up cleaner.)
 0:15  Scallion whites in. Toss 30 sec.
 0:17  Spinach in by the handful, stirring until just wilted — about 60 sec. Keep it green, don't stew it.
 0:20  Off heat. Taste. Salt, a few grinds of pepper, squeeze half the lime over and toss. Reserve the other half for Sam's portion — lime added fresh at the end is what keeps it from tasting "leftover."
 0:22  Plate yours. Move Sam's half into a container, lid loose, to release steam.
 0:25  Container goes in the fridge once it's stopped steaming.

SAM'S REHEAT (after service)
Skillet preferred: medium heat, 3–4 min, splash of water to wake the rice up, fresh squeeze of lime, scallion greens on top. Microwave works: 60–90 sec covered with a damp paper towel, same fresh-lime finish at the end.

CLEANUP
One skillet, one board, one knife, the unused lime half back in the fridge. Done.

One judgment call: if your skillet runs hot or the rice is going brown before it's hot through, drop to medium — you're warming and toasting, not stir-frying at full blast.

That is **three timing points on the same wetness curve**, with one variable moved each time. You asked two questions: (a) is the timing sufficiently bounded now, and (b) should the next study keep 5:30 fixed and change only brush moisture.

**On "sufficiently bounded":**

You have a wetness window with three sampled states:
- 5:00 → bloom (too wet)
- 5:30 → integrated mark with mild lower-end feather (working, with one residual)
- 6:00 → crisp rejection (too dry)

The lever is **real and isolated** — that's confirmed. What 5:30 gave you that 5:00 and 6:00 didn't is *the right kind of failure mode*: the wash and the warm edge both held, so you know the integrated-mark zone is reachable, but the lower-end feather means you haven't pinned the *uniform* working zone.

So the honest read is: timing is **bounded at the outer ends**, and you have a **single confirmed working point** at 5:30. You do not yet know whether 5:30 is the only point that works (a narrow zone), or whether 5:15–5:45 all integrate cleanly (a wide zone). That distinction is the only remaining ambiguity, and it matters because a narrow zone means timing has to be a controlled, repeatable step in your process; a wide zone means timing is forgiving and you can move on.

**On "keep 5:30 fixed and change only brush moisture":**

This is the right kind of question to ask, but it's the *next* question, not the *current* one. Before changing brush moisture, you need to know whether the lower-end feather at 5:30 is:
1. A timing-zone signal (you need to test 5:15 or 5:45 to see if the feather moves with timing), or
2. A brush-moisture signal (a slightly damper brush on the lower section would have killed the feather without changing timing).

If you change brush moisture first, you won't know which lever was responsible, and you'll have spent a session without isolating anything. That's the classic confound I flagged in the 8/9 sequence.

**Recommended next study — one controlled test:**

Keep paper, blue+brown mix, brush load on the cool wash, cool wash extent, warm-edge hue, and 5:30 timing all constant. Change **only the brush dampness on the dark rain interruption**, applied *uniformly across the rain mark* (not just the lower section).

Why this specific change rather than the "lower section only" patch I floated last turn: your residual is at the **lower end** of the rain mark. That has two plausible causes — pigment pooling at the bottom under gravity (timing/wash-volume signal), or the lower portion of the rain mark was applied when the brush had partially dried mid-stroke (brush-dampness signal). If you change brush dampness *only on the lower section*, you can't separate "fixing the feather" from "I just added water to that spot," and you also can't tell whether the upper section would have feathered under the same brush state. Uniformly changing brush dampness across the whole rain mark isolates the variable cleanly: if the feather disappears everywhere at 5:30 with a damper brush, you've learned brush moisture is the lever and timing was a near-miss; if the feather persists or moves, you've learned timing is still load-bearing.

Two sub-cases you should run **separately**, not in the same session:

- **Sub-case A — brush slightly damper than today's:** the brush you used today was at whatever its natural state was. Dampen it one notch (a touch more water on the brush, same pigment load) and re-run at 5:30. If the feather disappears: brush moisture is the lever. Move on.
- **Sub-case B — only if A does NOT clean the feather:** the brush was already wet enough and the feather is a wash-state artifact. Then a timing-pair is the right next move — 5:15 and 5:45 at the same brush state as today.

Don't run both A and B in the same block. Run A first, evaluate, then decide.

**On your specific framing question — "keep 5:30 fixed, change only brush moisture?":**

Yes to keeping 5:30 fixed. Yes to changing only brush moisture. But the change should be **uniform across the rain mark**, not localized to the lower end, and you should run it as a single-variable test before deciding whether a timing-pair is still needed.

**What success looks like:**

- Best outcome: feather gone at 5:30 with damper brush, upper mark still integrates cleanly, wash and warm edge unchanged. You've identified the lever, you've earned a repeatable process step ("dampen the rain-mark brush one notch, interrupt at 5:30"), and you're done with this study series.
- Acceptable outcome: feather reduced but not gone, or feather gone but upper mark slightly softened. You've learned brush moisture is *partly* the lever; one more session at the intermediate dampness level is justified.
- Failure outcome: feather unchanged, or feather gone but rain mark now blooms like the 5:00 case. Brush moisture was either already correct or you've overcorrected; revert to today's brush state and move to sub-case B (the 5:15 / 5:45 timing pair).

**One thing I'd flag about your question's premise:**

You asked whether timing is "sufficiently bounded now." Bounded at the outer ends, yes — you won't paint a 5:00 bloom or a 6:00 crisp rejection by accident, because you know what those look like. Bounded in the sense of "I know the full working zone," no — you have one confirmed point inside it. If "sufficiently bounded" means "I can trust this in a finished piece," I'd say yes for the next finished piece at 5:30 with today's brush state; if it means "I have a process I can repeat under varying conditions," the brush-moisture test below is the move.

SUMMARY
- Cut the dishwasher breaker NOW. Do not run another cycle to "see if it drains." A sustained hum from a pump = locked rotor = the windings are heating up; the longer it sits energized, the more you risk motor or control-board damage.
- This is a NORMAL-PRIORITY maintenance request, not an emergency. None of the escalation triggers (active leak, smoke, breaker trip, burning odor, sparking, sink backup) are present.
- Most likely fault given the signature (water above the filter, hum on restart, no leak, no trip): drain pump impeller jammed by a small object (glass, bone, pit, label), or a clogged drain hose / air gap / disposer knock-out. All consistent with what you described.

CONSERVATIVE SHUTDOWN (in order)
1. Cycle is already stopped. Leave the control set to OFF, not Cancel — Cancel often keeps the board live.
2. Door is open — leave it cracked for ventilation. The standing water is HOT (140F+) after a wash cycle; do not reach into it yet.
3. Go to the breaker panel. Flip the dishwasher breaker fully OFF. Label is usually "DW" / "DISH" / "KITCHEN DISHWASHER"; commonly a 15A or 20A single-pole, sometimes a dual-pole. Confirm the unit is dead (no lights, no response) before the next step.
4. Keep Kibo crated or in another room until the breaker is off AND the standing water is bailed or has cooled. Detergent residue plus any small parts that come loose during inspection are a real hazard for a kitchen-employed dog.
5. Let the tub cool 15-20 minutes before touching the water, or bail carefully with a cup into a bucket, pouring away from skin.

SAFE USER CHECKS (breaker confirmed OFF)
- Flashlight visual of the tub bottom around the filter: any glass, bone, label, cherry pit, toothpick?
- Remove the filter assembly (usually a twist-out cylinder at the tub floor). Check the well under it for the same debris. Manufacturers intend this to be user-serviceable.
- Under the sink, if accessible: check the dishwasher drain hose connection at the tailpiece or disposer. If you have a garbage disposal, is the knock-out port still intact? Is the hose kinked?
- Air gap (the small chrome cylinder on the sink near the faucet, if one is installed): pop the cap, look for debris clogging it. A very common cause of exactly this symptom.
- Look under the unit with a flashlight: any drips, warped floor, signs of a slow historical leak?
- Once cool, bail standing water to expose the filter and take weight off the door seal.

DO NOT DISASSEMBLE
- The drain pump itself — it sits under the tub and requires pulling the unit. Not user-serviceable, has electrical connections.
- The control board — electrical, ribbon connectors are fragile.
- The door latch / interlock switch — not relevant to this fault and easy to break.
- The spray arm — fine to remove for cleaning but it isn't the fault here; the plastic bearing cracks if over-tightened.
- Heating element, sump seal, any sealed system — not relevant.
- Hose clamps under the unit — pulling the dishwasher out is a two-person job and risks kinking the water supply line.

WHEN NOT TO TRY ANOTHER CYCLE
- After killing the breaker, do NOT re-energize and run a cycle without first addressing the cause. The hum will resume, the pump will re-lock, and you'll compound the damage.
- One narrow exception (drain-only cycle, breaker re-energized): you cleared visible debris from the filter well, you verified the drain hose is clear, AND the air gap is clear. If it hums again on restart — stop, breaker off, file the maintenance request.

WHEN TO SUBMIT A MAINTENANCE REQUEST (normal priority)
- After the breaker is off and the basic checks above are done, file through your normal Cherrywood channel. I don't have the tenant portal URL or property-manager contact saved for Cherrywood — use whatever you normally use, and tell me what it is so I can keep it on file for next time.

- Likely outcome: tech pulls the unit, clears or replaces the drain pump, verifies hose and air gap. Same-day or next-day is typical for a non-emergency in a rental.

WHEN TO SEEK EMERGENCY HELP INSTEAD
Escalate to after-hours / on-call if any of these appear:
- Water actively leaking onto the floor
- Smoke or burning odor from the unit
- The breaker trips the moment you re-energize the dishwasher circuit
- Visible sparks or arcing
- Water backing up into the kitchen sink through the drain line (a main-drain issue, not a dishwasher issue)
- Multiple kitchen fixtures affected at once

  1. Wash and dry hands thoroughly; no lotion, no rings. Clean nitrile gloves are the safer choice here — cotton gloves can snag dry flakes and pull them off. If you only have cotton, handle with extreme care around the residue corners and keep handling time short.
  2. Clear a flat workspace. Lay down a clean sheet of acid-free paper or a clean cotton cloth as a base.
  3. Slide a piece of acid-free paper or a clean piece of card UNDER the print rather than picking it up by the edges. The two residue corners are mechanically weakened; don't lift from those points or pinch them.
  4. Keep the print flat at all times. Don't flex, tilt, or wave it — barely-adhered flakes will drop.
  5. Set it on the prepared surface. Image-side up if the residue is on the back, residue-side up if the residue is on the front. Don't flip-flop it.

ISOLATION (KEEP FLAKES WITH THE PRINT)

  1. Best enclosure: a four-sided Mylar (polyester) sleeve. Detached flakes stay inside the sleeve with the print instead of falling into a drawer and being lost. Mylar is chemically stable.
  2. Acceptable fallback if you don't have Mylar: sandwich the print between two sheets of unbuffered, acid-free tissue inside a rigid acid-free folder. Place the print face-up on the lower tissue, then lift and lay the upper tissue on top — don't slide it.
  3. Any flakes you find detached during enclosure go into a small labeled paper envelope (unbuffered, acid-free), kept with the print. Do not throw them away. They are provenance; a conservator may be able to match them to a specific album page.
  4. Keep P05 physically with the 01–06 set in the same drawer/box, but in its own enclosure so flakes can't migrate onto the other five.

STORAGE — ENVIRONMENT AND POSITION

  1. Flat. Never on edge, never stacked under heavy objects.
  2. Cool: roughly 65–70°F (18–21°C).
  3. Dry: 30–50% RH. Stability matters more than hitting a specific number — avoid swings.
  4. Dark. Light damage is cumulative; even brief direct sun matters.
  5. In a closed cabinet or drawer, away from exterior walls, radiators, water pipes, and any window.
  6. Inside its enclosure, ideally inside a rigid archival box. A clean, dry, lidded plastic or metal container is fine for now. Avoid cardboard food boxes (acidic, off-gas) and avoid any unsealed wood drawer (wood off-gases acids).
  7. Not in a bathroom, kitchen, attic, basement, or garage.

LABELING

  On the OUTSIDE of the enclosure, in pencil only: "P05 — DO NOT CLEAN — dry black album-paper residue, two corners — observed 2025-09-14 — [your initials]."

MATERIALS TO AVOID

  - PVC / vinyl sleeves, "magnetic" photo album pages, self-adhesive album pages
  - Plain office paper, copy paper, newsprint, paper towels, tissue with lotion
  - Paperclips, rubber bands, staples, binder clips
  - Any kind of tape, even "archival" tape — adhesion is a treatment, not a step
  - Lamination, dry-mounting, glue sticks, photo corners (the triangular stick-on kind)
  - Markers or pens on the print or its back; pencil directly on the print
  - Household cleaners, water, saliva, solvents, erasers (even soft white plastic), furniture polishes
  - Anything labeled "acid-free" only by a maker you don't trust — when in doubt, food-grade unbuffered tissue from a conservation supplier is the safer bet

ACTIONS TO AVOID

  - Touching the residue with bare fingers (oils and salts accelerate deterioration and can detach flakes)
  - Brushing, blowing on, or "dusting" the residue
  - Scraping, picking, peeling, or pressing flakes back down
  - Pressing anything onto either surface of the print
  - Folding, bending, rolling, or standing the print on edge
  - Photocopying or scanning with a flatbed that presses the lid onto the print (scan through the Mylar sleeve or with the lid raised, and only after the print is fully enclosed)
  - Leaving it in direct sun, near a heat source, or anywhere with humidity swings
  - Writing on the print or its back — write on the enclosure

SIGNS THAT JUSTIFY INVOLVING A PHOTOGRAPH CONSERVATOR (ANY ONE IS ENOUGH)

  - Residue sits on or overlaps the image layer, not just the corners
  - Flakes continue to detach between handling sessions (active loss)
  - Image layer shows damage: silver mirroring (a bluish/purplish sheen on B&W prints), fading, yellowing, staining, tears, creases, cracking or flaking of the emulsion itself
  - The handwriting on the back is at risk or already partially abraded/smudged
  - You find mold (often looks like fuzzy spots, sometimes white/green/black), foxing (small reddish-brown spots), or any biological growth
  - Water damage, tide-line staining, or warping
  - The print is one-of-a-kind and you want it preserved across generations rather than just stabilized for now
  - You'd like the residue removed, the back safely cleaned, or the surface cleaned
  - Any time you feel tempted to do something beyond enclosing and storing

WHEN YOU INVOLVE ONE

  Ask specifically for a photograph conservator — paper conservators don't always specialize in photographic processes, and the chemistry (silver gelatin, albumen, platinum, chromogenic, etc.) matters. The American Institute for Conservation (conservation-us.org) maintains a "Find a Conservator" directory searchable by specialty and region. University art-conservation programs and the photo collection at a regional archive or museum can also refer. Expect an initial consultation to be modest in cost; full treatment is quoted after examination.

WHAT A CONSERVATOR CAN DO THAT YOU SHOULD NOT

  - Consolidate lifting flakes in place so they stop falling off
  - Safely reduce or remove the album-paper residue if that's appropriate for the specific photographic process
  - Surface-clean the print without damaging the emulsion or the back inscription
  - Stabilize tears, creases, or other damage
  - Re-house it in materials matched to the actual photographic process (buffered vs. unbuffered, etc.)
  - Tell you what the print is (process, approximate date) and whether the residue matches a known album, which can recover lost provenance

A small note on the index: when you do update the pair index for P05, it's worth recording this residue observation alongside the unresolved identification — it doesn't move P05 closer to being identified, but it does pin down one piece of its history (album-mounted, black paper), and it tells future-you (or a conservator) that this print was treated as evidence, not cleaned.

CONSERVATIVE TWO-WEEK PLAN (post clean 35-min test in the 9.2oz pair)

Premise
- Pre-test baseline: 2 sessions/week, 30 min each.
- Validated this week: one 35-min session in the new pair — clean during run, 0-2h post, and following-morning walking + stairs.
- Rule held throughout: advance duration OR frequency per week, never both.
- Ankle-and-calf strengthening continues, unchanged, 2-3x/week on non-run days.
- Session + following-day symptom check is the gate before any next-session decision.

Week 1 — bump duration, hold frequency
- Both sessions: 30 → 35 min, easy effort, same lake-trail route.
- Frequency stays at 2/week, with ≥48h between sessions.
- No third session this week.
- Shoes: 9.2oz replacement pair only. No rotation.
- Promotion gate to Week 2: BOTH 35-min sessions clean through the following morning.

Week 2 — bump frequency, hold duration
- Hold both 35-min sessions unchanged.
- Add a third session: 20-25 min, easy, on a day ≥48h from the prior run. Keep it short; this is a frequency probe, not a duration probe.
- Strengthening unchanged.
- Promotion gate beyond Week 2: the new third session AND both 35-min sessions all clean through their following mornings.

Symptom check (every session)
- Checkpoints: during the run, 0-2h post, and the following morning (walking, stairs, single-leg calf raise).
- "Clean" = no focal ankle or calf pain, no gait change, no swelling, no limp, no next-day stiffness that doesn't resolve with normal warm-up of ordinary activity.
- Any flag pauses the planned progression for that week — do not stack a second advance on a flagged session.

Rollback conditions
1. Focal pain or gait change during a run: stop the run; downgrade the next session ~10% in duration (e.g., 35 → 30) and/or drop back to 2 sessions; do not advance that week.
2. Focal pain or gait change showing up only the following morning: same response — downgrade the next session, hold the line on frequency.
3. Two consecutive flagged sessions (whether the flag is intra-run or next-day): revert full prescription to 2x30 for one full week before any further progression.
4. Sharp pain, visible swelling, limp, or pain that does not fully resolve by 48h post-session: pause all running; in-person eval before resuming.
5. Same-location symptom recurring across two separate sessions: pause progression; the question is shoe or strengthening load, not just running dose — revisit both before re-advancing.

Spacing
- ≥48h between running sessions; no back-to-back run days.
- Running slots around the existing bike days (Tue/Thu/Fri), not on top of them.
- The third session in Week 2 should land on a day with clear recovery margin around it (not the day before a long bike effort).

Alternative path if you want to be even more conservative
- Week 1: hold one session at 30, raise the other to 35 (the already-validated duration). Week 2: raise the remaining session to 35. Week 3: add the third short session. This pushes the full 2x35 + third-session build out to three weeks instead of two. Use this if you'd rather not put two 35-min loads on the leg in the same week as the test session.

Good afternoon. I'm Riley Tanaka, and I'm here to talk about how our restaurant approaches private events.

Sam, our private dining lead, holds final authority on the menu and the production plan for any private event. What that means in practice: menu, purchasing, prep, and final guest count are treated as one production decision, made together, based on the advance count. Nothing moves forward until that package is settled.

That has two consequences I want to be clear about, because they come up often.

First, approval and service attendance are separate questions. Sam signs off on whether an event can run and how it runs. That is not the same as committing to be on the floor for every service, and we don't conflate the two.

Second, customization is bounded. We'll customize when a request is executable inside our production sequence, our allergen handling, and our team's capacity. When a request would break any of those, we decline and explain why. We'd rather hold the line on what we can execute well than promise something we can't.

One example: a roasted chicken course is available as an advance-count private-event option. It is not a standing weekly menu item, because it only works when we can plan for it against the headcount. That's the model in miniature — say yes to what's producible, scope it correctly, and make the advance count do its job.

Renewal comparison

Annual premiums:
- Plan A (deductible $500, +behavioral): $61 × 12 = $732
- Plan B (deductible $750, no behavioral): $48 × 12 = $576
- Prior plan: $49 × 12 = $588

Plan A costs +$156/yr over prior; Plan B saves $12/yr.

Total annual cost (premium + deductible + 20% on the excess), as a function of covered claim spend X:

Plan A = 732 + 500 + 0.20·(X − 500) = 1,132 + 0.20X
Plan B = 576 + 750 + 0.20·(X − 750) = 1,226 + 0.20X

Setting them equal: 1,132 + 0.20X = 1,226 + 0.20X → never equal, because A is $94 cheaper at the deductible layer and then identical at the 20% layer. So **Plan A is exactly $94 cheaper than Plan B at every positive claim level**, and $156 cheaper at X = 0. Plan A dominates Plan B on pure claims math, independent of how much Kibo uses it.

Plan A − Plan B at various X:
- X = $0: $732 − $576 = +$156 (A costs more)
- X = $1,000: $1,332 − $1,426 = −$94 (A saves $94)
- X = $2,000: $1,532 − $1,626 = −$94
- X = $5,000: $2,132 − $2,226 = −$94
- X = $10,000: $3,132 − $3,226 = −$94

So if Kibo uses no claims at all in the next year, Plan B is cheaper by $156. The moment there is any covered spend, Plan A pulls ahead and stays ahead by $94 forever after — the breakeven on "savings vs. Plan B" happens the instant X > $0, and A is also $156/yr more expensive than your current plan in that case.

What matters for the decision
- **Behavioral-care eligibility after the deductible** — this is the only thing Plan A actually buys you that Plan B doesn't. Plan B simply has no behavioral coverage. The $156/yr "extra" over your prior plan is essentially the price of that rider.
- Trazodone and routine vet visits are already covered under the base policy on both plans; the behavioral rider is what would matter if a behavioral issue emerged.

Recommendation
If Kibo has no new condition and no pending claim — which is what you've told me — then **stay on the equivalent of your current plan (Plan B) and save $12/yr**, unless there's a realistic chance of needing behavioral care in the next 12 months. The behavioral rider only pays for itself if you actually use it, and the math shows you'd need roughly $200+ of behavioral spend just to recover the $156 annual premium increase; from there it's pure savings up to the $10k cap.

If behavioral coverage is something you'd want to have in your back pocket (storm-anxiety escalation, new behavior consult, etc.), then Plan A is the cheaper of the two options the moment any claim is filed — and the $156/yr cost is modest insurance for that.

The transparency-vs-answerability distinction is the load-bearing one. A count (or a dashboard, or a published FOIA log) is a disclosure; it does nothing to the question of who can compel a response when the count is wrong, missing, or contested. The two book-club points are really arguing the same thing from opposite ends: residents need a *corrective* lever (one), and an appeals process only counts when the institution doesn't get to pick which grievances are legible (two). Performative appeals are usually the moment where category-design quietly substitutes for adjudication.

The standardized-categories debate is downstream of that. The reason standardized categories lose local context is precisely because they re-import the institution's authority to define what counts — exactly the failure mode the second point named. So the disagreement in the group may not really be about whether to standardize; it may be about whether *standardization with a local override channel* is just category-control in a friendlier costume, or whether it can actually route around it.

  - Transparency ≠ answerability. Publishing a count is disclosure, not a remedy. The open question isn't whether data is visible — it's who can compel a response when the data is wrong, missing, or contested.

The other said appeals become performative when the institution still controls which evidence categories count. These are two ends of the same argument: an appeals lever that doesn't include category-disputing authority is just disclosure in a robe.

  - Standardization's hidden cost. The group split on whether standardized categories preserve enough local context. Downstream point: standardized categories lose local context precisely because they re-import the institution's authority to define what counts. The real split may be whether standardization with a local override channel is a genuine route around category-control, or just category-control in friendlier clothing.

One open question, framed on correction rather than category-challenge:

  Does the corrective authority sit with whoever wrote the record, or with whoever is named in it? Because if the institution that produced the record also decides what a correction looks like, then "appeals process" is structurally a confirmation step, not an adjudication — and the inspector-and-correct point collapses into the performative-appeals point, with the standardized-categories debate being a downstream symptom rather than the actual fault line.

Good instinct to interrogate this before locking it in. Here's my read of what has to hold for a one-off monthly snapshot cadence to stay sound, and where the design is fragile.

What has to be true for it to hold up:

1. The snapshot is genuinely comprehensive. The 11/4 anchor had 131 source rows, 7 validated dupes → 124 unique, every campaign with a status and owner. If Maya's sanitizer ever drops edge-case rows (archived-with-no-status-history, owner-on-leave, recently-renamed, campaign split from a parent), the inventory silently undercounts and every downstream review inherits that gap.

2. The five business-day window is real headroom, not a coincidence. 2BD Maya → 4BD Ines → 5BD Owen → 6BD you is 1-day buffers between steps. That buffer assumes no one's out, no source-export delay, no re-work loop. One slip cascades to the next person.

3. "State-changing or exception-heavy" actually routes to you and not to Ines/Owen. If the operational bar drifts — e.g. Ines starts closing state-meaning disputes, Owen starts signing off on exec claims — the 6BD escalation stop turns into a 6BD rubber-stamp and the cadence holds the shape but loses the safety.

4. Maya's prep-only scope stays narrow. She sees sanitized exports and approved examples. The moment she gets even read access to Customer.io or sees unmasked data, the audit trail blurs and her work can no longer be treated as "prep-only" — it'd be co-authoring.

5. The handoff map stays clean: Ines=gov, Owen=sem, Riley=exec/risk, Daniela=eng. Cross-ownership (e.g. Ines reviewing reporting semantics, Owen making a lifecycle call) is where the cadence frays.

Where the design is fragile:

A. Single-snapshot anchor. The whole month derives from one point-in-time export. If the export is taken at the wrong moment — mid-sync, during a lag window, before a nightly job lands — the inventory is wrong but looks complete. The lag-recovery rule ("delayed export/refresh resolves → recheck; do NOT restore pre-lag eligibility") partly addresses this for events but doesn't address "we captured a bad snapshot on day 2 and now run five days of reviews on bad data."

B. No explicit re-anchor trigger. What happens if Maya's 2BD inventory is materially wrong and only Ines catches it on 4BD? Does the cadence re-anchor from Ines' finding (resetting Owen's 5BD and your 6BD), or does Ines patch and the clock keeps running? This isn't specified, and the cadence assumes the upstream artifact is correct.

C. Owner state is a moving target during the window. Between Maya's 2BD snapshot and your 6BD sign-off, an owner can leave, change teams, or take over a campaign. The cadence assumes Ines' owner-state review at 4BD is sufficient, but for a fast-moving org, 2 days of drift between 4BD and 6BD is real.

D. "Validated duplicate" depends on definition. Seven dupes removed on 11/4 — what counts as a duplicate? Same name? Same campaign_id? Same audience + send window? If the dedupe rule is implicit (Maya's judgment), two months from now Maya or her successor might dedupe differently and the count of 124 won't reconcile against the 131 source. The cadence has no documented dedupe policy.

E. Exception-heavy work isn't bounded. "State-changing or exception-heavy work" is a wide bucket. If exception work clusters in a given month (say, a pricing change touches 30 campaigns' targeting), your 6BD window collapses. The cadence has no surge protocol.

F. One snapshot per month means stale-data window is up to ~30 days. A campaign that becomes unowned on day 7 won't surface in governance until the next month's 2BD. For high-risk surfaces that's too long.

G. Linear dependency means any link failure is a full stop. There's no parallelism, no async branches. That's a deliberate choice (clean signal, your pref) but it means a single person's unavailability stalls the whole month.

Tradeoffs vs. alternatives:

- Continuous/rolling governance (no monthly anchor): catches drift sooner, no "stale until next month" window, but more noise, no clean monthly checkpoint for exec claims, harder to coordinate handoff.
- Weekly snapshot with same review ladder: halves the staleness window, but doubles the operational load and probably overwhelms Ines/Owen given current cadence.
- Event-triggered re-anchor: keep monthly as the floor, but define explicit re-anchor triggers (material ownership change, schema change in source export, lag incident affecting >X% of rows). Keeps the cadence but adds a safety valve.

The core tension: monthly-once gives you a clean audit trail and a stable handoff map, at the cost of up-to-30-day staleness and tight coupling to a single snapshot's quality. If the snapshot is wrong, everything downstream is wrong; if the cadence slips, the whole month slips.

Want me to draft a "what would re-anchor the cadence" trigger list, or a dedupe policy that locks in what counts as a duplicate row, before we commit this to memory? Both would address the two biggest fragilities (B and D). Or if you'd rather discuss a different design — rolling, weekly, event-triggered — I can walk through what that would change operationally.

One-skillet potato hash with baked eggs & cheddar. ~30 min, one pan, reset takes 5 min.

Why it works: small-dice potatoes (1/2") hit a fast golden crust in 10 min, then the same pan runs the aromatics, greens, eggs, and cheese — no transfers, nothing to wash beyond a board, knife, and spatula.

Mise en place (do this first, ~5 min)
- 12 oz Yukon gold potatoes → 1/2" dice (smaller = faster + better crust)
- 2 scallions → whites and greens separated
- 4 oz baby spinach → rinsed, not dried (the water steams the wilt)
- 4 oz sharp cheddar → shredded
- 4 eggs → cracked into a small bowl (so they pour in fast)
- Have a lid or large plate ready

Cook sequence (T-30 → serve)

T-25  Heat 2 Tbsp olive oil + 1 Tbsp butter in a 12" skillet over medium-high. Add potatoes in a single layer with 1/2 tsp salt and pepper. Don't stir.

T-20  First flip — let them crust undisturbed until golden underneath, then toss every 2-3 min.

T-15  Add scallion whites, toss 30 sec. Pile spinach on top, cover, 2 min to wilt.

T-10  Uncover, stir spinach through. Make 4 wells, pour eggs in, season. Cover, drop heat to low.

T-7   Whites set, yolks still runny (lid on another minute if tops look wet).

T-5   Kill heat. Scatter cheddar + scallion greens. Cover 30-60 sec to melt.

T-3   Serve straight from the skillet on a trivet. Hot sauce and toast on the side if you want.

Reset before Sam heads out
- Soak the skillet in hot water while you eat (skip soap if cast iron)
- One wash: board, knife, spatula, small bowl
- Wipe the counter, you're done in under 5 min

If the dice feels slow: parboil potatoes 4 min, drain, dry, then start at T-25 — guaranteed on time.

Recommendation: change only the SHAPE of the darkest accent. Replace the rectangular doorway with an L-shaped (or notched-rectangle) silhouette in the same position, occupying roughly the same total dark area.

Held fixed across the two studies:
- paper
- pigment family (both cool wash and warm-edge pigments)
- large cool wash (same dilution, same wetness, same coverage)
- value-separated warm edge (same value steps, same placement along the interior)
- darkest value of the accent
- outer footprint of the accent (its bounding rectangle stays put)

Single variable changed: silhouette shape — specifically, introducing one inward step so the dark mass reads as a jamb or wall-thickness rather than a flat cutout.

Rationale, tied to your diagnosis: a uniformly dark rectangle with four equally weighted edges reads as a 2D shape pasted onto the warm field — that's the flattening you saw. An L (or notch) breaks the symmetry of the silhouette just enough for the eye to interpret the mass as a recessed opening with a side wall, which restores interior depth without touching values or edge quality. This isolates "uniform silhouette" as the culprit before you spend a study on edge softness or value gradation.

If the L still flattens after drying, the next controlled change to test is edge quality (hard three sides, soft one side meeting the interior floor) — but try the shape change first, since silhouette is the cheaper variable to rule out.

One small operational note: when you paint the L, load the inboard corner of the notch a hair earlier than the rest of the shape so the inner edge sets up while the outer edges still flow — that keeps the notch crisp without losing the wet-into-wet feel of the original study.

A few things worth knowing before you decide what to do with it:

1. The "high" flags on portal results are usually population reference ranges, not treatment thresholds. Your PCP will interpret an LDL of 118 against your personal 10-year ASCVD risk (age, BP, smoking, diabetes, family history, etc.). For low-risk adults the LDL goal is often <100 or <130; for higher-risk groups it's <70. So 118 doesn't automatically mean a statin conversation — it means the panel deserves a conversation.

Low TGs plus HDL in the 60s is the metabolic picture associated with larger, more buoyant LDL particles rather than the small-dense pattern that drives more atherogenic risk. So the same LDL number sitting next to TGs of 220 and HDL of 35 would read very differently than this one does.

If you don't already have a 10-year ASCVD risk score on file with your PCP, that's worth asking about; it puts the LDL number in context.

PRE-WORK
- Photograph the shifted corner and the full piece before touching anything.
- Clear a flat, padded, lint-free surface (glass table with a clean cotton cloth, or foam board + cloth).
- Wash and dry hands; nitrile or clean cotton gloves for the sheet itself.
- Stage supplies: notepad, clean soft brush (to lift dust), replacement corner pockets (paper or Tyvek, unbuffered, acid-free) if needed. No tape, glue dots, or self-stick corners.

OPENING THE FRAME (face-up, back toward you)
1. Bend out the flexible points / turn buttons. Lift the backer and the kraft dust cover as a stack, in order.
2. Lift the glazing out; set acrylic face-down if it's plexi to avoid scratches. Never slide it.
3. Lift the mat+artwork out as a unit if hinged; if loose, lift the mat and treat the sheet separately.
4. Lay the sheet face-up on the clean surface. Inspect the existing corner pockets and the sheet edges.

RESEATING THE SHEET
- If pockets are square and intact and only the mat shifted in the frame, just re-square the sheet in the window and re-tension the backer. No adhesive needed.
- If a pocket is bent, splayed, or no longer grips, replace just that one. Slip the corner flush into the new pocket — no overlap onto the image area. Friction alone holds it.
- The only archival adhesives appropriate to paper are wheat starch paste or methylcellulose under a Japanese tissue hinge, and only if you're trained. For a corner-pocket reset, no adhesive should touch the sheet.
- Replace the mat in the frame, lay glazing, spacer (if used), backer, refasten points. Rehang and recheck level after 24 hours — paper and wood settle.

STOP SIGNS — STOP HANDLING AND CALL A PAPER CONSERVATOR
- Tide lines, foxing, or any discoloration/ringing that wasn't there when framed
- Tears, creases, losses, or punctures, however small
- Flaking, powdering, or lifting pigment (especially gouache, pastel, soft charcoal)
- Yellowed carrier or residue from any pressure-sensitive tape, masking tape, or adhesive label — never peel at home
- Cockling, warping, or rippling beyond a gentle, even wave (suggests moisture history)
- Any mold, mildew, or biological growth
- A brittle or friable sheet that powders at the edges
- Existing tissue patches, fills, or retouching (prior repairs can be disturbed easily)
- Work that is signed, editioned, or has documented provenance — treat any intervention as "document and consult," not "fix at home," even for an 1/8" shift. A short consult is far cheaper than undoing a mistake on an irreplaceable sheet.

For the condition you described — flat sheet, no moisture/torn/abraded surface, no adhesive contact, mount-only shift — the home sequence above is appropriate. The discipline is: corners only, no adhesive on the sheet, stop the moment any of the signs above appears.

Here is a five-minute setup that should give you a faithful, archival-quality phone shot:

1. Kill the variables you can't control
   - Turn off every room light; use only the corner's indirect daylight. Mixed color temps are what make auto-WB drift blue/orange.
   - In the camera app, disable HDR, "Scene optimizer," "Vivid," and any AI enhancement. Long-press the painting to lock AE/AF.
   - Switch to RAW / ProRAW (or open a RAW app like Halide or Lightroom Mobile). JPEG processing is the single biggest reason the cool wash goes cobalt and the warm edge goes neon.

2. Light placement (~30 seconds)
   - Aim for a single soft source from roughly 45 degrees to one side, not dead-on (flat) and not raking (exaggerates paper tooth).
   - If one side of the paper is darker, prop a white board or sheet on that side as a bounce fill.
   - If a sunbeam is hitting, tape a sheet of tracing paper or a sheer cloth over it to diffuse.

3. Camera alignment (~60 seconds)
   - Prop the phone on a stack of books, mug, or tripod so the lens axis is exactly perpendicular to the painting, centered. Any tilt = uneven light across the frame.
   - Frame so the painting fills ~70 percent of the shot, with the reference card visible in one corner for the WB shot.
   - Use the 2-3 second timer so your finger doesn't jiggle.

4. Neutral reference + WB correction (~90 seconds)
   - Put an 18% gray card (or a clean white sheet, in the same light, on the same plane) in frame and snap one shot.
   - Move the card out and snap the final shot, same settings.
   - In the editor: eyedropper the gray patch in the reference shot, apply that WB to the final shot, drop saturation 5-10 percent, and check the histogram so the brightest paper sits below clipping.

That sequence is repeatable, takes about five minutes, and the RAW + neutral-WB step is what eliminates the blue/orange split you're seeing.

ONE-POT CHICKPEA ORZO WITH KALE
Serves 2 dinner + 1 lunch | ~25 min active | 1 pot

QUANTITIES
  1.5 cups (300g) dry orzo
  2 cans (15 oz ea) chickpeas, drained + rinsed
  2 cups crushed tomatoes (about 2/3 of a 28 oz can)
  4 cups broth (chicken or veg)
  1 bunch kale, stems out, leaves torn (~6 cups packed)
  4-5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced
  1/2 cup grated Parmesan (+ rind if you have one)
  3 Tbsp olive oil, salt, pepper, chili flakes (opt.)

TIMED PLAN

  0:00  Heat oil in a wide pot over medium. Add garlic + pinch chili flakes; stir 60 sec, don't brown.

  1:00  Add orzo. Toast, stirring, 90 sec until a few grains go golden and it smells nutty.

  2:30  Add tomatoes, broth, chickpeas, Parmesan rind, 1 tsp salt, pepper. Stir, bring to a boil.

  5:00  Drop to a steady simmer (medium-low). Cook UNcovered, stirring every 2-3 min so nothing sticks, 10-12 min. Splash in water if it tightens up before the orzo is done.

 16:00  Add kale by the handful, stirring to wilt. 3-4 min, just tender, still bright green.

 20:00  Kill heat. Stir in grated Parmesan. Cover, rest 2 min.

 22:00  Uncover, fish out the rind, taste for salt, drizzle olive oil, crack pepper. Serve.

NOTES
  Cleanup is 1 pot, 1 spoon, 1 board, 1 knife.
  Lunch portion: fridge up to 3 days; loosen with a splash of broth or water when reheating.
  If Sam's late: kill heat at 20:00 and cover — holds 10 min without overcooking, orzo keeps absorbing.

Good — I have the original palette and setup context (the Feb 15 plan called for burnt sienna + ultramarine darks with yellow ochre "kept quiet," so what you're seeing now is ochre creeping too loud at the focal cup). Here's the fix.

The problem is value compression, not hue. The pale cup is being read as one band with the ochre tabletop because they share a middle value, so the cup's edge dies. The fix is to push the tabletop darker and slightly cooler so the pale cup reads as light against it — keeping the same three pigments.

ONE RESTRAINED ADJUSTMENT: glaze a thin, cool, dilute ultramarine+burnt-sienna mix (mostly ultramarine, a touch of burnt sienna to keep it from looking chalky-blue) over the tabletop area, just enough to drop it one value step darker than the cup's body. You stay inside the palette, and because the glaze is cool it also reinforces the warm/cool separation without adding a fourth color.

BRUSH-AND-WATER SEQUENCE (work wet-on-dry, paper fully dry first):
1. Test swatch first — on scrap paper or the margin, mix about 4 parts water : 1 part ultramarine + a tiny half-pip of burnt sienna. Lay a stroke; it should read as a soft dusk blue-gray, not sky-blue. If it goes blue-pastel, add a fraction more burnt sienna or a drop more water.
2. Reload the mix, then tap out excess water and most of the pigment on a paper towel — you want a tea-stained consistency, almost a tint. A loaded round brush (size 8–10) is right; go flatter if your tabletop is a wide plane.
3. Lay the glaze in one confident pass along the tabletop, ending about a quarter inch short of the cup's shadow line. Don't push into the cup's wet edge. If a soft bloom appears as it dries, leave it — that's your subtle texture.
4. While that band is still damp (not wet), drop a slightly stronger mix of the same glaze only where the tabletop sits directly behind the cup — a half-inch halo — to deepen the value contrast at the focal point and pull the cup forward.
5. Walk away. Don't touch it for 15–20 minutes.

STOP CONDITION (any one of these means put the brush down):
- The tabletop reads one value step darker than the cup's body when you squint at it from arm's length. That's it. Done.
- The glaze starts to look streaky, mottled, or "painterly" in a fussy way — you've gone past one layer.
- The cup's edge starts to lose its soft lost-and-found line and goes sharp or muddy. The glaze has crept where it shouldn't.
- The yellow-ochre undertone has disappeared entirely from the tabletop. You want it dimmed, not erased — it should still register as warm when you look closely, just quieter than the cup.

If the squint test isn't passing after one dry glaze, do ONE more pass the same way tomorrow — don't chase it wet today. And if the ultramarine goes too cold on you, a single hair of yellow ochre in the mix warms it back without raising the value.

40-min stationary bike, seated only

Warmup (0-5 min)
  Spin at very low resistance. Bring cadence up from ~70 to ~85 rpm over the first few minutes. RPE 2 or less. Don't add resistance until the cadence feels natural.

Main easy effort (5-35 min)
  Cadence 80-90 rpm, seated the whole time — no standing climbs.
  Resistance light to moderate: you should feel the pedal under your foot, but never like you're pushing against it. Conversation pace. RPE 3-4.
  Favor smooth cadence over load. If a coworker could keep talking to you and your foot/ankle stays relaxed on the pedal, you're in the zone. The job here is circulation and easy aerobic work without loading the calf or Achilles.

Cooldown (35-40 min)
  Drop resistance, easy spin, RPE 2 or less, step off.

Resistance guidance (the only real knob)
  Backing off is always the conservative choice. If you can tell you're "pressing" the pedal, you're past easy — drop one notch of resistance and let cadence do the work. Low-cadence heavy-resistance is exactly the load profile you don't want on the ankle.

Stop conditions — end the session, do not push through
  - any sharp or focal ankle pain: joint line, behind/below the malleolus, or along the Achilles
  - an ache or pinch that doesn't ease within 1-2 minutes of dropping to very easy spin
  - calf cramping, gripping, or tightness that changes your pedal stroke
  - any limping or guarded gait when you stand up — treat that as a gait change
  - lightheadedness, chest discomfort, or unusual shortness of breath

Following-day symptom check (same pattern you already use)
  - walking gait unchanged — no favoring, no "walking carefully," no limp
  - no new ankle tenderness over the joint, behind the malleolus, or along the Achilles
  - no new swelling, no new morning stiffness, ankle feels like yesterday
  - calf soft to walk on, not tender
  - sleep and energy at baseline

If anything shows up
  - focal pain or gait change today → cut the next run to 30 min (your standing rule)
  - recurrent focal pain across sessions → clinical follow-up
  - ordinary muscle fatigue with no focal joint findings → proceed with the next scheduled run as planned

BEFORE YOU LEAVE WORK (or first thing when you get home)
- Empty the dishwasher last night — fewer dishes tonight
- Pre-cube a 6oz block of cheddar (½" cubes, back in the fridge in a container)
- Stage boards/trays/serving bowls on the counter so they're grab-and-go
- Toss a stack of napkins in a basket near where you'll set up

THE 45-MINUTE SETUP (do these in this order)

1. KIBO FIRST — 5 min
   Walk him to the quiet interior room with his water bowl, bed, and a long-lasting chew (frozen Kong, bully stick, whatever holds him). Close the door. Tape a note on it: "Kibo settling — please don't knock."
   Do this before you change so he doesn't shadow you for the next 40 minutes.

2. CHANGE & RESET YOURSELF — 3 min
   Work clothes off, quick counter wipe, breath check.

3. BEVERAGE STATION — 10 min
   - Open 2 bottles of wine (1 per ~3 people, with a buffer)
   - Ice in a bowl or small ice bucket; nestle sparkling water in
   - Kettle filled, set on its base
   - Stage: 6 wine glasses, 6 water glasses, 4 mugs, tea bags in a small dish, honey + sugar
   Put it all on one counter or side table so guests can self-serve.

4. SNACK PLATING — 8 min
   - One big bowl of popcorn (pre-buttered if you're feeling it, otherwise plain + salt + a small butter dish)
   - Crackers poured onto a board with a butter knife
   - Cheddar cubes arranged on the same board
   - Olives in a small bowl with a spoon + a tiny empty dish for pits
   No cooking, no stove, no timing.

5. SEATING — 10 min
   - Pull 6 chairs into a loose circle, not rows (book club works better facing each other)
   - One or two low side tables within reach of the circle for glasses/snacks
   - Lamps on, overhead off; one throw draped on a chair
   - Soft playlist already playing low

6. FINAL TOUCHES — last 4-5 min
   - Candle if using
   - Bathroom quick-check: clean hand towel, soap topped up
   - Door unlocked, porch light on
   - Coat pile spot set (bedroom door, or a chair by the entry)

DURING (7:00-9:00)
- Top up sparkling water around 8:00
- Click the kettle on around 8:30 for closing tea
- Don't fuss — let the book drive the conversation; the food is just set dressing

15-MINUTE CLEANUP (in this order)
1. (0-2 min) Stack everything in the kitchen; dump ice and wine dregs
2. (2-3 min) Foil/tin over leftover cheddar and olives → fridge
3. (3-8 min) Load the dishwasher, hit start
4. (8-12 min) Damp cloth over the snack board and any crumb zones; quick sweep of the seating area
5. (12-15 min) Tie off the trash, let Kibo out of the interior room
6. Couch + Kibo. Done.
