Decision math for the two unapproved Helio Start test shapes

Status: prep-only conversation, not a recommendation. Helio Start is still organic-only through 2026-03-31; separate budget approval is still pending; nothing below implies approval, launch authorization, acquisition authority, pipeline treatment, or forecast credit.

1. What the paired caps actually tell us

The recommended shape (min of $15,000 or 50 admitted workspaces) and the fallback (min of $8,000 or 25 admitted workspaces) are exposure caps, not cost projections. The $300 and $320 ratios are pure division — $15,000/50 and $8,000/25 — and they don't tell us any of the things a CAC figure would tell us:

- They are not expected acquisition cost. We have no paid-source conversion evidence yet (that's the whole reason the test is capped), so we cannot put a posterior on either ratio.
- They are not a cost-per-admission ceiling. A ceiling has to be set in dollars per admission; here the dollar side is an absolute ceiling and the admission side is an absolute ceiling, and we don't know which one binds first.
- They are not a target. Setting either ratio as a target before any paid run would be making a number the test is supposed to estimate, which inverts the experiment.

The only honest read of $300 and $320 is: "if we exhaust the dollar limit before the admission limit, every admitted workspace cost us at most this much in media spend; if we exhaust the admission limit first, we landed below this much per admission in media spend." Both arms give an upper bound, not an estimate, and the bound only binds in the direction where the dollar limit is the binding constraint.

2. What we can and can't infer under either cap reaching first

Spend limit binds first (i.e. we run out of dollars before we hit N admissions)
- We learn an *upper* cost-per-admission equal to the ratio ($300 or $320), and we learn it with however many admissions we produced before the spend ran out. That number is the maximum, not the expected cost; the true cost-per-admission could be much lower if late spend was inefficient relative to early spend, or much higher if the test was stopped early on a stop-rule trigger that consumed budget without admissions.
- We learn something about channel mix efficiency only to the extent the channel itself was varied or not.
- We do *not* learn conversion rate cleanly, because we censored on spend, not on time or on a complete funnel.

Admission limit binds first (i.e. we hit N admissions before spending the full budget)
- We learn that the channel produced at least N admitted workspaces within the cap, but we do *not* learn the cost-per-admission — only that it landed at-or-below the ratio as an average, and that number is contaminated by anything that biased early admissions (creative fatigue, audience saturation, day-of-week effects).
- We learn something about sustained volume only to the extent we kept running after hitting N; under the cap as written, the test would stop, so we don't learn that.
- We do *not* learn a CAC distribution, only a single mean that we can't validate.

In both cases, the cap as currently framed gives us a bound, not a calibration. That's fine for a first capped test — it's the right epistemic posture — but it means neither shape, on its own, produces a paid-source conversion number. Anything we report has to be labelled as an upper bound, never as a CAC.

3. 50-workspace vs. 25-workspace shapes — what each can teach against its exposure

50-workspace / $15,000 shape (recommended)
- Exposure: about 3x the dollar and 2x the admission budget of the fallback. Worst-case blast radius if the test misbehaves is bounded but non-trivial — 50 admitted workspaces is a population big enough that a support-load surprise or an unsupported-admission event would be visible, not a single-account anomaly.
- Learning: at 50 admitted workspaces, with paid-source attribution preserved eligibility→admission and complete outcome windows for paid-active, refund-adjusted collected cash, and account-level support effort, we get a read on Day-7 first integration as a leading indicator and the first credible signal on the three mature measures. But: the outcome windows have to fully close before we can call any of those "mature." A 50-workspace test that ends mid-window gives us leading reads only.
- Stop-rule surface area: 50 admits means roughly 50 chances for an unsupported-admission event to occur, which is the right resolution to actually exercise the immediate-stop guardrail. At 25, we get half the resolution.
- Ratio interpretation: $300/admission as an upper bound is a softer signal than $320 — the more permissive cap gives the looser bound.

25-workspace / $8,000 shape (fallback)
- Exposure: smaller blast radius, smaller support-load tail risk, and a tighter upper-bound on dollar-per-admission if spend binds first.
- Learning: at 25 admitted workspaces, we still get the same leading read on Day-7 first integration, but we get materially less power on the three mature measures. Outcome windows matter as much as admission count, and at 25 admits the mature-window read on support effort and refund-adjusted cash will be noisier — a single high-effort account or one larger refund can move the read.
- Stop-rule surface area: at 25 admits, an unsupported-admission event is still a halt, but with fewer admits in flight the chance of triggering the rule is mechanically lower, which means the rule is *less exercised*, not more reliable. If the goal of the capped test is also to validate that the stop rules actually trip, 25 is too small.
- Ratio interpretation: $320/admission as an upper bound is a tighter signal than $300 if spend binds first — a more informative cap, if and only if spend is the binding constraint.

Head-to-head: the 50-workspace shape trades a larger exposure for a larger sample and a higher-resolution stop-rule test. The 25-workspace shape trades learning for blast-radius insurance. There is no shape here that gives us both: a smaller admission cap is also a smaller admission cap. The right comparison is "how much insurance do we want against the worst-case" vs. "how much resolution do we need to call a mature read defensible." That is a Priya-and-budget-owner judgement, not a math judgement.

4. Remaining unknowns (not derivable from the caps alone)

- Channel and audience: still open per the working draft §4.3; CAC distribution depends entirely on this.
- Bid / pacing posture: a $15K cap spent in two weeks and a $15K cap spent in six weeks produce very different learning. The six-week framing in the recommended shape is calendar-time, not exposure-time.
- Baseline conversion assumption: we don't have a paid-source conversion prior to feed the cap-sizing, so the caps are set against exposure tolerance, not against a power calculation. We should be explicit with Priya that the cap sizes were not chosen for statistical power.
- Stop-rule thresholds: account-level-support-minutes threshold, Day-7 halt threshold, and how a stop interacts with the cap (does spend already spent count as exposure, or is the cap on committed spend?) — these still aren't set per §4.5 and §4.6.
- Outcome window length: how long after admission we wait before calling paid-active / refund-adjusted cash / support effort "mature" — still per §4.4 OPEN.
- Refund treatment policy: still per §4.7 OPEN. This affects whether refund-adjusted collected cash is a clean read or a noisy one.
- Whether the Q1 lane's missing-cohort-dates gap changes anything about how the caps are interpreted. Per the standing boundary, the missing-cohort-dates issue is a separate Q1-readiness item and does not block the Q2 prep conversation, but it does mean we are sizing a paid-acquisition test without the prior organic cohort dates in front of us — which is a meta-uncertainty worth naming.

5. Decision questions for Priya (proposal / launch authority)

1. Exposure tolerance: which blast radius is the company comfortable with for a first paid test — 50 admitted workspaces or 25? This is the cap question.
2. Stop-rule resolution: do we want the first capped test to be large enough that the immediate-stop guardrail on unsupported admissions actually gets exercised, or is 25 admits enough surface?
3. Outcome window length: how long is the mature window for paid-active, refund-adjusted collected cash, and account-level support effort — and is the 6-week calendar frame of the recommended shape compatible with that window, or does the window extend past the cap?
4. Day-7 first integration: confirm it stays a leading operating indicator only, with no decision weight in the go/no-go on extending paid acquisition. (This should be a confirmation, not a re-debate.)
5. Pipeline / forecast: confirm again that nothing in this prep shapes a pipeline or forecast number, regardless of outcome.
6. Missing cohort dates: is the Q1 not-board-ready status a constraint on how aggressively the Q2 cap can be sized, or is it treated as fully separate?

6. Decision questions for the budget owner (separate conversation)

1. Dollar ceiling semantics: when the cap says "earlier of $15,000 or 50 admitted workspaces," is the $15,000 a hard ceiling on committed spend, on invoiced spend, or on cash settled? Each reading has a different exposure profile.
2. Budget line and accrual: which budget line does this draw from, and is the full $15,000 reserved at approval or released incrementally against the admission count?
3. Stop-rule accounting: if a stop rule trips at admit #18 of 50 with $9,000 already spent, is that $9,000 the test's cost, or is the remainder of the $15,000 returnable? This matters for whether the cap functions as a true ceiling.
4. Refund-adjusted cash flowback: if refund-adjusted collected cash is a mature read, does the budget owner want the cash side reported on a cash-vs.-accrual basis for this test?

Decision rule for TC-5P8L2 (nontransferable $50, expires 5/13/26 11:59pm PT, that-airline-operated only):

Use it only if all three pass. If any fails, let it expire.

1. Would book anyway. You'd take this exact itinerary at the full pre-credit price on the same dates. The credit is pure upside, not the reason. If the trip only exists to "use the credit," it's manufactured — let it expire.

2. Net fare beats (or matches) your real alternative. Compare the post-credit total against the cheapest reasonable option elsewhere, factoring in your time, routing, and schedule. If this airline's flight is materially worse on price, timing, or convenience even after the $50, the credit doesn't change the math.

3. Change/cancel terms fit the trip's real risk. Read the fare class rules before booking. Nontransferable credits often pair with non-refundable, non-changeable fares. Don't trade $50 for a locked-in ticket on a date you might need to move.

Tie-breaker: if passes 1 and 3 but the post-credit fare is only marginally better than alternatives, default to the more flexible/cheaper option elsewhere. A $50 credit isn't worth a worse itinerary.

If none of your near-term travel plans hits all three, the right call is deliberate expiry. $50 is the ceiling, not the floor — don't let the deadline manufacture demand.

Three-value thumbnail

V1 (lightest): the warm floor strip where sun pools, plus the bright catch where it grazes Kibo's curled back. Leave paper white here; don't paint it.
V2 (midtone): the cool interior shadow on wall and floor surrounding him. This is the field Kibo sits in.
V3 (darkest): Kibo's coat, with the deepest notes only in the curl-crevice, under the chin, the eye, and the edge where his body meets the warm strip.

Read it as three shapes — light-strip, shadow-field, dog — not as fur. If the three shapes are clear, the study works.

Mixes (three pigments only)

  Cool interior shadow: ultramarine + a touch of burnt sienna. Dilute to mid value. If it goes too purple, add water, not pigment.
  Warm light strip: yellow ochre + a small touch of burnt sienna. Very dilute, almost tea-strength.
  Kibo's coat body: burnt sienna + ultramarine — your workhorse. Leans warm-neutral, sits darker than the background.
  Kibo's deepest darks: straight burnt sienna, or burnt sienna + ultramarine at full strength. No black.
  Edge note where Kibo crosses the warm strip: a touch more ultramarine in the coat mix along that edge so he doesn't dissolve into the warm.

Separation comes from value (Kibo's darks are darker than the field) and temperature (warm darks against a cool field). The merging you're seeing is the soft edge — let it happen wet-into-wet. A dry-brushed edge where he crosses the light strip gives you the hard edge.

Order

  1. Light strip first, wet-on-dry, dilute yellow ochre + burnt sienna. Let it dry fully.
  2. Cool shadow field, wet-on-dry around the dog's silhouette, or wet-into-wet where you want him to merge. Keep it loose — you're describing the room, not finishing it.
  3. Kibo's body in the mid-mix. Soft edges into shadow; harder edge across the dry light strip.
  4. Darks last and sparingly: straight burnt sienna in the curl, under the chin, the eye, nose. Two or three strokes, not twenty.
  5. If a highlight needs lifting on the coat, lift with a damp brush now — don't add white.

Stopping point

Stop when: the silhouette reads at arm's length, the eye is in, one warm-light edge is present, and the background is suggested rather than described. If you find yourself brushing individual fur strokes, you're past it. A dark coat flattens from overwork, not from undertreatment — every extra pass costs you the soft edge you came for.

Happy to help. Here's a plain-text rundown — tomorrow's the 6th, appointment at 8:30am.

  MORNING CHECKLIST
  - Normal breakfast — local anesthetic doesn't require fasting, so eat what you'd usually eat
  - Take any regular medications with water as usual
  - Brush and floss normally (clean mouth helps the procedure)
  - Plan to leave with enough time to arrive by 8:20am (10 min early)
  - Bring: ID, insurance card, payment method, a current medication list
  - Wear something comfortable
  - Local anesthetic typically doesn't impair driving, but if you'd rather not drive yourself, line up a ride — your call
  - Skip alcohol tonight and tomorrow morning (standard pre-op)

  PRACTICAL PRECAUTIONS
  - Numbness usually lasts 2–4 hours — be careful not to bite your cheek, lip, or tongue
  - Don't chew on the treated side until full feeling returns
  - Skip very hot drinks while numb — you can't reliably feel burns
  - Before you leave the chair, the dentist should check your bite; if the new filling feels "high" or your bite feels off, say so before you go (a small adjustment now saves a return trip)
  - Once numbness wears off, eat gently on that side for the first day; if it's a composite (tooth-colored) filling you can usually chew on it normally once tenderness fades
  - If you grind or clench, mention it — it influences material choice and follow-up

  EASY FOODS WHILE NUMB
  Best bets — minimal chewing, lukewarm temperature:
  - Smoothies or shakes (drink from a cup on the un-numb side, not a straw right away if there's any gum tenderness)
  - Yogurt, pudding, applesauce
  - Mashed potatoes, scrambled eggs, oatmeal (warm, not hot)
  - Soft pasta, well-cooked rice, soup
  - Hummus, very soft bread (no crusty rolls)

  Avoid while numb or on the treated side:
  - Anything requiring real chewing (nuts, raw veggies, meat, crusty bread)
  - Sticky things (caramel, taffy, gummy candy)
  - Very hot foods and drinks
  - Biting into things with the front teeth (apples, sandwiches, corn on the cob) — pull sideways with the untreated side instead

  NORMAL POST-FILLING SENSITIVITY vs. CALL THE DENTIST

  Usually fine, settles on its own:
  - Brief cold sensitivity (a zing that fades in seconds) for 1–2 weeks
  - Mild tenderness when biting that improves day over day
  - Gum soreness or a small bruise near the injection site for a day or two
  - A "high" or odd bite — worth popping back for a quick adjustment, not urgent
  - Mild ache relieved by OTC ibuprofen or acetaminophen

  Call the dentist (same day if severe):
  - Throbbing, spontaneous pain that doesn't respond to OTC pain relievers, or pain that wakes you at night
  - Pain or sensitivity that gets worse after 2–3 days instead of better
  - Swelling in the face, jaw, or gums around the tooth
  - Fever, or a bad taste / drainage suggesting infection
  - The filling feels loose, chips, or comes out
  - Lingering bite pain a few days in (often a simple bite adjustment, but worth checking)
  - Numbness that hasn't returned to normal after 4–5 hours
  - Any signs of allergic reaction — rash, hives, trouble breathing (call 911 for breathing issues)
  - Sharp pain on biting that lingers after release — can signal a deeper crack into the tooth

  Quick rule of thumb: mild and improving = watch and wait. Severe, worsening, swelling, fever, or a filling that feels loose = call.

Skillet gnocchi with burst tomatoes, spinach, and parmesan — one pan, ~25 min, minimal cleanup.

Approximate amounts (2 servings):
  Gnocchi: 14–16 oz (about 4/5 of the package; cook the rest as you like)
  Olive oil: 3 tbsp, plus a small drizzle to finish
  Garlic: 3–4 cloves, thinly sliced or minced
  Cherry tomatoes: the full pint, halved (or quarter any large ones)
  Baby spinach: all 5 oz, roughly torn if clumps are big
  Parmesan: 1/2 cup finely grated, plus a little extra to pass
  Salt, black pepper, optional pinch of red pepper flakes
  Optional: a squeeze of lemon at the end

Sequence:
  1. Prep (≈5 min): halve tomatoes, mince garlic, grate parm. No need to boil water — shelf-stable gnocchi goes straight into the pan.
  2. Crisp the gnocchi (≈8 min): heat 3 tbsp oil in a 12-inch skillet over medium-high until shimmering. Add gnocchi in a single layer, season with salt and pepper, and leave them alone for 4–5 min so they get a golden crust on the bottom. Toss and cook another 3–4 min until lightly crisped all over.
  3. Tomatoes + garlic (≈4 min): push gnocchi to one side. Add tomatoes and garlic to the cleared space with a pinch of salt and red pepper flakes if using. Cook 2–3 min, pressing a few tomatoes with the back of a spoon so they burst and start making a sauce, then stir everything together.
  4. Wilt spinach (≈2 min): add spinach in two handfuls, stirring until just wilted. If the pan looks dry, add a splash of water.
  5. Finish (≈1 min): off heat, scatter in the parmesan and toss so it melts into a light sauce. Taste for salt, finish with pepper and a tiny drizzle of olive oil or a squeeze of lemon.

Serve straight from the pan. Cleanup is basically the skillet, a cutting board, and a knife.

THREE-VALUE PLAN (dark glass bottle, cool interior shadow)

  Light   = the reflected window highlight. Preserve as paper white.
            No paint in this zone.
  Mid     = the bottle body in reflected cool shadow. Cool gray-blue,
            slightly green. Lean cool, never chromatic.
  Dark    = cast shadow on the surface + the deepest form core.
            Heavy ultramarine + burnt sienna (~2:1) reads as a
            chromatic near-black.
  Accent  = a single dry-brush yellow ochre on the rim/lip where warm
            light wraps. Optional, last thing, do not overdo.

MIXING ORDER

  1. Pre-mix on the palette before the brush touches paper.
        Dark: ultramarine + burnt sienna, 2:1, fully loaded (dries
              slowest, buys you working time).
        Mid : ultramarine + burnt sienna + a touch of yellow ochre,
              ~1.5 : 1 : 0.25. Pigment load LOW — granulating tea,
              not a puddle. Low load is exactly what keeps the
              highlight clean when you work beside it.
        Ochre puddle, slightly thicker, kept warm.

  2. Paper order:
        a. Cast shadow first — wet-into-wet on a pre-wet zone under
           the bottle for the soft edge.
        b. Mid wash on the body, wet-on-dry, advancing toward the
           highlight but never crossing it.
        c. Rim/lip ochre last, dry brush.

EDGE STRATEGY

  Hard  : where the cast shadow lands on a hard surface, and where the
          bottle's contour catches a clean line of light. Dry paper,
          loaded brush, one decisive stroke, leave it.
  Soft  : where the form shadow curves away from the window light, and
          the far-side contour where glass dissolves into background.
          Pre-wet a small zone, drop dark into it, tilt, walk away.
  Lost-and-found : alternate hard and soft along the contour in short
          ~1–2 cm sections. This is what reads as glass instead of a
          cutout. Do it last.

HIGHLIGHT PRESERVATION

  Pick one method. Don't blend them.

  Reserve + dry surround (default for a 45-min block):
    Leave the highlight zone bone-dry. Paint the midtone up to its
    edge, not across it. If you nudge into it, lift immediately with
    a clean damp brush before the wash sets. Once it dries you cannot
    fix it without roughing the paper.

  Masking fluid (safer if you're already nervous about it):
    Brush on first, let it fully dry, paint freely, remove at the end.

  Mud is what happens when a high-load midtone sits next to paper
  white and you go back in. Low load, one pass, then leave it.

STOP CONDITION

  Hard stop at 40 minutes. Five-minute buffer to dry and assess.

  Any one of these ends the block:
    - Squint test: the three values separate cleanly. Adding more
      collapses them.
    - The highlight is still paper white. If it isn't, fix it now with
      a damp lift — do not "improve" it with paint.
    - You reach for another stroke to darken, not to shape.
      Darken = stop.
    - The paper shows sheen loss or pilling at the edges. Stop now.

TIMING (within 45)

  00–05   Mask or reserve the highlight. Pencil sketch, no more.
  05–15   Pre-mix pools. Cast shadow wet-into-wet. Let dry.
  15–30   Mid wash on body, dry-brush toward highlight, never
          crossing the reserve.
  30–40   Rim ochre. Lost-and-found contour. Squint test.
  40–45   Stop. Lift any wet nudge into the highlight. Walk away.

Both critiques are right, and they connect.

The "hardest thing" prompt does two things at once that you don't want from a 5-minute opener: it commits the writer to the adversity genre before they've written a word, and it asks for disclosure that some kids won't safely hand to a peer 10 minutes later. The opener should be a low-stakes way to get pen moving — concrete, recent, sensory. Something like "write a moment from the last week you keep returning to" or "write about something you noticed that the person next to you probably didn't." Either produces specific material fast; neither requires a kid to mine their life for hardship in front of a room.

"Interesting" is the right thing to flag. It's a reader-reaction word that trains students to perform for approval rather than write for clarity, and it gives the partner nothing actionable to say. Better craft questions for the trade: "tell them the one sentence you actually remember" or "where does the writing get most specific?" The first tests what's landing; the second points at craft. Either gives the writer something concrete to use in the rewrite block.

The 15-minute rewrite is the strongest part of the structure as-is. Don't touch it.

Here's a 35-minute redesign that addresses Marcus's two critiques and adds the four pieces you asked for: ordinary-or-difficult choice, one concrete scene, specific feedback criteria, and an explicit opt-out from disclosure.

  35-MINUTE REDESIGN

  1. 5 MIN — PICK A MOMENT AND START WRITING

    Board prompt, read verbatim:

      "Write a moment you keep returning to. It can be ordinary —
       a routine, a place, a small encounter — or, if you choose,
       something difficult you've worked through. If you'd rather
       not draw on your own life today, write a scene you've
       observed: someone else's moment, a place, an object.
       You won't be asked which you chose, and you can change
       your mind halfway through."

    The last line is the opt-out: no student is on the hook to
    explain whether the scene is autobiographical, and no one
    is steered toward hardship.

  2. 10 MIN — DEVELOP ONE CONCRETE SCENE

    Zoom into a single moment. Stop summarising the whole
    story. Add three things on the page:

      - one physical detail (a texture, a sound, a light)
      - one line of dialogue, or one overheard phrase
      - one action the person in the scene takes

    If a student finishes early, they revise the same scene
    for more specificity — not more length.

  3. 10 MIN — TRADE AND ANSWER THREE QUESTIONS

    Partner writes answers directly on the draft. No talk yet:

      a. What's the one sentence you actually remember?
      b. Where does the writing get most specific? Where
         does it go vague?
      c. Can you picture one physical detail? Which one?

    These replace "interesting." Each is a craft question
    with a written answer the writer can act on. Trade back,
    read silently, no discussion.

  4. 10 MIN — REWRITE THE OPENING PARAGRAPH

    Use the partner's three written answers. Pick the one
    fix that matters most — the sentence they remembered,
    the spot that went vague, or the missing physical detail
    — and rewrite the opening to land it.

    This is the block from the original outline; it survives
    intact because it was already the strongest part.

  TOTAL: 5 + 10 + 10 + 10 = 35.

Two tradeoffs worth flagging for Marcus:

  - The volunteer read-aloud at the end is gone. In a
    35-minute slot that asks students to disclose, the share-out
    is the part most likely to make a kid regret what they wrote.
    If he wants it back, the cleanest cut is the rewrite block
    (10 → 8 min) plus 2 min share-out.

  - The rewrite is 10 min, not 15. That's still enough for an
    opening paragraph when the partner has handed the writer
    one specific fix. If students routinely need more, the
    place to recover time is the develop block, not the rewrite.

For a mild edge buckle on a fully dry 140-lb cold-press sheet, the safe path is gentle overall humidification followed by long, even pressing — nothing touches the painted face, no heat, no adhesive.

Sequence

  1. Inspect first. Confirm the buckle is only at the edge, the paint film is fully intact, and the sheet has no fiber damage, thinning, or foxing. If ripples cross the image area or the paper feels soft, skip to the stop condition.

  2. Build a press station on a flat surface:
       Bottom rigid board (foam core or plywood), larger than the sheet.
       3-4 clean blotters on the board (acid-free blotting paper or unprinted newsprint).
       One sheet of glassine or silicone release paper, slightly larger than the painting.
       Top: a second rigid board with 10-15 lb of books distributed evenly.

  3. Passive humidification (do this first — gentlest option):
       Lay the painting paint-side up on the blotter stack.
       Cover the painted face with the glassine/release sheet — it sits on the paint but is inert and non-adhesive.
       Place the whole stack inside a clean trash bag or closed plastic bin with a small dish of water 6+ inches away (not touching the sheet). Close for 45-60 minutes. The paper takes up ambient humidity evenly from both sides.
       Remove from the chamber.

  4. Press:
       Paint face stays up, glassine still covering it.
       Add 3-4 fresh dry blotters on top of the glassine.
       Place the top board and distribute the weight evenly.
       Leave undisturbed 24 hours.

  5. Check by lifting one corner. If flat, store between clean blotters in the portfolio. If a slight edge buckle remains, repeat steps 3-4 once with 60-90 minutes of humidification. Do not exceed two attempts.

Materials (all you need)
  - Blotting paper or plain unprinted newsprint
  - Glassine or silicone/parchment release sheet (art-supply or kitchen parchment)
  - Two rigid boards larger than the sheet
  - 10-15 lb of even weight
  - Clean plastic bag or bin + small dish of water for the humidity chamber

Stop condition — take it to a paper conservator if any of the following:
  - The buckle does not improve after two gentle attempts, or it worsens.
  - Any paint disturbance appears: edge bleed, lifting, tide lines, color shift, or white bloom.
  - The buckle extends across the image area rather than sitting at the edge.
  - The paper shows fiber damage, thinning, or you don't know its age or origin.
  - The sheet has meaningful sentimental or monetary value — at that point the conservator's fee is the cheaper risk.

Out-of-pocket formula (80% reimbursement after deductible):
- If covered expenses E ≤ deductible d: OOP = E
- If E > d: OOP = d + 0.20·(E − d) = 0.20·E + 0.80·d

Smoky Chickpea Tacos with Lime-Cabbage Slaw

Tonight: 2 tacos.  Lunch: 1 reserved tortilla + portion of chickpea mix + slaw, packed separate so nothing gets soggy.

Slaw (do first, lets it wilt while you cook):
- Half the cabbage, sliced thin (mandoline if you've got it, or just go thin with a knife)
- Half the lime, juiced over it
- Half the scallions, sliced (whites and a few greens)
- Pinch salt, toss, leave on the counter

Smoky chickpeas:
- Drain and rinse the can
- ~1.5 tbsp oil in a skillet, medium heat
- 1-2 garlic cloves, minced, 30 seconds
- Chickpeas in. Smash about half with a fork so you get some creamy chunks and some whole ones
- 1 tsp smoked paprika, salt, pepper. 4-5 min, stir occasionally, let the edges get a little crisp

Lime crema:
- ~3 tbsp Greek yogurt stirred with the rest of the lime and a splash of water to loosen. Pinch of salt.

Tortillas:
- Dry skillet or gas flame, ~30 sec a side. Stack and cover with a towel.

Build: slaw, chickpeas, drizzle of crema, scallion greens on top. Eat 2, pack the rest.

Lunch tomorrow: warm the chickpea mix in a skillet with a splash of water; warm the reserved tortilla; assemble with the slaw (it holds overnight fine, especially with the lime). Lime wedge in the bag if you want it bright again.

Total time: about 15-18 minutes, mostly hands-off.

CHICKPEA + CABBAGE SKILLET TACOS (one pan, ~20 min, serves 2-3)

Ingredients
  1 can (15 oz) chickpeas, drained
  1/2 small head green cabbage (~3 cups shredded)
  1 tbsp olive oil
  1 tsp ground cumin
  1 tsp chili powder
  1/2 tsp smoked paprika (or regular)
  1/2 tsp salt, plus more to taste
  1/4 tsp black pepper
  squeeze of lime (optional)
  tortillas, for serving (optional)

Sequence (≈18 min hands-on)
  0:00  Shred cabbage into rough 1/2-inch strips
  3:00  Heat oil in large skillet over medium-high until shimmering
  4:00  Add cabbage, toss to coat, spread in an even layer
  5:00  Let sit undisturbed 2 min to char, then stir; repeat once more
  9:00  Add chickpeas, all spices, and 2 tbsp water
 10:00  Smash ~1/3 of chickpeas with a wooden spoon or potato masher (gives the filling body)
 11:00  Stir, then leave to cook 4-5 min, stirring every minute, until chickpeas are hot and the mixture looks cohesive (not watery, not dry)
 16:00  Taste, adjust salt, squeeze lime over
 17:00  Warm tortillas directly over a gas flame or in a dry pan, 20 sec/side
 18:00  Serve

Notes
  - Cabbage chars faster than it wilts — don't stir constantly or it'll just steam gray.
  - The mash step is what makes it taste like a taco filling rather than a side dish.
  - If using salted canned chickpeas, drop the added salt to 1/4 tsp and adjust at the end.

Cleanup: one skillet, one cutting board, one knife, one spoon. Done.

Limited palette (3 pigments + paper white):
  - Payne's Gray — cool mass shadow
  - Burnt Sienna — warm reflected edge (dilute, low chroma)
  - Optional: Raw Umber or a pre-mixed chromatic black (ultramarine + burnt umber) for deepest accents only

Three-value plan:
  Value 1 (lightest) — paper white + the faintest warm reflected wash. Reserved ridges, eye catchlight, brightest underbelly curl. Either no pigment or a whisper of dilute sienna.
  Value 2 (mid) — cool Payne's Gray, slightly neutralized with a touch of sienna. The bulk of the dark coat in window shadow. This is the shape carrier.
  Value 3 (darkest) — neutral deep, small shapes only. Eye socket, deepest tuck of the curl, contact shadow on the rug.

Mixing order (do this before touching paper):
  1. Three water-heavy puddles: cool mass (Payne's + whisper of sienna), warm light (sienna, very dilute), deep accent (slightly stronger Payne's or a separate chromatic black).
  2. Test on scrap. The three puddles should read as 3 distinct steps — not 5, not muddy. If the warm puddle looks orange, add water until it reads as warm gray, not orange.

75-minute sequence:
  0-10  Gesture in pencil only — contour where the light/shadow divide crosses the silhouette. Dot the eye, nose, ear. Stop drawing.
  10-25 Warm reflected wash first. Damp (not wet) paper in the warm zones: underbelly, leg curls, edge facing the rug. Drop dilute sienna. If it goes orange anywhere, lift immediately with a clean damp brush.
  25-50 Cool mass shadow. Damp brush, Payne's Gray into the shadow side. Paint AROUND your reserved highlights, never over them. One connected shape for the whole body — don't segment into leg/leg/back. This is where the form lives.
  50-65 Darkest accents (value 3). Eye socket, deepest tuck, contact shadow on the rug. Small shapes, fully loaded pigment. Dry between each or they bloom together and lose punch.
  65-72 Face only. Eye catchlight = paper (just avoid it). Nose leather = one shape, one highlight. Muzzle as one soft value. No whiskers. No individual hairs. Stop at 72 even if you want more.

Edge strategy:
  Hard edges — outer silhouette against the rug, the eye, the nose, the deepest tuck. Save these for the last 10 minutes.
  Soft / lost edges — where the dark body curves into shadow internally, and the transition from cool mass to warm reflected light inside the form.
  The hard/soft split is what keeps the coat from flattening into one value.

Face priorities (in order — stop after #3):
  1. Eye — one dark shape with one reserved catchlight. This single mark does most of the work.
  2. Nose leather — single value, one highlight, hard edge on the lit side, soft on the shadow side.
  3. Muzzle — one soft value, lost edge into the cheek. Done.

Stop condition (any one ends the session):
  - Clock hits 75 min.
  - A fourth value is creeping in (you overmixed — accept the three you have).
  - The warm reflected edge reads orange (it isn't, once dry, against the cool gray — don't add pigment to "fix" it).
  - You reach for the face to "improve" it. The face is the first thing that dies from overwork. If it's reading at 65 min, leave it alone.

After 75: don't judge. Put it on the drying rack face-out, look tomorrow with fresh eyes.

HEALTH PLAN ARITHMETIC — FRAMEWORK
================================================================

1) ANNUAL PREMIUM (employee share only, what you pay)
----------------------------------------------------------------
Annual premium = employee contribution per pay period x pay periods
                + 2 (if biweekly) or x 12 (if monthly)
If your employer picks up a %, use only your share:
  Your annual premium = Total annual premium x (1 - employer %)

Often the cheapest-looking plan on premium is the HDHP; the
employer HSA contribution is the offset that often makes it cheaper
in low-claim years.

2) HDHP EMPLOYER HSA CONTRIBUTION (the offset)
----------------------------------------------------------------
This is free money toward your deductible — treat it as a credit:
  Effective premium (HDHP) = Annual premium - Employer HSA contribution

For a PPO/HMO, the employer usually contributes $0 to anything
medical-equivalent, so no offset.

3) EFFECTIVE FIXED ANNUAL COST BEFORE ANY CARE
----------------------------------------------------------------
This is what you pay in a year where you only get preventive care
(which ACA-compliant plans cover at $0, so it bypasses deductible):
  HDHP:  Annual premium - Employer HSA contribution
         (+ any HSA contribution YOU make, if you want to net that out)
  PPO:   Annual premium
         (+ any employer-funded HRA/FSA credit if applicable)

----------------------------------------------------------------
Allowed = negotiated rate, post-network discount, pre-OOP-max.
This is the right denominator — never the billed/sticker amount.

For each plan, walk through:
  a) You pay 100% up to the deductible
  b) After deductible: you pay coinsurance % (e.g. 20%) up to

  c) Above OOP max: plan pays 100%

  If allowed <= deductible:
     Your cost = allowed
  Else if allowed <= OOP max:
     Your cost = deductible + (allowed - deductible) x coinsurance
  Else:
     Your cost = OOP max

  Total = Annual premium (+/- HSA contribution) + Your cost above

TIRE PRESSURE — CONSERVATIVE IMMEDIATE SEQUENCE

CONTEXT
Three tires at placard (34-35) and one at 29 = ~6 psi shortfall on the front-right. Cold weather alone typically drops pressure 1-2 psi per 10°F; a 6 psi gap on a single tire is more than weather explains — treat it as a probable slow leak until you prove otherwise. No visible damage and no audible hiss doesn't rule it out; most slow leaks are silent.

STEP 1 — CONFIRM COLD BASELINE BEFORE INFLATING
- Tire must be truly cold: parked 3+ hours, or driven under 1 mile at low speed.
- Re-measure all four with the same gauge. Record FR psi, time, ambient temp.
- If FR is now 30+, weather is contributing; if still ~29 cold, leak is more likely.

STEP 2 — INFLATE TO PLACARD, NOT ABOVE
- Bring FR to 35 psi cold (door-sticker value, NOT the sidewall max).
- Top off the other three only if under 35; do not over-inflate any.
- Compressors heat air and over-read — re-measure after a minute or two, expect to settle.

STEP 3 — SAME-DAY RECHECK
- Drive locally (see limits below).
- After 2-4 hours of sitting, re-measure FR. Convert to cold-equivalent by subtracting ~2-3 psi from a hot reading.
- If cold-equivalent has dropped more than ~1 psi since inflation, you have a measurable leak.

STEP 4 — 24-HOUR AND 48-HOUR COLD RECHECKS
- Next morning before driving, FR should still read ~35 psi (±1) if there's no leak.
- Repeat once more the following morning.
- Two consecutive mornings of measurable drop = book the shop before any highway trip.

STEP 5 — LOCAL-DRIVING LIMITS UNTIL CLEARED
- Stay off highway/freeway speeds until pressure holds overnight.
- No heavy loads (no passengers + cargo piled up, no towing).
- Keep speed moderate (~50 mph or under); avoid long loaded sweeping curves.
- Re-check FR before every drive for the first several days.
- For the airport run with extra weight (Mom + luggage), run fronts a couple psi above placard — but only after confirming no leak.

DO NOT DRIVE IF ANY OF THESE ARE TRUE
- Visible sidewall bulge, crack, or cut exposing casing or threads.
- Hissing or obvious air loss.
- TPMS warning returns right after inflation.
- Tire visibly sagging or you feel a soft "thump" over bumps.
- Pressure below ~25 psi cold (sidewall failure risk, especially on a front steering tire).
- New or worsening vibration, pulling, or thumping after inflation.

GO DIRECTLY TO A TIRE SHOP (DON'T JUST KEEP TOPPING OFF) IF
- Pressure drops more than 1-2 psi per day cold, or any unexpected drop overnight.
- You find a nail, screw, or embedded debris. Don't pull it — driving on it to a shop is usually fine; pulling it can dump the tire fast.
- TPMS light returns after a confirmed correct inflation.
- FR ends up more than ~3 psi below the other front once everything's settled — leak or failing bead/seal.
- Uneven tread wear visible on FR that wasn't there before (it may have been low longer than you noticed).

FOR MOM'S AIRPORT PICKUP
- Don't take a highway trip until FR has held pressure at least 48 hours through a normal day/night cycle.
- If the timeline is tight, book a tire shop visit within the next couple of days. A plug/patch on a small puncture is typically 30-60 minutes and cheap — much better than a roadside failure at highway speed.
- Last resort: a properly inflated tire with a slow leak can usually be driven cautiously to a shop. If it's losing more than ~1 psi per hour, do not start that drive.

Here's how to explain it to her, in plain language:

"$49 copay after the deductible" means the $49 is the price Mom pays *only once the plan's $615 deductible has been satisfied for the year*. Until that $615 is reached, the $49 copay doesn't apply to Ventolin — instead she pays the plan's negotiated price for the inhaler (the actual cost the plan has arranged), and 100% of what she pays counts toward getting to $615. The two tier-1 generics are different: their $0 preferred-pharmacy copay applies from day one, regardless of whether the deductible has been met, so those never cost her anything at a preferred pharmacy.

Two simple examples, using a representative $48 negotiated price for Ventolin:

Before the $615 deductible is met
- Ventolin fill at preferred pharmacy → Mom pays $48 (the negotiated price, not $49). That $48 counts toward the deductible; $567 still needed.
- A tier-1 generic at the same pharmacy → Mom pays $0. Nothing is subtracted from the deductible because there was nothing to pay.

After the $615 deductible is met
- Ventolin fill at preferred pharmacy → Mom pays $49, plan covers the rest of the drug cost.
- A tier-1 generic → still $0.

So the only Ventolin-specific change in plain terms is: until $615 of out-of-pocket spending has been tallied for the year, each Ventolin fill costs the full negotiated price (often in the $30–$60 range for this inhaler) instead of a flat $49; once $615 is reached, every preferred-pharmacy Ventolin fill is exactly $49 for the rest of the plan year. The two generics stay free either way.

One precise question worth confirming with the plan (or the ANOC's deductible section), because the wording can mean different things:

"Does spending on the $0 tier-1 generics count toward the $615 deductible, or only spending on drugs with a copay-after-deductible structure like Ventolin?"

That single answer tells her whether the generics are truly 'free and irrelevant to the deductible' or whether every fill — including the $0 ones — quietly chips away at the $615. It doesn't change anything about today's review; it's just the one fact worth pinning down so the rest of the math in the ANOC makes sense.

Decision checklist — fill new Rx now vs. keep current glasses

Reasons to fill now
- End-of-screen-day blur is happening often enough that you noticed it and called it out
- New Rx is modest, so adaptation should be quick and cheap
- Updated Rx on file is useful even if you wait to buy lenses (lets you order online, backup pair, etc.)
- If your current frames are aging (loose hinges, worn coating, scratches in your central vision), frame condition alone can justify a refresh

Reasons to keep current for now
- No safety or comfort problem at distance, driving, or daily wear
- Mild end-of-day blur could be dry eye or fatigue rather than Rx change — an artificial-lube drop, a 20-20-20 break habit, or screen-distance tweak is essentially free to try first
- Filling "because it's new" costs ~$150–$400+ for a small visual gain you may not subjectively notice
- Insurance / FSA timing — if you've already used this year's benefit, waiting until January is rational

A reasonable middle path
- Buy just the updated lenses for your existing frames if frames are in good shape
- Or get a separate dedicated computer pair (cheap single-vision or occupational Rx, often +0.25 to +0.50 over your distance Rx) and keep current glasses for everything else
- Order lenses only after wearing the new Rx in the exam-room trial for a full day if your provider offers a trial frame

Re-evaluate / re-check trigger
- New onset: blur at distance, double vision, night-driving difficulty, or any of the red flags you already screened (pain, flashes, new floaters, headache, nausea, imbalance) → fill sooner and call the clinic
- Otherwise, default decision is fine to revisit at your next annual exam

Bottom line
- No urgency either way. The mild end-of-day blur is the only signal pointing toward filling; try a dry-eye / ergonomics fix first if you want a no-cost test, or get a cheap dedicated computer pair if you want the visual comfort without replacing your main glasses.

This is a decision aid, not a clinical recommendation. If anything in the red-flag list appears, contact your eye-care provider directly.

Lamp placement (do these in order, ~2 minutes):

1. Put the lamp on the side of the paper opposite your painting hand, head angled ~30–45° down toward the block. If you paint right-handed, that means upper-left of the paper; left-handed, upper-right. The bulb/diffuser should not be visible from your normal seated posture — tilt the head until you can only see the lit paper.
2. Raise the lamp so the hot spot sits on the paper, not on your hand or brush. ~18–24" above the block works for most task lamps; closer = more glare risk on wet washes, farther = uneven falloff.
3. Set the foam board on the side of the paper opposite the lamp, tilted up ~30° to bounce spill light back into the shadow side. Same-side placement does nothing; flipping it later will tell you why — you'll see values collapse on the shadow side.
4. Glare verify: lay down a wet wash across the block, then move your head through every angle you'd actually view from while painting. If a specular hotspot tracks your head, rotate the lamp head 5–10° (around the vertical axis, not the tilt — tilt changes coverage) until the wet surface reads as a flat, uniform value. Recheck; this is the only step that has to be repeated.

Checking sequence (run once, then anytime you swap lamps or seasons):

5. Spectrum sanity check — paint small labeled swatches of your trouble pairs (ultramarine vs. cerulean, viridian vs. sap green, burnt sienna vs. burnt umber, yellow ochre vs. raw sienna) plus a complement-mixed gray. View under the lamp, then the next overcast midday hold them next to a north-facing window. If a swatch shifts hue or value materially, the lamp is biased there — note the direction and pre-adjust your mixes under that lamp (e.g., if ultramarine reads too cool, expect it to warm and violet-shift in daylight). "Neutral-daylight" LEDs without a stated CRI ≥95 / R9 ≥90 are the usual culprit; if R9 isn't published, that's your hint.
6. Value ladder check — paint a 6–7 step single-pigment value scale (payne's gray thinned in even steps is fine). Under the lamp, every step must stay distinguishable. If steps 2 and 3 merge, either the foam board is filling too aggressively (tip it flatter or move it farther) or the lamp is washing out mid-values (drop brightness one notch).
7. Adaptation buffer — give yourself ~5–10 minutes under the lamp before judging color on a real piece. The first few minutes of any lighting change carry bias from the prior room light, and that's the most common reason a "painting problem" turns out to be a lamp effect.

Two notes worth keeping in mind: the lamp's white balance is irrelevant to value judgments and very relevant to hue judgments, so use the foam-board-lit side for value checks and a quick head-tilt to shade the paper from the lamp for hue-mixing decisions. And if you photograph work under the lamp, set a custom white balance off a neutral card under it — otherwise the photo lies about what you saw, and you'll second-guess real problems later.

Practical comparison across the three options. I don't have specifics on your vision plan, FSA/HSA status, or which online retailer you're considering, so dollar figures below are typical ranges — verify against your actual terms before deciding.

Cost
  In-network: insurer covers a frame allowance (commonly $130–$200) and lenses after a copay ($10–$25). You pay the overage on frames above the allowance plus any add-ons (blue-light, photochromic, progressive upgrades, high-index). Total out-of-pocket typically $0 to a few hundred dollars.
  Online: no insurance applied at checkout unless the retailer is in-network with your plan. Retail base $30–$200 for frames+lenses. Out-of-network reimbursement later can claw back part of it but rarely the full price.
  Wait: $0 now. Cost: if current pair fails before you reorder, you have no backup; if you time it to plan-year reset, you forfeit the 2026 benefit if unused.

Adjustment
  In-network: walk-in, free, same-day. Optician reshapes temples, swaps nose pads, tightens screws.
  Online: DIY or ship back (often at your cost, 1–2 weeks round-trip). Higher risk if the new Rx is progressive or includes prism — small fitting errors cause real discomfort.
  Wait: not applicable. Side note: 6+ months of waiting also ages the current pair's hardware (screws, spring hinges, nose pads).

Remake
  In-network: prescription-error and manufacturer-defect remakes typically covered 30–90 days at no charge. The optician owns the problem.
  Online: policies vary. Many offer a 30-day prescription remake; some charge a restocking fee on frames. Quality variance (axis, optical center, PD) is higher — errors only show up after you wear them.
  Wait: not applicable.

Reimbursement
  In-network: provider bills insurer directly; you owe only copay + overages. No paperwork.
  Online (out-of-network): pay full at checkout, submit itemized receipt (frame + lens breakdown, Rx, date of service) for reimbursement per your plan's out-of-network schedule — usually a smaller allowance than in-network.
  Online (in-network partnership): some retailers (e.g., Warby Parker, GlassesUSA, EyeBuyDirect depending on your carrier) bill your insurer directly; works like option 1.
  Wait: not applicable.

Timing
  In-network: lab turnaround typically 5–10 business days; same/next-day possible on simple single-vision.
  Online: 7–21 days (lab + shipping), plus another week if a remake is needed.
  Wait: flexible, but bounded by FSA/HSA "use it or lose it" deadline (often 12/31 with grace period or partial carryover), plan-year frequency limit (most vision plans allow one pair every 12 or 24 months), and current pair's condition.

Terms to verify before deciding

1. Vision plan specifics: in-network frame allowance, lens copay, frequency limit (12 vs 24 months), plan-year reset date, and whether the 2026 benefit has already been used.
2. Whether the new Rx requires specialty lenses (progressive, high-index, prism, photochromic) — this filters which online retailers can deliver acceptably.
3. Online retailer's status with your insurer: in-network partnership, or out-of-network only, and whether they file claims or you do.
4. Online retailer's remake/return policy in writing: window length (30 vs 60 days), who pays return shipping, restocking fee on frames, warranty on lens defects.
5. Online retailer's quality controls: lab identity/certification, how PD is sourced (your old Rx, or you self-measure), and stated tolerance on prescription accuracy.
6. FSA balance and forfeiture rules — many plans have a 12/31 deadline with either a grace period into Q1 or full forfeiture. If you have unused FSA funds, the calculus changes.
7. Whether your current pair can serve as a backup if you order online and need a remake — i.e. are you functionally dependent on the new pair arriving right?
8. Online retailer's current turnaround if ordered today (Nov 10) — would it arrive before any FSA deadline?
9. Whether the Rx includes PD; some online retailers won't fill without it and require self-measurement, which adds error.
10. All-in cost per option: in-network (copay + frame overage + add-ons); online (retail price − expected reimbursement + shipping); wait ($0 with the risks above).

The decision reduces to "is the cost of buying now less than the option value of waiting?" — and that hinges almost entirely on whether your 2026 benefit is unused and whether FSA funds are at risk of expiring. Check those two first; everything else is secondary.

The Rx is optional, current glasses are comfortable, and spending $118-125 on eyewear you don't need yet is just inventory. The 12/31 year-end pressure is the classic sunk-cost frame that pushes bad purchases — don't buy glasses just to use a benefit. A new benefit year starts Jan 1, 2027 anyway.

If you do decide a backup pair is worth banking the benefit for (or an Rx change is coming), the in-network shop wins easily:

- $7 cheaper online on paper, but you lose that to OON reimbursement paperwork time and any return shipping on a remake.
- Local fit adjustments are the durable advantage — glasses that sit wrong cost you headaches and days. Online has no remedy except a remake-with-shipping-deducted.
- 60-day no-charge remake vs. 30-day with shipping deducted.
- Shop files the benefit; one less thing on your plate.

Net: defer unless there's a real reason; if you buy, in-network.

Three options, four dimensions — comparison only (no medical angle).

OPTION A — In-network ($125)
OPTION B — Online ($118)
OPTION C — Wait (current pair)

1. ADJUSTMENT ACCESS
  A: Walk-in, same-day, included at the shop. Durable value over
     years — frame drift, nose-pad wear, screw loosening, seasonal
     fit.
  B: None locally. DIY or ship back at your cost; 1–2 weeks round-
     trip per visit.
  C: No new purchase, no adjustment need; current pair continues
     to age on its own hardware.

2. REMAKE TERMS
  A: One no-charge lens remake within 60 days if the prescribing
     clinician changes the Rx. Provider-owns-the-problem shape.
  B: One return or remake within 30 days, return shipping
     deducted. Tighter window, more friction.
  C: N/A. Risk: if current pair fails during the wait window,
     no backup.

3. REIMBURSEMENT WORK
  A: Shop files the claim. Zero paperwork.
  B: You submit an itemized OON claim after purchase. Plan-
     specific allowance (typically lower than the in-network
     frame allowance) — net online cost = $118 minus that.
  C: No claim. Either the 2026 allowance goes unused or it
     resets 1/1/27, depending on plan rules (separate item to
     confirm — most vision plans do NOT carry frame/contact
     allowances, though some have a grace period).

4. DECEMBER 31 BENEFIT TIMING
  A: ~7 weeks until 12/31/26. In-network lab lead time 1–2
     weeks. Order must be placed with enough runway for delivery
     AND any 60-day remake, or you risk a 2026 order filing
     against the 2027 benefit. Ask the shop what date-of-service
     they use (order date vs. dispense date).
  B: Lead time 1–3 weeks plus remake round-trip if needed. Same
     service-date question. OON claim itself can usually be filed
     anytime post-purchase, but the benefit-year cut-off still
     applies.
  C: Forfeits the 2026 allowance (assuming no carryover/grace
     period). New benefit year starts 1/1/27 with a fresh
     allowance and a new frequency clock. Worth checking your
     plan's frequency rule — 12 vs. 24 months between pairs —
     before assuming "wait until January" is free.

NET ON THE $7 SPREAD
  The $7 is the only dimension where B wins on paper. On each of
  the other three, A has the structural advantage, and any of
  (AR quality, PD accuracy on a self-reported Rx, OON reimburse-
  ment net, return-shipping on a remake) erases the $7 quickly.
  C is a separate bet — you're trading a 2026 benefit for a 2027
  one, with no second-pair insurance during the gap.

Two things still worth confirming before any order:
  1. Whether your plan carries allowance across plan years or
     has a grace period (affects C).
  2. The shop's date-of-service convention (affects A and B
     timing math for the 12/31 cutoff).

SHORT SEQUENCE — lamp height, reflector distance, neutral-value check

0. Ground truth first (do this before touching the setup)
   - Kill or shield the lamp for ~10 seconds. Read the cup under ambient room light only.
   - Note on scrap: where the primary shadow edge falls on the cup, how bright the reflected side is, where the cast shadow lands on the table.
   - That ambient reading is what the painting has to match. The lamp is a tool, not the reference.

1. Lamp height
   - Start high and slightly forward of the cup, so the cast shadow falls behind or beside, not directly under the base.
   - Lower in small steps (roughly 10–15% of height at a time), pausing 5–10 seconds between each.
   - Stop lowering the moment the cast shadow on the table reads as one confident shape with a soft outer edge — no doubled edge, no hard inner rim.

2. Reflector distance
   - Place the foam board at cup-height on the shadow side, but start FURTHER than feels natural.
   - Walk it closer in 2–3 inch increments.
   - The reflected side should brighten smoothly. The instant you see a new terminator line forming on the dark side of the cup, stop. Do not move it closer.

3. Neutral-value check (no wet-wash glare)
   - Squint until the lamp's hotspot diffuses into a soft patch — specular glare drops out, value masses remain.
   - Or: phone photo, desaturate to grayscale, view at an angle that doesn't mirror the lamp back to the lens.
   - For wet washes specifically: tilt the painting ~20–30° so the wet sheen reflects away from your eye, or hold a dried test swatch (same pigment, same dilution) next to the wet area. The dry swatch is what the wash will become, so it's the honest comparison.

STOP CONDITION (the one that protects the painting)

If at any point "matching the setup" would require you to ADD a second shadow edge to the cup, the setup is wrong — not the painting.

Concrete rule: when the reflector's reflected side begins to develop its own terminator line, back the reflector OFF until that line disappears, even if the reflected side then reads a touch darker than ideal. A slightly under-lit reflected side is honest form; a painted second edge is a fake chasing two competing key lights.

Translation: preserve the single primary shadow that's already on the paper. The artificial second edge is reflector glare, not the still life.

TIMING SNAPSHOT
- 12:55pm — preheat oven to 425°F
- 1:00pm — sheet pan in (sweet potatoes only)
- 1:10pm — chicken thighs join the pan
- 1:35pm — green beans go in; start stuffing on the stove
- 1:50pm — pull everything, rest 5 min
- 1:55pm — plate both meals
- 2:00pm — you eat; Sam's plate starts cooling
- by 2:45pm — Sam's plate in the fridge

THE TWO-PIECE COOKWARE SET (minimal cleanup)
- One rimmed sheet pan lined with foil
- One medium pot for the stuffing
- One cutting board, one knife, one spoon

PREP (~10 min, by 1:00pm)
1. Cube the sweet potato into ~1-inch pieces. Toss with 1 Tbsp olive oil, ½ tsp salt, pepper, ½ tsp garlic powder. Pile on the left third of the sheet pan.
2. Pat the 4 chicken thighs dry. Season both sides with salt, pepper, garlic powder, paprika, lemon zest. Drizzle the skin with a little olive oil and rub it in. Place skin-up on the right third of the pan, not touching the sweet potatoes.
3. Trim the green beans; mince 2 garlic cloves; zest the lemon.

OVEN SEQUENCE
- 1:00 — Sheet pan in with just the sweet potatoes.
- 1:10 — Add the chicken thighs (give them space; skin-up).
- 1:35 — Pull the pan for 30 seconds. Toss the green beans with 1 Tbsp melted butter, the minced garlic, salt, pepper, and a pinch of lemon zest; slide them into any gap (or onto a small foil-lined dish on the rack next to the pan). Back in.
- 1:50 — Pull everything. Chicken should read ~175°F at the thickest part; sweet potatoes browned and fork-tender; beans bright green with a little char. If the chicken skin isn't crisped enough, 2-3 min under the broiler finishes it.

STOVE-TOP STUFFING (~10 min, start at 1:40)
- Melt 3 Tbsp butter in the pot. Add the stuffing mix, stir to coat. Pour in 1½ cups stock (use stock, not water — it's worth it). Cover, rest off-heat per box (~5 min), fluff with a fork.

PLATING (do both at once, ~1:55pm)
- Your plate: 1 thigh, ~¼ of the sweet potatoes, a handful of beans, a scoop of stuffing. Squeeze lemon over the chicken and beans.
- Sam's plate: same portions, on a plate or in a shallow container (shallow = faster, safer cooling). Cover loosely.

SAM'S PLATE — COOLING + REFRIGERATION
- Don't let it sit out longer than ~30-45 min. The food-safety window for cooked poultry/vegetables at room temp is 2 hours total — staying well under that keeps the late plate in good shape.
- Speed the cool-down: spread the food in a thin layer (not piled high), or set the covered plate on a tray of ice water in the sink for 5-10 min before going into the fridge.
- Cover and refrigerate by ~2:45pm. ~8 hours in the fridge is no problem.

SAM'S REHEAT (whenever he eats)
- Microwave (easiest): cover the plate with a damp paper towel. Microwave at 70% power for ~3-4 min total, rotating/stirring once at the halfway point. If he wants the skin crisp again, a quick 1-2 min under the broiler at the end fixes it.
- Oven (if he wants): 350°F, plate covered with foil, 15-20 min. Stuffing and beans heat fastest; chicken should be the last thing to come out.
- Heat the chicken all the way to 165°F internal — cut into the thickest part, no pink, juices run clear.

ONE SMALL NOTE
- If you'd rather start 15 min later (1:15pm), put the cubed sweet potatoes and chicken on the pan at the same time, add beans + start stuffing at 1:40, and you'll still plate by 1:55. Same food, slightly less time for the sweet potatoes to caramelize — totally fine.

 4:30  Add stuffing on top in chunks (don't crumble — chunks crisp better), press down, 2-3 min.

 7:00  Toss spuds + stuffing together, spread to the pan edges. Nestle the whole thigh in the center, skin/top side up. Splash 1-2 Tbsp water around the edge (not on the chicken), cover. 3-4 min covered — the trapped steam brings the thigh to 165°F without driving off moisture.

11:00  Add green beans on top, lid back on for 30-60 sec. Just warm them through.

12:00  Lid off. Salt, pepper, pinch of sage/poultry seasoning/paprika; a few drops of vinegar or a pat of butter brightens the whole plate. If anything's pale, give it 60 sec uncovered to re-crisp.

13:30  Slice or pull the thigh on the board (not in the pan — juices stay in the meat). Plate.

Don't-dry-out rules:
- Thigh is dark meat + skin-side cap = naturally forgiving; the lid-and-splash step is the safety net.
- Don't slice before reheating — exposed cross-sections dry out fast.
- Medium heat the whole time. High heat overcooks the outside before the center warms.

Food-safety check (since you asked):
- Day-2 post-Thanksgiving leftovers are comfortably within the 3-4 day window.
- Target internal temp 165°F on the thigh; with a covered steam step of 3-4 min off a not-fully-cold start, you'll clear it. If you want certainty, an instant-read in the thickest part of the thigh is cheap insurance — especially with stuffing-adjacent meat.
- Eat off the plate; don't let the finished hash sit on the counter more than ~20 min before you sit down.

Serve with hot sauce, cranberry sauce if you have any left, or a fried egg on top if you want to push it into brunch territory.

A couple of notes on the draft:
- Bracketed placeholders for the clinician/clinic name and any MRN/DOB header your portal requires — fill those in as needed.
- The phrase "focal pain" and the 2/10 score, plus the 10-minute resolution and absence of red-flag findings, give the clinician enough to triage without you naming a cause.

Sixty minutes, one study, no rescue passes. Work the sequence as written; the stop condition is the point.

0:00–0:05 — Value map (no paint yet)
  Sketch a 3-value notan thumbnail first: light (catching planes), mid (the bulk of ribbon mass), dark (deepest folds and the shadow under the ribbon on the kraft). Mark the 3–5 pin-point highlights you will reserve. Sort every fold edge into two piles: hard (catching plane against shadow) and lost (shadow side rolling into kraft or into itself).

0:05–0:15 — Reserve + ground
  Reserve the brightest highlights two ways: (a) leave the paper untouched where they sit, and (b) mask the smallest pin-points with masking fluid if they would otherwise get kissed by a wet edge. Let the mask dry.
  Lay a single thin wash over the kraft area — raw umber + a touch of burnt sienna, low chroma, just warm enough to push the silver cool. Bone dry before the next step. On cold-press this gives you granulation and a value to push against; do not glaze it later.

0:15–0:20 — Mix once, then stop mixing
  One puddle: ultramarine blue + burnt sienna (≈2:1), diluted to a mid-value gray-violet. That is your workhorse. Add a second smaller puddle of the same mix, slightly darker (more ultramarine, less water) for the deepest folds. No third puddle. No Payne's gray, no black. Black muddies silver; the umber is doing the warming.

0:20–0:35 — First pass on the ribbon (the value map)
  Paint the ribbon's mid-to-dark shapes in one connected wash onto dry kraft. Drop the darker puddle into the deepest folds while still damp — a soft bleed reads as reflected cool shadow, which is what silver actually does. Keep the brush away from the reserved highlights. Do not chase individual reflections yet.

0:35–0:50 — Edges, the only place decisions live
  Hard edges: where a catching plane meets a shadow fold, let the wash dry to a crisp line, or reinforce with a damp-but-not-wet brush stroke if it softened too much.
  Lost edges: at terminations into kraft or into self-shadow, lift with a clean damp brush and pull the pigment outward — let it fade.
  One, at most one, secondary cool: a faint blue-green or violet tinge in a single fold that clearly reflects a specific ambient. Everywhere else stays the gray-violet mix. Peek and lift any halo around the masked highlights.

0:50–0:58 — Squint test and the one permitted correction
  Squint at the painting. It should read as three values — light, mid, dark — not as "ribbon." If a fourth value is forming, you are overworking. Permit yourself exactly one finishing move: deepen one deepest fold, or soften one edge. Not both.

0:58–1:00 — Stop
  Peel mask, dry the page flat, sign it. The painting is done when:
   • the squint test still passes,
   • the reserved highlights are still the brightest things on the page,
   • no area has been re-wet more than twice,
   • the cool of the ribbon and the warm of the kraft sit in tension, not harmony.

If you find yourself reaching for the brush to add a fourth local color, a fifth reflection, or a "just one more" fold — that is the overwork edge. Put the brush down. The study is the value map, not the inventory of reflections.

The IRS annual limit is on the COMBINED total (your contributions + employer contributions + any other contributions) flowing into the HSA in 2027. So:

HOPPIN' JOHN BOWL WITH COLLARDS

  New Year's Day classic — peas for luck, greens for prosperity,
  rice for abundance. All pantry, no shopping.

  Serves 2. About 30 minutes, mostly hands-off.

WHAT YOU HAVE, PUT TO WORK

  - 2 cans black-eyed peas → drained, rinsed
  - 1 bunch collards → stems out, leaves sliced into ribbons
  - 3 cups cooked rice → reheated with a splash of water
  - Garlic → 3-4 cloves, minced; split between peas and greens
  - 1 lemon → half into the peas, half into the collards, last wedge for the table
  - Vegetable broth → ~1 cup total, split
  - Olive oil, salt, black pepper, smoked paprika

STEPS

  1. Collards first (longest cook). In a wide skillet, warm 2 tbsp
     olive oil over medium. Add half the garlic, stir 30 seconds.
     Add collards in handfuls with a pinch of salt; toss until
     wilted. Pour in about 1/2 cup broth, cover, drop heat to low,
     and simmer 10-12 minutes until tender. Uncover, squeeze in
     juice from one lemon half, black pepper to taste. Hold warm.

  2. Peas next. Same skillet (or a small pot), 1 tbsp olive oil,
     remaining garlic, 30 seconds. Add the drained peas, another
     1/2 cup broth, a generous teaspoon of smoked paprika, salt,
     pepper. Simmer 5-7 minutes, mashing a few peas against the
     side of the pot to thicken the sauce. Taste — if it needs
     lift, a small squeeze of lemon.

  3. Rice. Warm covered with a splash of water, or microwave with
     a damp paper towel over the top.

  4. Plate. Rice on the bottom, peas and their sauce on one side,
     collards on the other. Dust with smoked paprika, crack pepper
     over the top, set the remaining lemon on the table.

WHY THIS WORKS

  - Smoked paprika stands in for the bacon a traditional Hoppin'
     John would carry — you get the smoky depth without a meat
     run.
  - Collards + peas + rice is the classic Southern New Year plate,
     so the meal earns its moment without feeling themed.
  - Peas and collards both reheat well, so if Sam is too tired to
     eat right away, lunch waits an hour with no loss.

For Sam, after a late NYE close, this is the right weight: warm,
soft, restorative, and you did the work.

ONE-POT COCONUT CHICKEN RICE WITH SPINACH
Serves 2 + 1 leftover (about 3 portions)

You'll need:
  - 1.5 lb boneless skinless chicken thighs, cut into 1" pieces
  - 1.5 cups jasmine or basmati rice, rinsed
  - 1 can (14 oz) full-fat coconut milk
  - 2 cups low-sodium chicken broth
  - 1 medium onion, small dice
  - 4 garlic cloves, minced
  - 1 tbsp grated fresh ginger
  - 1 tbsp curry powder (or 1.5 tsp red curry paste)
  - 3 tbsp neutral oil, 1 tsp kosher salt, black pepper
  - 5 oz baby spinach (3 big handfuls)
  - 1 lime
  - optional: 1 cup frozen peas, cilantro, chili crisp

You'll also need a Dutch oven or deep lidded skillet — that's the only pot.

Timing (about 30 minutes):

  0:00  Heat 2 tbsp oil over medium-high. Season chicken with salt and pepper; brown in 2 batches, about 3 min per side. Transfer to a plate.

  0:06  Lower heat to medium. Add remaining oil and onion; cook 3 min. Add garlic, ginger, curry powder; cook 1 min until fragrant.

  0:10  Stir in rice for 1 min to coat. Pour in coconut milk and broth; scrape up any browned bits. Return chicken and any juices.

  0:12  Bring to a simmer, cover, drop heat to low. Cook 13-15 min until rice is tender and liquid is absorbed. (Stir in peas at minute 10 if using.)

  0:25  Off heat. Scatter spinach on top, cover, rest 2 min. Uncover, stir spinach through, squeeze in lime. Taste for salt.

  0:28  Plate two portions; the third starts cooling now.

Cooling the leftover safely:

  - Get it out of the hot pot. Spoon the leftover into a shallow container no deeper than 2 inches. Depth is what slows cooling, not portion size, so a wide shallow box beats a tall deep one.

  - Targets: drop from about 140°F to about 70°F within roughly 30 minutes, then under 40°F within another 90 minutes. Total time in the danger zone (40-140°F) should stay under 2 hours combined.

  - Faster path: set the shallow container inside a larger bowl of ice water and stir gently for 5-10 minutes before fridging. This usually pulls it well under 70°F.

  - Don't seal it airtight while it's still steaming-warm. Vent the lid or leave it slightly cracked for the first 10-15 minutes in the fridge, then close.

  - Store at 40°F or below. Use within 3-4 days. Reheat to a steady 165°F — steam rising through the middle, not just hot edges. A splash of water or broth when reheating keeps the rice from drying out.

Here's a conservative sequence for a 31°F morning with deicing granules on the ground. Keep the walk short and assume the granules are the standard toxic kind (NaCl / calcium chloride / magnesium chloride) unless you know otherwise.

Walk
- Pre-walk: if you have dog booties or a paw balm (musher's wax / bag balm), apply now as a barrier. Short leash, route along the clearest path, avoid slushy puddles and piles where melt concentrates.
- During: brief — just necessary business. Watch Kibo for sudden paw-licking, limping, or stopping to chew; any of those is a signal to head home.
- On return: do not let him lie down or lick before you've cleaned him.

Paw check (do this before wiping, while you can still see granules)
- Look at each pad, between every toe, around the nail beds, and up to the wrist/hock.
- Note: stuck granules, redness, cracks, cuts, swelling, bleeding, dampness, or any pad that looks pale/white/bluish.

Wiping
- Damp warm cloth or unscented pet wipe. One cloth per paw (don't reuse — you can drag chemicals between feet).
- Wipe pads, between toes, and around nails. Pay extra attention to the webbing between toes where granules hide.

Rinsing (only if you saw heavy exposure or granules still on after wiping)
- Lukewarm water in a low basin or the tub. Dip each paw and gently work between toes with your fingers.
- Towel dry thoroughly, especially between toes — trapped moisture + cold is its own irritation source.
- Skip rinses on days with light exposure; wiping is enough.

Red flags → call the vet
- Repeated licking, chewing, or biting at the feet after you're done cleaning.
- Limping, reluctance to bear weight, or picking up a paw mid-walk.
- Visible burns, blisters, raw/red patches, cracked or split pads, or bleeding.
- A pad that looks pale, white, or bluish (possible cold injury), or any swelling.
- Granules you can't fully remove, especially packed between toes.
- Vomiting, excessive drooling, lethargy, or loss of appetite (possible ingestion of a toxic deicer).

Two small habits that prevent most of this from becoming a problem: towel-dry between toes every time, and keep a damp cloth by the door so the wipe happens within a minute of coming inside — before he can lick anything off.

If it does, skip the vinegar and just rely on the wash.

Wash:
- Cold cycle, per label. Turn the jacket inside out to protect the outer face from any further agitation at the spot. Wash alone or with similar colors (don't mix with anything that could pick up a dye transfer since the dye isn't confirmed fast).

Dry and verify:
- Air dry only — the label excludes the dryer, and you also don't want heat setting any residual stain. Hang or lay flat.
- Check the spot fully dry before deciding you're done. Tannin shadows often look gone wet and reappear as the fabric dries. If it's still visible, repeat the soap/vinega steps and wash again rather than reaching for heat.

What to avoid here:
- No bleach (label, and it would be harsh on untested dye anyway).

Here is a conservative stain-removal sequence that holds across most fabrics and most stains. The five operations are in their natural order; the bracketed sub-steps are the points where stains commonly go wrong, with the safe move called out.

1. READ THE CARE LABEL FIRST
   - Confirm fiber, max wash temp, bleach code, dry method.
   - "Dry clean only" or "do not wash" → take it to a cleaner. Point out the stain and identify it if you can.
   - If the label permits only a non-water solvent → use that, not water.

2. BLOT (never rub)
   - Place the stain face-down on a clean white cloth or paper towel.
   - Press a second clean white cloth onto the back; lift, don't smear.
   - Work from the OUTER edge of the stain toward the center. This is the main anti-spread step.
   - Rotate to a clean section of cloth each pass; stop when no more transfers.

3. SPOT-TEST
   - Pick a hidden spot: inside seam, hem, under a pocket flap, inside cuff.
   - Test whatever you'll use next (cold water, dish soap, solvent, etc.).
   - Wait ~5 minutes. Look for color loss, bleeding, surface change, or texture distortion.
   - If anything shifts → stop and bring to a professional cleaner. Don't proceed.

4. RINSE FROM THE BACK WITH COLD WATER
   - Cold only at this stage. Hot water at this point is the #1 heat-set risk and is irreversible on protein and tannin stains.
   - Hold the fabric taut over a basin or cup, stained side down, and run cold water through the back so the stain pushes OUT of the fibers, not deeper in.
   - 1-2 minutes of steady flow is usually enough. Don't let the rinse water pool across the surface — that re-spreads.

5. PRE-TREAT (gentle, matched to stain — see notes below)
   - Safe default: a drop or two of clear dish soap worked in lightly with a fingertip, OR a laundry pre-treatment gel.
   - Let it sit 5-10 minutes. Don't let it dry on the fabric.
   - Avoid until you've spot-tested: chlorine bleach on wool/silk/many synthetics, hydrogen peroxide on dark colors, vinegar on fresh protein stains, anything involving heat.

6. WASH PER THE CARE LABEL
   - Coldest effective temperature the label allows.
   - Use the labeled cycle. Hand-wash or delicate if the label says so.
   - Wash the item alone or with similar colors — pre-treated spots can bleed.
   - Standard detergent dose. No "extra" — more soap doesn't rinse cleaner and can leave a ring.

7. INSPECT WHILE STILL WET — THE HEAT-SET CHECKPOINT
   - This is the gate before drying. In good light, stretch the stained area flat and look at it.
   - If any shadow, ring, or color remains → DO NOT dry. Repeat steps 2-6, or take it to a cleaner.
   - The dryer, iron, radiator, or hair dryer will permanently fuse most remaining stains into the fiber.

8. AIR-DRY
   - Lay flat or hang, away from direct sunlight (sun fades some dyes) and away from heaters/radiators.
   - Reshape knits and knits/wools while damp; don't wring.
   - Only machine-dry or iron after the stain is fully gone.

DEVIATIONS BY STAIN TYPE (apply on top of the above)
- Protein (blood, dairy, egg, sweat, vomit): cold only, always. Enzyme cleaner helps. Hot water cooks the protein in.
- Tannin (coffee, tea, wine, fruit juice, soda): cold water first; baking soda paste or oxygen bleach (if label permits) after.
- Oil/grease (butter, salad dressing, cosmetics, bike chain): dish soap directly on the spot, let it emulsify 10-15 min, then warm (not hot) water OK.
- Ink / ballpoint / marker: rubbing alcohol on a cotton ball, blot-and-roll (test first — alcohol can dissolve some synthetics and finishes).
- Mud: let it DRY fully first, brush off the crust, then run the normal sequence. Water on wet mud grinds it in.
- Pet (urine, feces, vomit): cold rinse, then an enzyme cleaner formulated for pet stains. Regular detergent doesn't break down uric acid and the stain can return.

WHEN TO STOP AND CALL A PROFESSIONAL
- "Dry clean only" on the label.
- Silk, wool, rayon, viscose, vintage or unknown fiber.
- Structured garment (suit jacket, lined dress, anything with interfacing).
- Large stain, old stain, or unknown stain.
- Spot test failed, or the stain is still visible after one full cycle.
