SUMMARY
~35 min total, 1 sheet pan + 1 pot + 1 bowl. Lunch portion pulled hot into a shallow container for fast, safe cooling.

PREP (5 min, do first)
  Oven 425°F, rack center. Line sheet pan with parchment (no scrubbing = less ankle strain).
  Drain 1 can chickpeas; pat dry with towel.
  1 sweet potato: 3/4-inch cubes (smaller = matches broccoli cook time).
  1 head broccoli: ~2-inch florets (bigger so they don't burn before potato is done).
  Zest half the lemon now; juice later. Mince 2 garlic cloves.

SEASON + ROAST (3 min hands-on)
  On sheet pan: sweet potato + chickpeas + broccoli in one layer (crowded = steam, not roast).
  Drizzle ~3 Tbsp olive oil; add 1 tsp smoked paprika, 3/4 tsp salt, several grinds pepper, half the garlic. Toss.
  Roast 22-26 min. Shake the pan once at 12 min. Done when sweet potato is tender and chickpeas crisp at edges.

WHILE IT ROASTS (passive)
  Couscous: bring 3/4 cup water + pinch salt to boil; kill heat; stir in 1/2 cup couscous; cover; rest 5 min; fluff with fork.
  Lemon-tahini sauce (small bowl): whisk 3 Tbsp tahini + juice of half lemon + remaining garlic + 2 Tbsp warm water + pinch salt. Loosen with more water if thick.

PLATE + LUNCH PORTION
  Plate dinner: couscous base, sheet-pan veg + chickpeas on top, sauce drizzled over.
  Lunch portion: scoop remaining veg/chickpeas + couscous into a SHALLOW container (≤2 inches deep — spreads heat, cools fast).

SAFE COOLING (don't skip)
  Fridge within 1 hour of coming out of oven (target: 140°F→70°F under 2 hr; faster is safer).
  Leave lid slightly ajar or vented for the first 20-30 min in the fridge, then seal. Sealing hot = trapped steam = sogginess and slower cooling inside.
  Eat within 3-4 days. Reheat to steaming hot throughout (165°F).

ANKLE NOTES
  All chopping on counter; no low-cabinet bending.
  One carry out of the oven — slide the pan onto the stovetop, no long hold.
  No standing stir-watch; the timer does the work, one shake at 12 min only.

SUBSTITUTIONS (in case something is off)
  No smoked paprika → 1/2 tsp regular paprika + pinch cumin.
  Tahini thick → loosen sauce with warm water 1 tsp at a time; it seizes up cold, then relaxes.
  Sweet potato large → cube a bit smaller; large head broccoli → cut florets bigger to keep pace.

Lay the cool shadow first, then drop the warm reflection into/next to it. Don't keep the mug white until the end.

Why this order works in watercolor:

  - The structural shadow is what turns a white shape into a mug. It wants to go on while the paper is fresh, light-to-dark.
  - If you glaze the warm over a dry cool, the bounce sits cleanly as a tint and the cool stays cool — they meet at a soft edge instead of muddying.
  - Reverse it (warm first, cool on top) and the cool tends to push into the warm, killing the glow exactly where the orange should be talking to the mug.
  - The parts to reserve as paper are the lit curve, the rim catch, and any small specular — not the whole mug. The mug has to do some work; the paper just has to hold the brightest note.

For the 75 minutes, a workable sequence:

  1. Block the orange first. It sets the warm key and calibrates your eye for how much bounce the mug actually receives.
  2. On the mug, dry-brush or mask the lit curve and rim, then lay the blue-gray form shadow on the window-away side — soft edge toward the light, slightly firmer where it tucks into the cast shadow on the table.
  3. Let it set until just-damp (or bone-dry if your paper is sizing-thirsty — the 140-lb cold-press will tell you).
  4. Drop the warm reflection as a thin wash on the shadow-side curve and let it bleed a hair into the cool edge. That's where the "warm next to cool" optical effect lives.
  5. If the warm keeps lifting the cool instead of sitting beside it, switch to glazing: cool fully dry, warm on top as a transparent pass.

One judgment call: the cast shadow on the table is cooler and bluer than the form shadow on the mug. Paint them as two different washes, not one — the form shadow picks up bounce light, the cast shadow doesn't.

The underpass workaround, read neutrally

Immediate value:
- Unblocks daily movement now: residents have a working route where the institution's own asset does not.
- Cheap for the city: the work is done by residents, off-budget, without a capital project.
- Politically legible: "resilience" is a vocabulary the planner can use in a memo without admitting anything failed.
- Preserves optionality for the city — the underpass is still there, still nominally in service, so a future fix is not foreclosed.

How success conceals failure:
- Each successful rerouting removes a pressure signal. The volume of complaints, the visible queue at the underpass, the case for capital spend — all drop — because the workaround has absorbed them. The metric that justified action goes quiet precisely because of the workaround's success.
- The planner's "resilience" framing re-encodes the workaround as an institutional asset. Residents' private labor is converted into public-language cover. Whoever audits the system later sees a success story.
- The institution loses the ability to see the cost, because the cost has been displaced onto the people doing the rerouting — time, detour, risk, weather exposure — and those costs are not measured by the city.
- Durability is the tell: a true interim adaptation usually has an "until" attached. Once the workaround has been named as the resolution, the conditional tends to drop.

Two questions that leave both readings unsettled:

1. If a real fix were proposed tomorrow — fully funded, technically sound, ready to build — would the planner engage with it on its merits, or would the conversation shift to "but the community has already adapted, and disruption during construction would be worse than the current arrangement"? What they do in that moment is the disambiguating scene, and the book hasn't shown it to us yet.

2. Whose language ends up in the official record after the workaround is named? If the residents' own vocabulary for what they're doing (mutual aid, looking out for each other, just getting to work) survives into the city's documents, that's one reading. If the planner's word — "resilience" — is the only one that makes it into the file, and the residents' account is treated as anecdote rather than evidence, the workaround has already been converted into an institutional asset, and the question of whether it was ever genuinely theirs is partly settled by the answer.

For watercolor specifically — not drawing — I'd flip your two options and start with the bag as a unified mass, not the apple.

The folds are reading as their own drawing because you're giving them equal value range and equal edge articulation to the apple. In watercolor the fix is hierarchy through sequence, not through outlining.

Practical sequence for your 75 minutes:

  1. Light pencil only the apple's silhouette as one closed shape. Do not draw any folds.
  2. Mix a thin burnt sienna plus a touch of umber. Wet the paper around the apple — not the apple — and drop this in as one connected mid-value wash. Let it dry.
  3. Mix your red. Drop the apple in last, letting its edge slightly overlap the dried bag so the silhouette reads as decisive rather than tentative.
  4. Only after both are dry, suggest folds — and only the folds that touch or relate to the apple. Folds away from the apple stay as soft value shifts, not lines.

Why this works: the bag's overall value becomes the negative space that defines the apple's edge, instead of you drawing the apple and then drawing the bag around it. The folds stop being their own drawing because they only exist where they meet the apple. Everything else is value mass supporting the silhouette.

Spend your refinement time at the contact point where the bag's rim curls against the apple. That is the one place a fold should read crisply.

Dry-down (room temp, no heat, no machine):

1. Wipe uppers and insoles with a clean dry cloth; remove insoles and laces.
2. Open the tongue fully; stuff each shoe with loosely crumpled paper towels (or plain newspaper) to absorb interior moisture and hold shape. Replace the stuffing once at the ~2-hour mark if still damp; brief shower usually only needs the first round.
3. Set shoes in a spot with good ambient airflow — near (not on) a room vent, or in front of a fan. Upright or heel-down; do not stack or lean them against a wall.
4. Leave insoles and laces out separately, flat on a dry surface.
5. Plan on 24 h before reuse; 48 h is safer if the insoles or footbed felt wet through. No radiator, no dryer, no hair dryer, no sunlight through a window, no car dashboard.

Damage check before the next rehab session (replace stuffing / re-lace only after this passes):

- Smell: any musty or sour note = not fully dry, extend drying another 12–24 h.
- Sole bond: pinch the sidewall where upper meets midsole and along the toe/heel; any new gap, peeling, or audible squish = shoe is done for rehab, retire to casual or replace.
- Upper: delamination (overlay flapping), torn seam, or fabric thinning that exposes the backing = retire.
- Insole: curled edges, compressed/flat foam, or visible peeling of the top fabric = replace insole at minimum; if midsole beneath feels uneven, retire.
- Heel counter: squeeze both sides; if it collapses or twists where it used to be rigid, stability is compromised — retire from rehab use.
- Tread: confirm lugs/pattern still clear of packed debris (you said none) and that depth still looks even; if the outsole is smooth under the ball of the foot, swap in a fresh pair for rehab.

Rehab-specific call: given the right ankle is still in the pre-run gate, treat these shoes as load-bearing equipment. If any check above fails, do not use them for the return-to-run walk-runs — use a different pair, since a softened midsole or shifted heel counter will change your loading pattern and quietly undo the gate. Dry pavement ride or commute is fine in the meantime.

READ
- Hard backrun = pigment tide-line dried in. Once the sheet is fully dry, plain water lifts only a fraction of what's there — at best you'll soften the edge, not erase the mark.

SEQUENCE
1. Dry assessment under raking light. Note bloom density, edge sharpness, and proximity to the window edge. Plan the wet footprint before any water touches paper.
2. Lift attempt 1: small clean mop or #6 round, damp not dripping. Touch only the bloom, ~20–30s dwell, blot firmly with lint-free tissue (not paper towel — it leaves lint). Dry 5 min, re-evaluate.
3. Lift attempt 2 (only if attempt 1 actually moved pigment): repeat with slightly damper brush, slightly longer dwell, same tight footprint.
4. If a soft ghost remains: stop. For a kitchen-window study, a faint tonal mark reads as steam, condensation, dust, or weathered putty — often a feature, not a flaw.
5. If the hard edge persists and you want it gone: glaze, don't abrade. Mix the surrounding wash color/value, test on a scrap of the same pad first. - Surface disturbance: pilling, fuzzing, matte sizing, paper going soft under the blot. That spot is finished; go to step 5 or leave it.
- Pigment migrating into the surrounding wash on the first blot. Surrounding wash becomes the priority.
- Two lift cycles done and the edge still reads hard. More water won't help without abrasion.
- Hand reaching for a Magic Eraser, sanding stick, blade, or dry scrub on the paper. Stop. Re-render on a fresh sheet — a 10-sheet pad at ~3 studies/month is worth more than one overworked fix.

ONE-LINE RULE
If a third damp brushstroke is starting to feel tempting, you're already past "preserving the surrounding wash."

Conservative sequence, in order:

1. Quarantine now
   - Move the bag to a separate spot (different shelf, a lidded bin, or a closed box) so it can't be grabbed by mistake during the next feeding.
   - Don't tape, fold, or "fix" the split; don't cut the bag open further; don't transfer kibble into another container.
   - Keep it cool and dry. Don't rinse, toast, or otherwise treat the kibble.

2. Document before anything else
   - Photos in good light: close-up of the split seam, the full bag (brand/size/flavor), the lot code and expiration, and the shipping box showing it arrived intact.
   - Write down: brand, product/size/flavor, lot code, expiration, retailer and order #, date received, date discovered.
   - Save the order confirmation and any shipping notification emails.

3. Open the replacement request
   - Contact the manufacturer first (they own the damaged-product process); only loop in the retailer if you bought direct or the manufacturer points you there.
   - Send the photos plus lot/expiration/order info, and ask for: a replacement, a prepaid return or disposal instruction, and a reference/case number. Note the rep's name.

4. While you wait for a reply
   - Do not feed from the split bag, regardless of smell or appearance. Use your existing unopened stock first; rotate by expiration.
   - If you'd run out before they respond, buy a fresh bag at retail and keep the receipt — ask whether it's reimbursable under their damaged-bag policy.
   - Hold the quarantined bag in its current state until they tell you what to do with it. Don't discard it preemptively.

5. What not to assume
   - Dry look + normal odor ≠ safe. Once the factory seal is broken, you can no longer verify barrier integrity, fat stability, or that nothing entered the bag in transit.
   - An intact shipping box doesn't rule out bag damage — the split can occur before packing, during handling, or in transit.
   - "I'll just use it and see" defeats the point of the manufacturer's quality/recall process, and there's no early signal for the failure modes you'd actually worry about (oxidation, micronutrient loss, opportunistic contamination).

Net call: the bag stays sealed, separate, and unused until the manufacturer tells you otherwise. Existing unopened stock carries you in the meantime; a retail replacement is a fallback, not a substitute.

Diagnosis up front: small holes plus a dry, empty casing on a stored wool throw, with cotton untouched, is the classic signature of clothes moths (webbing or case-bearing). Wool/animal fiber is their preferred food; they leave cotton alone unless starving. The casing being "empty" means the larva already emerged and moved on, so treat this as a potentially active problem, not just historical damage. Plan below is dog-safe — no foggers, mothballs, or sprays.

PET-CONSCIOUS ISOLATION

  1. Brush or shake the throw over a white sheet outside or in the bathtub (not on the carpet). Seal it in a tied plastic bag at the spot you found it.
  2. Move the sealed bag somewhere Kibo can't reach — garage, car trunk, or a closed-off room for the hold.
  3. Vacuum where the throw was stored: seams, floor edges, baseboards, shelf undersides. Slow passes with the hose attachment. Empty the canister or seal the bag and dispose of it OUTSIDE — larvae left in a vacuum can re-emerge.
  4. Vacuum Kibo's bed and any nearby wool/fleece throws. Bag his bed separately if it's wool/fleece (his own dander buildup can be a reservoir).
  5. Look for the actual source: closet back edges, under furniture, wool carpet edges, feather/down items, lint buildup behind doors. Moths usually originate from one hotspot and spread.

INSPECTION (keep the throw sealed during this)

  - Over a white surface, run your fingers along every seam, hem, fold, cuff, and tassel. Look for live larvae, more casings, webbing, or fine powdery frass.
  - Shake suspect areas over a white sheet with a flashlight — disturbed larvae drop.
  - Webbing on the fiber surface = webbing moth. Portable silk tubes = case-bearing moth. Treatment is the same either way.

WOOL-APPROPRIATE CLEANING (pick ONE — do not combine)

  - Cold: seal in plastic, freeze at 0°F / -18°C for 72 hours, thaw 24 hours, refreeze 72 hours. Kills eggs, larvae, and adults. Works for any wool item the care label allows.
  - Heat (best for casings): hottest dryer cycle the care label allows, OR a low oven ~120°F / 50°C for 30+ minutes for items that can't be tumbled. Heat must reach the fiber core.
  - Wash: cool water, wool-safe detergent (Eucalin, Soak, or similar no-rinse), gentle hand agitation. Submerge long enough for larvae to drown. Lay flat to dry.
  - Dry clean: perchloroethylene kills all life stages. Air the item out fully before returning it to Kibo's room.

  After treatment, store the throw in a sealed plastic bin or a zipped clean garment bag — not back into the same drawer until monitoring is clear.

MONITORING (4 weeks minimum)

  - Pheromone traps: wing-shaped sticky traps with a moth pheromone lure. Non-toxic, no spray. Place where Kibo can't reach the sticky surface — top of closet, behind dresser, or inside a closed shoebox with an entry slit. Replace every 8–12 weeks. Trap count tells you if adults are still active.
  - White-sheet shake test: once a week for 4 weeks, shake the throw and any other wool/fur items over a white sheet in good light. Any larvae, casings, or frass = still active.
  - Re-inspect the storage area weekly before the throw goes back.

CALL A PROFESSIONAL IF

  - More casings, larvae, or new holes appear on other wool items within 2–4 weeks despite cleaning and trapping.
  - Damage shows up on upholstered furniture, wool carpet edges, or feather/down items — that's structural, not a single-garment problem.
  - You see multiple adult moths resting on walls/ceilings (small, ~½", gold/buff colored).
  - Kibo or anyone develops skin irritation, sneezing, or coughing that improves when out of the room — moth particulate can trigger allergies in sensitive individuals.
  - The source appears to be in the building (shared walls, adjacent unit) rather than the textiles.

DON'TS (dog-safety reasons)

  - Mothballs — naphthalene or paradichlorobenzene; toxic to dogs (liver and CNS effects).
  - Pesticide sprays, foggers, or "bug bombs" — already off the table; also avoid residual spray on wool.
  - Concentrated essential-oil repellents (cedar, lavender, peppermint) sprayed on fabric — can irritate if Kibo licks the treated fiber. Untreated cedar blocks hung in the closet are fine as long as he isn't chewing them.

Removing a Sheet from a Glued Watercolor Block (140-lb cold-press)

Before you start
- Locate the unglued gap. On most glued blocks (Arches, Saunders Waterford, Fabriano Artistico, Strathmore 500) one short edge is left unbonded, usually near a corner, leaving a millimeter or two where the top sheet is free. Run a clean fingernail along all four edges to feel where it lifts microscopically while staying glued everywhere else. That is your entry point.
- Pick a blunt tool. Best choices for cold-press, in order: a wide painting palette knife with a dull edge, a bone folder, or a stiff plastic card (old credit card, library card). Avoid kitchen knives, X-Acto blades, razor blades. Anything sharp will catch in the tooth of the sheet below and dig in.
- Set up a clean, flat surface. A sheet of glass, a self-healing mat, or a smooth tabletop free of grit. A single particle under the block will emboss the next sheet.

The sequence

1. Stabilize the block. Place it flat. Lay your non-dominant hand across the top of the block with the palm flat and fingers spread, pressing down on the stack, NOT on the sheet you intend to remove. Keep that hand still throughout. The block should not be able to slide or bow.

2. Open the unglued corner. With your free hand, lift the top sheet at the gap by just a millimeter or two. The paint film is dry, so a light pinch at the corner margin is fine, but keep the lift minimal. If it won't lift, you have the wrong spot; re-scan the edges.

3. Insert the tool. Slide the tool's edge into the gap so its flat face is parallel to, and barely above, the sheet beneath. This geometry is the whole game: you want to shear the glue line BETWEEN sheet 1 and sheet 2, not press down into sheet 2. If the tool is angled, stop and re-flatten it.

4. Cut along the glued edge. Push the tool along the edge in the direction the glue runs (the short edge where the gap is located). Keep strokes long and slow. On cold-press the tooth gives the tool micro-bumps of resistance; that is normal. Steady pressure rides over them. Do not saw.

5. Pause and inspect every 2-3 cm. Look at the block from the side. The top sheet should be separating cleanly; the sheet below should be flat and unmarked. If you see a faint line, dimple, or bow in sheet 2, the tool is too deep; back it out a hair and resume.

6. Free additional edges if they are glued. Most blocks glue 2-3 sides plus the gap. Once one side is free, you can reinsert the tool and shear along the other bonded edges the same way. The more perimeter you free before lifting, the less the painting has to flex.

7. Lift the sheet. Hold it by two opposite corners (or with clean fingertips on the unpainted margins) and lift straight up, parallel to the block. Do not peel from one corner like a sticker. A straight lift keeps the paint film from cockling.

When to stop, immediately

Stop and re-set if any of these happen:
- The tool tip feels like it has caught on the sheet below. Resistance jumps, or you hear or feel a faint scratch that was not there a moment ago. Pull back, lift the tool a fraction, and try again flatter.
- You see a faint mark, line, or dimple on the sheet beneath where you are working. The tool is too deep. Back out, re-flatten, resume.
- The top sheet buckles or wrinkles ahead of the tool. You are pushing too fast, or the glue has grabbed a fiber and is tugging the painting. Stop pushing; ease the tool back, let the sheet relax, and resume with lighter pressure.
- You hit a hard spot that will not yield to steady pressure. Do not force it. Pull out, re-angle slightly flatter, and approach from the other side of the stuck spot. Forcing past it risks tearing the painting or scoring sheet 2.

If the glue resists throughout, some 140-lb blocks are more aggressively bonded than others. Do not increase force; switch to a sharper-blunt tool (palette knife before card) and slower strokes. The block is reusable. The painting is not.

After it is free
- Lay the painting face-up on a clean surface. If it wants to curl, let it relax on its own; do not weight it for several hours, since the paint film is still relatively fresh and can take impressions.
- Cover the remaining block with its dust sheet or a clean sheet of paper so the next sheet stays clean.

HEADLINE
This is a diagnostic, not a top-off. A 12+ psi shortfall below the tire's marked minimum is too large to dismiss. Inflation alone is not clearance — what you learn in the next 1–24 hours is. Since the ankle rehab has the bike parked anyway, use that time.

WHY 38 PSI IS A FLAG, NOT JUST "A BIT LOW"
- Marked minimums aren't cosmetic. They're the lower bound the sidewall casing and bead are designed for. Below it you risk sidewall flex failure, bead unseat in a turn, and rim strikes on rough pavement — which is exactly what you commute on.
- 38 from a presumably-full prior fill means slow leak, valve issue, bead problem, or a meaningful ambient-temp swing. None of those is "add air and forget."

CONSERVATIVE STATIONARY INFLATION (no ride yet)
1. Bike in a stand, upside-down against a wall, or hung — wheels free to spin. Not loaded by your weight or a rack.
2. Inflate the REAR only to the MIDDLE of its marked range, not the top. If the range is 50–70, target ~58–60. You're testing whether it holds, not setting commuting pressure.
3. Front at 54 is within range — leave it alone. Don't mix variables.
4. Add air in short bursts (2–3 sec pump, pause, gauge). During each pause, listen at the valve and around both bead shoulders for hiss.
5. While inflating, watch the sidewall profile for any egg-shape, ripple, or visibly thinner spot. Stop on sight of any.
6. Record the exact landing psi, the time, and ambient temp.

SHORT-INTERVAL PRESSURE RECHECK
- T+10 min: must hold exactly. Any drop = fast leak.
- T+1 hr: drop >2–3 psi = fast leak. Shop now.
- T+24 hr: drop >5 psi from your landing pressure = slow leak. Shop before road use.
- Flat across all three checks → ambient-temp drop or normal seepage, not a defect. Then top to your normal commuting pressure and the bike is road-ready.

VISIBLE-DAMAGE SEQUENCE — DO THIS BEFORE YOU ADD AIR
With the tire still slack, spin the wheel slowly by hand against a fixed reference (zip tie on chainstay works). Look and feel for:
  - Embedded object in tread — run a gloved fingertip across the tread in 3–4 spots. Glass, wire, thorn head, staple.
  - Sidewall bulge, ripple, or a soft patch when you squeeze both sides.
  - Bead: both shoulders must sit evenly on the rim all the way around. Any section sitting higher or visibly lifting = bead or rim problem.
  - Tread cuts that reach the casing ply — same rule as your sidewall rule applies: visible casing = shop.
  - Valve: stem straight (not tilted), no hiss at the base when you push the tire sideways at the valve, no bubbles if you dribble water around the stem/rim interface.
  - Rim: sight along the brake track or rim edge as it rotates — any hop, dent, or visible deformation.
  - Rim tape: if spoke-hole nipples are visible through gaps, the tape has shifted and will eat tubes.

CONDITIONS FOR SHOP (leave the bike unridden)
Stop and don't treat inflation as proof of road-ready if any of these shows up:
- Any pressure drop in the first 10 minutes, or >2–3 psi in the first hour.
- >5 psi drop across 24 hours from your landing pressure.
- Any sidewall bulge, ripple, or egg-shape — even if pressure holds.
- Any cut reaching casing on sidewall OR deep in tread.
- Any embedded object found, even small.
- Bead won't sit evenly all the way around.
- Valve stem tilted, hiss at base, or wet around it.
- Rim hop, dent, or visible deformation.
- You can't plausibly explain the loss (the bike hasn't been ridden hard enough lately for temp drop alone to account for 12+ psi).

ANKLE-REHAB NOTE
You're not riding this as part of the current rehab anyway, so the timeline is in your favor. Don't shortcut the 24-hour recheck just because the tire "feels fine at 60 psi in the driveway." Stationary inflation tells you it holds air; only the recheck tells you it holds air at a rate that's safe to ride on.

Rosemary moved indoors usually browns at the tips and droops new growth for one of three reasons: indoor winter air is drier than outdoors, total light dropped sharply, and the rootball got a little too dry between waterings. With free drainage, no standing water, and no pest/disease signs, the right move is to stabilize conditions first and not do anything dramatic. Here is the conservative sequence, in order.

WATERING (today and ongoing)
  1. Water thoroughly with room-temperature water until you see a small amount drain out the bottom. Cold water shocks the roots and is a common cause of tip burn in rosemary.
  2. Because the upper inch was dry, the rootball may have shrunk slightly away from the pot wall. If water runs straight through without wetting the soil, set the pot in a shallow tray of room-temp water for 15-20 minutes so it wicks up from below, then lift it out and let the excess drain.
  3. From here on, let the top 1-2 inches dry between waterings, then water thoroughly each time. Pot weight is more reliable than a calendar — in a Cherrywood winter with forced-air heat, that usually lands around once a week, sometimes less.
  4. Do not fertilize. Stressed plants cannot use the nitrogen well, and pushing soft new growth now usually ends in collapse.

LIGHT
  1. Keep it in your brightest window. South- or east-facing is best; west-facing late-afternoon sun can be strong, so if that's the case, ease it in — a few hours of direct sun for the first 3-4 days, then full exposure.
  2. Rotate the pot a quarter-turn every few days so all sides get light and the plant doesn't lean.
  3. Indoor winter light is dimmer than people expect. If you can clearly tell the plant is getting under about 6 hours of usable light, a basic full-spectrum LED on a 12-hour timer, 8-12 inches above the plant, is the single most useful upgrade. Add it gradually — 2-3 hours on day one, building up over a week — to avoid another shock.

DRAINAGE
  - You said it drains freely with no standing water. That is the right setup. Do not repot. Do not add a gravel layer at the bottom — it actually raises the water table in the pot.

ACCLIMATION
  1. Leave the brown tips alone for now. They are protecting the green tissue underneath; cutting them off invites more loss.
  2. No fertilizer for at least 3-4 weeks.
  3. No repotting unless you see roots circling the surface or coming out of the drainage holes — nothing in your description suggests that.
  4. Keep it away from both the cold draft at the window and the heating vent. You've already done that; just keep doing it.
  5. Humidity: rosemary tolerates dry indoor air, but if Cherrywood is very dry in winter, a pebble tray with water below (not touching) the pot gives a gentle bump. Don't mist the foliage — wet needles in still indoor air invite problems you do not need.

MONITORING (this is the part that actually tells you what's happening)
  - Day 1 (right after the watering): note how the foliage looks and remember the pot's weight. If the droop was water stress, you should see some softening within hours.
  - Day 3: finger-test the top inch. If dry to 1-2 inches, water thoroughly again. New growth tips should look less limp.
  - Day 7: a few more brown tips are normal as the plant sheds stressed foliage. The signal of recovery is firm, upright new tips and the silvery-green color coming back. No fertilizer yet.
  - Day 14: you should be in one of three trajectories — clearly recovering (firm new growth, browning stopped), stable but quiet (fine, hold conditions and reassess in another 2 weeks), or worsening (see below).

ESCALATE TO A LOCAL PLANT PROFESSIONAL IF YOU SEE ANY OF THESE
  - Soft, black, or mushy stems or roots, or a sour/rotting smell from the soil.
  - Rapid generalized yellowing across the whole plant, not just older tips.
  - Sudden drop of a large amount of foliage.
  - White fuzzy growth on the soil surface, or any visible pests you cannot identify — webbing, sticky residue, scale, mealybugs. None are present right now; this is a future trigger, not a current finding.
  - No meaningful improvement after 3-4 weeks of stable conditions despite the steps above.

A nursery staffer or independent horticulturist can usually tell a lot from a single photo of the whole plant plus a close-up of the browning tip — that's worth bringing along when you go in.

A careful tape-free sequence for today. The logic behind all of it: your block already gives you a clean margin (the glue band is reserved) — your job today is to never threaten it, not to fight it with tape.

PRE-FLIGHT (before anything wet)

  1. Inspect the seam. Run a clean dry finger, or a bone folder held flat (never the point), along all four glued edges of the painting sheet. You're confirming the bond is intact everywhere and that your earlier tape test didn't disturb anything. Note any soft spot — that side gets extra caution today.

  2. Seat the block on a rigid support. Glass, plexiglass, or a smooth board underneath. The glued sheet is already flat in the middle; the rigid base keeps the edges from flexing up when you tilt.

  3. Weight the back cover only. Small coins, paperweights, or binder clips on the back cover corners. Nothing on the painting sheet.

  4. Decide your margin. Your usable painting area is roughly 6–10 mm in from the page edge — that's the glue band, and it's already reserved. Don't design a composition that needs paint on the very last millimeter; treat the white margin as part of the picture.

  5. Mark the margin without scoring the sheet, only if you need a guide:
       - Best: don't mark at all — use the block edge itself as your visual reference.
       - If you must mark, dot a 2H pencil corner to corner, not a continuous line. A continuous graphite line shows under washes and is annoying to remove later.

DURING PAINTING

  6. Tilt intentionally. Prop the rigid support at a gentle 5–10° tilt. Tilt AWAY from whichever block edge you're working near, so gravity pulls wash into the sheet, not into the seam.

  7. Control wash creep without tape.
       - Loaded brush, not flooded. Keep water-to-pigment tight.
       - When a wash approaches your margin, "pull" a clean damp line just inside it with a damp brush — the damp zone holds the wash back from crossing.
       - Keep a thirsty brush and a folded tissue within reach. If wash creeps, blot (don't rub) and lift with the thirsty brush.
       - For a straight edge you can't freehand, hold a scrap paper strip as a moving shield — laid down and lifted as you work, never adhered.

  8. For controlled washes, paint the margin edge first while the inside is still dry, then work inward wet-into-wet. The first stroke defines the boundary; everything after flows against it.

STOP-EARLY SIGNALS — pause painting the moment you see any of these:

    - a tide line or pooling forming at the margin
    - wash wicking sideways into the glue seam
    - any lifting, bubbling, softening, or rippling of the paper edge
    - the page "tenting" upward at a corner

CATCH PROTOCOL (the safe-stop sequence if an edge begins to catch)

  9. Stop adding water and pigment immediately. No "one more stroke."

 10. Blot, don't rub. Press a folded tissue to the affected edge, lift straight up. Repeat with a clean spot until no more pigment transfers.

 11. Tilt the block so any remaining moisture flows toward the center of the sheet, away from the seam. Hold the tilt until the area looks matte-damp, not glossy-wet.

 12. Lift residual moisture with a thirsty brush — clean, damp, then blotted on a tissue. One pass at a time, not scrubbing.

 13. Air-dry only. No hairdryer on a lifting or saturated edge — heat can set a buckle permanently. Patience fixes this.

 14. Once fully dry, recheck the seam. If an edge has lifted noticeably, weight it gently through the back cover (paperweight on the back, over the affected margin). Don't press on the painting sheet.

 15. Reassess. If the seam reseats and the sheet lies flat again, you can continue painting on a different part of the sheet, keeping clear of the affected edge for the rest of the session. If the lift or tide line is visible in the painting, end the session — the block needs to dry thoroughly before the next pass, and you'd rather lose today than lose the sheet.

Cheat-sheet version to keep next to the easel: seat on a rigid board, weight the back only, reserve the glue band as your margin, tilt away from the working edge, pull a damp boundary line, blot don't rub if it creeps, air-dry if the seam complains, stop and reassess rather than push.

The principle first, then the specifics.

PRINCIPLE

  The preservation master must be a faithful capture of the physical original —
  bit-for-bit reproducible from a clean re-scan of the same source. Every
  automatic that "improves" the image is a guess about intent; guesses belong
  in derivatives, not in the master. Output controls should make that
  boundary mechanical: master file never opened for editing, every adjustment
  written into a sibling derivative.

WHICH AUTOMATICS TO DISABLE

  Capture / exposure
    - Auto-exposure
    - Auto-gain / auto-levels
    - Auto white balance (for reflective prints: use a fixed neutral profile;
      for negatives/positives: keep the calibration but disable per-frame drift)
    - Highlight / shadow recovery
    - Dynamic range optimization / "exposure compensation"

  Color
    - Color correction / color restoration (the "faded photo" auto-rebuild)
    - Saturation, hue, or tone-curve auto-adjust
    - Skin-tone, sky-tone, or scene-type detection
    - Color space conversion at scan time (scan into the largest working
      space, convert deliberately later)

  Sharpening / noise
    - Unsharp mask / "sharpen" at any level
    - Noise reduction (luminance and chrominance)
    - Edge enhancement / outline filters

  Restoration (the big one for prints)
    - Dust and scratch removal — hardware ICE / infrared cleaning, AND the
      software equivalent (Digital ICE, Magic Touch, etc.)
    - Fading / color restoration
    - Grain reduction
    - Backlight correction
    - Red-eye (not applicable here, but disable it on principle)

  Geometry
    - Auto-crop
    - Auto-rotate / "auto-straighten" / deskew
    - Auto-sizing / auto-resolution adjustment
    - Perspective correction

  Format-level
    - Any "save with adjustments" default
    - Embedded previews that bake in edits (turn these off or accept they
      exist; the master file itself is what matters)
    - Auto file naming that overwrites (set an explicit, monotonic scheme)

  What to KEEP on
    - Resolution / bit depth at their maximum
    - A neutral target profile if your scanner insists on one
    - Multi-sampling / multi-pass if available — that improves fidelity,
      it doesn't alter content

  One-line test: if flipping it changes any pixel that isn't sensor noise,
  it's an alteration. Turn it off.

OUTPUT CONTROLS — KEEPING ADJUSTMENTS IN A DERIVATIVE

  File format for the master
    - Uncompressed or lossless only: TIFF (LZW or uncompressed), DNG
      (lossless), PNG for smaller items. Never JPEG for the master.
    - Bit depth: 16-bit per channel even if the source looks 8-bit — gives
      headroom and is still faithful.
    - Color space: a large, well-defined one (ProPhoto RGB or scanner RGB);
      assign output space at export, not at capture.

  Folder / file layout
    /masters/        untouched captures, read-only
    /derivatives/    working files, edits, exports
    /metadata/       sidecar XMP, OCR, provenance notes
    Naming: stable, sortable, and never reused. A print ID + sequence number
    beats a descriptive name — descriptive names rot, IDs don't.

  File system hygiene
    - Set the masters folder read-only at the OS level once the session
      closes. This is the mechanical guard against accidental save-back.
    - Checksums (SHA-256) written to a sidecar manifest immediately after
      each scan. Re-verify at session end. The checksum is what makes
      "unaltered" provable later.

  Editing workflow
    - Open the derivative, not the master. In Photoshop / Lightroom /
      Affinity / GIMP: import the master, immediately "save as" a working
      file in the derivatives folder, and never touch the original again.
    - All edits non-destructive: adjustment layers / smart objects / XMP
      sidecars. The master can be regenerated from source at any time.
    - Versioning: derivatives get explicit version suffixes
      (IMG_001_v1.tif, _v2.tif, _export_web.jpg). No "final_FINAL2" names.

  What "optional later adjustment" looks like in practice
    - Color rebuild, dust pass, crop, straighten, output sharpening — all
      happen in a derivative file whose lineage is "from master IMG_001".
    - The master stays the artifact you'd hand a conservator; the
      derivative is the artifact you'd share, print, or post.
    - If a derivative edit turns out to be wrong, you delete it and start
      from the master. The master is never the thing you "undo."

CHECKLIST FOR THE 2/14 SESSION

    [ ] Scanner software: every auto above turned off, verified on a test scan
    [ ] Output: 16-bit TIFF, lossless, large gamut
    [ ] Folder structure created before first scan
    [ ] Masters folder flagged read-only after scanning
    [ ] Checksum manifest generated at scan time and again at session end
    [ ] Working files (any color rebuild, dust pass, crop) saved into /derivatives only
    [ ] Provenance note (which print, which sleeve, condition) written before
        the print goes back in its sleeve
    [ ] Unresolved dates and source provenance preserved as captured, not guessed

The discipline is small but mechanical: capture is honest, edits live one
folder over, and the master is provably untouched by the time you put the
sleeve back on the print.

A split in the rubber edge is end-of-life for that blade, even if small. Once the rubber is compromised, contact across the glass is uneven and the defect grows with use. The passenger blade is fine; the windshield is intact. Treat this as a real visibility restriction in rain, not a cosmetic issue.

CONSERVATIVE SHORT-TERM DRIVING BOUNDARY

The streak sits in your main sight line, so treat it as restricted forward visibility in rain.

  - Avoid driving in rain if at all possible until the blade is replaced.
  - If you must drive before replacement:
      - Daytime only. Not dusk, dawn, or night - oncoming headlights through a smear are much worse than the smear alone.
      - Light rain only. Moderate or heavy rain overwhelms a single working blade and the streak widens with road spray.
      - Low speed, surface streets. No highway - sustained spray defeats the smear.
      - Use the passenger blade on intermittent, defogger on, headlights on so others see you.
      - Increase following distance; expect a real reaction-time deficit.
  - Do NOT run the damaged blade on a dry windshield - the torn rubber can score the glass over time. Same for washer fluid: it just smears through the split and makes the streak worse.
  - Do NOT try to "baby it along" for weeks. Replace within the day if rain is in the forecast.

REPLACEMENT SEQUENCE

  1. Confirm the correct length. Driver-side length is usually 22-26 in depending on vehicle; check the owner's manual or measure the old blade. Don't guess - too long and the arms clash, too short and you lose coverage.
  2. Buy a pair. Even though the passenger side is intact, mismatched wear causes uneven pressure and the other blade usually fails within weeks. Replace both at the same time.
  3. Park on level ground, engine off, key out.
  4. Protect the cowl/hood. Drape a thick towel over the area beneath the arm pivot. If the spring-loaded arm slips, the metal hook can dent the hood or crack the windshield.
  5. Lift only the driver arm. Hold it steady - the spring tension is real.
  6. Rotate the old blade perpendicular to the arm and look for a small release tab under the hook. Press/slide the tab while pulling the blade down and out of the hook. Most modern vehicles use a J-hook (side pin) connector.
  7. Match the new blade's adapter to the old connector. Many new blades ship with several adapters in the box - pick the one that matches the J-hook exactly. A loose or wrong adapter is the most common install mistake.
  8. Slide the new blade up into the hook until it clicks audibly. Tug gently to confirm it is locked.
  9. Lower the arm gently onto the glass. Do NOT let it snap down.
 10. Repeat for the passenger side if also replacing.
 11. Test before driving - see below.

WHAT TO VERIFY AFTER FITTING

  - The new blade sits flat with even contact across its full length - no lift at the ends, no gap in the middle.
  - Run the wipers on a dry (or very lightly misted) windshield. Watch for chatter, skip, or any lift.
  - Spray washer fluid and run a full cycle. One pass should clear completely. Any residual streak, smear, or unwiped band means the install is wrong.
  - Both arcs clear evenly; no new ticking or clicking.
  - When the wipers park, the blades sit below the hood line and do not overlap the dark frit band at the top of the glass.
  - Confirm the area that previously streaked is now clean - that is the only test that matters.

WHEN NOT TO DRIVE IN RAIN

  - Until the new blade is fitted AND the wet-test above is clean.
  - If replacement cannot happen the same day: do not drive in rain at all. Main-sight-line streak + oncoming headlights + road spray is a genuine visibility loss, not a minor annoyance.
  - Even after a successful install: skip heavy rain at highway speed for the first short drive - it is a cheap final confirmation that the blades are tracking correctly under load.
  - If the post-fit wet test still shows any streak, chatter, or skip, do not drive in rain. The blade is mis-seated, the wrong adapter, or the arm itself is bent (a common prior impact from ice, snow, or curb contact). Re-seat and re-verify; if it still fails, the arm is suspect and a shop should check it before you rely on the wipers.

ONE-POT WHITE BEAN & KALE STEW ON TOAST
(~25 min; 2 dinner + 1 lunch)

 1. Heat 3 tbsp olive oil in a Dutch oven or deep pot over medium. Add the half onion (diced small) and a pinch of salt; cook 3-4 min until soft. Add 2 minced garlic cloves and 1/2 tsp dried rosemary; stir 30 sec. (~5 min in)

 2. Add the 14 oz can of diced tomatoes (with juice), 1 cup vegetable broth, and both cans of drained/rinsed white beans. Bring to a gentle simmer. (~7 min in)

 3. Stir in the kale leaves (stems torn off and discarded, or chopped and added with the onion if tender). Cover and simmer 8-10 min until kale is soft and the broth has thickened slightly. (~15-17 min in)

 4. At the 5-min mark, toast all 4 bread slices: brush lightly with olive oil, 400F oven or dry pan, 6-8 min until crisp. Rubbing the dinner-toast and the lunch-toast slices with a raw garlic clove is nice.

 5. Off the heat (~18 min): squeeze in 1-2 tbsp lemon juice, then salt and pepper to taste. Don't add the lemon earlier — citrus dulls on reheat, so the lunch portion gets a fresh squeeze.

LUNCH PORTION + SAFE COOLING

- Ladle about 1.5 cups (roughly 1/3) into a SHALLOW glass or metal container — wide and no more than ~3 in deep. A deep lidded tub will stay in the danger zone too long.

- Speed-cool: set the container on a rack or in an ice-water bath for ~10 min, then lid and refrigerate. Goal: pot to fridge within 30-45 min, crossing 140 to 70F inside 2 hr and 70 to 40F within 4 more hr (USDA).

- The bread does NOT travel with the stew. Store it at room temp in a bag/tin and toast it fresh at lunch (~3 min under the broiler); spoon the reheated stew over. Pre-toasted bread stored with stew goes soggy overnight.

- At lunch: bring the stew back to a full simmer for 1-2 min (kills anything that grew in the cool window), squeeze fresh lemon over, serve on the just-toasted bread.

If you want, swap the rosemary for thyme, or add a pinch of red pepper flakes with the garlic for warmth. The other 2 cans of beans and the rest of the kale keep fine in the fridge for 3-4 days.

The first drawing mistake is that you've drawn three closed contours — a finished outline around the bow, a finished outline around the shaft, a finished outline around the teeth cluster — instead of one continuous silhouette that all three parts share. Whenever each sub-shape has its own hard outline, the eye reads them as three small objects in proximity rather than as one object with internal structure. That's exactly the "separate little symbols" symptom.

Redraw the outer envelope of the whole key as a single unbroken contour first. Then put the interior divisions in afterward as lighter, softer lines that sit *inside* that envelope, where they read as articulation rather than as boundaries.

A quick check: squint at the drawing. If you still see three dark little islands, the silhouette is still broken. If it collapses into one brass-colored slug with notches at the end, the contour is doing its unifying job and you can proceed to value and cloth.

Two junctions to watch while you redo it:

- Bow-to-shaft. The shaft should appear to grow out of the bow, not butt up against it. The outer contour has to pass through that junction as one continuous line, not two ends meeting.
- Shaft-to-teeth. Same thing at the other end — the teeth are the termination of the shaft, not a separate object pressed against it. The bottom edge of the key should be one wavy line, not three flat bottoms.

Fix those, and the parts will hold together when you lay in brass value and cloth folds.

The two fields answer different questions and answer them on different clocks:

- **Owner-level permission / network-allowlist action** — authorization. Has the owner explicitly granted access, and has the required network path been approved? This is deliberate policy, flips on human/admin action, and is owned by governance/security.

**Semantic problem.** Collapsing them into one boolean ("ready") makes a single value carry two meanings that don't share a lifecycle. A merged field can't represent "connector green, permission unresolved" or "permission green, connector stale" — it can only show some composite. Anyone reading it has to guess which gate is actually driving the state.

That breaks fail-closed (any gate not affirmatively green should block action), breaks audit (when something goes wrong, you can't tell which gate failed), breaks owner lanes (connector on-call vs. governance on-call, different SLAs, different remediation), and exposes customer action — downstream UI, billing, or notifications can light up green on a record that isn't actually authorized.

TWO-COMPONENT PLAN

COMPONENT 1 — CRISPY TOFU (held separate, re-crisped at service)

Press and cube:
- 8 oz firm tofu, pressed 15-20 min under a weighted plate
- Cube into ~1-inch pieces (about 2 cups)
- Toss with 1.5 tsp cornstarch + a pinch of salt

Pan-fry:
- 1.5 tbsp neutral oil (vegetable, canola) over medium-high
- Single layer, work in two batches if needed — don't crowd
- 2-3 min per side until deeply golden and crisp on multiple faces
- Drain on a paper-towel-lined plate

Sauce (toss AT service, not now):
- 1 tbsp soy sauce
- 1 tsp rice vinegar
- 1 tsp sesame oil (stir in off the heat so it doesn't burn)
- 1 small garlic clove, grated
- 1/2 tsp grated fresh ginger

Holding Sam's portion (this is the whole trick):
- Keep it UNSAUCED, on a paper-towel-lined plate, uncovered
- Up to 1 hr at room temp: fine as is
- Up to 3 hrs: fridge loosely covered; re-crisp in a hot dry skillet 2-3 min, then toss with sauce
- Do not sauce ahead — sauce is what makes crisp tofu go limp

COMPONENT 2 — BROCCOLI + BELL PEPPER (held without getting watery)

Cut:
- 1 head broccoli: florets ~1.5 inches; peel and slice the stems thin (don't waste them)
- 1/2 red bell pepper: 1/4-inch strips (~1 cup)
- Pat everything dry with a towel — surface water is the enemy, it turns to steam and pools

Cook now, slightly under-done:
- 1 tbsp neutral oil + 1 tsp sesame oil in a wide skillet over HIGH heat
- Broccoli first, 2-3 min undisturbed to get a little char
- Stir in garlic + ginger (same amounts as the tofu sauce), 30 sec
- Add pepper strips, 1-2 min more — keep it moving, you want bright color and crisp-tender
- Pull off heat while there's still bite; it'll cook a touch more on hold/reheat

Holding strategy (pick one):
- Cleaner option: hold UNCOOKED veg in the fridge, finish-fresh in a hot pan when Sam arrives (~3 min total)
- Easier option: cook now under-done, then a 60-90 sec reheat in a hot dry pan with sauce at service

The non-watery rules — repeat after me:
- Pat dry before cooking
- High heat, wide pan, never cover with a lid (steam = water)
- Salt and sauce go in at the end, not the start — salt pulls moisture out
- Store loose/uncovered, not sealed tight
- Sauce pooled at the bottom of a held container is the classic soggy-veg failure

RICE — SEASONING + HOLD

Per portion (~1 cup cooked):
- Warm gently with 1 tsp sesame oil, 1 tsp rice vinegar, a pinch of salt
- Fluff with a fork; taste
- Optional finish: a few drops of soy, tiny squeeze of lime

Hold:
- Loosely covered at room temp ~30 min, or in a container in the fridge
- Reheat: microwave covered with a few drops of water 60-90 sec, or in a small pan with a splash of water and a lid on low, 2-3 min

TIMING FOR TONIGHT

1. Press tofu (start 15-20 min before cooking)
2. Cut veg, pat dry, set aside
3. Reheat + season your rice; portion Sam's rice into its container
4. Pan-fry tofu (longest cook); set Sam's portion aside UNSAUCED
5. Stir-fry veg slightly under-done; set Sam's portion aside UNSAUCED, UNCOVERED
6. Eat yours: tofu + veg tossed with sauce over rice
7. When Sam gets home: hot dry pan 2-3 min for tofu to re-crisp; same pan, 60-90 sec for veg with sauce; rice 60-90 sec with a few drops of water. Toss together at service

THE TWO MOVES THAT FIX YOUR TWO PROBLEMS

- Crisp tofu stays crisp: cornstarch coating + single layer + sauce added at service + re-crisped in a dry pan (not nuked)
- Vegetables don't go watery: patted dry + high heat + no lid + salt/sauce at the end + slightly under-done now + finished at service + stored uncovered

Pre-wash setup (do this before loading the brush)

- Block support: rest the block on a closed book or dense foam pad, both palms under it for any repositioning. No thumbs on the painted face.
- Map the buckle: find its high ridge. The first wash dried into that shape, so water will want to travel from ridge → low spot. If the low spot is on the light-edge side, that's your problem.
- Counter-tilt: raise the light-edge side of the block ~5° with a folded towel under that edge. The goal is net flow away from the light edge, even against the buckle's pull. Verify the tilt with a water drop on a scrap strip laid on the block.
- Rotate, don't slide: if the buckle is severe, rotate the whole block 180° so the ridge sits between you and the light edge. Paint that way, then rotate back when the wash is set. Rotating mid-wash is fine if done in one clean lift-and-set.

Brush load

- Two jars (rinse + clean). Squeeze the brush to a damp mop after every rinse.
- Drag the loaded brush once across a paper towel before touching the sheet. That's your working load.
- For a graded wash that fades toward the light edge: start on the dark side wetter, and end drier as the leading edge approaches the protected margin. Don't try to lay it all uniformly wet.

Protecting the light edge

- Leave a 2–3 mm dry margin right up against the light edge. The wash stops at dry paper on its own; this is the single most reliable guard.
- Keep a thirsty brush (rinsed, blotted) in your off hand. If the leading edge creeps toward the margin, touch the thirsty brush to the head of the bead and pull it back into the body of the wash — away from the light edge, never across it.
- Never rewet the dry margin to "blend" it. A clean hard edge there is what you want.

Laying the wash

- One confident pass, dark side first, pulled toward the buckle ridge and stopped short of the margin.
- Keep the leading edge uniformly moving. Slow = pooling in the buckle's low spot; too fast = streaks and ridges.
- If the buckle acts as a channel, let the wash flow along it — don't fight it. Just make sure the channel points away from the light edge.

Pool stop (if it puddles)

- Set the brush down. No more loading.
- Touch a thirsty brush to the puddle, lift straight up. One pass, no scrubbing.
- Press a paper towel to the spot for one second, lift. Don't rub.
- If pooling is creeping toward the light edge, lift it back into the dark wash with the thirsty brush, not outward.

Don't do mid-painting

- Don't press the buckle flat or lay anything on the damp sheet.
- Don't blow on the wash — it drives water into blooms.
- Don't rewet an area that's already starting to set.
- Don't lift the paper off the block; the block is what holds the sheet stable.
- Rest the brush on the block's taped edge, never across the sheet.

After this wash, leave the block at the same tilt until dry. The buckle relaxes as it dries; chasing it wet just shifts the problem to the next pass.

PREPARE
Turn the trouser inside out. Lay the leg flat on the ironing board with the opened inch centered. Don't fold anything yet.

PRESS (restore the original crease only)
Iron on cotton with steam, or use a damp pressing cloth. Press only along the existing fold crease to reactivate the memory of the fabric, then press the hem allowance flat. Do not introduce a new fold line.

PIN
Refold the allowance along the original crease. Pin perpendicular to the hem line, each pin catching a thread of the trouser body so the two layers don't shift. Use 2–3 pins across the 1" opening, placed just inside the original stitch line so the new stitches land as close as possible to the old holes.

THREAD + START
~20" of single-strand matching thread (single is more flexible and less visible than doubled). Thread the needle with even ends and tie a small quilter's knot at the tail. Anchor by passing the needle into the fold of the intact hem, running it inside the fold ~1/2", and exiting at one end of the opened section. The knot stays buried in the existing stitching.

STITCH — blind hem from the wrong side
With the fold edge of the allowance facing you:
  1. Slip the needle ~1/8" horizontally inside the fold.
  2. Angle down and pick up 1–2 threads of the trouser body just below the original stitch line.
  3. Angle back up into the fold and slip another ~1/8".
  4. Repeat across the opening, spacing picks ~1/8" apart, snug tension but never pulling the fabric flat — let the hem hang naturally and check every few stitches.

END KNOT
At the far end, take one tiny backstitch inside the fold, then run the needle through the inside of the fold ~1/2" and exit. Pull taut and trim flush — the tail disappears into the fold.

FINAL PRESS
Turn right-side out. Press the hem with a pressing cloth and steam, lifting and setting the iron rather than sliding. This sets the crease and the stitches.

CHECK
- Right side: hem line straight and continuous, no puckers, only faint thread flecks visible on close inspection.
- Wrong side: stitches lying flat inside the fold, no loose loops, no thread bridges across.
- Tug test: gently pull the allowance away from the leg along the stitched section — no gap opens.
- Transition: where new stitches meet the old intact stitching, no step, ridge, or change in hem depth.
- Crease: after cooling, the pressed line is continuous with the rest of the hem.

WASH NOTE
Turn inside out, wash cold, hang or tumble low. The 1/8" blind-hem picks anchored inside the intact fold on both ends are the standard for trouser hems and will hold normal laundering.

Most likely cause: surface oil or residue (often a fingerprint) sitting on top of the sizing, not sizing failure. The sizing is probably intact. Sequence:

1. Hands off until it's bone dry.
   Don't blot, don't add water, don't add heat. Air-dry at room temperature, 30-60 minutes minimum; longer is safer. Heat from a hair dryer or lamp bonds residue into the sizing rather than releasing it. The beading you saw will keep happening until the sheet is in equilibrium.

2. Inspect under raking light, no contact.
   Tilt the sheet near a window so light skims across it. Oil/residue reads as a faint sheen or ring even when fully dry. If the sheen disappears at full dryness, the contaminant was water-soluble and a normal wash will flow next pass. Don't press a finger, brush, or cloth to it - that's how you turn a recoverable spot into an abraded one.

3. Diagnostic wash, in two parts.
   First, on a scrap of the same paper (or a clean corner of this sheet that's outside your planned image), lay a single pale stroke - one brushload, heavily diluted. If that flows clean, the issue is localized.
   Then lay the same stroke directly over the spot. Three outcomes:
   - Flows normally: residue is gone or soluble. Repaint freely.
   - Beads persist: residue is bonded. Do not keep washing over it - you'll only drive it deeper and risk the sizing.
   - Sits in a defined pool/ring: partial. You can paint right up to its edge; the wash won't spread through it.

4. Integrate, don't disguise.
   Three preservation-first options:
   - Read the bead-shape as part of the design. Round voids of this size pass as stones, fruit, dew, leaves, or pearls once surrounded by pigment.
   - Reserve it as paper white. Lay the wash right up to its edge so the beaded outline becomes a soft dry border instead of an interruption.
   - Work the wash outward from the spot so it stays a light passage framed by color.
   Avoid gouache, opaque white, or heavy paint over the top - those sit on the surface as a patch and read as a repair.

5. Hard stop conditions - set the brush down the moment any of these appear:
   - Fibers raising, fuzzing, or pilling at the spot
   - Puckering past the normal wet/dry cycle
   - Pigment lifting back into the brush on a pass (sizing gone)
   - Visible thinning at the edges of the spot
   More water on a lifting area makes it worse. Air-dry flat and accept. Recovery options are limited to cropping tighter, backing the sheet, or routing it to studies - there's no in-painting fix for lifted sizing.

Things to avoid on principle:
   - No kneaded eraser, no dry-brush scrub, no paper-towel rub.
   - No ox gall, alcohol, or soap on cold-press - they tend to drive residue into the tooth rather than lift it.
   - No hair dryer.
   - No opaque cover-up.

If the sheen is still visible at full dryness and you want one gentle removal attempt: a clean, damp (not wet) brush drawn once across the spot and immediately blotted with a lint-free cloth. Once only, on a bone-dry sheet, stop the instant anything fuzzes. Most sheen spots on cold-press lose visibility under a wash once dry and don't need intervention - usually step 4 is the whole answer.

Plan for a warm chickpea-fennel bowl over couscous, two servings.

Approximate amounts
  - 1 can (15 oz) chickpeas, drained and rinsed — about 1.5 cups
  - 1 small fennel bulb (~8-10 oz): sliced into 1/4-inch wedges with core attached, plus a few fronds reserved for garnish
  - 1 pint cherry tomatoes (~2 cups), halved if large
  - 2/3 cup dry couscous (yields ~2 cups cooked)
  - 3-4 oz feta, crumbled (about 2/3 cup)
  - 1 small lemon: zest the whole thing, juice half (~2 tablespoons)
  - 3 garlic cloves, thinly sliced
  - 3-4 tablespoons olive oil, plus more for finishing
  - 1 teaspoon dried oregano (or thyme)
  - Salt and black pepper

How to cook the fennel so it softens without disappearing

The two failure modes are crunchy-raw in the middle (too thick or too hot) or dissolved into mush (too thin or cooked too long). The fix:

  - Cut the bulb in half lengthwise, then slice into 1/4-inch wedges, keeping each slice attached to the core. The core acts as a backbone and stops the slices from falling apart.
  - Use a wide skillet, not a small one. Crowding steams the fennel instead of browning it.
  - Heat 2 tablespoons olive oil over medium (not medium-high). Add fennel and a pinch of salt. Cook 8-10 minutes, stirring every couple of minutes. Medium heat lets the inside soften before the outside burns.
  - If the pan dries out before the fennel is tender, splash in 1-2 tablespoons of water — the steam finishes the softening without scorching.
  - You're done when you can pierce a slice with a knife tip and meet only slight resistance. The slices should look translucent at the edges with golden-brown patches.

When to add feta and lemon

Both are finishing moves, but for different reasons.

  - Lemon zest: add it early with the garlic and oregano. The aromatic oils in zest bloom in warm fat and spread through the dish. Heat-stable.
  - Lemon juice: add it off heat, just before serving. Acid is volatile and disappears if cooked; adding it at the end keeps the dish bright and cuts through the richness of olive oil and feta.
  - Feta: stir half of it in off heat so it melts into creamy streaks through the vegetables, and save the rest to crumble on top of the plated couscous so each bite has a cold-creamy contrast against the warm food. If you add feta during cooking it dissolves into a salty puddle and you lose both the texture and the visual.

Putting it together

  1. Boil 1 cup water with a pinch of salt. Pour over couscous in a bowl, cover, rest 5 minutes, fluff with a fork. Drizzle with a little olive oil.

  2. In a wide skillet, heat 2 tablespoons olive oil over medium. Add fennel and a pinch of salt. Cook 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until softened and lightly golden. Splash in water if dry.

  3. Add garlic, oregano, and lemon zest. Cook 30-60 seconds until fragrant.

  4. Add cherry tomatoes and chickpeas. Cook 5-7 minutes, pressing some tomatoes to release their juices, until you have a light glossy sauce coating everything.

  5. Off heat: stir in lemon juice and half the feta. Season with salt and pepper to taste.

  6. Spoon over couscous, top with remaining feta, reserved fennel fronds, and a final drizzle of olive oil.

Total active time: about 25 minutes. The fennel is the long pole — start it first.

1. Lay the sweater flat, front side up, on a clean hard surface. Smooth the area around the loop so the surrounding stitches sit at their natural size — do this before touching the loop.

2. Do not pull on the loop itself. With the blunt tapestry needle, work the tip into the base of the loop where it emerges from the surrounding knit, not into the yarn of the loop. Wiggle gently to loosen the small stitch that is holding it.

3. Once loosened, push the loop through the fabric to the wrong (inside) side using the needle tip as a guide — front to back, slowly. If you feel resistance, stop and reposition; do not tug.

4. From the inside, weave the freed yarn tail into the surrounding backing fibers for about 1–2 cm with the needle to hold it without a knot. Leave the tail uncut.

5. Redistribute tension on the front: with a flat hand, pat and ease the area in small circles so neighboring stitches return to even size. If a single stitch looks pinched or stretched, touch its loop lightly with the needle tip to nudge it — do not pull lengthwise along any column, which distorts the rib.

6. Inspect both sides before washing:
    - Front: no visible loop, even surface, no shine or stretched marks.
    - Back: tail lies flat, nothing protruding that you'd feel against the body.
    - Tug test: stretch the area gently in both directions — it should behave like the surrounding fabric with no return loop.

7. Wash inside-out on a gentle cycle per the care label, then lay flat to dry.

If at any point the loop tightens instead of releasing, stop — forcing it risks a run. Leaving it as-is and bringing it to an alterations shop is the safer move than proceeding under resistance.

For two, generous supper portions:

Pantry math
  - Lentils: the whole can, drained and rinsed (see below)
  - Short pasta: all 8 oz
  - Cherry tomatoes: about 2/3 of the pint, halved (save the rest for tomorrow)
  - Garlic: 3 cloves, thinly sliced
  - Spinach: 3 to 4 good handfuls (about 3 oz)
  - Dried herbs: 1 tsp oregano or thyme
  - Olive oil: 3 tbsp for the pot, plus a drizzle to finish
  - Parmesan: a 1 oz wedge to grate, plus the rind if you have it
  - Liquid: 5 cups of water or low-sodium broth
  - Lemon: zest from the whole lemon, juice from half, more at the table

Rinse the lentils — yes
Canned lentils sit in a starchy, slightly tinny liquid that will cloud the broth and mute everything you're trying to make bright. Drain them in a fine strainer and rinse under cool running water until the water runs clear. Shake off the excess. For a brothy dish especially, you want clean lentils that taste like lentils, not like the can.

Cook
  1. Warm the olive oil in a wide pot over medium-low. Add the garlic, lemon zest, and dried herbs. Cook gently for about a minute — you want the garlic fragrant and soft, not browned. Brown garlic turns the whole pot heavy.
  2. Add the halved tomatoes with a pinch of salt. Let them collapse and burst for 5 to 7 minutes, pressing a few with the back of a spoon so you get a quick sauce base.
  3. Add the lentils, the pasta, the parmesan rind (if you have it), and the 5 cups of liquid. Season lightly — the cheese will add salt later, so go easy.
  4. Simmer 10 to 12 minutes, stirring now and then so the pasta doesn't catch on the bottom. Cook to al dente. The pot should still look brothy and loose, not tight like a risotto. If it tightens up, loosen with a splash of water.
  5. Fish out and discard the rind.

Finish bright, off the heat
This is where the bowl stays lively instead of turning into a stewed, heavy thing.

  - Spinach: pull the pot off the burner entirely. Pile the spinach on top and stir it in. It wilts in about 45 seconds from the residual heat only. No more cooking. This keeps the color vivid green and the flavor fresh-green instead of cooked-down.
  - Parmesan: finely grate it on a microplane (powdery, not shredded). Off heat, ladle a small splash of the hot broth into a bowl with the cheese and stir to make a thin slurry. Stir that back into the pot. This emulsifies into a light silky body without cream. A big mound of shredded cheese dropped straight in would clump and turn the broth gluey.
  - Lemon: squeeze in the juice from half a lemon, taste, then decide if you want more. Acid at the very end lifts everything. If you squeeze it in while the pot is boiling, the flavor dulls and disappears.
  - Finish each bowl with a drizzle of good olive oil, a little more grated cheese, and an extra lemon wedge for whoever wants more brightness.

The principle: heavy flavors (cheese, starch, cooked greens, acid that's been boiled off) all want to be added after the heat is off or in the last moments. That's what keeps a brothy bowl tasting like broth with things in it, rather than a thick casserole.

1. Rinse test. Run one of the cloudy glasses under the tap or wipe it firmly with a damp microfiber cloth. If the film wipes or rinses away, it is residue (detergent or mineral) and is fixable. If it does not, it is almost certainly etching — a permanent chemical interaction on the glass surface, not a fault in the machine, and no further cleaning step on that glass will help.

2. Detergent. Confirm you are using the right amount (most people over-scoop; on most pods/cubes the dose is the whole unit, not two), that the detergent matches your water hardness, that the cube/powder is fresh and not caked, and that the main-wash compartment lid actually pops open mid-cycle. A caked or over-full compartment leaves a film exactly like this.

3. Rinse aid. Top up the dispenser even if it looks partly full — many machines have an indicator window and a low/empty rinse-aid reservoir is a very common cause of film on glassware because water no longer sheets off during the final rinse.

4. Removable filter only. If your model has a bottom-rack filter (usually under the lower spray arm), lift it out, rinse it under the tap, soft-brush the mesh, and reseat it. Do not go further than that — no prying, no grinding, no interior scrubbing.

Stop conditions: do not reach for scouring pads, steel wool, or abrasive powders on the glass, and do not treat permanent, non-rinsing cloudiness as a dishwasher defect. Etching is a chemistry issue (typically soft water + high heat + alkaline detergent + glass age); the remedy is adjusting detergent/rinse-aid use and replacing the affected glasses, not appliance service.

Inspection sequence
1. Lay it flat under bright light. Look at the whole toy, not just the seam — check for other thin spots, loose eyes/tags/squeaker remnants, and any stuffing tufts on the floor or crate that you can't account for.
2. Open the seam gently and measure it for real (often longer than it looks). Note whether it split along stitching or tore through fabric, and whether edges are frayed.
3. Pull out only stuffing that comes out freely with your fingers. Do not cut or dig — if stuffing is matted or beaded (foam pellets), that's a discard signal.
4. Re-check size vs. Kibo's mouth. Anything he could swallow whole or in large chunks → discard now, no repair discussion.
5. Decide who's likely to be right about Kibo's behavior. If he's ever destroyed a plush before, that's the most relevant data point.

On hand repair — generally not recommended for plush dog toys:
- Most hand stitching won't survive a determined chewer, and re-opening usually happens within days.
- Suture-style thread can become a linear foreign body if swallowed (one of the higher-risk ingestions).
- Fabric glues are often not pet-safe once chewed.

A repair is reasonable only if ALL are true: toy is too large to swallow in chunks, fabric is heavy (canvas/denim/fleece, not thin plush), you use heavy-duty thread with buried/knotted ends, you accept daily inspection going forward, and Kibo doesn't have a history of destroying plush toys. Otherwise discard.

Discard now if any of: small parts exposed or detachable; thin/typical plush fabric; seam in a high-stress area (neck, belly, leg join); foam beads/pellets inside; seam tears through fabric instead of splitting at stitching; Kibo has a prior plush-destruction history; or you find unaccounted-for stuffing tufts (possible prior ingestion).

Vet advice — call or visit promptly if any of these appear in the next 24–72 hours:
- Vomiting (single or repeated), gagging, or persistent cough
- Diarrhea, especially with blood or mucus; straining or no stool
- Refusing food for more than one meal
- Lethargy, hiding, or unusual quietness
- Abdominal pain: "prayer posture" (front down, rear up), tense belly, flinching when picked up
- Frantic grass-eating or repeated lip-licking

If you find tufts of missing stuffing but Kibo is asymptomatic now, a call to your vet for guidance is reasonable — they'll likely give you a 48–72 hour watch protocol rather than imaging. Given no symptoms, no small parts, and seam still intact with stuffing present, this is low-but-not-zero risk; the main job now is deciding whether this toy is durable enough to survive a second pass.

Dry inspection (do all in order, brush dry):

1. Visual on the ferrule seam — look along the crimp at the handle side and the bristle side in good light. Note any gap, lifted crimp fold, discoloration, or rust specks. A visible gap that catches light = retire.
2. Fingernail tap — hold the brush horizontal and tap the ferrule with a fingernail. Listen for a rattle or hollow click. Rattle that comes from the bristle end = retire; rattle only at the handle end is a yellow flag, continue.
3. Gentle dry twist — with clean dry fingers, try to rotate the ferrule a fraction against the handle and against the bristles. Any movement at the bristle end = retire. Slight movement only at the handle end = continue, but the brush is on notice.
4. Bristle tug — dry-pull a few hairs from the bundle. One or two strays is normal; a tuft that releases easily = retire.
5. Handle entry — check the wood just under the ferrule for cracks, swelling, or soft spots. Any of those = retire.

Optional low-stress wet test (only if every dry step passes):

- Plain water, no pigment. Dip bristles only — do not submerge the ferrule.
- Make a handful of strokes on scrap paper. Watch the ferrule-handle joint while the brush is wet and again as it dries.
- Water wicking up into the gap, any new movement appearing, or bristles twisting inside the ferrule = retire immediately, rinse and dry the brush before storage either way.

Retire if any of the following is true:

- Movement at the bristle-side crimp, or any movement that grows between checks.
- Visible ferrule-handle gap that catches light or wicks water.
- Rust, exposed metal edge, or a crimp fold that has lifted.
- Bristle loss beyond a stray hair or two, or bristles twisting inside the ferrule.
- Handle swelling, cracking, or softness at the ferrule entry.
- Any rattle originating from the bristle end, not just the handle end.

If it passes everything, keep it as a backup only:

- Reserve for sketches, color mixing, and large washes — not detail or final pieces.
- Store dry, flat or hanging bristles-down; never standing on the bristles.
- Re-run the dry inspection before each use. Retire at the first sign of progression; do not attempt to re-glue or re-crimp at home.

The cast shadow — specifically the contact point where the spoon meets the linen.

Before you touch a single reflection, look at where the bowl of the spoon is touching the cloth. Three things to verify there:

1. The contact mark is darker than any reflection on the spoon. On stainless against white linen the contact is the darkest local value in the whole setup; if it's not, the spoon is floating and no reflection work will seat it.

2. The cast shadow's direction agrees with the brightest highlight on the bowl. If your highlight says "light from upper left" but the cast shadow runs off to the right, the reflections will read as decal no matter how carefully you paint them — the light story is contradicting itself.

3. The cast shadow's edge has the soft, slightly broken quality of shadow falling on white weave. A hard-edged cutout shadow on linen reads as cardboard on paper, not metal on cloth.

If that contact is weak or inconsistent, fix it first and let it dry. Then when you repaint the reflections, bend them to follow the same terminator curve that the cast shadow implies — the shadow tells the viewer the cylinder's axis, and the reflections have to wrap that axis, not decorate it.

1. Edge test first. Touch only the very corner of the patch with a clean rubber-cement pickup (best) or a clean fingertip through a smooth tissue. Press lightly and roll a few mm along the film — across the paper, not up. Expected result: it lifts as one thin continuous sheet.

2. Slow peel. Keep the already-lifted portion laid flat against the paper right next to the still-adhered film. Advance a few mm at a time. Work from the edge that lifted first, across the patch — never from the center outward, never pinching upward.

3. Stop and rehydrate if any of these appear: the edge won't release, the film tears into crumbs or powder instead of a sheet, any fiber comes up with it, or the paper surface pills or scuffs. Do not keep picking at a resistant patch.

4. Rehydrate only if needed. Hold the sheet flat. Barely dampen a soft sable or synthetic brush and touch the damp bristles to the patch — do not stroke. Wait 60–90 seconds, then re-run the edge test from step 1.

5. Final tidy. One light pass with a clean rubber-cement pickup over the area, no pressure. Leave any faint residual stain in place — don't chase it; it will lift in a later wash if you choose.

Do not: rub any eraser (kneaded or otherwise) over the surrounding wash, apply heat, use saliva or tape, or pick at a patch that resists the edge test.

If the edge test still won't release after one rehydration cycle, stop and leave it until the sheet can be soaked from the back — that's the next step up, not more picking.
