CONSERVATIVE SEQUENCE (BEFORE PAYING)

1. Pause at the counter. Ask the pharmacist to show the adjudicated claim line — billed amount, plan-paid amount, member responsibility, NDC, days' supply, quantity, dispense date, and the network tier it processed under. Do not pay until those line up with what you expect.
2. Verify network status on this specific fill. Confirm River Park is adjudicated as a preferred in-network pharmacy for Golden State Rx Saver on this transaction (network flags can differ by plan, by date, and by claim).
3. Verify drug and tier. Confirm the NDC dispensed is lisinopril 10 mg and that the plan is pricing it as a preferred-tier generic with a $0 preferred-pharmacy copay, not as a non-preferred or non-formulary product.
4. Check for deductible or benefit phase interference. Ask whether any portion of this fill is being applied to a deductible, a benefit-stage reset, or a "first-fill" rule that could change the member cost.
5. If anything looks off, ask the pharmacy to set the fill aside (or reverse and resubmit) rather than paying cash and chasing reimbursement. Cash-pay usually forfeits the ability to simply reprocess.
6. Only after the line items match the verified 2027 terms, complete payment. Save the itemized printout or screen — the EOB/claim record is what any later dispute will rest on.

NEUTRAL QUESTIONS — PLAN (GOLDEN STATE RX SAVER)

Summary: likely appealable — "routine/preventive not covered" is a red flag, not a clean denial.

Why this looks off
  Routine wellness exam is the textbook ACA preventive service. Plans that cover it do so at $0 member cost. A blanket "not covered" reason usually means one of three things went wrong upstream: (1) the claim was misrouted/classified, (2) the provider used a problem-focused E/M code or a non-preventive diagnosis instead of a preventive code, or (3) the plan is genuinely a preventive-excluding design (grandfathered, short-term, or a plan where preventive is in-network-only and the clinic is out-of-network).

What I need to know before recommending action
  - CPT code on the claim (preventive adult medicine is 99381–99397; sick-visit codes 99202–99215 would explain the denial)
  - Diagnosis/ICD code (Z00.00, Z00.01 for routine adult exam w/ or w/o abnormal findings)
  - Plan type / carrier product name on the ID card
  - Clinic network status (in-network or out-of-network for this plan)

Recommended path, in order
  1. Pull the actual claim detail from CompanionCare Plus member portal or EOB line items — confirm what codes were submitted.

  3. If the codes are problem-focused: ask the clinic to rebill under preventive codes. Common with clinics that default to sick-visit coding if any concern was discussed during the visit.
  4. If the plan truly excludes preventive: confirm in writing via the Summary Plan Description, then decide whether to pay or escalate. This is rare for employer plans but not unheard of.

Tick removal sequence — fine-tipped tweezers

Setup
- Nitrile gloves, fine-tipped tweezers (the slimmer the better), a small sealable container with a few drops of isopropyl alcohol OR a ziplock with a barely-damp paper towel, antiseptic (chlorhexidine 2% or diluted povidone-iodine), clean gauze, treats.
- A second person to steady Kibo helps. Stay calm — your dog reads you.

Before pulling
- Take a photo of the tick attached, with a coin or ruler in frame for scale. Useful later if a vet wants species, size, or attachment stage.
- Note the date, body location (outside of shoulder), and roughly how long it might have been on (check against last walk/grooming if you track that).

Removal
1. Part the fur so you can see the mouthparts meeting the skin.
2. Grasp with the tweezers as close to the skin as possible — at the head/mouthparts, NOT the swollen body. Squeezing the body can push saliva/regurgitant into the bite.
3. Pull straight up with slow, steady, even pressure. No jerking, twisting, or crushing. A few seconds of constant pull is normal.
4. After release, inspect: mouthparts should be intact and still attached to the body. If a tiny dark fragment stays in the skin, leave it — it usually works out on itself. Don't dig for it.
5. Skip the folk methods (matches, vaseline, nail polish, etc.) — they make the tick salivate and regurgitate.

Specimen / photo preservation
- Photo: keep the in-place photo with its timestamp, plus a second photo of the removed tick next to a ruler for ID and size reference.
- Specimen: drop the intact tick into the alcohol vial (or the ziplock with a damp paper towel). Label with date and body location. Many vets, and some state or university labs, will accept it for species ID or limited pathogen testing if symptoms develop. Keep it for the full monitoring window below; discard at 4 weeks if Kibo stays well.

Cleaning the bite site
- Wipe gently with gauze dampened in diluted chlorhexidine or diluted povidone-iodine (Betadine diluted to weak-tea color).
- Pat dry. Don't bandage unless the spot keeps getting irritated.
- Avoid pouring alcohol or hydrogen peroxide directly into the wound — both sting and can delay healing.

Monitoring — contact the vet if you see any of these

Bite-site / local (days 1–14)
- Spreading redness, swelling, or a target/bull's-eye lesion around the site
- Discharge, crusting, or a sore that doesn't heal within a few days
- A lump or nodule that appears 2–8 weeks later

Systemic (typical onset 2 days to 4 weeks, depending on pathogen)
- Tick paralysis: any new weakness, wobbly gait, or hind-leg trouble in the first 24–72 hrs (rare, but urgent if it appears)
- Lethargy, fever (warm ears, panting at rest), decreased appetite
- Shifting-leg lameness or reluctance to move; swollen or painful joints
- Bruising, pinpoint red dots on gums or belly, pale gums, or unusual bleeding
- Vomiting, diarrhea, or dark urine
- Any neurologic change (head tilt, facial droop, seizure)

Keep the photo and specimen until well past 4 weeks of clean monitoring — if anything above shows up, the vet can use both. Most single-bite encounters resolve without incident, but tick-borne illness has a real incubation window, so a calm watch beats an early dismissal.

Worth raising at Kibo's next routine visit: whether your area's tick species warrant a baseline 4Dx or similar screen at his next checkup, and what prevention product fits the bike-commute + outdoor routine.

Yes — home monitoring is still appropriate based on what you're describing. A firm ~4 mm bump at a healed tick bite site, with closed skin and no redness, heat, discharge, or systemic signs, is most often a small granuloma (your dog's local tissue reaction to retained tick mouthparts or to the healing wound). These are common and usually shrink on their own over 2–6 weeks.

At home
- Warm compress (clean damp washcloth, comfortably warm, not hot) 2–3x/day for 5–10 minutes
- Do not squeeze, lance, or pick at it
- Re-photo the site every 2–3 days in the same lighting and angle so you can compare objectively
- Keep the area clean; no ointments needed unless the skin opens

Send the saved photo or call the vet if you see any of these

Local (site) changes — sooner rather than later:
- Diameter grows past ~1 cm, or you can see it enlarging day-over-day
- Spreading redness, especially an expanding ring or erythema >2 cm around the site
- New warmth, swelling, or tenderness when you touch near it
- The bump softens (becomes fluctuant) rather than staying firm
- Discharge, pus, bleeding, crusting, ulceration, or the skin breaking open

Systemic (whole-dog) changes — call same day regardless of how the bump looks:
- Lethargy, reluctance to move, or unexplained lameness — especially shifting-leg lameness, which is the classic early Lyme presentation
- Drop in appetite or water intake
- Vomiting or diarrhea
- Feverish behavior: panting at rest, warm ears/groin, seeking cool surfaces
- Stiffness, joint swelling, or apparent pain on handling
- Any neurologic change (head tilt, stumbling, facial asymmetry)
- Pale or tacky gums

Tick-borne disease window — watch through ~early June (2–4 weeks post-bite):
- Lyme (Borrelia): shifting lameness, fever, lethargy, inappetence; sometimes an expanding target lesion elsewhere on the body
- Ehrlichiosis / Anaplasmosis: lethargy, fever, joint pain, inappetence
- RMSF: fever, lethargy, joint pain, sometimes small red/purple spots on gums or skin

Quick rule of thumb:
- Site-only change and stable → photo it, reassess in a day, call if it grows or breaks down
- Site change plus any behavior change → call same day
- Any systemic sign → call same day regardless of the bump

If a 4Dx/Accuplex snap test was run at the time of the bite, a retest at the 4-week mark catches seroconversion; if none was run then, the vet may want one now as a baseline.

This is general guidance for what you're describing — not a substitute for your vet. If anything in the list shows up, send the photo alongside a same-day call.

TEN-MINUTE TWO-VALUE NOTAN SEQUENCE
(before you touch the watercolor sheet)

0:00–2:00  SILHOUETTE + LIGHT LOCK
  Scribble the setup's outer shape in 30 seconds. Don't think, just get contours down.
  Pick the dominant light direction and mark it with an arrow. This is the only decision you have to defend for the rest of the ten minutes.
  Name the focal subject. One shape, not three.

2:00–5:00  MASS ASSIGNMENT (the hard part)
  Fill the dark mass solid. Everything else is light — no midtones.
  For each reflected-light shape, force the binary: it joins the dark mass (and the dark mass holds), or it stays light (and competes with the lit side). Pick one. No third option.
  The reflected lights tempting you right now are the ones that, in two-value, will either dissolve into shadow or punch a hole in the form. Let one of those happen — that's the design working.

5:00–7:00  FOCAL READ CHECK
  Hold the thumbnail at arm's length. The focal shape should still be the first thing you see.
  If a reflected-light shape is drawing the eye more than the focal subject, demote it to dark next pass. Don't argue with it.
  Cover the focal shape with your thumb. The rest of the composition should still feel arranged — that's how you know the supporting masses are doing compositional work, not just filling space.

7:00–9:00  OMISSION PASS
  Walk the thumbnail and ask of each light shape inside the dark mass: is this earning its keep, or am I keeping it because I can see it in the setup?
  "I can see it" is not the same as "it belongs." Cut anything that justifies itself only by accuracy, not by composition.
  Same pass for small dark shapes inside the light mass — if a detail exists only because the real object has it, omit it.

9:00–10:00  FINAL READ
  One last arm's-length look.
  Confirm: one dominant dark mass, one dominant light mass, focal shape intact at distance, supporting shapes simplified past the point of competition.
  If yes — you have a value map. Carry it to the sheet.
  If no — you have nine more minutes on this same thumbnail before any paper. That's the trade.

The single rule holding the whole sequence together: if a reflected-light shape survives the notan at distance and in service of the focal read, it earns a place on the sheet. If it only survives because the setup has it, it's gone.

REVISED BREAK-EVEN VALUE OF THE 1,800 "EXTRA POINTS"

The arithmetic on the prior analysis was $1,800 × 0.5 = 900 extra points/year at $0 fee differential, which gave a per-point break-even of $0.00/pt — i.e., any positive redemption value favored the current card.

With $500 as ordinary planned spend, the earn-rate gap produces 250 extra points/year on the current card, not 900. The *literal* per-point break-even is still $0.00/pt (because both paths are $0 fee, $0/$0.0050 = 0). What changes is the dollar magnitude of the differential — that's the practical break-even to anchor on:

  At 0.5¢/pt:  250 pts = $1.25/yr
  At 1.0¢/pt:  250 pts = $2.50/yr
  At 1.5¢/pt:  250 pts = $3.75/yr
  At 2.0¢/pt:  250 pts = $5.00/yr
  At 2.5¢/pt:  250 pts = $6.25/yr

Realistic range for a program of this shape is 1.0–2.0¢/pt (cash/statement-credit floor to transfer-partner ceiling). The marginal value of staying on the current card is therefore ~$2.50–$5.00/yr, contingent on redemption value — down from the ~$9–$18/yr the $1,800 baseline produced.

If the $500 ends up being a floor rather than a ceiling (i.e., you charge more on top of it), the differential scales linearly; if it's the total, the upside is roughly the band above.

PRODUCT-RETENTION RISK

The risk in this category is what happens to the product itself if you downgrade — not to your account, but to the no-fee replacement:

  - Sub-product discontinuation. Issuers periodically sunset no-fee product-change targets. If the current no-fee option is retired in the next 12 months and you downgraded into it, you may be auto-migrated to a different (possibly less favorable) card with new earn terms, new fee, or both. Holding the current card preserves the right to PC into the version whose terms you actually read.

  - Re-upgrade friction. Some issuers treat a later upgrade from a no-fee PC as a *new* account rather than a product change: new annual fee, new SUB with spend requirements, possible inquiry on credit report, and possibly loss of account-opening date for relationship purposes. Downgrade may not be freely reversible — "free" only at the moment of the button click.

  - PC eligibility windows. Issuers often impose a 12–24 month cooldown before a second product change on the same account. If you downgrade in June 2027 and want back in by, say, Q1 2028, you may be blocked.

  - Erosion of remaining benefits. The current card's non-earn-rate perks (if any residual Cardmember Agreement protections remain — rental car coverage, purchase protection, trip delay, etc.) may or may not survive onto the no-fee PC. Downgrading quietly drops them if they don't.

POSTING-TIMING RISK

The risk here is what happens around the June 15, 2027 effective date and how spend counts:

  - Cutover ambiguity. If the card's terms are "beginning June 15, 2027," transactions that post *on* June 15 (or in the issuer's batch window straddling the change) may earn at the new rate, the old rate, or pro-rated — the notice doesn't specify. A single large travel charge that posts in that window could earn meaningfully less than expected.

  - Billing-cycle boundary. Earn is typically pegged to transaction post date, not swipe date. Pre-authorization holds that post after a statement cut can shift a charge's earn category. A travel booking on June 14 that posts June 16 may earn at the new (lower) rate even though you "spent" it on the current card.

  - Travel+dining classification. Merchant category coding (MCC) determines the 1.5x bucket. Hotels booked through third-party aggregators, in-app dining orders, and certain airline tickets often code as "other" (1x) regardless of how the issuer markets them. If you assume $500 of ordinary travel+dining and several hundred dollars code as "other," the actual 250-point differential is overstated.

  - Statement-closing vs. effective-date interaction. If a charge posts in the final days of the current card's last statement, it may count toward the current cycle's earn even if the effective date has technically passed. Conversely, charges early in the new cycle lock in the new earn rate. There's a ~2-week window where the timing of any large purchase is non-trivial.

  - Refund/reversal timing. If a travel booking is canceled and the refund posts a cycle later, the points clawback may apply against the new earn rate, not the original. Net earn on the year can be slightly negative on refunds that cross the boundary.

  - Pending-points treatment. Pending rewards on the current card post to the same rewards account; the notice confirms this. But "pending" → "posted" timing around the change isn't guaranteed to be seamless — there's a small operational risk of points being held in pending limbo during the cutover and resolving at the lower rate.

These are the categories of risk you asked about. The break-even math ($0.00/pt, ~$2.50–$5.00/yr differential magnitude) is unchanged in structure from the prior analysis; only the magnitude moves with the $500 spend assumption. Whether any of the above risks is worth that band is a judgment call I'm not making.

Compact preservation-safe workflow — single session, no contact with the image area.

Setup
- Light: north-facing or shaded window, no direct sun on the paper. If the sun shifts onto the sheet, drape a sheer white cloth as a scrim between window and paper — do not move the painting into direct sun.
- Background: matte neutral gray (18% gray card or matte poster board), larger than the sheet. No glossy surfaces.
- Phone: RAW / ProRAW if available; flash off; HDR off; AE/AF lock ready.
- Hands: clean, dry, lotion-free. White cotton gloves preferred. Touch edges only.

Placement
- Paper flat on the background. If a corner curls, clip outside the borders only — never across the painted surface.
- Phone on a small tripod or stacked books so the lens axis is centered over the sheet and perpendicular to the paper plane (parallel placement, no keystoning).
- Frame the whole sheet with ~2–3 cm of background visible on every side.

Color neutrality
- Set a custom white balance from a neutral card in a test frame, then remove the card.
- Histogram should sit mid-tone, no clipping at either end. Even illumination, no hot spots.

Glare check (before each shot)
- Take one test frame, scan for hotspots on cold-press texture or any sheen.
- If glare appears: nudge the paper 2–3°, lower the indirect light, or shift the camera slightly off-axis — then re-verify parallel.
- Re-shoot and re-check.

Sequence
1. Full-sheet frame (RAW, even light, no glare, no keystoning).
2. One reference frame with an 18% gray card placed in the lower margin, for later color correction.
3. 3–5 detail frames at the same angle and lighting — signature / corners, paint texture, any passage worth remembering.

After capture
- Return the painting to its original sleeve or storage immediately. No new handling, no cleaning, no flattening, no insert between paper and storage.
- Leave the gray card and gloves in place if more pieces from the same batch are next.

Here's the Growth team's draft method — and what's broken about it. I'm going to stay descriptive per the standing rule, and call out the structural issues without rewriting their protocol.

---

**What's in the draft**

> "Run for seven days. Check the primary conversion result each day. If treatment reaches p<0.05 on any daily read, stop and roll out. Effect-size reporting is optional. No separate stabilization cohort is planned."

**Why this method doesn't hold up**

1. **The 7-day peeking inflates Type I error well past 5%.** If the null is true, each daily p-read at α=0.05 carries a ~5% false-positive rate. Seven independent looks give a cumulative false-positive probability of 1 − 0.95⁷ ≈ **30.6%** — i.e. nearly a one-in-three chance of a spurious "winner" on at least one day, not 5%. Anyone reading a single daily p<0.05 won't see that.

2. **Early stopping on the first p<0.05 biases the effect-size upward.** A read that crosses significance first is, by construction, one of the more extreme draws in the noise distribution. Without a pre-specified stopping rule (e.g. an alpha-spending function, sequential bounds, or a fixed horizon), the magnitude reported at stop-time will systematically overstate the true effect. This is why their "effect-size reporting is optional" line is a problem on its own — the *only* thing stopping buys you is a biased point estimate.

3. **"Stop and roll out" removes the confirmation window.** Once you ship on the first significant day, you've spent your budget on a peek. A separate stabilization cohort (or even a fixed-horizon read at day 7 with no peeking) exists to verify the effect holds rather than to discover it. Skipping it means there's no internal replication step before rollout.

4. **No correction for the metric, either.** The above assumes a *single* primary metric tested daily. If the team also glances at secondary conversions during those 7 days, the family-wise error rate compounds further. Not stated either way — that's the gap.

5. **"Optional" effect-size reporting is the load-bearing risk.** Point estimates without confidence intervals, on a stopping-rule that selects for extremeness, will be presented to leadership as if they were stable lift. That's the part most likely to cause downstream harm — the decision reads cleaner than the evidence supports.

**What a sound version of this experiment needs (descriptive, not prescriptive drafting)**

- A pre-registered stopping rule: either a fixed horizon (don't peek; analyze once at day 7) **or** a sequential design with an alpha-spending function (e.g. O'Brien-Fleming) so the cumulative Type I error stays bounded at 5%.
- Effect-size reporting as **required**, not optional — point estimate with CI, reported at the analysis horizon, not at the stopping moment.
- Either a stabilization cohort / holdback for confirmation, or an explicit justification for shipping on the primary analysis alone (e.g. reversibility + low blast radius).
- A locked primary metric and a locked cohort definition before the run starts, so day-1 looks aren't quietly expanding the hypothesis space.

**Net call:** the method as written will produce a "significant" result roughly 30% of the time under the null, and when it does, the reported lift will be biased upward. Shipping on that signal without a confirmation read is the failure mode worth flagging in review.

Short sequence for the thumbnail pass:

1. THREE-VALUE NOTAN FIRST
Draw a 2×3 thumbnail. Block only three values: light (paper), mid (window mullion/wood), dark (cast shadow). No hue yet — pencil or one neutral wash. Confirm the warm wood reads as a distinct mid against the cool dark, with at least one full value-step separation. If the dark swallows the edge, the warm won't survive no matter what color it is.

2. RESERVE THE WARM EDGES
On the working thumbnail (and transfer to the final block-in), mask or leave dry the narrow wood edges before any cool dark goes down. Two reasons: ultramarine + burnt sienna mixtures are unforgiving over wet paper and will creep into adjacent warm passages; and the warmth has to be the *base* layer reading, not a topcoat trying to recover lost ground. Decide now which edges are crisp (frame contact), which are soft/lost (shadow wrapping onto the casing).

3. MIX THE COOL DARK ONCE, USE IT TWICE
On the palette: ultramarine + burnt sienna in roughly 2:1 leans a clean violet-gray; pull a touch of yellow ochre into a separate well to *gray* the chromatic punch if it goes too purple. Test the mix on scrap at three dilutions — the shadow core, the shadow penumbra, and the reflection in the deepest corner. You want one cool family that just gets diluted/thinned for the mid-shadow passages. Mixing fresh per passage is where warm edges get contaminated by accident.

4. EDGE HIERARCHY CHECK BEFORE COMMITTING DARK
Lay the darkest mix only on a *dry* test strip (or scrap paper sized the same as your final). Paint the three edge types side by side: crisp mullion-against-shadow, soft shadow-falling-on-wall, and the warm wood edge you reserved. Stand back at arm's length. The hierarchy should be: warm wood edge = softest or lost-and-found (it's narrow, let it breathe); wall shadow = mid-soft; mullion contact = crispest. If the wood edge is competing in sharpness with the mullion, the value separation is doing too much work and the edges need to be softened, not the color pushed.

5. COMMIT THE DARK PASSAGES
With hierarchy confirmed, run the shadow in two passes: first the mid-shadow dilution everywhere, let dry, then the core dark only where the hierarchy test said it belonged. Warm wood edges stay untouched — they'll read warm by contrast against the cool dark, which is exactly the separation you wanted instead of cranking saturation.

One nudge: since your concern is preserving warmth without orange saturation, keep yellow ochre (not burnt sienna) as the warm-edge modifier on the final pass — it'll tint the edge warm without raising the chroma the way sienna would.

Short answer: the 30-minute cap is a clinical prescription, so the clean path is to ask the clinic before stepping over it. Your data supports asking — it doesn't replace asking.

Why your case is reasonable to bring up
  - 30 → 35 min is ~17% over your current cap, at the upper edge of the usual ~10%/wk progression rule. It's a real change, not a trivial one, but it's also a single-session test, not a permanent step-up.
  - You've been at 30 min, 2x/wk, nonconsecutive, with no focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, gait change, or next-day symptoms. That's the cleanest possible "tolerance" signal at the current load.
  - Plateau at the cap is the standard trigger for a progression conversation — staying flat doesn't generate new information.

Concise evidence to give the clinic (copy-paste ready)

  Status / adherence
    - Running: 30 min easy, 2x/wk, nonconsecutive days — within prescribed cap.
    - Cross-training: Tue/Thu bike commute, each leg ≤25 min, easy effort — within cap.

  Symptom surveillance (all negative)
    - No focal ankle pain
    - No swelling
    - No instability
    - No gait change
    - No following-day symptoms (next-day pain, stiffness, or soreness flare)

  Proposed change
    - One 35-min easy-effort run this week as a single-session test, not a permanent step-up.
    - Revert immediately if any of the above symptoms appear.

  Question
    - OK to do one 35-min test this week, or do you want formal reassessment first?

Two things worth avoiding

  - Don't do the 35-min run before the clinic replies. The cap is the cap for a reason — the clinic may have set it against a specific tissue-healing or biomechanical window that hasn't expired. One self-override is how a prescription loses authority, and how you lose the option of a quick, low-friction "yes" next time.

  - Don't frame it as "I'm fine, can I just go?" Frame it as "tolerance data looks clean, here's the single test I'd like to run, here's how I'd revert." That gives the clinic something to approve, not something to argue with.

If the clinic says no or wants reassessment, ask one clarifying question: is the cap time-based (a healing window that expires on a date) or symptom-based (clean tolerance signals unlock progression)? The answer tells you exactly what evidence moves the needle next time.

    keep $125: $3,675 combined, $825 unused

  If 2 of 4 occur:

    raise $175: $4,050 combined, $450 unused

Verification checklist before electing

1. 2027 IRS self-only HSA limit. You've stated $4,500; confirm the actual Rev. Proc. figure on irs.gov or with your HSA custodian. If the real limit is lower than $4,500, raising to $175 risks excess-contribution exposure (see #7). If higher, raising still leaves room.

2. Whether the $225 deposits count toward the annual limit. Most employer HSA contributions do. Ask HR/benefits how these are categorized — (a) employer HSA contributions (count toward the $4,500), (b) Section 213(d) wellness rewards paid from a separate account (typically do not count), or (c) something else. The categorization changes everything.

3. Realism of "contingent." If these deposits are conditional on program completion, tenure, employment status, or any other gate, estimate the expected count rather than the optimistic count. The math above assumes all 4 hit.

4. Outside contributions for tax year 2027. Direct contributions from your bank to the same HSA, a spouse's HSA contributions, an IRA→HSA rollover (executed in 2028 but counted for 2027), or catch-up contributions if you're 55+ in 2027 — each dollar reduces remaining headroom.

5. Mid-year election mechanics. Confirm (a) the July 12 cutoff yields a prospective rate applying to remaining paychecks only (not retroactive to the 12 already processed), and (b) your plan permits the change without a qualifying life event. Some plans lock the election outside QLE windows.

6. HDHP eligibility for the full year. If you weren't HSA-eligible for part of 2027, the limit may be pro-rated; if you use the last-month rule (eligible Dec 1, 2027), you must remain HSA-eligible through Dec 1, 2028 or the excess is taxable.

7. Asymmetry of error. Excess contributions trigger a 6% excise tax annually until corrected. Falling short just leaves a small amount of tax-free growth on the table. If anything is uncertain, lean toward leaving a $50–$200 buffer rather than maxing exactly.

Dry flatten (140-lb cold-press 9x12, finished watercolor):

Sequence
1. Sheet is already dry — proceed.
2. Stage on a flat, rigid base larger than the sheet (foam board, clean melamine, glass). Sheet lies paint-side UP; base is grit-free.
3. Interleave directly on the paint: one sheet of glassine or silicone release paper. Not tissue, plastic wrap, or newsprint.
4. Platen on top of the interleaving: a second rigid clean board, or a sheet of acrylic/glass, covering the sheet fully. This carries the weight; the paint never does.
5. Light distributed weight on the platen — roughly 5 lb total for a 9x12. Enough to hold geometry, not enough to crush fibers or flatten cold-press tooth.
6. Leave undisturbed 48–72 h at stable room humidity (45–55% RH). The ambient humidity equalizes front-to-back; pressure only holds the geometry.
7. Lift a corner gently to check. Flat = done. Soft wave remaining = another 48 h. Stubborn curl past ~7 days of continuous gentle pressing = stop.

Stop and leave alone when
- Sheet is flat on its own when the platen lifts — success, store flat with interleaving.
- Residual curl after ~7 days of patient pressing — the paper has set a drying memory; further weight will emboss without resolving. Mat/mount at framing instead.

Why this path
- Curl is a moisture-gradient memory from how the sheet dried. Gentle constraint + ambient humidity equalizes it slowly.
- Heat, steam, direct water, and face pressure all risk reactivating pigment or shocking the fibers — ruled out per your brief.
- Interleaving + platen keeps every load off the paint surface.
- "Light" matters more for cold-press than hot-press: heavy weight over time can compress out the tooth that's part of the work.

Avoid
- Flipping the sheet paint-down under weight (face pressure).
- Sticky or textured interleaving on the paint side.
- Heavy weight — it won't speed relaxation, only emboss.
- Lifting to check more than once or twice — every lift resets the equalization.

The pattern you describe — continuous call, weak supply that intermittently drops further, indoor above setpoint, no safety trips — fits two common causes: the indoor coil starting to freeze (almost always from a restricted return or dirty filter) or the outdoor unit not actually carrying the load (compressor struggling to start, very common capacitor/contact failure in summer heat). Either way the right move right now is the same.

Do this now:

  1. At the thermostat, switch the system to OFF. Not fan-only, not cool. Letting it keep calling while airflow is already compromised is what turns a fixable problem into a frozen coil or a damaged compressor.
  2. While you're near the return grille, swap the filter if you have a spare. A clogged filter is the single most common cause of this exact pattern and is renter-friendly. Note the size off the old one so you buy the right replacement if you don't already have it.
  3. Do not open any equipment panel.

With the system off:

  - If a coil was starting to freeze, give it 2–4 hours to thaw before any restart. The thaw itself is when water shows up — be ready for that.
  - Optional quick read on the outdoor unit: step outside and listen for 30 seconds. If the condenser fan is running, the outdoor side is at least trying. If the whole outdoor unit is completely silent while the thermostat was calling, the compressor isn't engaging — that's a Saturday-morning HVAC call, not a tonight emergency.

When you restart (filter swapped, system rested):

  - Cool, setpoint 76. You should feel strong, cold supply within a couple of minutes. If airflow is still weak or the indoor temp climbs back above setpoint, leave it OFF and book the pro.

Escalate tonight only if you see something new:

  - Water appearing where there wasn't water before — if a frozen coil thaws fast it can dump a lot of condensate; pull the breaker to the air handler if that happens.
  - Burning smell, new breaker trip, or sparking.
  - Kibo showing heat distress: excessive panting, drooling, wobbliness, or stopping responding normally. At 82°F, in the coolest interior room, with water, behaving normally, a dog is fine for a short outage. If indoor climbs into the high 80s+ overnight and the pro can't come Saturday morning, that's the line for displacing to somewhere with AC (your renter's policy has $10K loss-of-use if it comes to that, but it's not the right call yet).

Saturday morning: call an HVAC tech and describe the symptoms — "thermostat calling continuously, supply air weak and dropping further intermittently, indoor 82 vs 76 setpoint, no water/smoke/breaker trip, filter just swapped." That's enough for them to triage over the phone and likely get you on the Saturday route.

     - sha256, sha1, md5. Multiple algorithms protect against single-
       algorithm false positives and tooling quirks.
     - Redirect tool output to a fresh log path; verify nothing was written
       back to the originals.

  3. Byte-level comparison
     - cmp / sha256sum across the two files. Don't infer equality from hash
       alone — actually byte-compare.
     - If hashes differ, run cmp -l to localize the first differing byte and
       the offset class (header, EXIF/APP segment, preview/thumbnail block,
       moov, footer). Where the mismatch sits is itself evidence.

  4. Container and format metadata (read-only tools only)
     - file -b to confirm declared format.
     - JPEG/TIFF/HEIC: exiftool -G:1 -s -n  (no -overwrite_original, no -o)
                       exiv2 pr -a -u
     - RAW (CR2/NEF/ARW/DNG): dcraw -i -v  (info only); exiftool as above.
     - Video (MP4/MOV/MKV): mediainfo  (default = read-only)
                            ffprobe  (read-only)
                            exiv2 pr for MP4/MOV tags
     - PSD/XCF: identify or file.

  5. Date-bearing fields (record, do not act on)
     - EXIF: DateTimeOriginal, CreateDate, ModifyDate (+SubSec), OffsetTime/
       Original. Subsec and offset are weak by themselves.
     - IPTC: Date/Time Created, Digital Creation Date.
     - XMP: xmp:CreateDate vs photoshop:DateCreated — record both, they
       diverge under edit. Also xmpMM:History, xmpMM:InstanceID.
     - Video: com.apple.quicktime creationdate, MediaCreated, TrackCreateDate,
       ModifyDate.
     - Container-level: filesystem mtime/ctime/atime — treat as weak; these
       drift on every copy.

  6. Sidecars
     - .xmp, .aae, .thm, .mov, .json, .csv, .txt, .lrcat, .cr3, .dng.xmp, etc.
     - Hash each sidecar that exists. A sidecar present on only one side is
       meaningful evidence.

----------------------------------------------------------------
PHASE 2 — CHARACTERIZE THE MISMATCH
----------------------------------------------------------------
A) Byte-identical, metadata matches
   The "checksum mismatch" was likely about a stored/expected checksum,
   not the file content. Re-pull the stored checksum AND the recomputed one,
   confirm both correspond to the same object (version ID, etag match).
   Still record the finding — sometimes "checksum mismatch" means the
   expected record is stale.

B) Bytes differ, format and most metadata match
   Local has been modified (re-encoded, metadata pruned, re-exported), or
   cloud was updated. Compare the byte-offset class from Phase 1.3 against
   known re-edit signatures:
     - thumbnail block rebuilt while main image unchanged
     - APP1/APP13 segments stripped or rewritten
     - preview atom (MOV) re-written
   These localize "modified" vs "untouched". They do NOT speak to the
   April 1994 day.

C) Bytes differ and key date fields differ
   Now you have a real provenance question. Don't pick a winner. Go to
   Phase 3.

----------------------------------------------------------------
PHASE 3 — WHAT ESTABLISHES THE PRESERVATION MASTER
----------------------------------------------------------------
A preservation master is established by INDEPENDENT, EXTERNAL, IMMUTABLE
evidence — never by the file's own metadata (which can be edited).

Strongest to weakest:
  1. External contemporaneous evidence — a contact sheet, notepad, email,
     or calendar entry from the period that names the file or its subject.
     Dispositive; overrides hash records if they conflict.
  2. Ingest-time checksum on a trusted third record — the hash as captured
     at first write, stored in a manifest/log/redundant store. Dispositive
     if no post-ingest edits are documented.
  3. Provenance chain to ingestion — object version ID, multipart upload
     ID, ingest job log; cloud hash matches the ingest record's hash.
  4. Container structural integrity — intact APP segments, coherent moov,
     no re-encode artifacts; outranks a copy that shows edit signs.
  5. Downstream-edit indicators on a candidate — editor temp/lock files
     (.psd~, ~original, Icon\r, .DS_Store, .lrcat, AAE), ResourceFork,
     stripped EXIF, xmpMM:History showing software after ingest. These
     WEAKEN a copy's claim to be the master.
  6. Internal metadata only — suggestive, never dispositive.

Decision rule:
  - Cloud hash matches an independent ingest-time record AND local shows
    downstream-edit indicators → cloud is the master. Local is a working
    derivative. Do not promote local.
  - Both copies match independent records (rare) → the older ingest
    timestamp is authoritative.
  - Neither copy matches any independent record → neither is established.
    Do not pick. Preserve both, escalate to whoever can produce the
    ingest record.
  - A sidecar exists on only one side → that side has richer provenance,
    but still requires ingest-time evidence before it is declared the
    master.

----------------------------------------------------------------
PHASE 4 — CATALOG-DATE DISCIPLINE
----------------------------------------------------------------
- The April 1994 Portland garden outing with day unresolved is the known-
  good catalog state. Do NOT change it.
- Do NOT use EXIF/XMP/IPTC date fields to narrow the day. They could be a
  correct camera clock, a wrong camera clock, a re-saved timestamp, or
  deliberately stripped. Treat any surfaced date as a lead, not an answer.
- If the comparison surfaces a date in one file but not the other, record
  the field name and source in the ledger with no inference.
- The unresolved day remains unresolved until external contemporaneous
  evidence (Phase 3.1) narrows it. The byte mismatch did not introduce
  date provenance; it is a separate question.

----------------------------------------------------------------
PHASE 5 — CLOSURE
----------------------------------------------------------------
- Master identified → write a short ledger entry naming it, citing the
  evidence (e.g., "cloud sha256 matches ingest manifest entry dated …
  local shows … edit indicators"). Do NOT edit the catalog date.
- Master not identified → log the escalation; leave both files untouched;
  route to whoever holds the ingest record. Do not promote a candidate.
- Either way, leave both copies byte-for-byte unchanged from the start.

----------------------------------------------------------------
FORBIDDEN THROUGHOUT
----------------------------------------------------------------
- cp/rsync that overwrite, especially --delete or "sync to canonical".
- Opening the file in any editor that saves, including "Save As" / Export.
- exiftool with -overwrite_original, -o, or any in-place write flag.
- ffprobe / mediainfo used to remux or transcode.
- Editing the stored checksum record to match either copy.
- Editing the catalog to "use the EXIF date" — the EXIF date is not
  authoritative for the unresolved day.

----------------------------------------------------------------
WHAT THIS BUYS YOU
----------------------------------------------------------------
- Both files remain byte-for-byte as you found them.
- The mismatch is localized to a byte range and a metadata diff, not a
  guess about "which is right".
- The master, if one is established, is established by something outside
  both files — so the answer survives a future re-check.
- The unresolved April 1994 day stays unresolved, on purpose, until
  external evidence earns a narrowing.

hash line, metadata fields, evidence column) so you can populate it once
you run Phase 1. That stays out of the originals by construction.

Call (method): Retain the fully backfilled 45-minute interval in the original denominator. Document the incident as reliability evidence (operational footnote + a disclosed sensitivity check, not the headline analysis). Do not exclude the interval.

Why this is the principled default, not a favorable post hoc cut:

  1. Pre-declaration discipline. Any exclusion from the analysis population belongs in the analysis plan written before outcomes are observed. No ingestion-incident exclusion rule was predeclared here, so the default is to keep the denominator as randomized.

  2. ITT baseline. Post-hoc trimming reintroduces the selection bias randomization was designed to remove. The cost of an unjustified cut is larger than the cost of carrying clean-but-late data.

  3. Symmetry, not asymmetry. The delay hit both arms; assignment logs are intact; backfill is complete. There is no differential missingness to motivate a carve-out. The threat here is the principle, not bias direction.

  4. Ingestion delay is not measurement corruption. Late events are still valid observations of what actually happened. Exclusion is justified by whether the primary metric's validity was compromised by the delay itself, not by whether events arrived late.

The condition that would justify different treatment — i.e., the only thing that should flip the default to exclude the interval:

  - The 45-min delay corrupted measurement validity in the primary metric (e.g., the metric depends on event-timing precision the skew breaks). Plausible for time-to-event metrics, implausible for windowed yes/no conversion.
  - Missingness was asymmetric across arms, or backfill was incomplete / non-random, so post-delay observations are no longer exchangeable across arms.
  - The delay was caused by the treatment itself (e.g., the variant broke event firing), so missingness is an outcome, not noise.
  - A pre-declared reliability rule in the analysis plan was actually triggered by this incident.

None of those are reported here. The first is the only one worth a probing sentence in the reliability note; the rest would be visible in the incident postmortem.

Boundary: this is a judgment on the analysis population and how the incident is recorded, not a ship call, not an effect read, and not an authority claim. The standing growth method (predeclared primary + min effect, 21-day powered read, effect size + CI, safety-only interim, full stabilization cohort pre-ship) governs the read itself; the 45-min window enters as reliability evidence, not as a denominator cut.

P027 — three-copy comparison

SUMMARY
All three P027 copies share: TIFF / 600 ppi / 4284 × 2860 px / embedded scan date 2027-03-14. The cloud and local SHA-256 differ (8b0c...41e2 vs. d739...a118). The retained worksheet has no checksum or byte count recorded, so it cannot be hash-compared to either digital copy. Both checksummed copies open normally; neither has been renamed or overwritten.

WHY
  - Visible/embedded metadata is identical on all three. The two checksummed copies therefore cannot be separated on format, ppi, dimensions, or scan date.
  - The two SHA-256 hashes differ in both prefix and suffix (8b0c vs. d739; 41e2 vs. a118), so they are different full hashes. Cloud and local are NOT bit-identical.
  - No rename, no overwrite, both open normally → identity/labelling and corruption are ruled out as the cause of the divergence.
  - A byte-level divergence that leaves visible metadata intact points to a non-content field having been touched (XMP state, ICC variant, padding, or strip/tile re-layout on save) — not to pixel or EXIF/date corruption.

CUTS — what is NOT a discriminator
  - Format, ppi, dimensions, embedded scan date: identical across all three.
  - Open behaviour: both checksummed copies open normally.
  - Rename / overwrite history: neither occurred.
  - "Looks the same": true, but does not imply byte-identity.

P — PRINCIPLE
Two files with identical visible metadata but different SHA-256 are not the same file. Without a recorded checksum on the retained worksheet, no copy can be declared bit-true against the worksheet. The worksheet cannot currently act as a hash oracle.

EFFECT
  - Worksheet gap: missing checksum + missing byte count. The worksheet still records provenance (scan date, settings) but cannot prove byte-identity to either digital copy.
  - Cloud vs. local: at least one of cloud/local has been altered post-scan. Which one cannot be determined, because there is no third checksummed reference to triangulate against.
  - Surviving truth: 4284 × 2860 px and embedded 2027-03-14 are intact on both checksummed copies, so any alteration did not reach those fields.

CALL
  1. Record both hashes against P027 in the catalog: cloud = 8b0c...41e2, local = d739...a118. Mark both "known on arrival, not reconciled."
  2. Backfill checksum + byte count on the retained worksheet — compute from the original scan if reproducible, otherwise stamp a post-scan hash and label it as such.
  3. Going forward: capture SHA-256 + byte size on the retained worksheet at scan time, before any cloud/local duplication, so future three-way comparisons are decidable.
  4. Do not declare a canonical digital copy yet. If byte-identity is required downstream, re-derive from a fresh scan or from the original source the worksheet points to.

Short answer: no. Descriptive metadata agreement is not a basis for selecting a preservation master when the hashes diverge and neither copy carries an anchored checksum.

Why this fails the bar:

  - Descriptive metadata (title, extent, date, format label, creator) describes the object at the label level. It says nothing about the bytes. Two objects with identical descriptive metadata are still two distinct objects.
  - Hash mismatch with metadata match is itself a signal, not a coincidence. It usually means one of the copies was silently re-saved, re-exported, or drifted, while the human-curated description was not updated. The asymmetry is information.
  - A retained worksheet with no recorded checksum and no byte count cannot be defended as a master. You cannot match it against any prior record, you cannot detect bit-rot in the keeper, and you cannot reproduce the choice for a reviewer later.

What you can safely do right now, without overwriting either copy:

  1. Compute sha256 and byte count for BOTH copies and write each as a sidecar file next to (not into) the object. A sidecar is not an overwrite of the copy itself — confirm that interpretation with your preservation policy if there is any doubt, but the bytes of the object are untouched.
  2. Put both objects into read-only / quarantine state.
  3. Treat them as working copies, not masters. Do not designate a preservation master.

The next authoritative record that resolves the question is the ingest-time checksum and byte count — the record that captured what was actually accepted at deposit. Typical homes for that record:

  - the accession record in your archival management system (ArchivesSpace, Preservica, etc.)
  - the AIP / SIP checksum manifest generated at ingest
  - the BagIt manifest if the transfer was bagged
  - the deposit or transfer manifest from the donor system

That record is the only thing that lets you say "copy A is the master because its hash matches what was accepted on YYYY-MM-DD" or "neither copy matches; the accession is under-documented."

Once you have it:

  - If one current copy matches the ingest hash, that copy is the master. The other is a derivative or a drift candidate — classify it, don't promote it.
  - If neither matches, do not promote either. Flag the accession as under-documented and reconstruct provenance before designating anything. Picking one anyway is the kind of decision that becomes unrecoverable later.
  - The structural / visual diff between the two copies is useful for characterizing the gap, but only AFTER you have the ingest hash to anchor which side is canonical. Don't let the diff choose for you.

Compact sequence — three elements working together (bead control, moisture checks, drying order):

1. Pre-mix both pools to identical flow. Tape the sheet flat so cockling can't shift your bead. Plan the seam: leave a 2–3 mm dry gutter between the two passages.

2. Paint passage 1 in one continuous pass, working away from the seam. Keep the bead even. At the inner edge, pull the bead OFF the seam — either drag it back into the wet zone with a thirsty brush, or tilt the board so gravity pulls it away. The inner edge should lose its wet shine first. (Bead control.)

3. Moisture check on passage 1's inner edge: back of hand or a clean dry brush tip. No coolness, no pigment pickup → proceed. If it still feels damp, wait, or set it with a hairdryer on COOL (heat lifts transparent pigment and shifts tone).

4. Confirm passage 1 is bone-dry to the touch before you load passage 2's brush. Drying order: 1 must be fully dry before 2's bead approaches — a partially-dried edge is exactly what causes backruns.

5. Paint passage 2 starting from the OUTER edge and working TOWARD the seam. Stop the bead 1–2 mm short of passage 1 — never let wet paint touch the dried passage. The dry gutter is your safety margin. (Bead control again.)

6. As passage 2 lays down, pull its bead off the OUTER edge (away from passage 1) so it doesn't bloom back toward the seam while it itself dries.

7. Final moisture check on passage 2 before any further glazing — touch-dry, not just surface-tack.

Why it works without scrubbing: backruns need a moisture gradient — a wetter edge meeting a zone that's just beginning to set. Fully drying passage 1 before approach, plus parking passage 2's bead short of the seam, removes the gradient entirely. Bead discipline replaces re-wetting.

Two small reminders for transparent darks specifically: keep pigment load consistent between the two mixes (otherwise the seam reads as a tone shift, not just an edge), and don't chase passage 2's bead into the gutter "to blend" — that IS the scrubbing you're trying to avoid.

A. AT AUS, BEFORE LEAVING THE AIRPORT
  - Get the PIR (Property Irregularity Report) number in writing. This is the single most important reference for everything that follows.

  - Confirm how they'll reach you (text vs. email) and whether purchases above a threshold need pre-approval. Some carriers require a yes before you buy.
  - Ask the standard timeline: when is the next status check, and at what point does it convert from "delayed" to "lost."

B. BAG DESCRIPTION — PRESERVE NOW, WHILE IT'S FRESH
  - Bag tag number (or any tag, even a partial one).
  - Airline, flight number, origin, check-in date/time.
  - Brand, color, size, hard/soft shell, wheels, distinguishing marks (ribbon, scuff, strap).
  - Rough contents list, especially irreplaceables: meds not in carry-on, prescription glasses, jewelry, documents, chargers.
  - Save the photo of the bag if one exists from check-in or from a past trip.

C. TONIGHT AT CHERRYWOOD — KEEP IT SIMPLE
  - Get her settled with what's already in the carry-on (meds, ID, charger, one change of clothes).
  - Do not run out to buy anything tonight. There's no urgency, and you'll want to know whether the bag is located before spending.
  - If she's missing one small thing (toothbrush, sleepwear), use what you have at home before buying.
  - Quiet evening, normal dinner, no extra logistics on top of an already long travel day.

D. WHEN YOU DO BUY — NECESSARY PURCHASES + RECEIPTS TO KEEP
  - Buy only what is essential to bridge until the bag arrives: basic toiletries, underwear, a top, basic meds not in carry-on.
  - Skip anything that could read as "replacement wardrobe" — airlines routinely push back on non-essential spend.
  - Keep every receipt. Photograph paper receipts the moment you get them.
  - On each receipt, jot date + one-line reason ("delayed bag, PIR #___"). This saves headaches at reimbursement time.
  - Pay with a card you can identify later; avoid cash-only when possible.

E. DO NOT DISCARD — KEEP THROUGH RESOLUTION
  - PIR printout and the email confirming it.
  - Claim ticket stubs and any bag tags.
  - All purchase receipts from 8/1 forward until the bag is returned or formally declared lost.
  - The bag itself once it arrives — inspect before accepting it back if there's damage, and photograph the condition.
  - The full text/email thread with the airline about the claim.

F. WHILE YOU WAIT
  - Status updates typically come within 24–48 hours. Track via the airline's app/website with the PIR number.
  - If silent by tomorrow morning, call the AUS baggage office number you captured — don't wait for them.
  - Domestic bags that don't surface are usually declared "lost" around the 5-day mark; the airline then owes a settlement, not just reimbursement. Note that threshold.
  - Reimbursement policies vary by carrier and even by fare class — when the dust settles, ask the airline for their specific written policy so you're comparing apples to apples.

ONE LINE TO REMEMBER: the PIR number + dated receipts are the whole game. Everything else is optional.

RULING — authority-holder coordination on the certified support measure

SUMMARY
Keep coordination time IN the certified measure. Do not reclassify as external waiting time.

WHY
External waiting time, as a category, is reserved for parties outside the customer-CS relationship (third-party vendors, processors, payment rails). An owner-level permission or network-allowlist holder is account-attached — they sit inside the account's authority graph, and the action you're waiting on (state change, suppression, lifecycle hold, owner action) is itself the deliverable in many cases. Pulling that time out would (a) hide real cycle time, (b) make authority-gated cases look artificially fast, (c) break comparability with cases that hit the same gate. It also conflicts with how lifecycle holds / state changes / owner-action triggers are already tracked — those are part of the support outcome, not external to it.

CUTS — what "external waiting time" actually excludes
Excludes:
  - Third-party vendor response time
  - Payment / processor / rail delay
  - Customer-side silence past the documented ask window
Does NOT exclude:
  - Owner / allowlist / authority-holder response time
  - Passive elapsed time waiting on the authority-holder after CS has issued the ask
  - Coordination work CS does to prepare, follow up, or escalate to the holder

PROCESS
  - Tag the case sub-state as "awaiting authority-holder" with ask-timestamp and response-timestamp.
  - CS-active time (composing ask, follow-ups, escalation) counts fully in the certified measure.
  - Passive waiting on the holder counts in elapsed-cycle for the certified measure, but is annotated for analytics — not reclassified out.
  - Update the CS measurement-definition doc to make the carve-out explicit so audits can verify.

EFFECT
Certified cycle time reflects true elapsed time per case. Authority-holder bottlenecks stay visible in the data instead of being hidden in a reclassification. Comparability across case types is preserved.

CALL
Keep authority-holder coordination inside the certified measure. Patch the measurement-definition doc so the carve-out is unambiguous, and have Ines confirm the sub-state tag is being applied consistently on her next audit pass.

THE POINT (state in the first 30 seconds)
The chapter traces one institutional move: rely on hidden labor, blame the person who stops, then "fix" it by writing the duty down without changing the conditions that made it unfair.

WALK THE BEATS (~6 min, one per minute)
1. The kitchen ran because someone quietly carried a rotating duty. The institution never recorded, staffed, or paid for it.
2. The duty was treated as if it ran itself — until it didn't.
3. When it stopped, the story flipped. The framing became that resident's personal failure, not the institution's missing support.
4. The final chapter adds the duty to the official rota.
5. Adding it to the rota doesn't change time, authority, or support. So the formal version inherits the same unfairness — with a paper trail.

THE QUESTION UNDER THE CHAPTER (~1 min)
Putting a hidden duty on paper is not the same as making it doable. Formalization without resourcing is how institutions keep the work and shed the responsibility for it.

HANDOFF TO THE ROOM (~2-3 min, pick the one that fits the room)
- Where have you seen an institution keep the work and shed the responsibility?
- What's the difference between a duty being on the rota and being doable?
- Who gets blamed when an informal system breaks, and why them?

GROUND RULES FOR THE OPENING
- Frame, don't resolve. Save "is the final chapter too easy on the institution" for later in the meeting.
- If someone jumps in early, take the question, hold it: "I'll come back to that after we walk the chapter."

Compact sequence for a wet-on-dry cool glaze with a preserved warm edge:

1. Mix and test on a scrap of the same 140-lb cold-press. Try a chromatic cool (ultramarine + a touch of burnt sienna, or Payne's grey straight) at glaze strength — tea, not milk. Lay one stroke, let it dry, and judge: does it stay cool, darken to your target value, and dry without a tide line? Adjust ratio here, not on the painting.

2. Verify value separation before glazing. The warm wood edge should already be lighter in value than where you want the cool shadow to land. Glaze darkens everything it touches; if the two values are too close, lift from the warm edge first so the later value jump reads as form, not as a line.

3. Pre-wet a 1–2 mm feather band on the shadow side of the boundary only. Use a clean round, damp then blotted so it's moist, not wet. Do not cross into the warm edge. This is your planned stopping edge — the paint will diffuse into the damp zone and die into dry paper, which is what kills the tide line.

4. One pass with the tested mix. Start well inside the shadow, sweep outward, and stop inside the pre-wet band. No second stroke, no scrubbing, no re-entry. The cool mass reads as a mass because you didn't disturb the deposit.

5. Leave it flat and untouched until bone dry. No hairdryer blast on wet glaze — the airflow pushes pigment outward and recreates the very tide line you set up to avoid. Air-dry, or low heat from a distance if you must.

6. Judge dry, then decide. If the shadow needs more depth, glaze again only when fully dry — never wet-on-wet for a second layer in the same zone, that's where orange mud and blooms come from. Each dry layer adds value without re-saturating hue.

The warm edge stays untouched because you never crossed it; the separation is value, not edge.

RULING — CS draft: "owner checklist would improve support performance"
Format: 1-pager. Summary first. why/cuts/p/effect/call.
Suggested route: #growth-investigations (Priya).

SUMMARY
Decline as written. The cited evidence supports a hypothesis worth testing — not a conclusion that a checklist fixes support. The draft treats a within-high-support-tail correlation (4/5 needed separate permission-holder coordination) as proof of a fix; there's no comparison group, no intervention, no measurement of change, and the audit packet isn't closed. Hold external distribution until the cohort cut is complete, the packet is closed/audited, and a pre-registered experiment with a defined min-effect + 21-day powered read has been designed. If the hypothesis is worth pursuing, route through the standard growth-brief path.

WHY — reasoning failures in the draft

  Selection on outcome. Only the 5 high-support workspaces (5/25 = 20%) are characterized. The 20 low-support workspaces are never described. We don't know whether coordination load discriminates high- from low-support, or whether it's just common. Without the comparison cut, "4 of 5" is uninformative.

  Correlation ≠ causation. Even if 5/5 high-support had coordination needs (it was 4/5 — 1 did not), that wouldn't prove a checklist reduces support time. Claiming a fix requires pre/post or treatment/control with effect size + CI on a primary metric.

  Confound. Workspaces needing a separate owner-level permission or network-allowlist holder skew larger, more regulated, in restricted industries — those factors independently drive support load. Coordination is a marker, not necessarily a cause.

  The unexamined 1. The single high-support workspace that did NOT need coordination is the most informative case in the set, and the draft ignores it. Whatever is driving its load isn't coordination; that's relevant to any proposed intervention.

  Existing-system overlap. An auth-checklist workflow is already live (Ines H2: rev approved 7/12; 4th-wkly declined 7/13 — ceiling ≠ auth). An "owner checklist" needs to be reconciled against the existing authority/auth framework before it ships as a separate construct, otherwise we duplicate or drift authority.

  Packet integrity. The packet hasn't been assembled, closed, or audited. Circulating "evidence" from an unaudited packet breaks the investigation protocol.

CUTS — what to remove before any re-circulation
  - Strike "this is evidence that the checklist fixes the support problem." Replace with: "hypothesis: a checklist may reduce coordination-driven support load; needs test."
  - Strike the implicit causal framing around the 4/5. Keep as a descriptive observation only.
  - Hold distribution outside the investigation channel until the packet is closed and audited.

P — primary metric (if hypothesis proceeds)
Support minutes per active workspace per month, segmented by complexity tier. Secondary: time-to-resolution, escalation rate. Process measure: owner-coordination events per workspace per month (not the primary).

EFFECT — minimum detectable + read window
Pre-register the minimum effect before queueing the experiment. For a ~10-15% relative reduction in support minutes to be detectable at 80% power given paid-cohort variance, expect a 4-6 week read across a randomized treatment/control split. Interim reads = safety guardrails only (per growth method, eff 7/6/27). Full stabilization cohort required pre-ship.

CALL
Decline as written. Re-circulate as a hypothesis to evaluate, not evidence of a fix. If CS wants to pursue, route through the growth-brief + experiment path with: (a) the 20 low-support workspaces in the cohort cut for comparison; (b) audit packet closed; (c) pre-registered hypothesis + min effect + 21-day powered read; (d) reconciliation against the existing auth-checklist workflow before any "owner checklist" is scoped.

Compact lost-and-found-edge sequence

Pre-work
  1. Mix a cool shadow value on the palette. Lean toward blue or violet-grey, not toward orange — anything warmer will fight the pale ceramic and brighten the shadow instead of swallowing it. Test on a scrap of the same 140-lb cold-press: confirm it's deep enough to read as a shadow next to the pale, and that the wet mix flows without flooding.
  2. Decide the two zones before touching the painting:
     - lost-edge section — the ceramic edge will melt into the shadow
     - found-edge section — the ceramic edge will stay crisp
     Don't pencil the dividing line; graphite wicks pigment and contaminates the edge.

Execution (paper fully dry, brush damp-clean, no soap)
  3. Found edge first. Load a brush with the shadow mix and lay one confident stroke along the section you want crisp. Stop the brush tip exactly at the pale ceramic's edge — don't cross it, don't retrace. Wet pigment against dry paper = hard edge. Let it set ~30–60 seconds.
  4. Lost edge second. In the section you want to lose, take a damp (not wet) brush and lightly rewet only the shadow side of the line — a thin damp margin forms beside the ceramic. Then drop a small amount of the same shadow mix into that damp margin. It bleeds outward a millimeter or two and softens the shadow's own edge. The pale ceramic, untouched and still bone-dry, visually dissolves into the softened shadow.
  5. Stop. Don't tidy the found edge. Don't chase the lost-edge bleed past where it landed. No second pass anywhere.

Judge
  6. Full dry before judging — air-dry or hair-dryer on low. Edge reads crisp where you planned crisp, dissolves where you planned soft. If the value is off, fix on the next wash, not this one.

Why this honors the constraints
  - No lifting: nothing below is reactivated.
  - No scrubbing: brush lays pigment and stops; no friction on the cold-press tooth.
  - No added orange: the mix stays cool, the rewetting is clean water only.
  - Rewetting is beside, not over, the pale edge — the damp brush only touches the shadow side; the pale ceramic stays dry through the whole pass.

Two cold-press specifics worth knowing
  - Blot the damp brush on a tissue before the rewetting pass. Cold-press valleys wick extra water and will leave a tide line if the brush is too wet.
  - Cold-press's slight tooth already breaks a "hard" edge at micro-scale, which is why a lost edge beside it reads convincingly without any scrubbing.

Ruling — historical replay vs. intake spec (CS-suppression rule on the reminder)

1. Summary
Growth's first historical replay is non-compliant with the intake. The intake explicitly required that active Customer Success adoption or renewal work suppress the reminder; the replay omitted that check and instead surfaced 12 accounts. Growth's post-hoc justification ("in-product reminder, not a send") is rejected. Surface is not the discriminator — concurrent CS work on the same account is. Treat the replay as in-error, do not read signal from it, and re-run with the intake's suppression check restored.

2. Why
- The suppression rule is keyed on a condition (active CS adoption/renewal work on the account), not on a delivery surface. In-product reminder and outbound send are both touches to the same admin during the same window. If either counts as a touch, the rule applies; if the rule were surface-gated, the intake would have said so. It did not.
- This is the same duplicate-touch concern as the Acme 2024-01 infra-migration suppression (registry marker only; enforcement at the (account, message_class) layer in Customer.io). That precedent suppresses by class, not by channel. The intake rule is the lifecycle analogue: suppress by workstream presence, regardless of whether the touch is in-app or sent.
- Spec is fixed at intake, not at replay. Redefining the rule to fit a cleaner-looking output inverts the growth method (eff. 7/6/27): scope and intent are set pre-launch. A replay is allowed to surface implementation bugs; it is not allowed to silently rewrite the spec.
- Growth's framing assumes the reminder is low-cost if no message is sent. It isn't. It competes for the same admin's attention during a window when CS is actively working adoption or renewal — i.e., the exact coordination cost the intake rule was written to prevent.

3. Cuts
- Re-run the replay with the intake's CS-suppression check restored. Expected count drops by however many of the 12 have active CS adoption or renewal work in the replay window. Expect a non-trivial share, not zero — the rule was written because the overlap is real.
- Show, per account in the 12: whether CS adoption/renewal work was active in the replay window, and whether the reminder would have been suppressed under the intake spec. That is the audit trail the intake requires.
- Hold any narrative or cohort decisions off this replay until the corrected read is in. Do not pre-justify shipping on the 12-count subset.

4. P / effect
- P (risk of leaving as-is): CS reps walk into accounts where the reminder has already primed the admin to push back on the CS-led conversation; expansion and renewal motions get harder for those reps in that window. Also, we lose the ability to distinguish "reminder drove the outcome" from "CS drove the outcome" — which contaminates both the lifecycle read and the CS read.
- Effect of fixing: small one-time engineering cost (restore the suppression check in the replay harness); preserves the intake's coordination guarantee; keeps the lifecycle and CS reads independently attributable.

5. Call
- Replay as-shipped is out-of-spec. Do not act on its output.
- Restore the intake's CS-suppression check and re-run before any ship/hold decision.
- Route: lifecycle/suppression lane owns the rule and the re-run (Ines, per the Acme precedent on Customer.io push). Eng (Daniela) confirms the suppression check is wired at the same layer the intake specified, not papered over at the UI layer. CS is informed that the replay temporarily violated the coordination guarantee so they can flag any accounts they noticed concurrent motion on.
- Add to the experiment/brief notes: a one-line statement that surface (in-product vs. send) is not a valid carve-out from the CS-suppression rule, so this doesn't get re-argued at the next replay.

Develop the second. The offset is the version that will actually feel quiet.

The centered thumbnail reads decorative precisely because the margins are equal — that symmetry signals arrangement rather than presence. An eye in a room with a centered window and balanced walls knows where to land and has nowhere else to go; tidy, but not still. The offset version inverts that relationship: the window becomes a small event held inside a larger field of dark. Quiet in painting almost always comes from this inversion — the lit thing is subordinate to the field around it, so the room is the subject and the light is something happening inside it. Vermeer, Hammershøi, most of what gets called contemplative interior work works on exactly this principle.

Two things to watch as you take it further:

- The right-side dark mass needs at least a single quiet break — a picture edge, a chair-back, a jamb, a fold — or it will read as dead weight rather than silence. One break, not several.
- Keep the window from being the brightest value in the painting. If the wall it's in can hold its own temperature against it, the window stops being a pasted-on shape and starts feeling like weather in the room. A centered window tends to want to be the loudest note; an offset window can afford to be quieter.

The binary value structure you already have in the second thumbnail is the right discipline for this kind of study. Resist the urge to add a third value mid-painting.

I don't see any thumbnails attached to your message — this session has no image channel, so nothing rendered on my side. If you can drop them into a shared folder and give me paths, or paste them into the chat on a channel that carries media, I can give you a real comparison.

In the meantime, here are the criteria I'd use to judge "quiet interior emphasis," and the one pre-sheet check I'd run on whichever thumbnail wins.

What supports a quiet interior emphasis:
  - Value structure: deepest darks and highest lights clustered around the focal interior; edges fall off into a low-contrast envelope (atmospheric or hard vignetting both work, but the contrast lives inside).
  - Chroma: muted, low-saturation palette overall, with any warmer note reserved for the interior moment.
  - Detail hierarchy: most rendering inside the focal zone; the surround reads as shape, not subject.
  - Edge quality: soft / lost edges around the interior; harder edges only where the eye should land.
  - Negative space and enclosure: the interior feels held — a wall, window frame, or table-edge closes the composition inward rather than letting it breathe outward.
  - Rhythm: low-frequency, slow shapes; no competing verticals pulling the eye to the frame.
  - Single quiet thing: one clear anchor (a hand, a cup, a fold of cloth) — not two.

The one practical check before drawing on the full sheet:
  Do a notan study — squint at the chosen thumbnail, then reduce it to a 2–3 value black-and-white (graphite or a quick digital desaturation). If the quiet interior still reads as the lightest, most enclosed shape with the deepest pocket of dark inside it, the structure will hold when scaled up and pigmented. If it doesn't, fix the value map first — no amount of beautiful washes will rescue a weak notan.

Test on an offcut first, then one pass on the passage.

TEST STRIP (same paper, margin if you have it):
  Three ratios by volume in a flat well:  1:8  /  1:12  /  1:16  pigment:water.
  Same brush (#10 round), same tilt (~15 degrees), one stroke each, dry flat untouched.
  Pick the ratio that reads quiet + transparent with no speckle settling into the tooth.
  For a pale wall passage it's usually 1:12 or 1:16.

APPLY (one chance, no fixing-up):
  1. Pre-wet the area with clean water — even sheen, no puddles. Sized tooth lets pigment glide instead of biting in.
  2. Remix at the chosen ratio in a wide, shallow well (deep cups let ochre settle in the cup; flat keeps it mobile).
  3. Load the brush fully — juicy, not dripping. A thirsty brush dumps pigment into the texture instantly.
  4. Board at ~15 degrees — enough that gravity carries the bead steadily down, not steep enough to run.
  5. One continuous stroke, bead leading, no overlap, no return at the edge.
  6. While the sheen is just leaving (not dry), one light connecting pass to close any dry-edge marks. Still no scrubbing.
  7. Dry flat. Do not blot.

KEEPING IT QUIET (the orange trap):
  Dilution is what pulls ochre away from orange. Adding more pigment to "fix" transparency deepens it toward red-brown, not toward pale wall.
  If granulation still shows, one drop of ox gall in the well keeps pigment suspended a beat longer — skip if the pre-wet + angle solve it.
  Never go back over a drying wash to even it out. That's scrubbing, and scrubbing is what lifts and re-saturates.

Conservative call: leave it. A light construction line on cold-press in a pale, dry, non-focal margin is generally lower-risk to keep than to disturb. The reasons line up with what you already noticed:

- Cold-press has visible tooth — graphite sits in the texture and is visually absorbed under most lighting.
- Even careful erasing can scuff the tooth or push graphite sideways into surrounding pale washes.
- Dry paint at the margin is at risk of micro-lift even when it looks set, especially if the wash was thin.

If it genuinely bothers you, the gentlest removal is a kneaded eraser used as a pick, not a wipe: condition it until pliable (not sticky), dab straight down on the line, lift straight up, and stop the instant you see any pigment disturbance or sheen change. Skip vinyl/plastic erasers here — they polish the tooth and leave a shiny patch that will show under any later glaze.

Under the conditions you described, the line almost certainly won't read in the finished study, and the risk/reward favors leaving it as part of the working drawing.

Cold-press watercolor paper — stray line removal, conservative sequence:

0.  Live-with check first. If you've been staring at it 20+ min, that's the signal. If covering it with a card/masking tape makes the painting read cleaner, removal is warranted; if it reads the same, leave it.

1.  Test OFF the line — on a non-critical margin or back edge, same paint layer. Same pressure you'll use on the actual mark.

2.  Low-pressure test, in this order, stop after each:
    a.  Kneaded eraser, dabbed (not dragged). Fresh spot per pass. Follow the tooth, never cross it.
    b.  Damp (not wet) clean brush, blotted first, then touch-and-lift. One pass, then dry.
    c.  Vinyl/cleaner eraser, lightest hand, only if (a) and (b) didn't touch it.

3.  STOP if cold-press resists:
       - any pilling, fuzzing, or visible tooth disturbance on the test patch
       - pigment doesn't lift under light pressure (forcing harder damages surface more than the line does)
       - more than two passes on the test area

4.  If it resists: it's part of the painting now. Reincorporate — deepen adjacent pigment, extend it into a contour, or add a small intentional mark that makes it read as a choice. Don't chase it on the main sheet.

Rule of thumb: on 140-lb cold-press, the surface will forgive one gentle pass; it will not forgive a second one in the same spot. When in doubt, leave it.
