Bottom line: this is normal, expected local reactogenicity — exactly how a healthy arm responds the day after an intramuscular vaccine. Nothing you've described is a red flag.

What it is: your immune system reacting to the injection at the site. Local soreness without spreading redness, swelling, hives, systemic symptoms, or breathing issues is the textbook mild post-vaccination presentation and typically resolves within 24–72 hours.

Comfort measures (optional):
- Move the arm normally; gentle use actually reduces soreness vs. guarding it
- Cool compress for 15–20 min at a time if it feels hot or tender
- OTC pain reliever (acetaminophen or ibuprofen) at label dose if you want it; no need to pre-medicate next time unless your clinician has specifically said otherwise

When to actually seek care (none of these apply to you now, but for the record):
- Spreading redness, streaking, or a hard, expanding lump at the site
- Hives, lip/tongue swelling, wheezing, or throat tightness → emergency (anaphylaxis, even hours later)
- Fever ≥102°F, fainting, or weakness beyond the sore arm
- Soreness that worsens after day 3 or hasn't improved by day 5

You're fine. Hydrate, use the arm, and ignore it.

General info, not medical advice — if anything below doesn't fit your situation, defer to a clinician.

Ordinary self-care for isolated mild arm soreness:
- Relative rest for 24–48 hours; avoid the specific motion that triggered it, but keep the arm generally moving within comfort.
- Ice 10–15 minutes on / 45–60 minutes off for the first 48 hours if there's a clear acute strain or tenderness; switch to warmth after that if it feels better.
- OTC pain relief at labeled doses (e.g., acetaminophen or ibuprofen) if you tolerate them and have no contraindications.
- Gentle range-of-motion work a couple of times a day (slow circles, elbow flex/ext, wrist rotations) to prevent stiffness.
- Check workspace/setup if it's work-related (mouse height, keyboard, sleep position) so you don't re-aggravate.

See a clinician promptly if you notice any of the following:
- Sudden severe pain, visible deformity, or a snap/pop you heard or felt at onset.
- Rapid swelling, spreading redness, warm/hot skin, or fever — possible infection or significant soft-tissue injury.
- Inability to bear weight through the arm, lift anything, or move a joint through its normal range.
- Numbness, tingling, weakness, or color change in the hand or fingers (circulation or nerve involvement).
- Pain that wakes you at night, is constant at rest, or doesn't improve after ~2 weeks of self-care.
- Chest pressure, shortness of breath, pain radiating to the jaw or left arm, or sudden shoulder/arm pain with sweating — treat as an emergency.

TEST SEQUENCE — run all four on the dry strip before touching the wall:

1. Mix volume. Mix in a wide flat well, not a tube-touched one. Aim for ~1.5× what the area looks like it needs. Consistency check: dip a ¾" mop, hold it vertical over the well. It should run off in a steady ~1-second stream — not cling, not drip. If it clings, add water a drop at a time. These two pigments settle fast, so stir (don't shake) just before loading.

2. Brush load. Wet the brush fully first, blot on a damp sponge, then load. Tap the rim twice — don't wipe. Test stroke on a scrap corner: uniform bead, no dry patch mid-stroke, no puddle at the end. Adjust load until both conditions hold.

3. Board angle. Prop at ~15°. Paint a 4" stroke down the test strip. The wash should pool into a clean teardrop at the bottom edge in 2–3 seconds — running off the page = too steep; standing still = too flat. Tune ±5°.

4. Re-pass window. Paint four identical 2" swatches; under each, try a second stroke at 30s / 2m / 5m / 10m. The 30s pass will bloom and shift orange. 5m and 10m should accept a clean glaze. Your rule: second pass = fully matte (no sheen, cool to the touch), never "almost dry."

APPLICATION SEQUENCE:

1. Mix once, mix enough. Same well, same 1.5× rule, same consistency, stirred again right before loading.

2. Load as tested. Lead with the belly of the brush, start ½" off the top edge so the leading bead forms off-page.

3. One continuous passage, top to bottom (or left to right), single slow stroke. Keep the leading edge wet, the trailing edge just behind. Don't chase the bead back upward.

4. Let the wash settle to matte. Don't tilt-flatten to chase a final drop — that creates the orange bloom at the bottom edge.

5. If a second value is needed, wait until fully dry, then glaze a fresh wet wash over the whole area. Never spot-fix.

Why your second pass goes orange and streaky: ultramarine is finer-particle and lifts first; burnt sienna is heavier and granulates, so it stays put. The moment you re-wet, scrub, or overlap a partially-dry pass, you selectively remove the blue and shift the mix toward sienna. One continuous wet passage + dry-on-dry glazes only is the fix.

FOUR-DINNER FREEZER PLAN — Oct Thu late closes (10/7, 10/14, 10/21, 10/28)

One batch-cook on Sun Oct 3, ~2.5 hr active. Each dinner is a 1-qt zip-bag portion, single serving, reheats from frozen in 12–15 min. No calendar event, no shared-time, Mon stays protected.

THE FOUR
1. Chicken thigh braise — boneless thighs, crushed tomato, castelvetrano olives, lemon, oregano. Serve over a couscous pouch or toast.
2. Beef + mushroom stew — chuck, cremini, carrot, red wine (or stock + splash red-wine vinegar), thyme.
3. Red lentil + coconut curry — veg; ginger, garlic, garam masala, spinach stirred in at end. Serve over rice.
4. Pork + white bean chili — ground pork, white beans, green chile, cumin, lime.

WHY IT BATCHES COMPACTLY
  - Pantry overlap: oil, onion, garlic, canned tomato, broth, salt/pepper, thyme/oregano, a few spices.
  - Protein split: poultry / red / legume / ground — nothing repeats.
  - One session: brown chicken + beef in parallel pots, simmer 35–75 min. Cook lentils and chili sequentially in the same pot.

FREEZING (ordinary — no vacuum sealer needed)
  - Cool to room temp, then fridge uncovered for ~1 hr so the bags stop steaming.
  - Portion into 1-qt heavy zip bags, lay flat, press air out, label (dinner # + date).
  - Freeze flat on a sheet pan; stack once solid. Good 2–3 months.

REHEATING (Thu night — pick one)
  Microwave: drop frozen block in a bowl, loose cover, 5 min @ 50%, stir, then 4–6 min @ full.
  Stovetop: small pot + 2 Tbsp water, covered, low heat 12–15 min, stir once. Better texture on the stew and braise.

AVOID
  - Pasta cooked in sauce (mushy on reheat). Cook pasta day-of or use rice/couscous/polenta.
  - Cream-based sauces (break when thawed).
  - Raw veg frozen solo (zucchini, cucumber) — mushy. Fine cooked into the stew/curry.

THU PLATE-UP
  ~15 min, solo, quiet. A handful of pre-washed greens with olive oil + lemon is the only "fresh" add; anything more turns the night into a project.

SHOPPING (~ $35–45)
  1.5 lb boneless chicken thighs · 1.5 lb chuck stew beef · 1 lb ground pork · 1 cup red lentils · cremini 8 oz · 1 onion · garlic · carrots · crushed tomato 14 oz · white beans 15 oz · coconut milk 13 oz · green chile 4 oz · castelvetrano olives · chicken broth 1 qt · small bottle red wine · couscous pouches x2 · frozen rice pouches x2 · thyme, oregano, cumin, garam masala, smoked paprika.

Summary first: a lever that suddenly pulls further than usual is almost always cable stretch, pad wear, housing compression, or a developing cable failure — not a barrel-adjuster problem you can twist out at the trailhead. Leave the bike locked indoors at Helio, get home without it, and book a qualified brake inspection before it moves under power again.

Same-day transport home (no riding)

Pick whichever fits your schedule and your distance from Helio:

  1. Walk-bike home. If Helio is within ~20 min walk of your place, this is the lowest-risk, lowest-cost option. Walking pace, no brake demand, no disassembly.
  2. Rideshare (XL / SUV). Take the front wheel off, lay the bike flat or hang it; fits in most cargo areas. Tell the driver before they arrive.
  3. Bus with a front-mounted rack. Most transit systems hold 2–3 bikes without disassembly. Confirm the rack is deployed and operational on your specific route before you commit to it.
  4. Pickup from someone you know with a hatchback, SUV, or truck bed. Same logistics as rideshare, minus the wait.

If none of those land in the next hour or two, leave the bike locked where it is and pick it up later today or tomorrow morning. Helio is indoor-secured per your notes, so it's not going anywhere. Don't rush the bike somewhere sketchy to save 30 minutes.

Bike handling until inspection

  - Don't ride it. Not even a "just a few feet in the lot to see if it grabs." A lever that bottoms against the bar can mean near-zero braking force, and you only find that out when you need it.
  - Don't squeeze the lever hard against the bar to "set" anything. That can mushroom a cable head or crush a housing end and turn a small repair into a larger one.
  - Don't twist the barrel adjuster to take up slack. A longer-than-normal pull is pad/cable wear, not cable tension. Twisting the adjuster masks the wear and can leave you with a lever that bottoms out and a wheel that barely slows.
  - Keep it upright. Kickstand, wall, or rack. If the brake is hydraulic, don't lay it on the right side or upside down for long — some calipers don't like inverted storage.
  - If you walk it, walk next to it. Don't coast down any slope. Gravity alone shouldn't be the first real test of a brake you're not sure about.

What to book

Call your shop (or any competent LBS) and describe it as a "rear brake pull-to-bar diagnostic" or "brake won't hold adjustment." Walk-in is usually fine for this. Ask the mechanic to:

  - Measure pad thickness (front vs. rear for comparison)
  - Inspect the cable head and cable end for fraying
  - Check housing ends for compression, kinks, contamination
  - Check the lever body and pivot for play or damage
  - Spin the wheel and watch the caliper for smooth engagement
  - If hydraulic: lever feel, pad auto-adjust, fluid level
  - Adjust or replace pads as needed
  - Replace cable and/or housing if there's any sign of wear
  - Test-ride the bike after the work before returning it to you

You don't need to pre-order parts. The diagnostic comes first, then the quote.

Don't ride it again until

  - The mechanic has test-ridden it
  - The lever returns to its normal position under normal hand pressure
  - The rear brake locks the wheel with authority, or holds the bike stationary on a steep with normal lever force

One last line, because this is the part people always negotiate with themselves on: don't ride it home "just this once." A lever that pulls to the bar is one cable snap away from no rear brake at all, and that is not the margin you want on a 25-minute commute.

DECISION: Cross-workspace collapsing — REJECTED

Summary
  Cross-workspace collapsing of shared addresses is rejected. Dedup is
  permitted only within a single workspace, keyed by workspace identity
  + exact normalized destination. The only carve-out is verified
  mailbox-equivalent addresses. Cross-workspace shared addresses must
  remain distinct; ordinary suppression and fail-closed checks stand.

Why
  Collapsing across workspaces erases workspace identity as an
  address-distinguishing boundary. Two workspaces sharing an address
  (forwarder, alias, role inbox, vendor mailbox) are operationally
  distinct senders — different audiences, opt-in posture, contractual
  context. Collapsing produces wrong dedup, suppresses legitimate
  cross-workspace reach, and breaks the per-workspace fail-closed
  posture currently enforced.

Scope
  IN:  any proposal treating an address as identical across workspaces
       for routing, suppression, or dedup purposes.
  OUT: within-workspace dedup — unchanged, permitted.

Exception (only)
  Verified mailbox-equivalent addresses — receiving system guarantees
  a single shared inbox regardless of declared workspace (confirmed
  shared mailbox, or DL with a single physical recipient). Verification
  requires documented proof, not assertion. No carve-outs by analogy.

p / confidence
  Operational / contractual, not statistical. High confidence that
  collapsing is unsafe by default; fail-closed is the only consistent
  posture absent verified mailbox-equivalence. Effect size / CI not
  applicable — this is a guardrail ruling, not a launch metric call.

Effect
  No behavior change. Within-workspace dedup continues as today.
  Cross-workspace shared addresses stay distinct. Ordinary suppression
  rules unchanged. Fail-closed checks remain on.

Call
  Reject the proposed cross-workspace collapsing. Reaffirm
  per-workspace identity + exact-normalized-destination as the dedup
  key. Carve-outs only with documented mailbox-equivalence proof.

Ruling — Decline as drafted.

Summary
The claim "active CS work predicts renewal" is unsupported by any outcome data in the aggregate CS shared, and a system check confirms no renewal/churn outcomes are currently available (list_recent_churn over 120d = 0 events; get_churn_metrics all-tier = no snapshot). Prioritizing on a proxy whose correlation with renewal is unknown is selection, not signal.

Why
- Outcome missing. The aggregate cuts are: renewal month (62/59/60/5), entitlement (154/18/14), active CS work (49/137). None is a renewal outcome. Renewal month is *when*, not *whether*. We have no way to tell if active-CS-work=yes renews at a different rate than active-CS-work=no.
- Selection on a proxy. Active CS work is endogenous to CS — it's the set already being touched. Treating "yes" as priority over "no" is partly tautological: those accounts already get attention.
- 26/74 split. Yes=49 is a minority of active-entitlement (49/154 ≈ 32%). Prioritizing the smaller half deprioritizes 105 active-entitlement accounts with no current CS work, plus 18 pending and 14 inactive, on a hypothesis with no measured effect.
- Pending vs. inactive is orthogonal. Pending (18) and inactive (14) are entitlement-status workstreams; folding them into a CS-prioritization rule conflates two problems.

Cuts
- Required: renewal outcome (renewed / churned / lapsed) × active CS work. The aggregate doesn't allow it.
- Useful: renewal outcome × entitlement status. The aggregate doesn't allow it.
- Useful: renewal outcome × tier. get_churn_metrics returns per-tier snapshots — try mid_seg / growth / starter once an asof_date is set, if a churn snapshot exists.

p / effect
- Pre-launch min effect not defined. Growth method requires a metric + min-effect bar before launch; this draft has neither.
- If outcome data becomes available, a 21-day read on the 49 vs. 137 split is feasible only with a control arm and effect size + CI, not a directional claim.

Call
- Decline the prioritization as drafted.
- Unblocker: pull renewal outcomes from the system of record (Stripe sub status changes, or whatever is downstream of the churn metric). Until that exists, no prioritization rule on CS work is evidence-based.
- Interim hygiene (separate, do not bundle):
  • Assign the 5 unassigned renewal-month accounts.
  • Triage the 18 pending-entitlement and 14 inactive on their own tracks.
- Once outcome data lands, reopen with: defined comparison (yes/no × renewed/churned), min effect pre-launch, 21-day read with CI, and a stabilization cohort.

Watchouts
- Don't ship a "prioritize active CS work" rule without outcome data — it codifies current attention as the priority signal and locks in selection bias.
- Don't merge pending/inactive entitlement into a renewal-prioritization doc — they're a different workstream and a different owner.
- Renewal-month timing ≠ renewal risk. Don't let the 62 Aug / 59 Sep / 60 Oct cadence imply anything about likelihood without outcome.

  1. SHALLOW PORTION (do this first, while hot)
     - Spread each serving in a container no deeper than ~2–3 inches.
     - Single-serving dinners already give the right width-to-depth ratio; just confirm the food is in a flat layer, not mounded.
     - Smaller exposed surface = slower cooling. If anything is thick/stacked, split it into two shallower containers now.

  2. PROMPT COOLING (active phase — goal: 140→70°F within 2 hrs, 70→40°F within 4 more)
     - Set containers in an ice-water bath in the sink or a roasting pan. Stir/rotate the container every 10–15 min so the center doesn't stay hot.
     - Don't seal lids yet — venting lets steam escape, and a closed lid traps heat and extends the danger zone.
     - If you have a freezer-safe metal pan, pour the food into it (metal conducts cold much faster than plastic) and sit that pan on top of an ice bath.
     - Target: refrigerator-ready (~40°F) in roughly 60–90 minutes for shallow single servings.

  3. WHEN TO CLOSE THE CONTAINERS
     - Don't close lids while hot or warm. Two checkpoints:
       a) Move to fridge: cool to room-temp / ~70°F first, then lid on loosely for the fridge, or fully sealed if going straight to freezer.
       b) Move to freezer: cool to ~40°F or at least no longer steaming before lid goes on tight. Putting warm food in the freezer raises the ambient temp and slows freezing for everything else, including these portions themselves.

  4. LABELING (do before lids go on tight)
     Write on the lid or tape a label with:
       - Contents (one or two words)
       - Date cooked: 9/26/27
       - Target Thursday: "Thurs 10/7", "10/14", "10/21", "10/28"
       - Reheat to 165°F
     If two dinners look similar (e.g. two chicken + rice), the Thursday date is what prevents mix-ups.

  5. FREEZING
     - All four must be frozen, not just refrigerated. Cooked food held at 40°F is safe only ~3–4 days; your last Thursday is 32 days away, so refrigeration alone is out.
     - 0°F keeps them safe indefinitely for safety; quality is best within 2–3 months — all four are well inside that window.
     - Freeze flat on a sheet pan first if you can, then stack once solid. Faster freeze = smaller ice crystals = better texture on reheat.
     - Leave ~½ inch headspace if the food expands (sauces/stews) — most single dinners don't, but check.

  6. THAWING FOR EACH THURSDAY
     - Move one container from freezer to refrigerator the evening before (Wed ~24 hrs ahead) or the morning of (~12 hrs). Single-serving shallow portions thaw overnight in the fridge.
     - Don't thaw on the counter — that's the classic danger-zone path.
     - Don't refreeze a thawed-then-reheated portion. Each dinner is one use.
     - If you forget to thaw: cold-water bath in the sealed container (change water every 30 min) is the next-safe option, then cook/reheat from there.

  7. REHEATING (each Thursday close — 3pm to 11pm shift)
     - Reheat to 165°F internal, all the way through — that's the safe threshold for previously cooked food.
     - Microwave: vented or loose cover, stir/rotate midway, check temp in the center.
     - Skillet/saucepan: medium-low, covered, stir often; add a splash of water if it's drying.
     - Oven: 350°F, covered with foil, ~15–20 min for a single portion.
     - Soups/stews/sauces: bring to a full rolling boil for at least 1 minute.
     - Eat within 2 hours of coming out of the fridge; don't reheat a half-eaten portion and re-store.

Order of operations tonight: portion shallow → ice bath to ~70°F → lid loose or off → finish cooling to ~40°F → label tight → freeze flat → Wed evenings, one at a time, move to fridge → reheat to 165°F before the shift.

Practical fix: yes, decant it.

Since the cap is compromised the tube will dry out or crust at the threads even if you try to seal it with tape/cling, and ultramarine dries hard enough to be unusable once that happens. The half pan is the right call.

Quick steps:

  1. Squeeze the paint into the half pan in one mound, or a few smaller mounds if it's a lot — mounds re-wet faster than a flat layer.
  2. Tap the pan gently on the table to settle and pop air bubbles.
  3. Let it dry fully before closing the palette — lid on while still damp = fuzzy mold risk. Air-dry an hour or two, or 5-10 min with a hairdryer on low.
  4. Label the slot "Ultramarine" (and the brand/series if you care to track it later — useful for replacing).

Working notes for once it's dry: pan paint re-wets slower than tube, so give it an extra few seconds of water on the brush before you commit to the stroke. Pigment load is the same, just the activation is slower.

Nothing leaked onto paper or other materials — good. The split-at-the-threads failure mode is usually the plastic getting brittle with age rather than anything you did, so don't beat yourself up about it.

Toss the tube (or keep it empty if you want to decant other colors into it later with a replacement cap from the same brand if they sell spares). Replace the ultramarine when convenient — no rush since the pan will carry you.

Short preservation-conscious sequence (no water introduced to the tube; cap never loaded):

  1. Stage over a disposable sheet (parchment/wax paper): clean palette knife, soft cloth pad, parafilm or cling wrap, small zip bag, labeling pen — all within reach before touching the tube.
  2. Set the tube on the pad with the split cap UP, unsupported, never bearing weight or being pinched.
  3. Access paint from the CRIMP end — unroll the back of the tube and extrude a small bead away from the cap, or gently roll from crimp toward the shoulder. Do not compress near the split.
  4. Lift the bead on the knife and press it into the empty pan well. Tube and pan stay dry at this stage; no wet brush, no口水, no solvent near the opening.
  5. Wipe the knife clean before it touches anything else, so the source pigment and the pan stay uncontaminated.
  6. Label the pan now — pigment name, brand, date — while the transfer is traceable.
  7. Contain the tube: wrap the split cap snugly with parafilm (or a piece of tape/cling), then place the whole tube in the zip bag so any future weep is captured. Fold the disposable sheet to trap any residue.

Net effect: a dry, labeled pan; an intact, isolated bead of pigment; a sealed, bagged tube with no load on the split cap and no contamination path back into the stock.

Standing rule check: Expansion Assist is descriptive only, dispute preserved, no line-edit of the draft, release/readback routes to Daniela. Working from the text you supplied; not modifying the draft body.

What the draft claim is doing

The claim does two things at once: it states an observed rate (4 expansions / 16 exposures = 25% per-exposure in a 45-day window) and it asserts forecastability ("four forecastable expansions per comparable exposure cycle"). The second half is the load-bearing part — it assumes the observed rate is attributable to Expansion Assist and will repeat under similar conditions.

What the evidence actually supports

16 exposures with complete 45-day windows. This is a defined denominator for one observation window, nothing more. It does not establish cohort composition, exposure dose, or that the rate is stable across windows. It also implies there are additional exposures still in flight whose windows have not closed — so the 16 is a subset, not the universe.

6 help-or-options requests. This is a competing observable of equal or larger magnitude than the 4 expansions. If Expansion Assist is surfacing help/options at a 6/16 rate and expansions at a 4/16 rate, the per-exposure contribution is mixed, not cleanly an expansion driver. A forecast that uses only the expansion channel ignores this.

4 expansions. The numerator. Observed within the window. No causal weight without a counterfactual.

No randomized control. The 4 expansions may be secular baseline, in-flight product adoption, or coincidence inside a 45-day window. Without a control, EA-attributable share of the 4 is unknown.

No exposed account had active CS adoption/renewal work at exposure. This rules out one specific confound (CS-driven expansion) but does not control for the rest. It also makes the sample non-representative of the broader population, so any forecast baked on this subset does not transfer cleanly to accounts with active CS engagement.

What the claim does not survive

"Four forecastable expansions per comparable exposure cycle" overreaches on three counts: (1) no counterfactual, so the 4 may not be EA-attributable; (2) no temporal replication across windows, so 4/16 in one window may not generalize; (3) the help/options signal at 6/16 suggests the per-exposure effect is mixed, not a clean expansion driver. The incomplete-window exposures are an additional reason "comparable cycle" is not yet defined.

What I will not do

I will not propagate "4 expansions per 16 exposures" into a forecast, batch, budget, paid-traffic, pipeline-transaction, or production-change decision. Per the standing rule, paid traffic stays off and downstream forecast references stay off until Daniela's check. The draft line itself remains as written — disputed, not deleted.

Route the dispute to Daniela as Expansion Assist owner. Her check needs to answer two questions: (i) what share of the 4 expansions is attributable to Expansion Assist vs. secular baseline, and (ii) what a comparable-cycle forecast should be conditional on that attribution. Sequence (do steps 1–4 before any mounting; nothing touches the sheet until the gate passes):

1. Baseline record. Photograph the sheet flat under raking light from the upper left, plus a 1:1 scan or full-size tracing. On the trace mark: painted image boundary, signature/inscriptions, deckle or watermark, and the four sheet edges. Measure the painted margin on each side — those values are what the mat opening must not steal.

2. Define the "must-show" zone. Anything signed, dated, titled, or composed to the edge belongs in the window. Working rule for this sheet: if the 0.375" left/right overlap or the 0.875" top/bottom overlap crosses paint, a signature, or a deliberately edge-touched passage, the mat fails.

3. Dry test, no adhesive. Lay the mat over the sheet on a clean surface. Inspect all four covered edges under raking light. The top/bottom coverage is the bigger risk — watercolorists often place a horizon, signature line, or breathing margin there. Confirm the visible 8.25 × 10.25 still reads as a complete composition with intended margins.

4. Decision gate. Reject the mat if any "must-show" element is hidden. Do not alter the sheet to fit; cut or commission a new mat with a smaller opening, or shift the window off-center to clear the signature and critical edges. Centering is optional.

5. Materials (only after the gate passes):
   - Mat and mount board: 100% cotton rag, alkaline-buffered (unbuffered only if you suspect light-sensitive pigments; buffered rag is standard for watercolor).
   - Corners: polyester or polypropylene conservation corners only. No PVC — it off-gases and damages paper.
   - Hinging tape: linen or Japanese tissue with starch paste or methyl cellulose. No pressure-sensitive acrylic tape.

6. Mount. Clean hands or cotton/nitrile gloves, clean surface. Sheet face-up on the mount board; the four corners grip only the four corners of the sheet — minimum contact, no pressure on the painted area.

7. Keep the mount reversible. Hinge the mat to the backing along the top edge with linen tape so the sheet can be lifted out for inspection. Do not hinge the artwork itself.

8. Label the back in pencil on the backing: artist, title (Quiet Offset), date, sheet dimensions, mounting date, "conservation corners, no adhesive contact," and your name. That label is what makes the intervention legible — and undoable — for the next handler.

9. Storage (no display commitment yet). Interleave with archival sheets, store flat in a clean folder away from light. If you frame later, use UV-filtering glazing and a spacer so the mat never touches the glass.

Reject triggers — any one is enough: opening covers signature, date, or inscription; opening crosses a painted edge meant to show; mat or corners are not specified archival (acidic board, wood pulp, PVC); sheet must be trimmed, folded, or pressed to fit.

Yes — reject the mat. Dry-laying it before mounting was the right test, and the test gave you the answer: the centered opening eats the painted mullion. That's a mat problem, not a painting problem, and the mat is the variable you adjust.

Why not mount: mounting is irreversible at the level that matters. Adhering the sheet to "fix" a framing mistake means recovering the mullion later would require separating paper from backing, with the usual risks — surface disturbance, adhesive residue, cockling, possible tear. You're spending irreversibility to solve something that has several reversible solutions.

Why not trim: worse path. Trimming cuts into a 140-lb cold-press sheet that's already painted to fix a mat choice. It destroys original material and forfeits every future option — different opening size, deeper mat, asymmetric reveal — none of which require touching the sheet. A limited-supply sheet (~3/mo) shouldn't be spent compensating for a framing decision.

Better paths, all reversible:
  - Asymmetric opening: smaller top margin, larger bottom, so the mullion clears the reveal
  - Smaller or differently proportioned opening, still centered
  - Deeper mat with the same opening, if you want more breathing room around the composition

Rule of thumb: when a mat opening obscures a painted edge that carries composition, the opening is wrong, not the painting. The painting is the fixed asset; the opening is the design choice you redo.

Sequence for transparent glass with one reserved reflection (140-lb cold-press, damp-paper method):

1. Mark only the endpoints. Light 2H tick at top and bottom of the planned strip, on the same side. These are bead-alignment guides, not an outline — a continuous pencil line here is the most reliable way to guarantee a mechanical edge later. Strip interior stays untouched.

2. Pre-wet evenly on both sides of the reserved zone. Damp, not flooded — surface sheen gone, paper still cool. Load a full brush so the wash flows under gravity.

3. Tilt the board and lay both sides in one motion. Angle so the bead on each side runs parallel to the strip, falling away from it. Keep the bead moving across the strip without stopping or reloading near it. The dampness makes the wash feather to a halt just shy of the strip; the tilt makes it refuse to cross. Don't aim at it.

4. Soften the edge before it sets. While still wet, the boundary between wash and reserved paper should feather to nothing. If a bead is drying hard right at the strip's edge, breathe on it or touch the edge with a clean damp brush to break the drying front. A crisp line forming now becomes a mechanical outline later.

5. Bone-dry before any next glaze. Hair dryer on low, or air-dry until no cool spots and no sheen. Any residual dampness will bloom or mud the following pass.

6. Each subsequent glaze repeats the choreography with the strip still reserved. Same tilt, same soft feather at the boundary — never a hard stop. The strip stays paper from first wash to last.

7. Check at arm's length, or under raking light. The reflection should read as light without edges. If you can trace the strip's boundary as a line, it has become mechanical — usually a hard-dried wash edge meeting dry paper. Under your constraints (no lift, no opaque), the only recovery is integration: lay a thin pale glaze that feathers across from the lighter side to soften the boundary by lowering local contrast at the edge, not by reclaiming the strip.

The whole technique depends on steps 1 and 3 being right. Step 1 is restraint (almost no mark); step 3 is choreography (bead direction, not brush target). If those are sound, the strip survives untouched and un-outlined.

CALL: Wait until admission 10. Don't evaluate the pause rule at admission 1.

Why the empty-state framing is wrong:
- The rule's job is detecting whether the launch cohort is generating *systemic* support burden vs baseline. One account cannot answer that. Single-tenant outliers routinely cross any fixed "10% above 90th-pct" line because of one customer's config, one migration, one bug affecting that tenant — not because the rollout is hot.
- A false pause at n=1 is operationally expensive: halt the gated rollout over a spike that would have self-resolved. Cost of false-pause >> cost of an honest empty monitor for a window.
- Same failure mode as the expansion_nudge_60d_v1 near-miss: don't act on a partial read. Acting on a 1-admission read is that failure in miniature.

Cuts to Owen's framing:
- "Empty monitor" is a UX concern dressed as a methodology question. Fix the framing, not the data. Ship a "warming up — first read at admission 10" placeholder rather than backfilling with n=1 numbers that train the team to react to noise.

P (rule fires correctly at exactly n=10):
- Modest, and worth telling Owen this directly. The "10% above 90th pct" comparison depends on a stable *baseline* 90th-pct — which itself needs adequate baseline n. If the baseline cohort is small, the baseline 90th-pct moves as new data lands, and your "above 90th" reading swings. Frame admission 10 as first read, not a definitive pause/no-pause verdict; revisit at 25/50/100 as rollout widens.

Effect:
- At admission 10 the comparison is smoothed enough that one bad apple doesn't dominate, but still early enough to catch a real cohort-level shift before more accounts are admitted. Keeps the rule doing its actual job (catch systematic burden) rather than its shadow job (react to single high-touch accounts).

Next message to Owen, if useful:
"Wait until 10. The empty state is honest signal, not a bug — a monitor that displays n=1 will train us to react to single-tenant noise. Re-evals at 10/25/50/100; 10 is first read, not final call."

Expansion Assist — pause-rule clarification (draft, for your review)

  Summary
  Early operational support observations stay visible in our reporting from day one. They inform our read of operational health but do not, on their own, trigger any pause. The formal pause evaluation is gated: it begins only once at least 10 workspaces have been admitted, and applies only when, on an evaluation cycle, more than 10% of admitted workspaces exceed 90 cumulative account-level support minutes.

  What stays visible before the gate
  - First-contact volume, repeat-issue patterns, qualitative notes from the early cohort.
  - Recorded and reviewable. Used for learning, not for the pause decision.

  When the gate activates
  - Formal pause evaluation starts at ≥10 admitted workspaces.
  - Below that, we observe; we do not run the gate.

  What the gate checks (once active)
  - Per evaluation cycle: share of admitted workspaces whose cumulative account-level support minutes exceed 90.
  - If that share is >10%, the pause evaluation applies per the existing rule.

  How account-level support minutes are counted
  - Continuous from each workspace's first support contact. No reset at the 10-admission gate, no reset at any evaluation cycle.
  - "First contact" = the workspace's first logged support interaction, regardless of admission status at the time.
  - A workspace that crossed 90 minutes pre-gate carries that into the post-gate evaluation; it does not reset to zero.

  Why the distinction
  - Visibility vs. gating: small-sample noise from a few high-touch early adopters should not dictate the pause decision, but we still want the signal.
  - Continuity: resetting the counter at the gate would let a workspace that already burned 90+ minutes pre-gate "reset" at evaluation and inflate the pass rate. Continuous accounting prevents that.

SUMMARY
- Don't approve. Five claim-to-boundary conflicts, each load-bearing — not stylistic.
- This is offline review only. No publish, no staging spin-up, no traffic enablement. Per the standing pre-launch QA rule, running it against the live campaign would be a V11 bypass and would contaminate the 11/1 P1 trace.
- Recommendation: return to acquisition with the conflict map; do not have me redraft the copy (Expansion Assist is descriptive only). Routing: rel/rb → Daniela.

WHY — claim × boundary

1.  "for every team" vs. eligibility
    Helio Start is conditionally approved, not universally available. "Every team" sweeps in non-eligible accounts (refusal-required, connector-pending, external-authority). The universal eligibility claim is unsupported.

2.  "launch in minutes" vs. refusal + connector-access
    Segments must still be refused at intake; others cannot launch until connector access resolves. A "minutes" TTV implies neither gate exists. Both gates are unchanged.

3.  "Skip assisted handoffs" vs. assisted-routing
    Direct contradiction. Assisted routing is an unchanged boundary; the copy tells the reader to bypass it. Beyond accuracy, it primes inbound traffic to ignore legitimate handoffs and raises refund / expectation-mismatch load.

4.  "Skip assisted handoffs and start setup immediately" vs. external-authority
    In segments where launch / spend decisions sit with an external authority (client security, IT, legal, partner-side), a self-service "immediate" start is not available. The copy overpromises a unilateral launch path that does not exist for those segments.

5.  Cross-boundary effect
    The five conflicts compound: universal reach + minute-level TTV + no handoff = a population the product cannot serve at that shape. Even if any single claim were defensible (none are), the combination is not.

EFFECT (downstream)
- Paid-search compliance smell: broad claims now, narrow product later. Reads worse than modest claims + modest product and is the version that draws partner / regulatory scrutiny.
- Attribution contamination for the 11/1 P1 trace: a cohort entering on this copy will have a TTV distribution dominated by the population that could never meet the promise. First-paid-month + activation metrics will be misread from day one.
- Support / refund load: the assisted-routing bypass promise guarantees a wave of "I thought I could skip this" tickets.

CALL

Test swatch first
  On a corner of the actual sheet or a scrap of the same 140-lb cold-press:
   - Lay a flat wash of the cool pigment at working dilution (transparent, pale tint)
   - Touch it with a barely-damp brush 60 sec later — observe bleed distance and granulation
   - Time how long the surface goes from damp sheen to matte so you know your rewet window
   - Confirm the cool wash won't back-run into the pale passage on its own

Protect the crisp edge
  Study is bone-dry before you start. Don't let anything wet come within ~3mm of that edge.
  - Hold a small scrap of paper against the edge as a shield (fingertip or clip)
  - Or pre-dampen a thin strip of paper just OUTSIDE the edge with clean water, let it dry — this leaves a faint capillary gradient that pulls the wash away from the edge instead of across it
  - Either way, the edge stays dry and untouched the whole session

Controlled rewet of the pale passage
  - Large clean mop or hake, damp not wet
  - Load it, then blot twice on a clean paper towel — brush should be just barely moist
  - One even pass over the pale passage, working outward from (and stopping well short of) the crisp edge
  - Wait 20–40 sec until the surface goes from glossy to a uniform damp sheen — that's your window
  - If beads form, blot. If it goes matte, re-dampen with the same barely-moist brush

Brush moisture for the cool wash
  - Mix cool pigment in a separate well at the dilution you tested
  - Fully load the brush, then touch the ferrule to a paper towel — flow without flooding
  - Brush should not be wetter than the dampened pale passage underneath

Application order
  - Touch the brush into the damp pale passage AT the interface with the cool shape, working AWAY from the crisp edge
  - Let the damp paper pull pigment outward at the interface — that's your soft transition, no extra strokes
  - Stop the wash ~1mm short of the crisp edge so the damp halo carries nothing across
  - If the soft edge is too abrupt: one pass with a barely-moist thirsty brush, perpendicular to the interface, to pull pigment outward. One pass only.

Drying order
  - Hold the study perfectly flat. Do not tilt until the surface sheen is gone — tilt = wash drifts toward the edge you want crisp
  - Remove the shield while the surface is still damp, so it doesn't wick pigment back from the edge
  - Dry flat with gentle horizontal airflow. No fan aimed at the crisp edge.
  - Don't rest anything on the surface until bone dry.

If something goes wrong mid-pass
  Stop. Don't lift, don't scrub, don't add pigment.
  Let it dry fully (10–15 min under gentle airflow), then read the dry result.
  A transparent cool over a pale passage is usually re-fixable by re-dampening and re-blending the same passage — the underlying tone survives a controlled re-wet, which is the whole point of the test swatch.

Tuesday bike commute — 42°F, light N wind, ≤25 min/leg easy. Prep sequence:

LAYERS (dress cool for minute 1, vent before minute 8)
- Base: long-sleeve merino or thin synthetic. No cotton.
- Mid: zippable vest or jersey so you can dump heat before you sweat.
- Shell: packable wind jacket in the back pocket; on only if gusts spike or on the descent.
- Legs: thermal bibs, or shorts + leg warmers you can push to the calves once warm.
- Feet: same shoes; toe covers or wool socks. Keep ankles covered (you've been nursing that ankle).

HANDS & EARS
- Full-finger gloves with a wind shell; liner gloves underneath if fingers run cold.
- Thin headband under helmet — covers ears without a hat-brim-shadow or overheating.

WARM-UP (stay in easy, do NOT push to "get warm")
- 5 min spinning at ~85–90 rpm in an easier gear than you'd pick on a warm day.
- Two short 30-second easy accelerations to wake the legs.
- Effort stays at easy the whole time. The 25-min cap means harder ≠ warmer.

VISIBILITY (Nov overcast, low sun angle on the commute)
- Front light on steady or pulse even in daylight.
- Rear light, brighter than you think you need.
- Hi-vis vest or a bright panel on the jacket.
- Reflective ankle band — motion catches the eye more than static reflectors on the bike.

DON'T CHASE WARMTH WITH EFFORT
- Cold at minute 2 = add a layer before you leave, not after you're moving.
- Climb hills seated; standing cools you fast in a north wind.
- Tuck on descents to cut wind chill rather than pedaling harder into it.
- If you feel sweat starting, unzip or strip the vest at the next light — sweat + 42°F wind on the back half is the actual chill risk, not the first mile.
- Stop and add a layer if your fingers go numb; numb fingers don't warn you before they get bad.

- $36.50 twice monthly: 24 payments × $36.50 = $876.00

Both rebuild the full renewal amount over 12 months (Nov 2027–Oct 2028) and arrive at $876 by the 11/1/28 renewal date. There is no interest, no fee, and no rounding gap — these are arithmetically equivalent sinks.

CASH-FLOW DIFFERENCE

The only real difference is granularity and alignment:

Frequency. Twice-monthly means 24 outflows instead of 12. Half the dollar amount per event, but twice as many events hitting the household budget.

Lumpiness. $73 once a month is a single moderate-sized line item that competes with rent, utilities, and other monthly bills. $36.50 twice a month is two small pulls that blend more easily into everyday spending but require tracking 24 dates.

Payday alignment. This is the deciding factor for most households. If you and Sam get paid on the 1st and 15th (or biweekly with two paydays per month), $36.50 twice monthly lines up cleanly with each paycheck — the contribution is funded before it can drift. If income is monthly or weekly, $73 monthly reduces administrative friction.

Failure mode. A missed $36.50 is half the setback of a missed $73, but twice-monthly gives you twice as many chances to miss one. The reverse is also true: it's easier to backfill a smaller gap.

HOW THE SINKING FUND STAYS SEPARATE

This matters more than the cadence choice.

Account-level separation. The fund should live in its own sub-account, savings bucket, YNAB category, or envelope — never in the operating checking account that pays rent and groceries. The current $876 premium was paid out of household cash on 8/2/27; the new fund's job is to pre-fund next year's outlay, not to "pay back" the old one.

Independence from the policy. The premium is a fixed cost of coverage. It is owed whether or not Kibo files a single claim during the 11/1/27–10/31/28 term. The fund accumulates regardless of vet visits, accidents, or behavioral episodes. Conversely, a heavy claims year (even one that approaches the $10,000 annual cap) does not raise next year's premium through any mechanism the household controls — that is CompanionCare Plus's underwriting, not Riley's savings discipline.

Independence from coverage terms. The $500 deductible, 80% reimbursement, $10,000 annual limit, and behavioral-care (post-deductible) terms are governed by the policy contract. Nothing done with the sinking fund changes them. The fund is a household cash-management tool, not a coverage modifier.

Refund scenario. If the policy is cancelled mid-term, any premium refund comes from CompanionCare Plus pro-rated against their rules — not from the sinking fund. If cancellation happens, you stop funding, and the accumulated balance reverts to available household cash. The fund never becomes the insurer's money.

CALL

Pick the cadence that matches your and Sam's pay schedule. Twice-monthly wins if income arrives twice a month and you want each contribution to feel weightless; monthly wins if you'd rather see one line item on the budget and reduce the number of moving dates. Either way, the arithmetic is identical, and the fund stays a separate pot that does not touch current coverage or claims.

A practical temporary mount. Test before committing the full sheet.

1. Backer
   Rigid board at least 1 in larger than the sheet on every side (Masonite, sealed foam core, gator, or sealed plywood). Wipe with a damp cloth and dry. Dust or oil breaks adhesion and lifts fibers on removal.

2. Expendable margin
   Reserve a 1 in border all around as the tape zone. Pencil-mark the corners if it helps keep the painted area clear. The painted area stays free of adhesive.

3. Tape test
   Use 1 in yellow drafting tape or artists' low-tack tape. 140 lb cold press needs only mild adhesive; avoid household masking tape and Frisket. Stick a 2 in strip on a corner of the margin, burnish 30 sec, peel at low angle. Right result: releases cleanly, no fibers raised, no adhesive halo. If fibers lift, step down. If it pops off under its own weight, step up.

4. Mount
   Lay the sheet on the dry board. Lightly mist the front with clean water until a uniform sheen appears, then wait about 30 sec for the sheen to start breaking. Apply tape along all four edges with slight outward tension as you lay each strip. Burnish the full length, especially the inner edge against the paper. Once the corners are down, do not lift them again.

5. Tension dry (the no-stretch flat result)
   Let the board sit flat until the paper is dry to the touch, 30 to 60 min depending on humidity. The paper tightens as it dries and pulls taut against the tape; that tension is what keeps broad washes flat without aggressive stretching. Do not paint until dry; painting while still damp invites buckling and tape release mid-wash.

6. Wash window
   For each broad wash, mist the front again and wait for the sheen to disappear (matte, not shiny, not bone dry). Paint in that window. Tilt the board slightly so the wash flows; the rigid backer prevents cockling under the water.

7. Between washes
   Let each wash dry fully before the next, especially before a glaze or a rewet. Hair dryer on low, held off the surface, is fine. Trapped moisture under a new wash is the usual cause of tide marks and lifted tape.

8. Removal
   Remove tape while the sheet is still slightly damp from the final pass. If it has gone fully dry, mist the taped edges and wait about 60 sec. Damp release is the key to a clean lift on cold press. Pull at a low angle, almost parallel to the paper, slow and steady, leading away from the painted area. Do not lift straight up; straight up is what tears the surface. If a strip resists, mist that edge again, wait a minute, resume. Any faint adhesive sheen on the margin wipes off with a soft eraser or a damp cotton swab; it should not reach the image area if the margin held.

Result: flat sheet, broad washes stable, no adhesive on the image, no scrubbing stretch, no surface tear on removal.

Good call shutting it off. A few things worth knowing:

  What you smelled vs. normal first-heat smell
    - Normal first-cycle smell is brief (a few minutes) and reads as "burning dust" or a faint oily scent — dust + manufacturing residue on the heat exchanger burning off.
    - A sharp, electrical-or-hot-plastic odor that persists for 15 minutes is NOT the dust-burn-off. It usually points to something overheating under load: blower motor bearings, a failing run capacitor, wire/insulation near the heat exchanger, or in the worst case a cracked heat exchanger (which is also a CO concern, even though your alarm is silent right now).
    - The right move is exactly what you did: stop running it and get it inspected before the next call for heat.

  Don't restart the system
    - One short test run after the smell has fully cleared won't make it more dangerous, but it also won't help diagnose anything and risks reigniting whatever is overheating. Wait for a tech to look at it.

  Contact Cherrywood property management today
    - This is a landlord-handled item — HVAC is almost certainly their responsibility under the lease, and a first-heat electrical smell with a pet in the unit is the kind of thing that gets same-day dispatch from most properties. Ask for an HVAC tech (not just general maintenance). Most properties have a 24/7 emergency maintenance line for situations like this; if it's after-hours, that line is the one to use.
    - If you don't have the emergency maintenance number handy, I can look it up in your inbox / portal and draft the request — just say the word.

  Escalate if anything changes
    - Leave the unit with Kibo and call 911 (or the non-emergency fire line) if you notice any of: visible smoke or haze, scorch marks around supply registers or the air handler, a tripped breaker that won't reset, repeated CO alarm chirps after a battery pull, or the smell returning strongly when the system is off (which can indicate an active electrical fault).
    - Kibo behaving normally is reassuring. Cats mask respiratory distress well, so if you do run the system again post-repair, watch for hiding, fast breathing, or drooling in the first hour or two.

  One more thing
    - If the tech finds a cracked heat exchanger, that's typically a furnace-replacement-level finding and worth pushing back on with the property given the unit's age. Not worth raising now — just worth knowing that's a real possibility, not a worst-case fantasy.

25 minutes off the heat is well inside the safe window — the food-safety rule of thumb is that cooked food should not sit at room temperature for more than 2 hours total (1 hour if the kitchen is above about 90°F). You're nowhere near that.

Two things to do promptly so it cools through the danger zone (40–140°F) as fast as possible:

1. Divide into shallow containers, no more than about 2–3 inches deep. One tall tupperware of chicken thighs + sweet potatoes will hold heat in the middle and stay in the danger zone for a long time; spread across two or three shallow containers drops the temp quickly.
2. Refrigerate uncovered or loosely covered for the first 30–60 minutes, then seal. A tight lid on warm food traps steam and slows cooling. If you want to lid them right away, leave the corner cracked.

Storage times in the fridge (cover once cool):
- Chicken thighs: 3–4 days
- Sweet potatoes: 3–4 days
- Green beans: 3–5 days
- Cranberry relish (if cooked): 10–14 days

Don't stack the containers in the fridge until they've lost their warmth, or the bottom ones won't cool. Reheat any leftovers to steaming before eating, especially the chicken.

Cooling → shallow storage → fridge → bone separation → reheat, with Kibo security at every step:

1. Cool fast. Ladle into containers ≤3" deep (metal/glass cool fastest). For a big pot, ice-bath the pot 10–15 min first. Don't leave at room temp more than 2 hrs total.

2. Shallow storage. Fill containers ≤3", leave lids ajar until steam stops, then seal and date. Cool to ~70°F before the next step.

3. Refrigerate. Middle shelf (coldest, most even). Don't crowd — air needs to flow around containers. Use within 3–4 days, or freeze.

4. Separate bones. Strip meat off while it's still warm enough to handle easily. Meat goes into the shallow containers above. Bones + scraps go into a heavy zip bag or lidded tin → straight into a secured spot: latched trash, freezer, or a cabinet Kibo can't open. Cooked bones splinter and can kill a dog — assume counter-surfing risk and never leave them on the counter or in a soft bag.

5. Reheat one portion at a time, covered, to 165°F internal (steaming hot all the way through). Microwave with a splash of water and a loose lid, stir halfway. Don't reheat the same batch twice — pull what you'll eat, fridge the rest.

2. Ornament first (fragile, hardest to redo). Wrap the ceramic in clean packing paper with a 4–6 layer cocoon: 2 sheets flat under the base, gather around the sides, twist top closed, then a second outer wrap. Tape the tail flat. No exposed corners. Set aside in the Sacramento zone.

3. Book + card as a unit (Portland). Open the hardcover and slide the flat paper card inside the front cover, against the endpapers, so the book's own rigidity flattens and protects it. If the card is larger than the book, sandwich it between two stiff sheets of the packing paper first. Close the book, then wrap the whole book in 2 sheets packing paper, banded at the middle with a small piece of tape so it doesn't unravel. Set aside in the Portland zone.

4. Cushion and pack each box separately.
   - Sacramento: 1–2″ crumpled paper on the bottom, place the wrapped ornament in the center, fill all sides and top with crumpled paper so nothing shifts when you shake the box (no audible thunk).
   - Portland: same pattern, but the wrapped book is the cushion — center it flat, crumpled paper only at the short ends and top, no weight on the spine.

5. Seal, then label in two places. Fold flaps flush, one continuous tape seam across the center plus a short piece on each end seam. Write the recipient name, full address, and a destination arrow on the top. Repeat the name + city on a side panel. Do not write contents.

6. Receipts stay separate. Slip each receipt into its own small envelope, write the recipient name on the envelope, and tape the envelope to the underside of its box (so it ships with the package but doesn't smear the address label). Do not tape one recipient's receipt to the other box.

7. Stage for Dec 4. Stack both sealed boxes in a single "Dec 4 mail" area away from foot traffic. Place the two receipts on top in their own envelopes if you prefer to carry them to the post office separately rather than ship them attached. Re-check labels the morning of Dec 4 before sealing the mailer bag or handoff.

One guardrail: once a box is sealed and labeled, it does not move back to the prep counter — only forward to the staging area. That eliminates the swap risk.

DECISION FRAMEWORK — PAID-INTAKE ROTA TRANSITION

Context: CS asks whether the dedicated paid-intake owner-and-backup rota can close now that paid traffic is off, while 25 admitted workspaces still need ordinary support and continuous account-level support records through incomplete day-90 windows.

CORE SEPARATION
The rota has been carrying two functions at once. The decision turns on splitting them:

  A) Paid-intake coverage — triage of new paid-source leads entering 19=paid-source eligibility-flow (admit 8 / assist 6 / ineligible 5, tracked separately per 11/9).

  B) Ordinary support ownership — ongoing handling of admitted workspaces: tickets, questions, escalations, account-level support records, day-90 obligations.

These are independent. Closing A does not close B.

DECISION 1 — PAID-INTAKE COVERAGE: CLOSE
Closure is permitted because the demand the rota exists to serve is gone:
  - No new paid-source start can enter the 19-flow while paid traffic is off.
  - The dedicated owner-and-backup pair exists specifically to staff that intake stream.

Closure mechanics:
  - Set a closure date. Stop routing new paid-source leads to the rota on that date.
  - In-flight leads already in admission / assist / ineligible processing stay with the existing rota owners until each is cleared (separate tallies, not collapsed).
  - Once the in-flight set is empty, the dedicated rota stands down.

DECISION 2 — ORDINARY SUPPORT OWNERSHIP: CONTINUE
The 25 admitted workspaces are active CS accounts through their incomplete day-90 windows and beyond.
  - Each workspace transfers to a standard CS pod owner, with the pod lead as backup. The backup function is preserved; only its source changes (pod structure instead of dedicated rota).
  - Account-level support records stay continuous. No close-and-reopen, no ownership gap.
  - Day-90 obligations are ordinary support work, not paid-intake work. They ride with the workspace under the new pod owner.

EVIDENCE CONTINUITY
Continuity is preserved by an explicit handoff artifact, not by assumption:
  - Per-workspace handoff log: timestamp, outgoing paid-intake owner, incoming pod owner, open tickets, current day-90 milestone.
  - Rota-level audit entry: closure date, reason (paid traffic off, no new 19-flow entries), authorization.
  - Support thread: owner transfer is a metadata change on the existing ticket history, not a new ticket.
  - Day-90 tracker moves with the workspace. It does not remain parked on the paid-intake rota.

AFTER-HOURS HANDLING
The closure does not imply expanded coverage. No new after-hours rota is created.
  - Standard CS hours remain 8a–6p Central.
  - After-hours incidents for the 25 admitted workspaces follow standard on-call / escalation, not a paid-source path.
  - A paid-source tag is not, by itself, an after-hours trigger. Routing is governed by severity and tier, not by acquisition source.

DANIELA'S RELEASE AND ROLLBACK AUTHORITY
Unchanged. Rota closure does not narrow or widen her scope.
  - rel/rb routing remains with Daniela across the transition.
  - Any release or rollback decision during the closure window is still her call, whether it touches the paid-intake rota, the pod transition, or anything else in the admitted cohort's stack.
  - Handoff log records that her authority is preserved, so a future reader does not infer an authority change from rota closure.

WHAT THIS IS NOT
  - Not a declaration of mature outcomes. Day-90 windows are incomplete; outcomes are not claimed.
  - Not another batch. No new paid-source intake is opened.
  - Not an authority change. Daniela's rel/rb routing is preserved.
  - Not a reduction in support coverage. Each of the 25 workspaces still has an owner + backup.

CONDITIONS UNDER WHICH A DEDICATED ROTA WOULD RETURN
Listed for completeness, not as a present commitment:
  - Explicit reactivation of paid traffic, AND
  - New paid-source leads actually entering the 19-flow, AND
  - Daniela ack on the reactivation shape (consistent with the staging / isolated-campaign / $0 / no-eligibility-flow-entry precedent that governs reopens).
Day-90 completion alone does not bring the rota back. It just retires a day-90 obligation while ordinary CS ownership continues.
